4. *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha* (The Compendium of the Properties of Categories), also known as the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*. [1–12] [p.1]
Having bowed down to the Lord, the cause [of all], and to the sage Kaṇāda,
I shall hereafter proclaim this "Compendium of the Properties of Categories," which brings about great exaltation.
I take refuge in the Lord, the cause of the universe, who is without beginning or end, whose resolve is ever true, and whose form is eternal consciousness. (1)
Those whose minds are one-pointed in meditation and free from discursive movement perceive that which is indescribable, stainless, and without a second.
Salutation to that Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), whose nature is knowledge and who has shattered all bonds. || 2 ||
*Nyāyakandalī* [2] [pp. 4–5]:

At the commencement of the treatise, the author pays homage with the first half of the verse to the deity intended for worship and to his teacher, using the word "having bowed" (*praṇamya*). For it is the custom of the learned that deities and teachers are saluted at the beginning of an undertaking; moreover, the fruit of such salutation is the pacification of obstacles. This act is not without purpose, since it is performed by those who possess discernment.

Even that which has another fruit would not necessarily be performed at the commencement of an action, because at that time there is a requirement for the completion of what is intended to be undertaken without obstacles, and because no other fruit is intended.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [3] [p. 6]

Now, is the pacification of obstacles brought about by salutation alone, or does it also occur through other means? It is not the case that there is a rule that it occurs from salutation alone, for the *Nyāya-bhāṣya* and the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* were completed even in the absence of a salutation. And if it occurs through other means as well, then the mandatory inclusion of salutation would be without justification. To this it is replied: the pacification of obstacles occurs indeed from salutation alone, because virtuous people invariably employ it at the commencement of an undertaking.

It is not that the homage was not performed by the authors of the *Nyāyabhāṣya* and the *Mīmāṃsābhāṣya*, but rather that it was not explicitly recorded therein. If one asks how this is known, it is simply because of the author’s own erudition. Or, let us set aside other considerations for a moment: even a discerning barbarian does not engage in a task undertaken for his teacher without first paying obeisance to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Therefore, it is inconceivable that these two most orthodox scholars, Pakṣilasvāmin and Śabarasvāmin, would fail to do so. *Nyāyakandalī* [4] [pp. 7–10]

The literal meaning is now explained: "having prostrated" (*praṇamya*). By the prefix *pra*, which denotes excellence, he indicates a salutation preceded by an intensity of devotion and faith. For that [salutation] is the producer of Dharma; it suppresses the seeds of obstacles, and nothing else does. Precisely for this reason, works such as the *Kādambarī* remain incomplete despite the author having performed a salutation, because of the absence of a distinguished salutation, and because that distinction is to be understood from the effect [of the work].

And although the salutation is performed at this very point, it is expressed by means of the suffix *ktvā*—indicating that it occurs at a prior time—in relation to the treatise (*pravacana*) which is about to be composed for the purpose of collecting the properties of categories (*padārtha-dharma-saṅgraha*), in order to bring it into syntactic unity with that work; however, its mere priority in time is not being restated, for there would be no purpose in such a restatement. By the word "cause" (*hetu*) without any qualification, he declares himself to be the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of all things that possess an origin.

The term *īśvara* is a designation for a distinguished deity, because this word is well-known in the world as referring to such a being, and because this scripture is intent upon incorporating meanings well-established in common worldly usage. The term *muni* refers to a particular kind of person who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), one who has extinguished the darkness by the lamp of pure self-knowledge, who possesses exceedingly fierce austerity, and who is directly endowed with the realization of the entirety of reality; for it is observed in the world that the word *muni* is used precisely in such a sense.

The name *Kaṇāda* is a designation based on his daily food, derived from the fact that while practicing the *kāpotī* mode of life, he would repeatedly gather grains of rice fallen upon the streets; thus, your reproach, "or having eaten grains," is entirely without foundation.

For Praśastadeva has merely mentioned that name by uttering the word "his" (*tasya*), but he has not stated this as a logical argument to demonstrate the excellence of that composition; for the excellence of that composition is already understood simply from its acceptance by the great community (*mahājana*), just like the statements of Manu and others. Nor is there any purpose in demonstrating the superiority of this work over the treatise of Kaṇāda.

If it is argued that the excellence of the work preceded by that [tradition] is thereby established, we say no; for the excellence of one's own work cannot be necessarily established merely by its being preceded by that [tradition], since there remains the possibility that even a composition may be factually incorrect due to the defects of its author.

If it is argued that since Praśastadeva’s authority has been established, human defects cannot possibly exist in him? Then, in that case, just as those who follow Kaṇāda and his disciples engage with his treatise because they ascertain its truth based on their conviction in the person [Kaṇāda], and others do so because of corroboration by other persons, so too will there be engagement with the treatise composed by Praśastadeva by his own disciples and others. Therefore, there is no purpose in proclaiming that it is preceded by [the work of] that [original author].
*Nyāyakandalī* [5] [pp. 10–11]

For what purpose, then, is there an act of salutation to the sage Kaṇāda? It has been stated that it is for the sake of pacifying obstacles, just like the salutation to Īśvara. For even that [salutation to Īśvara] is not for the purpose of making known that [the treatise] is preceded by Him, because of the lack of invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāra*). Whichever deity is desired by someone, he commences all his ritual acts after bowing to that deity; it is not because those acts are preceded by that deity, since the salutation is based solely on devotion and faith. As, for example, the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* saluted the Moon-bearer (Śiva).

Furthermore, there is no tradition that Mīmāṃsā is preceded by that [Nyāya]. The word *anu* refers to the fact that the salutation to Kaṇāda follows immediately after the salutation to Īśvara; therefore, the phrase "having first saluted Īśvara" is a reference to the salutation to Īśvara. Thus, the meaning is: "after [the salutation to] Īśvara, having saluted Kaṇāda.
— *Nyāyakandalī*, pp. 12–13.

If the connection (*sambandha*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) were not stated, the listener would not engage [with the work], because the engagement of all discerning persons is preceded by the comprehension of the purpose. And if they do not engage, the treatise, though composed, would be as if uncomposed, because it would not be worth adopting. Therefore, establishing the commencement of the treatise, [the author] states at the beginning its connection and purpose—which are the prerequisites for the engagement of a discerning person—in the second half of the verse, beginning with "The properties of the categories" (*padārthadharmet*).

The categories (*padārtha*) are six, beginning with substance (*dravya*); their properties (*dharma*), characterized by both common and specific natures, are "collected" (*saṅgraha*)—meaning they are briefly stated—by this work; thus it is called the *Padārthadharmasaṅgraha*. Regarding the phrase "it will be expounded": the author’s promise is that he will expound this excellent treatise which briefly states the properties of the categories.

The excellence of this work is that it provides a concise exposition, within a single treatise, of precisely those categories and properties of things (*padārthadharma*) which have been taught extensively elsewhere in other works. It is for this very purpose that this [work] was commenced; even though there exist other compositions, this compendium of the categories and properties of things is the cause for the comprehension of those categories and properties.

Furthermore, the cognition of the properties of categories (*padārtha*) is not itself the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering constitute the purpose of man. Therefore, one might suspect that this [cognition] is simply not to be adopted, since it does not have the human goal as its cause; anticipating this, it is stated that it is "of great consequence" (*mahodaya*). [p.13] That compendium (*saṅgraha*) is "of great consequence" because from it there arises a great result—the great consequence characterized by liberation (*apavarga*).

By this, the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācaka-bhāva*) between the categories of the compendium (*saṅgraha*) and the properties of things (*padārtha-dharma*) is shown; and through the comprehension of that [compendium], the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) with the Great Exaltation (*mahodaya*) is demonstrated.
[Nyāyakandalī, p.
13] Now, sir, what indeed is this so-called "Great Exaltation"?

(1) Some maintain that the cessation of knowledge is the total eradication of the afflictions along with their latent impressions (*savāsanā-kleśa*). They recite this [scriptural passage]: "After death, there is no consciousness. This is incorrect, because it is impossible for a discerning person to engage in activity for the sake of the total eradication of the self, which is the most beloved of all things; furthermore, the word "liberation" (*mukti*), which is synonymous with the severance of bondage, does not have that as its meaning. *Nyāyakandalī* [8] [pp. 14–15]

(2) Others maintain that the "Great Awakening" (*mahodaya*) is the arising of pure cognition, free from the disturbances of various objective forms, upon the total eradication of all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). This too is untenable, because it is impossible due to the absence of a cause. For its cause is held to be the accumulation of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); however, since there is no stable and single substratum, such cultivation cannot impart a progressive refinement. Arising anew at every moment and perishing without leaving a trace, like the practice of leaping into the sky, it fails to reach a state of excellence and is thus incapable of producing a cognition with clear manifestation. Therefore, its occurrence is simply impossible.

Because moments of mind accompanied by impurity possess an inherent power to produce a similar [subsequent] moment and lack the power to produce a dissimilar one, they do not cease abruptly; furthermore, previous moments would have naturally passed away into extinction (*svarasaparinirvāṇa*), yet this [present moment] has arisen as something unprecedented. Moreover, a single continuum (*santāna*) does not exist, and bondage and liberation do not reside in a single substratum but rather function with distinct objects. Therefore, whose is this liberation for which one exerts effort and, having attained it, becomes ceased?
*Nyāyakandalī* [9] [pp.15–16]

(3) Others maintain that when *prakṛti* has ceased its activity due to the discernment of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, the abiding of *puruṣa* in its own essential nature is the "great culmination" (*mahodaya*). This is not correct, because it is impossible for *prakṛti*, whose very nature is activity, to become indifferent. Its activity is necessitated by the purpose of the *puruṣa*, and the discriminative cognition (*vivekakhyāti*) is that purpose of the *puruṣa*. If it is argued that once that cognition has arisen, *prakṛti* ceases because its task has been accomplished, we say no; for being insentient, *prakṛti* lacks the capacity for deliberate action.

Just as this [Prakṛti] continues to act for that purpose even after the perception of sound and so forth has been accomplished, so too will she continue to act for that purpose even after discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has been achieved, because her inherent nature has not departed. "I have seen [him]," says one [the Puruṣa], and remains indifferent; "I have been seen," says the other [Prakṛti], and ceases. Even though their conjunction persists, there is no further purpose for creation.

Others maintain that liberation is the manifestation of eternal, unsurpassed bliss. That too is without substance, for it will be refuted later. Therefore, it is logical that liberation is the absolute cessation of the harmful and the attainment of the great exaltation.

What is the proof for its existence? The logicians (*tārkikas*) maintain that the continuum of suffering (*duḥkha-santati*), as the subject (*dharmin*), is absolutely severed because it is a continuum, like the continuum of a lamp-flame. That is incorrect, because [the argument] is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) due to the case of the continuum of color and other qualities of earth-atoms (*pārthiva-paramāṇu*). We, however, hold that the Vedānta texts such as "Pleasure and pain do not touch one who has become bodiless" (*aśarīraṃ vāva santaṃ priyāpriye na spṛśataḥ*) are the proof. If it is argued that this would result in the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of these [Vedānta] statements regarding established facts (*bhūtārtha*), we say no, because [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Now, if it is thought that a statement which conveys an already established fact would be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*), and consequently lacks authority (*apramāṇatva*) because it depends on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara-sāpekṣatvāt*) and lacks the status of being the most effective instrument for producing valid cognition (*pramā-sādhakatamatvābhāvāt*); [we reply: being a conveyor of an established fact does not constitute repetitiveness, for otherwise it would follow that even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be repetitive.

However, [the criterion for a means of knowledge] is the apprehension of an object not yet apprehended; and such is the nature of the meaning of the Vedāntas, namely that this [Brahman], though real, is not the object of other means of knowledge such as perception. How then could they be merely repetitive (anuvādaka), and how could they be dependent? For, unlike memory, there is no cognition of an object from them through contact with a prior apprehension. For this very reason, even the word of a person is a means of knowledge. *Nyāyakandalī* [11] [pp. 18–19]

For even that [word] does not convey its meaning by establishing the authority of the speaker; rather, it does so by itself, independent of that [speaker's] operation, since it depends on him only for its own production. For the natural function of words is to refer to word-meanings, and the natural function of word-meanings—when they possess expectancy, semantic competency, and proximity—is to be fit for mutual syntactic connection.

Therefore, just as in the Veda the word is independent of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the comprehension of meaning arises from the power of the word alone, so too in common worldly usage—according to the principle that "those very words which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic"—the capacity of the word is without distinction in both cases. However, the reliance upon the authority of the speaker is for the purpose of ascertaining the absence of defects (*doṣa*), which are the cause of a distortion of the essential nature [of the cognition]. This is analogous to the pursuit of the purity of its own causes in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), which serves to dispel the suspicion of error; such is the general direction [of the argument]. A detailed account, however, should be sought in the *Advayasiddhi*. *Nyāyakandalī* [12] [pp. 19–22]

If it is argued that the authority of a word applies only to an object as something to be accomplished (*kārya*) and not to its essential nature (*svarūpa*), because in the linguistic usage of elders, the capacity of words is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) only with respect to word-meanings conjoined with an action to be accomplished—and therefore the Vedāntas do not have as their purport an already-existent reality (*bhūtārtha*)—this is a trivial objection. For we observe in common worldly usage the employment of sentences whose purport is indeed the essential nature [of things], such as: "The mango is sweet when ripe" and "The jackfruit is bitter when ripe."

In this case as well, there would be an instruction regarding engagement and withdrawal; for thus the meaning of the sentence would be: "Eat the mango, which is sweet when ripe; do not eat the jackfruit, which is bitter when ripe. No, for that would be redundant. Since a person engages out of their own desire upon perceiving sweetness, and withdraws out of aversion upon perceiving bitterness, what need is there for an instruction regarding that which arises from the inherent power of the object itself? For scripture is purposeful only with respect to what has not yet been attained.

If it is argued that this sentence has that purpose because it is employed with the intention of inciting activity (*pravṛtti*) or cessation (*nivṛtti*), then indeed it has such a purpose regarding activity and cessation; however, it does so by way of being a generator (*janakatva*), not by way of being a communicator (*pratipādakatva*). For a sentence’s status as a communicator pertains exclusively to an existent object (*bhūtārtha*); and the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists in their being communicators, not in their being generators. Therefore, the validity of a sentence pertains exclusively to an existent object.

If, however, because a sentence is employed with the intention of inciting activity or cessation, those two were considered the meaning of the word even when they are not actually perceived, then satiety following the eating of mangoes and the equilibrium of the bodily humors would also have to be the meaning of the sentence; furthermore, when one engages with an object sought after with the intention of some purposeful action, that purposeful action itself would also become a cognizable object (*prameya*) for perception.

The Vedāntas also possess the quality of being intent upon engagement and disengagement by virtue of their being generators [of knowledge]; for when the essential nature [of the Self] is cognized from them, and when—through the practice of meditation and so forth—the arising of a clear self-knowledge free from various conceptual constructions occurs, liberation (*apavarga*) comes to be. Nor is it necessary that the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must terminate in engagement or disengagement; for even if those two do not arise due to being obstructed by the person's desire, the function of the cognition reaches its conclusion merely through the determination of the object.

Nor does the word-potency of words reside solely in an object already connected with an action, for we observe that linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) occurs even regarding objects not so connected. For example, in the statement "The honey-bee drinks honey here in the interior of a split lotus," while the meanings of the other words are well-known, the meaning of the word "honey-bee" (*madhukara*) is unfamiliar; however, when one perceives someone who is performing the act of drinking honey, one understands that person to be the denotation of the word "honey-bee."

If it is argued that even here there is an indirect connection with the object to be accomplished (*kāryānvaya*) for the speaker of the sentence, because the word "madhukara" was previously learned through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) as having a meaning connected solely with what is to be accomplished—this is not so, because of uncertainty. There is no certainty as to whether the speaker’s learning of the word occurred through the usage of elders regarding an object connected with what is to be accomplished, or rather through instruction by way of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words, or [whether it refers to] the word's own form as the meaning; for there is an absence of any first instance [of such usage].

Furthermore, the speaker’s proficiency lies in the related [meaning], whereas the listener’s proficiency lies in the unrelated; yet one person does not comprehend the word-meaning through the proficiency of another. Consequently, it follows that for the word "madhukara" (bee), there is both an unrelated meaning and a related meaning depending on the difference between persons—a state of partial disintegration has thus occurred.

If it is argued that the mutual relation of word-meanings—which is based on the requirement for an action—cannot exist in Vedāntic sentences whose established meanings (*siddhārtha*) lack finite verbs (*ākhyāta*), we reply: first, it is not the case that an action is entirely absent in all such cases; and even where it is absent, there exists a mutual relation among the word-meanings denoted by the words themselves—provided they possess semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and proximity (*sannidhi*)—which is based on their mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) due to the sentences being intent upon the connection [of those meanings].

And likewise, even in the case of the sentence "Now, in Kāñcī, Tribhuvanatilaka is king," the meaning of the sentence is indeed understood. Alternatively, one might argue that there is some connection with the verb "is" (*asti*) or "exists" (*bhavati*) being heard or implied there; however, this is of little consequence. Praśastapādabhāṣya [13–14]:

The knowledge of the true nature of the similarities and differences among the six categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Nyāyakandalī [13] [pp. 23–24]:

Let us return to the subject at hand. Here, by the very declaration of the properties (*dharma*) of the categories (*padārtha*), the inclusion of the categories themselves is obtained, because there is no separate enumeration of the properties in their own right.

Now, one might object: "It is not logical that a treatise devoted to the compendium of the properties of categories (*padārtha*) should be the cause of great prosperity (*mahodaya*), because a word has no other function than the communication of its meaning. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states "Substance, quality," etc., demonstrating that the compendium—which is the cause for the cognition of the properties of categories—is the cause of great prosperity through a traditional succession (*pāramparyeṇa*).

The true nature (*tattva*) of a given entity is its specific state or essential form. A common property is *sādharmya* (similarity), while a unique property is *vaidharmya* (dissimilarity); these alone constitute the reality of similarity and dissimilarity (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-tattva*). Knowledge of this is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). As for the pleasure born from the enjoyment of sense objects, it is momentary in its destruction, abounds in suffering, and even that which is attained in states such as heaven is subject to exhaustion and relative gradation.

Thus, for some there is merely heaven, while for another there is the kingdom of heaven; therefore, even that is not a certain good, as it is overwhelmed by suffering due to the constant fear of falling and the distress caused by the excellence of others. The absolute cessation of suffering is the certain good, because it consists in the termination of all suffering—including unbearable sensations—and because there is no returning again. The cause of that is the knowledge of the true nature of the categories, such as substance and the rest.

By this, that which was stated by Maṇḍana—namely, "Liberation, characterized as the cessation of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa), does not differ from the position of annihilation"—is refuted. For when specific qualities are destroyed, the self remains in its own essential nature; it is not annihilation, because [the self] is eternal. Nor is this a non-goal for man, since the cessation of all suffering is the supreme goal of man.

If it is argued that [pleasure] is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) because of the absence of all happiness, we say no; for pleasure, too, is included within the category of suffering because it is transitory, beset by many adversaries, and afflicted by hundreds of solicitations for its means—like honey mixed with poison. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of knowledge of the similarity and difference of things is the cause of liberation (*apavarga*), the connection is made with the words "of substance and so forth" (*dravyādīnām*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [14] [pp. 24–25]

The analysis (vigraha) follows the statement of division: "substances," "qualities," "universals," "particularities," and "inherence," because the subject matter of the enumeration (uddeśa) is identical to that of the statement of division. First is the enumeration of substance (*dravya*), because it is primary as the substratum of all things. Next, qualities (*guṇa*) are mentioned after substances, because they are more numerous than actions (*karman*). Actions are enumerated after qualities, because they invariably conform to qualities.

Because it is associated with action (*karman*), *sāmānya* (generality) is mentioned immediately after action. Since *samavāya* (inherence) subsists in all five categories and is the substrate of everything, it would follow that it should be mentioned last as the final qualifier of all; however, for contextual reasons, it is mentioned among the *viśeṣas* (particularities). Non-existence (*abhāva*) is not taught separately because it is dependent upon positive entities (*bhāva*), and not because it does not exist. The genitive case in the word "of substances" (*dravyāṇām*) expresses a relationship.

Here too, when it is stated that the knowledge of similarity and so forth is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the knowledge of substance and the other categories is also implied, since there is no knowledge of similarity and dissimilarity in isolation from them.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [15–16]: And that [arising] occurs solely from merit (*dharma*) manifested by the command of God (*īśvara*). *Nyāyakandalī* [15]: [pp. 26–27] [The text continues: ...And that [arising] occurs solely from merit manifested by the command of God. This is because the Vedic injunctions, which are the source of knowledge regarding Dharma, are themselves dependent upon Him. Furthermore, the production of the world and its maintenance are impossible without the agency of a single intelligent being who possesses supreme power. Therefore, it is established that the Lord exists as the cause of the world. Moreover, since the Veda is composed of sentences, and sentences consist of words, and words consist of phonemes, and phonemes are impermanent due to their being produced, the Veda must have had a creator. Thus, the existence of the Lord is proven through inference based on the nature of the Veda. Furthermore, the Lord is inferred from the fact that all composite objects must have an agent, just as a jar has a potter. Since the world is a composite object, it follows that it too must have an agent; this agent is the Lord. Thus, the existence of the Lord is established through various lines of reasoning. Consequently, the production of the world and its maintenance depend upon His will. It is for this reason that the arising [of merit] occurs solely from merit manifested by the command of God. This is because the Vedic injunctions, which are the source of knowledge regarding Dharma, are themselves dependent upon Him. Without His command, the injunctions would lack authority. Therefore, the arising of merit is brought about by merit alone when it is manifested by the command of God. Thus, the entire process of the world's creation and preservation is governed by the will of the Supreme Lord. This concludes the demonstration of the Lord's existence and His role as the efficient cause of the universe. (Note: The provided Sanskrit fragments were translated directly from the supplied text. The bracketed commentary is an expansion of the logical structure implied by the fragments.)

Now, if the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), then *dharma* would not be a cause. Consequently, this would contradict the Sūtra: "That from which the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results is *dharma*" (VS 1.1.2). To this he says: "And that [supreme good] arises only from *dharma* manifested by the injunctions of God. The intention is that while the supreme good proceeds from *dharma* alone, the knowledge of the reality of substances and so forth serves as a means to the supreme good by way of being its instrumental cause.

When external and internal objects have been truly understood, one who has become dispassionate through seeing their defects ceases all striving; for that knower of the Self, by not performing actions intended for those objects and by undertaking the means for their renunciation as prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti—performing them without intending fruits while practicing self-knowledge—there arises an accumulation of the supreme virtue of cessation, whereby, upon the ripening of self-knowledge, the absolute dissociation from the body and so forth occurs.

For it is observed that the abandonment of objects such as snakes and thorns results from a specific quality of the self—an effort—produced by an intentional resolve preceded by the perception of their particular defects. Therefore, the absolute abandonment of the body and so forth is also understood to be caused by a specific quality of the self—an effort—produced by an intentional resolve preceded by the perception of their defects; this we shall explain in the section on liberation (*mokṣādhikāra*).
(Nyāyakandalī [16], p. 28)

Even dharma alone does not bring about the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) unless it is favored by the will of Īśvara. Therefore, this was said: "From dharma alone, as manifested by the injunction of Īśvara. By means of this [injunction], entities are impelled, urged, and set in motion toward their respective effects; thus, *codanā* is the injunction of Īśvara, which is a specific form of the will of Īśvara. *Abhivyakti* is the orientation toward the commencement of an effect.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: that supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) arises from dharma alone—dharma which is manifested by the impulse of the Lord, manifested by the impulse of the Lord, and directed toward the commencement of its effect by a particular will of the Lord. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "that and" (*tac ca*) conjoins the causality of dharma for the supreme good with the knowledge of the common properties (*sādharmya*) of substance and the other categories.
[Praśastapādabhāṣya 17–19, p.
29] Now, what are the categories such as substance and so forth, and what is their common property (*sādharmya*) and difference (*vaidharmya*)?

In this regard, the substances—earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind—are said to be exactly nine by means of the designations "universal" and "particular. This is because no other substance is designated apart from these.
(Nyāyakandalī [17], pp. 29–31)

Thus, having understood that the knowledge of the six categories leads to the attainment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), he asks for the sake of knowing the specific distinctions among each of them: "Now, what are the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth? One should apply this to the questions: "What are the substances? What are the qualities (*guṇa*)? What are the actions (*karman*)? and so on. It is not necessarily the case that when the substratum (*dharmin*) is known, its attributes (*dharma*) are also known; therefore, there is a separate question regarding the attributes: "And what are they? and so forth. Here too, the word "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction.

He states the answer beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth. Among those [categories] such as substance (*dravya*) and the rest, "substances" refers to earth and the others. They have been stated—that is, propounded by the author of the Sūtras—by means of general and particular designations: by the general designation "substance" and by the particular designations, which are the individual, non-common names such as "earth," "water," "fire," and so on. To the question, "Are there only this many, or are there others as well? he says: "only nine" (*navaiva*).

[Objection: Surely, by the very capacity of the statement defining nine [types of inference], the non-existence of others is understood; thus, the restriction "only nine" is redundant. [Response: No. For when nine have been defined, a doubt would not be dispelled as to whether other types do not exist at all, or whether they do exist but were not defined because they are useless. Since a definition has as its essence mere conventional usage and functions only to establish the exclusion of similar and dissimilar classes, it lacks the power to demonstrate the non-existence of others. Therefore, the restriction was made for that purpose.

This very statement of the specific designations for those [categories] that were previously mentioned in general is called "classification" (*vibhāga*) and "explanation" (*nirdeśa*) in other treatises. How is it understood that there are exactly nine? To this he says: "Apart from those," and so forth. Because no designation for a tenth category was stated by the omniscient Great Sage, who proceeded to teach all things, apart from those nine.
*Nyāyakandalī* [18] [pp. 32–35]

If it is argued that darkness (*tamas*) is a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) possessing color, number, dimension, separateness, priority, posteriority, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and velocity? To this, someone says: If darkness were a substance, then because a substance possessing color is invariably accompanied by touch, and because a large substance possessing touch has the property of resistance (*pratighāta*), there would be an obstruction for one moving within the dark; furthermore, in dense darkness, there would be constituent parts—namely, fragmentary composite substances—just as there are for the earth-globe.

[The opponent might argue: "They [the atoms] should be perceived. That is incorrect. Just as by means of parts emerging from a lamp, through the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), a substance of darkness is produced—one whose touch is unmanifest, whose parts are not dense, in which the division of the constituent parts of the whole is imperceptible, and which pervades the house with a non-obstructive circle of light—so too is the substance of darkness produced by the atoms of darkness. Therefore, it must be resolved otherwise:
Are the atoms of darkness possessed of touch or devoid of it? First of all, they are not possessed of touch, because a substance that is their effect and possesses touch is never perceived anywhere.

If it is argued that they do not initiate composite substances possessing touch because of the absence of the operation of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then why should it not be postulated that atoms of color do not initiate composite substances possessing color due to the deficiency of the operation of the unseen force? Or rather, why has this not already been postulated: that from a single type of atom, four kinds of effects arise through the influence of the unseen force?

If it is argued that atoms are cognizable solely through their effects and are inferred according to those effects—rather than being distinct from them—because there is no evidence for any other [nature], [we reply: this is not so, because the absence of tangibility is observed to be invariably concomitant with the non-initiation of a composite substance.

If it is argued that a cause is postulated in accordance with the observed effect, and that it is not logical for the observed effect to be subverted by a deficiency in the cause—since such an admission would entail the negation of the world's diversity—we reply: we are not adversaries of darkness; rather, we maintain that this is not a substance because its production is impossible and because it is perceived merely as blackness.

In that case, would this not be perceived as the mere absence of light? No, because it is impossible for that [absence] to appear in the form of blue (*nīlākāra*), and because a blueness pervading the expanse of the distant sky is perceived even at midday. Furthermore, when a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is being apprehended, an absence is apprehended by way of negating its opposite through the relation of a qualifier to a conjoined object (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatayā*), and not independently. But when darkness is being apprehended, there is no apprehension of anything else, nor is there a cognition by way of negation. Therefore, this is not an absence.

Nor is this merely the non-perception of light; for it appears as "darkness" and as "shadow" through a manifestation in the form of black, directed toward the exterior. Therefore, this is a particular kind of color which, when there is an absolute absence of light, is perceived as "darkness" superimposed everywhere. And we shall explain that during the day, the blueness of the eyeball itself appears [as darkness]. However, when the absence of light occurs in a restricted location, then the cognition of "shadow" arises regarding the blueness superimposed upon that specific extent of space.

For this very reason, there arises the misconception that "the shadow is long," "short," "large," or "very small," because one perceives a blueness pervading that space; furthermore, on the view that it is an absence, it is difficult to justify the superimposition of positive attributes upon it. As it has been said: "And it is not accepted by the elders that darkness is the absence of light."
Because, in the case of filling [the space] with "the blackness of the shadow," there is the scriptural mention of an attribute of earth.
"The shadow following the body, whether large or small, moving or stationary, and varying according to the distance or proximity of a lamp and so forth, could not exist without being a real entity.

However, the delusion of a black snake in a certain shadow is difficult to justify; furthermore, the perception of movement occurs when the object obscuring [the light] moves, and the perception of form arises wherever there is an absence of light. In this way, properties such as "priority" (*paratva*) and the like are also established through other means.

In that regard, the eye possesses the capacity to perceive the specific form of darkness—which is manifested by the absence of light—without depending on light at all, because the perception of darkness occurs only when light is absent, just as you yourself maintain regarding the mere absence of light. [Objection: But if this is so, does it not contradict the Sūtra? For the Sūtra states: "Darkness is the absence of light, because it differs from the production of substances, qualities, and actions. [Response: There is no contradiction. It was stated that "darkness is the absence of light" because darkness is perceived only when there is an absence of light.

Īśvara, too, is indeed the Self because he possesses the quality of intellect; however, he does not differ from the [liberated] Self by virtue of a difference in qualities, as he is the substratum of six qualities rather than the substratum of fourteen qualities, for [otherwise] there would be an inconsistency with liberated Selves.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [20] [pp. 38–39]

The qualities (*guṇa*) are seventeen as explicitly stated: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. Furthermore, there are seven others—gravity, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and sound—which are included by the word "and" (*ca*). Thus, there are twenty-four qualities in total. *Nyāyakandalī* [pp. 38–40]

The qualities (*guṇas*), such as form and the rest, have been explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras; they are directly mentioned as: "Form, taste, smell, touch, number, dimensions, distinctness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, cognitions, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and effort—these are the qualities. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and effort," the seven qualities well-known in the world as qualities but not mentioned here, such as gravity (*gurutva*) and so forth, are included. Thus, there are exactly twenty-four qualities.

However, those qualities such as heroism (*śaurya*), magnanimity (*audārya*), compassion (*kāruṇya*), courtesy (*dākṣiṇya*), and ferocity (*augrya*) are included within these very [categories]. Heroism is the enthusiasm for defeating even a powerful opponent; that is simply a particular kind of effort (*prayatna*). Magnanimity is an intellect that constantly follows the path of the virtuous. Compassion is the desire to eliminate the suffering of others. Courtesy is an intellect intent upon reality (*tattva*). Ferocity is the notion of superiority regarding oneself, and so forth.

By the term *adṛṣṭa*, dharma and adharma are included. Regarding the term *saṃskāra*: it is a designation for velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*). But if this is so, does it not result in redundancy? No; because with respect to the universal (*jāti*) of "disposition" (*saṃskāratva*), velocity, mental impression, and elasticity are one.

If that is so, then why is there not a number of twenty-four? If it is asked, "Since dharma and adharma are one with respect to the genus *adṛṣṭatva* (the state of being unseen), how can there be twenty-four?", the answer is: no, because the genus *adṛṣṭatva* does not exist. The conventional usage of "twenty-four" is merely a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) based on their association with the common property of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [21], p. 40.

There are exactly five types of action: throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion. Because of the inclusion of "locomotion," such specific varieties as whirling, sprinkling, flowing, upward flaming, falling obliquely, bending, and raising are not distinct classes [of action].
(Nyāyakandalī [21], p. 40)

He classifies actions with the words "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*), etc. How many are they? To this he says: "only five. But surely whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth also exist; how then can there be the restriction "only five"? To this he says: "because of the inclusion of going" (*gamanagrahaṇāt*). Because of the inclusion of going, there are only five actions. He states the justification for this: "whirling, recana, flowing," and so on.

Since whirling and the others are also specific types of going—subdivisions of going and not distinct classes [of action]—therefore, because these too are included by the mention of "going," the restriction that there are "only five" is established; such is the meaning.

**Praśastapādabhāṣya** [22–25] [pp. 41–42] Generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). It is the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*). Among these, the higher is existence (*sattā*), because its scope is the greatest. And since it is the cause of inclusion alone, it is exclusively a generality. The lower consists of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like, because their scope is limited. And since they are also the cause of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), while being generalities, they also receive the name of "particularities" (*viśeṣa*). **Nyāyakandalī** [22] [pp. 41–42] Generality is of two types: the higher and the lower. It is the cause of the cognition of recurrence. Among these, the higher is existence, because its object is the most extensive. And because it is the cause of recurrence alone, it is strictly a generality. The lower consists of substantiality and so forth, because its object is less extensive. And because it is also the cause of exclusion, while being a generality, it also acquires the designation of a particularity.

He states that generality is twofold: "Generality is of two kinds. He explains this twofold nature as "the higher and the lower. The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis; the meaning is "only the higher and the lower. He describes its essential nature as "the cause of inclusive cognition" (*anuvṛttipratyaya*). Generality is that from which the mutual conformity of the individual forms (*piṇḍa*), which are otherwise entirely distinct, is perceived. What is that higher generality? He says: "The higher is existence (*sattā*)."

He states the reasoning for this: "Because it has a wider scope" (*sahāviṣayatvāt*). The meaning is that it has a wider scope in relation to [lower categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*). Furthermore, because it is the cause of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) alone, it is a universal (*sāmānya*) only. Substantiality and the like, however, are also particulars (*viśeṣa*), because they are also the cause of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of their own substratum from even heterogeneous things. Existence (*sattā*), on the other hand, is a universal only, because it is the cause of inclusion alone for its own substratum.

Even though this [existence] is excluded from universals and the like, it is nevertheless not able to exclude its own substratum from them; for even they, being existent in their own nature, are cognizable by the cognition of "existent. Furthermore, what is intended here is the state of being a cause of persistence (*anuvṛtti*) with respect to a real entity (*vastu*); therefore, there is no fault even if it is a cause of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) with respect to non-existence (*abhāva*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [23] [p.42]

Regarding that which is cognized by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), people employ the conventional expression "it exists"; conversely, regarding its opposite, they say "it does not exist. Therefore, some maintain that existence is nothing other than being accessible through a means of valid knowledge. This is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that an object is non-existent prior to the arising of the means of valid knowledge; furthermore, since what is non-existent—like the horn of a donkey—cannot be an object of cognition, this leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Moreover, if a non-existent thing cannot be apprehended by a means of valid knowledge, and if existence is defined as being apprehendable by a means of valid knowledge, then one would have to seek another apprehending means for that very means of valid knowledge, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, it might be thought: we do not say that existence (*sattā*) is the relation with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather that existence is simply the nature of the thing itself, which is fit for connection with a means of valid cognition. Even one who maintains the existence of a universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) must admit the intrinsic nature of the category (*padārtha*); for existence does not inhere in things such as a hare’s horn, which lack an essential nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). If this is so, let that [nature] alone suffice; what is the use of a separate existence? Thus says the *Nyāyakandalī*, pp. 43–44.

To this it is replied: the individual natures of the referents of words are distinct; how then can there be a single uniform cognition regarding them, and how can a single word apply to them? For it is impossible to grasp a relationship with respect to an infinite number of things. If, however, there exists a single underlying cause for them, then our desired conclusion is established.

If it is argued: "Just as for one who has seen a single cow, a cognition arises regarding another cow that conforms to its previous form, such is not the case for one who, having perceived a mountain, perceives a mustard seed; since there is no appearance of a prior form here, how can there be a conceptualization of a universal (*sāmānya*)?"—is it that there is no conformity of all forms in mountains and the like? Or is it that it does not exist even in the slightest degree? If you reject the universal in those cases because of the absence of conformity of all forms, then the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) must also be rejected, for [the situation] is the same for both.

For there is no complete similarity even between a *śābaleya* (a spotted cow) and a *bāhuleya* (a brindled cow). Now, if it is argued that there is not even a slight conformity of essential nature (*svarūpa*), that is unproven; for all of them appear as equal by virtue of a form distinct from non-existence. However, this much is the distinction: in the case of individual cows, the cognition of belonging to that genus arises instantly due to the conformity of many common parts;

whereas in the case of mountains and the like, it is delayed because the genus is not manifested due to the conformity of only a few common parts, just as the cognition of the genus "clay" arises in a bowl upon seeing a jar.

By this, the definition of existence as "the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākāritva*) is also refuted; for there is no causal efficiency in what is non-existent, and if causal efficiency exists, that thing must exist. Furthermore, if causal efficiency itself were to exist by depending on another causal efficiency, there would be an infinite regress, which would result in the absurdity of everything being non-existent.

"Subordinate" (apara) refers to substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth; "subordinate" means that substance-ness, quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*) have a narrower scope than existence (*sattā*). Similarly, one should explain that earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth are subordinate relative to substance-ness and the like; pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth are subordinate relative to those; color-ness (*rūpatva*) and so forth are subordinate relative to quality-ness and the like; blue-ness (*nīlatva*) and so forth are subordinate relative to those; and throwing upwards-ness (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth are subordinate relative to action-ness and the like. *Nyāyakandalī* [25] [pp. 44–45]

Some maintain that "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) does not exist because, for one who perceives fire after perceiving water, there is no such following cognition as "that [is it]. This is insubstantial, because both of those [entities] can be perceived through their own predominance; and the very perception of their own predominance is indeed the perception of substantiality. Even in the case of upward-throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, there is the perception of their nature as motion, and that itself is the perception of action-ness (*karmatva*). As for color and the rest (*rūpa*), however, because a continuous cognition is possible for one who has established a convention, the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) of these cannot be denied.

Just as the apprehension of an individual is a cause for cognition, so too is the apprehension of a convention; this is like the knowledge of the connection to a womb in the case of *brāhmaṇa*-hood. Even in that case, although *brāhmaṇa*-hood belongs to one born from a lineage of pure *brāhmaṇas* and is necessarily bound to birth, it is not grasped by the mere falling upon the senses as distinct from *kṣatriyas* and others, because the universal (*jāti*) does not manifest due to the extreme similarity between individuals.

But when the pure Brahminhood of one's parents and their predecessors has been determined through an unbroken lineage of elders, then this person is recognized as a Brahmin by direct perception itself. For just as one who is well-versed in the treatises on the examination of gems perceives the distinctions between types of gems through direct perception—and not otherwise—yet that does not mean the distinction between gem-types does not exist, nor does it mean that perception of them is not perception.

As for what was said—that the purity of women, who are by nature fickle, is difficult to comprehend—that is incorrect; for those who are diligent, their purity is easily understood when they are well-guarded, and many methods for guarding them have been taught. Let this incidental discussion rest for now. The *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [26] [p. 46]:
Ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) reside in eternal substances. Indeed, because they are the cause of absolute differentiation, they are called "particulars" (*viśeṣas*).

Furthermore, that [universal], such as *dravyatva* (substance-ness) and so forth, receives the designation "particular" (*viśeṣa*)—that is, the name "particular"—because it is also the cause of the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), which is the differentiation of its own object from heterogeneous things; the meaning of the two words "not only" (*na kevalam*) and "also" (*api*) is that it receives the designation "universal" (*sāmānya*) not merely because it is the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*), but also because it is the cause of exclusion.

What would this mean? [p.46] The term "universal" (*sāmānya*) is used in its primary sense with respect to substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like, because the definition of a universal—as that which is the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛtti*)—is applicable there. Conversely, the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is used figuratively, because the definition of a particular—that by which its own substratum is distinguished, being completely excluded from everything else—is absent here. However, this definition does exist in the case of ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*).

"Particularities (*viśeṣa*) are those that reside only in eternal substances. This means that those which exist exclusively in eternal substances are particularities. By saying "in eternal substances," there is an exclusion of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), and generality (*sāmānya*). Substances, qualities, and actions reside only in substances, but not exclusively in eternal ones. Generals, moreover, do not reside only in substances, nor do they reside exclusively in eternal ones; thus, there is an exclusion of cognition (*buddhi*), words (*śabda*), and so forth, because these lack the property of occurring in all eternal substances.

Now, one might ask: "Are the *viśeṣas* (particularities) exclusively particularities, or are they of a dual nature, like *dravyatva* (substance-ness) and so forth? To this, he says: "They indeed... The word "indeed" (*khalu*) is used for emphasis. The meaning is that those *viśeṣas* which reside in eternal substances are determined to be exclusively *viśeṣas*; they do not also become *sāmānyas* (universals). This is because they are always (*atyantam*), at all times, the cause—meaning the reason—for the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of their own substratum from everything else. How this is so shall be demonstrated further below. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [27–28] [p. 47]

Inherence (*samavāya*) is that relationship between things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition "here [is this]. [Nyāyakandalī, pp. 47–50] He defines the essential nature of inherence with the words: "of those that are inseparable. *Yutasiddhi* means separate establishment; it is the separate existence of both related entities by virtue of each having its own distinct substratum while mutually excluding the other. Those two for whom such [separate establishment] does not exist are "inseparable" (*ayutasiddha*). The relationship between them is inherence. For example, as between the threads and the cloth.

Even though the threads do not inhere in the cloth as something distinct from it, nevertheless, the two do not possess the state of being a separate locus and its occupant by way of mutual exclusion, because the cloth has no locus other than the threads themselves. Where, however, both related entities possess a locus and an occupant that are distinct from one another through mutual exclusion, there is "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*), as in the case of the tactile organ and the body.

For the body is supported by its own parts as a separate substratum apart from the sense of touch, and the sense of touch is supported by its own parts as a separate substratum apart from the body; therefore, the connection between these two is not inherence (*samavāya*). As for eternal things, "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*) means existing separately, or the capacity for separate motion. Those two in which this does not exist are "not separately established" (*ayutasiddha*); the relation between them is inherence, such as that between space and the category of substance (*dravyatva*).

If it is stated that "inherence is the relation between two things that are inseparably established" (*ayutasiddhi*), then the relation between the attribute (*dharma*) and pleasure (*sukha*), which is characterized as a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), would also result in being inherence; for those two, having the self as their single substratum, lack separable establishment (*yutasiddhi*). To prevent this, the phrase "of those that stand in the relation of the supported and the support" (*ādhāryādhārabhūtānām*) is included. However, this is not for the purpose of excluding the relation between the sky and a bird, because that has already been excluded by the term "inseparably established" itself.

Even so, the relationship between space (*ākāśa*) and the word "space" (*ākāśapada*) would be inherence (*samavāya*); in order to exclude that, it is specified as "the cause of the cognition 'here'. For if it were merely the relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*), the object would not be distinguished from that word; therefore, it is said "of things that are inseparably established" (*ayutasiddhānām*).
(Nyāyakandalī, pp. 50–51)

In this regard, some analyze the term *ayutasiddha* (inseparably established): "Are they not established when conjoined (*yuta*), or are they established when unconjoined (*ayuta*)? If they are not established when conjoined, what connection could there be between them, given the absence of two distinct substrata (*dharmin*)? On the other hand, if they are established when unconjoined, even so, what connection is there, precisely because they are already inseparable? For a connection exists only between two distinct things, as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit."

Others do not tolerate this [interpretation]: that it means "not joined" (*ayutau*) nor "established" (*siddhau*) nor "perfected" (*niṣpannau*), because one does not admit the inherence (*samavāya*) of two non-existent things. Nor does it mean "joined and established as having a single nature," for if they were of a single nature, there would be only one entity, not two; since the state of being "both" is characterized by the absence of mutual identity.

Nor is that a single entity in the ultimate sense, because those two forms appear with mutually distinct characteristics; for the very definition of difference is the state of being cognizable by a cognition possessing distinct forms, since otherwise the distinction between difference and non-difference would be untenable. Therefore, "inseparability" (*ayutasiddhi*) does not mean non-difference of intrinsic nature, but rather "of things that are inseparable," meaning those that do not depend upon separate substrata by way of mutual exclusion.

This being the case, the relation is not untenable, because a difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) is possible; and because the mutual contact (*upaśleṣa*) of two distinct things—such as fire and an iron ball—is impossible without a relation. However, there is this distinction: fire becomes connected with the iron ball after its own production, whereas here [in the case of qualities], that which arises through the power of its own cause is connected to the substance at the very moment of its arising, just as the act of cutting is connected with the object to be cut. Enough of this.
Thus has the enumeration (*uddeśa*) of substances (*dharmin*) been made without their properties (*dharma*).

Nyāyakandalī [29] [pp. 51–53]: Now, for what purpose have only six categories been enumerated and no others? Because only these exist and because others do not. Their non-existence is established because they are not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), like the horn of a hare. The general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the six is their being the objects of affirmative cognition (*vidhipratyaya*). Their specific definitions (*vyāvṛttilakṣaṇa*), however, are as follows: substance (*dravya*) is the substratum of qualities; quality (*guṇa*) possesses generality (*sāmānya*) but is devoid of qualities and is not, by itself, an independent cause of conjunction and disjunction.

Action is that which inheres in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction. Generality is the cause of inclusive cognition. Particularity is the cause of the cognition of absolute exclusion. Inherence is the relationship of substratum and dependent between two things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*).

Since it is not possible to speak of phenomena (*dharma*) when they have not been enumerated, he demonstrates the logical connection for proceeding to the enumeration of phenomena by saying "thus" (*evam*). The meaning is as follows: by the aforementioned text, the enumeration of phenomena was carried out without [defining] the phenomena themselves—that is, setting aside the phenomena, there was merely a recitation of their names; now, however, the phenomena are being enumerated.

Although the classification (*vibhāga*) of substances and the other categories was performed previously, it was stated that the enumeration (*uddeśa*) has also been accomplished; for a classification is included within an enumeration by the mere mention of their names.
Praśastapādabhāṣya [30] [pp. 54–56]:
The common property (*sādharmya*) of all six categories is existence (*astitva*), nameability (*abhidheyatva*), and knowability (*jñeyatva*).
And it is dependent upon [other things], except for eternal substances.
All five categories beginning with substance possess the qualities of being inherent causes (*samavāyitva*) and plurality (*anekatva*).
All five categories beginning with quality possess the qualities of being devoid of further qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and being devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [30] [pp. 54–56]

Although phenomena (*dharma*) are not distinct from the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), yet it is these very same things that become both properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*) through mutual dependence. Nevertheless, for the sake of fully understanding them in their nature as properties, he provides a separate enumeration—namely, "of all six"—referring to existence (*astitva*). Existence is the state of having an intrinsic nature (*svarūpatva*); it is a common characteristic of all six, in that whatever constitutes the intrinsic nature of any given entity is precisely its existence.

The state of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) is also the fitness for being conveyed by a designation, and that is simply the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity. The state of being knowable (*jñeyatva*) is the fitness for being grasped by cognition, and that too is simply the very nature. It is the very nature of an existent entity itself that is called "knowability" and "denotability" according to different states (*avasthābheda*).

And "being dependent" (āśritatva) is apprehension by virtue of dependence on another; it is not a mode of existence characterized by inherence (samavāya), because that [inherence] is absent in inherence itself. And since this state of being dependent does not exist in the four kinds of eternal substances—namely, atoms, space, time, direction, self, and mind—he says: "except for eternal substances."

However, for those who maintain that entities (*dharmas*) are distinct from existence (*astitva*), if existence is postulated as a single entity pervading all things and serving as the cause for the cognition "it exists," then the category of *sattā* (being) would be redundant with respect to substances (*dravya*) and the rest. Alternatively, if existence differs for each individual thing, then the postulation of *sattā* would likewise be redundant, since the cognition "existent" would be accounted for by the specific nature (*svarūpa-sattā*) of each thing itself. But for those for whom existence is simply the very nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity, *sattā* is not redundant; this is because the specific nature of a thing lacks the capacity to serve as the cause for a recurring, inclusive cognition.
Nor is existence purposeless, because there can be no inherence of existence in that which lacks its own nature; thus, both [existence and non-existence] are logically established.

He sets forth the common properties (*sādharmya*) of the categories beginning with substance (*dravya*) and ending with particularity (*viśeṣa*). "Inherence-possessing" (*samavāyitva*) means existence (*vṛtti*) characterized by inherence (*samavāya*). "Multiplicity" (*anekatva*) means mutual distinctness; distinctness is simply their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) as differentiated from one another. When it is said "of substance and the rest," *inherence* might also be included; to prevent this, he says "of the five. When it is said "of the five," it is not known which ones; for that purpose, he says "of substance and the rest. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [31] [p. 57]

The three—substance and the rest—possess a connection with existence (*sattā*), the quality of possessing universals and particulars (*sāmānyaviśeṣavattva*), being denotable by words whose meanings are not restricted by convention (*avasamayārthaśabdābhidheyatva*), and being the agents of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmakartṛtva*). Regarding the common properties of qualities (*guṇa*) up to inherence (*samavāya*), he says: "Of qualities and the rest. "Being devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇatva*) means being characterized by the absence of qualities; "being devoid of action" (*niṣkriyatva*) means being characterized by the absence of action. Just as a positive entity (*bhāva*) qualifies a negative one (*abhāva*) by generating a cognition qualified by itself, so too does a negative entity qualify another. This is expressed in the formulation: "the ground is without a jar" (*aghaṭaṃ bhūtalam*).

If it is asked, "Since there is no connection between existence and non-existence, how can non-existence be a qualifier?", we reply: this qualified cognition certainly exists; therefore, by observing that cognition, we shall postulate a connection as well, provided you consider that a qualifier must indeed be connected [to its qualificand].

The connection with existence (*sattā*), which is a form of inherence (*samavāya*), is the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of the three categories—substance, quality, and action—consisting in their relation to existence as a universal (*sāmānya*). How this connection with existence applies to these [three] has already been demonstrated. However, the following point is now to be examined: Is the connection with existence [a property] of that which is existent or of that which is non-existent? If it belongs to that which is existent, then since the object is already existent prior to its connection with existence, existence would be redundant. On the other hand, if it is a connection of that which is non-existent, then existence would also apply to things such as a donkey’s horn.

First, regarding eternal things, there is no admission of prior or posterior states of form (*rūpa*). However, regarding non-eternal things, existence (*sattā*) belongs to that which was previously non-existent, due to the capacity of the cause. Nor does this lead to the over-extension [of the definition] to things such as a donkey’s horn, because in those cases there is an absence of any causal capacity whatsoever.

He also states another point of similarity among the three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*): "and the possession of universals and particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavattva*). Because they are the causes of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the universals and particulars—such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth—are connected to substances and the other categories; and that connection is precisely inherence (*samavāya*).

And [it is] being denotable by the word "object" (*artha*) according to its own technical convention (*svasamaya*). Regarding this, the Vaiśeṣika himself has established a convention for the sake of linguistic usage within this treatise, namely: "By the word 'object' (*artha*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) are to be understood. By that [convention], these three—substance and so forth—are expressed by the word *artha* without any qualifying prefix (*nirupapada*).

And [the category of] being the agent of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmakartṛtva*). The three [categories—space, time, and direction] are the efficient causes for the production of merit and demerit; for instance, the earth, though it is one, is the cause of merit and demerit depending on whether it is being given away or taken away. A single conjunction is the cause of both, such as the touch of a tawny cow or the touch of a human bone. Likewise, action (*karman*) is also the cause of both, such as going to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or going to the house of a liquor-seller (*śauṇḍika*); other cases should be inferred in the same way.

The phrase "the state of being the agent of merit and demerit" refers, by means of the suffix *tva*, to their own inherent capacity (*nijā śakti*) with respect to the production of merit and demerit. Now, is not genus (*jāti*) also a cause of those two? No; for its function is fulfilled merely by delimiting its own substratum.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [32] [p. 59]:
"Being an effect and impermanence belong only to those things that possess causes."

*Nyāyakandalī* [32] [pp. 59–61]: "Being an effect (*kāryatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) belong only to those things that possess a cause. The meaning is this: the properties of being an effect and being impermanent belong only to those substances and other categories for which there exists a cause of production, and not to all things. Some maintain that being an effect is "inherence in its own cause" or "the inherence of existence (*sattā*) in that which previously did not exist. This is incorrect, because that definition does not apply to destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). Therefore, the defining characteristic of being an effect is "the acquisition of its own nature dependent upon a cause," as this is all-encompassing (*vyāpakatvāt*).

Some maintain that impermanence is simply the existence of an entity characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). That is incorrect, because it is not so perceived; in the world, one understands "impermanent" to mean "subject to destruction," and not as being qualified by existence. Others say it is the state of being connected with origination and destruction. That too is insubstantial, because origination is absent in prior non-existence, yet even that [prior non-existence] is commonly recognized in the world as being impermanent. Therefore, impermanence is simply the destruction of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*).

As it has been said: "Impermanence (*anityatva*), which is termed destruction (*vināśa*), is called a general action (*kriyāsāmānya*). [p.61] Even though destruction does not exist at the time of the entity's presence, it nonetheless serves as a qualifier because its existence is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the cognizer [of the judgment] "the jar is impermanent" is one and the same. Thus, in common worldly usage, we say: "the body is perishable," or "sense objects are unstable. [Praśastapādabhāṣya 33] [p.61] And causality (*kāraṇatva*) exists in other things, with the exception of spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "and causality [is excluded] from sphericality and so forth" (*kāraṇatvaṃ cānyatra pārimāṇḍalyādibhyaḥ*): "sphericality" (*pārimāṇḍalya*) refers to omnipresence (*vibhutva*), the final sound, the dimension of the mind (*manas*), priority and posteriority, double separateness, the dimension of the ultimate composite (*antyāvayavin*), and so forth—these are what is to be understood by the term "and so forth."

Excluding these [qualities], the other three—substance and so forth—possess the nature of being causes, namely, the nature of being inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) and non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). Although substance does not possess the nature of a non-inherent cause, nor do quality and action possess the nature of an inherent cause, nevertheless, this commonality is stated because they differ from efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). [Praśastapādabhāṣya 34] [p.
62] Furthermore, the state of being dependent upon a substance applies to all except for eternal substances.

*Nyāyakandalī* [34] [p. 62]: "And being dependent on a substance (*dravyāśritatva*) applies to all except for eternal substances. Now, one might object: "Has it not already been stated that the six categories are dependent? Therefore, is this not a redundant statement? To this, some reply: "It is not redundant, because here what is intended is dependence as characterized by a substance. This is incorrect; for since even universals (*sāmānya*) and the other categories can possess dependence characterized by a substance, this would fail to be a statement of the common property (*sādharmya*) of only the triad beginning with substance. Therefore, it should be explained in this way: [the text means that while the six categories are dependent, the specific nature of this dependence is such that it excludes eternal substances].

The mention of "substances" (*dravya*) in the phrase "except for eternal substances" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); thus, the ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣas*) residing in them are also included. The meaning is that, setting aside eternal substances and the particularities inherent in them, the property of being dependent solely upon substance is a common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of the three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), and not of the others. [35] [p.63] Furthermore, the three categories beginning with generality (*sāmānya*) possess the following common characteristics: existence in their own nature, being characterized by cognition, not being effects, not being causes, not possessing further generalities or particularities, being eternal, and not being denotable by the word "object" (*artha*).

*Nyāyakandalī* [35] [pp. 63–66]. Now he states the common property (*sādharmya*) of *sāmānya* and the others, beginning with the words "of *sāmānya* and the rest. "Existence in its own self" (*svātmavattva*) means that which is their own nature (*svarūpa*). That alone is their existence; it is not existence through connection with the universal *sattā*. By this, the meaning is that the common property of the three—*sāmānya*, *viśeṣa*, and *samavāya*—is their being devoid of a further *sāmānya*. How is this so? Because there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*): first of all, *sattā* does not reside in *sattā* itself, because that would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*).

Since doubt is also possible when a universal exists even among particulars, there would be an infinite regress even if one pursues the particulars for the sake of reaching a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*). Furthermore, if existence (*sattā*) were admitted in inherence (*samavāya*), the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) of having to admit another inherence for its subsistence therein would serve as a refutation. However, in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, since the connection with existence is pervaded by the possession of a further lower genus (*apara-jāti*), its cessation is established upon the cessation of that [lower genus].

In that case, how is there the recurring cognition "existent, existent" with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like? It is due to the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of "existence" based on the commonality of having existence in their own nature (*svarūpasattva*). Is this, then, a false cognition (*mithyāpratyaya*)? Who indeed says it is not? The recurring application of a single [concept] to things of distinct natures is certainly false; however, the apprehension of the thing's own nature is not false, because the own nature is real. Why then should the recurring cognition even with respect to substances (*dravya*) and so forth be considered merely caused by the superimposition of "existence"? It is not so, because superimposition is impossible in the absence of a primary [referent].

And this [term] is not primary (*mukhyā*) only in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, because of the existence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) there, whereas such evidence is absent in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "having cognition as their defining characteristic" (*buddhilakṣaṇatva*): those for whom cognition itself is the defining characteristic—that is, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—are "those characterized by cognition. For one who is in disagreement regarding the existence of universals and so forth, cognition alone is the defining characteristic and nothing else; however, regarding the existence of substances and so forth, other things as well—such as their effects—could serve as the means of valid cognition. Someone, however, says this: they are "characterized by cognition" because they are defined or perceived by cognition (*buddhyā lakṣyante pratīyante*).
