That is incorrect; since substances and so forth are also characterized by their own cognitions, this would not have been stated as a point of dissimilarity.

Non-effectness is the nature of being independent of causes. And that is apprehended by perception itself—just like pervasion—with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), through the apprehension of its existence prior to, after, and at the time of the individual (*vyakti*), aided by the impressions produced by repeated observation and assisted by the non-perception of a cause.

Inherence (*samavāya*) must also be unproduced (*akṛtaka*), because it cannot be established as existing prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with its effect. For if inherence were to exist prior to the cloth, then in the absence of the related object (the cloth), to what would it belong? If it were produced simultaneously with the cloth, then the cloth would lack a substratum (*anādhāratva*). And if it exists subsequently, the cloth would likewise lack a substratum; yet it is not logical for an effect to be without a substratum. Therefore, inherence is uncreated.

Furthermore, the fact that particulars (*viśeṣa*) are not effects is established—given that they are real entities—by their being distinct from substances, qualities, and actions, just like universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*).

"Being without a cause" means the absence of being either an inherent (samavāyin) or a non-inherent (asamavāyin) cause; it does not, however, prohibit its being an efficient (nimitta) cause, since its status as an efficient cause for cognition is admitted. "The state of lacking generality and particularity" means the absence of any lower genus (*aparajāti*). Among generalities, there is no further generality called "generality," because that too would result in an infinite regress due to the recurrence of generality. As for particulars and inherence, the same reasoning applies regarding the absence of generality.

How, then, is there a recurrence of the same cognition regarding universals, such as "universal, universal"? Even though they are particulars, the application of a single word occurs due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of inherence (*samavāya*) in multiple individuals, because the capacity to produce a cognition of absolute exclusion is possible everywhere. Eternity is the state of being devoid of destruction; this too is ascertained with respect to the universal by means of a pure perception (*nirupādhi-pratyakṣa*) that occurs repeatedly and perceives its persistence through the production and destruction of individuals, just like the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Intrinsic inherence (*samavāya*), however, is inferred from the fact that its effects are perceived everywhere and because it is uncreated; furthermore, it is not denotable by the word "object" (*artha*). Moreover, their common characteristic (*sādharmya*) is that they are not denotable by the word "object" according to their own technical system (*svasamaya*); the word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [36], p. 67: For all nine substances beginning with earth, there is the following commonality: connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*), being productive of themselves, possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*), non-contradiction with cause and effect, and possession of ultimate particulars (*anyaviśeṣavattva*).
Nyāyakandalī [36] [pp. 67–68]:

Now he describes the common properties (*sādharmya*) of substances alone, beginning with the words "of earth and so forth" (*pṛthivyādīnām*). The connection—that is, the relation—of earth and the others with the generality (*sāmānya*) of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) belongs to them alone. To the question "To how many? he replies: "Of all nine. The word "also" (*api*) has the sense of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). By this, the definition of the category of substance as distinct from the others has been stated, and the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term "substance" has been considered.

Here someone raises an objection: "The connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*) is the inherence of substantiality (*dravyatva-samavāya*); and since that is a property of the five categories (*padārtha*), how can it be the definition of substance? Another replies: "Even though inherence is non-different everywhere, nevertheless, due to the distinction provided by the limiting adjunct (*upakṣaṇa*) of substantiality, it serves as the definition of substance. For it is observed that even for space (*ākāśa*), which is conceptually differentiated, there is a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by virtue of its being the auditory organ (*śrotra*)."

Both of these points are incorrect. It is not the case that the ear is related to space; rather, conjunction (*yoga*) is the definition of a substance, for it is simply the state of being a substance (*dravyatva*). A definition that is not connected to reality would be no definition at all; thus, the mention of conjunction is the statement of the existence of the mark (*liṅga*) in the subject (*dharmin*). And so the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: earth and the other [elements] are distinct from others because they possess the state of being a substance (*dravyatva*); those things which do not have distinction from others do not possess the state of being a substance, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and the like. Therefore, this is both a false objection and a fallacious reply.

He states another point of similarity among substances: "the state of being a producer within itself. The meaning of "the state of being a producer within itself" is the production of an effect that is of the same nature as oneself. "Quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is the relation of inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Both of these are points of dissimilarity between substances and qualities (and so forth), because they are impossible elsewhere [than in substances]. [Another point is] "the non-opposition to cause and effect. For a quality is sometimes destroyed by its effect, as for example, the first sound is destroyed by the second sound.

In some cases, [a substance] is destroyed by its cause, as for example, the final sound is destroyed by the penultimate sound. It is destroyed by its effect, as for example, by subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*). Substances, however, are not destroyed by their own effects, nor are they destroyed by their own causes; thus, they are non-opposed to their effects and causes. Regarding eternal substances, there is no destruction by a cause precisely because of the absence of both cause and destruction; regarding non-eternal substances, although both cause and destruction are possible, there is no destruction by the cause, but rather by something else—this is the distinction.
Likewise, "possessing ultimate particularity" (*antya-viśeṣavattva*) means the state of being endowed with ultimate particulars (*antya-viśeṣa*).
Non-dependence and eternity belong [to these] except for composite substances.
Earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind possess multiplicity and the possession of lower genera.
Earth, water, fire, air, and mind possess activity, corporeality, priority, posteriority, and velocity.
*Nyāyakandalī* [37] [pp. 69–70]

Non-dependence (*anāśritatva*), which is the state of not being inherent in anything (*asamavetatva*), and eternality (*nityatva*), which is the state of being devoid of destruction (*vināśarahitatva*), are the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) of substances. To the question, "Is this the common characteristic of all [substances]? he says: "Other than composite substances" (*avayavidravyebhyo 'nyatra*). The meaning is that, setting aside composite substances, non-dependence, eternality, and possession of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣavatva*) exist elsewhere. The word "and" (*ca*) implies that these are not only the previously mentioned properties of earth and so forth, but also non-dependence and eternality.

Now, demonstrating the mutual similarity and dissimilarity of substances themselves, he says: "Of earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind. "Multiplicity" refers to the distinction between each individual instance. "Possessing a lower genus" means being related to a genus such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.

Earth, water, light, air, mind, and time possess the qualities of having action, having form, priority, posteriority, and velocity. Having action (*kriyāvattva*) is the conjunction with actions such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*). Having form (*mūrttatva*) is the conjunction with limited dimension (*avacchinna-parimāṇa*). Priority, posteriority, and velocity consist in the inherence (*samavāya*) of priority, posteriority, and velocity.

Some maintain that "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "nearness" (*aparatva*) do not exist as distinct qualities, because the designations "remote" and "near" are caused solely by the lesser or greater number of "conjoined-conjunctions" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*). This is not so; for even when there exists a lesser or greater number of conjoined-conjunctions between two objects situated in different directions, and even when the cognitions of "proximity" and "distance" arise relative to the observer's own body, the cognitions of "remoteness" and "nearness" do not occur.

If it is argued that the cognition is thus [different] because of two masses situated in one direction, then there must indeed be a distinct object based on the lesser or greater degree of conjunction, since a cognition characterized by a difference in its objects would not otherwise arise. Velocity (*vega*) is also a distinct quality (*guṇa*), and not merely a succession of actions (*kriyāsantati*), because velocity is not perceived in slow motion.

If it is argued that the conventional usage of "velocity" (*vega*) is based on the rapid production of moments of action (*kriyākṣaṇa*), we say no. For in the case of a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*) and similar phenomena, although the moments of action possess uninterrupted production and destruction, their rapid production is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because each interval between them is not grasped; yet, the cognition of velocity still occurs. Furthermore, in the world, the distinction between action and velocity is clearly understood, as evidenced by the common perception, "He goes with velocity. Praśastapādabhāṣya [38] [p.71]:

Space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*dik*), and the self (*ātman*) are all-pervading (*sarvagata*), possess supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*), and occupy the same location as all things with which they are conjoined (*sarvasaṃyogisamānadeśatva*).

*Nyāyakandalī* [38] [p.71]: "The all-pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*) of ether, time, space, and the self," and so forth. Here, by the word "all" (*sarva*), the material substances (*mūrtadravya*) mentioned immediately prior in relation to the context are referred to. The all-pervasiveness of ether and the others is their conjunction with all material things; it does not mean moving everywhere, because they are devoid of action (*niṣkriya*). Their "supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattva*) consists in possessing a dimension that is not limited by any measure.

"Being in the same location as all conjoined things" means that for all corporeal substances possessing conjunction, space (*ākāśa*) is the common location—that is, the single substratum. This should be explained in the same way regarding direction (*diś*) and the others as well. Although space and so forth do not serve as the substratum for all conjoined things in the sense of being their immediate support—since they do not abide as such a support nonetheless, because they are the substratum of all conjunctions, it is said that there exists a conjunction with the substratum of all conjoined things; here, however, it is stated that they are the "substratum of all. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [39] [p.72]

The five elements, beginning with earth, possess the properties of being elemental substances (*bhūtatva*), being the material causes of the sense organs (*indriyaprakṛtitva*), and possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are each perceivable by one of the external sense organs.
*Nyāyakandalī* [39] [pp. 72–75]

He states the commonality (*sādharmya*) of the elements beginning with earth and ending with space by way of their difference from other things—namely, "of earth and the others. "Element-ness" (*bhūtatva*) means being denotable by the word "element" (*bhūta*). The application of a single term to multiple entities such as earth and so forth, in the absence of a single underlying cause, is like the case of the word "akṣa": just as the word "akṣa" is applied conventionally to dice, sense organs, and the *bibhītaka* tree due to their connection with the three universals (*sāmānya*) of "gambleness," "sensory organ-ness," and "bibhītaka-ness," likewise, the conventional designation of the word "element" applies to the four starting with earth by virtue of the universals of "earth-ness" and so forth.

In the case of space, however, the cognition "element, element" is based solely on its individual manifestation; it is permeated by that word and produced by the limiting condition (upādhi) of being denotable by that word, just as there is the single cognition "die" applied to the dice and so forth.

The state of being the nature of the sense-faculties (*indriya-prakṛtitva*) means having the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the sense-faculties. Some maintain that the sense-faculties do not have the elements (*bhūta*) as their intrinsic nature, because they function without reaching [their object] (*aprāpyakāritva*); for functioning by reaching [the object] is a property of material things (*bhautika*), such as a lamp. That is incorrect, because there would be no perception of objects obstructed by barriers; if the sense-faculty functions without reaching [the object], it would perceive even an object obstructed by a wall or the like, since there is no distinction in the lack of contact.

If it is argued that there is no apprehension of an object because of a lack of fitness (*yogyatā*), [we reply: the sense organ certainly possesses the fitness consisting in the capacity to grasp an object at that time, since it does grasp an unobstructed object. Furthermore, the fitness of the object—which consists in its being coexistent, possessing multiple substances, and having specific qualities such as form—is not at all lost even when there is an obstruction; its state of being situated directly in front remains exactly as it was.

Now, it might be thought: "The absence of an obstruction is also a cause for the cognition of an object, just as the absence of contact is a cause for the action of falling; when an obstruction exists, the absence of that obstruction ceases, and thus the non-arising of cognition is due to the absence of its cause. This is not sound, because an obstruction is perceived as having the function of preventing the reaching of a tangible substance; for instance, an umbrella and the like prevent the reaching of falling water and solar light, but they do not merely eliminate their own non-existence.

This being the case, the following inference is easily established: the eye reveals what it has reached, because it does not reveal objects that are obstructed, like a lamp; or, because it is an external sense organ, like the sense of touch. [Objection: But if this is so, then how is there the apprehension of distant objects? [Reply: Due to the contact between the ray and the object, the ocular rays—which possess unmanifest color and touch—travel to a distance and apprehend the existing object. For this very reason, since it reveals both the large and the minute, why is the elemental nature of the sense organ not established? This is possible through the medium of its rays, just as in the case of a lamp.

Where the sense-faculties (raśmayaḥ) are connected with their own constituent parts, along with the object as a whole and its parts, there is a distinct apprehension due to the grasping of the object as it is overwhelmed by all its specific qualities. However, where there is a connection with the whole alone, there is an indistinct apprehension because the subject (dharmin) is grasped only as qualified by its general characteristics. That which moves reaches two objects—one proximate and one remote—in succession.

If it is asked, "How then can there be a simultaneous perception of the branch and the moon? [the answer is: because the activity of the sense organ proceeds with such rapidity—like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals—this is an illusion caused by the non-perception of succession, and not a case of actual simultaneity. [Objection: But if the theory of direct contact (*prāpti*) were true, there could be no perception of this [moon] as being at a distance; [Response: No, for that is possible in another way.

Since the connection with the sense organs is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), the cognitions of "with an interval" and "without an interval" do not arise from the absence of that [connection]; rather, they are produced by the presence or absence of the connection with the body. Where there is the apprehension of an object connected to the body, there arises the cognition "this is without an interval"; but where there is the apprehension of an object not so connected, there arises the cognition "it is with an interval."

"Because they possess specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are perceptible by each of the external sense organs individually. This means that earth and the other elements possess those specific qualities, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are perceptible by each of the external sense organs, such as the eye and so forth. Since these qualities are also perceptible by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), their being "perceptible by each of the [external] sense organs" would otherwise be unestablished; therefore, the term "external" (*bāhya*) is included. The inclusion of the word "each" (*ekaika*) is for the purpose of stating their essential nature.
[40] [Page 76] "The four [elements] have the properties of being originators of substances (*dravyārambhakatva*) and possessing touch (*sparśavattva*)."

The three possess perceptibility, possession of form, and fluidity; [these are the qualities of earth, water, and fire]. The four possess the quality of being the originators of substances and the quality of possessing touch; these are earth, water, fire, and air. Being the originator of substances means having the status of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to a substance, and that is simply its own innate power (*nijā śakti*). Possession of touch means the inherence (*samavāya*) of touch.

The three [substances] possess perceptibility, possession of color, and fluidity. Perceptibility—defined as being manifest to cognition born of the external senses—belongs to the three: earth, water, and fire; it does not, however, consist in the conjunction with causes such as magnitude (*mahattva*), for that would result in the redundancy of the term "possession of color" (*rūpavattva*). One might object: "But isn't the self (*ātman*) also perceptible? True; however, it was stated that the three possess perceptibility with respect to the external sense organs. Likewise, "possession of color" means the inherence (*samavāya*) of color. Fluidity is the state of being fluid (*drava*) among substances, and this is a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*).
In two [substances], there is gravity and possession of taste. The elements and the self possess specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*).
Earth, water, and the self possess fourteen qualities each. Ether and the self possess specific qualities that are momentary and reside in only a portion of their substratum.
(Nyāyakandalī, p. 77)

There is heaviness in two [substances]. In the two—earth and water—heaviness is a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*); because of its presence, the term "heavy" is applied to earth and water. Furthermore, "possessing taste" means the inherence of taste; the meaning of "and" (*ca*) is that they possess not only heaviness but also the state of possessing taste.

The possession of specific qualities by the elements and the self. The conjunction of specific qualities belongs to the elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—and to the selves. "Specific" (*viśeṣa*) means differentiation; those things, such as color and so forth, which are capable of effecting differentiation—that is, the exclusion—of their own substratum from others are called "specific qualities" (*vaiśeṣika*). The conjunction of these belongs to the elements and the selves. Earth, water, and the selves possess fourteen qualities; that is, earth, water, and the selves are endowed with fourteen qualities.

And he states that there exists a conjunction of space and selves with particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are momentary and reside in only one part [of their substratum], by saying "of space and selves. Particular qualities belong to earth and the other elements as well; therefore, the term "residing in one part" is used for the purpose of excluding them. Furthermore, since those particular qualities of space and selves which do not pervade [their substratum] have the nature of being very rapidly perishable, the mention of "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) is made. [42] Space and time possess five qualities and serve as the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) of all things that arise.
The *Nyāyakandalī* [42] [p.78]:

He states that "in space and time" (*dikkālayoḥ*)—namely, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction—these five qualities alone reside. Not only do these two possess the common property (*sādharmya*) of having five qualities, but they also share the common property of being efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) for all things that originate.

Now, how is it to be understood that space and time are the efficient causes (*nimitta*) of all things that possess an origin? If it is by their mere presence (*sannidhi*), then ether (*ākāśa*) would also have to be a cause. If it is because of the designation [of birth] as such, that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since we see expressions such as "born in the house" or "born in the cow-pen," even though these are not the actual causes.

To this it is replied: First of all, the production of all things occurs due to the restriction of specific places and the restriction of specific times—just as the production of cloth and so forth occurs due to the specific restriction of threads and so forth. If specific place and time were not also causes, then causes would produce their effects anywhere at all, because there would be no distinction.

If it is argued that there is no production of an effect because its causes are absent at all times and in all places, we reply: it is accepted that causes possess their generative power only in those specific places and times where they exist, and not elsewhere; thus, particular place and time function as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*), since they must be depended upon by the causes for the production of the effect. This indeed constitutes the causal status (*nimittatva*) of place and time: namely, that the effect arises in one location and does not arise in another. [43] [p.79] Earth and fire possess occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*).

*Nyāyakandalī* [43] [pp. 79–81]: Earth and fire possess occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*). That which is produced from a cause is "occasional" (*naimittika*); that which is occasional and is fluidity is "occasional fluidity. Earth and fire are conjoined with this, because substances such as clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) belonging to earth, and substances such as gold and silver belonging to fire, undergo liquefaction through contact with fire. Some maintain that fluidity, like gravity, belongs exclusively to earth; it is perceived in burning gold and other such substances through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).

No, because the liquidity of earthy substances is observed to be reduced to ashes through contact with intense fire, whereas this [liquidity of gold] does not cease. For this very reason, the claim of some that gold and such are indeed earthy is also refuted; for if they were earthy, it would follow—just as in the case of ghee and similar substances—that their liquidity would be destroyed by contact with intense fire.

As for this argument that was stated—that earthly gold and the like possess gravity because they lack fluidity by nature while being substrata of gravity, like a clod of earth—that too is without substance; for the doubt remains unresolved as to whether the perception of gravity therein is due to its being an inherent quality (*guṇa*), or rather, even if it were not an inherent quality, it occurs through proximity to its own substrate, just as viscosity (*sneha*) exists in substances like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Furthermore, the other proof offered—that [earth] is manifested by another—also fails as a proof, since it can be accounted for by the presence of unmanifested color-form (*anudbhūtarūpa*). We have provided only a mere indication.

*Praśastapādabhāṣyam*: Thus, in all cases, similarity (*sādharmya*) and its opposite, dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), should be stated. *Nyāyakandalī*: [44] [pp. 82–83] Thus, in every instance, similarity is to be stated, and dissimilarity as its reverse. This means that wherever there is a commonality between two things, that constitutes their similarity; conversely, where there is a lack of such commonality, that constitutes their dissimilarity. For example, earth possesses qualities such as smell, whereas water does not; therefore, the absence of smell in water is its dissimilarity to earth. In this manner, one should describe the similarities and dissimilarities among all substances, qualities, and actions. Furthermore, when a specific property is mentioned in relation to a particular category, it should be understood that the remaining properties of that same category constitute its similarity to others within that class. Conversely, the absence of those properties in other categories constitutes its dissimilarity to them. Thus, through the systematic presentation of these similarities and dissimilarities, the essential nature of each category is fully elucidated. This method of exposition serves to distinguish each entity from all others and establishes the basis for inference. Therefore, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has provided this instruction so that students may correctly identify and articulate the defining characteristics of all categories. This concludes the section on the classification of substances. Now, the following section concerns the examination of qualities. Regarding the question of whether qualities are eternal or non-eternal, the author states: "Qualities are of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. This indicates that qualities are divided into these two categories based on their respective substrates. Among these, those residing in eternal substances are themselves eternal, while those residing in non-eternal substances are non-eternal. This distinction is established by the nature of their substrates. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether qualities are produced or unproduced, the author states: "They are both produced and unproduced. This means that some qualities arise from the production of their substrates, while others do not. Those that arise from the production of their substrates are called "produced," whereas those that do not are called "unproduced. This division is also determined by the nature of their substrates. For instance, qualities such as number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, fluidity, viscidity, sound, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and cognition are produced, because they arise from the production of their substrates. On the other hand, qualities such as gravity, elasticity, and the internal organ are unproduced, because they do not arise from the production of their substrates. This distinction is likewise established by the nature of their substrates. Moreover, regarding the inquiry into whether qualities are manifested or unmanifested, the author states: "They are both manifested and unmanifested. This means that some qualities are perceived through the senses, while others are not. Those that are perceived are called "manifested," and those that are not are called "unmanifested. This distinction is also determined by the nature of their substrates. For example, qualities such as color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, fluidity, viscidity, sound, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and cognition are manifested, because they are perceived by the senses. Conversely, qualities such as gravity, elasticity, and the internal organ are unmanifested, because they are not perceived by the senses. This distinction is likewise established by the nature of their substrates. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether qualities are causes or non-causes, the author states: "They are both causes and non-causes. This means that some qualities function as causes, while others do not. Those that function as causes are called "causes," and those that do not are called "non-causes. This distinction is also determined by the nature of their substrates. For example, qualities such as conjunction, disjunction, speed, merit, demerit, and cognition are causes, because they produce effects. On the other hand, qualities such as gravity, elasticity, fluidity, viscidity, internal organ, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are non-causes, because they do not produce effects. This distinction is likewise established by the nature of their substrates. Finally, regarding the inquiry into whether qualities are pervasive or non-pervasive, the author states: "They are both pervasive and non-pervasive. This means that some qualities extend throughout their entire substrate, while others do not. Those that extend throughout are called "pervasive," and those that do not are called "non-pervasive. This distinction is also determined by the nature of their substrates. For example, qualities such as number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, fluidity, viscidity, sound, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and cognition are pervasive, because they occupy the entire extent of their substrate. Conversely, qualities such as color, taste, smell, touch, gravity, elasticity, and the internal organ are non-pervasive, because they do not occupy the entire extent of their substrate. This distinction is likewise established by the nature of their substrates. Thus, the various classifications of qualities have been explained. Now, the following section concerns the examination of actions. Regarding the question of whether actions are eternal or non-eternal, the author states: "Action is non-eternal. This means that action is invariably non-eternal. Why is this? Because action arises from conjunction and disjunction, and since conjunction and disjunction are non-eternal, action must also be non-eternal. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether action is produced or unproduced, the author states: "It is produced. This means that action is invariably produced. Why is this? Because action arises from conjunction and disjunction, and since conjunction and disjunction are produced, action must also be produced. Moreover, regarding the inquiry into whether action is manifested or unmanifested, the author states: "It is manifested. This means that action is invariably manifested. Why is this? Because action is perceived by the senses. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether action is a cause or a non-cause, the author states: "It is a cause. This means that action is invariably a cause. Why is this? Because action produces conjunction and disjunction. Moreover, regarding the inquiry into whether action is pervasive or non-pervasive, the author states: "It is non-pervasive. This means that action is invariably non-pervasive. Why is this? Because action occupies only a portion of its substrate. Thus, the various classifications of action have been explained. Now, the following section concerns the examination of generality (*sāmānya*). Regarding the question of whether generality is eternal or non-eternal, the author states: "Generality is eternal. This means that generality is invariably eternal. Why is this? Because generality is the cause of the cognition of "being" (*sat*), and since the cognition of "being" is eternal, generality must also be eternal. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether generality is produced or unproduced, the author states: "It is unproduced. This means that generality is invariably unproduced. Why is this? Because generality is the cause of the cognition of "being," and since the cognition of "being" is unproduced, generality must also be unproduced. Moreover, regarding the inquiry into whether generality is manifested or unmanifested, the author states: "It is manifested. This means that generality is invariably manifested. Why is this? Because generality is perceived by the senses. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether generality is a cause or a non-cause, the author states: "It is a cause. This means that generality is invariably a cause. Why is this? Because generality is the cause of the cognition of "being. Moreover, regarding the inquiry into whether generality is pervasive or non-pervasive, the author states: "It is pervasive. This means that generality is invariably pervasive. Why is this? Because generality extends throughout its entire substrate. Thus, the various classifications of generality have been explained. Now, the following section concerns the examination of particularity (*viśeṣa*). Regarding the question of whether particularity is eternal or non-eternal, the author states: "Particularity is eternal. This means that particularity is invariably eternal. Why is this? Because particularity is the cause of the cognition of ultimate difference, and since that cognition is eternal, particularity must also be eternal. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether particularity is produced or unproduced, the author states: "It is unproduced. This means that particularity is invariably unproduced. Why is this? Because particularity is the cause of the cognition of ultimate difference, and since that cognition is unproduced, particularity must also be unproduced. Moreover, regarding the inquiry into whether particularity is manifested or unmanifested, the author states: "It is manifested. This means that particularity is invariably manifested. Why is this? Because particularity is perceived by the senses. Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into whether particularity is a cause or a non-cause, the author states: "It is a cause. This means that particularity is invariably a cause. Why

By this very method, other similarities (*sādharmya*) among all categories (*padārtha*) should be stated by oneself; and from the opposite [of similarity], their dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), which consists in the exclusion of others (*itaravyāvṛtti*), should also be stated. Thus he says "in this way" (*evam*) to his students. For regarding categories that have not been mentioned (*anuddiṣṭa*), their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) do not apply because they lack an object; and for those that are not defined (*alakṣita*), there is no cognition of their true nature (*tattvapratīti*) due to the absence of a cause. Therefore, for a treatise (*śāstra*) engaged in the exposition of categories, its operation is twofold: mention (*uddeśa*) and definition (*lakṣaṇa*). But for indirect knowledge (*parokṣā*), only the latter [is required].

Where, once a definition has been stated, the ascertainment of reality does not occur due to the distraction caused by opposing doctrines, there the procedure of critical examination (*parīkṣā*) is undertaken for the purpose of refuting the positions of others. However, where the ascertainment of reality would arise from the very power of the statement of the definition itself, there this [examination] is useless and is not required.

For even one who maintains that the operation of a treatise (*śāstra*) is threefold, there is still no examination of the purpose (*prayojana*) and the other [elements], for what reason? Because those [elements] are understood from the mere definition (*lakṣaṇa*) alone. If this is so, then the operation of a treatise is not necessarily threefold, as it follows from the comprehension of the subject matter (*artha*). The enunciation (*uddeśa*) is the naming of categories (*padārtha*) by means of their designations. The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the property (*dharma*) of that which has been enounced, which distinguishes it from both its own and other classes.

Investigation (*parīkṣā*) is the examination, according to their definitions, of those things that have been characterized (*lakṣita*). However, the enumeration of divisions (*uddiṣṭavibhāga*) is not a separate method, because it is already subsumed within the definition itself. Nevertheless, it is stated separately for the purpose of restriction—namely, to establish that "these alone [are the categories]"—and for the purpose of introducing the specific definitions (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). For specific definitions apply only when the categories have been divided; otherwise, they would be without a subject matter.

Among those, substances were first enumerated as "substance, quality, and action," and then substances were classified as "earth, water, fire," and so forth. Now, this section is commenced for the purpose of defining their specific characteristics. (Praśastapādabhāṣya) [45] [pp. 84–85]
Now, the dissimilarities are stated one by one:
earth is so called because of its connection with the universal "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*).
[Earth] possesses color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and faculty (*saṃskāra*).

These specific qualities, beginning with color, are established in the section on the classification of qualities. Number and the others are established by the mention of visibility; gravity is established by the teaching regarding falling.
*Nyāyakandalī* [45] [pp. 84–86]

Regarding the phrase "here now": previously, the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between two or many things was stated through their mutual dependence on one another. Here, in the section about to be explained, the defining characteristic (*vyāvartaka-dharma*) that distinguishes each individual substance is being described. The suffix *-śas* in the word *ekaikaśaḥ* is used to indicate repetition (*vīpsā*), demonstrating an extremely extensive pervasion.

Following the order of enumeration, he first states the dissimilarity of earth: "Earth is [defined] by its connection with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*). For one who, although knowing earth by its own nature, does not employ the conventional designation "earth" due to some delusion, this unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is stated—in order to establish that conventional usage through an infallible connection with the opposite [of the error]: "Earth is [defined] by its connection with earth-ness."

This should be designated as "earth" because it is connected with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*). Whatever is not designated as "earth" is not connected with earth-ness, such as water and so forth; yet this [subject] is not unconnected with earth-ness. Therefore, it should be designated as "earth."

Alternatively, for one who hears in the world that "this is earth" but does not know what its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is like, the unique property (*asādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) is stated in order to demonstrate its essential nature as excluded from both its own and other classes: "That which is designated as 'earth' in the world is earth, because of its connection with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*)."

As Uddyotakara said: "The purpose of a definition (*lakṭaṇa*) is the exclusion [of the defined object] from things of the same and different classes" (*Nyāyavārttika*). By this, the following argument is also refuted, which was stated by others: "If categories are already well-known, they need not be defined; if they are unknown, they even less so, because it is impossible [to define them]. Furthermore, a definition is employed for the sake of establishing specific usage regarding that which is understood in its own nature, and for the sake of understanding its specific features regarding that which is known only in a general sense. This is refuted because the purpose of a definition is precisely the exclusion of the object from things of the same and different classes.

If it is argued that this being the case, there would be an infinite regress—since, like the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) itself must be defined by something else—we say no. This is because a definition is required only when there is non-cognition, and non-cognition does not exist in all cases. For instance, the wise track cattle by their heads or their feet, yet they do not look for another means to perceive even these two. Furthermore, instruction is not intended for one who is entirely without cognition, for such a person lacks the capacity for it, like a child or a mute.

Demonstrating that the possession of fourteen qualities, including odor (*gandha*), also constitutes the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of earth from the others, he says: "color, taste, odor... (*rūpa-rasa-gandha...*). Here, because the suffix *matup* follows a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the connection of each [quality]—color and so forth—with earth individually is obtained. He further states: "And these... (*ete ca...*), indicating that these qualities are also intended by the author of the Sūtras to reside in earth.

The "Section on the Inherence of Qualities" (*guṇaviniveśādhikāra*) is the second chapter, so called because it is devoted to the exposition of the subsistence of qualities within substances. In that [chapter], the author of the Sūtras established and expounded color, taste, smell, and touch as residing in earth: "Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.1). From the mention of visibility, the seven [qualities] beginning with number are also [established].

From the statement regarding visual perception, "Number, dimensions, distinctness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, and action are visible because of their inherence in substances possessing color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.14), the seven qualities beginning with number are established in earth, which possesses color. The meaning is that if these [qualities] did not exist in substances possessing color, the author of the Sūtras would not have stated that they are perceptible through their inherence therein.

"Heaviness [is known] from the instruction on falling. Because of the instruction in the Sūtra, "In the absence of conjunction, velocity, and effort, falling occurs due to heaviness" (Vaiśeṣika-sūtra 5.1.7), the author of the Sūtras has effectively stated that heaviness exists in the earth which is connected with falling; for that which resides in a different locus cannot be the cause.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [46–47–48], p. 87.

From the statement regarding their commonality with water, [earth possesses] fluidity; from the statement regarding subsequent action, it possesses *saṃskāra* (elasticity). Odor exists only in earth. Color (*rūpa*) is of many kinds, such as white and so forth. Taste (*rasa*) is of six kinds, beginning with sweet. Odor (*gandha*) is of two kinds: fragrant and foul. Touch (*sparśa*) is produced by heating (*pākaja*), provided that it is neither hot nor cold. *Nyāyakandalī* [46] [p.87]

Because of the statement [in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra]: "Fluidity [is established] through the commonality with water; the flowing of clarified butter (*śarpi*), lac (*jatu*), and beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*)—which are earthen—is due to contact with fire; flowing is a commonality with water" (Vaiśū. 2.1.7), it is stated that there is occasional (*naimittika*) fluidity in earth. By the word *madhūcchiṣṭa*, beeswax (*siktha*) is denoted.

It is called *saṃskāra* because of the statement regarding subsequent action: "The first action of an arrow is caused by impulsion; and from that *saṃskāra*, produced by that action, there arise subsequent and further [actions]" (VaiSū 5.1.17). By showing that *saṃskāra* is the cause of action in the case of an arrow—which is an earthly substance—the author of the Sūtras has indicated that velocity (*vega*) exists in earth, for that which does not exist cannot be a cause. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate how this single *saṃskāra* persists until the fall.

Odor exists only in earth. This is its meaning: it is exclusively this unique property. If it is argued that odor exists in other substances as well—on account of such cognitions as "fragrant water" and "fragrant wind"—this is not so, because those qualities are perceived only through their inherence in a substance composed of earth. If it is asked how this certainty is established, it is because they are not perceived in the absence of that [earth].
*Nyāyakandalī* [47] [pp. 88–90]

Although color (*rūpa*) is common to the [first] three [elements], nevertheless, with respect to internal distinctions, he states that even this is a property unique to earth alone: "color is of many kinds. Here too, it should be understood as applying to earth alone. The meaning is that color, which is of various types such as white, yellow, and so forth, exists in earth alone and not elsewhere. Multiple colors inhere in the single genus *pṛthivītva* (earthness) according to the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*).

In some cases, even within a single individual entity (*vyakti*), there is the coexistence of multiple types of color, where a whole (*avayavin*) is produced by parts (*avayava*) that possess various kinds of colors. If one asks how this is so, it is said: just as the whole is produced by its parts, so too must color be produced in the whole by the colors of the parts; and among the parts, there is not only white color, nor only black, but rather black, white, green, and so forth.

Nor is there a fixed rule that [the sense organ] initiates only the form of those [atoms] and not others, for the capacity of all [atoms] is observed individually elsewhere. Nor is it logical to claim that all [atoms] fail to initiate [the effect] due to mutual contradiction, because a composite whole possessing variegated color (*citrarūpa*) is perceived, and because a substance devoid of color cannot be an object of direct perception.

Furthermore, the forms of the parts, when aggregated, are not perceived here by the variegated cognition; for if one were to imagine that the whole (*avayavin*) is perceived through those very parts, it would follow that the same would apply elsewhere as well, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the form of the whole. Therefore, [the whole] is produced by them acting together. And that which is being produced, because it conforms to the natures of its various causes, must consist of black, white, and green components, and is thus designated as "variegated" (*citram*).

If it is argued that it is illogical for a single entity to possess multiple natures due to contradiction—just as the common saying of the sophists goes: "That which is both one and manifold is more manifold than the manifold itself"—then what is the contradiction among blue and the other colors? It cannot be a contradiction consisting of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), because they follow the nature of being (*bhāvasvabhāva*) and because they are mutually dependent. If it is argued that contradiction consists in the difference of intrinsic nature (*svarūpānyatva*), then that is indeed true.

Nevertheless, there is no inconsistency in the nature of variegated form (*citrātman*), because that which arises from the causal capacity of diverse causes is established by perception itself, which is renowned to all the world.

If it is argued that—just as in the case of a cloth—the variegated form residing in its substrate would necessarily be perceived on a non-variegated side because of its unity, we say no; for, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the perception of the various forms of the parts, whose causal capacity has been established, is also the cause for the perception of variegated form, and that [perception] is absent on the other side.

[Objection: But if that is the case, then in a substance composed of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) possessing various colors, there would be no perception of a variegated color, because there is no perception of the colors of its constituent parts. [Response: Who says it is not so? For the color of an extremely subtle entity is not perceived in isolation; however, when the color of something *is* perceived in isolation, the colors of its constituent parts are also perceived.

As for one who maintains that there are many non-pervasive variegated colors (*citrarūpa*), for him there would be no production of color in a double-threaded fabric (*dvitantuka*) commenced by blue and yellow, because the color of each individual part does not initiate [a new color]. Now, if it is thought that a single variegated color is produced there from two [colors], then it should be the same elsewhere as well, since there is no distinction.

The variegated substance under dispute is connected with a single-colored substance, because it is a substance, like any other substance; and the color residing therein is single, because it is the color of a whole composed of parts, like the color of any other substance composed of parts.

In the statement "taste is of six kinds," the explanation is as before. With the intention that the determination of the varieties of smell is, by extension, a description of the essential nature of earth as well, he says: "smell is of two kinds. He demonstrates that very twofold nature: "namely, fragrant and non-fragrant."

*Asurabhi* (non-fragrant) is another kind of odor (*gandhāntara*) that is contrary to fragrance, inherent in various substances and so forth, and perceived as disagreeable; it is not merely the absence of fragrance, because it is experienced as a positive entity (*vidhirūpa*) and as possessing degrees of intensity. As for the neutral odor, it is not mentioned separately because it is simply a non-manifestation of the distinctions between fragrant and non-fragrant odors. Alternatively, even that [neutral odor] is indeed non-fragrant, based on the etymological derivation that "non-fragrant" means that which is other than fragrant odor.

He demonstrates her dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from touch (*sparśa*) as it truly is by stating, "her touch. The touch produced by heating (*pākaja*) is the dissimilarity of earth; its essential nature is described as being "neither hot nor cold" (*anuṣṇāśīta*). Although color (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), which are also produced by heating and possess touch, are likewise dissimilar to her, the fact that they are produced by heating is not mentioned here. This is because their dissimilarity exists even otherwise, and the intention is merely to establish the general state of dissimilarity.

The fact that touch in pillars and other such objects, whose baking is not perceptible, is produced by baking (*pākaja*) is established through inference: "The touch in pillars and other such objects is produced by baking, because it is a touch belonging to an earthy substance, like the touch of a jar and so forth. Furthermore, the touch of a jar and so forth is also produced by baking, because, while being perceivable by a single sense organ, it is a quality of that substance, like the color residing therein. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [49] [p.93]: And that [substance] is of two kinds—eternal and non-eternal. That characterized as atoms is eternal; however, that characterized as an effect is non-eternal.

And that [earth], characterized by the arrangement of its parts such as stability and so forth, possesses a multiplicity of lower genera (*apara-jāti*) and serves many purposes, such as providing beds, seats, and the like. In order to define its internal subdivisions, [the author] says: "It is both eternal and non-eternal. The two words "and" (*ca*) serve to indicate the absence of any other categories. To the question, "Which is eternal and which is non-eternal? he replies: "That characterized as atoms (*paramāṇu-lakṣaṇā*) is eternal, while that characterized as an effect (*kārya-lakṣaṇā*) is non-eternal. In both instances, the word "characterized" (*lakṣaṇa*) has the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).

What is the proof for the existence of earth whose nature is that of an atom (*paramāṇu*)? It is inference (*anumāna*): the gradation of atomic dimensions must terminate somewhere, because it is a gradation of dimension, just like the gradation of large dimensions; that wherein this gradation terminates, beyond which no further atom exists, is the atom.

For this very reason, [the atom] is eternal, because while being a substance, it is partless, like space. Alternatively, if this [atom] were possessed of parts, then it would not be an atom; for in the world, the dimension of the parts of an effect is perceived to be smaller and smaller than the dimension of that effect itself, and that which is its part will be the atom.

Now, if it is argued that even that [composite] does not exist because other parts exist, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, there could be no gradation of size among composites—such as being smaller, smaller still, and so on—because, since all things would equally be produced by an infinite number of causes, the two factors of the greater or lesser number of constituent causes (which are the grounds for the excellence or non-excellence of magnitude) would be impossible. Yet, this distinction of magnitude certainly exists; therefore, the atomic dimension must be somewhere unsurpassable, and thus the eternal atom (*paramāṇu*) is established.

Furthermore, that single [atom] cannot be a producer, because if a single eternal entity were a producer, the effect would arise continuously due to the absence of anything else to be depended upon, and moreover, its indestructibility would follow, since there would be no cause for the destruction of its substratum or the disjunction of its parts. Nor is it logical for all three [atoms] to be producers; for here, in the production of a large effect-substance, we observe that only an effect-substance possessing a dimension smaller than its own is capable [of producing it].

A triad (tryaṇuka) is produced only by an effect-substance, because it possesses the dimension of largeness (mahat-parimāṇa), like a jar. Thus, having rejected that three or one [atoms] are the originators, it is established that what is originated by exactly two atoms is a dyad (dvyaṇuka). Nor is there a rule that it must be originated by many dyads; for if it were originated by two, since the cause for the production of the dimension of minuteness (aṇu-parimāṇa) would already exist, the production of minuteness would be redundant. However, regarding many [dyads], there is no fixed rule.

Sometimes it is said that a triad (tryaṇuka) is commenced by three [atoms], sometimes it is commenced by four, and sometimes by five; such is the conceptualization according to one's preference. Nor is the effect purposeless, for as the number of causes increases, so too is a corresponding gradation of magnitude perceived.

And this being the case, it does not follow that only dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) are the originators of a jar; for when a jar is broken, one observes parts that are progressively smaller and smaller, and thus one postulates the originators in that very same manner. Thus, in this way, earth characterized as an effect is produced through the sequence beginning with dyads.

And that [earth] is impermanent, because its causes—the disjunction of parts and the destruction of the substratum—are possible. By stating "And that," he adds another property to earth, which is characterized as an effect, alongside its impermanence. *Aitharyam* means density (*nibiḍatvam*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), looseness and so forth are included. The "arrangement of parts" (*avayavānāṃ sanniveśaḥ*) is a particular conjunction of parts.

The meaning is as follows: they are characterized by stability and so forth, as well as by specific arrangements of parts; "endowed with a plurality of subordinate universals" means being possessed of a multiplicity of universals such as "cowness," "horseness," and so on. Even though there is no subordinate universal in atoms and the like, their configuration (*vyūha*) occurs in various ways through the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), such that the subordinate universals are manifested in the effects produced from them.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the creation of all entities is caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa)? Earth, characterized as an effect, produces some purposeful action for a person; therefore, it is by this unseen force that it is created. To this, he says: "Sleeping, sitting," etc. There are many benefits such as sleeping, sitting, and so forth; earth is "characterized as an effect" because it performs those functions. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [50] [p. 97]

Its effect is threefold, consisting of what is known as the body, the sense organs, and their objects. The body is of two kinds: born from a womb (*yonija*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*). Among these, the non-womb-born body of the gods and sages arises from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*), without depending on semen and blood. The bodies of punishment for minute creatures arise from atoms accompanied by a specific demerit (*adharma*). That which is produced from the union of semen and blood is womb-born; it is of two types: viviparous (*jarāyuja*) and oviparous (*aṇḍaja*). The viviparous belong to humans, domestic animals, and wild beasts. The oviparous belong to birds and reptiles.

The *Nyāyakandalī* [50] [pp. 97–103]: It enumerates its other effects with the words "and threefold. It demonstrates the threefold nature of the effect itself with the words "and threefold. It demonstrates that very threefold nature of the effect with the words "the body," and so forth. That effect which has the designations "body," "sense organ," and "object" is described as such. The body is the locus of experience for the enjoyer; it is designated as such even in a dead body because it possesses that potentiality. A sense organ is a substance that serves as the substratum for the soul and is the means for the knower’s direct perception [p. 98].

The object (*viṣaya*) is a substance that serves as the means for the self's enjoyment and is distinct from the body and the sense organs. He explains the distinction of the body: "born from a womb (*yonija*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*). A "womb" (*yoni*) is the union of semen and blood; that which is born from that is "born from a womb," while the opposite is "not born from a womb. He demonstrates this very point by saying, "among those, the one not born from a womb. Between those two—the womb-born and the non-womb-born—the body not born from a womb is produced without depending on semen and blood. To the question "Of whom? he replies: "Of the gods and the sages (*devarṣīṇām*)."

The meaning is "of the gods and the sages. To the question, "In the absence of semen and blood, whose causal status is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), how can the body arise?", he says: "from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma-viśeṣa*). That which is distinguished is a "specific" (*viśeṣa*); merit itself is the specific, thus "specific merit" (*dharma-viśeṣa*), meaning preeminent merit; [the body arises] from atoms accompanied by that.

This is the underlying intention: at the commencement of the body, atoms alone are the cause, and not the union of semen and blood; for once those two have perished through the logical process of action and disjunction, the body is originated by atoms in which the qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) have arisen. Nor is there any distinction between the atoms of semen and blood and other atoms, since they are indistinguishable in their earth-nature (*pārthivatva*).

In this case as well, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) alone is the cause for the restriction of the genus (*jāti*) in the effect. Thus, the production of a non-maternal body from atoms favored by specific merits (*dharma*) is not untenable.

Now, it might be argued: "Is it not observed that in all cases of the production of a body, there is a rule of priority for semen and blood? Therefore, just as the hypothesis of a stone floating up is untenable because it contradicts other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which apprehend the sinking of another similar stone, so too is the hypothesis of a non-womb-born (ayonija) body. This is not so; for we observe bodies such as those of locusts even in the absence of semen and the like.

If it is argued that the body’s possession of a specific configuration is understood to be preceded by semen and other such factors, [p. 100] this is true; nevertheless, the rule is not established, because of the doubt as to whether our own bodies and those like them are preceded by semen and so forth due to the absence of a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force), or rather, due to being invariably connected with the mere possession of a specific configuration. By this, the counter-inference (*bādhakānumāna*) is also refuted, because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is subject to doubt. Whatever remains to be said on this matter, we shall explain at the occasion of the investigation into the direct perception of yogis (*yogipratyakṣa*).

He states that even through a particular kind of demerit (*adharma*), a body may be born without a womb (*ayonija*)—namely, "of small creatures. Small creatures refer to gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like; their "torment" (*yātanā*) means suffering. A body for that purpose is a "body of torment. That [body] is produced from atoms accompanied by that particular demerit. This, however, is well known in the world. He describes the womb-born body (*yonija*): "born from the union of semen and blood."

Semen and blood—their conjunction (*sannipāta*) being a specific kind of union—from that which is born is called "born from a womb" (*yonija*). Following the conjunction of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood, due to contact with the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) within the womb, there occurs the process of action, disjunction, and so forth among the atoms (*paramāṇu*) that constitute the semen and blood. Upon the dissolution of the semen and blood, through contact with fire, the previous color and other qualities of the atoms perish; then, when new qualities of the same kind arise, the process begins with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and so on.

The production of the *kalala* body occurs there, with the entry of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), but not while in the state of semen and blood, because the mind has the body as its substrate. Therein, the essence of the mother’s food is transmitted in due measure by the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

Furthermore, in that case, due to the connection with the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*), the embryo (*kalala*) is destroyed through the process of action, disjunction, and so forth among the atoms constituting the *kalala*. Then, by the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), the atoms of food—which have acquired action and possess qualities identical to those of the atoms constituting the *kalala*—unite with those atoms produced by maturation (*pākaja*) and together initiate another body. This conceptualization is to be observed for the body every day.
Śrī: What is the proof for non-difference? It is the difference in dimension (*parimāṇabheda*), because a large dimension cannot be fully contained within a substratum delimited by a small dimension.

If it is argued that the body, having undergone a change of state (*avasthāntarāpanna*), becomes the substratum [for that large dimension], [we reply: either new parts of the body, assisted by the parts of the food, would originate the new state, or the body itself, assisted by them, would do so. In either case, as with threads and the like in the production of cloth, there would have to be the perception of multiple bodies with smaller or larger dimensions at the end; yet this is not so. Therefore, the previous body has perished and another body has arisen.

In respect to the dimensions under dispute, which have distinct substrata, [the proof is: because they possess lesser or greater dimensions, like the dimensions of a jar and a bowl; or, the dimension under dispute perishes solely through the destruction of its substratum, because it is a dimension, like a dimension that has been destroyed by a blow from a mallet. If it is argued that the unity of the body is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), we say no, for that [recognition] is also possible as having similarity as its object.

Since the causes of error—namely, the non-perception of an interval due to the production of individuals without interruption, and extreme similarity—are always present, there exists a possibility of sublation through reasoning, even though no sublation such as "this is not that" arises [as in the case of individual flames].

He shows its classification by saying "of two kinds" (*dvividham*). The explanation is that "of two kinds" means that which has two types or modes. "Jarāyu" is a designation for the womb; that which is born enveloped by that is "jarāyuja" (placental-born). An "aṇḍa" is an egg; that which is born enveloped by that is "aṇḍaja" (egg-born). To the question of for whom there is the placental-born and for whom the egg-born, he says "human," and so forth.

Humans are those such as ourselves; cattle are goats, based on the scriptural observation: "One should sacrifice a beast for Agni and Soma," and "One should sacrifice seventeen beasts dedicated to Prajāpati. Wild animals are the black antelope and others; their bodies are born from the womb (*jarāyuja*). This is also illustrative, since quadrupeds in general are born from the womb. Birds are well known. Reptiles are snakes; their bodies are egg-born (*aṇḍaja*). This too is not intended as a restrictive rule, because others, such as fish, are also egg-born. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [51], p. 104.
The sense organ that manifests odor, belonging to all living beings, is the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*), which is composed of earthy atoms not overcome by water and other elements;
this is the *Nyāyakandalī* [51] [pp. 104–105].

In order to define the essential nature of the sense organs, he says: "The sense organ. That sense organ which manifests odor and perceives odor for all living beings is composed of earthy atoms. By this much alone, the restrictive rule—that only this [organ] manifests odor and no other earthly substance does so—is not obtained; therefore, he says: the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) is composed of earthy atoms that are not overwhelmed by water and the other [elements].

This [organ] has been produced by parts that are not overwhelmed by water and the other elements, whose capacities are unimpeded, and which, by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), are distinct from others; therefore, because of this specific production, only this [organ] is capable of manifesting odor, and nothing else—this is the meaning. "Ghrāṇa" is its designation.

The self smells because it apprehends odor by means of this [organ]; thus, the very perception of odor is the proof for its existence, since an action must be accomplished by an instrument (karaṇa), and such perception does not arise when the eyes and other organs are active. Furthermore, even though it is composed of earth, the fact that it manifests only odor among the qualities such as form is the proof, just like clarified butter which manifests the fragrance of saffron.

Just as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), being accompanied by its own fragrance, manifests the fragrance of saffron (*kuṅkuma*), so too the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) is an organ that is itself accompanied by its own fragrance; therefore, it is not the perceiver of its own fragrance, because a thing cannot be perceived by that very same thing. Just as with the sense of smell, so it is with the senses of taste, sight, and touch: by the force of the examples to be stated, they are inferred to be organs only when conjoined with their respective qualities of taste, color, and touch, and thus they do not perceive their own qualities. The ear (*śrotra*), however, is an organ whose quality is sound; therefore, the perception of sound occurs through it alone.

*Praśastapādabhāṣyam*: The object, however, which is produced through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), is threefold, characterized as earth, stone, and immobile things (*sthāvara*). Among these, varieties of earth consist of regions of the ground, walls, bricks, and so forth. Stones consist of rocks, gems, diamonds, and so forth. Immobile things consist of grass, medicinal herbs, trees, shrubs, creepers, spreading plants, and forest giants (*vanaspati*). *Nyāyakandalī*: [pp. 106–107] The object of earth is threefold: earth, stone, and immobile things. Earth is of many kinds, such as the surface of the ground, walls, bricks, and the like. Stones include rocks, gems, diamonds, and so on. Immobile things comprise grass, medicinal herbs, trees, shrubs, creepers, spreading plants, and forest giants. Among these, trees are those that possess fruits and flowers; shrubs are those that bear fruit without flowers; creepers are those that require support to grow; spreading plants are those that grow horizontally; and forest giants are those that produce fruit without flowers and are large in size. Grass, medicinal herbs, and the like are also included among immobile things because they are fixed in one place and do not move about. Thus, the objects of earth have been explained. Regarding water: its quality is taste, which is of six kinds—sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. Its function is to moisten. Its manifestation is cooling. Its production is by means of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with fire. Its destruction is by means of conjunction with fire. Its substrata are rivers, oceans, rain, dew, frost, hail, and so forth.
