By the word "but" (*tu*), showing the specific nature of the object as distinct from the body and the senses, he demonstrates the difference [between them] with the words "the object, however. The phrase "begun by the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth" is a restatement of its common form. "Characterized by earth, stone, and stationary things" means having the nature of earth, stone, plants, and so on. Among these, specifying earth by way of its own nature, he says "therein. Therein, "regions of the earth" refers to regions conceived as the terrestrial globe.

Elevations, depressions, and so forth; walls, bricks, and so forth—all these are varieties of earth; the meaning is that they are different forms of clay. He speaks of the varieties of stone: "stones" (*pāṣāṇāḥ*). *Upalāḥ* refers to rocks; *maṇayaḥ* refers to sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*) and the like; *vajra* refers to thunderbolts and diamonds. *Tṛṇa* refers to grasses such as *ulapa*; *auṣadhayaḥ* refers to plants that end with the ripening of their fruit, such as wheat and the like; those which possess flowers and fruit are *vṛkṣāḥ*, such as the *kovidāra* and others; *gulmāḥ* are shrubs, such as bamboos, sugarcane, and the like.

A *latā* (creeper) is well known; *avatanvat* (creepers that spread) refers to those such as the *viṭapa*, *ketakī*, and *bījapūra*. Those which bear fruit without flowers are *vanaspati* (trees), such as the *udumbara* and others. Now, one might object: "Immobility (*sthāvaratva*) consists in the absence of activity dependent on one's own will, and that indeed exists even in earth and stone. True; however, because other forms [of existence] are also possible for those two, they have not been designated by this specific term. Praśastapādabhāṣya [53]: Water is that which is connected with the quality of water-ness (*aptva*).
They possess color, taste, touch, fluidity, viscidity, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, weight, and impression.
Their establishment is as before.
Their color, taste, and touch are exclusively white, sweet, and cold.

In the *Nyāyakandalī* [53] [pp. 107–109], he states the definition of water: "Water is that which is connected with the property of water-ness (*aptva*). Here too, as before, the purpose of a definition is either to establish conventional usage or to exclude what is of the same and different classes. Everything else is as previously explained. However, this must be stated here: one who has personally apprehended the distinction between categories through perception should communicate it to another by means of a definition, for that which is not itself understood cannot be communicated. Furthermore, the distinction between categories is characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

And that [negation] is apprehended by the apprehension of both that which is the absence and that wherein the absence occurs; otherwise, a negation restricted to its own specific nature would be untenable, as in the case of "a cow is not a horse. In this regard, does the apprehension of mutual absence arise from the apprehension of both [entities] as having mixed natures, or as being mutually distinct? First, if there were an apprehension of them as mixed, the very cognition "this is not that" would be impossible.

If non-existence is cognized through the perception of two things as mutually distinct, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): for the cognition of non-existence occurs when there is the perception of the two distinct things, and the perception of the two distinct things occurs when there is the cognition of non-existence; since non-existence itself is what constitutes distinction. To this it is replied: the absence of one from another belongs to two things that are already distinct, but the absence of one from another is not itself the distinction.

That which is the individual, intrinsic nature (*prātyātmika-svarūpa*) of an object is itself its differentiation (*bheda*). And that [nature], being perceived through the mere contact of the sense organs without depending on any other cognition, is experienced as distinct in each case. For instance, one who seeks a cow does not act upon seeing a horse, nor does he recall the word "cow"; since the horse and the cow are apprehended each by its own respective essence, the cognition of their mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*) is not untenable due to the restriction of their specific natures.

And this being the case, one should not say: "Let there be only a difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*); what is the use of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)? for that too is experienced as an object of negation. Demonstrating that not only is the state of being water (*aptva*) a property distinguishing water from others, but also its possession of fourteen qualities accompanied by viscidity (*sneha*), he says: "color, taste... [p.109]. Here, the possessive suffix *matup* should be applied after the copulative compound (*dvandva*).

Their establishment is as before; that is to say, just as the establishment and comprehension of these qualities—color and the rest—was previously established in earth on the basis of the words of the author of the Sūtras, so too it is in water. And thus the Sūtra states: "Water possesses color, taste, and touch; it is fluid and viscous" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.2). However, the Sūtra that establishes number and the other [qualities] is indeed common to all.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to mention color and other qualities—which are common to earth and the other elements—at the occasion of defining dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya*), he demonstrates their specific uniqueness through internal subdivisions, beginning with "white" and so forth: "The color of water is exclusively white, its taste is exclusively sweet, and its touch is exclusively cold. The perception of other colors in water is due to the difference in the color of its substrate.

If it is asked, "How is this so?"—the answer is that when those very fibers are extracted and scattered in the air, there is the perception of whiteness alone; however, when they fall back down, they conform to the form of their substrate. If it is argued that there is no sweet taste in them because, unlike molasses and such, it does not manifest, we say no; for a taste is experienced that is distinct from pungent, astringent, bitter, salty, and sour. The non-manifestation of sweetness, as in the case of molasses, is due to the absence of an excess of sweetness. In water alone is viscidity (*sneha*), and fluidity (*dravatva*) is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*). *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [54] [p.109]

*Nyāyakandalī* [54] [pp. 109–110]: It is implied that viscosity (*sneha*) without qualification is the specific property (*vaidharmya*) of water—expressed by the statement "viscosity exists only in water. Now, one might object: "But this [viscosity] also exists in earth, as it is observed in milk, oil, and clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*. [The author replies: "It does not exist everywhere, because it is absent in stones, bricks, cotton, fuel, and so forth. As for its occasional observation in things such as milk, that is due to *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) with water itself; just as natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*) is perceived in milk and oil through its contact with its own substratum [water]."

Moisture, however, is the inherent nature of water everywhere, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance [of water]. Thus, there is moisture in trees, grasses, and so forth, which grow in regions where no irrigation is provided; and there is dryness in those growing in arid regions. Even in that case, those whose roots are constantly being drenched possess moisture, while those lacking such [water] do not.

"And fluidity is innate. The meaning is that it is not only viscidity; fluidity is established by its very nature in water alone. In milk and oil, its perception occurs through contact with their own substrates, because in some cases their density is perceived. [55] [p.110] But these [qualities] are, as before, of two kinds, due to the existence of eternal and non-eternal states. Their effects, however, are threefold, being designated as body, sense organ, and object.

In that regard, the body in the world of Varuṇa is indeed not born from a womb (*ayonija*); yet, through the support of earthly particles (*pārthivāvayava*), it is capable of experience. *Nyāyakandalī* [55] [pp. 111–112]:

Just as earth, water also possesses a twofold nature due to internal distinctions; thus he says: "But those... Water is eternal when it has the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), but it is non-eternal when it has the nature of an effect (*kārya*). And the effect is threefold. Here too, the connection is as before: just as the effect of earth is threefold—consisting of what is designated as body, sense-organ, and object—so too is it for water.

In this regard, the meaning is that there is a distinction: the body is exclusively non-womb-born (*ayonija*); the earthly (*pārthiva*) body is both womb-born (*yonija*) and non-womb-born, whereas the watery (*āpya*) body is exclusively non-womb-born. Now, one might object: "The human body is indeed earthly, because the quality of odor is perceived; but where does the watery body exist? To this he says: "In the world of Varuṇa. This body is to be understood as being composed of water on the basis of scriptural tradition (*āgama*).

Since water has the single nature of fluidity, a body composed of it would primarily consist of water-bubbles and would be unfit for specific practical activities; how then could it be capable of experience? To this he says: "It is capable of experience due to the support of earthy atoms. Due to the support—that is, the specific conjunction—of earthy atoms, the aqueous body becomes capable of experience.

In the production of a watery body, the particles of earth are the efficient cause; because of their conjunction, the fluidity of the watery particles is obstructed, and thus this specific body is produced, rather than being merely like a mass of water bubbles—this is the meaning.

However, for those who maintain that the body has the five elements as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the body would be odorless, because a single causal odor cannot initiate [an effect]. Furthermore, it would follow that the body possesses variegated color, taste, and touch, since multiple colors and touches are possible among the causes. But this is not observed; therefore, the body is not composed of the five elements as its material cause.

For this very reason, it could not have earth and water as its material cause; for this very reason, it could not have earth, water, and air as its material causes either. If it had earth, air, and space as its material causes, it would be devoid of color, taste, and smell. If it had earth, fire, and air as its material causes, it would be devoid of smell and taste. If it had fire, air, and space as its material causes, it would be devoid of smell, taste, and color—and so on; these points should be applied accordingly, as the case may be.

Nor does the body attain oneness despite having the five elements as its inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because difference is established through the distinction of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāvabheda*). A human body consists of earth, because it possesses odor, like earth characterized by atoms. If it is asked how the properties of water and so forth are perceived here, the answer is simply that it is due to inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).

The sense organ is the tongue, which manifests taste for all living beings; it is composed of water-particles that are not overpowered by particles of a different kind. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [56] [p. 112]
The objects, however, are rivers, oceans, hailstones, and so forth. (Nyāyakandalī, p.

113) "The sense organ that manifests taste for all living beings... Regarding this: the sense organ which manifests taste for all living beings is composed of water-particles. Nevertheless, why should only that [organ] be the manifester of taste, and not other substances consisting of water? To this he says: "by those not overwhelmed by a different species" (*vijātyanabhibhūtaiḥ*).

The meaning is as follows: by those watery atoms (*āpyāvayava*), whose capacities are unimpeded because they are not overwhelmed by heterogeneous earthly parts, a substance is produced that is distinct from other substances; therefore, this sense organ is a "color-apprehender" (*rañjaka*) due to its specific production, and not a separate substance, because such a substance does not arise in this manner. And this is postulated solely on the basis of observation (*darśana*). Regarding the existence of the gustatory sense organ (*rasanendriya*), the apprehension of taste itself is the proof, since an action must be accomplished by means of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

The state of being water (*āpyatva*) is established because, among the qualities such as color and so forth, it is specifically the manifestor of taste, like saliva and other substances in those whose mouths are parched. To define its objects, he says: "But the object... Rivers, oceans, hailstones, ice, and so forth are the objects, because they serve as the means for the experiencer's enjoyment by virtue of their being enjoyable.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [57] [p. 114]

It is fire (*tejas*) because of its connection with the nature of fire. It possesses color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, and faculty (*saṃskāra*). Their establishment is as before. Among these, its color is white and luminous; its touch is exclusively hot. *Nyāyakandalī* [57] [pp.114–115]

"Because of its connection with *tejastva* (the nature of fire), it is called fire. The explanation is as before. He shows that, like *tejastva*, the possession of the eleven qualities beginning with color (*rūpa*) is also its specific property (*vaidharmya*)—this is indicated by the words "color," etc. "Their establishment is as before" means that just as the existence of color and the other qualities in earth is established from the words of the author of the Sūtras, so too is their existence in fire; such is the meaning. And thus the Sūtra says: "Fire possesses color and touch" (VSū 2.1.3). However, the Sūtra that establishes number and the other qualities is indeed common to all [substances].

He demonstrates its specific form by stating: "white and luminous. While the color white exists in both earth and water, it is not luminous—that is, it does not illuminate itself or others—whereas the white color in fire is indeed luminous; this constitutes the point of distinction.

As for its red or tawny color that is perceived in some instances, that is produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of its substrate, because when devoid of a substrate, only whiteness is perceived everywhere—just as in the case of the circle of light from a lamp or the illumination of the sun and moon, whose touch is exclusively hot. Earth, water, and air possess touches that are neither hot nor cold, whereas the touch in fire is exclusively hot; this constitutes their difference in nature (*vaidharmya*).
[Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
115] That [fire] is also of two kinds, due to its existence as atoms (*aṇu*) and as effects (*kārya*). And the effects consist of the triad beginning with the body.
In the world of the Sun, the body is indeed not born from a womb; it is capable of experience due to the support provided by earthly particles.
As for the sense organ, the eye is that which manifests color for all living beings; it is composed of fiery particles that are not overwhelmed by other constituent parts.
*Nyāyakandalī* [58] [pp. 115–116]

Anticipating that fire (*tejas*) also possesses a twofold nature, just like earth and water, he says "that too" (*tad api*). Because it exists both as an atom (*aṇu*) and as an effect (*kārya*), fire is also of two kinds. And the effects are the triad beginning with the body; the triad consisting of the body, the sense organ, and the object is the effect of fire. The body [of fire] is exclusively non-maternal (not born from a womb), existing in the world of the sun (*ādityaloka*).

[Objection: Since fire is by nature hot, a body composed of it would be like a mass of flames; because it would be unfit for specific practical activity (*viśiṣṭavyavahāra*), it could not serve as a locus of experience (*upabhoga*). To this, he says: "And because of the support of earthy atoms" (*pārthivāvayavopaṣṭambhāt*). The intention is that, through the support—that is, the particular conjunction—of earthy atoms acting as instrumental causes, the parts of fire produce a body that is specifically fit for experience, rather than one that is merely like a mass of flames.

"The sense faculty is that which manifests color-form for all living beings. That sense faculty which manifests color-form for all living beings is composed of parts of fire (*tejas*). Why is this very faculty the manifestor of color-form, and not some other substance of fire? The proof for this is: "by those [parts] which are not overwhelmed by other [substances]."

The eye is composed of those parts of light whose capacities are unimpeded by the constituent parts of earth and water; therefore, because of this specific production, it is the sense organ that manifests color, and not any other. That it is produced in such a manner is due solely to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), for the restriction regarding the effect itself is the proof [of its cause]. Its luminous nature (*taijasatva*), however, is established because, among color and the other qualities, it invariably manifests color, like a lamp. Yet, by virtue of the unseen force, its color and touch are non-manifest (*anudbhūta*); consequently, it does not burn its own substrate, nor is it perceived.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [59–60] [p. 116]: That which is designated as "object" (viṣaya) is of four kinds: terrestrial, celestial, digestive, and mineral. Among these, terrestrial fire originates from wood-fuel, has the nature of upward flaming, and is capable of cooking, burning, sweating, and so forth. Celestial fire has no fuel; it includes solar light, lightning, and the like. Digestive fire is for the purpose of transforming the food consumed into chyle and other bodily constituents. Mineral fire includes gold and similar substances. That which is designated as "object" (*viṣaya*) is fourfold. That fire whose designation is "object" is the effect of fire; it is fourfold. He demonstrates this very fourfold nature with the words "terrestrial" (*bhauma*) and so forth. Regarding the term "therein" (*tatra*): here *tatra* has the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). "Terrestrial" means that which exists on the earth; it originates—that is, arises—from fuel consisting of wood, having the nature of wood, because that which lacks a support does not arise.

The mention of "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) is for the purpose of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), since grass, husks, and so forth are also causes. "Having the nature of upward flaming" means that upward flaming is a specific action; that which has this as its nature possesses that property. "Capable of cooking, steaming, and so forth": cooking is the production of another quality distinct from the previous qualities; steaming is the destruction of rigidity; by the word "and so forth," burning—which is characterized by the production of blisters and the like—is included; thus, the description is of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Divine light is that which has the sun as its fuel (*sauram*), while light such as lightning and the like is "without fuel" (*anindhana*). By the etymological derivation "that whose fuel is water," the term refers to solar light, lightning, and so forth—the word "and the like" (*ādi*) including meteors. The gastric fire (*audaryam*) exists within the stomach for the purpose of transforming consumed food into chyle and other constituents; it is the light produced in the abdomen whose function is the transformation of ingested food into the states of chyle, waste, and bodily tissues. And there is also that which is born from mines, such as gold and the like.

A mine (*ākara*) is a specific location; therein, fiery substances such as gold, silver, and so forth, are produced. Regarding the fact that gold and the like are fiery (*taijasa*), scripture (*āgama*) is the authority, and the reasoning (*nyāya*) has already been stated. If so, how is it that odor, taste, non-warm-and-cold touch, and weight are perceived? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*).

Due to the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of many enjoyers, gold and other substances—which possess unmanifest color and touch and are capable of forming a solid mass—are produced through the support of numerous earthy atoms. In that case, these tastes and other qualities are perceived as inherent in the earthly substance. The word "iti" marks the conclusion.

If it is argued that we do not accept that gold and the like possess unmanifest color and touch because there is no distinct substance apart from the perceived color and touch, we say no; for there is a perception of distinct configurations in each instance, such as "this is a pillar" or "this is a pot," whereas the nature of color and the rest remains the same everywhere. If it is argued that the difference in cognition for each aggregate is due to a difference in mental impressions (*vāsanā*), then let the difference in the cognition of blue and so forth also be produced by mental impressions alone, and there would be no need for a distinction in the objects themselves, such as blue and so on.

If it is argued that, in the absence of external objects, since the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—which arises depending solely upon one's own mental continuum—cannot be occasional, it is impossible for the cognition of blue and so forth, which has that [maturation] alone as its cause, to be occasional; and therefore, there must be a conceptual construction of distinctions such as "blue" and so on [based on internal factors]: [we reply that] even the distinction between the cognitions of pillars and other things would not be possible as something occasional if it did not conform to an external object. Consequently, one must postulate a distinct specific configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*), different from color-form (*rūpa*) and the like, which serves as the cause for the awakening of specific latent impressions at every moment of perception.

By means of which the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching is also established; for this [apprehension] is impossible even with respect to an entity consisting of mere color-form and so forth, because of the restriction that each of those is apprehended by a single sense-faculty.

Furthermore, since form and the other [sensory objects] consist of atoms (*paramāṇu*) that are each individually beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), and there is no "collection" (*saṃcaya*) distinct from them, what object of yours could possibly be the domain of seeing and touching? If it is argued that although the atoms are individually beyond the senses, they become perceptible (*aindriyaka*) when they arise with capacity in the presence of mental attention (*manaskāra*), the sense organs, and so forth—this is not so. For even when they arise with capacity, they do not transcend their extremely subtle nature; and if visual perception occurred merely through such a capacity for arising, then [the same would apply to] mental attention and the sense organs.

Furthermore, [the atoms] would have to be perceptible, as there is no distinction [between them and the whole]. Now, if it is thought: "Although individual atoms are not gross, when they are aggregated like a mass of hair, they become the objects of visual perception by appearing as gross; and because they are without intervals, they are determined as being one"—if this is so, then among these many [atoms], does a single gross form arise at that time? Or is it perceived as superimposed, though non-existent, as in the case of [individual] hairs? If it arises, then that is our "composite" (avayavin).

If, however, that which does not exist is perceived, then it is an illusion (*bhrānti*). And since illusion is the opposite of non-illusion, one must admit that in some cases there exists a single, gross, and real entity. Nor is its reality in consciousness logical, because the perception "I am gross" does not arise, and because it would follow that it could not be common to multiple perceivers. Therefore, this single, gross object is indeed the external referent (*viṣaya*), because it appears with a distinct form at all times and because it accomplishes causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); thus, the existence of the whole (*avayavin*) is established.

[Objection: Surely, when there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), that which is established by cognition is treated as being so; however, in the case of the existence of a whole (*avayavin*), there is indeed a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, when the hand is trembling, the body resting upon it does not tremble; or when the foot is trembling, the body situated upon it does not tremble. Thus, there would follow the absurdity (*prasaṅga*) of a single entity possessing contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmatā*). [Reply: That is incorrect, because there is no necessary rule that the body must necessarily tremble when the hand is trembling.

When there is a cause to move only the hand, then only that much moves and not the body, due to the absence of a cause [for the latter]. But when there is a cause for the movement of the body as well, then the body certainly moves.

Since there is no lack of motion in this [body], how can there be a contradiction? If the hand moves but the body does not, then would it not follow that the part and the whole possess "separate existence" (*yutasiddhi*)? Not so; for separate existence consists in having distinct substrata, not in being mobile and immobile. Even when a substance moves while a quality remains stationary, there is no separate existence between the two. Furthermore, since the part and the whole do not have distinct substrata even though they are different, they do not possess separate existence.

As for the other objection that was stated—that when one part is covered, the whole (avayavin) inherent in it would not be perceived, whereas when uncovered parts are perceived, it would be perceived, resulting in the simultaneous perception and non-perception of a single entity—that too is without substance, because there is no covering of the whole when a single part is covered.

For that [whole], existing as a single entity in many constituent parts, is perceived when some parts are covered by the perception of other uncovered parts, since it is undifferentiated throughout. However, that does not result in the cognition of "grossness" (sthūla) like the perception of many parts, because there is an absence of the perception of an accumulation of parts—which is the cause for the cognition of the excellence of dimension (parimāṇa)—in that state.

However, where there is an obstruction of most of the parts and only a very few parts are perceived, there is no perception of the whole, as in the case of seeing only the head of one submerged in water. As for the objection that if one part is colored, the whole would be colored in that region while being uncolored in other regions—thus resulting in the absurdity of a single thing being both colored and uncolored—that is not a valid refutation, because there is no contradiction. Being colored consists in conjunction with a coloring substance, and being uncolored is the absence of that;
both can indeed belong to a single entity, since conjunction exists as non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti).

Nyāyakandalī [60] [pp. 121–124]: This is another point: does the whole (avayavin) subsist in each of its parts by way of a single part, or in its entirety? For there is no other possible mode. First, it cannot subsist by way of a single part, because apart from the parts themselves, there is no "single part" belonging to it. Nor can it subsist in its entirety, for in that case, there would be no subsistence in the other parts; this is because the nature of the whole, as delimited by its connection with one part, leaves no room for the other parts, and because there is no other nature for it apart from that specific nature.

In this regard, it is further examined: does that which exists exist by way of a part or in its entirety? Is this stated as something established for oneself or as something established for another? First of all, for the Buddhists themselves, the existence of anything anywhere is unestablished; nor is existence established for another [opponent] by way of parts or in its entirety, because those two [modes] do not exist and because they are not causes for existence.

Whatever exists exists by way of its own nature through a mode of operation characterized by the relationship between the locus and that which is located therein. Nor is the connection of a single entity with multiple things contradictory; for it is observed in the case of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*)—delimited by the form of blue—that there is a connection with forms such as yellow and so forth. Nor does that cognition possess a difference for each individual form, because for you [the Yogācāras], it would follow that there could be no experience of variegation, since it is impossible for a single [cognition] to grasp multiple forms. Nor, on account of the unity of consciousness, can the forms themselves be one, for that would contradict the experience of variegation.

Just as in the case of a single whole whose nature is delimited by one part, there is the inclusion of other parts—since it is perceived as connected with multiple parts—so too, because of the cognition of a single gross object, the connection of the manifold within the one is established; and while this is merely a difference in formulation (that "the manifold is connected in one" versus "one is connected in many"), there is no distinction between the two cases regarding the delimitation of the manifold's connection within the one.

And thus, the two following undesirable consequences (*prasaṅga*) have been refuted: first, that whatever is one must reside in only one place, just as a single color or a single composite whole (*avayavin*); and second, that whatever resides in many places must be manifold, just as palm fruits contained in many vessels—and yet the composite whole resides in many [parts]. This is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished both from our own perspective and from the opponent’s. From our own perspective, a single cognition resides in multiple objects, sense-faculties, and mental attentions by way of its arising with an undifferentiated nature; and for the opponent as well, a single [composite]...

A thread exists in many jewels by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) without distinction; likewise, it will exist in parts (*avayava*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), and yet there will be no such thing as a "whole" (*avayavin*). Furthermore, every reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) that destroys its substratum (*āśraya*) also destroys itself. For if the whole were non-existent and the world consisted of mere atoms, the cognition of properties, subjects, examples, and so forth would be unestablished, because there can be no occurrence (*vṛtti*) for that which lacks a substratum.

Therefore, the whole (*avayavin*), which is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), cannot be refuted by this [inference], because that [inference], being dependent upon direct perception, is weaker than it. If it is argued that "direct perception is erroneous," from what does this follow? If it is argued that "it is because its object is discarded by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*)," then there is mutual dependence: direct perception would be erroneous if the subverting cognition were valid, and the subverting cognition would be valid if direct perception were erroneous. However, this logic does not apply to direct perception, because it is independent.

Nor is it logical to claim that what is established for all the world through correspondence with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) and possesses a clear manifestation is erroneous; for if that were so, it would follow that even the direct perception of blue and other such objects would be erroneous. This is the rebuttal of the subverting argument (*bādhaka*). Furthermore, atoms, although they are to be inferred from the existence of composite wholes (*avayavin*), must nonetheless be treated as real entities in conventional discourse.

If it is argued that the simultaneous conjunction of six [atoms] with a single atom results in that one atom having six parts, thereby subverting the existence of the atom—what is this so-called "simultaneous conjunction"? Does it mean the simultaneous production of a single atom together with six other atoms, or simultaneous conjunction? As for simultaneous production, if it were dependent on the simultaneity of causes, what contradiction would there be even if it occurred in a partless [atom]? Furthermore, simultaneous conjunction is not untenable either; for indeed...

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) has parts as its locus in the case of substances, because it exists even in space (*ākāśa*), which is partless; furthermore, if conjunction were to reside only in atoms (*paramāṇu*)—even if those parts themselves possessed further parts—the consequence would be that such conjunction would be imperceptible. Rather, conjunction has the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as its locus. If this is so, then just as in the case of a substance with parts, it is indeed possible for a single partless atom to serve as the locus of multiple conjunctions simultaneously when the conditions for causality are present; thus, there is no rejection of that [possibility]. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [61] [pp. 124–126]

Air is that which is connected with the nature of air (*vāyutva*). It possesses touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and impression (*saṃskāra*). Its touch is established as being neither hot nor cold and not produced by heat (*apākaja*), because it is included among the qualities [in the *Guṇasūtra*]. Number and the other [qualities] up to distinctness are established because it is stated [in the *Guṇasūtra*] that it is formless and invisible. Impression is established because the action of grass [being moved by it] is mentioned.

And this [earth] is of two kinds, due to its existence as both atoms and effects. Among these, that characterized as an effect is fourfold: the body, the sense organ, the object, and the vital breath.
In the world of the Maruts, the body is indeed born from a womb (*yoni*), and it is capable of experience due to the support provided by the constituent parts of earth (*pārthivāvayava*).

The sense organ is that which perceives touch for all living beings; it is the tactile sense (*tvagindriya*) which pervades the entire body and is composed of particles of air (*vāyvavayava*) that are not overwhelmed by earth and the other elements.
*Nyāyakandalī* [61] [pp. 124–127]

Having explained the three [substances] beginning with earth—which are perceptible—and having reached the occasion for explaining substances that are imperceptible, [the author] explains air (*vāyu*), since it is the contextually relevant matter to define a substance that possesses both eternal and non-eternal natures: "Air is so called because of its connection with the property of air-ness (*vāyutva*). The explanation is as before. He states its qualities, beginning with "touch" (*sparśa*), etc.; here too, the explanation is as before.

He demonstrates what kind of touch exists in air with the word "touch. The touch of earth is produced by heating (*pākaja*) in its atoms, and is likewise [produced by heating] in its own effects; the touch of this air, however, is not produced by heating, and for this reason it is dissimilar. Its state of not being produced by heating is due to its not having earth as its substratum, like the touches of water and fire. By specifying that it is "neither hot nor cold," its dissimilarity to the touches of water and fire is stated.

And he states that this [air] is established as existing in air by the sūtra from the second chapter, "Air possesses touch" (VaiSū 2.1.4), saying: "Because of the assignment of qualities. Regarding the statement "in those without form, they are not visible," the seven [qualities] beginning with number are [meant]; because it is declared that in substances devoid of color, the [qualities] beginning with number are not perceptible to the eye, the existence of number and the others in formless things is thereby stated; otherwise, the declaration of their imperceptibility when residing in such [substances] would be incoherent.

"Because of the mention of action in grass, there is *saṃskāra*. From the statement, "Action in grass [arises] from conjunction with air" (VaiSū 5.1.14), *saṃskāra* is shown to exist in air, because it is not observed that the conjunction of a substance devoid of velocity (*vega*) can be a cause of action. To define its specific divisions, he says: "And this... Here, "and this" (*sa ca ayam*) refers to that which was brought to mind by memory and present in the intellect; subsequently, it is referred to as "this" (*ayam*) as if it were perceived through direct perception.

The meaning is that not only are the earth-based [elements] of two kinds, but this one is also of two kinds. The meaning of "having the nature of an effect" (*kāryasvabhāva*) is that it is characterized as an effect and is fourfold. To the question "In what way is it fourfold?", he says: "body, sense organ, object, and vital breath. Among these, he specifies the body by its genus:

Regarding the term "body" (*śarīra*) therein: it is specifically non-uterine (*ayonija*), meaning that while it is not uterine like an earthly body, it is nonetheless non-uterine. The phrase "in the world of the Maruts" is a mention of its location. Through the support—that is, the specific conjunction—of a great number of earthly atoms acting as instrumental causes, it arises as stable and compact in nature, capable of experience just like an earthly body.

"The sense-faculty is that which perceives touch for all living beings. The meaning is this: that sense-faculty which perceives touch for all living beings is composed of wind-particles whose capacities are unimpeded and not overcome by earth and the other elements; therefore, due to its specific production, it constitutes a sense-faculty. As for its existence, the very perception of touch is the proof.

Its nature as air is established because, among the qualities such as color and the rest, it manifests touch alone, like the breeze that manifests the coldness of water clinging to the body. Furthermore, it pervades the entire body, because its effect—the perception of touch—is present everywhere.

If it is argued that the designation "skin-faculty" (*tvagindriya*) refers to the faculty located in the skin—so called because of the metaphorical attribution of the whole to its parts—and that the skin pervades the bases of all faculties such that perception of color-form and so forth occurs when the skin is present and does not occur when it is absent; therefore, the skin-faculty serves all objects and is not merely a grasper of touch—this is incorrect. For it would entail the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and others. If one were to admit a differentiation of its powers according to the differences of those respective bases, then this would amount to admitting a differentiation of the faculties by another means altogether.

Praśastapādabhāṣya [62]: Air, however, is that which is the substrate of the perceived touch; it is characterized by touch, sound, support, and motion; its nature is horizontal movement; and it possesses the capacity for the production and maintenance of clouds and the like. Nyāyakandalī [62] [pp. 127–130]: Regarding air (*vāyu*), its existence is established through inference based on its effects. It is the substratum of the touch that is being perceived. Its specific qualities—touch, sound, support, and motion—serve as its marks. Its inherent nature is horizontal movement (*tiryyaggamana*). Furthermore, it is capable of producing and sustaining phenomena such as clouds, lightning, and rain. Thus, air is an entity distinct from earth, water, and fire, possessing the aforementioned characteristics.
In order to define the determination and regulation of the object, he says: "But the object" means that which is the locus and support of the perceived touch; that is the object.

"What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence? Some say it is perception itself, because through the operation of the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*), there arises an immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*) that 'the wind blows. This is not so; for no other entity distinct from touch is perceived. In immediate cognition, only touch manifests, and nothing else. Even the cognition that 'the wind blows' is an inference based on touch, independent of the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth due to the excellence of proficiency gained through practice—just as the action residing in a tree and such is apprehended by the eye."

Even the recognition of wind, which transcends the distinctions of cold and hot touch, occurs only through the inference of a substance that serves as its substratum. For there is no manifestation of anything other than cold and hot touch by means of the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*). The inference that "wind is perceptible to the sense of touch because it is the locus of a perceived touch, like a jar" is as unestablished by perception as the inference of horns from the fact that animals such as rabbits possess the nature of being quadrupeds.

The tactile nature of a substance is understood to be pervaded by its visibility, as seen in the case of jars and other such objects; since visibility is absent in air, the absence of tactile nature can be inferred therefrom. Therefore, he sets forth an inference for the existence of that [air], which is not perceived by the senses, stating: "It has touch, sound, support, and motion as its marks. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning: that of which touch, sound, support, and motion are the marks (*liṅga*).

This tactile sensation (*sparśa*) which is perceived as being devoid of color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest must reside in something, because it is a tactile sensation, like any other tactile sensation. Nor can earth alone be its substrate, because of its dissociation from color-form. If it is argued that "there is also unmanifest color-form present here," we say no; for the tactile sensation of earth that is being perceived is observed to be invariably concomitant only with color-form that is itself being perceived. Since no such perception of color-form exists here, this tactile sensation is not of earth.

Nor is this [touch] dependent on water or fire, because it is neither hot nor cold, like the touch of a jar or similar objects. Nor does it reside in the formless entities—space, time, direction, and the self—since touch is observed to be invariably concomitant with corporeal matter (*mūrta*). Furthermore, if the internal organs (*manas*) possessed touch, they would, like atoms, initiate substances of their own kind; but this is not the case. Therefore, touch does not belong to them either. Consequently, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), that upon which this [touch] depends is air (*vāyu*).

Likewise, sound is also its mark. This "shuk-shuka" sound that is heard suddenly among leaves and such—the first of these sounds is produced by conjunction with a substance possessing touch, because it is an initial sound occurring in a substance whose parts are not being divided, like the sound of a drum struck by a staff; and that which possesses touch is air (*vāyu*). For ether (*ākāśa*) and the rest lack touch, and if earth, water, and fire—which possess color—were the cause of that sound, they would necessarily be perceptible.

The phrase "while being related to a substance whose parts are not being divided" is stated in order to exclude sound produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-śabda*). Likewise, the support or maintenance (*dhṛti*) of leaves and other objects in the atmosphere is the effect of conjunction with a tangible substance; for, in the absence of causes such as effort or velocity, it is a case of support, just like the support of leaves and other objects situated upon water. And that tangible substance is none of the triad beginning with earth, precisely because it is imperceptible; thus, there is the establishment of another substance. The phrase "in the absence of causes such as effort" is intended to exclude the maintenance of arrows and birds.

Likewise, the specific trembling of trees and such things is produced by conjunction with a substance possessing touch, because it is a specific kind of trembling, like the trembling of cane-reeds and forests caused by a river flood. If it is argued that there is an inconclusive deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to earthquakes, we say no; for that is known to have a different cause. However, in the case of trembling produced by conjunction with a substance possessing touch, the fact of being a specific kind of trembling itself is the proof; thus, there is no inconclusiveness.

But surely, that very substance which is inferred by touch is also inferred by sound and the other [qualities]; it is not the case that a different substance is inferred for each respective mark. What is the proof here for saying that "air has touch, sound, support, and trembling as its marks"? This is the proof: since sound and the others can be accounted for simply as effects of the substance already inferred through touch, the postulation of a separate substance would be redundant.

Wind being thus established, its properties are shown: "its intrinsic nature is horizontal movement" (*tiryyaggamanasvabhāva*). This means that horizontal movement is its inherent nature. It is capable of impelling clouds and the like, leading them here and there; of supporting, which is the counteracting of gravity; and, by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), of friction. By the phrase "clouds and the like," vessels for travel and so forth are included, since these too are impelled by wind.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [63] [p.131]

Although that [air] is not perceptible, its plurality is inferred from its coalescence (*sammūrcchana*). Coalescence, moreover, is the collision of two air-currents of equal velocity moving in opposite directions; that too is inferred from the upward movement of the two composite air-masses, and that again from the movement of grass and other objects.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [63] [pp. 131–132]

When doubt arises regarding the perception of unity or plurality in respect to space, the self, and so forth—which are themselves objects of inference—he says, "even though that [space] is imperceptible," in order to dispel that doubt. Furthermore, since even "intermingling" (*sammūrcchana*) is not understood, he states its meaning as "intermingling."

The conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of two things possessing equal velocity when their actions are directed toward opposite directions is a specific type of contact (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*) that causes a mutual obstruction of their motions; this is called "collision" (*sammūrcchana*). By means of this, the manifold nature of air (*vāyu*) is inferred, because such a collision is impossible for a single substance. Just as there is no collision between two things set out in the same direction and moving according to their respective courses, [it is said] "of those whose actions are in opposite directions"—meaning those whose actions are in different directions.

Conjunction does not occur between two things of unequal velocity, because one would overcome the other; therefore, it is said that they must have "equal speed. Just as their distinctness is imperceptible when they are imperceptible, so too is their conjunction; thus, he says "that also" (so 'pi) to indicate that it exists. Conjunction also [exists]. It is inferred from the upward movement of two portions of air possessing parts, since the upward movement of air is preceded by mutual obstruction when no other cause is possible, because it is the upward movement of a substance whose nature is horizontal motion, like the upward movement of water waves struck against each other.

Although one should have said "of two wholes" (*avayavinoh*), it is stated as "of two things possessing parts" (*sāvayavinoh*) [p.132] because there is a desire to include even parts as wholes for the sake of encompassing gross air; for an atom-sized dimension lacks the capacity to impel grass and such. Furthermore, their upward movement is imperceptible; therefore, he states an inference for its cognition: "it is inferred by the movement of grass and so forth. Praśastapādabhāṣya [64] [p.132]:

Vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a single entity within the body that is the cause of the impelling and other functions of the fluids, wastes, and constituent elements (*dhātu*); being one, it receives the designations of *apāna* and so on due to the difference in its activities.
In the *Nyāyakandalī* [64] [pp.

132–133], he states the essential nature of that which is known as *prāṇa*, distinguished from the *viṣayavāyu* (the air of the sense-objects) both in common worldly usage and in the Yoga scriptures: "The *prāṇa* is within the body. That wind which exists within the body is called *prāṇa*. He describes its functional activity (*arthakriyā*) as follows: "It is the cause of the impelling and so forth of the *rasa*, *mala*, and *dhātu*s. By *rasa* is meant the specific substance produced from food and drink through the process of digestion. By *mala* is meant the designation for urine and feces.

The elements (*dhātavaḥ*) are skin, flesh, bone, blood, and so forth; it is the cause of their impelling—that is, their being led here and there—and, by the force of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), their arranging as well. Since there is a doubt as to whether that [wind] is one or many, he says: "being one. But surely five winds are heard of in the body? To this he replies: "due to the difference in activity."

It is called *apāna* because it leads urine and feces downward; *vyāna* because it extends the essence (*rasa*) throughout the channels of the fetus; *udāna* because it leads food, drink, and so forth upward; *prāṇa* because it exits through the mouth and nose; and *samāna* because it moves equally everywhere within the stomach for the sake of digesting food by means of the gastric fire. However, this fivefold division is not real, but merely conceptualized. Why? Because there can be no coexistence of material entities within a single substratum. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [65], pp. 134–136.

Now, the procedure for the creation and dissolution of the four great elements is described here: at the end of a hundred years according to the measurement of Brahmā, at the time of the final liberation of Brahmā, when the unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in all individual selves—which bind together the body, the sense organs, and the great elements—cease their activity simultaneously with Maheśvara’s desire to withdraw the entire world-system, so that all living beings exhausted by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) may find rest during the night.

From actions born of the conjunction of atoms with the soul, which is itself the will of Maheśvara, there arise disjunctions among the atoms that are the causes of bodies and sense organs; upon the cessation of those conjunctions, their destruction occurs down to the level of the individual atoms. In the same manner, among the great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—the preceding element is destroyed when each subsequent one comes into being. Thereafter, the atoms remain separated, and the selves (ātman), permeated by merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), and mental impressions (saṃskāra), likewise remain for that same duration of time.
Having explained in detail the four substances that undergo origination,
an effort is now made for the purpose of examining their agent.

The origin and destruction of the four elements, beginning with earth, are to be examined. Since an examination of each of these individually would result in excessive prolixity of the text, this chapter is commenced to examine them all together under a common principle—beginning with the words "of the four. The method (*vidhi*) or manner of their creation and dissolution—that is, their origin and destruction—is now described.

Although the creation and dissolution of all four [elements] are mentioned in one place, this is nevertheless not a statement of their common characteristics (*sādharmya*), because they are described as being distinct in each case. When it is said "of the great elements" (*mahābhūtānām*), there would be the inclusion of only three, since the number "many" (*bahutva*)—as in the injunction "one should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds"—is satisfied by that many alone; therefore, it is stated "of the four."

When "of four" is stated, the very set of four just mentioned—the body, the sense organ, the object, and the vital breath (prāṇa)—which are the effects of air, would enter the mind; to exclude that, [the author] says "of the great elements" (mahābhūtānām). [Objection: But in that case, the production and destruction of dyads (dvyaṇuka) would not be asserted, because they are atomic (aṇu). [Reply: Not so, because of the employment of the word "rule" (vidhi). It was stated that the manner in which the production and destruction of the great elements occurs is the manner that is being described.

And their production proceeds by way of the sequence beginning with dyads and ending with atoms, while their destruction likewise ends with the atoms. Therefore, the creation and dissolution of dyads as well would be implied, since the intention was merely to explain the meaning.

Although the dissolution was mentioned later, he explains it first, saying "by the Brahma-measure. Fifteen *nimeṣas* of ours constitute a *kāṣṭhā*. Thirty *kāṣṭhās* make a *kalā*. Fifteen *kalās* make a *nāḍikā*. Thirty *kalās* make a *muhūrta*. Thirty *muhūrtas* make a day and night (*ahorātra*). Fifteen days and nights make a fortnight (*pakṣa*). Two fortnights make a month (*māsa*). Two months make a season (*ṛtu*). Six seasons, or twelve months, make a year (*saṃvatsara*).

Three seasons constitute the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), and three seasons constitute the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). The northern course is a day for the gods, and the southern course is a night for the gods. Three hundred and sixty such days and nights constitute a year. Twelve thousand years constitute a cycle of four ages (caturyuga). One thousand cycles of four ages constitute a single day of Brahmā.

By this measure, at the end of a hundred years, at the conclusion of the current Brahmā’s term, at the time of liberation, for the sake of rest—that is, for the cessation of suffering—for a short time, for the sake of the living beings who are exhausted by repeatedly assuming bodies and so forth in various places within *saṃsāra* and afflicted by the manifold sufferings such as those in the womb; there arises the desire to withdraw (*sañjihīrṣā*), the will to dissolve the universe, of Maheśvara, the Lord of all worlds, whose power is unimpeded everywhere.

Simultaneously with that, or immediately following it, there occurs the cessation of the activity—the obstruction of the power—of all *adṛṣṭas* residing in every self (*ātman*) and inherent in all selves, which are the causes for the binding together of the body, the sense organs, and the great elements, and which initiate the body, the sense organs, and the great elements. When that [cessation] exists, there is the non-arising of future bodies, sense organs, and great elements; and for the sake of the destruction of those already arisen, actions are produced from the conjunctions of the Great Lord’s will, the selves, and the atoms.

The dissolution [occurs] at the moment of Maheśvara’s desire to withdraw [the world]. The term "atom" (*aṇu*) refers to the inclusion of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). The analysis of the compound is: "Maheśvara’s desire and the conjunctions of the self with the atoms. From these—namely, those produced from Maheśvara’s desire, the self, and the conjunctions with the atoms—arise actions produced by Maheśvara’s desire, the self, and the conjunctions with the atoms. From those actions, disjunctions occur among the atoms which are the successive causes of bodies and sense organs. From these disjunctions follows the cessation of the conjunctions of those atoms.

When conjunction ceases, there is the destruction of those [composite bodies] down to the level of the atoms. The destruction of those bodies and sense organs occurs through the process of the destruction of dyads and so forth, continuing until the atom.

Regarding what has been said by some—that this [Creator] would be merciless and act arbitrarily by destroying living beings out of season—the rebuttal to that is: "[He does so] for the sake of the rest of living beings during the night. Furthermore, as for what was stated: "While the infinite unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) of infinite selves are ripening in succession, some cease from experiencing them due to the exhaustion of their unseen forces, while others continue to be experienced."

"But others, being oriented toward enjoyment," and so on—in this way, it is not possible for there to be a simultaneous absence of the body and other factors during every engagement with objects; thus, by this [argument], the claim that "there is an obstruction of function due to unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*)" is refuted. It was stated that at the time of Brahmā’s liberation, "it is night"; this is said metaphorically, based on the commonality between the cessation of awakening for all living beings and the state of night. He says "likewise" regarding the destruction of the great elements as well.

Just as the dissolution of the body and the sense organs occurs down to the level of the atoms (*paramāṇu*), so too does the dissolution of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) follow this same sequence. That is to say, through the sequence of atomic activity, disjunction, and so forth, when each subsequent element is present, each preceding one is destroyed. The meaning is that while water remains, earth is first destroyed; while fire remains, water is destroyed; and while air remains, fire is destroyed.

Thereupon, the atoms remain separated, permeated and sustained by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) known as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and they persist for that same duration—the lifespan of Brahmā. The directions (*diś*) and so forth also persist because they are eternal. However, due to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of the selves (*ātman*), the atoms will not begin [creation] again. Because of its predominance, the persistence of the selves and the atoms is mentioned here specifically due to the influence of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [65–a] [pp. 137–139]

Then again, for the sake of the enjoyment of living beings, immediately following Maheśvara’s desire to create, and depending upon the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) residing within all souls which has acquired its functional capacity, motion arises in the atoms of air due to their conjunctions with those [souls]. From the mutual conjunctions of these atoms, through the process beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka), a great wind is produced, which remains vibrating in the sky.

Immediately thereafter, from those very atoms of air, by that same process, a great ocean of water arises and remains floating about. Immediately thereafter, within that very ocean, from the atoms of earth, the great earth arises and remains in a solid mass.

Immediately thereafter, within that very great ocean, from the atoms of fire, a great mass of fire arises through the process beginning with dyads and so forth, and it remains blazing brightly because it is not overcome by anything else.

When the four great elements have thus arisen, Maheśvara, by mere volition (*abhidhyāna*), initiates the formation of a vast cosmic egg (*maheṇḍa*) from fiery atoms conjoined with earthly atoms. Having produced within that egg Brahmā—the Grandfather of all worlds, whose lotus-face consists of four faces—along with the entire universe, he appoints him to the task of creating living beings.

Having thus established the process of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*), he speaks while establishing the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*): "Then again... Although at that time there is no connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for the selves (*ātman*), they are nevertheless called "living beings" (*prāṇin*) due to their inherent fitness [for such a state]. For the sake of their experience—that is, for the arising of the perception of pleasure and pain—the Great Lord’s desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*), the will to emanate, arises. Immediately thereafter, the unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in all the selves obtain their respective functions.

Although the single will of the Lord—which, like space and other eternal entities, consists of the power of action and is engaged in the simultaneous production of innumerable effects—is indeed one, nevertheless, upon obtaining the assistance of specific times, it sometimes serves the purpose of dissolution and sometimes serves the purpose of creation. When it serves the purpose of dissolution, then, in accordance with that, the cessation of the activity of unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*), characterized by indifference, arises.

But when that [unseen force] becomes intent upon creation, then there is the "attainment of function," which is the activity directed toward the production of its own effects. Those by whom the function has been attained are called "function-attainers" (*vṛttilabdhāḥ*). The prior placement of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) follows the rule for the *āhitāgni* group, as in the example "one whose teeth have grown" (*dantajātaḥ*). Then, those conjunctions of the self and the atoms—which depend upon all the functions residing in the selves, those functions that have been attained, and the unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*)—give rise to actions in the atoms of air. From these [conjunctions], motions are produced in the atoms of wind.

The atoms of air (*pavanaparamāṇu*) are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). The conjunction of the atoms with the self (*ātman*) which possesses unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭavat*) and has attained its functional state is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Unseen merit or demerit is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Thus, upon the production of action, mutual conjunctions arise among those atoms of air; and from those conjunctions, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) are produced.

Thereafter, by this sequence beginning with "the triads," the great wind arises; shaking in the sky—that is, in space—it remains possessed of an extraordinary velocity because it encounters no obstruction anywhere. Immediately after that, within that very wind, from the aqueous atoms and by that same sequence starting with dyads, the great ocean is produced; floating—that is, remaining buoyant everywhere due to the absence of any obstructing agent—it remains.

Immediately after that, following the emergence from the ocean, the great earth arises from those very atoms of earth (*pārthiva-paramāṇu*) within that same ocean; it exists as a solid mass with a stable nature. Immediately after that, within that same great ocean, a vast mass of fire arises from fiery atoms (*taijasa-aṇu*) through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*); it remains blazing because it is not overcome by anything else.
Although there is a natural opposition between water and fire, nevertheless, their relationship as container and contained is not untenable due to the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

Thus, when the great elements have arisen through the process just described, by the mere volition and mere intention of Maheśvara, a great egg—a vast cosmic form—is commenced from fiery atoms conjoined with earthly atoms. In the commencement of this cosmic form, the earthly components serve as a supporting basis; therefore, it did not become a mere mass of fire.

Having brought forth from that egg Brahmā, whose lotus-face is fourfold, the grandfather of all worlds and the primordial person of all worlds, together with all the realms of existence, he appoints him to the creation and generation of living beings, saying: "You must do this."

And he, commissioned by Maheśvara, is endowed with supreme knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty—namely, knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty (*jñāna-vairāgyaiśvaryāṇi*). Being enriched and perfected by these supreme forms of knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty, he perceives the merit and demerit of living beings exactly as they are through his superior knowledge. Due to his detachment, he does not act with partiality; due to his sovereignty, he causes them to experience the fruits of their actions. Thus, it is said: "having understood the ripening of the karma of living beings."

"Vipāka" means ripening in various ways; "karmavipāka" is the ripening of actions. Having known—that is, having understood that such will be the fruit of this action—he created the Prajāpatis, Dakṣa and others, who were his mental sons (*mānasa*), produced solely by the resolve of his mind: namely, the Manus, the gods, the sages (*ṛṣis*), and the hosts of ancestors (*pitṛgaṇas*). These sons possessed knowledge, enjoyments, and lifespans corresponding to their respective actions.

Having created the four castes from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—namely, Brāhmaṇas from his mouth, Kṣatriyas from his two arms, Vaiśyas from his thighs, and Śūdras from his feet—and having created other beings, high and low, minute and more minute, he endows them with qualities corresponding to their latent dispositions (*āśaya*). "Latent disposition" (*āśaya*) refers to action (*karman*), for it lies within the self until the time of the enjoyment of its fruit; he joins them with virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and power according to those [dispositions], such that each being receives knowledge and the rest in accordance with the specific nature of its own action.
It joins correctly; the meaning is that it does not act otherwise, even by way of measure.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [66–69] [pp. 139–140]

And he, commissioned by Maheśvara, endowed with supreme knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty regarding Brahman, having understood the ripening of the karma of living beings, created the Prajāpatis—his mind-born sons—who possess knowledge, experience, and lifespan according to their respective karma; and having created the four castes from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, as well as other high and low beings, he endows them with dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty that correspond to their latent dispositions (*āśaya*).
— *Nyāyakandalī* [66] [pp. 140–141]

Now, as for what some have asserted—that the activity of a discerning being must be for the sake of attaining a desired object or avoiding an undesired one, and that since neither the attainment of the desired nor the avoidance of the undesired is possible in the case of Īśvara, who has all his desires fulfilled, his engagement in the creation of the world is therefore untenable—the answer to that is: "for the sake of the enjoyment and prosperity of living beings. The intention is that his engagement in the desire to create is for the sake of others, and is not based on any need of his own.

Now, if this is so, one might object: "Why does he not create a creation consisting solely of happiness rather than one variegated with suffering, since he is impelled by compassion? To this, the following is the resolution: "Having understood the ripening of the karma of living beings. Although he acts for the sake of others, he does not create a world consisting solely of happiness, because his role as a creator is assisted by the diverse momentum of karma; this is the meaning. Nor does this entail a contradiction with compassion, because even the production of suffering serves as a cause for the supreme human goal by way of generating detachment.

If [it is argued that] He acts in dependence upon merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and thus lacks independent agency, which constitutes the fault of non-sovereignty (*anīśvaratā*), this too is answered as follows: He unites [beings] with virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty in accordance with their dispositions (*āśaya*). For how could He not be sovereign while bestowing fruits upon all living beings in accordance with their karma? Indeed, a master who grants specific rewards to his servants in accordance with their fitness does not thereby cease to be a master.

This is the seed of the rebuttal to the objection that, since it is impossible to establish linguistic conventions for living beings produced at the beginning of a kalpa who are unacquainted with all words and their referents, verbal communication would be untenable: "They are mental [bodies]. For one born from a womb, whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been obliterated by the great succession of sufferings such as dwelling in the womb, does not remember anything experienced in a previous birth.

The ṛṣis, the Prajāpatis, and the Manus, however—possessing unimpaired mental impressions through a connection with unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) associated with bodies not born from a womb—reconnect, like one waking from sleep, to the entire linguistic usage of words and their meanings experienced in another *kalpa*. And as they reconnect, they communicate with one another and engage in linguistic usage.

From their usage, the understanding of the living beings existing at that time arises; and from their usage, that of others arises. Thus, the meaning is that the understanding of the relationship between words and their meanings is established through a continuous succession of linguistic usage.

*Nyāyakandalī* [67] [pp. 141–147]: What, then, is the proof for the existence of God? It is both scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*). The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are preceded by one who possesses cognition; whatever is an effect is preceded by one who possesses cognition, just as a jar is. And the four great elements are effects; therefore, they too are preceded by one who possesses cognition.

If it is argued that the status of earth and other elements as effects is unestablished because their prior limit (beginning) is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it has already been stated: "Because they possess parts; for whatever possesses parts is an effect, just like a jar; and since earth and the rest possess parts, therefore these too are indeed effects. [Objection: But the operation of inference proceeds from the apprehension of a pervasion (*vyāpti*). And the apprehension of a pervasion between the state of being an effect and having a conscious agent as its cause is impossible, because at the very time one perceives an agent in the case of jars and the like, one perceives the absence of such an agent in sprouts and the like which are currently arising.

Nor is it logical that even the state of being a sprout (*aṅkuratva*) and so forth should constitute the subject (*pakṣa*). For the distinction between the subject and other members of the syllogism occurs in relation to the opponent at the time the inference proceeds once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped. In this case, however, because it is always overwhelmed by the perception of a counter-example, it has already been stated that the very apprehension of pervasion cannot be established.

To this, we reply: although there is a perception of being an effect preceded by an agent in the case of pots and the like, but not in the case of sprouts and the like—thus, despite the observation of such a duality—it is possible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and consequently, the inference that the earth and other elements are effects preceded by an intelligent being proceeds. Furthermore, if the absence of the grasp of pervasion were to follow from the non-observation of such a duality, then even the inference of the sun’s motion based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), which is favored by the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*, would not be established; for in that case as well, [the same logic would apply].

For at the very time one perceives Devadatta’s arrival at another location preceded by motion, one observes in the case of the stars and so forth merely the arrival at another location without [the perception of] motion. Now, even though it is possible that motion is not perceived in those cases due to the great distance of the locations, this does not obstruct the frequent observation (*bhūyodarśana*)—which functions without any limiting conditions—as the cause for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), because there is no equality of status between the two.

If this is so, then here too, since it is possible for an agent who is accepted as being bodiless to be perceived in sprouts and the like even through a spatial remoteness of his essential nature, the capacity of repeated observation—which functions without external conditions—is not impaired by that; thus, the case is the same.

Moreover, sir! Is it merely an agent that is being proved by inference, or one capable of constructing the earth and so forth? If it is merely an agent that is being proved, then there is no proof of what you intend; for an agent similar to ourselves is not what you intend, nor can this effect—the earth and so forth—be constructed by such a limited-sighted agent. However, an agent capable of constructing the earth and so forth is not established, because of the lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For it is by the force of positive concomitance that an agent similar to those observed in the example is established.

This is not a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*), because no specific quality of the agent has been established. When the general property of being preceded by an intelligent being is proven through the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the specific quality characterized by the capacity to construct the earth and so forth is indeed established as well; for a generality cannot be established without its particulars. If it is argued that the generality should not be established, we say no, because that pervasion with the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) cannot be denied.

For if even that which is pervaded were not established, then fire in its general form would not be established from smoke either, because a specific fire is unestablished as it lacks concomitance, and because a universal cannot exist without particulars.

Now this is said: the nature of inference consists of two factors—pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Among these, the universal is established through the power of pervasion, while the intended particular—the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire delimited by the mountain and so forth—is established by the force of its presence in the subject. Otherwise, what would be the use of its presence in the subject, and where would the validity of inference—which grasps what has already been grasped—lie? If this is the case, it is the same for the inference of God as well; the difference lies merely in one's dogmatic attachment.

Now, it might be thought: a particular (viśeṣa) is indeed established in inference where there is no contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, what inconsistency could there be in establishing a particular fire located on a mountain slope from smoke? Indeed, differences of place, time, and so forth are observed among individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, in the case of the inference for God (*īśvara*), a particular is not established, because it contradicts valid cognition.

For instance—it is not the fact of being preceded by a body that is to be proven here; because when a body exists, it is impossible for there to be agency if there is no possibility of fully knowing the capacities of the sense organs, as well as the imperceptible materials, instruments, and so forth required [for action].

Furthermore, the claim that [the world] is not preceded by a body is impossible to prove; for every agent first ascertains the nature of the instrument, then desires, "I shall accomplish this by means of this," then exerts effort, then sets the body into motion, then presides over the instruments, and finally acts. Since one who does not ascertain, does not exert effort, does not set the body into motion, and does not preside over the instruments does not act, it is established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the body, like the intellect, is a cause in the production of an effect.

It is the means [to liberation]. Since it has been ascertained by the very same valid cognition that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*) upon the abandonment of all adventitious attributes (*upādhi*), it cannot be abandoned—just as the capacity of fire to transform fuel cannot be abandoned when inferring smoke. And if that were abandoned, one would have to abandon intelligence (*buddhi*) as well; for by virtue of his preeminent power, this Lord will act even while being devoid of intelligence, like a physical body.

If it is argued that one who is ignorant of the nature of the material cause, the instruments, and so forth, is unable [to produce an effect], from what [source] is this known? If you say "because such a thing is not observed," then my own wish-fulfilling tree has borne fruit; for the intellect is not as useful in the production of an effect when it is mediated by desire and effort as this body is, whose operation is immediate.

If that is so, what is the status of the general property of "having an intelligent creator" in this case? It has no status at all, because neither of the two specific instances—possessing a body nor being bodiless—is tenable; furthermore, a universal devoid of particulars cannot be established anywhere.

What is the refutation of the inference? None whatsoever. Rather, it is the person himself who is defeated for employing a proof against a universal that, due to the absence of particulars, is like a hare's horn and thus unfit to be proven—just as someone might wield a sharpened sword against the uncuttable sky.

Now, if you are not satisfied without a refutation of inference, then this inference regarding the absence of a prior embodied creator (*aśarīripūrvakatva*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
