Furthermore, by the force of the pervasion, it contradicts the intended qualification of being "bodiless," and thus it is a "contradiction of a specific qualification" (*viśeṣaviruddha*); moreover, that is simply a sub-variety of the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) fallacy. This is the summary of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). *Nyāyakandalī* [68] [pp. 147–149]

To this, the rebuttal is as follows: Is agency (*kartṛtva*) merely the state of possessing a body, or is it the instigation of causal factors whose capacities are observed? Agency is not merely the state of possessing a body, because that would entail the status of being an agent for one who is in deep sleep or who is indifferent; rather, it is the instigation of causal factors whose capacities are observed, since the production of an effect occurs only when that [instigation] exists. And this [agency] is possible even for one who is bodiless, just as in the case of the self’s instigation of its own body.

If it is argued that even in that case, he possesses that very same body acquired through his own karma? True, it exists; however, it cannot serve as a means of impulsion, because action within oneself is a contradiction. If it is argued that there exists something to be impelled? Even for Īśvara, there exists an atom to be impelled.

If it is argued that, since an impulse arises within one's own body from desire and effort, and since desire and effort exist when the body exists and are absent when it does not, the body serves as the means for its own impulse by way of generating desire and effort—this is not so. For the body is a cause only with respect to the production of desire and effort; however, at the time of performing the impulse once desire and effort have already attained their own nature, the body is certainly not a means, as it is merely the object (*karman*) of that action. Thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Since it is observed that a conscious being— whose bodily activity is not required and who is aided by nothing more than desire and effort— is at times capable of producing the activity of an unconscious entity, and since the property of being an effect is never found apart from an intelligent agent, the existence of God is established.

If it is argued that even for the production of desire (*icchā*) and effort (*prayatna*), the body must be depended upon, [we reply]: let it be depended upon where these two are adventitious; however, where these two reside as inherent (*svābhāvika*), dependence on it is useless. Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the eternality of intellect (*buddhi*), desire, and effort. For we observe a twofold state among qualities (*guṇa*) such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth—namely, eternality and non-eternality—depending on the difference of their substrates (*āśrayabheda*). The same will hold true for intellect and the others as well. This is the ultimate limit of the proponents and opponents alike in the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*); beyond this, it is mere proliferation (*prapañca*).

If it is argued that atoms will proceed to act when presided over by a self (*ātman*), we say no; for prior to the production of a body, those selves—whose consciousness is dependent upon the collection of sense organs acquired through their own past karma—are devoid of cognition regarding all objects. If it is argued that selves possess an innate consciousness (*sahajacaitanya*) that pervades all objects, we say no; for what could have impaired that innate consciousness in those who possess a body, such that it would manifest everything as if it were something previously unknown?

If it is argued that because the body acts as a veil, consciousness is concentrated within itself alone and does not become outward-directed—then what is the meaning of the expression "concealment" (*tirodhāna*)? For, since [consciousness] is all-pervasive, its connection with objects is never severed; and since it is eternal, its nature as the illuminator of objects never ceases. If it is argued that concealment consists in the obstruction of the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) of consciousness, then how do embodied beings perceive objects at all? If it is replied that in some cases these modifications are not obstructed, from what cause does this distinction arise?

If it is argued that this is due to a specific proximity provided by the sense organs, then the consciousness's inclination toward objects is dependent upon the senses and is not caused by mere presence; for even though [consciousness] is all-pervasive, it does not function with respect to all objects, which would otherwise entail the uselessness of the sense organs. Thus, it has been well said that for disembodied selves, there is no cognition of objects.

And thus some say: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one sees what is outside, not the inner self. Since they lack understanding, there can be no presiding controller over them; therefore, someone superior to them must be postulated as a presiding controller, consisting of innate knowledge that perceives all objects and having the nature of an agent, because insentient things do not function without a sentient presiding controller.

Is He one or many? We say He is one. For if there were many, they would lack the capacity [for omniscience] like ourselves and others, since they would not be omniscient; whereas if there were omniscience, it would belong to only one, as the others would be useless. Furthermore, there is no cause for a perpetual consensus among many who are equally predominant, and thus there might even be the non-production of any effect. If all were to act in accordance with the intention of one, then that one alone would be the Lord (Īśvara) and not the others. If, on the other hand, there is no conflict among all of them in accordance with the production of the effect—as in the case of the members of a monastic assembly—then each one individually would lack lordship.

Thus, since the specific agent established by the particularity of his effects is omniscient, there is no non-perception of any distinction regarding any object whatsoever. Consequently, there is no false cognition based upon that; and in the absence of false cognition, there is no attachment or aversion rooted therein. Due to their absence, there is no activity preceded by them; and in the absence of activity, there is no merit or demerit to be accomplished by it. Because of their absence, there is also the absence of pleasure and pain produced by those two at all times.

Some maintain that because experience exists, memory and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) also exist; thus, they say the Lord, the Blessed One, is the substratum of eight qualities. Others, however, asserting that his unimpeded power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is nothing other than cognition itself, do not admit desire or effort, and thus declare him to be the substratum of six qualities. Is he bound or liberated? He is certainly not bound, for the afflictions and so forth—which are known as the causes of bondage—cannot possibly exist in one who is already characterized by bondage.

Even one who is liberated does not become [the Supreme Lord], because liberation is synonymous with the severance of bondage. However, He would be eternally liberated, as the venerable Patañjali stated: "The Lord is a distinct soul untouched by afflictions, actions, or their fruitions.
[Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
153] Since ether, time, and space are each singular, and thus lack intermediate universals (*aparajāti*), they possess three technical designations: ether, time, and space.
In that regard, the qualities of space (*ākāśa*) are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. [Nyāyakandalī, p.

153] He states the dissimilarities (*vaidharmya*) of the three—space, time, and direction—with a single passage for the sake of brevity: "Of space, time, and direction. Because space, time, and direction are each singular, there is no lower genus (*apara-jāti*) for them, since a genus must reside in a plurality of individuals. In the absence of a lower genus, the three designations "space," "time," and "direction" are technical terms (*pāribhāṣikyaḥ*); they are not based on a lower genus like the designations "earth" and so forth. This is the meaning.

The distinction between these [categories] is based solely on their designations (*saṃjñā*). That which is designated by convention (*saṅketa*) without a causal basis (*nimitta*), by way of specific pointing (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), is *pāribhāṣikī* (technical), such as "This is Devadatta. On the other hand, that which is designated by taking a causal basis into account is *naimittikī* (causal); this is the distinction. Now, for the purpose of defining each individually, he says: "Among those, the qualities of space (*ākāśa*). Among those three [substances], the qualities of space are sound, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. Furthermore, the possession of qualities such as sound constitutes the specific difference (*vaidharmya*) of space.
Praśastapādabhāṣya [71–72–73–74] [p.154]:

Sound is not a specific quality of tangible substances, because it is perceptible by the senses, because it does not presuppose a cause that is itself a quality, because it does not exist as long as its substance exists, and because it is perceived elsewhere than in its substratum. It is not a quality of the self, because it is perceptible by an external sense organ, because it can be apprehended by other selves, because it does not inhere in the self, and because it is perceived as distinct from the notion of "I. It does not belong to space, time, or the internal organ, because it is apprehended by the auditory organ and because it lacks the status of a specific quality (vaiśeṣika-guṇa) belonging to those. By process of elimination, being a quality, it is the inferential mark for the cognition of space.

*Nyāyakandalī* [71] [pp. 154–157]: Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of space (*ākāśa*)? Some maintain that it is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*), because when a bird is flying in the sky, through the operation of the eyes, there arises a cognition based on a restricted location: "This bird has reached here," or "It has not reached there. This is incorrect, because a substance devoid of color cannot be perceived by the eye.

Furthermore, regarding this notion of location (*adhikaraṇapratyaya*), no distinct substance appears there apart from the sphere of diffused light; therefore, by presenting a *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference for the existence of space, he negates that sound is a quality of another substance—stating: "sound...

Sound is not preceded by the qualities of its own inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because—unlike the color and other qualities of a cloth—it does not arise immediately after the production of its substrate. Therefore, like pleasure and so forth, it is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of that which possesses touch. One should not suspect that, upon the negation of its being a specific quality, it will therefore be a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*); for, since it possesses both generality and particularity and is perceptible by a single external sense organ, its status as a specific quality is established, just like color and the rest.

The color and other qualities of the earthly atom (*pārthivaparamāṇu*) are indeed particular qualities of a tangible substance, yet they are not preceded by qualities of their own causes, because the atom is not an effect. To exclude such cases, the qualification "while being perceptible" (*pratyakṣatve sati*) was added. Furthermore, sound exists only as long as its substance persists; since it perishes even while its substratum, such as a conch-shell, still exists, it follows that, like pleasure and other internal states, sound is not a particular quality of a tangible substance.

Even there, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains due to the color and other qualities of the side-particles (*pārśvaparamāṇu*); since these are destroyed by contact with fire even while their substrate, the atom, still exists, the phrase "while being perceptible" (*pratyakṣatve sati*) must be supplied as a qualification. He states another reason: "And because it is perceived elsewhere than its substrate. Furthermore, if sound were a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of something possessing touch (*sparśavat*), then a conch-shell or similar object would have to be declared its substrate.

Furthermore, it is perceived elsewhere than its source, at a distance in the region of the ear-cavity; yet there is no perception of a quality belonging to one thing in another place. Therefore, sound is not a specific quality of a substance possessing touch. If it is argued that sound is indeed perceived as situated in the very location of the conch-shell and so forth—on the grounds that the sense organs pervade the entire cosmic sphere (*maṇḍala*) from beginningless time—this is not so, for there would be no distinction in the perception of sounds whether they are near or far.

If it is argued that, although the sense organs are all-pervasive, when they are set in motion by the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha), their functional modifications (vṛtti)—which issue forth from their respective substrates and extend toward the objects in accordance with the apprehension of those objects—exist at that time; and because the apprehension of objects occurs, there is no lack of regularity (avyavasthā): [we reply] that the sense organs exist for the sake of apprehending objects, and the apprehension of objects is dependent upon the functional modification. Indeed, the sense organs are nothing other than these modifications themselves, because anything else would be useless and lacks any means of proof.

Furthermore, the auditory faculty does not perceive an object by traveling to the location of that object; for if it did, it would follow—just as in the case of visual perception—that doubt regarding direction (dik-sandeha) would be impossible even with respect to sound. Nor is there any movement of a quality (guṇa) away from its own substratum; nor can sound be initiated in the intervening space by that [quality] residing in the conch-shell, because we observe that a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) belonging to a tangible substance initiates another specific quality only in a substance initiated by its own substratum, and because no substance initiated by the conch-shell exists in the interval between the conch and the ear.

Because it is not perceived. Nor is there perception of that which has not reached [the sense organ], for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, if sound were a quality of substances such as conch-shells, there would simply be no perception of it. Yet, its perception does exist; this very fact establishes that it is a quality of a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), in which—pervading the intervening space—the perception of sound occurs through a sequence of the production of successive sounds until it reaches the vicinity of the ear. *Nyāyakandalī* [72] [pp. 157–158]

He states "because it is perceptible by an external sense organ" for the purpose of negating [sound] as a quality of the self (*ātman*). First of all, the auditory organ is an external sense organ because it invariably illuminates external objects, just like the visual organ; and sound is what is grasped by that [organ], because its cognition occurs only when that [organ] exists. Now, whatever is not graspable by an external sense organ is not a quality of the self, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; therefore, the meaning is that this [sound] also is not a quality of that [self].

For this reason also, sound is not a quality of the self (*ātman*); the meaning is that it is perceivable by the limits of other selves and is common to multiple perceivers. Indeed, a particular manifestation of sound produced by a lute, flute, or the like, which is perceived by one person through a continuous series, is perceived by another person situated in that same location; however, pleasure and so forth are not like this. Thus, because it possesses characteristics contrary to those of a quality of the self, sound is not a quality of the self. Furthermore, sound is not a quality of the self because it does not inhere in the self, just like color and other such qualities.

If it is argued that its non-inherence in the self (*ātman*) is unestablished, we say no; for, like color and other qualities, it is perceived as being directed outward, whereas the qualities of the self are understood to be internal. Furthermore, this is not a quality of the self because it is apprehended by the "I-notion" (*ahaṅkāra*) as something distinct and having a different locus. Indeed, whatever is a quality of the self is apprehended as having the same locus as the "I-notion," as in "I am happy" or "I am suffering"; however, sound is not apprehended in this way, and therefore it is not a quality of the self.

If it is argued that there exists the designation "I am one of pleasant speech"? True; however, this is due to the nature of its substratum, and not because it is the locus of that quality, for such a cognition is absent in the case of sounds from drums and the like.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [73] [p. 158]

Let it be granted then that [sound] is a quality of space, time, or the mind; to this he replies: "Because it is perceivable by the sense of hearing" (*śrotragrāhyatvāt*). What is meant? Those qualities of space, time, and the mind which are established by both parties as being conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, are not perceivable by the sense of hearing; but since this [sound] is perceivable by it, it cannot belong to them. Furthermore, space, time, and the mind possess no specific quality (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*), whereas this is a specific quality; for this reason also, it does not belong to them. He says: "And because of the absence of a specific quality" (*vaiśeṣikaguṇabhāvāc ca*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: sound is not a quality of space, time, or the mind, because it is a specific quality, like pleasure and so forth.
*Nyāyakandalī* [74] [pp. 159–160]:

Now, if it is argued that the presentation of multiple means of proof for a single object is useless, since the determination of that object is accomplished by even one alone—[we reply: Is there a uselessness of another means of proof once the object has been ascertained by one means of proof because of a lack of result (*phala*), or because of a lack of interest on the part of the person? It is not that there is no result, for just as before, so too hereafter, the cognition of that object exists. Nor is there a total lack of interest on the part of the person in every case.

Where there is an excellence of sweetness such that pleasure arises with every single experience, there indeed remains a desire to see again and again even after it has already been seen, as in the case of an extremely beloved son or the like. However, where there is no such expectation, even in that case—as before—there is no futility for one who has already begun [the activity], provided that the subsequent cause is present; for it possesses purposefulness precisely through the determination of its object. But in the case of grinding what is already ground, since it results in the failure of one's capacity, no fruit whatsoever arises.

Any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well consists merely in the delimitation of its object, because purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is accomplished by means of the object. If it is argued that when one [moment of the object] is delimited, there can be no status as the "most effective instrument" (*sādhakatamatva*) for a second [moment], we say: no, because in relation to its own effect, that very [first moment] possesses the status of being the most effective instrument. Otherwise, a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) would be invalid, since the object does not differ [from moment to moment]. Furthermore, in each cognition, the extremely subtle moments of time do not appear. And even if this were so, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because the process ceases when there is no further utility; thus, it is settled. *Nyāyakandalī* [75] [pp.160–161]

Now, one might object: even if sound is not a quality of the eight substances beginning with earth, what follows regarding the existence of space? To this he replies: "By elimination" (*pariśeṣāt*). Sound is a quality, and a quality cannot exist without a substratum possessing that quality (*guṇin*). Nor is this sound a quality of earth and the other [elements], and there exists no other substance [to which it could belong]. Therefore, that of which this is the quality is space; thus, the meaning of the statement is that [sound] is the mark (*liṅga*) for the cognition and apprehension of space by way of elimination.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Sound is a quality belonging to a substance other [than earth and the rest], because, while being a quality, it does not reside in the eight substances beginning with earth; for whatever is not a quality belonging to a substance other [than earth and the rest] does not, while being a quality, fail to reside in the eight substances beginning with earth—just like color (*rūpa*) and so forth. This is a negative inference (*vyatirekī*). From the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [75–a]:

The oneness of sound is established because its indicative mark (*liṅga*) is non-distinct. Its separateness from the one (*ekapṛthaktva*) follows from that [oneness]. Its dimension is that of the supreme magnitude (*paramamahatparimāṇa*), because of the statement regarding its pervasiveness (*vibhava*). Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) are its causes, because of the statement regarding its being the cause of sound.

Therefore, because it possesses qualities and is non-dependent, it is a substance (*dravya*); and because it lacks causes that are either homogeneous or heterogeneous, it is eternal. Furthermore, it serves as the cause for all living beings in the perception of sound by functioning as the auditory organ (*śrotra*).

Furthermore, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is a region of space (*nabhodeśa*) characterized by the cavity of the ear, which is bound by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) that bring about the experience of sound-objects. Since it is eternal, deafness occurs due to the deficiency of that which binds it.
*Nyāyakandalī* [75–a] [pp. 161–164]

From the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its existence, the fact that space has sound as its quality (*śabdaguṇatva*) is already understood. Now, he states what is worthy of establishing its qualities such as number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth: "Because there is no distinction in the mark [consisting of] sound" (*śabdaliṅgāviśeṣāt*). For sound is the mark of space, and since sound is everywhere undifferentiated and one, space is established as being of a single nature; the meaning is that there is an absence of any means of valid cognition that establishes difference.

But is not sound also indeed manifold, appearing in forms such as very loud and so forth? True; however, it is not in that form that it serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*), but rather by virtue of being a quality (*guṇatva*). And that [quality-ness] is indistinct and thus incapable of bringing about the cognition of a difference in its substratum (*āśraya*), because there is no contradiction in a single sound being produced with distinctions such as very loud and so forth from a single substratum due to a difference in its causes.

"From its conformity with that [unity], there is oneness-of-separateness (*ekapṛthaktvam*). This means that because of its conformity with unity, there is oneness-of-separateness. Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes difference in the case of space, its unity is established for all; therefore, its separateness is also established. Some say that unity is simply the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity itself, and not a specific number (*saṅkhyāviśeṣa*). For them, the co-usage of the expression "one jar" (*eko ghaṭaḥ*) would be untenable, as the two terms would be synonyms.

Even for those who claim that the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) of entities is intrinsic, it would follow—just as in the case of the conceptualization of unity—that there could be a conceptualization of distinctness even for one devoid of a reference to a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). But this cannot be so, because distinctness is conceptualized as "this is distinct from that. Therefore, there is no identity between the two.

From the statement regarding its omnipresence (*vibhava*), it follows that [space] possesses the dimension of supreme magnitude (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*). Since space possesses dimension because it is a substance, the dimension of supreme magnitude in space is established by the author of the Sūtras’ statement: "Space is omnipresent and great. Whatever is omnipresent is supremely great, as for example the Self; and since space is omnipresent, it too is supremely great.

If it is asked, "How is the all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) of space established? [The answer is: because sound is produced everywhere. For if that space were not pervasive, then sound would not be produced everywhere, since an effect cannot arise in the absence of its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa). Sounds produced in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space are inherent in a single substratum, because they are sounds, like the first sound currently being heard. And the inherence of the two sounds—the one currently being heard and the first one—in a single substratum is to be understood through their relationship as cause and effect, because that which resides in a different locus cannot function as an inherent cause.

Because of the statement regarding sound being a cause, [it follows that] conjunction and disjunction [are its causes]. By the sūtra, "The production of sound is from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound," it is stated that conjunction and disjunction are the causes with respect to sound, which is a quality of space (*ākāśa*). Therefore, conjunction and disjunction are established as existing in space, because that which resides in a different locus cannot be an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Therefore, because it possesses qualities and because it is non-dependent, space is a substance (*dravya*). Since space possesses qualities, it is a substance by virtue of possessing qualities, like a jar or similar objects; not only because it possesses qualities, but also because it is non-dependent, space is a substance, like an atom (*paramāṇu*). Furthermore, it is eternal because of the absence of causes—both homogeneous and heterogeneous. Homogeneous [causes] are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), while heterogeneous [causes] are non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*); due to the absence of these, it is eternal.

"It is the cause for the perception of sound by all living beings. [Objection: But if this were so, everyone would perceive all sounds, since space (*ākāśa*) is present everywhere without distinction. To this he says: "By way of being the auditory organ" (*śrotrabhāvena*). What, then, is the auditory organ? To that he says: "The auditory organ, moreover... That by which one hears is the faculty of hearing (*śravaṇa*); and that which is the cavity of the ear is the "cavity of hearing" (*śravaṇavivara*). That region of space which has that very thing as its designation is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), because when it is covered, sound is not perceived. He states its qualification with the words beginning "the cause of sound," etc.

Experience, which has sound as its cause, is the perception of pleasure and pain; it is bound by and assisted by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are its producers. This is the meaning: whichever sense organ perceives a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that is perceptible by each of the external senses individually, that sense organ possesses that same quality. For example, the eye, which perceives color, has color as its substratum; and the ear, which likewise perceives such a sound, must therefore also have sound as its quality. Furthermore, it has been established that sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*).

Therefore, the auditory organ is indeed space itself; and although it is all-pervading, it does not cause the perception of sound everywhere, because—by the power of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings—it is restricted as a sense-organ solely to that which is located within the cavity of the ear. This is just as, despite the self being omnipresent, its status as a knower occurs only in the region of the body and not elsewhere, because the body is the locus of experience; otherwise, the body would be purposeless.

[Objection: "But even so, would there not be perception of sound by a deaf person, since the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) exists? To this he says: "And of that... etc. Even though that ether (*ākāśa*) is eternal, deafness occurs due to the deficiency or absence of its two supporting factors, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which serve as its auxiliary causes. The word "iti" marks the conclusion. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [76–77] [pp. 164–165]

Time is characterized by the notions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, slowness and quickness. Since there is no other cause for the arising of those notions—which are distinct from previous cognitions regarding their respective objects—time is that which serves as the cause here.

It is also the cause of the production, maintenance, and destruction of all effects, because it is designated as such. Furthermore, it is the basis for the conventional usage of the divisions of time: the moment (kṣaṇa), the lava, the nimeṣa, the kāṣṭhā, the kalā, the muhūrta, the yāma, the day and night, the half-month, the month, the season (ṛtu), the solstice (ayana), the year, the yuga, the kalpa, the manvantara, the dissolution (pralaya), and the non-dissolution.
In the *Nyāyakandalī* [76] [pp.

164–166], for the purpose of defining time (*kāla*), he says: "Time. The cognition that something which is "prior" (*para*) with respect to a particular direction is "posterior" (*apara*), and the cognition that something which is "posterior" is "prior"—this is the transposition (*vyatikara*) or reversal of priority and posteriority. Furthermore, the simultaneous cognition, the non-simultaneous cognition, the cognition of quickness (*kṣipra*), and the cognition of slowness (*cira*) are the marks (*liṅga*) of time.

[Objection: Since time is not perceptible, there can be no apprehension of a pervasion (vyāpti) between it and cognitions such as "simultaneous" (*yugapat*), and so how can it function as a logical mark (*liṅga*)? To this, he says: "Of these... Of these cognitions—such as "simultaneous"—which arise with respect to their objects, such as substances, etc., and which are distinct from previous cognitions [of those same objects] and distinct from cognitions of non-substances, etc., there is no other cause for their production.

This is what is meant: with respect to objects such as substances, cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth arise; yet substances and the like are not their cause, because they are of a different nature from those cognitions. Furthermore, there can be no production of an effect without a cause. Therefore, that which is the cause in this case is time.

Some maintain that the conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior" based on the bodies of the young and the old is dependent upon the relative smallness of the revolutions of the sun; however, this is incorrect, because there is no connection between the revolutions of the sun and the young and the old, and if that which is unconnected were to serve as a cause, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [77] [pp. 166–169]

Others claim that "simultaneity" (*sahabhāva*) means "occurrence at the same time" (*yaugapadya*); this too is inconsistent, because they do not admit the existence of time and because the meaning of "together" (*saha*) is absent. If it is argued that the meaning of "together" is the state of entities being related to one another (*anyonyapratiyogitva*) with respect to some action, we say no; for entities that are unarisen, stationary, or ceased lack such mutual relation. Furthermore, if those existing simultaneously were indeed related to one another, then time itself could not be denied—this has already been stated. In this same manner, cognitions such as "not simultaneous" (*ayugapat*) and so forth are also to be explained.

If it is asked, "Since time is indivisible, how can there be a difference in cognitions? [the answer is: It is due to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). When two entities—their production and their existence—are grasped by a single cognition, time, acting as a non-cooperative cause for that [cognition], produces the notions of "prior" and "posterior. When many [entities] are grasped simultaneously by a single cognition acting as a cooperative cause for the activity of their production, a notion of simultaneity arises. And when the manyness or fewness of the moments of action intervening between the production and destruction of an effect is grasped by a single cognition acting as a cooperative cause, the notions of "long duration" and "short duration" arise.

It should be stated according to the circumstances. Now, one might object: let the distinction between cognitions be based solely on those respective causes; what is the use of time? No, for there is no arising of a real entity (*vastu*) in the absence of time. For there is no arising of that which is absolutely existent, such as space (*gagana*), nor of that which is absolutely non-existent, such as a human horn (*naraviṣāṇa*); rather, it is of that which was previously non-existent. However, if time did not exist, the word "prior" (*prāk*), which functions as a qualifier of non-existence, would lack its referent, and thus this specific distinction could not be established; consequently, the arising of anything whatsoever would be impossible.

If it is asked, "How can there be a qualified cognition by means of time, which is not perceptible? some reply to this: "Time is a cause for the arising of a qualified cognition just like a sense organ, but it does not function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) like a staff. This too is without substance, because for cognition—which has consciousness alone as its intrinsic nature—there is no other qualifier in the absence of a connection with an object. Therefore, it is stated otherwise.

When the connection with time has been inferred through the difference in the bodily states of the young and the old as being the cause thereof, there subsequently arises for the cognizer—since he is one—the cognition of those two as qualified by time; for there is no contradiction in a qualifier being brought forward even by another means of knowledge, just as in the case of "fragrant sandalwood."

Or, as for the Mīmāṃsakas' [example] "the floor is devoid of a jar," since jars and the like are inferred to have a connection with time—due to their being corporeal substances or due to their varying states, just like the body—the cognition of "simultaneous" and so forth arises as qualified by that [time]. Subsequently, its status as an inferential mark (liṅga) for time is established against those who dispute it on grounds such as its being an effect; thus, there is no fault.

It is the cause of the arising and destruction of all effects. Here he states the reasoning: "because of its designation" (*tadvyapadeśāt*). This means that because of the designation of arising and so forth by means of that time—such as designations like "the time of arising" or "the time of destruction"—time possesses the status of being the cause therein. He also describes another of its functions: "moment, instant," and so forth. A *kṣaṇa* is one-fourth of a *nimeṣa*; two *kṣaṇas* constitute a *lava*; and a *nimeṣa* is the time characterized by the movement of the eyelids; this is to be understood according to the treatises on calculation.

Praśastapādabhāṣya [78] [pp. 169–170]: Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. Unity is established because its indicative mark (liṅga) is non-specific. Distinctness follows from its being a substance. Maximum magnitude is established by the statement "Time exists as a cause. Conjunction follows from the mention of its being a cause of priority and so forth. Disjunction follows from its being the destroyer of that [conjunction].

Since its substantiality and eternity have been established as being like those of space, and since it is naturally one because there is no distinction in its marks, time is nevertheless metaphorically designated as manifold— like a jewel or like cooks— due to the differences in the commencement, accomplishment, duration, and cessation of all effects.
*Nyāyakandalī* [78] [pp.169–171]:
Thus, once the substratum (*dharmin*) has been established, he describes its qualities, saying: "Its qualities."

Since time is a flowing substance, its connection with number and other categories is established; however, in order to demonstrate its specific qualities, he says: "Because there is no distinction in the marks of time. This means that because there is no distinction among the marks of time—namely, the cognitions of simultaneity and so forth—time is one, as there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a plurality of time. [Objection: But is it not the very distinction between the cognitions of simultaneity and so forth that establishes its non-difference? [Reply: Not so; for even if time were non-different, the distinction in cognitions is possible due to the distinction in their auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). "From its conformity [to number], there is separateness (*pṛthaktva*)."

The concomitance of oneness with separateness is their coexistence; by this, separateness is established from oneness. By the statement "Time [is the cause] in respect to the cause" (Vaiśeṣikasūtra 7.1.25), he indicates the sūtra "In respect to the cause, [there is] time and space. The meaning of the sūtra is that the name "time," the designation "time," belongs to the cause of cognitions such as "simultaneous" and so forth. By this, time is obtained as all-pervasive, because the intention is that cognitions such as "simultaneous" exist everywhere.

Regarding the statement "because of priority with respect to its cause," it refers to conjunction (*saṃyoga*). In the sūtra, "Priority and posteriority arise from priority with respect to their causes and posteriority with respect to their causes" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.22), the phrase "priority with respect to their causes" denotes the conjunction between time and a substance. By this, its status as a quality consisting of conjunction is established. Regarding the statement "because it is the destroyer of that, it is disjunction (*vibhāga*)," since that conjunction is produced, it must necessarily perish; disjunction is its destroyer, because in all cases there is no destruction of the substratum [of the conjunction].
Therefore, disjunction is established in time, because a disjunction residing in a different locus cannot be its destroyer.

Its status as a substance and its eternity are established as being like those of space (*ākāśa*). Just as space is a substance because it possesses qualities and is non-dependent, so too is time. Just as space is eternal because it lacks causes of either the same or different classes, so too is time.

[Objection: If time is one, how is there a designation of it as manifold? [Response: He says: "Because the marks of time are indistinguishable. Since the marks of time—the cognitions of priority, posteriority, and so forth—are indistinguishable in that they do not indicate any difference, and since the oneness of time is thus established in its primary or literal sense, the designation of it as manifold occurs through a figurative application of multiplicity.

Why? Because "the beginning" (ārambha) of all effects is their commencement; "accomplishment" (abhinirvṛtti) is the completion of the action; "duration" (sthiti) is the persistence in its own nature; and "cessation" (nirodha) is destruction—it is due to the difference between these limiting adjuncts (upādhi) that there is the designation of manifoldness.

Just as a single gem, such as crystal, is designated as "blue" or "yellow" due to the differences in its adjuncts (*upādhi*), so too time, though singular, is designated as "the time of commencement," "the time of the manifestation of action," "the time of the duration of action," and "the time of cessation" due to the differences in its adjuncts; this is the meaning.

To demonstrate that the connection of a gem with its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not real, whereas the connection of time with action is real, he states another example: "as in the case of a cook" (*pācakavad vā*). Just as a single person receives designations such as "cook" or "reader" due to his engagement in actions like cooking or reading, so too does time; however, it is not the action itself—such as beginning—that is time, because time is cognized through a distinct cognition. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [79], p. 172.

Space (*dik*) is characterized by the notions of "east," "west," and so forth. Taking a corporeal substance as a limit, it is that from which there arise these ten notions regarding corporeal substances themselves—namely, "this is to the east of this," "to the south," "to the west," "to the north," "to the southeast," "to the southwest," "to the northwest," "to the northeast," "below," and "above"—since no other cause for these is possible.
Its qualities—number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction—are established to be the same as those of time (*kāla*).

Demonstrating that the distinction of space (*dik*) consists in its being characterized by notions such as "prior" and "posterior," just as time (*kāla*) is characterized by notions such as "simultaneous" and so forth, he says: "Space is characterized by the notions of prior, posterior, and so on. That direction for which the notion of "prior," "posterior," and so forth is the mark (*liṅga*) is described as such. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "material substance" (*mūrttadravya*). An immaterial substance cannot serve as a limit (*avadhi*), nor can it be the object of notions such as "prior" and "posterior," because its dimension (*parimāṇa*) is unconditioned (*anavacchinna*).

Therefore, this has been stated: taking a corporeal substance as a limit, that [direction] is *diś* (space/direction), from which notions such as "this is to the east of that" arise only with respect to corporeal substances. In the very sense of "this is prior to that," the term "to the east" (*pūrveṇa*) is used, because the third case ending is prescribed for the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Now, one might ask: since notions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth are effects, a cause is inferred; but how is it certain that this cause is *diś* alone? To this, he says: "because no other cause is possible."

First of all, a mere substance (*dravyamātra*) cannot be the cause of the notions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, because it would follow that these notions would arise whenever a substance exists in any way whatsoever. Even if one were to argue that two substances are the cause of their arising through mutual dependence, the same fault remains; moreover, there is the additional consequence that both [the prior and posterior] would be non-existent. Furthermore, if action, quality, and so forth were the cause, there would be no distinction in the notion regarding things possessing identical qualities or actions. Therefore, that which is the cause of these [notions] is "direction" (*dig*).

Where the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed as in "from this, that" (*ita ād idam*), otherwise even that [case] would be without an object. If it is argued that this ablative has a limit (*avadhi*)? True; however, this status of being a limit belongs in relation to *space* (*dik*), and not to substance (*dravya*) alone, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of its being indistinguishable everywhere. Even though it is imperceptible, it must be stated that, like time (*kāla*), it is the cause of specific cognitions. Demonstrating that the definition of a substance—namely, possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*)—applies to this [space], he says: "But its qualities," and so forth.

These [qualities] are established as being like time (*kāla*). Just as the oneness of time is established because there is no distinction in its marks, so too is there oneness of direction (*dik*) because there is no distinction in its marks. Just as there is separateness (*pṛthaktva*) in time because it conforms to that [oneness], so it is in direction. Just as there is the dimension of infinite magnitude (*paramamahatparimāṇa*) in time because of the statement, "Time is in the cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.25), so too there is the dimension of infinite magnitude in direction because of the statement, "Direction is in the cause. This is because its effect—the cognition of "east," "west," and so forth—is present everywhere.

Just as the possession of the quality of conjunction was established for time (*kāla*) on account of its priority with respect to causes and its posteriority with respect to causes, so it is for direction (*diś*) as well; and just as disjunction is established in time because it destroys conjunction, so it is in direction—this is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*).
*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [80] [p.174]

Although space is unitary by virtue of its lack of specific distinctions, the great sages have, for the sake of the practical conventions of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and worldly affairs, assigned ten conventional designations—namely "East" and so forth—to the conjunctions and disjunctions of the Lord Sun as he revolves clockwise around Mount Meru; these names correspond to the regions of the quarters presided over by the world-protectors (Lokapālas). Thus, the ten directions are established figuratively.

Due to the influence of their respective presiding deities, these very [directions] further possess ten designations: namely, Māhendrī, Vaiśvānarī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtī, Vāruṇī, Kauberī, Aiśānī, Brāhmī, and Nāgī.
*Nyāyakandalī* [80] [pp. 174–175]

[Objection: Is it not the case that the lack of distinction among the directions is not established, because the cognitions of "east," "west," and so forth are mutually distinct? And this being so, it is logical that there is a plurality of directions. [Reply: No, because in relation to a single object, cognitions such as "east" and "west" arise simultaneously depending upon other objects. For if there were a plurality of directions, the cognition of "west" would not occur with respect to what is "east. [Objection: Does it not have a connection with all directions? [Reply: If that were so, then for every object, all cognitions would result from all perspectives.
But it is not so; therefore, direction is one, and the difference in cognition arises from the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

The conventional designation "east" (*pūrva*) applies to the interval between the conjunction with the sun at its first rising and a substance situated in a straight line from it; "south" (*dakṣiṇā*) applies to the interval between the conjunction at midday and a substance situated in a straight line from it; and "west" (*paścima*) applies to the interval between the conjunction at sunset and a substance situated in a straight line from it. Where the conjunction with the sun is not perceived, there the designation "north" (*uttara*) is used in relation to a substance situated in a straight line from the midday conjunction. Between these [directions], the designations "southeast" (*pūrvadakṣiṇā*) and so forth are employed.

Thus, the distinction in cognition is established. [Objection: Let the cognition be based solely on conjunction with the sun. [Response: No, because that [sun] lacks conjunction with a corporeal substance, and it is impossible for that which is unconnected to be a cause of cognition. He demonstrates this very point with the words: "because there is no distinction in the marks of direction" (*digliṅgāviśeṣāt*). Even though direction is established as one, ten types of designations—such as "eastern" and so forth—have been made by the great sages. Of what nature are they? They are "significant" (*anvarthā*); that is, they are so called because their meaning follows from [the object itself].

For what things is their meaning applicable? It is for the regions of the directions presided over by the world-protectors (lokapālas), such as Indra and the others. The words "of the sun" (*savitur*) and "conjunctions and disjunctions" (*saṃyoga-vibhāgāḥ*) are to be supplied [to the sentence]. For instance: because the sun moves toward this [direction] first, it is called *prācī* (east); because it moves downward, it is *avācī* (south); because it moves upward, it is *udīcī* (north). Of what kind of sun? Of that which revolves clockwise around Meru—that is, which circumambulates Meru from left to right.

For what purpose were these designations made? They were made for the sake of the conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*) of the Vedas (*śruti*), the Smṛtis, and the world. That is, for the sake of correct worldly practice. Vedic usage includes such injunctions as "one should not sleep with one's head toward the west," and so forth. Smṛti usage includes such rules as "one eats while facing the east for the sake of longevity," and so forth. Worldly usage includes such expressions as "go forward" or "look to the south," and so forth. Since these ten designations were made, the ten directions are established and proven through figurative application (*bhakti*) or metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

However, the designations such as *māhendrī* (belonging to Mahendra) and so forth do not refer to different objects; rather, they apply to those very same things by virtue of other causal conditions. Thus he says: "To those very same... and so on. This is called *māhendrī* because it belongs to Mahendra; *vaiśvānarī* because it belongs to Vaiśvānara, and so on—this etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) applies everywhere.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [81] [p.176]

It is called the *ātman* because of its connection with the nature of self (*ātmatva*). Since it is imperceptible due to its subtlety (*saukṣmya*), its existence is established through the instruments—the ears and so forth—which are themselves inferred from the perception of sound and other objects. Just as tools such as axes are seen to be employed by an agent, and because of the well-known fact that one perceives sound and so forth through the sense organs directed toward sound and so forth, the one who accomplishes this [perception] is inferred.
*Nyāyakandalī* [81] [pp. 176–179]

Knowledge of reality leads to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), while erroneous knowledge is the cause of *saṃsāra*; therefore, for the purpose of explaining that for whose sake all beings exist, he says: "It is called the self (*ātman*) because of its connection with the property of selfhood (*ātmatva*). The meaning is that "selfhood" is a universal (*sāmānya*), and because of its connection with that, there is the conventional usage "self. This constitutes its specific difference from other things.

One might object: "The existence of a perceptible object is pervaded by the cognition of its form; yet there is no cognition of any [object] that has the Self as its form. Therefore, by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), its very existence is refuted; how, then, can there be a definition of its properties? Anticipating this, [the author] says "of that" (*tasya*), demonstrating that there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against its existence because direct non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalabdhi*) is otherwise established, and that there is indeed inferential evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) for it.

Subtlety (*saukṣmya*) is the absence of fitness for direct perception. Therefore, the perception of sound and other objects by means of the organs of the imperceptible self is accomplished through the ears and so forth, which are themselves inferred—on the grounds that they are instruments, like the act of cutting, because they are actions that must be accomplished by instruments. Why is this so? He says: because we observe that instruments such as axes and the like are employed by an agent. Whatever is an instrument is set in motion and applied to an effect by some agent, just as an axe or similar tool is used by a carpenter.

Furthermore, the instruments such as the ear must be employed by some agent; that which is their employer is the Self (*ātman*). Although there is no direct connection between the ether (which constitutes the ear) and the Self because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), nevertheless, the ear is employed by the Self through the mediation of the presiding of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), just as an iron ball is joined [to fire] by means of a pair of tongs joined to the hand. And the status of the ear and other organs as instruments is due to their grasping specific objects.

Like a lamp. Although the self is experienced by the mind as being permeated by agency and ownership—forms produced by the limiting conditions (upādhi) of the relationship between cause and effect acquired through its own karma, such as "I" and "mine"—nevertheless, the expression "not perceived here" is intended with respect to the external sense organs. Furthermore, the cognizer is inferred from the fact that there is a well-known manifestation regarding sound and other objects. Regarding the manifestation—that is, the cognition—concerning objects such as sound, the cognizer who brings it about is likewise inferred. And cognition must reside in something, because it is an action, like the act of cutting; that in which this [cognition] resides is the self.

If it is argued that this [consciousness] knows by itself and does not depend on another, is this [consciousness] permanent or does it perish at every moment? If it is permanent, there is merely a difference in terminology. If, however, it is momentary, there can be no recollection of what was experienced long ago, because the cognizer has changed.

As for the claim that memory of what was experienced in a preceding moment occurs because of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), whereas there is no such memory by a son of what was experienced by his father because of the absence of a causal relationship between the cognitions of the father and the son, and because the two bodies are likewise insentient—that is incorrect. For in the absence of a self (*ātman*), the causal relationship itself cannot be ascertained. At the time of the cognition of the cause, the cognition of the effect is yet to come; and at the time of the latter, the cause has already passed away.

And since there is no single seer other than those two, who could perceive the causal relationship between them as they occur in succession? Now, it might be argued that the preceding cognition, which grasps its own self, takes as its object its own nature as a cause, which is not distinct from itself.

If it is argued that the subsequent cognition also grasps its own nature as its object, and likewise grasps its own causality—which is not distinct from that [nature]—and that the causality and effectuality grasped individually by those two are then determined (*adhyavasīyate*) by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the force of a single latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by both; alas, what a far-fetched hypothesis! For the preceding and succeeding cognitions are restricted solely to their own selves; how then could there arise in them the realization: "I am the cause of this" and "I am the effect of that"?
Because they are unaware of each other's communications, how could one determine what has not been grasped by those two, given that cognition follows upon experience?
Praśastapādabhāṣya [82] [p.179]:

It is not [the case that consciousness belongs to] the body, the sense organs, or the mind, because they are insentient. Consciousness does not belong to the body, because it is an effect of the elements like a jar and so forth, and because it is impossible in a dead body. It does not belong to the sense organs, because they are instruments, and because recollection is observed even when they are impaired or when their objects are absent.
[82] Let it be granted that cognition is dependent upon something else; however, its substratum may be either the body, a sense organ, or the mind.

Regarding this, he says: "Not of the body, the senses, or the mind. The word *caitanya* (consciousness), which occurs in the subsequent sentence, is connected here [to the preceding negation]. Consciousness does not belong to the body, the senses, or the mind; why is that? He says: "Because of their lack of knowledge (*ajñatvāt*). The meaning is: because they lack the status of being the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of cognition. Now, one might object that this too is no different from the point yet to be proven (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not of the body."

Consciousness does not belong to the body because the body is an effect of the elements, like a jar; whatever is an effect of the elements is not conscious, just as a jar is, and the body is an effect of the elements; therefore, this too is unconscious. He states another argument: "And because [consciousness] is impossible in a dead [body]. By the phrase "because consciousness is impossible in a dead body," he intends to express that [consciousness] does not persist as long as the substance [of the body] exists.

Consciousness is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the body, because it does not persist as long as the substance [the body] exists, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For this very reason, its causes must also be unconscious; if they were conscious, consciousness would also exist in the effect [the body]. Furthermore, there would result a multiplicity of knowers within a single body. Consequently, there would be defects such as the absence of a rule governing activity based on a single intention. [Nor is it a quality] of the sense organs, because they are instruments (*karaṇa*); the sense organs are unconscious, because they are instruments, just like a staff.

And he adds another reason with the words "even when impaired": even when the sense organs have perished, an object previously experienced is remembered; yet it is not logical for memory to occur when the experiencer has perished. Therefore, cognition is not a quality of the sense organs. Furthermore, memory is observed to occur even in the absence of the previously experienced object, because the external sense organs function only by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*). Thus, memory does not belong to the sense organs.

The meaning is that in the absence of that [consciousness], there would be no experience as well, because one thing is not remembered when another is experienced. For this very reason, the object also does not possess consciousness, since it is impossible to remember an object once it has perished. Furthermore, it does not possess consciousness because the cognition of that place and the pleasure or other sensations produced by it are not experienced, and because there is an absence of specific purposeful activity preceded by awareness.

Furthermore, if consciousness belonged to the sense organs or to the objects, it would not be possible to have the realization of a single agent for the cognitions of form and so forth—such as "I saw a form," "I experienced a taste," "I touch a tangible," or "I shall smell an odor"—because there is a difference between the forms and the like, and the eyes and the other senses.

Nor can it belong to the mind (*manas*), because if it did not depend on another instrument, there would be the consequence of simultaneous perception and memory, and because the mind itself functions as an instrument. By process of elimination, since it is an effect of the self (*ātman*), the self is thereby established.

[83] Let it be, then, that cognition is a quality of the mind (*manas*). Since its being the object of all things and its permanence would account for the phenomenon of recognition (*pratisandhāna*) and so forth, he says in response: "Nor [is it] of the mind. If the mind were the knower and, depending on some other cause distinct from the eye and so forth, cognizes color and the rest, then the dispute would be merely over a difference in terminology. That which must be depended upon is the mind, and that which is the substratum of cognition is the mind; for us, that is the Self (*ātman*).

Now, if it does not depend on another instrument, then simultaneous perceptions of color, taste, and so forth—which are connected to their respective sense organs—would follow, due to the simultaneity of the causes. However, if there is dependence on another instrument, then because that [instrument] is atomic, its presence in all the sense organs simultaneously is impossible, and thus simultaneous perceptions do not arise. Likewise, in the absence of an internal instrument (antaḥkaraṇa), simultaneous recollections would occur, as there would be nothing further to depend upon; but when there is dependence on an instrument, the production of recollection occurs sequentially, because the conjunction with that [internal instrument] lacks the capacity for simultaneity.

As for what was stated by someone—that a single, eternal entity cannot produce effects either successively or simultaneously—that is incorrect. It is incorrect because simultaneous production is impossible, and non-production at a later time occurs simply because there is nothing further to be produced. Nor does its existence follow from this alone, since we do not accept that existence is anything other than the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

For this reason also, the quality of the mind (*manoguṇa*) is not knowledge, because the mind is itself an instrument (*karaṇa*); thus he says: "And because it is itself an instrument. The mind is not consciousness (*cetana*), because it is an instrument, like the sense of smell and so forth. If it is argued that the mind's status as an instrument is unestablished (*asiddha*), because its agency (*kartṛtva*) is accepted [by some], then [we reply]: if the mind were the agent, then just as with the eyes and other organs in the perception of form and so forth, another instrument would have to be sought for the perception of pleasure and so forth; for an action does not arise without an instrument.
Even if that were the case, there would be a mere difference in terminology, since both the agent and the instrument are already established.

[p.184] For this reason as well, the mind is insentient because it is corporeal, like a clod of earth. If knowledge is not a quality of the body, the senses, or the mind, then what follows for the proof of the self? To this he replies: "By elimination" (*pariśeṣāt*). Knowledge, being an effect, must be the effect of some inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); and the status of the body, the senses, and the mind as its substratum has been refuted.

Furthermore, by the reasoning to be stated later, there is no possibility that other things could be the cause of cognition; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), cognition is the effect of the self. And because it is the effect of the self, the self is apprehended through that cognition—this is the conclusion. [Objection: But all of this is incoherent, because due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), the relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) cannot exist. To explain: existence (*sattva*) consists in causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), and that is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, since no other alternative is possible for that which is neither successive nor simultaneous.

Succession (*krama*) is indeed the state of performing multiple purposeful actions at multiple times, while simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is the state of performing them at a single time. There is no mode other than these two—unity and multiplicity—because the negation of one between two mutually exclusive opposites is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other. However, if there were non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), succession would be impossible; for that which is capable cannot be delayed, and that which is incapable cannot produce an effect even at another time, since its nature has not ceased. If it is argued that "it acts successively by obtaining successive auxiliary causes," [the response follows in the Nyāyakandalī].

On this point, they say: If the auxiliaries do not produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the entity, they are not to be depended upon, because they contribute nothing. If, however, they do produce it, is that excellence distinct from the entity or non-distinct? In the first case, if it is distinct, then since the production of the effect occurs through that adventitious excellence alone—as established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—the non-momentary entity cannot be the cause, for the effect does not occur even when that [entity] is present.

If you argue that its capacity to produce [the effect] belongs to it when accompanied by the intention (*āśaya*) produced by the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then what kind of assistance is there if the excellence (*atiśaya*) does not initiate further excellences? And if it does initiate them, what is the remedy for infinite regress (*anavasthā*)? Furthermore, the claim that "the excellence produced by the auxiliaries belongs to the non-momentary entity" is a fine statement indeed, since there can be no relation between that which is not assisted and that which does not assist. Nor is it tenable to say that the excellence, being non-different from the entity itself, is produced by the auxiliaries; for an entity that has already arisen cannot arise again.
If it is argued that the original entity, being devoid of any excellence, ceases, while another entity, characterized by excellence, is born, then momentariness is established.

Now, one might ask: "What is done by the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) even for that which is momentary? Nothing at all. Why, then, are they required by it? Who indeed says they are required? For the moments existing in their final state are each individually capable of producing the effect; what mutual dependence could there be among them? As for the fact that they draw near to one another at that time, this is due to the necessary rule governing the cause of their approach, and not for the sake of performing the effect in concert; and the necessity of that approach at that specific time arises from the very nature of those things.

If each cause were individually capable, they would each produce only a single effect; why then do many produce one? In this regard, one must inquire into the reasons why these causes possess the nature of accomplishing a single purpose. We, however, as speakers of the nature of things as they are observed, are not subject to such questioning.

If it is asked, "Since the effect has already been produced by one alone, what do the others do?"—they do not produce what has already been produced; rather, while it is being produced by one, the others also assist in its production. If it is asked, "In a case where one alone is sufficient, what is the utility of the others?"—that is true; however, they are not acting with foresight, such that they would remain indifferent after having reflected in this manner.

If it is argued that "it is impossible for a single effect to arise from multiple causes, because the difference in causes must be the cause of a difference in effects," we say this is not so; for the difference in effects arises from the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), not from the difference in the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). Indeed, being an auxiliary factor consists precisely in contributing to a single effect. Therefore, if things were momentary, the production of effects in succession by entities occurring in a sequence would not be possible; however, the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) by a non-momentary entity is what is truly impossible.

Simultaneous action is also untenable, because the nature capable of performing those many effects does not cease even at a later time. If it is argued that there is no performance of what has already been done and nothing remains for it to do—since the entire collection of effects has been performed all at once, and therefore it does not act in subsequent moments—then, in that case, it would be non-existent at that time, due to the absence of all purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*).

Thus, since neither succession nor simultaneity—which are the two pervaders—are perceived in a non-momentary entity, existence (sattva), by being excluded from the non-momentary, is established as residing only in the momentary. This being the case, the inference of momentariness is easily obtained: "Whatever exists is momentary; and the twelve bases (āyatanas) exist.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [85] [pp. 188–193]

To this it is replied: existence does not establish momentariness, because there is no comprehension of its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). If it is argued that—"Whatever is devoid of succession and simultaneity is non-existent, like a horse's horn; and the non-momentary is devoid of succession and simultaneity"—and thus, by means of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), the exclusion of existence from the non-momentary is cognized through the exclusion of succession and simultaneity from the non-momentary—this is not so. For as long as the non-momentary is not cognized, the cognition of the exclusion of existence from it is impossible, just as [the exclusion of heat] cannot be cognized in water while the water itself is being perceived.

Just as there is the cognition of the absence of fire and smoke, so too, when a non-momentary entity is observed, the absence of existence must be cognized due to the absence of succession and simultaneity. If it is argued: "But for you [Buddhists], there is no such thing as a non-momentary entity; nevertheless, just as even when a *piśāca* (demon) is not being perceived, its exclusion from others is cognized—namely, that 'the pillar is not a *piśāca*'—so too will this case be," we reply: No, because exclusion is the exclusive domain of the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

Furthermore, since non-apprehension consists in the apprehension of an object other than that which is excluded, it cannot occur without the apprehension of its counter-positive; nor is it possible to cognize the exclusion of a piśāca from something else when the piśāca itself is remote by its very nature.

If it is asked, "How then is there the cognition that 'the pillar is not a *piśāca*?," this is not a negation of conjunction (*saṃsarga-pratiṣedha*), but rather a negation of identity (*tādātmya-pratiṣedha*). And this proceeds because the *piśāca*, which is hypothetically projected as having the nature of the pillar, is admitted to be perceptible, and not otherwise. As it has been said: "Whatever negation is made by way of identity, all of that is performed by accepting that [the object] meets the conditions for perception."

In that regard, the cognition of a pillar, which is restricted solely to the essential nature of the pillar, is the cause for the exclusion of what is not its self; for if the pillar were a *piśāca*, it would have been cognized as having that [demon's] nature. However, cognition does not apprehend the state of being a *piśāca* in the same way it apprehends the state of being a pillar; therefore, "this is not a *piśāca*."

Now, if it is thought that there is no such thing as a non-momentary or momentary entity distinct from blue and so forth; rather, a moment of blue perceived by a previous cognition, when superimposed as non-different from a moment of blue perceived by a present cognition, is called "non-momentary," whereas when established as different, it is called "momentary"—in that case, this realization of the absence of existence through the exclusion of succession and simultaneity applies only to blue and the like.

If this very moment that was previously perceived is now being perceived, then it should have performed its present causal efficiency (arthakriyā) at the earlier time, or its former efficiency at the present time; it could not perform them sequentially, because it is contradictory for a single entity to be both an agent and a non-agent. Nor does it perform everything only previously, because that would entail the consequence of its non-existence now, as it would be devoid of causal efficiency at the present moment.

In this case as well, is a real counter-example (*vipakṣa*) of the reason "existence" being shown here, or is one merely established through conceptual superimposition? First, it cannot be a real counter-example, because for blue and other such things, non-momentariness is unreal; and in whatever form they exist as real entities, in that very form they are indeed performers of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*), and thus they do not constitute a counter-example.

If it is argued that a counter-position (*vipakṣa*) superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is not a factor for inference (*anumāna*) which establishes a real entity—because such a [counter-position] is unreal, and because this entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference (*anumeya*) proceeds solely through a relationship of property and locus (*dharmadharmibhāva*) mounted upon the intellect—[we reply: no, because the distinction between a valid reason (*hetu*) and a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) would be untenable, since the status of being a thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, when merely superimposed by conceptual construction, is easily found everywhere. Therefore, for one who desires a real comprehension of the object through inference, there must be a determination of the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

In all cases, the status of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth must be demonstrated as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the inference from smoke, and not merely by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Since there exists no non-momentary entity that is of such a nature, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished. When that is unestablished, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is likewise unestablished because it is preceded by that; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).

Furthermore, although the exclusion of existence from non-momentary things has been established by a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), how is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between momentariness and existence established? Nor can there be the status of a logical reason (*hetu*) based merely on exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*), because that would entail the absurdity of even an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason being a valid reason. Moreover, inference based solely on negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireki-anumāna*) is not accepted [by us].

If it is argued that once it has been established that existence does not belong to the non-momentary, it follows by implication that existence is based on the momentary—thereby establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—we say no. This is because the phrase "by implication" does not constitute a reference to the reason (*hetu*), namely existence; for as long as its positive concomitance remains unestablished, it lacks the status of a valid reason.

However, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the operation of both [positive and negative concomitance] would have to establish it only within the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), because it is impossible to cognize a pervasion that lacks an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*), and because there exists no object apart from the twelve sense-bases. Furthermore, if positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were cognized among those [twelve bases], momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would also be cognized, since the cognition of a relation is inseparable from the cognition of its relata; thus, the property of existence (*sattva*) would be redundant.

If it is argued that the apprehension of pervasion occurs generally with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*), while existence (*sattva*) functions as the logical reason (*hetu*) with respect to the particular, we say no; for there is no cognition of a universal devoid of particulars. Furthermore, when the two universals of momentariness and existence—which are established in particulars—are being cognized, the momentariness residing in blue and other such things is already cognized; thus, it is rightly said that [the separate mention of] existence is redundant.

If it is argued that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs between the sublation [of existence] and the exclusion of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), while the cognition of momentariness—which is the very nature of the thing—arises from existence itself, we say no. This is because there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between two exclusions that are conceptually differentiated by the difference in their respective objects of exclusion (*vyāvartya*). Furthermore, identity has been stated to be a necessary factor for inference, since momentariness and existence, as the very nature of the thing, are identical.

If it is argued that there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), even though they are determined as being of the nature of that [object], we say no. For if the identity of real entities is not established through any other means, then even a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) would be useless. Furthermore, when the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between two exclusions is ascertained, there is no establishment of the real entity (*vastu*), because there is a difference between a real entity and a non-entity, and because there is no relation between them.
(Nyāyakandalī, pp. 193–197)

As for what was stated by Dharmottara—that having established the pervasion (vyāpti) in a jar by means of a subverting argument (bādhaka), one establishes momentariness in sound because of its existence [therein], and thus both arguments possess meaning due to a difference in their objects—there too this is the reply: since there is no contradiction in the operation of the subverting argument in sound just as in a jar, the pursuit of another means of knowledge is fruitless.
