Nor is it the case that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible for a non-momentary entity. For a thing possesses the nature of producing an effect when accompanied by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), rather than having a causal form that is independent of them. Thus, the production of an effect occurs in such a way that the auxiliary causes—whose capacities are known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—come together; in this manner, even a stable entity can act sequentially. This is because an effect dependent upon multiple causes cannot arise from a single one alone.

Nor is it correct to argue that since the effect arises from an excellence produced by the auxiliary causes when they are dependent upon them, the entity itself is not the agent; for we observe the production of the effect through the persistence of the entity's own nature. For if it were not the agent, then even when a barley seed is in proximity with earth and water, a rice sprout might arise as well, due to the absence of any restrictive cause.

Nor do the auxiliary causes impart any excellence (*atiśaya*) to the nature of the entity; rather, they are merely auxiliaries. Furthermore, its "excellence" is simply its association with those auxiliaries, while its "non-excellence" is simply their absence, because the effect exists when that [association] is present and does not exist when it is absent. As for the assumption of a distinction between moments that produce and moments that do not produce [the effect], this is contradicted by perception which apprehends [the entity] as persisting at all times. If it is argued that this is an illusion of persistence caused by the non-perception of an interval due to the production of highly similar moments without interruption—[we reply: such a thing being established...

If perception were momentary, it would be erroneous; and if it were erroneous, the establishment of momentariness would follow—thus there is mutual dependence. Furthermore, when the cause of a thing's production and the cause of its destruction have been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is not logical to postulate its production and destruction in the absence of those causes. Destruction cannot be without a cause, and the claim that even a seed is the cause of a seed [rather than its producer] is unproven.

The seed that produces the sprout does not possess the nature of being a seed [as a cause] when it has already produced the sprout, because it is a seed, just like a seed situated at the top of a stalk of rice. If it is argued that since a thing is partless, its status as both a producer and a non-producer is untenable, this is of little consequence.

Just as fire possesses both the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*) with respect to burning and the status of not being an agent (*akārakatva*) with respect to bathing, yet its essential nature (*svarūpa*) does not differ because of those two states; so too, for a single existence (*bhava*), there is the status of being an agent due to the presence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāribhāva*), and the status of not being an agent due to their absence. If it is asked: "How is it that one thing is an agent in the proximity of another, and even when it is an agent, why is it an agent only of some things and not of all?"—in this regard, the inherent natures of things (*vastusvabhāva*) must be accepted as the answer, and they are not to be further questioned.
But we, accepting that those very factors whose capacity we understand through positive and negative concomitance constitute the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), do not deserve censure.

In your own position as well, it is only earth, water, and the seed that possess the capacity for cooperation (*sahakāritā*) in the production of a sprout, and not other things; even there, what cause is there other than the very nature of the thing (*vastusvabhāva*)? If you argue that the seed and so forth are each individually capable and do not require mutual cooperation, then for what purpose does the farmer sow the seed and pour water upon the ploughed ground? If you say it is for the sake of generating, through their mutual influence, moments (*kṣaṇa*) in each of them that are fit for producing the sprout—[p.196] then...

If the seed has arisen from its own causes as capable of producing a momentary state conducive to the generation of a sprout, what is the use of earth and water? Or, if it is incapable, even then their proximity is of no avail, because the seed's intrinsic nature has not been abandoned.

If it is argued that through earth and water, the seed’s capacity to initiate a subsequent moment—which exists within its own continuum and is otherwise incapable—is suppressed? Let it be that, because of this, an incapable moment does not arise; however, the arising of a capable moment would be difficult to obtain due to the absence of its cause. Furthermore, there can be no suppression of a capacity that is inherent to the nature of a thing, for if there were, it would follow that the thing itself must also be suppressed.

Furthermore, destruction would follow as being caused; moreover, it is impossible for a seed to impart a capacity to produce a specific moment [of existence] because of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). And if a capacity distinct from its own nature were produced, there would be the undesirable consequence of producing what has already been produced. Therefore, there are only two possibilities: either that which is incapable does not act at any time despite having arisen, or that which is capable acts immediately after arising. It is not the case, however, that action occurs upon the accompaniment of another entity, because such an entity serves no purpose.

Now, if you think that because an effect does not arise from a single cause and is seen to arise from many, the causal capacity belongs only to them when combined—why do you become angry with us for saying this? Thus, since even a non-momentary entity can perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

As for what was also stated—that the destruction of produced entities is inevitable—it is by means of that as well that momentariness can be inferred. For instance: whatever is necessarily present in something does not depend upon other causes for its occurrence, just as the iron-nature of arrows, swords, and the like [does not depend on further causes]. And since the destruction of produced things is necessarily present, this inference rejects the dependence of destruction upon other causes.

For those things that depend upon other causes are not necessarily present; just as dyeing and the like [depend on conditions] in the case of cloth, so too, if entities were to depend on another cause for their destruction apart from their own causes, then—since it is possible for that other cause to be obstructed or deficient—might some produced thing not even perish? However, since things arise from their own causes with a perishable nature, they perish immediately after their production; thus, momentariness is established.

Moreover, if an entity possesses an indestructible nature, its destruction would be impossible to effect, just as coldness is impossible in fire; if it possesses a destructible nature, there is no need for causes [of destruction]. Furthermore, destruction cannot be produced by another cause when it is non-different from the entity itself, because difference in causes is the cause of difference [in effects]. And if something different were produced by another cause, it would follow that the original entity could still be perceived and so forth, since the production of one thing does not entail the loss of the nature of another.

Furthermore, the designation "the jar has perished" would not be one whose agent is an entity (*bhāva*); rather, it would have to be designated as "non-existence has arisen. And if that were the case, when the question "What became of the jar? is asked regarding its cessation, something entirely irrelevant would be stated. Therefore, destruction is indeed of the very nature of an entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*). *Nyāyakandalī* [87] [pp. 198–202]

To this it is replied: Is this entity that has arisen restricted to a single moment, or does it persist even into another moment? In the case of its persistence into another moment, there is a contradiction of its momentariness because it would endure for multiple periods of time. However, if it is restricted to a single moment, then it lacks persistence in any subsequent moment; thus, there is no identity between existence and non-existence, due to the difference in time.

Now, if it is thought: "We do not say that an entity is its own non-existence, but rather that the second moment is the non-existence of the preceding moment," that too is without substance; for even though there is a difference between the individual entities of the preceding and succeeding moments, there is no contradiction in their intrinsic natures.

Just as a jar coexists with another jar belonging to a different continuum, so too it would coexist with one belonging to the same continuum, because there is no proof for its negation at the first moment by a second means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apprehending the second moment—which has already fulfilled its purpose by establishing the jar's own nature. Furthermore, non-existence (*abhāva*) consists solely in the negation of existence, since the cognition "the jar does not exist" arises.

Therefore, it is logical that the arising of that entity is its cessation, the persistence of that entity is its non-persistence, and the perception of that entity is its non-perception, because they are mutually contradictory. This being the case, an entity cannot possess momentariness, since its subsequent non-existence depends upon another cause and thus lacks the necessity of following immediately after the entity. Furthermore, this is observed in the world: a jar that has arisen is destroyed only after a long time by the blow of a mallet.

It is inconsistent to claim that the destruction of a jar is an entity and that from the blow of a mallet there arises a continuum of shards; for as long as the power to produce similar [effects], which is bound to its own continuum, is not obstructed, the production of a dissimilar continuum is impossible. And if that power is obstructed by the impact of the mallet, what aversion is there to the obstruction of the entity itself? Nor does the fact that negation is an effect of a cause entail that non-existence is a real entity like existence, because negation, being of the nature of a prohibition, is established through perception and other means of valid cognition.

Such is its essential nature that, although it is produced, it does not perish like other entities, because once destroyed, it is no longer perceived. To negate the intrinsic nature of a thing established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) on the grounds of its similarity to something else would entail the negation of the world’s diversity itself. How the production of one thing involves the loss of the intrinsic nature of another is not subject to further questioning, due to the inherent nature of things (*vastusvābhāvya*). Furthermore, the designation "the jar is destroyed" occurs precisely through the arising of non-existence (*abhāva*), according to the principle of the motion of its parts and so forth.

For this very reason, this is the absence of that [specific object] alone, not of everything. Furthermore, it has no inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); due to the absence of such a cause, it likewise lacks a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Where has an effect ever been seen to exist without a substratum? Yet, this very thing is indeed observed: for this [absence] does not inhere in the jar because the jar is absent, nor does it inhere in the ground because it is a property of something else. How then is it perceived as restricted to a specific location? It is through the restriction of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

This is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): that when conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is negated, it appears as if conjoined; when inherence (*samavāya*) is negated, it appears as if inherent. The qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is likewise the same; however, it does not possess conjunction or inherence, because those two are properties of positive entities (*bhāvadharma*). Thus, non-existence (*abhāva*) is established as the opposite of existence, an object to be known by the cognition "it is not. It is this [non-existence] which causes even fire and snow to be in opposition.

The absence of fire in snow and the absence of snow in fire—there is no contradiction between these two, for there is no contradiction between one affirmation and another affirmation in their own nature. [p. 202] Furthermore, as for the claim that because non-existence is necessarily present, it does not depend on other causes, that too is inconclusive due to the rising and setting of the sun; for if those two were independent, there would be no distinction in time. The same fault applies even if they are obstructed by a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

For the cause of coloration in cloth is determinate and occurs at a determinate time; thus, it is established that the non-arising of coloration results merely from the absence of that [cause] at that particular time. However, the causes of destruction are infinite and occur at indeterminate times; since it is impossible for all of them to be obstructed at all times, one or another inevitably falls [upon the object]. Having fallen at a later time, it destroys the entity in a single moment. Thus, even though things are produced (*kṛtaka*), their destruction is certain. *Nyāyakandalī* [88] [pp. 203–206]

Furthermore, all these proofs for momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) are "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because there is a subsequent cognition of that which has already been cognized through the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Now, it might be argued that this cognition cannot establish the persistence of an entity across prior and posterior states, for this is not a single cognition, due to the absence of such a cause.

The sense faculty has a present object and does not penetrate into past time; the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as well, being restricted to its object through previous experience, does not touch upon another time; nor is there anything else distinct from these two that possesses both objects as its domain, which could produce this cognition.

For this reason as well, this is not a single cognition, because there is a difference in their intrinsic natures: for "this" refers to perceptibility, while "that" refers to non-perceptibility (remoteness). And perceptibility and non-perceptibility, being mutually contradictory, cannot belong to a single [cognition]. Therefore, these two cognitions, consisting of apprehension and recollection, have distinct objects.

To this we reply: First of all, from this cognition, a single reality delimited by prior and posterior time is indeed perceived; that this [perceived thing] is not its object contradicts experience. Furthermore, recognition and recollection do not take a single object as their support. Therefore, on the strength of the fact that it is experienced as a single cognition, it must be accepted that this [cognition] has both [the past and present moments] as its object.

Furthermore, scholars postulate even an unperceived cause for the production of a perceived effect; however, they do not deny a manifest effect simply because its cause is unperceived, for that would entail the absurd consequence of denying the very diversity of the world. Therefore, although the sense organ and the mental impression (saṃskāra) are individually incapable, through the power of their combined causes, they will apprehend both objects, and this cognition shall attain the status of perception (*pratyakṣatā*) by conforming to the capacities of both the object and the sense organ.

And is it not the case that where each individual member is incapable, there the collection of them together is also incapable? No, for we observe that earth, water, seeds, and so forth—though each acting individually—produce sprouts and the like when they possess mutual proximity. It is well-established that where the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is of a distinct nature, the effect is likewise of a distinct nature; therefore, its directness (*pratyakṣatā*) and indirectness (*aparokṣatā*), characterized by the objects being present or absent, will not be contradictory.

For this very reason, even in the absence of sensory contact, there is indeed perception belonging to the prior time, because perceptuality consists in being the object of a cognition born of the senses and because it is invariably concomitant with that alone. Even when determining what is not present, the sense organ determines only the state of prior time and not the state of future time, because in that case the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is absent as a cooperative cause.

Nor is there any logical inconsistency in a single entity existing at two different times, such that one who synthesizes its existence across both times would be deemed a mere conceptualizer (*kalpanā*). For it is observed that a single thing can be related to multiple qualifiers, as in the case of Caitra with respect to both an umbrella and a book. There is no difference between the simultaneous relation to an umbrella and a book and the successive relation to two points in time; for in both cases, there is no distinction in the cognition of a single entity being delimited by two qualifiers.

Thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), by determining a single reality (*vastutattva*) that persists through differences of place, time, and state, conceals the arising and perishing of entities at every moment. If it is argued that this cognition is erroneous, we say no, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). If it is argued that the very proof of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is the subverting evidence, we reply: an inference arises only when its object is not subverted by perception; yet if that inference has arisen, perception is subverted—this results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).

This rule does not apply to perception, because perception is independent [of other means of knowledge]. In cases such as a flame, perception has the universal (sāmānya) as its object, while inference has the particular (viśeṣa) as its object; thus, since there is no contradiction, there is no prohibition against the arising of inference from perception. Enough of this. — *Nyāyakandalī* [89] [pp. 207–210]

As for one who, out of excessive arrogance, asserts that momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the very absence of such experience is the answer. For the cognition is "this is blue," but not "this is momentary. Momentariness is not distinct from blueness, because it lacks any separate causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, when blueness is apprehended, momentariness is also apprehended, due to the non-apprehension of the difference between extremely similar moments.

If you say, "It is not so determined," oh, what another excellence of wisdom this is, that one speaks even after explaining experience itself! To say that "what is not determined is apprehended" is a mere mirage, because we do not admit any basis for establishing the status of being "seen by perception" other than a determination produced by the power of perception. To assert an identity between two things such that, when one is being determined, the other is necessarily not determined—like blue and yellow—is nothing but idle chatter.

If it is argued that momentary direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) grasps momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), which is the state of abiding for only a single moment, by delimiting the existence of an object as existing at its own [the cognition's] simultaneous time—thereby excluding its non-connection with that time and also excluding connection with another time which would deviate from its absence at that time; this is like clutching at a blade of *kāśa* or *kuśa* grass. Cognition does not even grasp itself; how then could it grasp the object’s existence at a time simultaneous with itself? Let it grasp it.

Or, even so, regarding the claim that "this did not exist previously and will not exist later," perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not alert here, because it does not grasp prior and posterior time. Furthermore, while the determination of the present time logically excludes what is not that time—due to the contradiction between two states of being—it does not exclude connection with other times, for there is no contradiction in a single entity having multiple connections, like a gem on a string. This point has been elaborated by us in the *Tattvaprabodha* and the *Tattvasaṃvādinī*, and thus is not expanded upon here.

Furthermore, if one accepts the momentariness of all entities, whose is *saṃsāra*? If it is argued that it belongs to the stream of consciousness (*jñānasantāna*), we say no; for there is no such thing as a "stream" apart from the members of the stream (*santānin*). Now, if it is thought that *saṃsāra* is not the connection of a single entity with multiple bodies and so forth, but rather the non-interruption of the stream of consciousness—and that this is not untenable even if things are momentary—that too is worthless. For there is no evidence that the consciousness of the womb and so forth is produced by a consciousness belonging to a previous existence; indeed, an object does not arise solely from something of the same class, since smoke can arise even from something of a different class, namely fire.

Now, it may be argued that the established rule is this: that which follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and the excellence (*atiśaya*) of another thing is of the same genus as that thing and is its material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, cognition possesses the excellence of having consciousness as its nature (*bodhātmakatva*), and this does not exist in the elements such as earth and the rest. Therefore, since it is established that whatever possesses this excellence has a homogeneous material cause, it is proven that embryonic cognition is preceded by another cognition; for if there were a deviation from a cause, it would follow that the effect is accidental (*ākasmika*).

That too is without substance; for just as fire, though produced from wood-drilling and other means that lack the nature of burning, arises with an excellence of burning, so too it is possible for an excellence of the nature of cognition to arise from the eyes and other organs despite their lacking the nature of cognition. Consequently, there is no occasion for postulating causes that possess the nature of cognition [as belonging to a previous life], and thus the establishment of a prior birth will not occur. Furthermore, even "another birth" is not established, because there is no evidence for the claim that at death, another cognition must be linked by the final cognition of the body.

If it is argued that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in this: "Whatever exists in a state where its causes are complete necessarily produces that effect—just as a seed in a state of complete production produces a sprout, and so too the final moment of consciousness exists in a state of complete production of knowledge"—we say no, because this is contradicted by the case of flames and the like. If it is argued that the final moment of a flame lacks completeness because its causal state is deficient due to the exhaustion of oil or the wick, then [the same applies to] the final consciousness, which is likewise impaired by the agony of death.

Is it not poorly argued to say that the state of being a complete cause for that which is afflicted is unestablished? As for the claim that there would be no future world (*paraloka*) if things were momentary (*kṣaṇikatva*), let us stop here.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [90], p. 210.

Furthermore, by means of effort, the conscious controller of the body is inferred—just as a charioteer is inferred from the movement of a chariot—through the activities of engagement and withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtti*) which inhere in the body and are capable of securing what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful; and also through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. How so? Because we observe modified movements in the air confined within the body, like a person blowing a bellows; because of the regular activity of closing and opening the eyes, like an operator of a wooden puppet; and because of being the cause of the body’s growth, healing of wounds, and the regrowth of broken parts, like a householder. (Nyāyakandalī, pp. 210–212)

In the *Ātmasiddhi*, he states another means of valid cognition as well: "by those two which inhere in the body. By means of activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*), an agent possessing effort is inferred as the controller of the *vigraha*, that is, the body. The phrase "which inhere in the body" is stated in order to exclude the activity and cessation of creepers and the like. Furthermore, the phrase "capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful" is used to exclude the activity and cessation of a dead body impelled by a stream of water. [p.211]

Beneficial is happiness and non-beneficial is suffering; the acquisition and avoidance of these two consist in the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the non-beneficial. In this context, "by means of those that are capable and competent" implies the undertaking of intentional activity. The phrase "like a charioteer by means of the movement of the chariot" provides an illustrative example. By way of the adoption of means for attainment and the avoidance of means for abandonment: activity capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the non-beneficial is preceded by effort, because it is a specific kind of action, just like the movement of a chariot.

Alternatively, the body is presided over by one possessing effort, because it is the locus of specific actions, like a chariot. And [the phrase] "by means of the vital breaths, etc."—it should be understood that an agent possessing effort is inferred by means of the vital breaths and so forth. By the expression "by means of the vital breaths, etc.," there is an inclusion of all the marks mentioned in the sūtra: "Inhalation, exhalation, opening and closing of the eyes, life, movement of the mind, and the modifications of the other sense organs, as well as pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, are the marks of the self" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.2.8).

He demonstrates that inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*) serve as marks [of the soul] by means of a question: "In the body... Air has the inherent nature of moving transversely; yet, in the air contained within the body—which is designated as *prāṇa* and *apāna*—one observes a modified action, namely upward movement and downward movement, which is contrary to its natural state. Therefore, an agent possessing effort who presides over the body is inferred, for it is he who impels the air in such a way, since otherwise this modification would be impossible. It is like one blowing a bellows.

The example is as follows: the body is presided over by an agent possessing effort, because it is the substratum of modified air preceded by volition, like a bellows. By the phrase "appropriated by the body," its being preceded by volition is demonstrated; for otherwise, there would be an inconclusive argument due to cases such as the movement of wind in a pair of bellows. By means of the regulated action of closing and opening the eyes, it is like the operator of a wooden mechanical doll; thus, "closing" (nimeṣa) is the action that causes the conjunction of the eyelids, and "opening" (unmeṣa) is the action for the purpose of their disjunction.

By that action, an exertive presiding agent is inferred for the body, just as one is for a wooden mechanical device. Even by the force of the wind, the opening and closing of the eyes of a wooden machine might occur; therefore, the term "regulated" (*niyatena*) is used to exclude that possibility. By this, he demonstrates dependence upon will. The body is presided over by an exertive agent because its opening and closing of the eyes are dependent on will, just like a wooden mechanical device.

He states the inference based on the mark of life (*jīvanaliṅgaka-anumāna*) with the words "of the body" (*dehasya*). Growth is well known. Furthermore, because of the healing—that is, the rejoining—of what is wounded or broken, an intelligent presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātā*) is inferred, like a house-owner who exerts effort. The growth and healing of wounds in a body are produced by one who possesses effort, because they consist of the growth and healing of wounds and fractures, just like the growth and healing of wounds and fractures in a house.

If it is argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because growth and so forth occur in trees and the like, we say no; for even those are created by the Lord (Īśvara). However, trees and the like do not possess a self (sātmaka), because they lack a specific connection with a self capable of producing cognition and other mental functions. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [91] [p. 213]

By means of mental activity—which is caused by the connection with the instruments that grasp desired objects—a single entity is known to be the observer of both, like a child who throws a ball in the corners of a house; for after the perception of an object of sight, one observes a modification of the sense of taste through the sequence of the recollection of flavor, just as a spectator looking through many windows perceives both sides.
Furthermore, the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is inferred from the qualities of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort.
*Nyāyakandalī* [91] [pp. 213–216]

He presents an inference based on the mark of mental activity (*manogatiliṅgaka*), beginning with the words "the desired object" (*abhimata*) and so forth. The "desired object" (*abhimato viṣayaḥ*) is the thing one wishes to grasp; its "grasper" (*grāhaka*) is the instrument such as the eye, and the "connection of the mind" (*manaḥ-sambandhaḥ*) with that [instrument]—it is by means of this, namely through the movement of the mind (*manaḥ-karma*) caused thereby, that an impeller of the mind is inferred. Just as a child who possesses effort is inferred as the impeller of a ball held in his hand toward a ball placed in the corners or rooms of a house upon the ground, so too is the impeller of the mind inferred.

The mind is to be impelled by one who exerts effort, because it is the locus of activity caused by connection with a desired object, like a child’s hand holding a ball. However, that which is impelled by wind and the like may also come into contact with what is undesired; therefore, the phrase "desired object" was stated [to exclude such cases]. [He demonstrates the modification of another sense organ: "the object of the eye," and so forth.

Immediately after perceiving—that is, grasping—a form that is the object of the eye, a transformation of another sense-organ, the tongue, is observed through the sequence of recollecting a taste; therefore, like an observer situated between two windows, a single entity who perceives both form and taste by means of two senses is inferred.

What is being said? Upon seeing the form of some desired object, there arises a desire for its associated flavor previously experienced, due to the recollection [of that flavor]; from that [desire], an effort—dependent upon the conjunction of the self and the mind—produces a modification in the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*).

That modification of the gustatory faculty, inferred from the flow of saliva, would not belong to the sensory consciousness (*indriyacaitanya*), because there is no perception of the concomitance between color and taste by the two distinct faculties of sight and taste respectively, and thus no recollection of taste upon seeing a color. Yet this modification exists; therefore, there must be some observer other than the sense-faculties who, having seen the color, remembers the taste.

If it is argued that the body itself will be the perceiver of both [the past and the present], we say no; for since the difference between the bodies of a child and an old man is established by their difference in size, it would follow that what was experienced in the state of childhood could not be remembered in the state of old age.

Not only by the reasons previously stated, but also by the qualities such as pleasure, pain, desire, and aversion, the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is inferred [as follows]: "Pleasure and the rest must reside in a substance because they are qualities, like color and so forth; that which is this possessor of qualities is the Self. Now, [an objection is raised: "But pleasure and the rest reside only in the body"; to this he replies: "And these are not qualities of the body or the sense organs. Since no matter can be established by a mere thesis alone, with this intention he asks: "Why?"

He states the reason: "Because there is no syntactic unity with the *ahaṅkāra*. Syntactic unity (*ekavākyatvam*) with the *ahaṅkāra*, that is, the notion "I," means having a common substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatvam*). This is because pleasure and the like are perceived as delimited by the *ahaṅkāra*, as in the cognitions "I am happy" and "I am miserable," where the object of the notion of "I" is that which is delimited by pleasure and so forth. Furthermore, the notion of "I" does not have the body as its objective support, for if it did, it would follow that such a notion would be absent in the bodies of others. If it is argued that this notion occurs only in one's own body, we say no, because there is no distinction [between one's own body and another's].

If the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), which has the body as its objective support, were to perceive another's body just as it does one's own, then—just as the cognition of grossness and so forth occurs regarding one's own body, it would likewise occur regarding another's body, since the essential nature [of the body] is no different in both cases. However, if there is a distinction based on the fact of being related to oneself, then this notion is produced solely by that [relation] and does not have the essential nature as its objective support; for if it had that as its objective support, it would not occur even when directed inwardly.

For this very reason, this [consciousness] does not have the sense organs as its support, because the sense organs are themselves beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), and because this [consciousness] is a perceptual cognition that does not depend on signs, words, or the like. Therefore, pleasure and the other [feelings] are also not objects of the body or the sense organs. Furthermore, for whomever there is an experiencer, for that very person there is recollection, desire, the appropriation of the means to pleasure, the arising of pleasure, and aversion toward pains; all this is self-evident to every embodied being. And it has already been stated that experience and recollection do not belong to the body or the sense organs. For this reason as well, pleasure and the others are not their objects.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya*: And these [qualities] are not qualities of the body or the sense organs; why? Because they do not form a single syntactical unit with the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), because they reside in specific locations, because they do not persist as long as the substance [in which they inhere] exists, and because they are not perceptible by the external senses; likewise, because the word "I" is distinct from words such as "earth" and so forth. *Nyāyakandalī*: [pp. 216–218] And these [qualities] are not qualities of the body or the sense organs. Why? First, because they do not form a single syntactical unit with the word "I. If they were qualities of the body or the sense organs, then the cognition "I am fair" or "I am blind" would be possible; however, since the word "I" is never used as a synonym for the body or the sense organs, it follows that the qualities denoted by "I" are distinct from those belonging to the body and the sense organs. Second, because they reside in specific locations (*pradeśavṛttitva*). Qualities such as color and so forth belong to the whole of their substrate, whereas pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and cognition are perceived as residing in specific parts of the body. Therefore, they are not qualities of the body. Third, because they do not persist as long as the substance exists (*ayāvaddravyabhāvitva*). Qualities such as color and so forth persist as long as the substance exists, whereas pleasure and the rest do not; therefore, they are not qualities of the body. Fourth, because they are not perceptible by the external senses (*bāhyendriyāpratyakṣatva*). Qualities such as color and so forth are perceptible by the external senses, whereas pleasure and the rest are not; therefore, they are not qualities of the body. Furthermore, because the word "I" is distinct from words such as "earth" and so forth, it is established that the object denoted by "I" is distinct from earth and the other elements. Thus, the self is established as a substance distinct from the body and the sense organs. It is not the case that the word "I" refers to the body or the sense organs, for if it did, there would be no distinction between the word "I" and words like "body" or "eye," and one would never hear the expression "my body" or "my eye. Since such expressions are indeed heard, it is clear that the word "I" denotes something other than the body and the sense organs. Consequently, the self is established as a substance distinct from the body and the sense organs. It is not the case that the word "I" refers to the mind (*manas*), for the mind is an instrument of cognition, whereas the word "I" denotes the cognizer. Moreover, the mind is imperceptible, whereas the word "I" is used in reference to something that is the subject of experience. Therefore, the self is a substance distinct from the body, the sense organs, and the mind. It is eternal, omnipresent, and the substratum of consciousness. It is the agent of action and the enjoyer of its fruits. It is distinct from the body, the sense organs, the mind, and all objects of cognition. Thus, the existence of the self is established through inference based on the nature of the word "I" and the characteristics of pleasure, pain, and so forth. It is not possible to deny the self, for its existence is proven by the very fact of our own experience and the linguistic usage of the first-person pronoun. Without a self, there could be no ownership of actions or experiences, nor could there be any continuity of personal identity across time. Therefore, the self is an undeniable reality. It is neither the body nor the sense organs, but a distinct, eternal, and omnipresent substance. This concludes the proof of the self. It is not the case that the self is merely a collection of aggregates, for the aggregates are momentary and lack the capacity for memory or recognition. Without a permanent self, the connection between past and future experiences would be impossible. Therefore, the self is a necessary postulate for the coherence of human experience and the validity of moral responsibility. It is the locus of consciousness and the ultimate subject of all inquiry. He states another argument: "Because they exist in a limited location (*pradeśavṛttitvāt*). It is observed that pleasure and the like exist in a limited location, based on such cognitions as "there is pleasure in my foot" or "there is pain in my head. Consequently, there is an absence of their being qualities of the body or the sense organs, because it is never the case that the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of those [two] exist in a non-pervasive manner (*avyāpyavṛtti*).

Pleasure and the like are not specific qualities of the body or the sense organs, because they do not exist as pervading occurrences (*avyāpyavṛttitvāt*). Those which are specific qualities of the body or the sense organs are observed to be pervading occurrences, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; however, pleasure and the like are not pervading occurrences. Therefore, they are not qualities of the body or the sense organs—this is a negative inference (*vyatirekī*). There is no deviation in this rule: the sound that is a quality of the portion of space delimited by the ear-canal—which has attained the state of the auditory organ—is pervasive throughout that cavity.

For this reason as well, pleasure and the like are not qualities of the body, because they are produced by a substance distinct from earth (the body), just as color and so forth are the illustration [of qualities belonging to a different substance]. However, this reason does not apply to the refutation of their being qualities of the sense organs, because it would lead to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to sound, which is a quality of the auditory organ. For this reason as well, pleasure and the like are not qualities of the body or the sense organs, because they are not perceptible by the external sense organs. There are two possible courses for qualities of the body and the sense organs: non-perceptibility, as in the case of gravity (*gurutva*) and so forth; and perceptibility by the external sense organs, as in the case of color (*rūpa*) and so forth.

But pleasure and the like belong to a different category; therefore, they are not qualities of that [body]. Since their status as qualities of the body and the sense organs has been refuted, it is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that the self is inferred by means of them.

Now, it may be objected that pleasure and pain are modifications, and thus cannot belong to the eternal self (*ātman*). If they were to exist, then the self would be non-eternal, like a piece of leather. This is not so; for although those two arise and perish, there is no loss of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the self, which is distinct from them. Indeed, for an eternal entity, modification is not accepted as the destruction of its own nature or the production of another nature; rather, the cessation of one quality (*guṇa*) and the production of another quality is entirely uncontradicted.

Now, what is produced for this eternal [self] by pleasure and pain? It is the experience of its own object. When there is the experience of pleasure and pain, what benefit is there for that which is devoid of increase or decrease? This very thing is the benefit for it, and this alone is the increase: namely, the state of being an enjoyer of pleasure and pain when such [experience] exists. The same applies to the word "I" as well.

Just as the self is inferred by means of pleasure and so forth, it is likewise inferred by the word "I. For the word "I," when employed by experts in both worldly and Vedic usage, cannot be devoid of a referent. Nor is it logical for its own form to be its referent, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself. As it has been said: "No word ever denotes itself."

Therefore, that which is its denotation is the Self. [Objection: But surely this will be a designator of earth and the other elements themselves. To this he replies: "Because of its distinction from words such as 'earth'. Whatever is the designator of a certain object is observed to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word for that object, as in "the substance is earth" or simply "earth."

However, the word "I" (ahaṃ) has a distinction from words denoting earth and so forth, namely, an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*), because expressions such as "I am earth" or "I am water" do not occur; therefore, this [word] does not have earth and so forth as its object. [Objection: But is it not observed that this [word] refers precisely to the body, as in "I am fat"? [Reply: No, because of the usage "I know" and "I remember. Furthermore, the status of the body as the substratum of knowledge and memory has been refuted. Therefore, the usage of that [word "I"] with respect to the body is by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the body's being an auxiliary to the self (*ātman*), just as there is the designation "this is indeed I" with respect to a servant.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [93–94] [p. 219]: Its qualities are cognition (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), mental impression (*saṃskāra*), number (*saṃkhyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and disjunction (*vibhāga*). In the section concerning the marks of the self (*ātmaliṅga*), those beginning with cognition and ending with effort have been established. Merit and demerit are established because it is stated that they are not the causes of the qualities of another self. Mental impression is established because it is stated to be the cause for the arising of memory. Number is established because of the statement regarding the distribution [of individual selves]. *Nyāyakandalī* [93] [pp. 219–221]: Regarding the qualities of the self: cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction are its qualities. Among these, from the section on the marks of the self, those starting with cognition and ending with effort are established as qualities of the self. Merit and demerit are established because it is stated that they are not the causes of the qualities belonging to other selves. Mental impression is established because it is stated to be the cause for the production of memory. Number is established by the statement regarding the distinct distribution [of individual selves]. Dimension is established by the statement regarding the size of the body. Distinctness is established by the statement regarding the difference between one self and another. Moreover, it is eternal because it is partless; that which has parts is non-eternal, whereas this [self] is partless. This being established, he describes the qualities of the self with the words "his qualities," and so forth. He shows the author of the *Sūtras*’ agreement regarding the existence of intellect (*buddhi*) and the other qualities in the self by stating: "[In the section on the marks of the self, those beginning with intellect and ending with effort are established]. The phrase "in the section on the marks of the self" refers to the *sūtra* concerning inhalation (*prāṇa*), exhalation (*apāna*), and so on (VS 3.2.4). Their establishment follows from the statement: "Because merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are not causes for the qualities of another self."

Refuting the view of some who maintain that the act of giving, residing in the donor, produces the act of receiving, which resides in the recipient, the author of the Sūtras stated: "Because the qualities of one self are not the cause of qualities in another self" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 6.1.7).

This is the meaning: because the qualities of one self, such as pleasure and so forth, lack causality with respect to the qualities of another self, such as pleasure and so forth, it is illogical for *dharma* and *adharma*, which reside in one place, to produce an effect in another. By this, the fact that *dharma* and *adharma* are qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇa*) is stated; otherwise, the argument for their non-productivity through the description of their similarity to pleasure and so forth would be incoherent. "Impression (*saṃskāra*) [is the cause] in the production of memory."

The sūtra, "Memory [arises] from the non-distinctness of the contact between the self and the mind, and from mental impressions" (Vaiśeṣika-sūtra 9.2.6), characterizes memory as follows: A previously experienced object is remembered; however, the [original] experience is not the cause therein, because it has long since perished. Nor is the absence of experience the cause, because since absence is devoid of degrees, the distinctions of memory—such as being vivid or faint—would be untenable, and furthermore, the practice of repetition would be rendered useless.

Therefore, it is postulated that a *saṃskāra* (latent impression) is produced in the self by experience, from which memory arises. However, for those who claim that even a destroyed experience itself is the cause of memory, it would follow that a destroyed *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth could serve as the means for attaining results such as heaven; thus, even the doctrine of the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) would be abolished. "Number [is established] because of the statement regarding their distinctness":

the meaning is that the number of plurality is established because the multiplicity of selves is demonstrated by the sūtra, "The selves are many because of their distinctness" (*Vaiśeṣikasūtra* 3.2.20, or alternatively 3.3.16).

Now, what is this established principle? It is the non-connection (*apratisandhāna*) of cognitions, pleasures, and so forth, which arise in various bodies. For if there were a single self (*aikātmya*), then just as that which was experienced in childhood is connected with in old age—thinking "I had pleasure" or "I had pain"—likewise, even that experienced in another body would be connected, because the experiencer is one and the same. But this is not the case; therefore, there are distinct selves for each body.

If it is argued that just as there is a fixed determination of the perception of sound everywhere through the single space (*ākāśa*) being the auditory organ (*śrotra*), due to the differences in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the ear-cavity, so too, despite the oneness of the Self (*ātman*), there is a fixed determination of experience and so forth due to the difference of bodies—this is an unequal comparison. For it is logical that there is a fixed determination in the apprehension of sound according to the restriction of its substratum, because the ear-cavities—which are the causes for the perception of sound—are themselves determined by the two attributes (*dharma*) residing in each individual person.

But if there were only one self (*aikātmya*), since there would be no fixed distribution of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), and thus no fixed distribution of bodies, by what would the distribution of the arising of pleasure, pain, and so forth be determined? For even the connection with the mind (*manas*) would be common to all. However, for one who holds that there are multiple selves (*nānātmānaḥ*), although all selves are connected to all bodies due to their omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), experience is not common to all.

That body which has been initiated by a particular action belongs as its locus of experience to that [agent] alone, not to everyone; likewise, that action belongs to that very person by whose body it was performed, and not to another. Thus, the restriction of one body follows from the restriction of another action, and so on ad infinitum. (Nyāyakandalī [94], pp. 222–223)

Now, if it is thought that even though the Supreme Self (paramātman) is one, there is a systematic distinction due to the mutual difference between the individual selves (jīvātman), that is incorrect; for if there were a difference between the Supreme Self and the individual selves, the doctrine of non-duality (advaita) would be undermined, and it would contradict the scriptural testimony regarding the identity of the individual self and the Supreme Self, namely: "Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms."

If it is argued that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is created by ignorance (*avidyā*), then whose is this ignorance? Is it of Brahman, or rather of the individual souls? First of all, there can be no connection with ignorance for Brahman, because its nature is pure and enlightened. Furthermore, the claim that ignorance resides in the individual soul is refuted by the fallacy of mutual dependence: the distinction of the soul is caused by ignorance, yet ignorance is said to reside in the soul.

If it is argued that the distinction between ignorance (*avidyā*) and the living being (*jīva*) is beginningless, like that of the seed and the sprout? This is untenable because, unlike the distinction between individual instances of seed and sprout, ignorance and the living being lack ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*). Furthermore, while the mutual causality of seed and sprout is established by way of distinct individual instances, the living being is one and the same throughout all millions of existences. This is evident from the similarity of species among newborn infants in various wombs—such as human, animal, or bird—as well as their desire for specific types of food, which results from actions performed in previous births within those respective species.

Because the connection with beginningless bodies is perceived through a succession of inferences based on the repeated practice of various specific births, and because the distinction between individual souls (*jīva*) therein is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), it is inconsistent to claim that [the world] is [produced] by ignorance.

Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is likewise without beginning or end, it is a reflection of Brahman; therefore, on the authority of the scripture stating, "Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined," one must conclude that it is the very reality of Brahman, without beginning or end, which manifests within all bodies. If that were the case, the established order [of experience] would be untenable; thus it is well said: "The selves are many, because of their distinct arrangements. As for the scriptural texts concerning non-difference, they have a figurative meaning—this is the general direction of the argument.

Furthermore, on the view that there are many selves, it is not the case that the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) would be utterly destroyed at the end when all have been liberated in succession; for it is impossible for an infinite number [of souls] to be finally diminished or increased. As the venerable authors of the *Vārttika* have said:
"And for this very reason, even as the wise are being constantly liberated, there is no emptiness [of the world], because the living beings in the world of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) are infinite."
"Being neither less nor more than the ultimate limit is possible for that which possesses magnitude;
however, in the case of an immeasurable entity, their occurrence is certainly impossible. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [95], p. 224.

Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is also established for this very reason. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement "the Self," it possesses the dimension of infinite magnitude (*paramamahatparimāṇa*). Since pleasure and the like arise from contact, [the Self] possesses conjunction (*saṃyoga*); and since it is the destroyer of that [conjunction], it possesses disjunction (*vibhāga*).
— *Nyāyakandalī*, pp. 224–226.

Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is also established for this very reason. The intention is that separateness is proven by the very statement, “They are not non-distinct, because they are established as such,” since separateness follows the pattern of number (*saṅkhyā*). Likewise, from the statement “the self” (*ātman*), its dimension is that of the supreme great (*paramamahatparimāṇa*). The meaning is that the dimension of the self is the supreme great, because the self is all-pervading (*vibhu*) like space, based on the words of the author of the Sūtras: “Space is great because of its pervasiveness” and “so too is the self” (VS 7.1.22).

Furthermore, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the self is understood from the upward flaming of fire and the horizontal movement of air; for these two are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). And that unseen force cannot exist without being connected to its substratum, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is a direct connection with another substance possible for an unseen force inherent in the self; thus, it follows that its connection occurs through the mediation of a connection with its own substratum.

From this, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the self, characterized by its connection with all corporeal substances, is established. If it is argued that the upward flaming of fire occurs by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*) and not through the power of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), then what is this so-called "nature"? Is it the state of being fire (*vahnitva*), or the capacity to burn (*dāhakatva*), or a specific quality of form (*rūpaviśeṣa*)? In the case of a heated iron ball, these properties would belong to the fire [present within it] as well.

Now, if you argue that the nature [of fire] consists in its arising from a specific kind of fuel, then upward flaming would not occur in cases where it arises without fuel or where it arises from lightning and the like. Or, if you claim that there exists some supersensible (atīndriya) nature in certain individuals for whom upward flaming is observed, then what is the objection against such a quality in the person (puruṣaguṇa)? For when an action has neither gravity, fluidity, nor momentum as its cause, its production must arise from a specific quality of the self (ātmaviśeṣaguṇa), just as the action of the hand arises from human effort.

Gravity and other such qualities are not the causes of upward flaming, horizontal movement, and so forth, because they are absent [in those cases] and because they are contrary to those specific effects. Therefore, it is logical that these too arise solely from a specific quality of the self (*ātmaviśeṣaguṇa*). Upward flaming, horizontal blowing, and so on are produced by a specific quality of the self, because—while lacking causes such as being a general quality—they are actions, like the action of the hand produced by human effort.

Because pleasure and the like arise from *sannikarṣa* (contact), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established. Since the qualities of the self, such as pleasure and so forth, are produced by the conjunction of the mind with the self, conjunction is proven to exist in the self; for that which resides in a different locus cannot function as an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause). "Because it causes the destruction of that, disjunction (*vibhāga*) [is established]" means: because it causes the destruction of that conjunction, disjunction is proven; since both the self and the mind are eternal, there is an absence of the destruction of the substratum, which is the cause of [conjunction's] destruction. This is the meaning.

But surely, if the self were eternal and remained so, then for one who perceives the self as eternal and is overwhelmed by thirst for pleasure, there would be attachment to the means of pleasure and aversion toward the means of pain; from these two come engagement and withdrawal, from which arise merit and demerit, and from those comes saṃsāra—thus, there would be no liberation.

If it is argued that liberation is possible because, in the absence of a self, one realizes "I myself do not exist," and thus, through the lack of reliance on anything, there is an absence of activity and so forth for one who is free from passion and aversion toward all things—this is not so. For even while maintaining the view of a permanent self, liberation arises by way of the production of dispassion through the perception of defects in sense objects; enough of this.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [96–97] [p. 226]: Mind is that which is conjoined with the quality of *manastva*. Even when the self, the senses, and their objects are present, since we observe that cognition, pleasure, and so forth arise after having not existed, another instrument (the mind) is inferred.

Because memory is observed to arise even when the ears and other [senses] are not functioning, and because pleasure and so forth are objects of internal apprehension that are not grasped by the external sense organs;
*Nyāyakandalī* [96] [pp. 226–230].

Having first described the self (*ātman*) because of its primacy, he speaks next for the purpose of defining the mind (*manas*): "It is called 'mind' due to its connection with the property of mindness (*manastva*). The explanation is as before. Mindness is a universal (*sāmānya*) that is to be inferred when the individual instances of mind (*manovyakti*) exist in a state of difference. For among those individuals whose qualities and effects are identical, another universal is observed, as in the case of jars and the like; and since the individual instances of mind possess identical qualities and effects, they therefore possess the connection with another universal.

Considering that the definition of its properties is improper as long as the mind is unestablished, he states the proof for its existence: "Even when the self, the sense organ, and the object are in proximity..."

Since the self (*ātman*) is omnipresent, it indeed possesses simultaneous contact with all the sense organs; likewise, the sense organs also come into contact with objects that are present before them. Nevertheless, it is observed that while one object is being perceived, cognition, pleasure, and so forth do not arise regarding other objects, and they arise upon the cessation [of that perception]. From this observation, an additional instrument (*karaṇa*) is inferred beyond the contact of the self, the sense organs, and the objects—an instrument by whose presence the production of cognition, pleasure, and the like occurs.

Furthermore, there is non-arising due to non-proximity. The contacts between the self, the sense organs, and their objects depend upon another instrument for the production of an effect, because even when they are present, they do not produce the effect—just like threads and other such materials. And that which is required as this dependent instrument is the mind (*manas*). What is the proof that there is contact of the sense organ with another object that is not perceived at the time of the perception of one object? It is simply the proximity of the sense organ to its own substrate.

At the time of perceiving a form (*rūpa*), odors and other objects are also brought into contact with the sense of smell and the rest, because they are situated in proximity to their respective bases, just like the odors and other objects currently being perceived.

He states another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well: "Because the arising of memory is observed even when the ear and other senses are not functioning. Memory, first of all, is produced by a sense faculty because it is a cognition, like the cognition of odors and so forth. Yet the ear and other senses are not its instruments, because memory is observed to arise in the deaf and others even in the absence of the operation of the ear and other senses. Therefore, that sense faculty which is its instrument is the mind (*manas*).

The inference of another instrument is not based on the aforementioned reason alone; rather, it is also because pleasure (*sukha*) and the like—which are not apprehended by external senses such as the eyes—are objects of a different kind of apprehension in relation to form (*rūpa*) and other such objects. Thus he says: "By the external senses. The cognition of pleasure and so forth is produced by a sense organ, because it is a direct perception (*aparokṣapratīti*), just like the cognition of form and the like. And that sense organ is the mind (*manas*), because the eyes and the other external senses have no operation with respect to it.

If it is argued that pleasure and so forth are of the nature of cognition because they share an identical cause, and thus are self-cognized and not apprehended by another instrument, we say no; for if pleasure and pain were of the nature of cognition, it would follow that there is no distinction between them. Furthermore, even if their aspect of awareness (*bodhākāra*) were common to both, pleasure and pain could not be of the nature of cognition if they were mutually distinct, because the aspects of pleasure and pain are themselves mutually exclusive.

Furthermore, these two [pleasure and pain] do not arise from an object that is non-different from the cognition, because cognition arises from an object, and because pleasure and pain arise from that [cognition] when assisted by latent impressions (*vāsanā*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of neutral cognition (*upekṣājñāna*). Nor is it established that cognition is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), for there is no example for a single entity occupying the roles of both object and instrument; if it is argued that a lamp which is self-illuminating serves as an example, it is not so, for even that is known by a person and made known by the eye.

Cognition is its activity (*kriyā*), but it is not itself the instrument (*karaṇa*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the activity. If it is argued that—just as for proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*), there is a simultaneous state of being both object and agent for the self in its own cognition, so too for cognition there is the status of being the instrument and so forth—that is not so, because there is no contradiction. Being the object consists in being the objective domain of the cognitive activity; and being the agent consists in independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to that very same activity. There is no contradiction between independence and being the objective domain.

The state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and the state of being an action (*kriyātva*) are mutually contradictory in a single entity due to their respective natures as accomplished and that which is to be accomplished, since there is no identity between a cause (*kāraṇa*) and an instrument (*karaṇa*). Likewise, there is a contradiction between these two: being an instrument consists in being prompted by another, whereas agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in not being prompted by another; this is because they possess the natures of affirmation and negation. Therefore, it is not logical for these to coexist in one and the same thing. *Nyāyakandalī* [97] [pp. 231–233]

Now, if it is thought that the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth does not constitute self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) for cognition, but rather that its very arising as something whose nature is self-luminous (*svaprakāśasvabhāva*) is what constitutes self-awareness—here too it is examined: Is that the manifestation of the object, or of itself? If it is the manifestation of the object, then from its arising there would be awareness of the object, but not of itself; thus, the fault of its own non-awareness remains.

Now, this [position] holds that the light itself is its own manifestation, and thus the light is both the manifestor and the manifested; consequently, the identity of the action and the instrument remains as it was. Nor is there any illustrative example for the claim that the very arising of a thing constitutes an action upon itself. Furthermore, as for the proof stated for the establishment of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*): "Whatever has its manifestation dependent on something else, that manifests when that [other thing] is manifesting—just as a jar, whose manifestation depends on a lamp, or form and so forth, whose manifestation depends on cognition."

In that case as well, if it is intended that cognition itself is the manifestation of the object, then it is unestablished that color-form and so forth have a manifestation dependent upon that [cognition], and the reason would be inconclusive with respect to the sense-faculties. Alternatively, if the manifestation of the object produced by cognition is not cognition itself but rather the manifestation of the object, then there is an absence of an example, because a lamp, which produces cognition, lacks the quality of being a manifestor of the object. By this, the following is also refuted:
"For one whose apprehension is not perceptible, the perception of an object is not established."

The perceptuality of cognition is not the seeing of an object, but rather the arising of consciousness. In that case, even if the cognition itself is not consciously apprehended, the awareness of the object is established by the mere fact of its arising. If it is asked, "How can the arising of one thing be the awareness of another?", what can we do? It is due to the very nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*). This being so, it does not follow that everything is perceived; for [cognition] arises with a nature restricted to the awareness of a specific object, determined by the totality of its own causes, and is perceivable only by a specific cognizer.

Others, however, say this: "When an object is manifested through its contact with cognition, consciousness itself is manifested because its nature is luminosity, just like a lamp; and the self is also manifested because it is the locus of that luminosity, just like the wick of a lamp. Thus, there is perception as a triad. This too is incorrect, because when the cognition "this is a jar" is being experienced, neither the knower nor the act of knowing appears therein.

However, where there is the appearance of these two—as in the cognition "I know the jar"—once that knowledge has arisen, the object as qualified by the knower and the knowledge is the object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). But there is no appearance of the knower and the knowledge within a visual cognition, for that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that those two too would be objects of visual perception.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [98] [pp. 233–237]

Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*). From the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition, its oneness in each body is established. Distinctness is also established for this very reason. From the statement of its absence [of magnitude], it possesses atomic dimension. From the statements regarding moving away and moving toward, it possesses conjunction and disjunction. Because it is corporeal, it possesses priority, posteriority, and mental impression. Because it lacks touch, it does not originate other substances. Because it possesses motion, it is corporeal.

It is non-conscious because it would follow that it possesses a common body; it exists for the sake of another because it is an instrument; it is a substance because it possesses qualities; and it moves rapidly due to the influence of effort and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Thus ends the section on substances in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.

*Nyāyakandalī* [98] [pp. 233–238]: Thus, the mind having been established, the author sets forth its qualities with the words "its qualities," and so on. Even the possession of the eight qualities beginning with number (*saṅkhyā*) constitutes the specific difference (*vaidharmya*) of the mind. He states the existence of number with the words "effort," and so on. When the doubt arises as to whether the mind is one in each body or manifold, the author of the Sūtras stated: "Because of the non-simultaneity of effort and the non-simultaneity of cognitions, there is one mind in each body" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.2.3).

Therefore, oneness is established for each individual body. For if there were a plurality of minds, there would be a plurality of soul-mind conjunctions, and consequently, cognitions and efforts would occur simultaneously; yet, as has been stated, a sequence of cognitions is observed, because when one is occupied with the apprehension of a single object, other objects are not perceived, whereas they are perceived once that occupation has ceased.

Thus, even for volitional efforts (*prayatna*), there is only sequential production, because one who is exerting effort toward one object lacks activity toward another, and because [the effort] exists only when the action is completed. Therefore, the mind (*manas*) is one. Indeed, given its unity, there is only a single conjunction at any one time; thus, it is logically established that there is only a single cognition and a single volitional effort at once. As for the notion of simultaneity in some cases, that is due to rapid succession—like a whirling firebrand—and not a real simultaneity. This is because, having observed a sequence of effects in one instance, one infers the capacity of that very same instrument (the mind) to produce them elsewhere as well.

If this is so, then how is there the appearance of multiple objects in the case of the verse "these trees are in bloom," which expresses two distinct meanings? And how is there the simultaneous impelling and supporting of one's own body? No; for we do not deny that a single cognition can have multiple objects as its basis. Rather, there is simply a distinction between cognitions, but no such simultaneous appearance, because each of those cognitions is restricted to a single object.

Thus, the impelling and sustaining of the body arise from a single specific effort (*prayatna*), just as a single cognition can have multiple objects; likewise, its causes—desire (*icchā*) and effort—are also so. Therefore, nothing is difficult to establish. "Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) also [is established] for this very reason" means that separateness is also proven precisely because of the conformity with number (*saṅkhyā*). From the statement of its absence, the atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) [is understood].

Having stated that "the self is likewise great like space" (*Vaiśeṣikasūtra* 7.1.22), the author of the Sūtras declared, "Because of the absence of that [pervasiveness], the mind is atomic" (*Vaiśeṣikasūtra* 7.1.23). Therefore, it is established that the mind has an atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*). This is because the absence of pervasiveness in eternal substances is invariably concomitant with atomic dimension. Furthermore, the absence of its pervasiveness is understood precisely from the impossibility of simultaneous cognitions.

If the mind were all-pervasive (*vibhu*), then due to its simultaneous connection with all the sense organs, there would be a simultaneity of cognitions regarding color and other objects in contact with the eyes and the rest.

Now, how is it that cognitions do not arise simultaneously regarding objects such as jars, which are perceivable by a single sense organ and are in contact with the eye presided over by the mind? [The answer is: They do not arise because of the simultaneity of the self, the senses, and the objects.

If it is argued that, for this reason, the incapacity of the single conjunction between the self and the mind to produce multiple cognitions simultaneously must be postulated, this is equally true even if the mind is omnipresent; therefore, even if it is not omnipresent, another argument must be stated. That is stated as follows: because of the omnipresence of the self and the mind, in the absence of their mutual conjunction, there would be no production of the qualities of the self—such as cognition, pleasure, and so forth—due to the absence of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

For if the conjunction with the self were the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), the cognition would arise at the location of the object, because qualities that reside in specific locations are produced without being separated from their non-inherent cause. Even if the conjunction of the self and the sense organ were the non-inherent cause, auditory cognition would not arise, because there is no conjunction of the self with the ear, which consists of space (*ākāśa*).

Furthermore, there is no cognition in an external location, nor is there a non-arising of verbal knowledge; therefore, since the conjunction of the self with objects and the conjunction of the self with the sense organs have been ruled out as non-inherent causes, by the method of elimination, the conjunction of the self and the mind is established as the non-inherent cause. And since that [conjunction] is not possible if the mind were all-pervading, there would be a total non-arising of cognitions, pleasure, and so forth; yet their arising does exist. That very fact negates the omnipresence of the mind.

"Conjunction and disjunction [of the mind] are established from the mention of 'departure' (apasarpaṇa) and 'approach' (upasarpaṇa). By the sūtra, "Departure, approach, conjunctions with what is eaten and drunk, and conjunctions with other bodies are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.11), it is stated that the mind's departure from the previous body and its approach to another body are caused by the unseen force; therefore, its conjunction and disjunction are established. Because it possesses corporeality (mūrtatva), it also possesses priority and posteriority (paratva-aparatva) and momentum (saṃskāra).

First, corporeality is established because of its possession of limited magnitude (*vibhava*); therefore, like a jar or similar objects, priority, posteriority, and velocity are established [as qualities] for it. Its non-origination of substance is due to its lack of tangibility. The mind’s lack of tangibility is established—just as in the case of the self—because, while being distinct from the body, it produces cognition of all objects; consequently, like the self, it does not originate substances of its own genus. And its corporeality follows from its possession of motion.

Although its corporeality is established by the demonstration of its atomicity, this is stated for the sake of clarity. Ignorance follows from the consequence that it would possess a body common to all. If the mind were the knower, this body would be a common locus of experience; but such is not the case, because its activity and cessation are always observed in accordance with the intention of a single [individual]. Therefore, the mind is ignorant. Although consciousness has already been refuted, this is stated again here due to the context of the discussion.

Since its insentience has been established, he says: "Because it is an instrument, it exists for the sake of another. This means that it is for the sake of another, serving as a means for the experience of another. Because it possesses qualities (*guṇa*), it is a substance (*dravya*), like earth and the other elements. It should be understood that it moves rapidly due to the influence of being grasped by effort (*prayatna*) and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Being grasped by an effort preceded by desire and aversion, or by an effort preceded by the mere maintenance of life, it moves rapidly from one location to another; likewise, being grasped by the unseen force, it moves rapidly from one body to another at death—this is how it should be understood. The word "iti" marks the conclusion.
