May this ocean of substances be resorted to, which is a source of clusters of pearls in the form of various pure logical principles and possesses corals in the form of clearly established tenets.
Thus ends the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*) in the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on the *Padārthapraveśaka*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrī Śrīdhara.
NK_3_G1ṭXT: Now begins the definition of the category of quality (guṇapadārtha);
Praśastapādabhāṣya [99] [p. 239].

All qualities, such as color and the rest, possess the following characteristics: connection with the nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*), dependence upon a substance (*dravyāśritatva*), the absence of further qualities (*nirguṇatva*), and the absence of activity (*niṣkriyatva*).
— *Nyāyakandalī* [99] [pp. 239–240] Ūṃ.
Homage to the enemy of Mura, who is dark blue like a rain cloud, who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa as his couch, and from whom flows the bliss of embracing the neck of Lakṣmī.

Having explained the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*), he speaks for the purpose of defining qualities (*guṇa*): "of the qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth. The connection with that universal (*sāmānya*) called "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) belongs to the qualities; this is a statement of their mutual similarity (*sādharmya*). It is also a statement of their dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from the other categories. Quality-ness is perceived by perception itself—assisted by instruction—in the case of color and the rest, just as "jewel-ness" is [perceived] in jewels.

As for the fact that this [quality] is not initially apprehended as distinct from action (*karman*) and so forth, that is because its dependence upon a substratum (*āśraya-pāratantrya*) and its extreme similarity [to them] are possible. The phrase "of qualities such as color" (*rūpādīnāṃ guṇānām*) is a statement of their essential nature (*svarūpa*). The word "all" (*sarveṣām*) is intended to demonstrate pervasion. "Residing in substance" (*dravyāśritatva*) means being subordinate to substance (*dravyopasarjanatva*). And this is a statement of a mere property (*dharma-mātra*), not an expression of a specific difference (*vaidharmya-abhidhāna*), since it is possible even in the case of substances, actions, and so forth.

Thus, "qualitylessness" (*nirguṇatva*) means being devoid of qualities; this is the very nature of qualities because they do not produce other qualities within themselves. And their non-productivity [of further qualities] is due to the non-perception of another color, etc., within colors, etc., and because of the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This being so, the conventional usage [of expressions] such as "one color," "another sound," and so forth, occurs only by way of metaphor (*upacāra*). Number and the like do not have color and the like as their substratum, because they are qualities, just like color and the like. He states another essential nature [of qualities]: "actionlessness" (*niṣkriyatva*).

If it is argued that when a substance moves, its color and other qualities also move, we say no. This is because action occurs in space and other [immaterial] entities through conjunction with a forceful wind, yet it does not occur in branches and the like; thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*) between corporeality (*mūrttatva*) and possession of action is established. Consequently, the cessation of action in color and other qualities is proven by the absence of corporeality.

How, then, is there the perception of motion in them? It is due to the action of their substratum. Just as existence (*sattā*) does not move along with its own substratum—for if one thing moved, it would follow that the entire universe moves—so too is this case.
Praśastapādabhāṣya [100–101]:
Color, taste, smell, touch, priority, posteriority, weight, fluidity, viscidity, and speed are the qualities of corporeal substances.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are the qualities of incorporeal substances.
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction are qualities belonging to both [substances].
Conjunction, disjunction, duality, dual distinctness, and so forth, are dependent upon multiple [substrata]. The remaining [qualities], however, reside in each individual [substratum].
Color, taste, smell, touch, natural fluidity, cognition, pleasure, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*).
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, artificial fluidity, and momentum are the general qualities (*sāmānya-guṇa*).
Sound, touch, color, taste, and smell are apprehended by each of the external sense organs individually.
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, viscidity, and momentum are apprehended by two sense organs.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, however, are apprehended by the internal organ.

Nyāyakandalī [100] [pp. 241–245]: Now, demonstrating their mutual similarities and dissimilarities, he says "rūpa" and so forth. These are the qualities of only those things that possess form (*mūrta*), not of those that are formless (*amūrta*). To explain: color, touch, priority, posteriority, and velocity exist in the three beginning with earth; in air, all except color; in the mind, all except color and touch; taste and heaviness in earth and water; fluidity in earth, water, and fire; viscidity in water; and odor in earth.

He describes the qualities of the formless (*amūrtta*)—namely, "intellect, pleasure, pain," and so forth. Intellect and the others, up to volition (*bhāvanā*), are the qualities of the self (*ātman*). Sound is the quality of space (*ākāśa*).
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction are qualities common to both; they are the qualities of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless.

Conjunction, disjunction, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, are dependent upon multiple substrates (*anekāśrita*). A single instance of conjunction and a single instance of disjunction both subsist in two substances; thus, they possess the quality of being dependent upon multiple substrates. The same applies to instances of duality and dual separateness. As for those instances included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), such as instances of triad-ness, triple separateness, and the like, they are dependent upon many substrates as the case may be. Furthermore, the word "multiple" (*aneka*)—derived from the etymology "that which is not one"—is common to both pairs and to many.

"But the remaining ones have a single-substrate occurrence. The "remaining ones" are the individual instances of color and so forth; they exist in only a single individual instance. The meaning is that a single instance of color does not exist by being distributed across both [substrates] simultaneously, as is the case with conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

He defines the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) with the words "color, taste, smell," and so forth. "Specific" (*viśeṣa*) means differentiation (*vyavaccheda*); those qualities which serve that purpose are the specific qualities, such as color and the rest. For these indeed differentiate their own substratum from others, whereas number and the other qualities do not, because they lack intrinsic differentiation. It should be understood that whatever differentiation exists among them is produced solely by the differentiation of their substrata. [p.243]

Number and the others are general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*). This means they are qualities that serve for the commonality of their own substrates—that is, for the similarity among them—rather than for the differentiation of their own substrates. Now, is it not the case that the atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*) of atoms is what establishes their distinctness? No; because that [atomic dimension] is common to atoms of other classes [such as those of fire]. Natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*) is exclusively a specific quality (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) of water; therefore, by this term, [the text] intends to include only that which is produced by external causes (*naimittika*). Sound, touch, color, taste, and smell are each perceivable by one of the external sense organs. The external organs are the eye and so forth, because they illuminate external objects. By these [organs], color and the other [qualities] are apprehended individually.

Number and the others, ending with velocity, are perceptible by two sense organs—that is, they are grasped by both the eye and the sense of touch. Just as there is the cognition "this is unctuous" through the eye, so too does it occur through the tactile organ; thus, like number and the others, unctuousness is also grasped by both.
Cognition and the others, ending with effort, are perceptible by the internal organ; the meaning is that they are cognized by the mind.

Some maintain that cognition (*buddhi*) is inferable and is not apprehended by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); this is incorrect, because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*). The mere object cannot be the mark, because it is fallible. If it is argued that the "known object" is the mark—that is, the state of being known (*jñātatā*), which is the status of being the object of cognition—then since that relation to cognition is not perceived while the cognition itself is being perceived (because the perception of a relation is necessarily concomitant with the perception of its relata), how could the object qualified by that [cognition] serve as the mark? For, like the mark itself, the qualifier of the mark must also be something already known to be a cause of inference.

Now, you might think: "Immediately after its own production, knowledge produces a certain state called 'knownness' (*jñātatā*) in the object, just as cooking produces 'cookedness' in rice grains; and since that [knownness] is a property of the object, it is perceived along with the object. This too is without substance, because it is not experienced. For just as the state of being cooked—the transformation of rice grains into boiled rice—is experienced, the knownness of an object is not experienced in such a way.

Furthermore, this state of being non-mediately perceived (*aparokṣarūpatā*) and its fitness for practical transactions such as avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth—which belong to that object—is indeed a relation with cognition, not a separate property (*dharmāntara*). Just as when an object is known there is "knownness" (*jñātatā*), so too when "knownness" itself is being known, there would be another "knownness," leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Or, if this [knownness] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*), then why this hostility toward cognition?

In reality, even an object qualified by the three times, when cognized by a cognition, is cognized as delimited by the present time. And that state of the [object] belonging to the three times which is delimited by the present time is "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*); because it is produced by cognition, some hold that it is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of that [cognition]. That too is nothing; for being delimited by the present is indeed being qualified by the present time. And that [qualification] belongs to the object naturally; it is not produced by cognition, but rather is cognized [by it].

For even he who maintains that cognition is to be inferred from the awareness of an object must be questioned in this way: Does the awareness of the object inhere in the self, or in the object? It cannot be in the object, because consciousness is denied to it. If, then, it inheres in the self, what other "cognition" is there that remains to be inferred? If you say that its cause—characterized as the activity of the knower—is that [inferred cognition], is that cause eternal or non-eternal? If it is non-eternal, then its own cause must also be stated at the time of its production.

If it is argued that the cause [of cognition] is the contact between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the self (*ātman*), which is assisted by the objects, the senses, and so forth—then that same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is sufficient for the arising of the awareness of the object; what is the use of this internal tumor (*antargaḍu*)? Furthermore, if that [contact] is eternal, you must accept that it produces the occasional awareness of objects only when assisted by occasional factors such as the contact between the sense organs and their objects. In that case, since the arising of the awareness of objects is established by the very collection of adventitious causes, the postulation of that [eternal contact] is useless.
This is because the comprehension of the object and the subsequent practical activity (*vyavahāra*) are both established through the awareness of the object itself.

Nyāyakandalī [101] [p.246]: Now, it might be argued: "How can cognition, which arises from the object, the sense organ, and so forth, inhere in the self alone? This would be so only if the self were not composed of innate consciousness (*sahajajñānamaya*). For if the self were insentient (*acetana*), then since there is no distinction in its being a cause, cognition would likewise inhere in the sense organs and other such factors as well. To this we reply: the restriction is established precisely through the necessity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaniyama*).

Just as, although threads do not constitute a cloth, inherence resides in them alone and not in the shuttle and other tools due to the restriction of the genus "thread-ness," so too, although the self is insentient by nature, there will be a restriction of the inherence of knowledge [only] in it due to the restriction of the genus "self-ness."

By this, the following claim is also refuted: that some say the self’s own consciousness is its intrinsic nature (*caitanya*). For [if that were so], it would follow that it must manifest even during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). If you argue that it is concealed by ignorance (*avidyā*), is there ignorance even for Brahman? And what kind of expression is "concealment" in the case of that which is eternal and self-luminous? Furthermore, when that [Self] is concealed, nothing else can appear, according to the Śruti: "By its light, all this shines."

If it does shine forth, then there would be liberation for everyone, because when knowledge (*vidyā*) manifests, ignorance (*avidyā*) dissolves. Or, if this ignorance does not dissolve, then the manifestation of knowledge cannot be the cause of its dissolution, and thus there is no liberation. Furthermore, the manifestation of a partless entity in one part is not to be suspected. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [102] [p.247]:
Weight, merit, demerit, and mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) are indeed supersensible (*atīndriya*).
The qualities of color, taste, smell, touch (produced not by heat), dimension, unity, separateness, heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, and velocity are preceded by the qualities of their causes.
[Nyāyakandalī, pp. 247–248]:
Heaviness, merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impression (*bhāvanā*) are beyond the senses; the meaning is that they are not perceived by any sense organ.

Color and other qualities that are not produced by disjunction (apākaja) have the qualities of their causes as their antecedents; that is, color and other qualities are preceded by the qualities of that which is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of their own substratum. For example, the color of a cloth is preceded by the color of the threads, because they invariably conform to those properties. If they were not preceded by those, there would be some other quality in the cloth, since there would be no cause for such a restriction. By this, the claim that "the white color is one and the same everywhere because of recognition" is refuted; for it would otherwise follow that the states of being more or less intense (taratama-bhāva) and so forth could not be established. Therefore, recognition is based on the universal (sāmānya).

The color and other qualities of the atoms of earth arise from heating—that is, from contact with fire—and do not have as their nature the color and other qualities residing in the inherent causes (the atoms) themselves; therefore, the term "not produced by heating" (*apākaja*) is included to exclude them. Once production is established, it must be examined whether it is preceded by the qualities of the causes or not preceded by the qualities of the causes. Furthermore, since the production of the color and other qualities of the atoms of water and so forth does not occur at all, there is no deviation [from the rule].

Furthermore, the statement that these qualities are preceded by the qualities of their causes is intended as a description of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), not as a restrictive definition (*avadhāraṇa*), because it is possible for occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*) and velocity (*vega*) to exist without being preceded by the qualities of their causes. In the case of these two [fluidity and velocity], their being preceded by the qualities of their causes should be understood as applying to those instances where they are inherent in a composite water-substance (*jalāvayavin*) produced from parts possessing velocity.

[103] Intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound (*śabda*) are not preceded by the qualities of their causes.

Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), sound, the dimension of cotton, subsequent conjunction, specific substance-ness, priority, posteriority, and those produced by heating are produced from conjunction.
*Nyāyakandalī*:

From intellect up to sound, these qualities are not preceded by the qualities of their own substratum’s inherent cause; that is, they do not originate from the qualities of the inherent cause of their own substratum, because they are qualities of eternal substances.

Cognition and the rest are born of conjunction (*saṃyogaja*). Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression (*bhāvanā*) are born of the conjunction of the self and the mind. Sound is born of the conjunction of the drum and space. The dimension of a tuft of cotton is born of the conjunction known as accumulation (*pracaya*). Subsequent conjunction is considered to be born of conjunction. Occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*) is born of conjunction with fire. Priority and posteriority are born of the conjunction of direction, time, and the substance. The color, taste, smell, and touch of the atoms of earth are born of conjunction with fire; such is the distinction. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [104], p. 249.
Conjunction, disjunction, and velocity are born of action. Sound and subsequent disjunction are born of disjunction.
Priority, posteriority, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, depend upon cognition.
Color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, sound, dimension, unity, individuality, and viscidity originate their own kind.
(Nyāyakandalī [104], p.

249) Conjunction, disjunction, and speed are born of action. The first instances of conjunction and disjunction are born of action; they may also be preceded by qualities that are not causes [of the substance].

Sound and the subsequent division are both produced by division. The distinction is that the first sound is produced from both [contact and] division, whereas the subsequent division is produced from division alone.

Remoteness, proximity, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, depend upon cognition. Cognition is the efficient cause for the production of these; by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of triplicity, triple separateness, and the like is intended.

Color and the other qualities ending with viscidity (sneha) originate [qualities] of their own kind: from the color of the cause arises the color of the effect, from taste arises taste, from smell arises smell, from touch arises touch, from viscidity arises viscidity, and from magnitude arises magnitude, and so forth—this should be applied accordingly. Sound, however, originates another sound only within its own substratum. And here, mere causality is intended, not specifically the status of being an *asamavāyi-kāraṇa* (non-inherent cause); otherwise, the exclusion of hot touch—which is a *nimitta-kāraṇa* (instrumental cause) for heterogeneous qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*)—would be irrelevant.

[Objection: If that is so, then how can form and the other [qualities] be causes of cognition? [Reply: No, because what is intended is their capacity to produce effects of the same genus as themselves, excluding those [cognitions]. [Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 250]:
Pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, however, originate effects of a different genus.
Conjunction, disjunction, number, gravity, fluidity, hot touch, cognition, merit, demerit, and mental impression originate both homogeneous and heterogeneous effects.
*Nyāyakandalī* [105] [pp. 250–251]

Pleasure and the like do not originate from causes of their own kind. Pleasure is the cause of desire; pain is the cause of aversion; desire and aversion are the causes of effort; and that [effort] is the cause of action. If it is argued that the pleasure derived from the company of a son produces pleasure [in the father], for otherwise his joy would be inexplicable—this is without substance. For it is by inferring the arising of pleasure in the son through such signs as the brightness of his face that pleasure subsequently arises in the father.
In this regard, the pleasure of this son is not the cause, because he has remained absent for so long; rather, the process is that the inferential cognition concerning him is the cause.

The qualities beginning with conjunction and ending with mental impression (saṃskāra) originate both homogeneous and heterogeneous effects. From conjunction arises a subsequent conjunction of the same class, as well as a heterogeneous large dimension in a double-cotton-wool ball; from disjunction arises disjunction and sound; from the number "one" residing in the cause arises the number "one" residing in the effect; from the numbers "two" and "many" arise minuteness and largeness; from gravity arises another instance of gravity and the action of falling; and from fluidity arises another instance of fluidity and the action of flowing.

From a hot touch, another hot touch arises; likewise, from the color and other qualities of an earth atom, further color and so forth arise. From cognition, another cognition and mental disposition (*saṃskāra*) arise; from merit (*dharma*), further merit and pleasure arise; from demerit (*adharma*), further demerit and pain arise; and from mental disposition, further mental disposition and memory arise. [Praśastapādabhāṣya 106, p.
251] Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, mental disposition, and sound are initiators of effects that are inherent in their own substratum.
Color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, viscidity, and effort originate effects in other substances.
Conjunction, disjunction, number, singleness, separateness, gravity, fluidity, speed, merit, and demerit, however, originate effects in both [the substance itself and another].
*Nyāyakandalī* [106] [pp. 251–252]

Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound are initiators [of effects] inherent in their own substrata. Pleasure and the others produce their effect only where they themselves reside. Cognition, however, even when initiating duality and so forth in another [substratum], produces its own specific quality (*ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*) as something inherent in its own substratum alone, and not elsewhere.

Color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, viscidity, and effort originate [qualities] in other things. Residing in the parts, color and the others, as far as possible, originate color and the like in the whole; effort inherent in the self is the cause of motion in the hands and so forth.

Conjunctions and the like are initiators in both cases; they are initiators both in their own substratum and elsewhere. Conjunction existing in the threads initiates a cloth in those very threads, and the conjunction of the object and the sense organ initiates cognition in the self. The disjunction of two bamboo segments initiates sound in the space adjacent to them, and the disjunction of the bamboo segment from space initiates sound in its own substratum, which is space.

The number one residing in the parts initiates the number one in the whole, while the numbers two and so forth are initiated in their own substrata. Likewise, the separateness-one (*eka-pṛthaktva*) residing in the parts initiates the separateness-one in the whole, while the separateness-two (*dvi-pṛthaktva*) and so forth are initiated in their own substrata. Furthermore, heaviness, fluidity, and velocity residing in the causes initiate heaviness, fluidity, and velocity in the effects, while motion is initiated in their own substrata. Similarly, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) [initiate] pleasure and pain in the self, and in external objects such as fire, they initiate actions such as flaming.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [107] [pp. 252, 254]
Gravity, fluidity, velocity, effort, merit, demerit, and particular conjunctions are the causes of action.
Color, taste, odor, non-hot touch, number, dimension, singleness, separateness, viscidity, and sound possess the nature of being non-inherent causes.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression possess the nature of efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇatva*).
Conjunction, disjunction, hot touch, gravity, fluidity, and velocity possess the nature of being causes in both ways (efficient and non-material).
*Nyāyakandalī* [107] [pp. 252–255]

Gravity and the like are the causes of action. From gravity comes falling; from fluidity comes flowing; from velocity come the subsequent actions of an arrow; from effort come the actions of the body and so forth; and from merit and demerit come the actions of fire and the like. That which distinguishes is a "particular" (*viśeṣa*); conjunction itself is the particular, thus it is a "particular conjunction. A specific conjunction—characterized as pushing (*nodana*) or striking (*abhighāta*)—is also a cause of action, as will be explained. [p.253]

Qualities beginning with color (rūpa) and ending with sound (śabda) are non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). A non-inherent cause is that which is proximate to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and whose causal efficacy has been ascertained. Proximity consists of both inherence in the inherent cause and inherence in the same object as the inherent cause. For pleasure (*sukha*) and the like, the self (*ātman*) is the inherent cause; because it inheres therein, the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*) is their non-inherent cause.

[Objection: If that were so, then merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) would also be non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). [Reply: No; for their capacity to produce all the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self has not been ascertained. To explain: there is no production of merit or pleasure from demerit, nor the production of demerit or pain from merit. In this way, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of each of the others, such as cognition (*jñāna*), must also be pointed out. However, since the conjunction of the knower and the mind (*jñātṛ-manaḥ-saṃyoga*) has its capacity ascertained in every case, by virtue of this distinction alone, it alone is the non-inherent cause.

Likewise, because the color of the threads (tanturūpa) inheres in the same substrate—the thread—as the cloth (paṭa), which is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of the cloth's color, the color of the threads is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) of the cloth's color, and not its taste and other qualities; for it is through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) that the capacity of that [color] alone to produce it is determined. This should be applied similarly to taste and the rest as well. Furthermore, hot touch also serves as an efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) in the production of qualities born of cooking (pākaja); it is for this reason that "not hot" (anuṣṇa) is specified.

Color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, dimension, and viscidity possess the status of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) through both inherence in the cause (*samavāyikāraṇasamavāya*) and inherence in the same object as the cause (*kāraṇaikārthasamavāya*), because these, residing in their causes, initiate effects belonging to the same genus as themselves. Sound possesses the status of a non-inherent cause through inherence in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇasamavāya*), because that which resides in space initiates another sound in space itself.

Number and separateness function as causes in both ways: when residing in the cause, they respectively initiate singleness and oneness-of-separateness in the effect; and when residing in their own substratum, they generate duality and twoness-of-separateness.

Intellect (*buddhi*) and the others possess the nature of efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇatva*). The meaning is that they are exclusively efficient causes. Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), hot touch (*uṣṇasparśa*), heaviness (*gurutva*), fluidity (*dravatva*), and velocity (*vega*) possess the nature of being causes in two ways; that is to say, they are both non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and efficient causes. For instance: the conjunction of a drum and a stick is the efficient cause for the production of sound, while the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause. Similarly, the disjunction of the bamboo slivers is the efficient cause, while the disjunction of the bamboo slivers and space is the non-inherent cause.

Heat (uṣṇasparśa) is the non-inherent cause of heat itself and the instrumental cause of qualities produced by cooking (pākaja). Gravity (gurutva) is the non-inherent cause of falling in its own substratum and the instrumental cause in the production of the actions of pushing and striking. The same should be applied to fluidity (dravatva) and velocity (vega).
In the case of priority (paratva), posteriority (aparatva), duality (dvitva), dual separateness (dvipṛthaktva), and so forth, there is no causality.
Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) reside in a limited portion of their substratum.

Regarding priority (*paratva*), posteriority (*aparatva*), and so forth, they lack the status of being causes; these are neither non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) nor efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). By the phrase "of duality, dual separateness, and so forth," there is the inclusion of triple separateness and the like, as well as atomic dimension (*paramāṇu-parimāṇa*) and the dimension of the infinitely large (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*).

"Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities [of the self] exist as partial-occupants (*pradeśavṛtti*). This means that those which exist as partial-occupants are non-pervasive-occupants (*avyāpyavṛtti*), in the sense that they both exist and do not exist within their own substratum. Now, this is untenable, because it is contradictory for a single thing to simultaneously possess existence and non-existence in one and the same place. It is not untenable, however, because such a state of affairs is perceived through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For instance: the conjunction of a large tree with a man is perceived at its top, while its absence is perceived at its root; even when the tree is perceived at the root, the conjunction is not perceived by anyone there, whereas it is perceived at the top. Nor do the conjunction and its absence belong solely to the root and the top respectively, because the presence and absence of the man are perceived in the tree itself, as delimited by those respective locations.

If conjunction belongs to the part (*pradeśa*) and not to the whole (*pradeśin*), then since the part itself is a "whole" in relation to its own parts, conjunction would have to reside in a mere atom (*paramāṇu*) which is itself partless. However, since that conjunction existing therein is not perceived, it results in the total absence of any cognition of conjunction. Just as a single composite whole is not divided despite the diversity of its color and other qualities, so too is conjunction; for in both cases—whether conjunction exists or does not exist—the oneness of that [composite] is established by perception.

Although conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is indeed perceived when both its substrates are perceived, nevertheless, because it is not perceived across all parts of the substrates being grasped—just like color and other qualities—it is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Likewise, sound (*śabda*) also does not pervade space (*ākāśa*), because its simultaneous presence and absence are possible there due to its perception and non-perception at different locations. For cognition (*buddhi*) and the rest are non-pervasive, as they are perceived internally but not externally.

If it is asked, "How then can there be action in fire and other substances caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), given that these two are not present in those locations?", we say no; for even though they are not present there, they act as causes merely by virtue of the proximity of their own substratum. This should be understood just as, for example, the touch of a *caṇḍāla* at one end of a cloth is a cause of transgression for a member of the three higher castes who is in contact with the other end.
The remaining qualities pervade their substrata. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [109] [p. 257]

The qualities of color, taste, smell, touch produced by non-maturation, dimension, individual separateness, natural fluidity, heaviness, and viscidity persist as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvitva*). All remaining qualities do not persist as long as the substance exists (*ayāvaddravyabhāvitva*).
All these qualities, beginning with color, receive their respective designations—such as "color" and so forth—due to their connection with subordinate universals (*aparasāmānya*).

*Nyāyakandalī* [109] [pp. 257–258]: "The remaining [qualities] pervade their substratum. Those other than those already mentioned are the "remaining" ones. Their "pervasion of the substratum" means that, like conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, they are not non-pervasive.

"Those qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and the rest which are not produced by heating (*apākaja*) exist as long as the substance [that is their] substratum exists. As long as the substance which is the substratum exists, color and the other qualities remain present. The term "not produced by heating" (*apākaja*) is included because color and the rest produced by heating do not exist even while the substratum is still present.

The remaining qualities exist as long as the substance exists. This means that qualities other than those such as color produced by cooking do not persist for the duration of the substance; they perish even while their substratum still exists.

Now, in order to demonstrate the mutual difference (*vaidharmya*) of each of the qualities, he says: "Of color and the rest" (*rūpādīnām*). Those qualities of which color (*rūpa*) is the first—due to their connection with lower universals (*aparasāmānya*) such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth, they receive the designations "color," "taste," and so on. These designations, such as "color" and "taste," are produced by the lower universals like "color-ness"; this constitutes the individual difference of each of the qualities, such as color.

Some maintain that there is no universal such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*); this is incorrect, because the cognition "this is color, this is color" persists across the various distinctions of blue, yellow, and so forth. If it is argued that this persistence is caused by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being perceptible by the eye, we say no, because those [specific colors] are not grasped by the eye in the form of the word "color. For if their perceptibility were the cause, the cognition would arise in that way only after they have been grasped.

If it is argued that "visibility" is the state of being graspable by the eye—that is, the capacity for such grasping—and that this exists in blue and other objects throughout the three periods of time, let it be so; however, if this capacity were to differ with each individual object, it would not follow as a common cognition, because there would be no single underlying cause. If, on the other hand, it were to persist across all objects, it would be a mere difference in designation. Taste and the other qualities are explained in the same manner.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [110–111], p. 259.

In this context, *rūpa* (color/form) is that which is apprehended by the eye; it functions within earth, water, and fire; it is the means for perceiving substances and so forth; it assists the eye; it is of many kinds, such as white and others; it is eternal in the atoms of water and other [elements], while in the atoms of earth it is opposed to contact with fire; in all effects, its form follows the qualities of its causes; and it perishes solely through the destruction of its substrate. — *Nyāyakandalī* [110] [pp. 259–260]

Because it is the cause for the manifestation of all categories of objects, he first defines *rūpa* (form/colour): "Among those [qualities], *rūpa* is that which is apprehended by the eye. Among those qualities, *rūpa* is apprehended by the eye alone and not by any other sense organ. [Objection: But isn't *rūpatva* (the generic property of being form) also apprehended by the eye? How then is this a point of distinction (*vaidharmya*) for *rūpa*? [Reply: No, because what is intended to be distinguished is its difference from the [other] qualities (*guṇa*). Thus, the word "among them" (*tatra*) is used in the present context to specify [it] from the primary elements (*prakṛti*).

Its dissimilarity [to the universal] consists in its being a possessor of universals (*sāmānyavattva*). It resides in earth, water, and fire; that is, it exists only in earth, water, and fire. It is the manifester of substances and so forth: it manifests the substance upon which it resides, as well as the qualities, actions, and universals belonging to that substance. It is an auxiliary to the eye: its own color (*rūpa*) acts as an auxiliary for the eye in the apprehension of objects. It is of many kinds, such as white and so forth.

That which possesses many varieties such as white and so forth is "of that kind. It is eternal in water and other atoms; it is eternal in water-atoms and fire-atoms. In earth-atoms, it is opposed by contact with fire. We shall explain later that contact with fire is the adversary—the destroyer—of the color of earth-atoms. In all effects, [color] is preceded by the qualities of the cause; the color residing in an effect-substance is preceded by the color of its own inherent substantial cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
It perishes precisely through the destruction of its substratum; for the destruction of a thing in the form of an effect has the destruction of its substratum as its sole cause.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [111] [pp. 260–261]

If it is argued that we do not accept the destruction of color (*rūpa*) due to the destruction of its substratum (*āśraya*), because the destruction of both the color and the substance is perceived simultaneously, we say: no. First, from the impact of a hammer, through the sequence of motion in the parts, disjunction, and so forth, there occurs the cessation of the conjunction that initiates the substance; thus, the destruction of the substance initiated by that [conjunction] follows from the destruction of its cause. But what is the cause for the destruction of the color residing therein? For if the destruction of color were to follow from the destruction of the conjunction of parts even though it is not its [direct] cause, then the colors of the potsherds would also [be destroyed] from that same [cause].

Otherwise, they would perish simultaneously without distinction. Therefore, we consider it logical that the substance perishes first and its color-form perishes thereafter; the sequence is not perceived because of its extreme rapidity.

However, those who maintain that there is identity (*tādātmya*) between form and substance, and who claim that the cause of the substance itself is the cause of the form, should be asked this: does the form of an atom produce another form or not? If it produces one, does it produce it within itself, or within its own substratum, the atom? If it does not produce it, or if it produces it both within itself and in its substratum, then in the absence of the production of form and so forth in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the dyad would prior to that be as formless as an elephant’s tusk.

Now, since it is impossible for sound to have its own substrate while the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is still being produced, one must necessarily admit that the production of color occurs in the dyad only after the dyad has been produced, because an effect cannot arise without a substrate. This being the case, how can there be identity [between the substance and its qualities], given that they exist at different times—[the substance] first and [the qualities] later?

Furthermore, it is your own accepted position that even while the jar remains present, its color and other qualities perish due to contact with fire, and likewise, they are produced again. This is the established procedure: when one thing arises and another does not arise, and when one ceases and another does not cease, there is no identity between those two. Nor does the consequence of separate perception follow from absolute difference, because color is always dependent upon a substance. Why is this so? It is due to the inherent nature of things (*vastusvābhāvyāt*). Enough of this contrary argument directed at the teachers! —*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [112], p. 262.

Taste is that which is apprehended by the sense of taste; it resides in earth and water; it is the cause of the nourishment, strength, and health of living beings; it assists the sense of taste; and it is divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are like those of color (*rūpa*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [112] [p.262]

Now, in the course of defining the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that reside in perceptible substances and are graspable by each of the external sense organs individually, the author first explains *rūpa* (color/form), and then explains *rasa* (taste), which is to be explained next, noting its distinction from color in that it resides in both types of substances. He states: "Taste is that which is grasped by the gustatory organ. Among the qualities, taste alone is what is grasped by the gustatory organ, and that which is grasped by the gustatory organ is taste alone. It resides in earth and water; it exists only in earth and water. It is the cause of life, nourishment, strength, and health.

Life is the maintenance of the vital breaths; nourishment is the growth of the bodily constituents; strength is a particular kind of enthusiasm; and health is the absence of disease—the *rasa* (taste/flavor) is the cause of these. All of this is to be understood from the medical treatises (*vaidya-śāstra*). It is an auxiliary to the sense of taste. The internal *rasa* is an auxiliary for the tongue in the perception of external *rasa*. It is divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent; the meaning is that it is of six types according to the divisions beginning with "sweet."

Its production, destruction, and permanence are like those of color (*rūpa*). Just as color in earth-atoms arises and perishes through conjunction with fire, whereas in water-atoms it is eternal, and in an effect it is preceded by the qualities of its causes and perishes upon the destruction of its substratum—so too is taste (*rasa*). Odor (*gandha*) is that which is apprehended by the sense of smell; it resides in earth, acts as an auxiliary to the sense of smell, and is either fragrant or foul. Its production and other characteristics are explained as before.

*Nyāyakandalī* [113] [p.263]: Odor is that which is perceivable by the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*). Odor alone is perceivable by the sense of smell, and what is perceivable by the sense of smell is nothing but odor. Now, how is this restriction established? It is due to the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niyama*). Such is the intrinsic nature of odor that it is perceived by the sense of smell alone and no other; for there is no denial of what is observed or inferred. It subsists in earth (*pṛthivī-vṛtti*); it exists in earth alone and nowhere else. It is an auxiliary to the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa-sahakārī*); the odor inherent in itself is the auxiliary of the sense of smell.

There is a distinction between fragrant and non-fragrant. Its production and other characteristics have been explained as before. Just as taste in the atoms of earth possesses production and destruction due to contact with fire, and in an effect is preceded by the qualities of its causes and perishes through the destruction of its substrate, so too is odor. Furthermore, it possesses no permanence whatsoever. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [114], p. 264.

Tactility (*sparśa*) is that which is apprehended by the tactile sense-organ (*tvag-indriya*); it resides in earth, water, fire, and air; it assists the tactile organ; it conforms to color (*rūpa*); and it is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold. Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are also as previously described.
*Nyāyakandalī* [114] [p. 264]

Tangible (sparśa) is that which is apprehended by the tactile faculty (tvag-indriya). The faculty situated in the skin perceives tangibility by that very organ and not by any other. It exists in earth, water, fire, and air; its occurrence is restricted to these alone. It is an auxiliary to the skin. The tangibility inherent in itself is an auxiliary for the tactile faculty in the apprehension of its object. It conforms to color (rūpa); it has the nature of following or conforming to color, because wherever there is color, tangibility is necessarily present there. It is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-cold-nor-hot.

The specific types of conjunction arising from hardness or softness are not distinct from touch (*sparśa*), because they are perceivable by both sense organs. Its properties regarding eternality, non-eternality, and production are as previously stated. There is perception of a distant taste but not of odor, because the latter lacks eternality. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [115] [p. 265]: The process of the production of qualities born of baking (*pākaja*) in the color and other attributes of earth-atoms. When a raw substance such as a jar comes into contact with fire, there is the destruction of the conjunctions; and from the destruction of those conjunctions, the effect-substance perishes.

When that [composite substance] has perished, in those independent atoms, there occurs the destruction of qualities such as blackness due to the conjunction with fire and the dependence upon heat; then, from another conjunction with fire and the dependence upon heat, qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise.
*Nyāyakandalī* [115] [pp. 265–267]

He describes the production and destruction of the color and other qualities of earth-atoms with the words: "of the color and other qualities of earth-atoms. Although atoms themselves are indeed earth, they are nevertheless called "earthly" (*pārthiva*) in relation to earth as an effect. These atoms are the causes of earth; thus, "earth-atoms" refers to them. The method—the manner—of the production of their color and other qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) is now stated.

[Objection: If this were the case, then the determination of the destruction of blackness and so forth would not have been promised. [Response: This is not so, because that is understood through the word "mode" (*prakāra*). For such is the mode of production of color and other qualities from baking: namely, that where there is the destruction of the former [qualities], there is the production of others. He demonstrates that very mode with the words, "of a raw substance such as a jar," and so on. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), bowls and the like are included. "Of a raw substance" (*āmadravyasya*) means "of an uncooked substance."

Actions arise in the atoms of a substance that is connected with fire for the purpose of cooking; since water-atoms exist even as conjuncts in the case of an uncooked object such as a jar, he says "in those that originate it" (*tadārambhakeṣu*) in order to exclude them. This means "in those that originate that [jar] and so forth. And he states that the atoms which originate the jar and so forth are the indirect cause of the actions, saying "from impact with fire or from impulsion."

The impact or the impulsion by fire upon an earthly atom is a specific kind of conjunction, and this will be explained in the section on action (*karma*). From those [impacts] arise disjunctions; from those actions arise the disjunctions of the atoms. From the disjunctions arise the destructions of the conjunctions that initiate dyads (*dvyaṇuka*); and from the destructions of those conjunctions, the effect-substance perishes—namely, the effect-substance characterized as a dyad perishes from the disjunctions.

When that [composite substance] has perished, in those independent atoms, due to contact with fire and depending on the heat residing in the fire, there is the destruction of the previous color, taste, smell, and touch, such as blackness and so forth. Then, from another contact with fire, qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise.

Regarding the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) in independent atoms, the proof is the observation that the production of color and other qualities occurs everywhere in a substance that is not occupied by an effect. The color and other qualities of atoms exist only in substances that are not occupied by effects, because they are qualities being produced [in a substance], like the color and other qualities of threads and the like. Furthermore, the production of another color and so forth even upon the destruction of the previous color and so forth is the proof.

Since it is impossible for another color-form (rūpa) and so forth to arise within that which already possesses color-form and the like, the red and other colors are not produced within those things possessing color-form, because they are color-forms, just like the color-forms of threads and such. Thus, once the destruction of the prior color-form and so forth in atoms is established, conjunction with fire alone remains as the cause of destruction, because destruction occurs only when that [conjunction] is present, and no other cause is possible.

Furthermore, it should not be understood that the very cause which destroys form (*rūpa*) and the other qualities is the same as the cause that produces them; for we observe that the form and other qualities of a thread arise from one cause and perish from another. Therefore, it is determined that in atoms, the production of form and the rest arises from one conjunction with fire, while their destruction arises from another conjunction with fire. The destruction and production of the form and other qualities of an atom do not have a single cause, because they are instances of the destruction and production of form and the rest, just like the destruction and production of the form and other qualities of a thread. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [116] [p. 267]

Immediately thereafter, due to the conjunction of the self and the atoms—dependent upon the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of sentient beings—action arises in those atoms in which qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) have emerged. From their mutual conjunction, the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) is produced through the sequence beginning with the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). In that process, the production of color and other qualities occurs according to the principle of the priority of the qualities of the cause (*kāraṇaguṇapūrvaprakrama*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [116] [pp. 267–269]:

Immediately thereafter, due to the conjunction of the self and the atoms—dependent upon the unseen merit and demerit of sentient beings—action arises in those [atoms] in which qualities produced by heating have emerged; from their mutual conjunction, the effect-substance is produced through the sequence beginning with the dyad.

When jars and other such objects have arisen, those for whom there will be the experience—that is, the enjoyment—of the pleasure and pain produced by them are called "enjoyers" (*bhogin*). Their unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), characterized as *dharma* and *adharma*, causes the mutual conjunctions of those atoms. From this, a binary compound (*dvyaṇuka*) arises from two atoms, and a tertiary compound (*tryaṇuka*) from three binary compounds; in this sequence, the effect-substance, such as a jar, is produced. In that process, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the prior succession of the qualities of the causes.

From the two forms of two atoms (*paramāṇu*), the form of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) arises; from the forms of dyads, the form of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) arises; and by this sequence, color, taste, smell, and touch are produced in jars and other objects. Number and the other qualities do not arise from heating (*pākaja*), because they are non-specific (*avikṣaṇatva*). Now, one might object that even in the case of touch, no difference is perceived; this is true, yet its arising from heating is established through inference, as was demonstrated in the section on Earth (*pṛthivī*).

Immediately after the production of the qualities resulting from baking (*pākaja*), motion arises in the atoms, but not at the very same moment as the cessation of the dark color and other qualities. This is inferred because we observe that motion, which serves as the cause for initiating a new substance possessing color and other qualities, occurs only in a substance that already possesses color and other qualities. The motion of the atoms arises only in that which possesses color and other qualities, because it is a motion that serves as the cause for initiating an effect possessing color and other qualities, just like the motion of the threads that produces the conjunction initiating a cloth.

Now, why is it not assumed that the production and destruction of color and other qualities occur only in the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) due to contact with fire? For jars and the like, when placed for the purpose of baking, are perceived directly in all their stages by one whose eye is directed through an opening; and they are recognized even after the baking as "these very same jars. To this, he says: "And not... He states the reasoning: "In all the parts..."

The sense is this: because there is no conjunction—which is a pervasive relation—of the fire existing externally with the whole (avayavin) that exists internally and is inherent (samaveta) in all its parts, the production and destruction of effects such as color and other qualities cannot be accounted for; otherwise, it would follow that the internal parts would not undergo baking (*apāka*). Furthermore, composite substances (*avayavidravya*) possess apertures. Even if a large fire-particle cannot enter the interior of the whole, it certainly can enter its constituent atoms (*paramāṇu*); thus, pervasion will indeed occur. Praśastapādabhāṣya [117–118] [p. 270]

Furthermore, the production or destruction of color and other qualities in an effect-substance (kāryadravya) is not possible, because fire cannot pervade it—both internally and externally—since it exists within all its constituent parts. Nor can pervasion occur even through the entry of atoms, because that would entail the destruction of the effect-substance.
(Nyāyakandalī [117], pp. 270–272)

Regarding this, he says: "Even in the case of entry into the minute. To begin with, atoms do not possess intervals between them, because they lack parts. Furthermore, it is impossible for a dyad (dvyaṇuka) to have intervals, because there would be no conjunction of that dyad with the two atoms. If these two [atoms] are conjoined, they must indeed be without intervals. For a conjunction with an interval occurs when two entities possessing parts are conjoined by means of some portion; however, this rule does not apply to two things that lack parts.

Furthermore, when gross objects are perceived, no interval at all appears; it is only in triads (tryaṇuka) that an interval exists, and because that is not capable of being perceived, this hypothesis is cumbersome. Therefore, jars and other such things are indeed without intervals. As long as there is no disintegration of the constituent parts of the earth, fire-atoms can enter into their interior.

In a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat*), when it is struck by another such substance, its parts are divided; then, according to the principle of action, disjunction, and so forth, the conjunction that initiates the substance is destroyed, which necessarily entails the destruction of the substance itself. Therefore, how could there be pervasion (*vyāpti*) even by the entry of atoms? Furthermore, in the case of effect-substances (*kāryadravya*), the destruction of color and other qualities is never observed to occur from any cause other than the destruction of their substratum, nor is their production ever observed to arise from causes other than the qualities of their own constituent causes (*kāraṇaguṇa*). Consequently, one should not postulate the production and destruction of color and other qualities resulting from the contact of a jar with fire.

The color and other qualities of a jar perish solely through the destruction of their substratum, because they are the color, taste, smell, and touch residing in an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), like the color and other qualities of a jar destroyed by the blow of a mallet. Likewise, the color and other qualities of a jar arise from the qualities of their causes alone, because they are the color and other qualities residing in an effect-substance, like the color and other qualities residing in a cloth.

Furthermore, previously there was a loose conjunction of the parts, whereas now hardness is perceived; and it is not logical for looseness and hardness to coexist in one place as they do in the cases of pushing and striking, because they are mutually contradictory. Therefore, upon the cessation of the previous configuration (*vyūha*), this other configuration has arisen. This being so, it is established that there is the destruction of the former substance due to the destruction of its causes, and the production of another substance due to the existence of other causes.

Recognition, moreover, concerns the universal (sāmānya), as in the case of a flame and the like. Furthermore, the perception of an effect in all its states occurs because the destruction of that which is perishing takes place gradually; for a jar is not composed of a mere collection of atoms such that it would be destroyed instantaneously when those atoms are separated, but rather it is composed through a process beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth.

In the case of those [substances] that are independent, as the atoms undergo a succession of destructions of dyads, triads, and so forth, up to an incalculable number of substances, they perish only after a long time; until their destruction occurs, perception certainly persists. On one side, the prior constituent parts perish, while on the other side, new dyads and so forth are produced in their very place by atoms in which the qualities resulting from heating (*pākaja*) have arisen, through the same process starting with dyads; thus, there is the observation of both cooked and uncooked parts.

And when, due to the destruction of the final constituent parts, the prior whole is in a state of perishing, at that very moment another whole is being produced from the arising of new constituent parts; thus, in the subsequent moment, there is the destruction of the prior whole and the production of the other whole. Consequently, the relationship of container and contained, as well as their distinct determination, would be possible. Furthermore, since there are exactly as many constituent parts in the latter as there were in the former, its dimension and its numerical measure are logically established. (Nyāyakandalī [118], pp. 273–275)

The process, however, is as follows: at one and the same time, there is the destruction of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the state of being about to perish (*vinaśyattā*) of the triad (*tryaṇuka*), the state of being about to perish of the black color and other qualities, the state of being in the process of arising (*utpadyamānatā*) of the disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*) in the active atom (*paramāṇu*), and the state of being in the process of arising of the conjunction with fire that produces the red color and other qualities.

Then, at one and the same time: the destruction of the triad; the state of being about to perish of its effect; the destruction of the dark color and other qualities; the production of the disjunction born of disjunction; the state of being about to perish of the [original] conjunction; the production of the fire-conjunction that produces the red color and other qualities; the state of being in the process of arising of the red color and other qualities; and the state of being about to perish of the fire-conjunction that removes the dark color and other qualities.

Then, at one and the same time: the destruction of the triad (tryaṇuka); the state of being about to perish in its effect; the destruction of the conjunction due to the disjunction produced by disjunction; the state of being about to arise in the subsequent conjunction; the production of redness and other qualities; the destruction of the fire-contact that destroyed the blackness and other qualities; and the state of being about to arise in the action that initiates a substance in the second atom.

Then, at one and the same time: the destruction of that effect; the state of being about to be destroyed of that effect; the production of the subsequent conjunction; the state of being about to be destroyed of the action, the disjunction, and the disjunction produced by disjunction; the production of action in the second atom; and the state of being in the process of arising of the disjunction.

Then, at one moment: the destruction of that effect; the state of perishing of that effect; the destruction of the action, the disjunction, and the disjunction produced by the disjunction; the production of the disjunction of the second atom from space; and the state of perishing of their conjunction. Then, at another moment: the destruction of that effect; the state of perishing of that effect; the destruction of the conjunction of the atom with space; and the state of being produced of the subsequent conjunction.

Then, at one and the same time: the destruction of that effect; the state of being destroyed (*vinaśyat-tā*) of that effect; the production of a subsequent conjunction of one atom with another atom; the state of being produced (*utpadyamāna-tā*) of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); and the state of being destroyed of the disjunction and the action. Then: the destruction of that effect; the state of being destroyed of that effect; the production of the dyad; the state of being produced of the color and other qualities residing therein; the destruction of the disjunction and the action. Thereafter, in the next moment, by the sequence of the qualities of the causes, other qualities are produced in the dyad. This is the conceptualization [of the process] for all dyads.

However, in the production of triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, action need not be considered; for when many atoms (*paramāṇu*) conjoin simultaneously, from the conjunction of one atom—which is the cause of one dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)—with another atom which is the cause of a different dyad, there arises the conjunction of that dyad with the atom that is the cause of yet another dyad, and from that, the conjunction of two dyads. By this sequence, these [triads] arise from conjunctions produced by conjunctions (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) alone within the dyads.
Thus has it been explained by us, according to the instruction and according to our understanding.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya*: Number is the cause of the verbal designation "one" and so forth. *Nyāyakandalī*: [pp. 275–278] Number is the cause for the application of linguistic expressions such as "one," "two," and so on. It is a quality that resides in substance; it is distinct from size (*parimāṇa*), because while size is perceived even in a single object, number is not. Furthermore, it is distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because conjunction exists between two or more objects, whereas number is established even in a single entity. It is also distinct from disjunction (*vibhāga*), because disjunction is a relation between two things, whereas number is a property inherent in a single thing. It is distinct from priority and posteriority (*paratva-aparatva*), because those are dependent upon direction and time, whereas number is independent of them. It is also distinct from cognition (*buddhi*), because cognition is an attribute of the self, whereas number is an attribute of substance. It is distinct from pleasure and pain, because pleasure and pain are feelings, whereas number is a quantitative property. It is also distinct from desire and aversion, because desire and aversion are mental states, whereas number is a physical quality. It is distinct from effort, because effort is an activity of the body, whereas number is a static quality. It is distinct from sound, because sound is a quality of ether, whereas number is a quality of substance. It is distinct from darkness, because darkness is merely the absence of light, whereas number is a positive entity. It is distinct from the universal (*sāmānya*), because the universal is a category of existence, whereas number is a specific quality. It is distinct from the particular (*viśeṣa*), because the particular is the ultimate differentiator of eternal substances, whereas number is a common property shared by many. It is distinct from inherence (*samavāya*), because inherence is the relation of inseparable connection, whereas number is a quality that inheres in its substratum. Thus, number is a distinct category of reality. It is eternal in eternal substances, such as atoms, and non-eternal in non-eternal substances, such as jars, being produced by the cognition of the enumerator and destroyed by the destruction of the substrate or the destruction of the cognition itself. It is of various kinds: unity, duality, plurality, and so forth. Unity is eternal in eternal substances and non-eternal in non-eternal substances. Duality and higher numbers are produced by the synthesis of unities through the operation of the mind and are destroyed by the destruction of their substrates or the destruction of the synthesizing cognition. This is the nature of number.

Even though the nature of number is well-known to the whole world, there are some whose intellects are obscured by the habit of extremely perverse views and who hold contrary opinions; with reference to them, he says: "Number is the cause of the linguistic usage of 'one' and so forth. Linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is the act of using; it is the cognition of the object to be known. Alternatively, it is that by which something is used, namely, speech (*śabda*). Thus, "the linguistic usage of one and so forth" refers both to the cognition—such as "one," "two," "three," and so on—and to the corresponding words. Number is the cause of these two.

In this way, the cognition of "two," "three," and so forth, is produced by a qualifier because it is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*), just like the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Likewise, taking the word itself as the subject (*pakṣa*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) should be shown as: "[The word 'two' is qualified] because it is a qualified word. [Page 276] But is this cognition not rather directed toward objects such as color (*rūpa*)? No, because it is distinct from the cognition of those [objects]. For a cognition caused by color would take the form "blue" or "yellow," but not "one," "two," and so forth. Well then, let it be that [this cognition] is without an object (*nirviṣaya*), since there is no entity existing apart from color and the other [sensory qualities].

From what does this form of one, two, three, and so forth arise in this [consciousness]? If you say it is from the ripening of latencies (*vāsanā*) bound to the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), then let the forms of blue and so forth also arise from that very same source. For there is no distinction made by experience between that form of blue mounted upon consciousness and the form of number, such that we could maintain that one is born from an object while the other is not born from an object. Now, if you argue that this is the distinction: "this form of blue is non-erroneous, whereas the form of number is distorted."

That is without substance, because there is no evidence for the non-erroneousness of the blue aspect here either. First of all, it has no correspondence with anything else, because it is restricted to that single cognition and because it is momentary. For this very reason, it also lacks causal efficiency.

Furthermore, there is no apprehension of similarity among the aspects belonging to preceding cognitions within each individual cognition that is concentrated solely upon its own aspect, by means of which a correspondence (*saṃvāda*) could be established based on the perception of a stream of similar aspects; nor is there the perception of similar aspects in all cases, since the perception of dissimilar aspects also occurs in some instances.

Nor is the non-erroneousness of the blue aspect established merely by its being produced from an object, because it is impossible to determine that it is produced from an object when the object itself is not perceived; furthermore, since the postulation of an aspect not perceived through another means of valid cognition would be futile, if one accepts that the object is established simply from the cognition of the aspect, then the establishment of the object follows from the cognition of a non-erroneous aspect, and once the object is established, the non-erroneousness of the aspect is established through the determination that it is produced from that object—thus there is mutual dependence.

Furthermore, non-contradiction (*abādhitatva*) exists for the form of number (*saṅkhyākāra*) just as it does for the form of blue (*nīlākāra*), since both are mounted upon cognition (*jñānārūḍha*). Moreover, the impossibility of contradiction by virtue of being located in an external object (*arthagatatvena*) is difficult to establish even in the case of blue and so forth, because their own nature is remote from [the cognition]. Therefore, there is only the awareness of the mere form (*ākāramātra-saṃvedana*) everywhere; if that [awareness] is not produced by an object in one case, it is likewise so in another, and thus there is no establishment of blue and the like.

If it is argued that—since there is no external object—the occasional occurrence of the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which arises depending solely upon one's own mental continuum, would be impossible; and since the occasional occurrence of the forms of blue and so forth, whose cause is that [maturation] alone, would likewise be impossible, the conceptualization of blue and so forth must be admitted—[we reply: even for forms such as one, two, or three, occasional occurrence would not be possible if they did not conform to an external object; therefore, number too must be conceptually constructed, as the logical justification is identical in both cases.

As for the claim that number does not exist as something distinct from substance because it is not perceived separately, that too is incorrect; for even when trees standing close together are not perceived as "one" and so forth from a distance, the perception of their own individual forms is still possible. In this way, the distinction from color and other qualities is also explained, since we observe the cognition of a substance even when its color is not perceived from a distance. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [120] [p. 278]

Furthermore, it (number) is both single-substantiated and multiple-substantiated. Among these, for that which is single-substantiated—such as the color and other qualities of water-atoms—the properties of eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of the atoms themselves. That which is multiple-substantiated, however, begins with duality and ends with the highest number (parārddha).

Thus, regarding the nature of number (*saṅkhyā*) as a quality, he explains its divisions: "Furthermore, it is both single-substance (*ekadravyā*) and multi-substance (*anekadravyā*). That which has a single substance as its substratum (*āśraya*) is single-substance; that which has multiple substances as its substratum is multi-substance. The two words "and" (*ca*) demonstrate the mutual conjunction of the single-substance and multi-substance types, thereby indicating the absence of any other categories.

Among those, regarding the two types—those residing in a single substance (*ekadravya*) and those residing in multiple substances (*anekadravya*)—the eternality, non-eternality, and production of that which resides in a single substance are like the color and other qualities of water-atoms (*salilaparamāṇu*) and so forth. Just as color, taste, and touch are eternal in a water-atom, so too is the number one (*ekatvasaṅkhyā*). And just as the color and other qualities of an effect-water (i.e., macroscopic water) are non-eternal, perishing upon the destruction of their substratum and being produced through the sequence of the qualities of the causes, so too is the number one.

But that which resides in multiple substances begins with duality and ends with the parārdha. "Beginning with duality" means that duality is its first; "ending with the parārdha" means that the parārdha is its final limit. The parārdha is that at which the conventional usage regarding numerical limits comes to an end. The word "but" (*tu*) is used to indicate the specific distinction of duality and the rest as residing in multiple substances, as opposed to the number one, which resides in a single substance. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [121][122][123] (p. 279)

Indeed, its production arises from unities associated with a cognition of multiple objects, and its destruction results from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). How so? When there is contact between two substances—one of the same class and one of a different class—by means of the observer's eye, and when there arises the cognition of the generality of unity inherent in that which is conjoined with what is conjoined (*tatsaṃyuktasamavetasamaveta*), then, from the cognitions of the generality of unity and its relations, a cognition having multiple objects arises regarding the two qualities of unity. At that time, depending upon that [cognition], [the duality] arises from the two unities.
Duality is initiated in its own two substrates. Then, from that [duality], the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*) arises.

From that cognition of the generality of duality, there is the state of the impending destruction (*vinaśyattā*) of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), while simultaneously, from the generality of duality, its relation, and the cognition thereof, the cognition of the quality of duality (*dvitvaguṇabuddhi*) arises; this constitutes one single moment.

Therefore, now, at this single moment: from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the state of being about to perish (*vinaśyattā*) of the quality of duality (*dvitva*); from the cognition of the quality of duality, there is also the state of being about to perish of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*); and from the knowledge of the quality of duality and its relations, there is the arising of the cognition of the substance as "two substances. This is one and the same time. (Nyāyakandalī [121], pp. 280–284)

Indeed, its production arises from unities accompanied by the cognition of multiple objects, and its destruction results from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). The word "indeed" (*khalu*) is used for emphasis; the meaning is that its production is solely from unities, and not merely the collection of individual qualities. The compound *ekatve caikatvāni ca* is employed [to form *ekatva-ekatve*]; otherwise, the cause for the production of duality would not have been stated. [The phrase is] "accompanied by the cognition of multiple objects."

The term *aneka* (many) does not mean "one"; rather, by way of its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), it should be understood as applying to two or many, referring to the cognition that arises regarding multiple objects. He explains this very point by means of a question, beginning with the words "How? and so forth.

When, at a certain time, there occurs a contact (saṃyoga) between the eyes of a cognizer and two jars that are either of the same class or of different classes—such as a jar and a cloth—there arises a cognition regarding the generality of unity (ekatvasāmānya) which inheres in each of the two qualities that respectively inhere in those two substances conjoined with the eyes. For the cognition of the qualifier is the cause of the cognition of the qualified.

Furthermore, when two qualified objects possess the quality of unity (*ekatva*), the universal of unity (*ekatvasāmānya*) serves as the qualifier; therefore, at the outset, cognition is considered to occur with respect to that very [universal]. Moreover, since visual cognition does not arise without proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the relationship characterized by "inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*) is demonstrated for the universal of unity with respect to the sense organ.

Thus, when knowledge has arisen, because of the commonality of oneness (*ekatva*), due to the connection of that oneness with the two single qualities (*ekaguṇa*), and because of that knowledge, a single cognition arises which has multiple objects as its domain and rests upon both single qualities.
