This is because it is impossible for the single eye-organ to simultaneously preside over both [objects] by means of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); for if only one were always the grasper of the object, the postulation of a second would be useless.

From both of its orbs, rays of light issue forth and become connected with their respective objects, just as those from a lamp situated inside a house through the openings of windows. In this process, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) directly presides over the eye, not because of a direct connection with the object, since it does not go outside; rather, it is precisely through its presiding over the eye that its connections become the cause for the arising of cognition.

This being the case, cognition indeed arises simultaneously with respect to multiple objects due to the efficacy of its causes; yet, that which arises is only one, because the single conjunction between the self and the internal organ has the capacity to produce only a single cognition.

For this very reason, even the arising of conceptual cognition occurs because, when multiple impressions—which have various conventional designations as their objects and serve as causes for memory—are manifested simultaneously, a single recollection having multiple objects is produced through the capacity of the contact between the self and the internal organ. To the question, "Even if a single cognition has arisen with multiple qualities as its objective support, what follows from that? he says: "At that time, depending upon that cognition, duality is initiated in the two substances (the two fingers) which are its own substrates, by means of the two unitary qualities [of those fingers]."

The two [entities] residing in their own substratum are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*); the two single units are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); and the cognition whose object is manifold is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). When a single cognition of unity arises regarding two single units, duality is produced by those two unities; thus, the mention of simultaneity is intended with reference to a period of time called a *lava*, which consists of two moments (*kṣaṇa*). However, with respect to the individual moments, there is indeed a difference in time, because the effect and the cause exist at prior and subsequent times respectively.

The claim that an object arises from cognition is not unworldly, because we observe the production of pleasure and so forth [from cognition]. It is not merely a matter of dissimilarity that the production of an external object is not observed, for there is no difference between the two cases regarding their conformity with the presence and absence [of the cause]. If it is argued that—once it is established that the cognition of the qualities of both [the self and the mind] serves as the manifestor of duality—the rule of immediate succession for the cognition "two" would not be possible, we say no, because that would lead to the consequence of non-restriction.

For if duality were not produced by cognition (*buddhija*), it would be perceived even by another person, just like color and so forth, because there would be no cause for restriction. But if it is produced by cognition, then that which is generated by the cognition of one person is perceived by that person alone; thus, the restriction is established. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Duality is produced by cognition, because it is invariably cognizable by a single perceiver. Whatever is invariably cognizable by a single perceiver is produced by cognition, just like pleasure and so forth.
And duality is invariably cognizable by a single perceiver; therefore, this too is produced by cognition.

In this way, he determines the cause for the cognition of the duality that has arisen, stating: "Then again. Following the production of duality (*dvitva*), a cognition of that universal of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*) arises. Here too, the cause is precisely the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). The expression "again" (*punar*) is used in view of the universal of unity (*ekatvasāmānya*). Duality is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); and since no cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) arises when the qualifier is not apprehended, the cognition of the universal is first described as the cause of the cognition of the qualified.

Even though this [number two] exists, the very cognition of duality (*dvitvabuddhi*) as qualified by the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even though that [cognition of duality] exists, the cognition "two substances" (*dve dravye*) is the means of valid knowledge. Since the cognition "two substances" is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), it is preceded by a cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), just like the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*); thus, when the cognition of the quality [of duality] has been inferred, its being preceded by a cognition of its own qualifier must also be inferred, because it too is a qualified cognition. *Nyāyakandalī* [122] [pp. 285–288]

As for those who claim that the qualifier and the qualified share a single cognition as their objective support (*ālambana*), what is their position regarding the case of "fragrant sandalwood"? For the eye does not have odor as its object, nor does the nose apprehend a substance. Therefore, the apprehension of the relation cannot occur through those two senses, since the apprehension of a relation is dependent upon the apprehension of both relata.

Just as the perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) produced by both mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the sense organ has as its object both prior and subsequent times due to the efficacy of both causes, so too some maintain that this [perception] produced jointly by the eye and the nose would have both as its object due to the efficacy of these two causes.

That too is not correct, because [knowledge] is partless (*nirbhāga*). If knowledge were possessed of parts, then it would be logically consistent to establish that one part of it is produced by the nose and another by the eye; however, this [cognition] is a single, undivided entity produced by both [senses]. If it perceives both the odor and the substance, then it follows that the odor is also visual and the substance is also accessible to the sense of smell, since the property of being apprehended by a particular sense is defined by its being the object of the cognition produced by that sense.

Furthermore, because the mind is atomic, it is impossible for it to simultaneously preside over both sense organs. Therefore, once an odor has been apprehended by the nose, this cognition of the qualified object—which has as its objective support the qualified object alone—is produced by the eye acting in conjunction with that apprehension; this must be admitted even by one who does not wish it. And this being the case, this same principle applies to other cognitions of qualified objects as well.

The cognition of a qualificandum under dispute has as its objective support (ālambana) the qualificandum alone, because, while being perceptual, it is a cognition of a qualificandum, like the cognition "fragrant sandalwood. The phrase "while being perceptual" is for the purpose of excluding inferential cognition. [Objection: If the objective support of the cognition of a qualificandum is merely the essential nature (svarūpa) of the substance itself, then such a cognition would occur even when the qualifier is absent.

Now, it might be argued that because the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is a cause [of its cognition], the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) does not arise in its absence; even so, this [cognition] is no different from the cognition of the substance-form (*dravyarūpa*), because there is no other distinction in the cognition except for a distinction in the object, and such a distinction is not admitted. We do not say that the mere nature of the substance is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the qualified cognition, but rather the qualified [object] itself. And this state of being qualified (*viśeṣṭatā*) is indeed something over and above the [substance's] own nature (*svarūpa*), which appears in the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍī*).

Indeed, in that case, there is no cognition of a mere person, nor of the mere state of being conjoined with a staff. Thus, in the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), the person is perceived as distinct from others; and this distinction consists precisely in his being subordinate to the staff. For this very reason, it is said that a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which effects exclusion (*vyavacchedaka*). For the staff, by producing in the person the cognition of its own subordination, excludes that person from others.

And this alone is its distinction from [mere] indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Indication also serves to exclude [others], but it is not the cause for the cognition of being subordinate to itself. For, just as in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), the subordination of the staff is cognized in the man, so it is not the case that in the expression "an ascetic by his matted locks" (*jaṭābhis tāpasaḥ*), the subordination of the matted locks is cognized in the ascetic. Furthermore, the predominance of the man characterized by the staff is due to the excellence of his capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and the excellence of his enjoyment.

If that is so, then this relationship between qualifier and qualified is merely relative and not real; have you not observed that the conventional usage of agent, instrument, and so forth is likewise relative yet real? Thus, enough with this prolixity; it has been dealt with in the *Saṃgrahaṭīkā*.

Through the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*), there is the state of perishing of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Enumerative cognition is defined as a cognition that has both unitary qualities (*ekaguṇa*) as its object. Through the cognition of the generality of duality, there is the state of perishing of that [enumerative cognition], which is the presence of the cause of destruction; this is due to the generality of duality, because of its connection with the quality of duality and because of the cognition thereof. From that, there is the state of being produced of the cognition of the quality of duality, which is the presence of the cause of production. The cognition of the generality of duality is the destroyer of the enumerative cognition and the producer of the cognition of the quality.

Therefore, it is established that the very arising of one thing is the perishing of another, and thus the state of perishing and the state of arising are simultaneous. Consequently, from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there follows the state of perishing of the duality (*dvitva*), and so forth. The destruction of the enumerative cognition is the cause of the destruction of the duality, because the latter is not perceived in its absence. Thus, the destruction of the enumerative cognition is the state of perishing of the duality.

It is observed that qualities (*guṇa*) may also be destroyed through the destruction of their instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), as for example, the destruction of the final moment of true knowledge (*antyatattvajñāna*) at the stage of attaining liberation (*mokṣa*) due to the destruction of the body.
*Nyāyakandalī* [123] [p.289]:

The cognition of the quality of duality (*dvitva*) is the cause of the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of duality, because one cognition is incompatible with another cognition. Likewise, it is also the cause of the cognition of the substance (*dravya*). Therefore, at the very moment the cognition of the quality arises, there would be the state of being produced for the one and the state of perishing for the other. [The phrase] "from the cognition of the quality of duality and its relations" (*dvitvaguṇajñānatatsambandhebhyaḥ*) is to be construed as: "the quality of duality (*dvitvaguṇa*), and its (*tasya*) cognition (*jñāna*), and the relations (*sambandha*). *Praśastapādabhāṣyam* [124] [p.290]:

Immediately thereafter, there is one single moment consisting of: the arising of the cognition of the two substances; the destruction of duality (*dvitva*); the state of the cognition of the quality of duality being about to perish; and the state of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) being produced from the cognition of the substances.

Immediately after that, from the cognition of the substances, there is the destruction of the cognition of the quality of duality, and from the mental impression, there is also the destruction of the cognition of the substances.
*Nyāyakandalī* [124] [p. 290]

Immediately thereafter, there is one single moment comprising the following: the arising of the cognition of the two substances (*dravyajñāna*), the destruction of duality (*dvitva*), the state of being about to perish of the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*), the state of being about to arise of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the destruction of the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*), and the state of being about to perish of the cognition of the quality. Although duality does not exist at the time of the arising of the cognition "two substances," it nevertheless remains its cause, because the persistence of a cause at the time of the arising of its effect is of no utility.

For the causality of a cause consists in its producing an activity conducive to the arising of the effect. If that [activity] has been produced by it, what is the use of its remaining at the time of the effect's arising? Since the production of the effect is established through the activity alone, it does not follow that the cause lacks agency; for it is precisely that [cause] which is the reason for the effect by means of the activity. Nor, this being the case, is its status as an agent merely figurative, because there is no intervention by its own activity.

Otherwise, for an archer who has fallen [to the ground] due to a harsh blow to his back at the very moment the arrow is released, there would be no agency regarding the piercing of the target occurring in a subsequent moment. Immediately after that, from the cognition of the substance (*dravya*), there is the destruction of the cognition of the quality (*guṇa*); simultaneously, there is the state of the impression (*saṃskāra*) being produced. Then, from the production of the impression, there is the state of the cognition of the substance being about to perish; and from the impression of the subsequent moment, there is the destruction of the cognition of the substance. Furthermore, the impression possesses the status of being the cause for the destruction of the cognition of the substance, because it exists only when that [destruction] exists, and because no other [cause] is possible.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya*: By this, the production of triad-ness (*tritva*) and so forth is explained. Their production arises from unities accompanied by a cognition whose object is multiple; their destruction arises from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). *Nyāyakandalī*: [pp. 291–294] The production of triad-ness and other such numbers is established in the same manner as the production of duality. Just as two unities, when assisted by a cognition that has multiple things as its object, produce duality, so too do three unities, when assisted by a cognition that has three things as its object, produce triad-ness. Likewise, four unities produce tetrad-ness, and five unities produce pentad-ness. Thus, the production of these numbers is explained. Furthermore, their destruction occurs through the destruction of the enumerative cognition. When the enumerative cognition ceases, the number produced by it also ceases. This is because the number is a quality (*guṇa*) that depends upon its substratum (*āśraya*), and since qualities cannot exist without a substratum, they perish when that substratum perishes. Alternatively, the destruction of the number may occur through the destruction of its substratum. For instance, when the substance that serves as the substratum for a triad-ness is destroyed, the triad-ness itself is destroyed along with it. This is because the number is a quality that is dependent upon the substance. Or, the destruction of the number may occur through the destruction of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that produces it. For example, when the conjunction of parts that produced a triad-ness is destroyed, the triad-ness is destroyed. This is because the conjunction is a cause for the production of the number, and when that cause is removed, the effect is likewise removed. In all cases, the destruction of the number is brought about either by the destruction of the enumerative cognition, the destruction of its substratum, or the destruction of the productive conjunction. Thus, the nature of the production and destruction of triad-ness and other higher numbers is fully accounted for.

By this, the production of triad-ness and so forth is explained. By this process of defining the production and destruction of duality, the production of triad-ness and the rest is explained. He demonstrates that very method: "Their production [occurs] from unities accompanied by a cognition of multiple objects, and their destruction occurs from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)."

By this, the production of the number "one hundred" and so forth is also established. When each individual quality has been experienced one by one, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising in succession are simultaneously manifested immediately after the experience of the final quality—due to the simultaneous manifestation of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors that bring about the conventional usage of "one hundred. Then, given the unity of conjunction and the arising of a single memory whose object is manifold, the number "one hundred" is produced in its own substrata by two enumerative cognitions (*apekṣābuddhi*) consisting of both experience and memory.

And that [number] is indeed perceptible, because it is the object of a sensory cognition associated with the final substance while accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding substances. As for the case where, after the countable objects have perished, a cognition consisting of a number arises—such as "one hundred ants have been killed by me"—how does the number one hundred arise there? Since there is no substratum, it simply does not arise there due to the absence of its cause. However, some maintain that the conventional usage of "one hundred" in such cases is figurative (*gauṇa*), just as it is in the case of colors and other qualities.

Others, however, disregarding the assumption of metaphorical usage because the cognition is identical [in both cases], maintain that past substances themselves serve as the substratum, since they are brought forth by latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*). That which is absolutely non-existent, such as a sky-flower and the like, is not a cause, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Past things, however, lack a connection with the present time, but not their own essential form; for them, when brought to mind through memory, it is not contradictory for them to function as inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) upon obtaining auxiliary conditions conducive to their effects.

And this being the case, it does not follow that everything exists in that manner, because things are established according to how they are perceived. If it is argued that since a past object can be a producer, experience itself may suffice as the cause of memory, making the postulation of a *saṃskāra* (latent impression) redundant—this is not so; for that which has perished without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-pradhvasta*) cannot function as a causal agent even if it is not present. However, when one postulates a continuity (*anvaya*) that brings that past object to mind, the existence of the *saṃskāra* is established.

And thus, at the time of the cognition of the final phoneme, although the preceding phonemes have perished, they nonetheless possess the status of instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) in the cognition of the meaning, because they are brought to mind by memory. Just as this is so, so too will some [phonemes] possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*). And just as the mind, when accompanied by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), possesses the capacity to produce memory regarding external objects, so too must it be admitted that it possesses the capacity to generate direct perceptual experience, since this is observed.
This being the case, there is no absence of blindness, deafness, and so forth, because [the mind] follows the activity of the external sense organs.

In a case where duality arises with respect to a substrate that has already perished but is brought to mind by memory, its destruction occurs solely due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition characterized by memory. However, in a case where it has arisen while the substrate still exists, its destruction does not occur merely from the destruction of the enumerative cognition; in some instances, it may also result from the destruction of the substrate itself.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [126] [pp. 294–295]

And in some cases, [the destruction of number occurs] even from the destruction of its substratum. How so? When an action arises in a constituent part that is the locus of the unitary character (*ekatva*), at that very moment a cognition of the universal "unity" (*ekatvasāmānya*) arises; by that action, a disjunction (*vibhāga*) is produced from another part, and a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Then, at the same time that the destruction of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) occurs due to that disjunction, duality (*dvitva*) arises. From the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance (*dravya*), and the cognition of the universal [duality] arises.

Therefore, at the very moment when the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs due to the general cognition (*sāmānyajñāna*), at that same moment the destruction of duality (*dvitva*) occurs due to the destruction of its substratum. This formulation is sound if one follows the "killer-and-the-killed" model of opposition; however, if opposition is characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition of the substance could not arise. How so? Because if duality were destroyed at the same time as the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*)—due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition—the cognition of the substance, namely "two substances," which depends upon that [duality], would necessarily fail to arise.
In the *Nyāyakandalī* [126] [pp.

294–296], he says, "Because there is no single substance or two substances, and because there is no cognition of 'two'," and then adds, "and sometimes also due to the destruction of the substratum. When asked by an ignorant person, "How so?", he explains that point, saying, "When..."

At the time when an action arises in a part of a substance that is the locus of the quality of oneness, at that same time, a cognition arises regarding the generality of oneness (*ekatvasāmānya*) residing in that single quality; in the subsequent moment, a disjunction from another part is produced by that action, and from the cognition of the generality of oneness and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the arising of duality. At the very same time that the destruction of the conjunction initiating the substance occurs due to the disjunction of the parts, then, from that relative cognition, duality arises; subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction, [there is the destruction] of the substance.
The destruction of [the substance] and the arising of the cognition of the generality of duality occur at one and the same time.

Then, at the moment when the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs due to the cognition of the generality of duality, at that very moment, the destruction of the duality occurs due to the destruction of the composite whole; however, the destruction of the enumerative cognition is not its cause, because they are co-existent. Although there is no purpose for the arising of the duality once it has been destroyed without having first produced the cognition "two substances," nevertheless, the arising of an effect—which follows from the capacity of its causes—does not depend upon a purpose; thus, an investigation into its arising was undertaken.

In this context, indeed, within the process of the production of duality (*dvitva*), the destruction of each preceding cognition by each succeeding cognition has been demonstrated. And this [destruction] is possible only when there is a contradiction (*virodha*) among cognitions. Regarding that contradiction, some maintain it to be of the nature of mutual annihilation (*vadhyaghātaka-svabhāva*), while others maintain it to be non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). In this regard, the Teacher, adopting the perspective of mutual annihilation, says: "This rule is excellent. This rule refers to this very manner of the production of duality.

The meaning is that in the case where the second cognition arises in the category of a "slayer" (*vadhyaghātaka*) and destroys the preceding cognition in the subsequent moment, this position is excellent and logical. However, regarding the contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), in the position where the arising of one cognition is the destruction of the other, there would be the consequence of two substances [existing simultaneously], which entails the impossibility of the cognition's production; therefore, the intention is that [contradiction] characterized by non-coexistence is not logical. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "How? (*katham*).

For, according to the theory of non-coexistence with dependence (*sahānavasthāna-apekṣā*), at the very moment the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitva-sāmānya-jñāna*) arises, the cognition of dependence (*apekṣā-buddhi*) perishes; thus, duality is in the process of perishing. And simultaneously with the cognition of the quality (*guṇa-buddhi*), duality is destroyed. Consequently, in the subsequent moment, the cognition "two substances" (*dve dravye*)—which depends upon duality—could not arise due to the absence of its cause. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [127], p. 297.

If it is argued that [the cognition of the substance] arises from mere cognition, just as in the case of inference? It might be thought: just as in the case of "an existent [is inferred] from an existent" even in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*), there is inference from mere cognition, so too, even upon the destruction of the quality, the cognition of the substance would arise from the mere cognition of the quality.

This is not so, because it is a cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*). For a cognition of a qualified object cannot occur through similarity alone without a connection to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "From the whiteness inherent [in the cloth] and from the cognition of whiteness, there arises the cognition of the white [cloth]; these two stand in the relation of cause and effect" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.1.9).

*Nyāyakandalī* [127] [pp. 297–298]: Here he raises an objection: "Like that which is based on a mark" (*laiṅgikavat*). He clarifies this with the words "It might be thought," and so forth. "In this way, your view might be as follows; this might be what you intend: just as when a person is inferred from a particular sound, immediately after the cognition has arisen, the mark characterized by the sound—though unbecome, non-existent, and already perished—serves as the mark for the particular person who has become, i.e., exists; thus, even in the absence of the mark, inferential knowledge arises from the mere cognition of that [mark], so too..."

[Objection: "Even when duality has perished simultaneously with the cognition of qualities, the cognition 'two substances' would still arise from that very cognition [of duality] alone. However, another [commentator] explains: "In the case of the statement, 'The non-existent action of raining is the mark (liṅga) of the existent conjunction of wind and cloud,' just as there is inference from the mere cognition of that [mark] even in the absence of the action of raining," this is inconsistent; for here it is not the action of raining that is the mark, but rather its absence.

And that [prior non-existence] exists at that very time, because prior non-existence is not destroyed when a thing is not produced in its own nature. Therefore, one must follow the method stated by us.

He states the rebuttal: "No, because it is a cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣyajñāna*). It is not the case that the cognition "two substances" arises from mere cognition alone; why? Because it is a cognition of a qualified object. [The opponent asks: "Granted that it is a cognition of a qualified object, even so, why does it not arise from mere cognition? To this he replies: "For not... A qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is of the same form as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), that which colors the qualified object, and—what amounts to the same—causes the perception of its own subordinate status within the qualified object.

Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is non-existent to possess the quality of being an attractor (*anurañjaka*) or to be the cause of the cognition of its own subordination; therefore, the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) cannot occur without a relation to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, regarding the point that the cognition of the qualified cannot occur without a relation to the qualifier because of its similarity [to it] and because the qualifier is not explicitly stated, he shows the agreement of the author of the Sūtras by saying, "And so he says."

From the inherence of whiteness—that is, from the quality of white—and from the cognition of whiteness, that is, the cognition of the quality of white, there arises the cognition of the white substance, namely, "the substance is white. These two cognitions—the cognition of the qualifier and the cognition of the qualified—are related as cause and effect, having the nature of cause and effect; by this sūtra, it is stated that the qualifier possesses the capacity to manifest [the qualified]. And the sense is that this capacity does not exist for that which is non-existent. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [128] [p. 299]

But inferential knowledge does not arise without differentiation; therefore, this comparison is unequal. No, because of its rapid production. Just as in the case of "space possesses sound," three cognitions arise rapidly, so too it is in the production of the cognition of duality and so forth; thus there is no fault. *Nyāyakandalī* [128] [pp. 299–300]

Now, indicating the distinction of inferential knowledge (*laiṅgikajñāna*) from the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñāna*) by means of the word "but" (*tu*), he says: "But not... Inferential knowledge does not arise by apprehending the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) as subordinate to the mark (*liṅga*) through non-difference from the mark. Therefore, this comparison is unequal; the meaning is that the comparison "like inferential knowledge" is not equal to the cognition "two substances."

At the time of the cognition "two substances," duality itself does not yet exist; how then can there be an apprehension qualified by it? No, because it exists in the moment immediately preceding the arising of the cognition. For in all cases, the object of perceptual cognition is precisely that which exists in the preceding moment; and since duality exists in the moment prior to the production of the cognition "two substances," the cognition of it as a subordinate attribute certainly occurs.

However, this must be addressed here: in the cognition "two substances," just as the substance appears, so too does duality appear as a subordinate factor (*upasarjanībhūta*). And it is not logical for a non-existent duality to appear. Therefore, that [duality] would have to be the objective support (*ālambana*) of the cognition of the qualified at that time, precisely because the definition of being its objective support is its appearing therein. To this, he says: "not before its arising."

It is not the case that duality has not perished at the time of the cognition of the substance; rather, because the cognition of the quality of duality and the cognition of the substance arise so rapidly, their sequence is not perceived, leading to the misconception that both duality and the substance appear in a single cognition. In reality, however, the meaning is that duality appears first, and subsequently the substance. To illustrate this with an example relevant to the present context, he says: "Just as..."

Just as in the case of the cognition "space possesses sound," three cognitions—the cognition of sound, the cognition of space, and the cognition of space as qualified by sound—arise almost simultaneously, so too is it in the production of cognitions such as duality and so forth. What is meant? Just as in the cognitions of sound and the like, due to their rapid succession, the order is not perceived and there is the misconception of simultaneity, so it is also with the cognitions of duality and substance.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [129–134] [pp. 300–301]

If it is argued that the same fault applies even in the case of the "slayer and the slain" (the theory of successive cognitions), one might think: "In that case, does it not follow that there would be no production of the cognition of the substance even in the 'slayer and the slain' model? How so? Because the determinate cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed at the same time as the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*), due to its dependence on the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). [Page 301] This is not so, because it is the cognition of the aggregate (*samūhajñāna*) that is the cause of the latent impression. Since it is the cognition of the aggregate itself—and not the initial sensory perception (*ālocanajñāna*)—that is the cause of the latent impression, there is no fault.

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions (*jñānayaugapadyaprasaṅga*), the following might be thought: "Surely, if there is a contradiction between cognitions in the manner of 'the slain and the slayer' (*vadhyaghātaka*), then the consequence of their simultaneity follows. This is not so, because what is being denied is the coexistence of two [cognitions] while they are both undestroyed. By the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of cognitions, the simultaneous arising of two cognitions and the simultaneous persistence of two undestroyed cognitions are both prohibited. For in the case of the contradiction between 'the slain and the slayer,' there is no such thing as the simultaneous arising of two cognitions or the simultaneous persistence of two undestroyed cognitions. *Nyāyakandalī* [129] [pp. 300–303]

Someone has stated that even in the case of the "mutual destruction" (vadhyaghātaka) model, there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the cognition of the substance would not arise; he raises this doubt with the words, "Even in the case of the mutual destruction model. He explains the meaning of this with the passage beginning, "It might be thought," and so on. If the cognition of the substance does not arise when the duality is destroyed at the same time as the cognition of the qualities, then its non-arising would follow even in the mutual destruction model. He states the reasoning for this here: "Because of the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) due to the mental impression (saṃskāra) at the same time as the cognition of the universal (sāmānya)."

Just as the cognition of expectation (*apekṣābuddhi*), having arisen, produces duality (*dvitva*), so too does it produce the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and that [impression] is its destroyer. Therefore, at one and the same time: while the latent impression and the duality are being produced, and the cognition of the universal of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*) is arising, the cognition of expectation is in the process of perishing. Then, at another moment: while the cognition of the universal of duality is being produced, the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) is arising, the cognition of expectation has perished, and the duality is in the process of perishing. This constitutes one single point in time.

Therefore, the arising of the cognition of quality (*guṇabuddhi*) is the destruction of duality; thus, in the next moment, there is the non-arising of the cognition "two" which depends upon that [duality]. This fault is equal even in the case of the "slayer and the slain" (*vadhyaghātaka*) model. He provides the resolution: "No, because the cognition of the aggregate is the cause of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). It is not the case that the destruction of the cognition of relative distinction (*apekṣābuddhi*) results from the latent impression; why? Because the cognition of the aggregate is the cause of the latent impression. He explains this very point with the words beginning "the aggregate," and so forth.

The meaning is that only the collective cognition (*samūhajñāna*)—which is the cognition of a substance qualified by the quality of duality (*dvitva*)—produces a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and not the initial sensory perception (*ālocanajñāna*), nor the non-conceptual cognition of relation (*nirvikalpakāpekṣājñāna*); therefore, its destruction does not occur through such a mental impression. Regarding the fact that the cognition of relation is not the cause of a mental impression, the proof is the recollection of two qualities as distinct from their substances; and regarding the fact that the cognition of a substance qualified by a quality is the cause, the proof is the recollection of the qualified substance.

If it is argued by someone that "if a subsequent cognition, having arisen, destroys a previously arisen cognition, then the two would coexist in a single moment; consequently, this contradicts the Sūtra which states that cognitions do not arise simultaneously," he raises this objection with the words, "If it be said that there is the consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions? He introduces this with "It might be thought," and so forth. He provides an explanation of this with "But surely," and so forth. He answers with "No."

The simultaneous existence of the cognition that perishes and the cognition that causes its perishing at a single moment is not a fault, because the sūtra "due to the non-simultaneity of cognitions" prohibits the coexistence of two [cognitions] that are not perishing. This very point is demonstrated: by the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of cognitions, both simultaneous production and the simultaneous abiding of two non-perishing [cognitions] are prohibited.

And regarding the position of the executioner and the victim: there is no simultaneous arising of two cognitions, nor is there coexistence of two that do not perish, because when one arises, the second is in a state of perishing. Thus he says: "For not... The word "iti" indicates the conclusion. *Nyāyakandalī* [130] [pp.303–306]

O sir, this entire investigation into the production and so forth of duality is untenable, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence. If it is argued that the cognition "two" is the means of valid cognition, we say no; because the defining characteristic of an object of apprehension (*grāhya-lakṣaṇa*) is absent. For, when an object becomes the content of a cognition, is it already produced or unproduced? In either case, it is untenable: because that which is unproduced lacks existence, and because that which is produced lacks stability [at the moment of cognition]. If it is argued that only a past object is the content of cognition because it is its producer, we say no; because this contradicts the manifestation of the object as present, and because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even the sense organ itself would be an object of apprehension.

If it is argued that such is the very nature of the object, produced by its own causal complex, whereby—despite the lack of distinction in their capacity to produce cognition—this [object] alone is the apprehended (*grāhya*) and not the sense organ and so forth, and that the appearance of "presentness" belongs to the object of the immediately subsequent moment; then, what indeed is this "apprehended-ness" (*grāhyatva*) of the object? If it is said to be the state of being a cause for cognition, then once again the status of being apprehended would accrue to the sense organ as well, since the mere fact of being a cause is no different in its case.

If it is argued that the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of cognition itself is the apprehension of the object, this is quite extraordinary: that the self-cognition of one thing is the apprehension of another. It is not extraordinary, because the nature of things cannot be questioned. For consciousness has the nature of grasping an object; therefore, the self-cognition of its own form constitutes the apprehension of the object. Furthermore, since this [consciousness] arises from a specific object, this apprehension belongs to that object alone and not to everything; thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasakti*). No, for they are one and the same.

"Being produced from an object" (*arthajatva*) means the arising of cognition from an object. And that [arising] is one; it cannot be a property belonging to both the cognition and the object, because if it were to reside in many, it would follow that they are multiple. If it were a property of the cognition, it would not restrict [the cognition] to the object; if it were a property of the object, it would not restrict [the object] to the cognition, since it would be a property of something else. Furthermore, the establishment of their mutual relationship as the grasped and the grasper depends on the restriction of both to a single related thing, not merely from the restriction to one side.

Furthermore, past and future objects possess no causal efficacy (*kārakatva*) with respect to cognition, because they do not exist. If it is argued that the restriction of the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) entails the restriction of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhakabhāva*), this is not so, because there is no difference [between them]. Being the grasped (*grāhyatva*) is itself being the object (*viṣayatva*), and being the grasper (*grāhakatva*) is itself being the subject (*viṣayitva*). When the cause for their respective restriction is asked, that very [fact of identity] is stated as the answer; thus, this shines forth in all superior cognitions.

If it is argued that the apprehension of a fixed object is also the very nature (*svabhāva*) of cognition? Well, if this nature of it were causeless, then there could be no restriction. Or, if it is due to the power of causes, then let that alone be stated; what is the use of proclaiming a "nature," for that [restriction] is nothing other than arising from those [causes]. We observe this.

Now it is said: that which produces and imparts its own form to cognition is what is apprehended by it, and nothing else. Furthermore, the object must necessarily be present within the cognition; otherwise, since pure consciousness devoid of form would be indistinguishable with respect to all objects, the determination that "this belongs to blue" and "this belongs to yellow" would be impossible, and consequently, there would be no cognition of the specific nature of the object. For this very reason, they say that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the form of the object itself.
And that [form], being unique, connects the cognition with the specific object, whereas common factors such as the sense organs do not. As it has been said: [p.306]
For it connects this [cognition] with the object, and not by abandoning its own objective form;
therefore, the conformity to the form of the object is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the apprehension of the object of knowledge (prameya).

And it has been stated elsewhere: "It is not logical that the mere existence of a cognition constitutes the awareness of its object, because that existence is indistinguishable in all cases. Rather, it is the cognition entering into similarity—that is, assuming a similar form—that can connect itself with the object. To this, it is replied: Is the object experienced by the cognition through its own form (*ākāra*), or is it its own form [that is experienced], or both? It cannot be both, because at all times only a single form is perceived, such as "this is blue."

Furthermore, the experience of an object through cognition is not tenable; for at the time when the object exists in its own nature (*svarūpasattā*), cognition has not yet arisen, and at the time of cognition, it is impossible for that which has already passed to appear as present. To claim that "this appearance of presentness belongs to the moment coexisting with the cognition" is merely the devotion of one who clings to their own tenet, since that [moment] cannot be apprehended by that [cognition]. And what is the reason here that cognition makes a specific object known and not everything? For there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between the two, and it has been stated that causal production (*tadutpatti*) is not the cause for such a restriction.

If it is argued that "having that form" (*tadākāratā*) is the restrictive cause [of cognition], then why does one blue object not apprehend another blue object of similar form? If it is argued that the nature of being an apprehender belongs only to cognition and not to the object, even so, a single cognition of blue would have to be the apprehender of all blue objects, since there is no difference in their having that form. If it is argued that an object-moment is apprehended only by that which produces it, on account of both its arising from that and its similarity to it, and not by all [blue objects]...

The same consequence of being an object of apprehension would also apply to the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). For cognition arises from these two as well, and it possesses a similarity (*sārūpya*) with them consisting in their respective restriction to the apprehension of objects and their nature as consciousness.

Now, it might be thought that both this specific determination of the apprehension of an object—which is the conformity of consciousness to the sense faculty—and its nature as cognition, which is the conformity to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), are common to all cognitions; whereas conformity to the object is unique [to each], since the form of blue can only occur in a cognition of blue when that cognition is produced from a blue [object].

The claim that "it is precisely that which is its unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) which acts as the determiner," and that by this much distinction cognition grasps the object and not the sense-faculty or the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), is also without substance; for it would entail the undesirable consequence that the immediately preceding condition, which shares the same object, would also be grasped.

If it is argued: "That which imparts the form of blue and so forth to consciousness is alone its object of apprehension (*grāhya*); moreover, in a continuous stream of consciousness (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*), the production of the form of blue and so forth does not arise from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), but rather from the object itself; for in the production of that [form], efficacy is perceived everywhere through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since efficacy is understood to belong to the object only in the production of the cognition's own form"—then we reply: whose command is this that "that which imparts the form of blue and so forth is the object of apprehension"? It belongs to no one else, but to that very [consciousness] itself.

The restriction of the nature of being an object (*grāhyatva*) is the regulator. Thus, let the restriction arise precisely from the restriction of nature; for cognition arises as having the very essence of the awareness of a specific object due to the specific determination of its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*). The object, too, is perceived precisely because of the restriction of its nature as something perceivable, and not because of the sense organs and so forth; thus, the form (*ākāra*) is not the cause.

For the act of cutting does not possess the form of the tree such that it would be connected with the tree alone and not with the axe; rather, the tree and this act possess such a nature that it is restricted to this very [tree] and not elsewhere. Furthermore, the determination that "this is the cognition of that" is based solely on the appearance of that object therein; therefore, for that purpose as well, a [representational] form is not to be sought.

Now, if the object is not cognized at all by means of a cognition possessing an aspect, but only its own aspect [is cognized], then the existence of that object lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First, there is no apprehension of the object, nor is there a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*); for it is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that performs determination. And although this [conceptual construction] functions merely through the operation of imagination (*utprekṣā*), because it arises in the wake of perception, it sets aside its own operation and adopts the operation of its cause—namely, perception—which has already functioned toward the object; thus, it directly grasps the thing-in-itself (*vastu*).

But where perception itself has not occurred, there conceptual construction (vikalpa) is likewise incapable, due to the absence of its cause. If it is argued that the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), by establishing a cause similar to itself, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of the object—well then, does the object exist externally as the provider of that form which bestows the gross appearance? What is the status of this statement:
"Therefore, the gross appearance in consciousness is not caused by an object;
because it has been refuted in the case of a single [atom], it is not possible even in the case of many"?

Now, if this [cognition] arises from what is not an object, it occurs at some time due to some cause, or it is perceived even though it does not exist; likewise, the other form [of the object] will also either come into being or be perceived even though it does not exist. Furthermore, it has already been largely established that in the theory of forms (ākāravāda), the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous forms of cognition is not easily discernible.

Furthermore, at that time, the form of cognition (*bodhākāra*) postulates an object as its cause only if it is understood that the object is exactly like the form of the cognition. However, such an understanding is not possible if the object is not itself perceived, because the ascertainment of both causality and similarity depends upon the apprehension of both [the cognition and the object]. Thus, the existence of an object is not established by means of the form [of the cognition]. Therefore, it is rightly said: neither is causality the defining characteristic of the apprehended (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*), nor is there causality capable of imparting a form [to the cognition]; consequently, due to the absence of the defining characteristic of the apprehended, there is no object of experience other than the cognition itself.

For this reason as well, there is no object distinct from cognition; for if that [object] were insentient, it would not manifest of its own accord. Nor do we perceive any other illuminator of it, since at all times only a single form is perceived. Furthermore, if there is illumination, that which is itself non-illuminating and lacking the nature of illumination could not illuminate the object either.

That which has an unmanifest manifestation is unmanifest, such as an object obstructed by a wall or similar barriers; and the external object of another [person] has an unmanifest manifestation. Likewise, that which illuminates another is independent of any other similar entity for its own manifestation, just as a lamp; and cognition is the illuminator of another. Therefore, this is consistent with the logical principle that it is only consciousness, while itself being manifest, that possesses the capacity to illuminate objects.

This being the case, because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there is non-difference between the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*), just as in the case of a real moon and an unreal moon. For the rule of non-simultaneous apprehension is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of difference, since there is no rule of simultaneous apprehension for blue and yellow perceived at once. And the rule of simultaneous apprehension is the opposite of the rule of non-simultaneous apprehension; thus, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader, the rule—being excluded from difference by the pervasion of non-rule—remains established in non-difference. This is the proof of the logical connection (*pratibandhasiddhi*).

Nor should it be argued that the meaning of the word "simultaneous" (*saha*) is either assistance or simultaneity, and that because these two are pervaded by difference, the reason is contradictory; for what is intended as the qualification of the reason is a *conceptual* (*ābhimānika*) coexistence. In the example of the double moon, the coexistence is conceptual and not real, since the moon is actually one. The moment of cognition of omniscience perceives all living beings simultaneously with its own self.

If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive because those [cognitions] are not non-different from the Omniscient One, we say no, because there is no such restriction. For, with respect to moments (*kṣaṇa*), the co-perception of two things is indeed restricted to those two, since each of the two momentary entities is not perceived individually. However, that is not what is intended here; rather, the meaning of the reason is the restriction of co-perception with respect to the continuum (*santāna*).

Furthermore, there is no simultaneous perception of the mental continuum of an omniscient being together with another mental continuum, because it is possible for the omniscient one at times to abide in his own self alone. Nor does he cease to be omniscient at that time, because the capacity for omniscient knowledge remains present.

Just as one who cooks is called a "cook" even when not currently cooking, so too that which is perceived by a particular cognition is not distinct from that cognition; for example, the self [is the perceiver] of knowledge, and blue and other objects are its objects of perception. For if there were a difference [between the cognition and its object], this object could not be perceived by that cognition, because the necessary condition—identity (*tādātmya*)—would be absent, and because origination from that (*tadutpatti*) is not a restrictive factor.

Furthermore, if one thing were cognizable by another with which it is unrelated, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, since the relation—which is the pervading cause that restricts [cognition]—is not perceived in the case of difference, the property of being cognizable (*vedyatva*), which is excluded from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of difference, is pervaded by non-difference; this establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason. By this, the non-difference of even the form "I" from cognition is established. As for this appearance of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the cognition as distinct, it is an illusion, like the appearance of duality in a single moon.
In that case as well, the cause is precisely the beginningless, uninterrupted, and undifferentiated latent impression (*vāsanā*). As it has been said:
"And difference would appear in a deluded cognition, just as [duality appears] in the non-dual moon.

Now, if there is no external object, what is the cause of that cognition which arises with the form of blue and so forth? As it has been said: "The cognition of an object bears its form; yet, being qualified by that form, it deserves this investigation: does it [arise] from an external object or from something else?"

Regarding this, they also say: if external objects exist, what is the cause for that [variety]? If you claim it is the object such as blue and so forth, this is not the case, because such an object is never perceived, since it is always beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). If you argue that it must be postulated on account of the variety of effects, then let the variety of potencies be postulated in the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which is itself perceptible; by this, the variety of appearances even in one's own cognition is accounted for. For in that case, there is no efficacy of objects separated by space and time, because they do not exist.

But in that case, even the cognition of a variegated object (*citrapratyaya*) would not occur; for if cognition were unitary, it would follow that its non-differentiated aspects must also be unitary. Alternatively, if cognition were to differ with each form, then since cognitions are each restricted to their own respective forms, there would be no distinct entity apart from them capable of grasping all the forms simultaneously.
(Nyāyakandalī [132], pp. 316–318)

To this we reply: First of all, does the variegated form not manifest? It does, because that would contradict direct experience (*saṃvitti*). Furthermore, it is impossible for an insentient thing to manifest. Therefore, this form is of the nature of cognition and is indeed one; nor is there a difference in cognitions due to a difference in forms, because a single variegated form lacks a plurality of forms. Just as a single blue object has a single blue nature as its form, so too a single variegated object has a variegated nature as its form.

And when cognition operates upon that which has become its very self, it operates either entirely or not at all; it does not operate by way of parts, because that [object] is partless. As for these parts that appear as mutually distinct, they are not the variegated form itself, so there is no inconsistency whatsoever. The gross form also should be explained in this same manner.

However, a single part (avayava) that is gross is not tenable, because it would follow that it is manifold due to its subsistence in multiple parts. But the form of cognition (jñānākāra), existing within a single cognition, is indeed one and gross. Some maintain that contradictions such as trembling and non-trembling are to be set aside on the grounds that they contradict consciousness itself (saṃvid).

Others, however, maintain that even the form of cognition—which appears by the force of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is unreal and incapable of withstanding analysis; this very unreality is its true nature. Thus: whatever is a cognition has no external object as its support, just like a cognition in dreams and the like; and this waking cognition of a pillar and so forth is also a cognition. For the lack of an objective support is seen to be invariably concomitant with cognition in dreams and such states; and since being a cognition is the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of even a waking cognition, if it...

If it were to abandon its lack of an objective support (*nirālambanatva*), then it would necessarily abandon its very nature. Now, if all cognitions (*pratyaya*) were without an objective support, then the cognitions of the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would also be without an objective support; consequently, because the status of being a subject, a reason, and so forth would be absent, inference (*anumāna*) could not function. If, on the other hand, those [cognitions] do have an objective support, then this reason is rendered inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) by them? Not so; for while they are ultimately without an external objective support, they serve as the cause for the operation of inference by way of mere conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

For it is observed that even from what is unreal (avidyā), the attainment of knowledge (vidyā) occurs; for example, the cognition of phonemes (*varṇa*) arises from written characters (*lipyakṣara*). Although the lines and so forth that represent the phonemes are real in their own nature, they are indeed real, yet they do not signify by virtue of their own form. They signify through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the forms of the letter *ka* and so forth; thus, the form of these [lines] that is useful for the effect [of signification] is simply unreal. This is the summary of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). *Nyāyakandalī* [133] [pp. 318–320]

As for what was stated—that because of the lack of connection with the definition of an object of apprehension—that does not prove the non-existence of the object, because it lacks the necessary force. For while an object would not be apprehended in the absence of the definition of an object of apprehension, its non-existence does not follow; since the absence of apprehension can be accounted for even by a spatial remoteness of its own nature, as in the case of a *piśāca* or similar beings.

If it is argued that non-existence is established because there is no apprehension despite the capacity for apprehension, how then is its capacity determined? For its apprehension has never been observed anywhere; if it were observed, it would not lack the characteristics of being an object of apprehension. Furthermore, apprehension is dependent upon an apprehending subject, and since the apprehending cognition is restricted solely to itself, by this alone the other thing is unapprehendable. Thus, the claim that this non-apprehension results from the absence of an object of apprehension is no different from the very point to be proven.

Moreover, being asked this, please explain: what is the "graspability" (*grāhyatā*) of the form of cognition? It cannot be its being a cause of cognition, because it is not distinct from it. Nor can it be its imparting a form [to cognition], since two forms are never experienced. Furthermore, graspability cannot consist merely in being of the same nature as cognition, because even that which is experienced as being of the nature of cognition during deep sleep—necessarily persisting like the continuum of cognition—is not grasped.

If it is argued that its very state of being manifest (*avabhāsamānatva*) constitutes its being an object of cognition (*grāhyatva*), then what is this manifestation of the form (*ākāra*)? If it is the attainment of a fitness for practical transactions (*vyavahāra*) such as rejection and so forth, which is tied to cognition, then that same fitness belongs to the external object as well; for instance, people are aware [of it] thinking, "This is blue," or "This is yellow."

They grasp, abandon, or remain indifferent to only the external object, and not to the internal form; thus, the application of the definition of the "graspable" (grāhya-lakṣaṇa) is unestablished. If it is asked: "How can the arising of one thing result in the suitability for conventional usage (vyavahāra-yogyatā) of another?"—the answer is that this is a trivial objection, because by the necessity of its own causal complex (svakāraṇa-sāmagrī), that [external object] produces a nature conducive to the conventional usage directed toward it. Thus, [the argument of the opponent] is of no consequence. *Nyāyakandalī* [134], pp. 321–327.

By this, the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) is also refuted; for even if there is a difference [between the cognition and its object], that [state of being known] is established simply through the restriction of the cognition's own causes, as its exclusion from the contrary case remains doubtful. As for the claim that "the insentient cannot be manifested," that too is intended to mean the absence of having manifestation as its very nature (*prakāśātmakatva*). If it is intended to mean a relation of conjunction (*saṃsarga*), it is a proof of what is already established and is devoid of logical justification.

There is no royal decree that an insentient object must not come into contact with illumination; for just as the act of cutting is connected with and cuts the object to be cut, so too will the act of cognition be connected with and cognize the object of cognition. Furthermore, the exclusion of the rule of "simultaneous apprehension" from the contrary case is doubtful, since the necessity of the simultaneous perception of the blue object and its cognition is established by the mere fact of the cognition's self-awareness.

If it is argued that cognition does not perceive another because of the non-existence of external objects, then there is a mutual dependence: the proof of the non-existence of external objects depends on the establishment of the reason’s exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and its status as a reason for that non-existence depends on the proof of that very exclusion. If it is claimed that the reason is valid once the non-existence of external objects is established by other means, then let that alone suffice; what is the use of this [reason]? Furthermore, the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is unestablished, for when an object such as "this is blue" is experienced through an outward-directed state, at that very moment there is an internal [state].

If it is argued that the necessity of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is established once the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of knowledge is proven—because the experience of that [knowledge] is itself experienced—if one asks what the proof for the establishment of self-cognition is: If it is argued that "whatever is illuminating is independent of anything else for its own illumination, just as a lamp," [we reply: the function of a lamp lies in bringing about the presence of objects located in its vicinity; and since this function is performed by the lamp itself, it does not require another lamp for that purpose, as that would be redundant.

In its own cognition, however, it certainly depends upon the eye and other [senses]; thus, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). Now, if by "illuminating nature" you intend "the state of being cognition," and therefore [you claim] it is independent of others, then the reason is unestablished (*asādhāraṇa*). Furthermore, as for what was said—that "whatever has an unmanifest illumination is itself unmanifest, like a covered object"—in that case too, the unmanifestness of the covered object is its non-illumination; yet, because that [non-illumination] is not due to its own unmanifest nature but rather due to its very absence, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished. And as for the argument "because it is a cognition" (*pratyayatvāt*), that too is baseless, since the example is unestablished.

Even cognitions such as those in dreams have superimposed external objects as their objective supports; they do not terminate in their own nature alone, because those very objects employed during the waking state appear in that manner by the force of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Otherwise, it would be impossible for them to arise with a necessary restriction regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced. Furthermore, if the external does not exist, what is it that is now perceived with a restricted form, such as "this is blue"? If you say, "This is a manifestation within consciousness," it is not so, because there is an awareness of something existing outside of consciousness.

If, however, [the object] were of the nature of the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), the cognition would be "I am blue," and not "this is blue. If it is argued that because cognitions each have distinct forms, for some there is the appearance "I" and for others the appearance "this is blue," we reply: no, because unlike the form of blue and so forth, the form "I" lacks any fixed determination.

And likewise, if it is argued that what is perceived as "I" by one is perceived as "you" by another, and that in one's own self-awareness it appears as "I," then does the other person also possess awareness? If it is argued that even regarding its own nature, there is a perception of difference due to error, then why is the difference perceived through direct perception not real? If it is argued that direct perception is erroneous, as it has been said:
"This portion which stands externally is a distinct determination;
for the appearance of difference in non-dual cognition is indeed a cognitive distortion (*upaplava*)."

[Page 324] Whence is this [conclusion] derived? If it is argued that it is because non-difference is established by inference (*anumāna*), then there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāpekṣitā*): the validity of the inference is obtained because perception (*pratyakṣa*) has an unsublated object due to its being non-erroneous; yet, once the inference has attained its own nature, the erroneousness of perception is established. Alternatively, even if the delusion of difference were granted, how could there be the cognition of a specific place as the locus [of the object]? For in that case, there is no restrictive cause such that "this [superimposition] must be imposed here and not elsewhere."

If it is argued that there is a restriction regarding the superimposed object due to a restriction in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), we say no; for even those impressions lack a cause for such spatial restriction. Indeed, when an external object exists, the experience occurs in the same location as the object, and the latent impression is preceded by that [experience] in that same location. But in the absence of an external object, what could determine the spatial restriction of that impression? There is certainly a restriction in the case of superimposition, and a specific effect cannot be accounted for without a specific cause, yet an external object does not exist.

If it is argued that the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) itself exists because that diversity is purposeful, and that this is due to the diversity of their causes, which is thus beginningless—[we reply: if the diversity of latent impressions is not other than the form of cognition itself, what distinction is there between them one from another? Or, if it is something else, why this hostility toward external objects, such that the common experience of all the world is denied?

And by what means is this form superimposed externally? If you say "by cognition," then does the superimposition consist merely in the cognition's awareness of the form within itself, or is it something else? In the first case, that very [awareness] would be its correct perception, yet it would also follow that it is false; for while the apprehension of the form as residing in the cognition is true, the awareness of its externality is incorrect. And if the two were distinct, they could not occur sequentially, because the cognition which is their cause is momentary.

Furthermore, it is impossible for a single [cognition] to be perceived simultaneously as both true and false; nor is there any other mode besides succession and simultaneity, wherein a present cognition could grasp a form within itself and yet superimpose that same form externally.

Moreover, if an object such as blue were a form of cognition, then only that person for whom this form belongs would perceive it, and another person would not perceive it. Yet this single object is perceived by many, because they all simultaneously act toward it with their faces directed toward it, and because of the subsequent recognition: "That which was seen by you was seen by me too. Therefore, this object is not a form of cognition.

However, for those who claim that blue and other such objects appear as mere illusions while denying even the form of cognition itself, there can be no restriction regarding their cause, their production, or their causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). Since there is no object, nothing could be the cause of anything, or everything would be the cause of everything; consequently, there would be no distinction between the correspondence or non-correspondence of causal efficacy. As the Teachers have said:
"For those who are satisfied by imaginary sweetmeats and those who have actually acquired sweetmeats, it would follow that the taste, potency, and post-digestive effect are identical for both."

If it is argued that the specific nature of that [result] is established from a specific latent impression (*vāsanā*), we ask: if that impression is the cause of the entirety of external purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then it is merely a difference in name, for "impression" is just another word for "object. Alternatively, if it consists of cognition itself, then in the absence of an object, its specific nature would be without foundation, because the material cause, which is mere consciousness, is undifferentiated everywhere. Furthermore, if one were to admit a specific feature that is not distinct from the form of consciousness, it would entail the admission of the actual existence of the object; this has already been stated.

Moreover, under this view, the occasional nature of cognitions such as that of "blue" would not be possible, because the continuum of moments capable of producing them would persist at all times; or, if it did not persist, such a cognition would be impossible even at another time, since there is no factor external to itself that could be required. If it is argued that the effect is occasional because the maturation of the cause is occasional, [we reply:]...

The maturation of a cause is its orientation toward the production of an effect; that too must depend solely upon self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and cannot be merely occasional. Yet, this perceptual manifestation is indeed occasional. This very manifestation, by establishing an external object restricted by place, time, cause, and intrinsic nature as the domain of cognition, subverts the proof of its non-existence. Thus, because the time for the [opponent's] argument has passed, their reasons are also refuted; let us now conclude. The enumeration [of the types of non-perception] has been established.

**Praśastapādabhāṣya**: Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause of the practical usage of measurement. It is of four kinds: atomic (*aṇu*), large (*mahat*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*). Among these, the large is of two types: eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). Eternal [largeness] is the supreme largeness (*paramamahattva*) found in ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and self (*ātman*). Non-eternal [largeness] exists only in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth. **Nyāyakandalī**: [pp. 327–330] Dimension is the instrumental cause for the linguistic and practical conventions regarding measurement. It is divided into four types: atomic, large, long, and short. Of these, largeness is twofold: eternal and non-eternal. Eternal largeness is the supreme largeness residing in ether, time, and the selves. Non-eternal largeness exists only in composite bodies such as the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and the like. Atomic dimension is likewise twofold: eternal and non-eternal. Eternal atomicity resides in the atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the ultimate indivisibles (*anuparimāṇa*). Non-eternal atomicity resides in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). Shortness and length are both non-eternal; they reside in dyads, triads, and other composite objects. Length and shortness are perceived through the conjunction of largeness and atomicity. However, in the case of a triad, it is not that largeness alone produces length; rather, it is the specific configuration of the constituent parts that brings about the perception of length. Thus, the dimension of a triad is produced by the dimension of its parts, while the dimension of a dyad is produced by number (*saṃkhyā*). The dimension of a dyad is atomic, whereas the dimension of a triad is large. This is because the dimension of a dyad is obstructed by the dimension of a triad, and conversely, the dimension of a triad is not obstructed by the dimension of a dyad. Furthermore, the dimension of a dyad is not produced by the dimension of its parts, because those parts are themselves atomic. Therefore, the dimension of a dyad is produced solely by the number of its constituent atoms. The dimension of a triad, however, is produced by the dimension of its parts, because the dimension of the triad is not obstructed by the dimension of the dyad. Thus, the dimension of a triad arises from the largeness of its parts. In this manner, the dimensions of all composite objects are produced by the dimensions of their constituent parts. Now, for the purpose of defining dimension (*parimāṇa*), he says: "Dimension is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement. Conventional usage of measurement consists of both the cognition—such as "minute," "large," "long," or "short"—and the verbal expression thereof; dimension is the cause of that. By this, he demonstrates the existence of dimension—even though it is established by perception—to one who is in disagreement, by means of its effect. Just as it has been stated that cognition establishes the object of knowledge, so too is this the case here. [p. 328]

But how is it with sound? It cannot have the object as its essence, for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of filling the mouth, burning it, or tearing it apart when uttering the words "food," "fire," or "sword. Nor is it produced from the object, because it arises from the impact of the internal air against the throat and other parts [of the vocal apparatus]. If something that does not possess the nature of the object and is not produced from it were to convey it, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To this it is replied: if sound were produced solely from the impact of the throat and so forth, it would not convey even the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), because it would lack a causal connection (*utpatti*) with it.

Furthermore, it would be a reckless assertion to say that words do not even indicate the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), since words are preceded by intention through a traditional lineage.
