If you argue that words convey intention because they are preceded by it, then they must likewise convey the experience of an object, since intention is itself preceded by the experience of an object.

If you claim that even in the absence of an actual experience of an object, one perceives the speaker’s intention regarding that object in the case of a deceiver, we reply: even in the absence of an intention regarding that object, a sentence concerning that object is observed in the case of a person under delusion. Thus the Teachers have said:
"For it is observed that when one who is deluded intends to say one thing, another sentence [actually] issues forth."

It is not possible for one expression to arise from a desire to speak something else; for, according to the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), if a specific cause is known to produce a specific effect, then if that cause were to deviate from its effect, it would follow that the entire world is accidental (*ākasmikatva*). Therefore, one might argue: "Even if the desire to speak that particular meaning is not perceived in a deluded person, it must be inferred from the resulting speech as something produced suddenly and in an indistinct form, like the cognition of the touch of grass while walking. If this is said, then even in the case of a deceiver, one must infer a specific desire to speak based on his experience of that object, since no object is experienced without being cognized.

Because a specific intention regarding that object is impossible at that time. If it is argued that the deceiver has no experience of that object at that moment, let it be so; however, a memory certainly exists, for the deceiver indeed describes an object previously experienced in one way as being otherwise.

In this regard, his intention to speak (vivakṣā) regarding that object, being directly caused by memory, is indirectly caused by the experience of that [object]; thus, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra), because even an intention preceded by a false experience is ultimately preceded by a true experience. And since experience does not deviate from the object, the object is established through the word.

Otherwise, upon hearing a sentence, because the listener would lack comprehension of the meaning and because the mere cognition of the speaker’s intention is not a human goal, verbal communication would be destroyed; furthermore, the determination of victory and defeat for the proponent and the opponent would be untenable, since both would be speakers of the actual state of affairs merely with respect to their own intentions.

As for the claim that dimension is non-different from the substance, because there is no cognition of it when the substance is not apprehended—that is unproven. For even when a substance is apprehended from a distance, its specific dimension is not apprehended. It is for this very reason that even a large object is seen through error as if it were minute.

Dimension (*parimāṇa*) being thus established, he describes its divisions, stating: "That is fourfold. He shows the basis upon which it is fourfold: namely, "atomic (*aṇu*), large (*mahat*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*). As for [the notions of] squareness and so forth, these are particular configurations (*saṃsthāna*) of parts and not a different kind of dimension. [Objection: Let length and so forth also be like that. [Reply: No, because even when the configuration of the parts is not perceived, the cognition of "long" and so forth is observed from a distance.

Moreover, sir! The dimension of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is indeed atomic (*aṇu*), because there is no cause for the production of a large dimension (*mahat-parimāṇa*). And from that [atomic dimension], the dimension of the atom (*paramāṇu*) is more minute, since it is observed that the dimension of the cause is inferior to the dimension of the effect. Therefore, the dimension of the atom is distinct from the dimension of the dyad.

Thus, the dimension of space and so forth, which reaches the ultimate limit of excellence, is indeed distinct from the dimensions of jars and the like; likewise, dimension is of eight kinds, including long and short. To the question, "Why then is there only a fourfold division? he says: "Among those. Among those four types of dimensions, the "large" (mahat) is twofold: eternal and non-eternal. Suspecting the question, "In what things is it eternal? he says: "It is eternal in ether, time, space, and the self. And that is called "supreme largeness" (paramamahattva).
The meaning is that non-eternal largeness exists only in triads (tryaṇuka) and the like, but not in ether and so forth.

Likewise, the minute (*aṇu*) is also of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is that spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) found in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and minds (*manas*). The non-eternal exists only in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Even among large objects such as the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits, the conventional usage of "minute" is figurative, depending on the presence or absence of the excellence of that [spherical dimension].
[Page 332]

Length and shortness are produced and reside in the same substrate as largeness and smallness. Even in things such as sacrificial fuel-sticks, sugarcane, and bamboo, which are directly long, the conventional usage of "shortness" occurs figuratively with respect to the presence or absence of that excellence [of length].
All four types of dimension are non-eternal and originate from number, dimension, and aggregation.

In that regard, the number "plurality" (*bahutva-saṃkhyā*) produced in atoms and dyads in dependence upon the cognition of God produces both largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) at the same time as the production of color and other qualities in the effect-substance characterized as a triad (*tryaṇuka*), etc., which is composed of those [atoms]. However, in an effect-substance composed by two or many large [substances], it is only the largenesses of the causes that produce largeness, not plurality; for when [effects] are composed by substances with an equal number [of constituent parts], a greater degree [of size] is observed.
*Nyāyakandalī* [136] [pp. 331–336]

Just as the large (*mahat*) is of two kinds, so too the minute (*aṇu*) is of two kinds: eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). In both cases, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to exclude any other alternative. Eternal minute dimension exists in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and in minds (*manas*), because there is an absence of causes for their production or destruction. Sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) is the most minimal dimension. Non-eternal minute dimension exists only in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and nowhere else; this is the meaning.

By this, the following is stated: the dimension of the atom (*paramāṇu-parimāṇa*) is merely a particular instance of the dimension of the minute (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), and the dimension of the supremely great (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*) is a particular instance of the dimension of the great (*mahat-parimāṇa*); otherwise, the qualification by the word "supreme" (*parama*) would be inappropriate. Indeed, that dimension which, accompanied by color (*rūpa*), makes its own substratum perceptible is designated as "great," whereas that which does not make it perceptible is conventionally termed "minute."

And this being the case, does it not follow that even a triad (tryaṇuka) would possess atomicity? No, because that too is perceptible; for a triad is perceptible to people like us because it is composed of many inherent causes, just like a jar. Furthermore, that substance which is perceptible yet whose constituent parts are not perceptible is precisely what constitutes a triad. As for the dimension of space, although it lacks the status of being a cause of perception, it nonetheless possesses magnitude (mahattva), because its substratum has a greater extension than that of a dyad (dvyaṇuka), just like the dimension of a jar.

It is incorrect to claim that the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) alone is the atom (*aṇu*) because it is impermanent; for we observe the conventional usage of the term "atom" applied to things such as the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits relative to one another. Therefore, he says: "In the case of the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, *bilva*, and so forth. The excellence (*prakarpa-bhāva*) in the *bilva*—namely, its possession of a superior magnitude (*mahat-parimāṇa*)—is absent in the *āmalaka*. It is with reference to this absence that the conventional usage of "atom" is applied to the *āmalaka* in a figurative sense (*bhākta*). "Figurative" (*bhākta*) means that which is derived from "figure" (*bhakti*), where "figure" is similarity (*sādṛśya*)—that which is shared by both—and "derived" (*bhākta*) means belonging to that [similarity]. The meaning is that it is secondary (*gauṇa*), based solely on similarity.

Thus, the conventional usage of the term "atom" (*aṇu*) with respect to a *kubala* fruit is based on the absence of any excess in its magnitude compared to that of an *āmalaka*. For where the minimum degree of minuteness is found in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), there the absence of large magnitude (*mahat-parimāṇa*) is observed. Even in the case of the *āmalaka*, the conventional usage proceeds by way of this similarity: namely, that it does not possess such a large magnitude as is found in a *bilva* fruit.

He shows the scope of length (*dīrghatva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) with the words: "and length and shortness. "Largeness and smallness" (*mahadaṇutve*) refers to largeness and smallness; "produced largeness and smallness" (*utpādyamahadaṇutve*) refers to those two, largeness and smallness, when they are produced. Length and shortness are inherent in a single object through these two. The meaning is that where produced largeness exists, as in a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, there produced length exists; and where produced smallness exists, as in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), there produced shortness exists.

Regarding this, some maintain that because the atom (*paramāṇu*) is spherical, it lacks shortness, and because space (*ākāśa*) is all-pervading, it lacks length. Others, however, argue that since the conventional designations of "supremely small" and "supremely large" are observed in the world just as there are designations for "atom" and "supremely great," so too are there designations of "supremely short" and "supremely long"; thus they say that supreme shortness resides in atoms and supreme length resides in space. Space is the substratum of the dimension of length, because it is the locus of the dimension of greatness, like a pillar or similar objects.
Likewise, the atom is the substratum of the dimension of shortness, because it is the locus of the atomic dimension, like a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

If shortness were produced as inhering in the same object as minuteness, how could there be the conventional usage of "short" elsewhere? To this he says: "In the case of sacrificial fuel, sugarcane, bamboo, and so forth. Here, *samidh* (sacrificial fuel), *ikṣu* (sugarcane), and *vaṃśa* (bamboo) constitute the compound *samidikṣuvaṃśāḥ*.

In these cases, although bamboo is long in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), the absence of that state of excellence in dimension—the possession of an extreme degree of length—is perceived in relation to sugarcane; thus, there is a figurative (*bhākta*) or secondary (*gauṇa*) conventional usage. Likewise, the absence of that excellence in sugarcane is perceived in relation to a *samidh* (sacrificial fuel stick), resulting in the conventional usage of "short. Indeed, in a *dvyaṇuka* (binary atomic aggregate), which is short in the ultimate sense, there is an absence of length; and even in sugarcane, there is no such length as that which belongs to bamboo—this is the metaphorical application (*upacāra*).

Now, why is it not accepted that the usage of "shortness" (*hrasvatva*) regarding these [sounds] is indeed real? It is not accepted, because within those very same sounds, one observes the usage of "longness" (*dīrghatva*) in relation to others. Furthermore, it is not logical for both longness and shortness to be real properties of a single entity, due to their mutual contradiction. If it is asked, "Why then is the usage of 'longness' itself not considered figurative (*gauṇa*)?"—it is because there exists a causal basis for its production. Let the usage of "shortness" then be figurative in all cases? No, for a figurative application is impossible in the absence of a primary (*mukhya*) sense.

Now, in order to determine the causes of the dimension that is produced, he says: "The non-eternal is also fourfold. Non-eternal dimension—whether long, large, small, or atomic—is of four kinds; it has number, dimension, and aggregation as its source (yoni), meaning it has number, dimension, and aggregation as its cause. First, he states that number is a cause: "In that regard" [p.335]. A dyad (dvyaṇuka) commenced by two atoms is called a "dyad of atoms" (paramāṇudvyaṇuka).

The number three, which arises in dependence upon the cognition of the Lord directed toward each of those three individual qualities as their objective support, produces both largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) in the effect-substance characterized as a triad (*tryaṇuka*), which is commenced by those three dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), at the very same time that color and other qualities arise. In this context, the word "therein" (*tatra*) is for the purpose of determining the cause of the dimension of largeness; and the phrase "triad and so forth" (*tryaṇukādi*) is for the purpose of including the tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) and subsequent aggregates.

But how is this determined—that for the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, it is specifically the plurality (*bahutva-saṃkhyā*) residing in the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) that is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*)? Because no other [cause] is possible. First of all, the color, taste, smell, touch, unity, individuality, heaviness, fluidity, and viscidity residing in the dyads cannot be its non-inherent cause; for it is observed that when qualities residing in the cause initiate a quality in the effect, they possess the capacity to initiate another quality of the same genus.

If the atomic dimensions of dyads were the originators [of magnitude], then the triad itself would possess only minuteness and not largeness, because it is understood that from a dimension only a dimension of the same genus arises. Yet, largeness exists here, because it is composed of more constituent parts, like a jar or similar objects. Furthermore, an effect is never produced without an inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa); and it is observed elsewhere that, even when two effects are composed of constituent parts of equal dimension, there is an excess of largeness in one due to the greater number of constituent parts.

Therefore, in this case, number alone is postulated as the cause. If it is argued that the production of largeness in a triad occurs from two conjunctions of dyads, we say no; for if conjunction were the originator of largeness, then largeness would also have to occur in a dyad. If, however, it is said that the conjunction of many parts is the cause, then by distinguishing between what is attained and what is not attained, it is established that the plurality of parts alone is the cause. [This applies] to the triadness which depends upon the intellect of God.

Its destruction occurs through the exhaustion of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) that is the cause of its persistence, but it is never destroyed by the destruction of its substrate; nor is it destroyed by the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), because the cognition of the Lord (*īśvara*) is eternal.

Now, he explains the production of largeness from largeness on account of its magnitude: "by two or by many large [things]. "Two" and "many" constitute "two-or-many"; in a causal substance produced by them, it is precisely the largenesses of the causes that produce largeness. Where a substance is produced by two large, non-accumulated [parts], there the production of largeness occurs solely from the largenesses of the parts, because of the absence of both the number "plurality" and accumulation (*pracaya*).

Furthermore, where an effect is produced by many large constituent parts (*avayava*), the largeness of the whole (*avayavin*) arises from the largenesses of the parts, not from the number "many" (*bahutva*). This is because, when two substances are composed of parts that are equal in number but differ in being coarse or subtle, a greater degree of largeness is observed in the substance composed of coarse parts. For if number were the cause, there would be no distinction in the effect, since number itself is without such distinction.

However, where a difference in magnitude is observed between two objects composed of parts of equal size—due to a greater number of constituent parts in one case—the number of parts must also be accepted as a cause; otherwise, the specific nature of the effect would be untenable. Where an effect is produced by causes that are equal in both name and magnitude, some maintain that both are causes for the production of largeness, because the capacity of both is observed individually and no distinction is seen between them in that instance.

Others, however, maintain that [number] is the cause of dimension (*parimāṇa*), because when the production of an effect from a homogeneous cause is possible, there is no occasion to postulate a heterogeneous cause. In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [137] [p. 337], it is stated: "Accumulation (*pracaya*), existing in two tufts of cotton, initiates largeness (*mahattva*) in the double-tuft (*dvitūlaka*), depending either on the loose conjunctions of the parts that constitute those tufts, or on the conjunctions between the parts of the respective tufts; it does not depend on plurality (*bahutva*) or largeness. This is because an excess [in size] is observed in what is produced by [tufts] having the same number and weight (*palaparimāṇa*)."
Nyāyakandalī [137] [pp. 337–339]:

He states that accumulation (*pracaya*) is also a cause: "And accumulation... Accumulation is a specific kind of loose conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) that initiates a substance. Now, this [conjunction], existing in two tufts (*tūla*) that initiate a double-tuft (*dvitūlaka*), either disregards the loose conjunctions of the parts belonging to each individual mass, or disregards the mutual conjunctions of the parts of the two masses; in either case, it initiates magnitude (*mahattva*) in the double-tuft.

Where the conjunction of two masses is itself loose and the conjunctions of their constituent parts are also loose, there is observed a greater degree of magnitude in the substance produced by those two masses compared to a substance produced by the dense conjunction of parts belonging to two other masses. Therefore, the loose conjunction of the two masses, depending upon the loose conjunctions of the parts that constitute the masses, is the cause of [their] magnitude.

However, where there is a loose conjunction of two masses (*piṇḍa*), such that the conjunctions of the parts of one mass with the parts of the other are also loose, yet the constituent parts of the two masses themselves are not loose—there, in the substance produced by those two masses, because a greater degree of largeness (*mahattva*) is observed compared to a substance produced by two masses whose mutual part-conjunctions are extremely dense, the distinction is this: the loose conjunction of the two masses, in relation to the conjunctions of the parts of each mass with one another, is the cause of largeness.

Now, why is it not accepted that in those cases plurality (*bahutva*) and magnitude (*mahattva*) alone—possessing the requisite capacity—are the causes? To this he says: "Not plurality and magnitude. The plural number in the phrase "plurality and magnitude" is used with respect to the distinction of instances. The meaning is: wherever there is the cognition of a specific dimension due to a specific constituent substance (*avayavin*), there plurality and magnitude are not the cause. The objection here is: because an excellence [of dimension] is observed in what is produced by [atoms] having an equal number and weight-measure (*palaparimāṇa*).

Number, weight, and dimension are "number-weight-dimensions. Because an excellence is observed in the effect produced by those things which possess equal number, weight, and dimensions—for instance, if number alone were the cause, then between two substances produced respectively by three or four [atoms] with loose conjunctions and by three or four with dense conjunctions, there would be no greater magnitude in the one produced by loose conjunctions compared to the one produced by dense conjunctions, since the number of causes is equal in both cases.

Likewise, if magnitude (*mahattva*) were also a cause [of dimension], then between two substances produced from [atoms] that are either accumulated or unaccumulated by equal magnitudes, there would be no excess of dimension in the one produced from the accumulated over the one produced from the unaccumulated; yet such a distinction does exist. Therefore, we infer through reasoning that neither number nor magnitude is the cause.

However, where there is the observation of an excellence of magnitude in a substance composed of accumulated large [atoms] as opposed to two substances composed respectively of unaccumulated atoms and accumulated large ones, in that case both magnitude and accumulation are the causes. Where there is the observation of an excellence in two substances composed respectively of many unaccumulated atoms of equal dimension but greater number, and of fewer accumulated atoms, and in a substance composed of those same many accumulated atoms, in that case both number and accumulation are the causes.

Where there is a perception of difference between that which is produced by a small number of non-accumulated atoms and that which is produced by a greater number of accumulated gross [atoms], in that case, it should be understood that this [distinction] pertains to these three [dimensions] alone. However, as for the one who thinks that in substances of equal magnitude, the *pala* (weight) residing in the causes is the cause for the production of magnitude, rather than the magnitudes themselves—in his view, the refutation is made while accepting the causality of the *pala*; but in our own system, the *pala* is not a cause.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [138] [pp. 340–341]
The number two, residing in two atoms, initiates minuteness in the dyad.

Just as largeness [arises], length arises in triads and so forth from the plurality of causes, from largeness, and from homogeneous accumulation. Just as minuteness [arises], shortness arises in the dyad from the number two.

Now, what is the mutual distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) as they exist in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, and what is the distinction between minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) as they exist in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)? In that regard, there is a mutual distinction between largeness and length, because we observe specific linguistic usage such as, "Let the long be brought from among the large," and "Let the large be brought from among the long. However, the mutual distinction between minuteness and shortness is perceptible to those who perceive it. Furthermore, all four types of dimension (*parimāṇa*) perish only through the destruction of their substratum once they have been produced.

The number two, residing in the two atoms, initiates minuteness (*aṇutva*) in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). As for one who maintains that the dimension of the dyad arises from the dimensions of the two atoms alone, against him it follows that the dyad would also be the most minute (*aṇutam*); thus the previous argument must be repeated. Furthermore, it is an additional point that the dimension of an eternal substance does not originate [other dimensions].

The dimension of an atom is not the producer of anything, because it is the dimension of an eternal substance, like the dimension of space and so forth; or else, because it is the dimension of an atom, like the dimension of the mind.

He states the production of length (*dīrghatva*) with the words "like largeness" (*mahattvavat*). Just as largeness arises from a plurality of causes, from a homogeneous cause which is the largeness of the constituent parts, and from accumulation (*pracaya*), so too does length arise from a plurality of causes and from accumulation; thus, everything regarding this is identical to its case regarding largeness. He states that in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), even for shortness (*hrasvatva*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is simply the number two (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*) with the words "like minuteness" (*aṇutvavat*).

How can there be a difference in effects from a single cause? It is due to the difference in the auxiliary factor (*sahakārī*), namely, the specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*). Thinking that "length is simply a particularity of magnitude (*mahattva*) and shortness is simply a particularity of minuteness (*aṇutva*"), he says: "Now [the opponent]... He provides the answer: "In that case, it exists... If there were no difference between length and magnitude, then the restrictive selection (specification) "let a large one be brought among the long ones" would not occur because of their non-difference. For such a selection does not occur in the case of "let a colored thing be brought among colored things," yet this selection does indeed exist here.

If it is argued that a distinction between length (*dīrghatva*) and largeness (*mahattva*) must be postulated because two dimensions cannot coexist in a single substance since dimension (*parimāṇa*) is necessarily pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛtti*), we say no; for there is no contradiction in two heterogeneous things existing in one place. If it is argued that even when there is a difference in sub-species (*avāntarajāti*), the coexistence of blue and red is never observed in a single locus, then let it be so for those two cases; however, the coexistence of length and largeness is established by the common experience of all people and is therefore impossible to deny.

However, the distinction between the atomicity and shortness residing in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is perceptible to yogis; thus he says: "But [the distinction] between atomicity and shortness... For people like us, however, since the atomicity and shortness are merely figurative, there can be no inference of a distinction even for those [qualities] in their primary sense. Furthermore, this fourfold dimension (*parimāṇa*) perishes only through the destruction of its substrate and not from any other cause; such is the rule. By the inclusion of the term "produced" (*utpādya*), there is an exclusion of the eternal atoms (*paramāṇu*), the infinitely small (*paramahrasva*), the infinitely large (*paramamahat*), and the infinitely long (*paramadīrgha*).

If it is argued that minuteness and largeness, as well as length and shortness, are produced through mutual dependence and are not inherent, [we reply: in that case, since no difference is perceived between the measurement delimited by a cubit, a span, and so forth, in its isolated state and in its state of dependence, it would follow that both states do not exist at all. For what purpose, then, is there dependence? It is for the sake of perceiving the presence or absence of excellence in two measurements already grasped upon the apprehension of their respective substrata, such that, through the cognition of these two, the conventional usage "this is long compared to this" or "this is short compared to this" may occur.
Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is the cause for the conventional usage of distinguishing one thing from another.
Furthermore, it resides in a single substance as well as in multiple substances.
However, its eternality, non-eternality, and production have been explained by means of number (*saṃkhyā*).

This much, however, is the distinction: unlike unity and so forth, there is no absence of lower universals (*aparasāmānya*) such as "single separateness" (*ekapṛthaktva*); rather, it is qualified by number, because we observe linguistic usage characterized by that [number].
(Nyāyakandalī [139], pp. 343–345)

Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is the cause of the conventional usage of distinction (*apoddhāra-vyavahāra*). This conventional usage of distinction consists of the cognition and verbal designation that "this is separate from that. Separateness is the cause of that; the explanation is as before. If it is argued that this conventional usage is caused by mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), we say no, because a negation cannot be the object of a positive conceptualization (*vidhi-pratyaya*). Furthermore, that [separateness] resides in a single substance and in multiple substances.

That which has a single substance as its substratum is "single-substance" (*ekadravya*); that which has multiple substances as its substratum is "multiple-substance" (*anekadravya*). The word "again" (*punar*) is intended to highlight the distinction between separateness (*pṛthaktva*), which resides in both single and multiple substances, and dimension (*parimāṇa*), which resides only in a single substance. Thus, the distinction is that dimension is exclusively single-substance, whereas separateness is both single-substance and multiple-substance.

However, its eternality, non-eternality, and production have been explained by means of number. For both kinds of separateness (*pṛthaktva*), its eternality, non-eternality, and production have been explained by means of number. Just as the number one in a single substance is eternal in atoms, while in an effect it is preceded by the qualities of its causes and perishes through the destruction of its substratum; so too is the separateness of a single substance.

The meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*) is as follows: just as number such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth, which resides in multiple substances, arises from a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) that has multiple qualities as its object, and perishes upon the destruction of that [cognition], and in some cases perishes through the destruction of its substratum; so too is it with non-dual distinctness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and so forth residing in multiple substances. Regarding the term *nityānityatvam*: since it is heard after a copulative compound (*dvandva*) consisting of "eternal" (*nitya*) and "non-eternal" (*anitya*), the suffix *-tva* is connected to each member individually. Thus, "eternal and non-eternal" refers to both states.

In this sentence as well, the word "tu" (but/however) is intended to highlight a distinction. The meaning is that its [the universal's] properties, such as eternity and so forth, have been explained by means of number, but not those of dimension (*parimāṇa*).

Having thus established the similarity between number (*saṃkhyā*) and separateness (*pṛthaktva*), he establishes their dissimilarity with the words "But this much... The difference of separateness from number is as follows: whereas there exist lower universals such as oneness, duality, and so forth, in relation to the higher universal of "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*), there do not exist lower universals such as "single-separateness," "dual-separateness," and so forth, in relation to the higher universal of "separateness-ness" (*pṛthaktvatva*).

How, then, is there a specific internal cognition regarding many instances of singularity, separateness, and so forth? To this he says: "But it is distinguished by number. In the case of separateness, we observe a linguistic usage qualified by numbers such as singularity and so on, as in: "This one is separate," or "These two are separate."

The intention is as follows: separateness (*pṛthaktva*) residing in a single substance is qualified by the number one (*ekatvasaṃkhyā*) inhering in the same object; that residing in two [substances] is qualified by the number two (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*) brought forward by memory. From these specific qualifications arises a specific distinction in intermediate linguistic usage, and the notion of recurrence (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) is produced solely by the generality (*sāmānya*) of separateness itself.

By this same reasoning, the status of "atom-ness" (*paramāṇutva*) in atoms must also be rejected as a commonality; for the continuity of linguistic usage is established simply from the generality of "minuteness" (*aṇutva*) as qualified by the word "supreme" (*parama*). Now, why is it not accepted that there is a single "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) inherent in all substances, which serves as the cause for the diversity of cognitions through the distinction of its qualifiers, such as the specific numbers one and so forth? It is not accepted because, in the case of substances arising sequentially, we do not observe the inherence of a quality in the same way we observe that of a universal.

"Could this be merely a generality (*sāmānya*)? No, because, unlike the cognition of a generality when there is no connection with other aggregates, there is an absence of a cognition of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*).
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [140–141] [p.346].
Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause of the cognition "conjoined."
And that [fire] is the cause of substance, quality, and action.
It is independent in the production of a substance, according to the statement: "From those which are dependent and from those which are independent" (VS 10.2.7).
However, it is dependent in the production of qualities and actions, according to the statement: "The specific quality of fire arises from conjunction with air" (VS 10.2.7).

In order to establish the existence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), [Praśastapāda] says: "Conjunction is the cause of the cognition 'conjoined'. There indeed exists among common people this cognition: "This is conjoined with that. And color and other such qualities cannot be its cause, because this cognition is distinct from the cognitions of those [qualities]. Therefore, that which is its cause is conjunction.

If it is argued that this cognition is not based on immediate contiguity (*nairantarya*), then what is this contiguity? Is it the mutual contact of two substances, or the absence of anything intervening between them? In the first case, nothing additional would have been stated; for us, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is precisely the mutual contact of two substances. In the second case, one must explain what cause other than conjunction brings about the absence of an interval between two things that previously had an interval.

If it is argued that "the very cause which brings about the conjunction of two things previously unjoined is itself the cause for us of the absence of the interval between two things that have an interval," let it be so for the sake of argument; however, does this [cause] produce the absence of the interval by reaching another location that is its own substrate, or without reaching it? In the first case—that of not reaching—it is difficult to establish the absence of the interval, because the object remains occupying precisely the space it already occupies.

But if one holds the position that [the atoms] reach another location, what indeed is this other conjunction that is being negated? If it is argued that the conventional usage of "conjunction" occurs when two substances arise in an adjacent location, we say no; the conventional usage of "conjunction" does not apply to mere arising, but rather to arising in adjacent locations. That very state of adjacency in which the two things being produced arise is itself conjunction.

And that [conjunction] is the cause of substance, quality, and action. The conjunction of threads is the cause of a substance; the conjunction of the self and the mind is the cause of qualities such as cognition. Likewise, the conjunction of a drum and space is the cause of sound, which is a quality; the conjunction of the self possessed of effort and the hand is the cause of the action of the hand; similarly, the conjunction of wind possessed of velocity and grass is the cause of the action of the grass—such cases are to be inferred accordingly. [p. 348]

He demonstrates the manner in which this [conjunction] initiates a substance and how it initiates qualities and actions by means of the passage beginning with "In the initiation of a substance," and so forth. When the initiation of a substance is to be performed, conjunction does not require anything other than its own substratum and its own efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

However, this meaning of "non-dependence" is not that it does not require another subsequent efficient cause; for otherwise, it would follow that the final conjunction of fire with an atom—which occurs immediately after the destruction of blackness and other qualities—would be a non-dependent cause even in the initiation of the qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*).

"How is it understood by you that this conjunction is independent in the production of a substance? To this he replies: "It is so because of the statement [in the Sūtra], 'From those that are dependent and from those that are independent' (10.7). Having previously established that the cognition arises—'the cloth will come into being'—with respect to the threads being employed for the sake of a cloth, the author of the Sūtras stated this: 'It is so because of [the distinction between] those that are dependent and those that are independent.'"

The meaning of this is as follows: just as there arises the cognition "the cloth will be" with respect to those [threads] being prepared, so too there arises the present-tense cognition "it is" with respect to both those that are dependent and those that are independent. Otherwise, the present-tense cognition "it is" would not arise with respect to both the dependent and the independent; for if some threads were joined together while others remained unjoined, then at that time the cognition "the cloth is" would have to arise with respect to them—this is the sense.

The intended meaning here is that since the word "independent" (*anapekṣa*) is applied to the threads being described in this sūtra as the cause of present cognition while they are already conjoined, it is understood that conjunction is independent in the production of a substance.

By using the word "but" (*tu*), he indicates a distinction from what preceded: "But in the production of qualities and actions, it is dependent. To the question "How is this known?", he says: "Because of inherence in the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāyāt*). By the phrase "the specific quality of fire" (*agner vaiśeṣikam*), the heat residing in fire is intended.

Since it is accepted that color and other qualities arise in an atom through inherence when fire is conjoined with an earthly atom, it is understood from this very reason that the conjunction of fire with an atom in the production of qualities depends upon the quality of heat (uṣṇasparśa); otherwise, it would be impossible to designate the touch of fire as the cause of the color and other qualities produced by conjunction with fire. Similarly, it should be inferred according to the circumstances that in the production of cognition, the conjunction of the self and the mind depends upon merit (dharma) and other factors, even apart from its own substratum and its own instrumental cause.

Even in the case of the initiation of action, conjunction is dependent on something else; for instance, the conjunction of grass with the wind initiates action in the grass only when it depends upon the velocity residing in the wind. If it is argued that because a sprout arises immediately after the destruction of the seed, and a jar arises immediately after the destruction of the lump of clay, therefore the production of a substance results from non-existence (*abhāva*) alone and not from conjunction—this is incorrect. This is because we observe the production of a substance from specific conjunctions of its constituent parts (*avayava*), and because if non-existence were devoid of distinctions (i.e., uniform), it would follow that specific effects arise without a cause (*akasmikatva*). *Nyāyakandalī* [141] [pp. 350–356]

This, however, is being examined here: is that which is produced already existent, or is it non-existent? The Sāṃkhyas maintain that it is produced as something already existent. Because there is no production of the non-existent—for it is not possible for anyone to bring about the existence of a sky-flower, which is non-existent—and because it is logical that an existent thing has a cause, since causality is a property of the existent. For it is observed that oil, which already exists in sesame seeds, is produced by pressing; but there is no example for the production of what is non-existent.

For this reason also, the effect exists [in the cause]: because of the selection of the material cause (*upādāna*). "Material causes" refers to the causal factors; their "selection" by the effect means the connection of the effect with them. Therefore, the effect is indeed existent [in the cause], because that which is non-existent lacks any connection. If it is argued that the effect is produced by the causes while being entirely unconnected [to them], we say no, because of the impossibility of everything arising from everything. If there were no distinction in being unconnected, then everything would arise from everything. But such is not the case; therefore, prior to its production, the effect is connected with its causes. As they have said:
"Because it is non-existent, there is no connection with causes that are associated with existence;
and for one who desires the production of what is unconnected, there is no systematic order.

Furthermore, does the capacity to produce belong to that which is capable or to that which is incapable? If it belongs to that which is incapable, there is an over-extension [of the definition]. If it belongs to that which is capable, is this capacity universal or restricted to certain instances? If it is universal, that same fault of over-extension occurs. If it is restricted to certain instances, then it must be explained how the cause has a restricted capacity with respect to that which is non-existent, since what is non-existent cannot function as an object.

Therefore, that which is possible for the capable—that is, the object which is the domain of capacity—is indeed existent even prior to its production. For this reason also, the effect is pre-existent (*satkārya*): because of the nature of the cause; the effect has the nature of the cause. [Objection: Is it not established by such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as "the whole is not other than the parts, because it occupies the same location as them," and "that which is not other than something does not occupy its location, just as a cow is not the location of a horse," that the effect is non-different from the cause? And since the cause is existent, the effect, being non-distinct from it, must also be existent. This has been stated:
"Because the non-existent cannot be produced, because of the necessity of employing a material cause, because everything is not possible from everything..."
Because that which is capable produces only that which it is capable of producing, and because the effect exists within the cause, the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkārya).

To this it is replied: if the cloth already exists in the threads even prior to the operation of the instruments, why is it not perceived when the causes of perception are present and there is even a desire to know it? If you say it is because of "non-manifestation" (*anabhivyakti*), what is this non-manifestation? If it is the absence of perception, then since the very impossibility of that [absence] has already been stated, how can that itself be the answer? Or if non-manifestation is the absence of that form which is capable of being perceived and capable of performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), then at that time you would be advocating the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*).

Because such a form, which did not previously exist, comes into being later. Now, if it is thought that—just as the eye and other [senses] are causes for the perception of a cloth—the operation of causes such as the weaver is also a cause for its perception; and that because of the absence of this [operation], there is no perception even though the object exists? No, for the operation of the causes is also always possible in that case. If it is argued that the operation itself was previously unmanifest and is now manifested by the causes, thereby making the entity perceptible? Then, if this manifestation is also non-existent, how could it [bring about perception]?

What is the reason? If you say it is because [the effect] exists, then the consequence that the entity would be perceived remains exactly as before; thus, without the production of some unprecedented distinction, the perception of what was previously unperceived later on is difficult to establish.

As for what was said—that "what is non-existent cannot be produced, like a sky-flower"—in that case, there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): a sky-flower has the single nature of being non-existent, whereas a jar or the like has the nature of being both existent and non-existent; that [jar], being previously non-existent, subsequently becomes existent. If it is asked how there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence in a single locus, [the answer is] because they coexist through a difference in time.

If it is asked, "Since the cloth—the substratum—does not exist prior to its production, how can non-existence be its property? [the answer is: As is the Yakṣa, so is the Baka; existence cannot be a property of the non-existent, but non-existence is indeed appropriate for that which is non-existent. If it is asked, "How can that which was previously non-existent possess existence? [the answer is: It is through the efficacy of the causes. There is a certain power in the shuttle and other implements such that, when they operate together, the cloth—which was previously non-existent—is produced.

If it is argued that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasakti*) if that which is non-existent and unconnected were produced, we say no; for there is a capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the class of threads to produce only the class of cloth. Why is this so? [The opponent asks: "Why is this so even in your own position? [The author replies: "Why is it that the nature of cloth resides only in the threads and not everywhere? [The opponent says: "Because of the inherent nature of things (*vastusvābhāvya*). [The author replies: That same [principle] will apply here as well. For this very reason, there is also a restriction regarding the material cause (*upādāna-niyama*), because through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one determines the capacity of a thing of a certain class to produce an effect of that same class.

Furthermore, as for the claim that because effect and cause are non-different, the persistence of the effect follows simply from the persistence of the cause—that is unproven, being established by what is itself unproven; for the difference between effect and cause in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), power (*śakti*), and configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moreover, it would entail the undesirable consequence that the universe, if identical with the primal matter (*pradhāna*), would be beyond the senses. As for the effect’s occupying the same space as the cause, that is based merely on its being dependent upon it; so enough of this excessive insistence on the views of the elders.

But let this be considered: what is this "power" (*śakti*)? The Noble Ones [the Buddhists] hold that it is some kind of supersensible entity. That is incorrect, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence. Now, if you think: "Just as it is understood that burning arises from fire in its ordinary state, so too it is not seen to arise when mantras or medicinal herbs are present; if the visible form alone were the cause of burning, then since that complete [cause] is present, burning would not fail to occur."

And there is this non-arising; this, indicating a deficiency in the perceived form [of the fuel], leads one to postulate the existence of a supersensuous power in the fire, which is either suppressed or destroyed by means of mantras and the like. In that case, where the effect arises again through the application of a remedy, it is "suppression"; but where there is no arising of the effect whatsoever, it is "destruction."

Nor should it be said: "The mantra is neither conjoined with fire nor inherent in it; how then could it destroy a potency residing in a different locus? If it were to destroy it, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the principle. This is because [the destruction] occurs by virtue of being directed toward that specific object. Just as malevolent magic (abhicāra), even though unconnected [to the victim], kills only the person for whose sake it is performed and not another person, so too the mantra, when employed while aiming at a particular individual, obstructs the potency of that individual alone and not of all.

Nor should it be proclaimed that: "If power (*śakti*) were of the nature of a substance, would it not perish upon the destruction of either the inherent (*samavāyin*) or non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) cause? Or, if it were not distinct from the quality (*guṇa*), would it not perish through the destruction of its substratum or the emergence of a contrary quality?"—for we do not accept *samavāya*. We state that very cause of destruction from which we perceive the destruction of a thing; however, we do not accept this convention (*samaya*) devised by you, because it is contradicted by experience (*pratīti*).

If it must necessarily be accepted, then let the destruction of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) alone be admitted where it is observed; as for this power (*śakti*), like similarity (*sādṛśya*), it will perish by another means as well. If it is asked, "Since power is understood in fire through the production and non-production of effects, on what basis is it postulated in all entities?", this is of little consequence, because that [power] which was postulated in one case as being conducive to the production of an effect is inferred here [in all cases] precisely from the production of that effect.

To this it is replied: the non-production of the effect in the presence of mantras and the like does not necessitate the postulation of an unseen form (*adṛṣṭa*). Just as fire, whose causal capacity has been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is the cause of burning, so too is the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of obstructing factors such as mantras a cause. And since that [absence] ceases when mantras and the like are employed, the non-production of the burning occurs solely due to a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaiguṇya*), and not from a lack of power (*śaktivaikalya*) [in the fire].

If it is argued that because an entity is observed to be invariably dependent on a cause that is itself an entity, a non-entity cannot be an effect, we say no. This is because from the non-performance of obligatory (*nitya*) rites, demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises; otherwise, if demerit did not arise from the non-performance of obligatory rites, there would be no performance of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), as such performance would be purposeless.

If it is argued that in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises from performing another act instead of the obligatory one, but not because the prior non-existence of the performance of the obligatory rite is the cause [of demerit], we say: no. For even the non-performance of the obligatory rite functions as an auxiliary factor, being invariably concomitant with that [demerit]. Now, if it is argued that when an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*) is applied, its absence ceases, and thus the burning does not occur, then in the case of an "obstructor of the obstructor" (*pratibandhakapratibandhaka*), burning would likewise not occur, because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—which is the cause of that burning—would have ceased.

Moreover, it is observed that when an obstacle is countered by another factor such as a mantra, the [effect] occurs; therefore, since it is established that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not the cause, power (*śakti*) must be the cause. And thus, the hypothesis that this power was previously obstructed and is now stimulated by a second factor gains ground. But even that is unsatisfactory, because when a visible explanation is possible, there is no room for the postulation of an invisible one.

In this hypothesis—that sometimes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) accompanied by the absence of obstructing mantras and so forth is the cause, while at other times the complex accompanied by a second mantra and so forth is the cause—what contradiction is there that would necessitate resorting to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)? For a difference in the causal complex is observed even for an effect that is uniform in nature; for example, fire produced from the friction of wood and fire produced from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*). This is the secret of the principles established by reasoning (*tarka*). As for the secret of the principles established by Mīmāṃsā, it has been explained by us in the *Tattvaprabodha*. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [142] [pp. 357–361]

Now, what is its definition, and how many kinds are there? Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the attainment of two things that were previously unattained. It is of three types: produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and conjunction-produced conjunction.
Among these, that produced by the action of one is the conjunction of a mobile object with an immobile one, such as a post with a hawk, or of all-pervading entities with material objects.
Conjunction produced by the action of both occurs when two things moving in opposite directions meet, as in the case of two wrestlers or two rams.

Conjunction produced by conjunction, however, is a conjunction occurring between an effect and a non-effect, preceded by a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause; it belongs to that which has just arisen or to that which has long since arisen and is now inactive, and it arises from one, from two, or from many.
First, from the conjunction of one thread with a *vīraṇa* grass stalk, there arises the conjunction of two-threaded cloth with a *vīraṇa* grass stalk.
From two conjunctions of a thread with space, there arises one conjunction of two-threaded cloth with space.
And from many conjunctions of threads and the shuttle, there arises a single conjunction of the cloth and the shuttle.
*Nyāyakandalī* [142] [pp. 357–363]

It has already been understood that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause of the cognition of things being conjoined; however, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its distinctions (*bheda*) are not yet known. To address this, he asks: "Now, what is its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and how many kinds are there? Here, the word *atha* introduces the question; the word *katham* has the sense of the interrogative *kim* (as in "What is dharma? What is its definition?"). The word *lakṣaṇa* denotes essential nature; thus, the question is: "What is the essential nature of conjunction? As for "how many kinds," the meaning is "of how many types."

He states the definition: conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the attainment of two things that were previously unattained. Conjunction is that mutual contact which is the subsequent attainment of two substances that were previously unattained. The phrase "of two things that were previously unattained" is for the purpose of excluding inherence (*samavāya*). Now he explains its divisions: "And it is of three kinds. [p.358]

The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis: conjunction is indeed of three kinds only. He demonstrates this threefold nature by means of the phrase beginning with "produced by the action of one" (*anyatarakarmaja*). Among two conjoined substances, that which is the action belonging to whichever one substance is the "action of one"; that which is produced from this is "produced by the action of one. The actions belonging to both substances are the "actions of both"; that which is produced from these is "produced by the actions of both. Furthermore, conjunction is also produced from conjunction.

Among those [three types of conjunction], that which arises from the action of one is as follows: among those three, the conjunction of an inactive substance with an active substance is "arisen from the action of one. An example of this is: as between a post and a hawk, or between all-pervading substances and material objects. The conjunction of the inactive post with the active hawk is produced by the action of the hawk.

Thus, the conjunction of all-pervading, inactive substances such as space with active, corporeal substances that possess the dimensions of non-pervasive entities arises from the action of the corporeal substance. Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that when one person moves slowly and another runs after him from behind, a conjunction arising from the action of either one occurs? How then can it be said that [conjunction] occurs between an active and an inactive substance? This is true; however, it should be understood that the expression "inactive" is intended with reference to the specific action that serves as the cause for the conjunction in question.

First, there is the conjunction between the hawk’s foot and the top of the post; subsequently, there is the conjunction between the hawk and the post as wholes. Regarding this, some maintain that the conjunction of the two parts is produced by action (*karmaja*), whereas the conjunction of the two wholes is a conjunction produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*). This too is without substance, because even for a whole that possesses motion, its conjunction with another whole arises from the motion of that very whole itself.

If this is not accepted, then since even parts would be wholes relative to their own parts, the conjunction produced by action would be eliminated in all wholes; and that being the case, one must either assert the absence of action in the whole or abandon the definition of action as "action is the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction.
How much stumbling we shall point out at every step on the part of those who are poorly lettered and pretentious, who discard both reasoning and the words of the Teacher, like blind men.

Conjunction produced by the action of both [substances] is the meeting of two things possessing actions in opposite directions. When two objects moving toward each other's location from two directions undergo mutual obstruction, those are "opposite directions," such as east and west, or south and north. Those substances which possess actions in opposite directions are "those with actions in opposite directions"; their meeting is conjunction produced by the action of both, because the capacity for each is determined to reside in both individually.
An example is that of two wrestlers or two rams.

Conjunction produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*), however, occurs when that which has just arisen or has long since arisen, being devoid of motion, comes into contact with non-causal factors that are themselves conjoined with its cause; it is preceded by a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause, and resides in both the effect and the non-effect. Here, the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is intended to mean the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), while the term "non-cause" (*akāraṇa*) refers to anything other than the inherent cause. We shall clarify the remainder through examples.

And that [conjunction] arises from one, from two, or from many. First, from one: from the conjunction of a single thread and a *vīraṇa* grass, there arises the conjunction of the two-threaded substance (*dvitantuka*) with the *vīraṇa*. When the two-threaded substance has just been produced and is yet motionless, its inherent cause—the single thread—is conjoined with the *vīraṇa*; thus, the conjunction of that thread with the *vīraṇa* arises from the prior conjunction of the thread and the *vīraṇa* alone. This is described as being preceded by the conjunction of the cause's own cause.

The thread is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the two-threaded cloth, while the *vīraṇa* grass is its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because [the cloth] is produced by the conjunction of those two. Furthermore, this [conjunction] resides in both the effect and the non-effect; since it inheres in the two-threaded cloth, which is the effect of the threads, and in the *vīraṇa* grass, which is not that effect, its status as the cause of conjunction is established by elimination (*pariśeṣasiddha*), as no other [cause] is possible.

And here, "proximity" (pratyāsatti) consists in inherence in a single object that is the effect [of the conjunction]. This is because the conjunction of the threads and the vīraṇa-grass inheres in the same object—the vīraṇa-grass—together with the effect, which is the conjunction of the two-threaded cloth and the vīraṇa-grass. Is there not a contradiction with the Sūtra—"qualities originate another quality"—if a single conjunction were the producer of a conjunction? No, for this is due to a misunderstanding of the meaning of the Sūtra.

It is stated by this [sūtra] that qualities also function as causes with respect to [other] qualities; however, it does not mean that only many qualities originate [a new quality], and not one or two, because no such restrictive rule (avadhāraṇa) is heard. As for the point here that "qualities originate another quality," the resolution—that this rule applies to those qualities functioning within a cause which originate their own kind, but not to all qualities—is convincing only to those of sharp intellect who have not heard the [correct] explanation, and not to us.

From two conjunctions of the threads with space, there arises the conjunction of the dyad (the two-threaded cloth) with space. First, space conjoins with the dyad as soon as it has been produced, because it is conjoined with the cause of that dyad, just as the vīraṇa grass is conjoined with the causes of the dyad. Furthermore, there is no other cause for that conjunction; therefore, its production occurs precisely from the two conjunctions of the threads—the causes of the dyad—with space.

And from many conjunctions of threads and the shuttle, there arises a single conjunction of the cloth and the shuttle; that is, from those many conjunctions of the individual threads—the causes of the cloth—with the shuttle, a single conjunction of the cloth and the shuttle is produced. Furthermore, the status of the threads as initiators of the cloth occurs through a succession of initiations of composite substances (*khaṇḍāvayavidravya*).

Nor is there the fault of multiple corporeal entities occupying the same location, because we do not admit the inherence of another whole in exactly those same threads—neither fewer nor more—in which one whole resides.

A two-threaded [fabric] inheres in two threads; a three-threaded [fabric], however, inheres in those two and in another thread, as well as in that additional substance. Thus, in the conceptualization of each subsequent stage, how could there be co-occupancy of space? For this very reason, when a cloth is torn, there is the perception of fragmentary wholes through the differentiation of states such as "smaller," "smallest," and so forth, while the original remains. But if a cloth were to be started again once those [threads] have perished, this would be difficult to establish.

But in that case, would not the parts of the body of a child, together with the parts of the food [ingested], begin another body while that [previous body] remains undestroyed? Let them begin it—if, as in the case of a cloth, the perception of the previous bodies is possible when the composite wholes remain in the old body or when it has been destroyed. But if this is not the case, then this rule does not apply there, because the determination is made according to what is observed.

By this, the objection that under the theory of the "beginning by what is already begun" (ārabhyārambhaka-vāda), there could be no perception of the world as existing in the state of atoms, is also refuted; for it has been demonstrated in the section on Earth (pṛthivī-adhikāra) that atoms lack the status of being the cause of triads (tryaṇuka) and so forth.

Alternatively, if atoms, having initiated a dyad, together with that dyad initiate a triad, and those together with the triad initiate another substance, even so, why would there be no perception of the universe? For the causes of perception—namely, magnitude (*mahattva*), possession of multiple constituent substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and specific qualities (*rūpaviśeṣa*)—are present. If it is argued that despite their presence, they are imperceptible because their substrata are beyond the senses (*atīndriyāśrayatva*), then this difficulty is equally unavoidable in your own position as well. Therefore, this is not an inconsistency here. Regarding the atoms' role in initiating triads, the same reasoning stated in the section on Earth (*pṛthivī*) should be followed.

And the production of two from one: how so? When there is a conjunction between an earth atom and a water atom, and simultaneously a conjunction occurs of the earth atom with another earth atom and of the water atom with another water atom, then by those two conjunctions, two dyads—one earthy and one watery—are produced simultaneously.

Then, at the very same time that color and other qualities arise in the two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) by the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes, there simultaneously arise two conjunctions: one between the cause and the non-cause, and another between the effect and the non-effect.

What is the reason? For it is a logical principle that an effect must necessarily be conjoined with a non-cause that is itself conjoined with its own cause. Therefore, the earth dyad is conjoined with the water atom which is conjoined with its own cause; likewise, the water dyad is conjoined with the earth atom which is conjoined with its own cause.

[Page 365] Now, how is there a mutual connection between two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) that are connected to each other’s cause and non-cause? Their connection is also through two conjunctions produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*).

There is no unproduced conjunction (*aja-saṃyoga*), like the eternal spherical dimension (*nitya-parimaṇḍala*), because it is not mentioned separately. For instance, after stating the four kinds of produced dimensions, [the author of the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra*] says, "The spherical is eternal" (VS 7.1.26). Similarly, after stating the produced conjunctions—such as those arising from the action of one of the two factors—he would have to state the eternal one separately; however, he did not do so. Therefore, there is no unproduced conjunction.

The partial occurrence of space and the other [all-pervading substances] in atoms is due to conjunction produced by the action of one or the other. However, there is no mutual conjunction among all-pervading substances (*vibhu*), because they lack separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*).
This [separate establishment], moreover, consists in either both or one of two things possessing distinct motion, or having distinct substrates as their support.

Regarding the question of how two conjunctions can arise from a single conjunction, the author, being asked by one who is ignorant, replies with the words "When... When a conjunction occurs between an earth atom and a water atom, there simultaneously arise two further conjunctions: one of the earth atom with another earth atom, and one of the water atom with another water atom. At that time, by means of those two conjunctions, two dyads—one composed of earth and one composed of water—are simultaneously produced.

Because the conjunction of homogeneous substances is the cause for the production of another substance, at the very same time that color and other qualities arise in the earthy and watery dyads through the sequence beginning with their causes, two conjunctions—arising from the mutual conjunction of the respective causes and non-causes—are produced simultaneously in the respective effects and non-effects.

In the case of two dyads, one earthy and one watery, their constituent causes—the earthy atom and the watery atom—are conjoined with one another. The earthy atom is the cause of the other earthy dyad, but is not the cause of the other watery dyad. Likewise, the watery atom is the cause of the other watery dyad, but is not the cause of the other earthy dyad.

From the conjunction of those two, there occurs a conjunction between the other earth atom—whose effect is the earth dyad (dvyaṇuka) and whose cause is the water atom—and that [water atom]. Likewise, from the conjunction of the other water atom—whose effect is the water dyad and whose cause is the earth atom—a conjunction also occurs between those two; thus, production arises from one [atom] with respect to two [atoms].

What is the reason? Being asked, "What is the proof for the conjunction of dissimilar atoms in the case of a binary compound (*dvyaṇuka*) consisting of an earth atom and a water atom? he states the proof: "By means of that which is conjoined with its cause. An earth atom is connected with a water binary compound because it is conjoined with the cause of that [binary compound], just as a shuttle is conjoined with a cloth. The same should be stated by taking a water atom as the subject (*pakṣa*).

Since an effect is conjoined with that which is conjoined with its cause, therefore an earthy dyad is connected with a watery atom conjoined with its own cause, and a watery dyad is connected with an earthy atom conjoined with its own cause; such is the summary.

Now, how is there a connection between the earth-dvyaṇuka and the water-dvyaṇuka, which are bound to each other by their respective causes? For how can there be a connection between the earth-dvyaṇuka—which is connected to its own cause, the water-dvyaṇuka’s cause, namely a water-atom (paramāṇu)—and the water-dvyaṇuka—which is connected to its own cause, the earth-dvyaṇuka’s cause, namely an earth-atom? Thus he asks. He provides the answer: "Of those two also... [iti].

The conjunction between the two dyads arises from two conjunctions produced by conjunction: namely, the conjunction produced by conjunction between the earthly dyad and a water atom, and the conjunction produced by conjunction between the water dyad and an earthly atom. From these two conjunctions of an earthly atom and a water atom with the two dyads, there occurs the mutual conjunction of the two dyads. In this case as well, the previously stated rule applies: "the effect is conjoined with that which is not its cause, by means of that which is conjoined with its cause."

It has been stated that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is of only three kinds. Some maintain that even eternal conjunction is possible; to refute this, he says: "There is no unproduced conjunction, because it is not mentioned separately, like the spherical [atoms]. Since the omniscient Great Sage, in his endeavor to teach all things, did not mention it separately, there is no unproduced conjunction, just like a sky-flower. He explains this very point with the words beginning "just as," and so forth.

The meaning of the thesis is that conjunction is not unproduced (*aja*), and not that there is no such thing as an unproduced conjunction, because [the latter claim] would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Now, one might object: the conjunction between an atom (*paramāṇu*) and space (*ākāśa*) is indeed eternal, because both of them are eternal and because there is no lack of contact (*aprāpti*) between them.

As for the fact that this was not stated by Kaṇāda, it is because error is a human attribute; therefore, he says: "of ether and the rest, [conjunction and disjunction] with atoms. Just as, in the case of a large banyan tree whose single root extends through its stones and parts, a person moving from the root to the top or from the top to the root simultaneously perceives conjunctions and disjunctions produced by the action of either one, so too, although ether is all-pervading, conjunctions and disjunctions with an atom—produced by the action of the atom—occur; of these two...

Because it is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), the conjunction of an atom with space is not eternal. This much has been refuted in the following manner: what is the response regarding the mutual conjunction of all-pervading (*vibhu*) entities? For this [conjunction] cannot be produced by the action of one of the two, nor can it be produced by the action of both, because they are devoid of motion (*niṣkriyatva*). Nor is it produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*), for a conjunction produced by conjunction occurs when an effect is conjoined with that which is not its cause, even though it is conjoined with its cause. And this is not possible for all-pervading entities, because they are eternal.

Furthermore, there exists a conjunction among them, because space is conjoined even with formless substances, since it possesses conjunction with material substances, like a cloth or similar objects; this is understood through inference. Since it is eternal, like existence and its cause, this [objection] that "there is no such thing as an unborn conjunction" is untenable. To this, he replies: "Of the all-pervading [substances]. Conjunction is observed only where there is separate establishment (yutasiddhi). However, separate establishment does not exist in the case of space and the others; therefore, due to the absence of the pervader, conjunction also does not occur in them.

Furthermore, that inference which was stated to establish conjunction is not a valid proof, because it applies equally to both positions. Just as this [inference] praises the conjunction of all-pervading entities (*vibhu*), so too does it [establish] their disjunction by means of those very same reasons and examples. If it is argued, "Let there be the establishment of both, since their existence as such is perceived through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," we say no; for if one of the two—conjunction or disjunction—is eternal, the other is impossible. Thus, neither is established, due to their mutual exclusion.

Now, what is this "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*), the absence of which prevents the conjunction of all-pervading entities from being established? To this he says: "That, moreover... [p. 368]. For eternal things, separate establishment consists in the separate movement of two things or of one of the two; for non-eternal things, it consists in the subsistence of two things or of one of them in separate substrata through mutual exclusion. The intention is that neither of these two types exists in the case of space and so forth.

The destruction of every conjunction, however, results from a disjunction inhering in the same object [as the conjunction]. This applies to that produced by the action of one [of two bodies], that produced by the action of both, and that produced by another conjunction; [all] result from a disjunction inhering in the same object. When a conjunction exists between two substances, the destruction of that conjunction occurs through their mutual disjunction. Although the conjunction still exists at the time of the disjunction, nevertheless their coexistence is no longer perceived, either because the destruction occurs so rapidly or because the perception of it is obstructed by the disjunction.

In some cases, conjunction is destroyed even by the destruction of its substratum. How so? When a conjunction exists between two threads, an action arises in one of them—specifically in the part (*aṃśu*) that constitutes the thread—due to some cause. By that action, a disjunction is produced from the other part; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction of the two parts, which leads to the destruction of the thread. Consequently, there is the destruction of the conjunction residing in it, because a conjunction that has both as its substrata is not observed to persist when one of its substrata no longer exists.
Praśastapādabhāṣya [144] [p.369]:
Disjunction (*vibhāga*) is the cause of the cognition of separation. It is also the cause of sound and disjunction.

Disjunction is non-attainment (*aprāpti*) preceded by attainment (*prāpti*). It is of three kinds: that produced by the action of one [of two things], that produced by the action of both, and disjunction produced by disjunction.
In that regard, [disjunction] arises from the action of one [of two bodies], or from the action of both, just like conjunction.
Disjunction, however, is of two kinds: arising from the disjunction of the cause, and arising from the disjunction of the cause of the cause.
*Nyāyakandalī* [144] [pp. 369–371]

Since disjunction is preceded by conjunction, he says—immediately following that—for the purpose of its definition: "Disjunction is the cause of the cognition of being separated. Here too, the explanation is as before. If it is argued that the cognition of being separated occurs when there is an absence of conjunction, [we ask]: in the absence of disjunction, from what does the absence of conjunction arise? If it is argued that it is produced by action (*karman*), no; for action is not observed to have the capacity to destroy a quality (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, it is observed that the destruction of qualities (guṇa) serves as the cause for other qualities; therefore, in this case as well, one must postulate another quality. Moreover, if conjunction were non-existent, there would be the cognition "these two are unjoined," but not the cognition "they are disjoined," because a negation cannot be apprehended through a positive mode of presentation. If you argue that this cognition is merely figurative (bhākta), then disjunction cannot be denied, for there can be no figurative usage in the absence of a primary referent.

He demonstrates its function: "and it is the cause of sound and disjunction. The meaning of "and" (*ca*) is that it is not only the cause of the cognition of separation, but also the cause of sound and disjunction. When a bamboo split is being split, this initial sound must have another quality as its cause, because it is a sound, like the sound produced by the conjunction of a drum and a stick. Nor is this [initial sound] produced by conjunction, because conjunction is absent [in that case]. Therefore, this is produced solely by the disjunction of the bamboo splits, because it exists only when that [disjunction] exists.
We shall explain the fact that disjunction is the cause of disjunction immediately hereafter.
