"Attainment is *vikā* (change), non-attainment is its definition. Regarding the term "non-dharma" (*adharma*), the negative particle (*nañ*) refers to another quality that is opposed to dharma, rather than to the mere absence of dharma; likewise, in the term "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*), the negative particle refers to another quality that is opposed to attainment, rather than to the absence of attainment. The meaning of the sentence is this: when attainment has previously existed, that which is non-attainment—a specific quality opposed to attainment—is disjunction (*vibhāga*).

Is it merely the prior state of conjunction, or does it also possess causality toward disjunction? We maintain that it is merely the state of abiding; for if conjunction were the cause of disjunction, then immediately after the conjunction of the parts, their disjunction would arise, resulting in the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the substance could not be produced. If it is argued that conjunction is the cause when assisted by action (karman), then let action alone be the cause—its capacity having been determined through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—and not conjunction, since [disjunction] does not occur even when that [conjunction] is present.

Just as there is a rule of temporal priority for the destruction of a thing with respect to its production, so too there is a rule of temporal priority for conjunction with respect to the production of disjunction, because disjunction has a nature that is opposed to it.

And that [disjunction] is of three kinds; this is the statement of its divisions. Here too, the word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis, meaning it is indeed of three kinds: disjunction produced by the action of one [of two bodies], disjunction produced by the action of both, and disjunction produced by another disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*). Among these, the disjunctions produced by the action of one and by the action of both are like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Just as the conjunction of an active body with an inactive one is produced by the action of one, so too is disjunction. And just as the conjunction of two wrestlers or two rams is produced by the action of both, so too is disjunction.

"Disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*) is of two kinds. By the word "but" (*tu*), its distinction from the two preceding types is stated. One disjunction arises from the disjunction of two causes; the other, however, arises from the disjunction of a cause and a non-cause—thus there is a twofold division. *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, [145] [pp. 372–375]

In this regard, first, concerning the division of the cause: when an action arises in a cause that is engaged with its effect, it effects a division from another constituent part, but not from a location such as space; however, when it effects a division from a location such as space, it does not then effect a division from another constituent part—this is the established rule. Therefore, the action of a constituent part initiates a division only from another constituent part, and from that division follows the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance.

When that [effect] has perished, there is the destruction of the whole because of the absence of its cause; at that time, the disjunction residing in the two causes, depending on the time characterized by the destruction of the effect or on the independent constituent part, initiates a disjunction of the very active constituent from a location such as space which was previously conjoined with the effect—but not of the inactive one, for if there were no subsequent conjunction due to the absence of a cause, the consequence would be that it could not be experienced.

However, that action of the part does not produce a disjunction from a location such as space, because the time for the production of that [disjunction] has already passed. But it certainly produces a conjunction with another location, because there is no lapse of time for an action that has not yet produced its conjunction.
(Nyāyakandalī [145], pp. 372–376)

The distinction [of disjunction] due to the distinction of its cause is now explained by the passage beginning with "occupied by the effect" (*kāryāviṣṭa*). When an action has arisen in a cause that is occupied, pervaded, or encompassed by an effect, and it produces a disjunction from another part of that [same] component which destroys the conjunction that initiates the substance, at that time it does not produce a disjunction from a location such as space (*ākāśa*) that is already encompassed by the substance. And when it [produces a disjunction] from a location such as space, it does not [produce one] from another part; this is the established rule.

Therefore, the action belonging to a part initiates disjunction from another part alone; for there is a rule that an action which is the cause of disjunction from space does not produce disjunction from another part. Consequently, an action that initiates disjunction from another part produces disjunction from that other part alone, and not from a location such as space.

This is the intended meaning (*abhisaṃdhi*): the status of being the agent of a spatial division (*ākāśa-vibhāga*) is pervaded by the non-production of a division that is opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance (*dravyārambhaka-saṃyoga*). And the production of a division opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance is contradictory to the non-production of a division opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance. Therefore, wherever this [latter property] is perceived, since the non-production of a division opposed to the conjunction initiating a substance is absent, the status of being the agent of a spatial division—which is pervaded by it—is also absent. Just as, for example, when fire is excluded, smoke is excluded.

If it is argued that there is merely a coexistence between the quality of being the agent of a division of space and the non-initiation of a division that opposes the conjunction initiating a substance, but not a necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*), we say no; for no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed. Wherever a deviation is seen between two things, there they have merely a coexistence, as in the case of "earthiness" and "scratchability by iron" in a diamond (*vajra*): despite its earthiness, it does not possess scratchability by iron, as this property is found in wood and other such things.

However, no deviation is observed regarding [the properties of] being the agent of the division of space and being the producer of a specific conjunction. Even if such a deviation were not observed, one might suspect that it could occur at some time, provided that the coexistence of these two were perceived as being caused by limiting conditions (*upādhi*), as is the case between a teacher and a pupil. But this is not so, because no such limiting conditions are perceived.

If coexistence that is unobserved to deviate and is free from limiting conditions were not the cause of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then there would be no pervasion even between fire and smoke; thus, the very discourse of inference in this world would now be cut off.

If the disjunction from another part is produced by the action of a constituent part, but not the disjunction from a location such as space, what is established thereby? To this he says: "And from disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance. The meaning is that if [the action] were the agent of disjunction from space, then because no specific disjunction would be produced, the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance would not occur.

To address what would happen upon the destruction of the conjunction, he says: "In that [conjunction]. When that conjunction, which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), is destroyed, the whole (*avayavin*) is destroyed according to the principle that "in the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect. To address what would happen when the substance consisting of the whole has been destroyed, he says: "Then."

When the substance has perished, the disjunction residing in its two constituent parts initiates, with respect to time characterized by the destruction of the effect or to an independent part, a disjunction of that very part—now inactive—from the location such as space that was previously conjoined with the effect. As long as the causal substance has not perished, the part possesses independence.

Since there is no capacity for the [parts] to go to separate locations, it is not possible for that disjunction to occur from the location of the whole; for this reason, it is stated that one must depend upon either a time characterized by the destruction of the effect or an independent part. If it is asked what the reason is for the disjunction existing between two causes producing a disjunction only in that which possesses action, he says: "No, because there is an absence of cause for that which is devoid of action."

When a disjunction arises from a [prior] disjunction, action (*karman*) is also an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); in its absence, there would be no disjunction for that which is devoid of action. For this very reason, he states another argument: "If a subsequent conjunction were not produced, there would follow the consequence of being non-enjoyable. For action arises primarily for the sake of a subsequent conjunction, since it accomplishes some human purpose through a substance that has reached another location.

In this regard, if there were no disjunction of the active part from a location such as space that is conjoined with the effect, then—because the prior conjunction acting as an obstacle would not have ceased—the subsequent conjunction could not arise; consequently, that [activity] would be useless and serve no purpose. But this is not tenable. Therefore, the intended meaning is that disjunction belongs only to that which possesses activity. It is not possible for the two activities of the parts to simultaneously act as the cause of the disjunction from space and so forth at the same time as the disjunction of the parts.

Let this [action] not produce two disjunctions simultaneously; however, what contradiction is there in its production occurring sequentially, such that one should abandon this [action], whose capacity for producing disjunction is observed, and instead resort to a disjunction—whose capacity is unobserved—as the cause of disjunction? To this, he says: "But that action of the part does not produce disjunction from a location such as space, because the [space] that initiated it has already passed away."

For such is the nature of action that, by not being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of disjunction, it initiates disjunction at the very moment immediately following its own production, and not at any other moment; and since that time of its initiating disjunction has passed by the time the second part is produced, disjunction does not arise from it.

But why does it also produce conjunction with another location? Because there is an interval of multiple moments; therefore, he says: "it produces conjunction with another location. Just as the moment immediately following the production of an action is the time for initiating disjunction, so too the moment immediately following the cessation of the prior conjunction is the time for initiating conjunction with another location, since it is impossible for a substance situated in its former place to reach another place [without such a process].

Furthermore, there has been no lapse—that is, no passing away—of the time at which that conjunction was to begin; for this time would have passed only if a conjunction with another location had been produced by the action, but such is not the case. Therefore, because there is no lapse of the time for the action to initiate the conjunction while the conjunction remains unproduced, the action produces conjunction and not disjunction.

In this case, since it is impossible for another [cause] to exist and because a thing is not produced without a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), it is established that disjunction inhering in the same object (*ekārthasamaveta*) is its cause. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the section.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [146] [pp. 376, 382]

How is it also through the disjunction between the cause and the non-cause? When an action arises in the hand, without producing a disjunction from another part, it initiates disjunctions from points of space and so forth, and subsequently initiates conjunctions with other points of space. At that time, those are the disjunctions between the cause and the non-cause. Then, depending on the direction toward which the action is oriented and facing the effect, they initiate disjunctions between the effect and the non-effect; immediately after that, from the conjunction of the cause and the non-cause, they initiate conjunctions between the effect and the non-effect. [p. 382]

If the production of the disjunction of the effect follows immediately after the disjunction of the cause, then the production of the conjunction of the effect follows immediately after the conjunction of the cause;
[Nyāyakandalī, pp. 376–382].

Having thus understood the disjunction preceded by the disjunction of the cause, one who wishes to understand the disjunction preceded by the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause asks: "How also from the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause? He provides the answer with the words beginning with "yadā" (when).

When an action has arisen in the hand due to some cause, and without producing a disjunction from other parts of that hand, it initiates disjunctions from locations such as space; when it then initiates conjunctions with other locations, those disjunctions between the cause and non-cause are the disjunctions of the hand—which is the cause of the body—from non-causes such as locations in space.

With respect to that direction toward which the action is oriented for the commencement of its effect—that is, the direction in which a subsequent conjunction is to be produced by the action—the action initiates the disjunctions between the hand, which is the agent of the effect, and those things that are not its effects, namely the points of space such as ether and so forth. For instance, when there is no disjunction of the hand from a location such as a wall, a disjunction of the body from that same location is likewise observed. And this [disjunction of the body] is not the result of an action belonging to the body itself, because at that moment the body is devoid of motion.

Nor can it be produced by manual action (*hastakriyā*), for it is never observed that an action residing in a different substratum is the cause of disjunction. Therefore, it is postulated that the cause of this [disjunction] is the disjunction between the cause and the non-cause (*kāraṇākāraṇavibhāga*). The phrase "in ether, etc. (*ākāśādau*) includes all pervasive substances (*vibhudravya*). For this very reason, the plural number is used in the word "disjunctions" (*vibhāgān*), because those disjunctions are many.

Regarding this, some say: "Since the simultaneous occurrence of the separation from the wall or other locations and the separation of the hand from the body is perceived, the assertion of a causal relationship between the two is contradicted by direct perception. This is incorrect, because at the time of the hand's separation, there is no cause for the production of the body's separation. Furthermore, an effect cannot arise in the absence of a cause, and it has already been stated that the action of the hand is not the cause [of the body's separation]. Therefore, the impression that these two occur simultaneously is an error.

Successive occurrence is to be inferred, whereas simultaneity is established by perception; and when perception stands as an obstacle, there is no arising of inference at all, because it lacks an uncontradicted object. If you ask, "How can perception be erroneous due to contradiction with that inference?", [we reply: why would inference even proceed in the case of piercing a hundred lotus petals? [Because] it would be contradicted by perception.

Now, you might think that in those cases where this [inference] would certainly subvert the object, inference does not arise due to contradiction with perception; however, here it is doubtful, because it is possible for the perception grasping simultaneity to occur even on the grounds of the rapid succession of the piercing of a hundred leaves.

Furthermore, there exists a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends a pervasion (vyāpti) well-known to all the world: "An extremely firm needle pierces what is not obstructed, but not what is obstructed. Therefore, by the force of this [pervasion], inference arises even when perception is possible.

Thus, in this case as well, since an action occurring in a different locus does not produce disjunction, the inference of sequence remains firmly established; for the means of valid cognition that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is extremely firm, and perception can be accounted for otherwise. For this very reason, perception is sublated by inference. For this [inference] possesses an object, whereas perception is without an object, because it functions merely through rapid succession.

Furthermore, that which possesses an object is strong because it obtains the assistance of the object as it exists in its true state, whereas that which is without an object is weak due to its lack of assistance. Indeed, since the sublation of perception arises through the very same perception that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is a sublation of perception by inference. Thus, the elders maintain that in cases such as disorientation regarding the directions, inference alone is stronger, saying: "Inference is indeed more powerful than even perception."

However, in the case of a perception that apprehends heat in fire, there is no other possible explanation; therefore, once the object has been determined by that [perception], there is no occurrence of inference when the object is sublated. For what purpose, then, is the relationship of the sublated and the sublator postulated between two cognitions? Because they are in contradiction regarding the same object: one cognition makes known that very same thing as "this is silver," while another makes known it as "this is mother-of-pearl."

Furthermore, the properties of being nacre and being silver cannot coexist in a single locus, because they are always observed to exist in mutual exclusion. Therefore, since there is a contradiction between the objects, and consequently a contradiction between their respective cognitions, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is postulated.

What is the sublation (*bādha*)? It is the removal of the object. [Objection: But surely the substrate (*dharmin*) manifested in the cognition of silver appears exactly as it was even when another cognition has arisen; it is only the "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) that does not exist. What, then, is being removed? [Response: Because "removal" means the disjunction of the relation [between the substrate and the attribute]. [Objection: That [silver-ness] appeared in the cognition. [Response: True, it appeared, but what has appeared cannot be removed, precisely because it has already occurred.
For an object that has appeared does not become non-appearing; although silver does not exist there in reality, it was presented by the cognition as if it were existing there.

If it is argued that "separation" consists precisely in the demonstration of non-existence—by way of directly demonstrating the contradiction of that cognition which has been produced—then what harm was done to the cognition of silver once the absence of silver had been demonstrated? For this [cognition of silver] has no function in the maintenance of the silver's existence; rather, its function lies in its manifestation, and that has already been accomplished by this very [cognition] as it arose. Thus, what is here being sublated? The harm done was this: upon the realization of the absence of silver, the nature of the previously arisen cognition of silver is realized as being unreal.

[Objection: But surely, in this way, sublation (*bādha*) is simply the removal of the result (*phala-apahāra*), because once a cognition is understood to be non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārtha*), it ceases to be a factor in practical activity (*vyavahāra*). [Reply: Not so. Because the removal of the result is necessarily concomitant with the removal of the object (*viṣaya-apahāra*). For a cognition is not, in all cases, restricted to its result; since that [cognition] depends on the person's desire, it terminates in the awareness of indifference (*upekṣā-saṃvitti*) when it is not produced.

Even in cases where there is a desire for a result, since that result is dependent upon its object, and the object is dependent upon cognition, it is the removal of the object alone that constitutes the sublation of the cognition, not the removal of the result itself; for the latter is necessarily concomitant with the former. Enough of this elaboration for the sake of the *Saṃgrahaṭīkā*.

[p.382] He now demonstrates the "conjunction produced by conjunction" (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*)—which was previously asserted as occurring immediately after the "division produced by division" (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*) and which arises after a long interval—with the words "immediately after that."

Therefore, immediately after the disjunction produced by disjunction, the conjunctions born of action—which involve the hand (the cause of the body) and the points of space such as ether (which are not its causes)—initiate conjunctions with the points of space such as ether (which are not the effects of the hand) belonging to the body (the effect of the hand), which is itself devoid of motion; it is not the action of the hand that initiates these, because that action has as its cause the reaching of another location by its own substratum. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the section.

Here he raises an objection with the words "yadi" (if). If the disjunction of the effect, the body, occurs after the disjunction of the cause, the hand, and likewise if the conjunction of the effect occurs after the conjunction of the cause, and not simultaneously with it; [then one might object: "But in that case, does this not entail the fault of the hand and the body being *yutasiddha* (separately established)? No, because there is a lack of understanding regarding what *yutasiddhi* actually is.

Furthermore, this [separate existence] consists in the possession of separate motion by two things or either one of them; this belongs to eternal things. For impermanent things, however, *yutasiddhi* (separate establishment) is inherence (*samavāya*) in distinct substrates.

The skin-faculty (*tvagindriya*) and the body do not possess separate motions; since they exist as inherence (*samavāya*) in their respective substrates, their mutual conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established. However, in the case of an atom (*aṇu*) and space (*ākāśa*), because there is no other substrate and one of the two possesses separate motion, conjunction and disjunction (*vibhāga*) are established. In the case of the yarn and the cloth, which are non-eternal, there is an absence of conjunction and disjunction with respect to each other because there is no other substrate. As for direction (*dik*) and the rest, however, because they lack separate motion, there is an absence of conjunction and disjunction with respect to each other. *Nyāyakandalī* [147] [pp. 383–385]

But if this were so, there would be "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*)—that is, separate existence or mutual independence—between the part and the whole. This is what is meant: if the body were dependent upon the hand, then when the hand moves, the body would necessarily move along with it; and if that were the case, there could be no sequence of conjunctions and disjunctions. If, however, these two possess conjunctions and disjunctions sequentially, then it follows that the body does not move when the hand moves, which entails its independence.

He refutes this, saying: "No. [The objection that] there would be the consequence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*) is not valid; why? Because separate existence is not properly understood. The meaning is that you do not understand the definition of separate existence as it truly is. What is its definition? To this he says: "That, moreover, belongs to two... Separate existence is the fitness for the inherence of actions that cause mutual conjunction and disjunction, belonging either to two things or to one of them.

The separate movement of two atoms, or the separate movement of one of the two when they are an atom and a space-atom—this, however, belongs to eternal things. The word "tu" (however) is used for emphasis; it should be understood as following the word "nityānām" (of eternal things), meaning that this kind of *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) belongs only to eternal things. As for non-eternal things, however, *yutasiddhi* is their inherence (*samavāya*) in separate substrates.

*Yutasiddhi* (separate existence) is the inherence (*samavāya*) of two things, or of either one of them, in a substrate other than [the other], through mutual exclusion; it pertains to impermanent things. For example, in the case of a jar and a cloth, there is the state of being a support and a supported in separate substrates for both. In the case of a bird and space, there is the state of being a support and a supported in a separate substrate for the bird alone. Even though there is also a separate movement of the bird, that separate movement is not what is grasped here, because that [definition] is explained as having only permanent things as its domain.

Why is it not said that even for non-eternal things, *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) consists precisely in separate movement? To this he replies: there is no separate movement of the skin-sense organ (*tvagindriya*) and the body; rather, because there is inherence (*samavāya*) in their respective substrates which are distinct, their mutual conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established. If, however, separate movement were defined as *yutasiddhi* even for non-eternal things, then due to the absence of separate movement between the skin-sense organ and the body, they would be *ayutasiddha* (inseparable).

Consequently, a conjunction between those two is not possible, because conjunction is necessarily pervaded by separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*). [And conjunction is their relation; it is not inherence (*samavāya*), because that is of a different nature. Therefore, for impermanent things, "separate establishment" means the absence of separate movement. Precisely because there is no substratum, the state of being a substratum and a dependent upon separate substrata does not exist in eternal things.

Since those [atoms] possess separate motion, their mutual conjunction and disjunction are established; therefore, with the intention that their "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*) consists precisely in their moving separately, he says: "But in the case of an atom and space, even though there is no other substratum, conjunction and disjunction are established because one of the two possesses separate motion.

Previously, it was stated that even in the absence of separate motion, because conjunction and disjunction are possible when the skin-sense organ and the body have separate substrata and superstrata, for impermanent things, "separate establishment" consists in having separate substrata and superstrata, not in moving separately.

Now, in order to support this very point, he demonstrates the absence of conjunction and disjunction—despite the impossibility of either the thread or the cloth having a separate motion—due to the lack of separate substrata, by means of the passage beginning with "of the thread and the cloth. However, in the case of all-pervading entities (*vibhu*), because neither both nor either of them possesses separate motion, there is no mutual conjunction, nor is there disjunction, since the latter is preceded by the former; rather, there is merely their abiding in their own essential nature. This he states with the words "of space and so forth."

By this much of the discussion, it has been established that while the hand moves, the body does not move; by this much, there is no separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*). If, however, the hand and the body were to have distinct substrata and superstrata, then there would be a separate establishment between them. But that is not the case, because the hand is inherently contained (*samaveta*) within the body.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [148] [pp. 386–387]

The destruction of every disjunction, however, occurs because it is momentary; it is momentary because its limit is the subsequent conjunction. But its destruction does not occur through the very same conjunction from which the disjunction arose, as is the case with conjunction. Why? Because, unlike the cognition of being conjoined, there is no persistence of the cognition of being disjoined. Therefore, it is momentary because its limit is the subsequent conjunction. [p. 387]

And in some cases, it perishes due to the destruction of its substratum. How so? When a part (*aṃśu*) produced in a constituent part of the two-threaded cloth (*dvitantuka*) begins a disjunction from another part, at that very same time, motion arises in the other thread as well; and from that disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread. Then, by the motion of the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this constitutes one moment of time.

Then, at the very moment when the destruction of the conjunction of the threads occurs due to disjunction, at that same moment, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread; and when that [thread] has perished, there is the destruction of the disjunction from the other thread which was dependent upon it.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [148]

The destruction of every disjunction, however, occurs because of its momentariness. As for the question—how is it established that every disjunction, whether produced by action (*karmaja*) or produced by another disjunction (*vibhāgaja*), and whether residing in the cause (*kāraṇavṛtti*) or residing in both the cause and the non-cause (*kāraṇākāraṇavṛtti*), possesses momentariness, that is, the quality of being destroyed very rapidly? To this he says: "Because of the existence of a limit in the form of a subsequent conjunction. Subsequent conjunction is the limit, the boundary; because of the existence of that [limit], disjunction is momentary.

What is being said? It is not that disjunction is without an end; rather, it has a subsequent conjunction as its limit, and this subsequent conjunction arises immediately thereafter. Therefore, since the subsequent conjunction—which perishes quickly—is the limit of the disjunction, why is this so? To this he says: "But not like conjunction."

Just as conjunction perishes through the mutual disjunction of its own two substrates, disjunction does not perish in the same way through the mutual conjunction of its own two substrates; rather, it perishes through the conjunction of its substrate with something else. For instance, the disjunction between a tree and a person at the base of the tree perishes either through the mutual conjunction of those two, or through the person's conjunction with another location.

If it is thus established that disjunction has subsequent conjunction as its limit—since the action that initiates it cannot reach its conclusion without bringing its own substrate to another location—then one might object: "Is this not also 'equal to the point to be proved' (sādhyasama), in that the cessation of disjunction occurs merely through conjunction? To this he replies: "Like the cognition of being conjoined. Just as the cognition of being conjoined persists for a long time, there is no such persistence of the cognition of being disjoined once the conjunction with another location of its own substrate has occurred.
Therefore, its cessation occurs through mere conjunction alone. He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

In some cases, however, destruction also occurs from the destruction of the substrate. How so? This is the question of the ignorant. The answer is: "When... [p.388]. When an action arises in a fiber (*aṃśu*), which is a part of the thread that is the cause of the two-threaded cloth, and it initiates the disjunction of that fiber from another fiber, at that very same time an action also arises in the other thread. And when, due to that disjunction, the conjunction that originated the thread is destroyed, at that same time the action in the thread effects a disjunction from the other thread; thus, these occur at one and the same time.

Then, at the very moment when the destruction of the conjunction between the two threads occurs due to disjunction, at that same moment, from the destruction of the conjunction between the two parts (*aṃśu*), there is the destruction of the thread (*tantu*) commenced by them. When that thread has perished, there is the destruction of the disjunction from the other thread which was dependent upon it; in this case, the destruction of the substratum (*āśraya-vināśa*) is the cause, because of the absence of any other cause for destruction. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [149] [pp. 388–392]

If that were the case, it would follow that no subsequent division could occur, because there is an absence of a cause for such division. Consequently, since there would be an absence of conjunction in that which possesses conjunction with another location, a contrary quality (virodhiguṇa) would be impossible; thus, the fault would be that action would persist over time, and that which inheres in an eternal substance would itself be eternal.

How so? When an action has arisen in a paramāṇu that is the originator of a dyad (dvyaṇuka), it produces a disjunction from another atom; at that very same time, an action also arises in the other atom. Then, at the same moment that the destruction of the conjunction initiating the substance occurs due to that disjunction, a disjunction between the dyad and the atom is produced by the action in the other atom. Then, at the very moment that the destruction of the conjunction between the dyad and the atom occurs due to that disjunction, at that same moment the destruction of the dyad occurs due to the destruction of its conjunction.

When that [substance] has perished, there follows the destruction of the disjunction between the dyad and the atom which was dependent upon it. Consequently, because a contrary quality cannot exist, action inherent in an eternal substance would be eternal. [Page 390] There is no fault here, for the disjunction arises from the disjunction of the thread from another part; thus, due to the destruction of the substratum, only the disjunction of the two threads is destroyed, not the disjunction of the thread from the other part. From this, a subsequent disjunction is produced, just as the disjunction of the body from space arises from the disjunction of the finger from space. In that case, the action, having produced a conjunction, perishes; thus, there is no fault.

Alternatively, at the same time that the disjunction from another part arises, an action is produced in that very thread. Then, from the disjunction from the other part, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread; and by the action of the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this constitutes one moment. Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread; and from its destruction, there is the simultaneous destruction of the disjunction and the action that depend upon it.

Or, when there is a conjunction between a thread and *vīraṇa* grass, since no new substance is produced, the destruction of the disjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa* occurs through the previously mentioned method, namely by the destruction of the substratum and by the [subsequent] conjunction. In this case, however, a disjunction born of disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*)—which would be with respect to a location such as space—is not produced for the moving thread, because the cause, namely the disjunction of the two threads, is absent. If the subsequent disjunction has not occurred, what follows from that? To this he says: "From that... (*tataḥ*).

Consequently, because no subsequent division arises and the prior conjunction of the thread with space—which acts as an obstacle—has not ceased, there can be no conjunction of the active thread with another location. For this reason, in the absence of the opposing quality of subsequent conjunction, the action would persist for a long duration; thus, the fault would arise that it lasts until the destruction of its substrate, or, in the case of that which inheres in an eternal substance, that it would be eternal itself.

"What is the question? "The answer is: 'When... When an action arises in the atom that is the originator (*ārambhaka*) of the dyad (*dvy-aṇuka*), it produces a disjunction from another atom; at that very same time, there is also an action in the other non-originating atom (*anārambhaka-paramāṇu*) which is conjoined with the dyad. Then, at the moment when the disjunction of the two atoms causes the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance, at that very same time, there is a disjunction of the dyad and the atom produced by the action of the atom.

Then, at the very moment when the conjunction of the two dyads is destroyed due to the disjunction of the atoms of those dyads, at that same moment, the dyad composed of them is destroyed because of the destruction of the conjunction of the atoms. When that dyad has been destroyed, the disjunction of the atoms of the dyad which was dependent upon it is destroyed. Then, due to the absence of the cause, namely disjunction, when the disjunction of the atom from the point of space occurs and the prior conjunction ceases, there arises the subsequent conjunction, which is a contradictory quality.
Since there is no cause for its destruction, action inherent in eternal atoms would be eternal.
First, he addresses the aforementioned objection: "There is no fault, because [the subsequent] disjunction arises from the disjunction of the thread from another part."

When the cause is occupied with an effect, the motion produced therein, while effecting a disjunction from another part of its own substratum, does not effect a disjunction from a location such as space; this is because its capacity to act as the agent of a disjunction from a location like space is pervaded by the non-initiation of a specific disjunction. However, it certainly effects [a disjunction] from another part that is conjoined with its own substratum, as there is no contradiction in that case.

Therefore, when an action has arisen in the thread that is the cause of a two-threaded dyad, at the same time as the disjunction from another thread, it initiates a disjunction with the fiber (*aṃśu*) that is conjoined with that thread. And since that disjunction remains until the destruction of its substratum, he says: "Due to the destruction of the substratum, the disjunction of the two threads themselves is destroyed, while the disjunction between the thread and the other fiber remains."

If this is so, what follows? To this he says: "From this. It is like the separation of the body from space resulting from the separation of a finger from space. Just as there is a separation of the body from space due to the action-born separation of a finger from space, so too is there a separation of the thread from space due to the action-born separation of the yarn from the thread; such is the meaning of the example.

If it is argued that the disjunction of the body from space is logically possible through the disjunction of the hand from space, but not through the disjunction of a finger from space—because the finger is not a cause with respect to the body—[we reply: the hand, too, is a support for the arm and not for the body; how then could there be a disjunction of the body even from the disjunction of that [hand]? Alternatively, if it is argued that because the body pervades all its parts, the hand is indeed a support [for the body], then the finger must likewise be a support, since the recognition of the body occurs within the aggregate of parts such as the hand and the finger.

When that division of space has occurred and the prior conjunction, which acted as an obstacle, has ceased, the action inherent in the thread produces a subsequent conjunction and then perishes; thus he says: "In that... [tasmin].

He explains destruction through the destruction of the substratum by another method as well, beginning with "Or else": at the same time that the production of a division from a different part occurs, an action arises in that very thread whose parts are being divided; then, from that division, there is the destruction of the conjunction with the fiber (*aṃśu*) which was the originator of the thread; and by the action of the thread, there is a division of that [thread] from the other thread—this constitutes one moment.

Thereafter, following that, due to the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread sustained by it; and from the destruction of that [thread], there is the simultaneous destruction of the disjunction and the action residing therein. As for the objection raised—that what is eternally inherent must be eternal—no rebuttal has been stated there, because that argument is irrelevant to the point at hand.

For when the cause is occupied with its own effect, the motion produced does not, at the same time as it effects the disjunction from another constituent part, bring about a disjunction from space and so forth; because there is a contradiction between being the agent of disjunction from space and the like, and producing a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction that initiates the substance.

In the case of an atom that is not the initiator [of a process] but possesses a conjunction with a dyad, the action simultaneously with the disjunction from the dyad indeed effects a disjunction from a point of space; then, upon the cessation of the atom's conjunction with space due to that disjunction, when a subsequent conjunction occurs, the destruction of the action residing therein necessarily takes place.

It has been stated that when there is a conjunction of homogeneous substances and a substance is produced, the destruction of disjunction and action occurs due to the destruction of the substratum; now, he explains the destruction of disjunction through both the destruction of the conjunction and its substratum when there is no production of a substance due to a conjunction of heterogeneous substances—namely, "when there is a conjunction between a thread and a vīraṇa grass, and no substance is produced, according to the previously mentioned method."

At the same time that the action arises in the constituent parts (*aṃśu*) that initiate the thread (*tantu*), an action also arises in the *vīraṇa* grass. Then, by the action of the parts, a disjunction is produced between one part and another part; and by the action of the *vīraṇa*, a disjunction is produced between that disjoining part and the thread, as well as a disjunction with a point of space. Thereafter, from the disjunction of the parts, the destruction of the conjunction of the parts occurs; and from the disjunction of the *vīraṇa*, the destruction of the conjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa*, as well as the conjunction between the *vīraṇa* and space, occurs. Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction of the parts, the destruction of the thread occurs, and likewise the destruction of the *vīraṇa*.

And then there is the subsequent conjunction; thereafter, through both that subsequent conjunction and the destruction of its substratum, the disjunction between the thread and the vīraṇa grass is destroyed—such is the process.
The *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [150] [pp. 393–394]:
Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are the causes for the application of the designations and cognitions "remote" and "proximate.

These are of two kinds: produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and produced by time (*kālakṛta*). Among these, that produced by space indicates a particular direction, while that produced by time indicates a difference in age.

In this regard, the production of that which is caused by direction (*dikkṛta*) is explained. How so? When there is a greater or lesser number of conjunctions with what is conjoined between two objects situated in the same direction, an observer—taking one of them as a proximate limit—forms the cognition "this is remote from that" regarding the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*). Then, depending upon that [cognition], there arises the production of "remoteness" through conjunction with a more distant spatial region (*dikpradeśa*).

Having taken a remote object as the limit, the cognition of proximity arises with respect to the other [near] object. Then, depending on that [proximity], there is the production of "remoteness" (*paratva*) from conjunction with another spatial region.
*Nyāyakandalī* [150] [pp. 393–395]:

"Remoteness and proximity are the causes of the designations and cognitions 'remote' and 'proximate. Remoteness is the cause of the designation and cognition 'remote'; proximity is the cause of the designation and cognition 'proximate. Thus, he establishes their existence by means of their effects.

Even though space and the conjunctions of space with the throat and so forth may be the causes for the designations "prior" and "posterior," and even though the conjunction of the self and the mind and so forth may be the cause for the cognition of priority and posteriority, nevertheless, another efficient cause (nimitta) is established; for a specific cognition cannot arise without an uncommon cause. The mention of both in one instance is because they are mutually dependent upon one another.

"That is twofold": "that," namely remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*), is "twofold," meaning of two kinds; this is the determination of their distinction. Anticipating the question of what causes the distinction between these two, he states the difference based on their respective causes: "produced by space (*dik*) and produced by time (*kāla*). That which is produced by the conjunction of space and a substance is "produced by space. That which is produced by the conjunction of time and a substance is "produced by time."

From what is the distinction between these two to be understood? He says: "From the difference in their effects. That which is produced by space (*dikkṛta*) causes the cognition of a specific direction, whereas that which is produced by time (*kālakṛta*) causes the cognition of a difference in age. The spatial "remoteness" (*paratva*) indicates distance from a location, while "nearness" (*aparatva*) indicates proximity to a location. However, temporal remoteness indicates the distance of an object from a point in time, and temporal nearness indicates its proximity to a point in time; such is the distinction.

Among those two—[the notions] produced by direction and produced by time—the production of that produced by direction is now explained. To the question "How so? he provides the answer: "In one [direction]. The notions of priority and posteriority do not occur between two objects situated in the eastern and western directions; for that reason, it is stated that they must be "situated in one direction."

When two masses are situated in one direction—either the east or the west—a single observer has a conjunction with the ground in proximity to one mass, and likewise a conjunction with the ground in proximity to the other. When there is a multiplicity or scarcity of such "conjunctions-with-what-is-conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*s), taking that mass possessing fewer conjunctions as the proximate limit, one perceives: "This [other] mass is distant from this [first] mass. Thus, in the mass which possesses a greater number of conjunctions, there arises *paratva* (remoteness).

A cognition of remoteness arises. Then, immediately after the arising of that cognition of remoteness, in dependence upon that cognition of remoteness, there occurs the production of "remoteness" (*paratva*) in the substance acting as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), due to a conjunction with a further spatial region (*dikpradeśa*) possessing a greater degree of conjunction, which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

For an observer, having established a remote limit relative to his own body by way of a greater number of conjunctions with the conjoined (saṃyuktasaṃyoga), there arises the cognition of "nearness" regarding another object that possesses a smaller number of such conjunctions. Taking that cognition of nearness as the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa), and through the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) which is the conjunction with another spatial region characterized by a smaller number of conjunctions with the conjoined, there occurs the production of "remoteness" (paratva) in the substance serving as the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).

If it is argued that because the cognitions of "near" and "far" are mutually dependent, there would follow the consequence of the non-existence of both, we say: no, for this is not accepted. It is not the case that the cognition of "far" arises in dependence on [the cognition] "this is near," nor does the cognition of "near" arise in dependence on the cognition "this is far. Rather, the cognition of "far"—which possesses a greater degree of conjunction—arises in dependence on perceiving an object associated with a lesser degree of conjunction.

Thus, it is precisely by depending on a cluster accompanied by a greater number of conjunctions that there arises, in relation to it, a cognition of proximity in that which possesses fewer conjunctions; therefore, these two do not depend upon one another.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [151] [pp. 396–398]

How [is it produced] even for those things conditioned by time? When two persons, a youth and an elder, existing in the present time and conjoined with points of space in no fixed direction, are present together—possessing respectively a smooth beard and the coarseness [of youth], and wrinkles and grey hair [in the case of the elder]—then for a single observer, having taken the youth as the limit (*avadhi*), there arises with respect to the elder a cognition of remoteness (*viprakṛṣṭā buddhiḥ*). Then, depending on that [cognition], through conjunction with a subsequent point of time, there is the production of "remoteness" (*paratva*). And having taken the elder as the limit, there arises with respect to the youth a cognition of proximity (*sannikṛṣṭā buddhiḥ*).
Then, depending on that [cognition], through conjunction with a preceding point of time, there is the production of "nearness" (*aparatva*).

Destruction, however, results from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), conjunction, and the substance. First, regarding destruction due to the destruction of the relative cognition: at the very moment that the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) has arisen once "priority" (*paratva*) has been produced, there is the state of the relative cognition being about to perish (*vinaśyattā*); and simultaneously, there is the state of the cognition of the quality of priority (*paratvaguṇabuddhi*) being about to arise from the cognition of the universal, its relation, and so forth—this constitutes one single moment.

Then, there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the arising of the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*). Then, from the destruction of the relative cognition, there is the state of the quality being about to perish; and from the cognition of the quality, its relation, and so forth, there is the state of the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*) being about to arise—this is one moment. Then follows the arising of the cognition of the substance and the destruction of the quality.

How [is the destruction of distance] also due to the destruction of conjunction? At the very same time as the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), an action arises in the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*). By that action, a disjunction from space and the object is produced. The production of remoteness from the relative cognition and the production of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*)—as well as the destruction of the conjunction between space and the object—occur at one and the same time. Then, at the very moment when the cognition of the quality of remoteness arises, the destruction of the quality occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction between space and the object.

How is it also due to the destruction of the substance (*dravyavināśāt*)? When an action has arisen in a part that is the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*), at the very moment it produces a disjunction from another part, at that same moment the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Then, at the very moment when the conjunction is destroyed by that disjunction, at that same moment "remoteness" (*paratva*) arises. Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance; and from the destruction of the substance comes the destruction of the quality (*guṇa*) that depends upon it. *Nyāyakandalī* [151] [pp. 396–399]

How is it that [priority and posteriority] are produced by time? First, the production of priority and posteriority as caused by space has been explained; the question is: how is the production of those two [qualities] caused by time? The answer is: "of two things existing at the present time. Priority and posteriority do not arise in the absence of two objects—or even one object—existing at the present time; for that reason, it is said "of two things existing at the present time."

Regarding those situated in indefinite directions—meaning those standing in the same direction or different directions, such as a youth and an elder, one with a grown beard and another with wrinkles, grey hair, and white hair—in the presence of these signs of temporal distance, for a single observer, having taken the youth as the proximate term (arvādha) by inferring his short duration of existence through the absence of a grown beard, coarseness, and so forth, there arises a remote cognition (viprakṛṣṭā buddhiḥ) regarding the elder who possesses a grown beard, wrinkles, grey hair, and the like; it is in relation to that [proximate cognition] [that the remote cognition occurs].

By means of a further spatial portion of time characterized by a greater number of solar revolutions, through conjunction as a non-inherent cause, there arises in that very elder the quality of "remoteness" (*paratva*). Taking the elder as the distant object, a cognition of proximity arises with respect to the youth; depending upon that cognition, through conjunction with a subsequent spatial portion of time marked by fewer solar revolutions, there arises in [the youth] the quality of "nearness" (*aparatva*). The lesser or greater degree of conjunction with time in the bodies of the youth and the elder is in reference to the continuum (*santāna*) of the bodies, and not with respect to the individual entities themselves, because those two perish at every moment.

[Page 397] That which is produced necessarily perishes, and that [perishing] does not occur without a cause; thus, he states the causes of destruction for *paratva* (priority) and *aparatva* (posteriority): "As for destruction... The destruction of priority and posteriority occurs through sevenfold stages of destruction: from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), from the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), from the destruction of the substance (*dravya*), from the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition, from the destruction of both the substance and the conjunction, from the destruction of both the conjunction and the relative cognition, and from the destruction of the relative cognition, the conjunction, and the substance. This is the sevenfold sequence of destruction.

(1) First, its destruction is said to result from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). At the very moment that the cognition of the universal "remoteness" (*paratvasāmānya*) arises regarding that [substance] in which "remoteness" has been produced—[the word] *tataḥ* is formed with the suffix *tasil* in the sense of the locative case according to Pāṇini 5.3.7 (*sārvavibhaktikas tasil*)—at that very same moment, there would be the state of "about-to-perish" (*vinaśyattā*) for the relative cognition, that is, the presence of the cause of its destruction.

From the cognition of the universal [of] priority (*paratva-sāmānya*), its relation [to the substance], the universal of priority itself, the cognition of that universal of priority, and the relation between the quality of priority and [its substrate], there arises the cognition of the quality of priority; this constitutes one single moment. The very cognition of the universal of priority is the cause for the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the cause for the production of the cognition of the quality; therefore, at the very moment of its production, the relative cognition is in the process of perishing, while the cognition of the quality is in the process of being produced.

Then, in the next moment, there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the arising of the cognition of the quality of "priority" (*paratva*). Thereafter, from that destruction of the relative cognition, the state of being destroyed belongs to the quality. At that very same time, the substance-cognition arises from those three: the quality, the cognition of the quality, and their mutual relation. This constitutes one single moment.

The destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the cause of the destruction of the quality (*guṇa*); the cognition of the quality is the cause of the cognition of the substance (*dravya*). Furthermore, the destruction of the relative cognition and the arising of the cognition of the quality would occur simultaneously; consequently, the state of the quality being in the process of destruction and the state of the cognition of the substance being in the process of arising would also be simultaneous. Thereafter, there is the arising of the cognition of the substance as qualified by "priority" (*paratva*) and the destruction of the quality of priority.

When the question is asked, "How does the destruction of conjunction also lead to the destruction of priority and posteriority? he says: At the very same time as the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), an action arises in the object (*piṇḍa*) which is the substratum of priority; in the subsequent moment, by that action, a disjunction is produced between the direction (*dik*) and the object which is the substratum of priority; and at that same time, the production of priority occurs from the relative cognition. Thus, it is one and the same time.

Then, when remoteness has arisen, there occurs the arising of the cognition of the generality of remoteness (*paratvasāmānya*) and the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the object due to disjunction; this constitutes one moment of time. Thereafter, at the very moment when the cognition of the quality arises from the cognition of the generality, at that same moment the destruction of remoteness occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the object, and not due to the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), because the relative cognition is also destroyed at that very time.

To explain how destruction occurs even from the destruction of the substance, he says: "in the part that is the substratum of remoteness. When an action arises in a part of the substance—which is the substratum of the future remoteness—and it effects a disjunction from another part, at that very same time the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Then, at the same moment that the disjunction causes the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, the relative cognition produces remoteness.

Then, from the destruction of the conjunction follows the destruction of the substance; then, from the destruction of the substance follows the destruction of the quality dependent upon it. At that very same time, there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) due to the cognition of the generality of "priority" (*paratvasāmānya*), and the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the object due to the destruction of its substratum. Thus, these two do not function as causes [for the destruction of priority], because they are co-existent with it.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [152] [p. 399]

How is it that [priority] also perishes simultaneously due to the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition? When motion arises in a constituent part of the substrate, at that very same time the relative cognition arises; by that motion, a disjunction from another constituent part is produced, and the production of priority occurs—all this takes place at one and the same moment.

Then, at the very same time that the conjunction which initiates the substance is destroyed due to the separation of its parts, at that same time the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) arises; immediately thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance, and from the cognition of the universal comes the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); thus these occur at one and the same time. Subsequently, from the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition, there follows the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [152] [p. 399]

How is it that [the qualities] perish simultaneously due to the simultaneous destruction of the substance and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? At the very moment that action arises in a part of the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*), at that same time the relative cognition arises; and by means of that action, a disjunction from another part is produced, while the production of "remoteness" occurs—this is one point in time. Then, at the moment when the conjunction that initiates the substance is destroyed due to the disjunction of the parts, at that very same moment the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of "remoteness" arises.

Immediately thereafter, due to the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the substance; and simultaneously with that, there is the destruction of the cognition of the universal and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Thus, these occur at one and the same time. Then, from the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition, there is the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*), for it is recognized that each of these two is a cause for the destruction of the other. And in this case, because no distinction between the two can be determined, both are causes for the destruction. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [153] [pp. 400–401]

How [does distance arise] even from the destruction of the substance-conjunction? When an action has arisen in a part of the substratum of "remoteness" (paratva) and produces a disjunction from another part, at that very same time there is the simultaneous production of the action in the whole (piṇḍa) and the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). Then, at the very same time that "remoteness" arises, there is the destruction of the substance-initiating conjunction due to the disjunction; and by the action in the whole, a disjunction between the direction (dik) and the whole is produced—this constitutes one single moment.

Then, at the very moment that the cognition of generality arises, at that same moment the mass is destroyed due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance; and from that destruction follows the destruction of the conjunction with the mass. Thereafter, simultaneously with the cognition of the quality, the destruction of the mass and the conjunction results in the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*).

How is it that [the destruction of distance occurs] also due to the simultaneous destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? At the very moment that "remoteness" (*paratva*) arises, there is motion in the substratum of that remoteness. Then, at the same time that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness arises, the disjunction between the direction and the object is produced by the motion of the object. Thereafter, from the cognition of the generality, the relative cognition is destroyed; and from the disjunction, the conjunction between the direction and the object is destroyed—this constitutes one single moment. Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition, the destruction of "remoteness" follows. [p. 401]

How [is it] also due to the simultaneous destruction of the three causes—the inherent, the non-inherent, and the instrumental? When the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises, at that very moment there is also motion in the constituent part of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*). Then, at the same time that the motion produces a disjunction from another constituent part and the production of "remoteness" (*paratva*), at that very time there is also motion in the aggregate. Thereafter, from the disjunction of the constituents, the conjunction that originates the aggregate is destroyed; and by the motion of the aggregate, a disjunction from the spatial direction (*dik*) is produced.

The cognition of the universal and the production [of relative distance] occur at one and the same time. Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction [of the substance with its parts], there is the destruction of the mass; from disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the mass; and from the cognition of the universal, there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Thus, through the simultaneous destruction of these three—the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)—there is the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*).

*Nyāyakandalī* [153] [pp. 400–402]: "Also from the destruction of the conjunction with the substance," and so forth. How does destruction occur even from the destruction of the conjunction with the substance? When an action has arisen in a part of the substratum of *paratva* (priority), it produces a disjunction from another part; at that very same time, there is the simultaneous arising of the action in the whole (*piṇḍa*) and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Then, at the very moment that *paratva* arises, at that same moment, the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance occurs due to the disjunction of the parts, and by means of the action in the whole, there is a disjunction between the direction (*dik*) and the whole.

"One time" refers to the fact that it is produced. Thus, at the very same time that the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises, the destruction of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*) occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance; and due to the disjunction between the direction and the aggregate, the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the aggregate occurs. Then, simultaneously with the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*), the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*) occurs because of the destruction of the conjunction between the aggregate and the direction-aggregate. However, the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is not the cause, because that [destruction of the relative cognition] exists at that very same moment as the cognition of the universal. [p. 401]

How [is this] also due to the simultaneous destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? When "remoteness" (*paratva*) arises, at that very moment there is motion (*karman*) in the substance which is the substratum of that remoteness. Then, at the same time that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness arises in the substratum of remoteness, the disjunction from the spatial point (*dikpiṇḍa*) is produced by the motion of the body. Thereafter, in one and the same moment, the destruction of the relative cognition occurs due to the cognition of the generality, and the destruction of the conjunction with the spatial point occurs due to the disjunction from the spatial point.

Consequently, due to the destruction of the relative cognition dependent upon that conjunction, there is the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*). However, since the destruction of the substance does not occur at that time, it cannot be the cause [of the destruction of priority].

How [is there destruction] even from the simultaneous destruction of the three—namely, the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)? "Inherent, non-inherent, and efficient" refers to the inherent, non-inherent, and efficient; these are the causes, thus they are called the inherent, non-inherent, and efficient causes, which consist of substance, conjunction, and cognition. When the question is asked, "How is there the destruction of 'remoteness' (*paratva*) due to the simultaneous destruction of those three?", he provides the answer with the words "When... (*yadā*).

When the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises, at that very moment action also occurs in the constituent part of the aggregate. Then, at the same time that the action effects a disjunction from another constituent part and the relative cognition produces "priority" (*paratva*), at that very same time action also occurs in the aggregate. Thereafter, from the disjunction of the constituents, the destruction of the conjunction that originated the aggregate occurs; and by the action in the aggregate, a disjunction from space is produced, as well as the arising of the cognition of the universal—this constitutes one single moment.

At that time, the destruction of the aggregate occurs due to the destruction of the originating conjunction; the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the aggregate occurs due to disjunction; and the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs due to the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyajñāna*). All of this happens simultaneously because of the simultaneity of the causes. Consequently, from the destruction of the three causes—the inherent (*samavāyi*), the non-inherent (*asamavāyi*), and the instrumental (*nimitta*)—there follows the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*). This mention of the destruction of priority is merely illustrative; the same sequence of destruction should be shown for "posteriority" (*aparatva*) as well. *Nyāyakandalī* 4.154. [p.402] Buddhi. *Praśastapādabhāṣya*. [154] [p.402]
Intellect (*buddhi*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and cognition (*pratyaya*) are synonyms.
It is of many kinds, because objects are infinite and because it is restricted to each respective object.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [154] [pp. 402–404]
Having established that priority and posteriority reside in cognition (*buddhi*), he now asks, "What is this cognition? and replies with the words beginning "Cognition" (*buddhir* etc.).

Cognition is the modification of *pradhāna* known as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) called "the Great One" (*mahat*), which has "mind" (*citta*) as its synonym. When cognition is colored by external objects through the channel of the senses, there arises a function (*vṛtti*) based on the quality of *sattva* that assumes the form of those objects; this is knowledge (*jñāna*). Furthermore, when the power of consciousness (*cetanā-śakti*) is reflected in the cognition that has assumed the form of the perceived object, there occurs an "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) that mimics the function of that cognition.

And thus the Blessed Lord Patañjali said: "For the power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigrating; yet, as if transmigrated into the changing object, it experiences its fluctuations. By "the power of the enjoyer," the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) is meant, and that is the Self itself. "Into the changing object" refers to the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*); "as if transmigrated" means as if reflected therein.

The meaning is that, being reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*), it experiences the modifications (*vṛtti*) of that [intellect], becoming an imitator of the intellectual modification through the falling of its shadow upon the intellect. The object of the intellect is the cognition (*pratyaya*) in the form of pleasure and so forth. Thus said the Blessed One: "Even though the *puruṣa* is pure, he observes the cognition belonging to the intellect; observing it, although not of the nature of that [cognition], he appears as if he were of the nature of that.
To refute this Sāṃkhya doctrine, he says: "The intellect," and so forth.

That which possesses these synonymous terms is *buddhi*. Furthermore, this process that has been demonstrated is refuted precisely because of its lack of perceptibility (*pratīti*). Both of these are experienced by each individual: one is characterized by arising and passing away, conforming to the abandonment or acquisition of objects; the other is its substratum, from whose arising activity and cessation would follow. There is no other mode [of experience].

Furthermore, is this activity (*vṛtti*) of that intellect (*buddhi*) different from the intellect or not? It cannot be different, because it is accepted that the activity and the possessor of the activity (*vṛttimad*) are invariably identical in nature. If, on the other hand, it is not different, then since the intellect is a single entity, its activities—which possess the forms of objects—would also be one; consequently, cognitions such as "three" or "four" would be impossible, because there would be no perception of mutually distinct forms, and the *puruṣa* perceives only the form as it has ascended into the intellect.

As it has been said: "The person is the witness of the intellect. Furthermore, one should infer such refutations as follows: if there were a plurality of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), there would also be a plurality of the intellect (*buddhi*), which would contradict its unity, and so forth.

He defines the differentiation of cognition (buddhi) with the words, "And that is of many kinds. He states the reason for this: "Because of the infinity of objects" (arthānantyāt). [An objection: Even if the objects—that is, the spheres of experience—are infinite, what follows regarding the manifold nature of cognition? To this he replies: "And because it is restricted to each respective object" (pratyarthaniyatatvāt). The cognitions of those such as ourselves are restricted to each respective object; and since objects are infinite, the cognitions restricted to them individually must also be infinite.
Even that single cognition which has multiple objects as its domain is indeed distinct from other cognitions because it is restricted to those specific objects; thus, there is no fault.
[Praśastapādabhāṣya 155–156, p.
405] Although that [cognition] is of many kinds, in brief there are two types: knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
In that regard, ignorance (*avidyā*) is fourfold, characterized by doubt, error, non-apprehension, and dreaming. [Nyāyakandalī, pp.

405–407] Although there is a distinction within cognition (*buddhi*) due to the difference in its objects, he states briefly that it is twofold: "Of that" (*tasyāḥ*). Knowledge (*vidyā*) is a cognition consisting of a non-doubtful and uncontradicted determination; ignorance (*avidyā*) is the opposite of that. Because his intention is merely to explain the meaning, he first discusses ignorance—even though it was mentioned later—saying: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
Between those two, knowledge and ignorance, ignorance is fourfold, consisting of four types characterized by doubt, error, non-determination, and dreaming.

But surely, since ignorance is enumerated as being of four kinds, that enumeration is untenable, because there is also the possibility of well-established *tarka*-knowledge (*tarkajñāna*). For indeed, between doubt and certainty, *tarka* is experienced. To illustrate: some hold that the self has the property of arising, while others hold that it does not have the property of arising. Consequently, due to this disagreement, when a doubt arises as to whether this [self] possesses the property of arising or whether it is otherwise, *tarka*, which consists of inquiry, proceeds.

If this [Self] were subject to origination (*utpattidharmaka*), then neither saṃsāra—characterized by the conjunction of one [Self] with multiple bodies and so forth—nor liberation (*apavarga*), which is the absolute release from that, would be possible. However, if the knower were not subject to origination (*anutpattidharmaka*), both saṃsāra and liberation would be possible; therefore, this [Self] must be something not subject to origination. What is the purpose of this probans based on possibility (*sambhāvanā-pratyaya*)? It is simply the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). For even when there is doubt regarding the counter-position—as in the case of a certainty regarding the opposite—the reason (*hetu*) simply does not function, because a real entity cannot possess two contradictory natures. As the venerable Bhaṭṭamiśra has said:

"As long as there is even a hundredth-part doubt regarding the non-exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), how can the logical force of the reason's capacity to reach [the probandum] exist?

However, by this [process], having set aside the state of being subject to origination (*utpattidharmakatva*) and considering the possibility of the state of not being subject to origination (*anutpattidharmakatva*), the object is discerned; once the object is thus discerned, inference proceeds because it is no longer countered by a false opponent. Thus, through the medium of discerning the object, *tarka* (reasoning) serves the purpose of attaining knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) by way of assisting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because a means of valid cognition, as an instrument, reaches its fulfillment in its own function only when assisted by *tarka*, which occupies the position of the "manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*).
