For indeed, even if it rolls within the hollow of a rogue’s hand-cage and is squeezed by a firm, unregarded grip, an axe with a sharp edge does not remain effective for the cutting of even a hard piece of wood unless it is struck forcefully. As it has been said: "In this world or in the Veda, there is no such instrument whatsoever that, in an action to be accomplished through a specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*), does not require the assistance of that [procedure]."

If, however, such reasoning (*tarka*) were not accepted as being of the nature of establishing what is undesirable for the opponent, then even the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) would not be acceptable. For that [reductio] does not differ in essence from reasoning; and yet there is indeed a *prasaṅga* even for the Vaiśeṣikas. [Objection: A *prasaṅga* is not a logical reason (*hetu*), because it suffers from defects such as the unestablished nature of its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). — *Nyāyakandalī* [156] [pp. 408–410]

To this it is replied: Is tarka the cognition of the non-existence of the opponent's position, or is it the possibility of one's own position? In the first case, this is simply a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If the cognition that "if the knower were impermanent, transmigration and liberation would be impossible" were not a valid knowledge, then the non-existence of the opposing view could not be established from it, because it is impossible for any object to be established by what is not a valid knowledge; thus, inference would simply not function here due to the absence of a discerned object.

Now, if the absence of the counter-example (vipakṣābhāva) is established from this [reasoning], then this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must—whether one likes it or not—be admitted to be included within one of the [accepted] means of valid cognition, such as perception (pratyakṣa) and so forth; for there exists no other means of establishing a cognition apart from those. A reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is also the manifestation of a contradiction, and that consists in the presentation of some stronger contrary means of valid cognition. In this case, what else could "reasoning" (tarka) be, other than that contrary means of valid cognition and the statement presenting it?

Now, is *tarka* (reasoning) a cognition consisting in the possibility of one's own position? What is the cause of its arising? It cannot be the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes one's own position, because such a means has not yet functioned. Once the object has been analyzed by *tarka*, the means of valid knowledge that establishes one's own position then proceeds. If that very [means] is the cause of *tarka*, then mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) is quite evident. If it is argued that the cause of this [tarka] is the cognition of the absence of the opposing position (*vipakṣa*), since the possibility of one's own position arises only when the absence of the opposing position is perceived?

In that case, this is indeed an inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) of the cognition of the absence of the counter-instance (*vipakṣa*), because the negation of one of two mutually contradictory things is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other. This would be so if it were to determine the object as "this is exactly thus. However, this [cognition] does not determine either of the two properties, though it does allow for one; nor is it even doubt (*saṃśaya*), because there is no contact with both alternatives. Rather, it is a distinct kind of cognition—a notion of possibility—that has neither fallen away from doubt nor reached certainty.

And thus people in the world say: "In this way I reason. No; for from the determination of fitness—where there is an absence of counter-examples (vipakṣa), there is the establishment of one of the two positions, whereas where its possibility exists, there is no such establishment—one who perceives positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and realizes the absence of counter-examples conceives that "this [subject] will be characterized by non-arising" (anutpattidharmaka). In this sense, this is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); it establishes the fitness of this object for being presented as a means of valid cognition.

Since it determines the object, it is indeed inference (*anumāna*). And it thus supports the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the apprehension of fitness (*yogyatā*) is the cause for the operation of the means of valid cognition. Otherwise, this would be a mere possibility and utterly useless, since it is not a constituent part of either the establishment or the perception of that which is itself not a means of valid cognition; for even the discernment of the object has already been accomplished by the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) itself, which demonstrates the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [157] [p. 405]

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is, first of all, a deliberation (*vimarśa*) directed toward both alternatives, characterized by the thought "What could this be?", arising from the perception of mere similarity between two well-known particulars, the recollection of their respective specific qualities, and demerit (*adharma*). Others, however, say that reasoning (*tarka*) is merely a variety of doubt, because its nature consists in non-ascertainment.

First, doubt (*saṃśaya*). The word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates sequence; the meaning is that doubt is stated first. Regarding the phrase "of two well-known particulars": *(Note: The provided text fragment ends here. The full definition of doubt typically continues with the standard Nyāya formulation: "Doubt arises from the perception of common properties, the non-perception of specific properties, and the recollection of those specific properties.")*

When there is the perception of mere similarity—meaning the mere possession of common attributes—between two things, such as a post and a person, which previously had their various specific, uncommon properties (such as crookedness and hollows, or a head and hands) well-known and recognized, then, due to the recollection of those previously perceived specific features of both the post and the person, and due to a lack of [decisive] characteristics, there arises a deliberation resting upon both possibilities in the form "What could this be? This is doubt (*saṃśaya*).

Is it a post? Or is it a person? Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a specific kind of cognition that, while touching upon the particulars of both sides, apprehends contradictory objects in an unstable manner characterized by both forms.

Regarding the phrase "from the perception of mere similarity": by the force of the inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*), the non-perception of the particulars is understood. The word "perception" (*darśana*) denotes apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and does not denote direct sensory perception (*pratyakṣa-pratīti*), because even a universal (*sāmānya*) that is to be inferred can serve as a cause for doubt. By the mention of the apprehension of similarity, the apprehension of the locus (*dharmin*) is also obtained.

Since that property of similarity is not perceived when the substratum is not perceived, doubt also resides only in the substratum (*dharmin*) and not in the similarity itself, because the similarity is already ascertained. Furthermore, "similarity" is stated here as merely a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and not as a similarity inherent in multiple objects; for we observe doubt regarding minuteness and magnitude in the self, even though the absence of touch—the non-existence of touch—is a property common to both ether and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

This, then, is the summary of the meaning: when this cognizer perceives a property common to both [alternatives] in some single locus, yet due to a certain cause does not perceive a specific distinction of that locus, remembers two previously cognized contradictory particulars, and does not conceive the presence of both in one place because they are contradictory; nor does he conceive their absence, because of the perception of the common property which is invariably concomitant with them.

Then, when the locus (*dharmin*) has been determined as having common properties as its object, there arises a cognition that is non-determinative in nature regarding its specific qualities; this is doubt (*saṃśaya*). [p.413] But surely, it is a contradiction to say "a cognition that is non-determinative in nature," for this very quality of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) consists in its determining an object. No, for both possibilities are indeed possible.

For this [cognition], being produced by the perception of a substratum qualified by its general property (*sāmānya*)—which is opposed by the non-perception of specific properties (*dharma-viśeṣa*)—and assisted by the recollection of two mutually exclusive specificities, determines the substratum as qualified by its general property in the form "this," yet, not determining the specific [nature] such as "it is a post" or "it is a person," it would be a cognition whose nature is non-determination (*anavadhāraṇātmaka*). Indeed, it is observed that where the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct, the effect is likewise distinct, as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is also ignorance (*avidyā*), and since that is undesirable for a person, its being an effect of demerit (*adharma*) has been demonstrated [by the phrase] "and from demerit. If it is argued that when, having perceived a commonality (*sāmānya*), one recollects one particular (*viśeṣa*) and then recollects another particular, then—because the perception of the commonality has by that time perished—it is impossible for it to be the cause of doubt, we say no. This is because two latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) whose objects are both particulars, having been simultaneously awakened, produce a single recollection whose object is both particulars; and at that time, the knowledge of the commonality is possible in its state of perishing.
And that [doubt] is of two kinds: internal and external. First, regarding the internal:
when an instructor, having correctly or incorrectly pointed out [an object], points it out again, doubt arises with respect to the three times as to whether "is this correct or incorrect?"
The external [object] is of two kinds: that which is within the range of perception and that which is beyond the range of perception.

Among these, first, with respect to that which is beyond the range of perception, doubt arises from the observation of a common mark, the recollection of both specific features, and the influence of past experience (adharma). For example, upon seeing only a horn in a forest, one wonders whether it is a cow or a gavaya.

Even regarding an object of perception, when one perceives only the similarity of mere height in a post (*sthāṇu*) and a person (*puruṣa*), and because the specific features such as curvature are not perceived, the particularities of the universal "post-ness" and so forth remain unmanifest; then, due to the recollection of the specific features of both, the cognition of the self—which is being drawn toward both—wavers: "Is this indeed a post, or rather a person?
(Nyāyakandalī [158], pp. 414–416).

And that [doubt] is of two kinds; this is the statement of its divisions. To the question "In what form?", he says: "Internal and external. That fivefold doubt which has been shown by those of our own school (sāmānatāntrika) due to the occurrence of common properties, the occurrence of multiple properties, conflicting testimony, the non-determination of perception, and the non-determination of non-perception—all of that is subsumed within these very two types.

"First, regarding the case of the predictor (*ādeśaka*): the predictor is an astrologer (*jyotirvit*). Having once perceived some omen such as the movement of a planet, he has predicted: 'In such-and-such a place, it was thus, it is now so, and it will be so in the future,' and that indeed came to pass accordingly. At another time, however, a prediction he made turned out to be false.

Now, having seen a similar omen arising for him at this present moment, as he makes his prediction, doubt arises within his own knowledge: 'Is this prognostic knowledge of mine which occurred previously true or false? [p. 415]

The external [object] is of two kinds: that which is within the range of perception (*pratyakṣa-viṣaya*) and that which is beyond the range of perception (*apratyakṣa-viṣaya*). Among these, regarding the latter—the object beyond the range of perception—doubt arises from the observation of a common mark (*sādhāraṇa-liṅga*), the recollection of both specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*), and the influence of mental disposition (*adharma*). For example, upon seeing only a horn in a forest, one wonders whether it is a cow or a *gavaya*. Since this doubt concerns an individual object (*piṇḍa*) that is not currently perceived but is inferred through the general observation of a mere horn, this doubt has as its object that which is beyond the range of perception.

He speaks even regarding an object of perception with the words "of the post and the man," and so forth. This is because one perceives in the subject (dharmin) standing before one—which is the object of perception—the mere verticality belonging to both the post and the man. By the phrase "due to the non-perception of specific features such as curvature," etc., there is the inclusion of the head, hands, and so on. This is due to the non-perception of the specific qualities of the post, such as curvature, hollows, and the like, and the specific qualities of the man, such as the head, hands, and so on.

In the phrase "due to the non-manifestation of the specific universals such as 'being a post' (*sthāṇutva*)," the word "etc. includes the exclusion of "being a person" (*puruṣatva*) and so forth. Crookedness, hollows, and the like are the causes for the manifestation of "being a post," while a head, hands, and so forth are the causes for the manifestation of "being a person"; these are not perceived here.

When the states of being a post and being a person are not manifested, and because the specific features of both the post and the person—each previously perceived individually—are not recollected, the cognizer is drawn toward both; that is, he is drawn toward both the post and the person. When, upon seeing the verticality [of the object], he desires to determine "this is a post," then he is drawn toward the person due to the recollection of the person's specific features. [And when he desires to determine "this is a person," then...]

Because one is drawn toward a post by the recollection of its specific features, and [simultaneously] toward a person, one is thus pulled in both directions; for this very reason, one's cognition wavers and does not remain fixed upon one object with certainty. This demonstrates that the similarity to a swing lies precisely in the instability of the cognition: "Could this indeed be a post, or rather a person?
Furthermore, error (*viparyaya*) occurs only within the domain of perception and inference.

First, regarding the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*): when two things possessing well-known distinct characteristics are perceived incorrectly due to the impairment of the sense organs by bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), or wind (*anila*), there arises—due to the contact of the self and the mind, depending on a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a cognition of an object not present, and from demerit (*adharma*)—the erroneous cognition (*viparyaya*) that "this is that" with respect to what is not that. For example, [mistaking] a cow for a horse.

Even when there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there occurs the conceit of direct perception, as for example: "The nocturnal darkness, resembling a cloudless ocean and dark like a heap of powdered collyrium, is the sky.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [159] [pp. 416–420]

Immediately after doubt, he defines error (*viparyaya*): "Error also occurs only with respect to the objects of perception and inference. The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that just as doubt occurs only with respect to the objects of perception and inference, so too does error occur with respect to those same objects. The phrase "it occurs only with respect to the objects of perception and inference" is stated because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apart from perception and inference.

Regarding the object of perception first: "between two things whose many specific features are well-known" means that those two, the cow and the horse, are such that their many specific features—the dewlap and so forth, and the mane and so forth—have been previously perceived and are thus well-known. Between those two, the cognition "this is it" directed toward what is not a horse—that is, the cognition "this is a horse" regarding a cow—is error (*viparyaya*).

[Objection: Surely, when the particularities such as cowness and the dewlap are apprehended in a cow, then no error occurs; and if it were to occur, there would be the undesirable consequence of its never ceasing. To this he replies: "Because of an observation that does not correspond to reality" (*ayathārthālocanāt*). An "observation that does not correspond to reality" is the absence of an observation that corresponds to reality; that is to say, the absence of apprehending the object—such as a cow possessing a dewlap—in the manner that it actually exists. Therefore, the cognition "that [is] in what is not that" arises. By this, the non-apprehension of the particularities is stated to be the cause. [p.418]

He asks: what is the cause for the non-perception of "cowness" (*gotva*) when the individual object (*piṇḍa*) is present, or what is the cause for the cognition of "horseness" (*aśvatva*) which is not present? He replies: "of one whose sense faculty is afflicted by bile, phlegm, and wind. That is, for one whose sense faculty is afflicted—that is, impaired—by bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), and wind (*anila*), there occurs this inversion. Thus, the capacity of defects such as wind, bile, and phlegm to produce the appearance of what is not present and the non-appearance of a present object has been established.

If it were the case that everything appeared everywhere simply through the power of defects, then everything would manifest in every place due to the absence of a cause for restriction; therefore, he says: "from the contact of the self and the mind, depending on the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a cognition whose object is not present."

The object, such as a horse, is not present; rather, it arises from a contact between the self and the mind that depends upon a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a cognition that arose previously. This is its meaning: although the sense organ in contact with the body of a cow does not grasp "cowness," it grasps that body as qualified by similarity, because an entity possesses parts. And by that grasping of similarity, the latent impression whose object is a horse is awakened.

And when that person has awakened and the recollection of the horse arises, due to a defect of the mind, he produces a cognition of the horse in the form of a direct experience with respect to the cow currently in contact with the senses; this occurs solely due to the influence of similarity. Therefore, there is no manifestation of everything everywhere, because similarity and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are the causes for specific determination. For this very reason, this error is said by the Teachers to be born of the senses (*indriyajā*).

For in this way, [the cognition] would not be born of the senses; if it were to apprehend only "horseness" as something non-present and without a substratum solely through the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it would occur even for one whose sensory activity has ceased. But since it apprehends the very cow-individual conjoined with the eye while the eye is active, by taking it to be of the nature of a horse—if this [cognition] is not born of the senses, then what indeed will be born of the senses? Moreover, it is precisely for this reason that even a "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) occurs, because one thing appears in the form of another.

Even in that case where there is an error based on non-apprehension (*viradhiṣṭhāna*), the object, though not present there, is perceived through a present form that is contrary to its own nature; thus, it is indeed a "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) and not a "perception of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*), because the object is possible in its own nature and because what is non-existent cannot appear.

Where error proceeds by taking a similar object as its basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there similarity is the cause; however, in an error that lacks a basis and is connected solely to a defect of the mind, this [similarity] is not possible, as in the case of a cognition in which a woman appears to one afflicted by passion. Furthermore, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause only in that case where the error is conceptual (*savikalpaka*); but in the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), the capacity belongs to the defect of the sense organ alone, because the error occurs only when that defect is present, as in the arising of the cognition of yellow in a conch shell.

He states another example of error with the words, "Even when there is no direct perception, there is the conceit of direct perception," and so forth: the rays of the eyes, sent upward out of curiosity to look at the sky, have their speed diminished by traveling a great distance; struck by the exceedingly powerful rays of the sun coming from the opposite direction, they return and cause the quality of blueness—which is without support in another location—to appear as belonging to one's own eyeball, [perceiving] the sky as being like a vast, waveless great ocean freed from the mass of clouds.

They produce a cognition of form as if it were directly perceived, even though the sky is not directly perceived. In this regard, the proof for the rule that the cognition conforms to the qualities of that [organ]—namely, that the sense organ manifests its own sphere as having space as its substratum—is as follows: indeed, one whose sense organ is affected by jaundice perceives the atmosphere as if it were smeared with the liquefied essence of gold; likewise, due to an excess of phlegm, one with a white eyeball sees it as having the luster of silver.

The darkness of night (*śārvara-tamaḥ*), being as dark as a mass of powdered collyrium, belongs to Śarvarī (Night). Thus, when absolute light is absent, *kevalajñāna* (absolute knowledge) perceives—as if it were direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—objects that are everywhere merely inferred forms, even though they are not directly perceived.
[Prashastapādabhāṣya, pp.

421] Even regarding the domain of inference (*anumāna*), there is the inference of fire from what is mistaken for smoke due to steam and the like, and the [inference] "it is a cow" from seeing the horn of a *gavaya*.

Error (*viparyaya*) is the false cognition that views the systems of Śākya and others—which are contrary to the vision of the Three Vedas—as being the highest good. It consists of: the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) regarding the body, the senses, and the mind; the perception of permanence in things that are produced; the knowledge that an effect arises despite the deficiency of its causes; the cognition that what is taught as beneficial is harmful; and the cognition that what is taught as harmful is beneficial. (Nyāyakandalī [160], pp. 421–422)

Even regarding the object of inference, when steam, dust, or banners are mistaken for smoke and known as such, one infers fire in a place where there is no fire. Similarly, the cognition that "this is a cow" upon seeing the horn of a *gavaya* is a fallacy of inference (*anumānaviparyaya*).

He states that a fallacy also arises from the habit of extreme misperception: "in cases contrary to the vision of the Threefold Way" (*trayīdarśanaviparīteṣu*). The term *trayī* is a collective designation for the three Vedas—*Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*; the *Atharvaveda*, however, is merely a part of the *Trayī*.

"Darśana" (vision/philosophy) is that by which an object serving as the means to heaven and liberation is perceived; thus, the three Vedas alone are "darśana," and the "Trayī-darśana" refers to them. Regarding the systems of Śākya and others—namely, the heterodox scriptures of the Buddhists, the Bhinnaka, the Nirgranthakas, the Saṃsāramocakas, and so forth—the cognition that "this is the highest good" and "this is authoritative" as they teach it is a false conviction (*mithyā-pratyaya*). This is because these systems are rejected by all members of the social classes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*), and because they contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, the misconception regarding the body, the senses, and the mind as being the self is an error, because it is established that the knower is distinct from them. The misconception among the Mīmāṃsakas that the Vedas—which are produced—are eternal is an error. The misconception among the Lokāyatikas, who maintain that an effect can arise even in the absence of its causes due to the non-existence of merit and demerit, and their knowledge of the diversity of pleasure, pain, and so forth, is an error.

When the elders learned in the Vedas teach what is beneficial—such as "living beings must not be harmed" and "impurities such as dirt and mud must not be worn"—the cognition that perceives this as harmful, namely the view held by the Kṣapaṇakas, Saṃsāramocakas, and others that "the highest dharma is the harming of living beings" and "wearing dirt, mud, and so forth is indeed the best," constitutes a misconception on the part of their disciples. This is the reversal of the cognition regarding what is beneficial.
*Nyāyakandalī* [161] [pp. 423–426]

On this point, some say: "Error does not exist, because there is no cause for it. Its absence [is established] because the sense organs have the inherent nature of producing knowledge that corresponds to reality. If it is argued that "the sense organs produce even non-corresponding knowledge due to the influence of defects (*doṣa*)," we say no; for defects are merely causes of the obstruction of capacity. A sense organ in contact with mother-of-pearl, its capacity impaired by a defect, fails to grasp the "mother-of-pearl-ness," but it does not manifest silver that is not present, because that would entail the absurd consequence that defects function as positive embellishments (*saṃskāraka*).

And if the eye perceives even that which is not itself perceptible, by what means could the omniscience of everyone be prevented? Furthermore, it is contrary to experience (*saṃvid-viruddha*) to claim that the cognition "this is silver" has mother-of-pearl as its objective support (*ālambana*). For whatever object appears in a cognition is the objective support of that cognition; and in the cognition of silver, it is silver that manifests, not mother-of-pearl. Moreover, there can be no error regarding silver in mother-of-pearl for one who has not apprehended silver.

Therefore, these two cognitions—"this" (referring to the experience of the nacre) and "silver"—have distinct objects: the former is an experience of the nacre, while the latter is a recollection of silver produced solely by a latent impression awakened by a perception of similarity and caused by a defect, consisting in the loss of the "that" (tad-) component.

To this, it is replied: if the cognition of silver does not have the nacre as its object but is merely a recollection of silver, then a person seeking silver would act toward the silver previously experienced, and not toward the nacre; for a recollection causes action only toward the locus of the original experience.

Now, you might think: the common form of silver is apprehended by the sense organ in the mother-of-pearl, but its specific nature as mother-of-pearl is not; and by the recollection of silver—which possesses only the form of an apprehension devoid of the mental reference "that"—mere silver is presented without determination of its direction or location. Then, due to the similarity between these two (the perceived and the remembered) and between the acts of perception and recollection, and because of the non-apprehension of their distinction, one fails to discern the difference and proceeds toward the location of the mother-of-pearl, [resulting in] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

One determines that "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl and silver; that too is incorrect, because even non-discrimination is not a case of non-apprehension. For it is the apprehension of non-difference from silver, and not similarity, that is the cause for one desiring silver to act toward the mother-of-pearl; and the apprehension of difference is the cause for desisting from it. In the absence of both of these, one would neither act nor desist; however, one invariably acts, because there is no distinguishing factor [to prevent it].

In this way, even grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not be possible, since the non-apprehension of difference—which is the cause of grammatical non-coreferentiality—is likewise possible. And thus, even the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) that arises after the initial activity, "This is not silver," would not be tenable; for the difference between the mother-of-pearl and the silver was not apprehended, rather than identity having been determined, such that it could now be negated.

If it is argued that this is a negation of the practical usage of "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl—which is occasioned by the non-apprehension of their difference—we say no; for it is possible for the engagement in a practice not directed toward that object to arise from the non-apprehension of non-difference. Indeed, there is the engagement of one seeking silver toward a location containing mother-of-pearl; there is the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the form "this is silver"; and there is a sublating cognition which aims at negating the identity of the substrate of "this-ness" with silver.

From this we understand that, by means of a sense-organ in contact with the mother-of-pearl, aided by a defect and accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of silver, an erroneous determination (*adhyavasāya*) of silver is produced with respect to the mother-of-pearl, while conforming to its similarity [to silver]. As for the objection that it is contrary to experience to hold that the mother-of-pearl is the objective support (*ālambana*), that is without substance; for even the fragment of mother-of-pearl, characterized by its glitter and situated in a specific location as "this," does indeed appear. Furthermore, the meaning of being an "objective support" is the fitness for practical activity such as avoidance (*hāna*), and that is possible precisely in this case.

Even he who maintains that the engagement in the practical usage of "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl occurs due to the non-apprehension of their difference has nonetheless admitted error (*viparyaya*), because error consists precisely in the engagement in practical usage regarding something as being what it is not. Furthermore, as for the claim that defects (*doṣa*) function merely by obstructing the capacity [of the sense organs], that too is of no consequence, since we observe that bodily constituents (*dhātu*) corrupted by defects such as wind (*vāta*) give rise to entirely different diseases. Moreover, the possibility of everyone knowing everything is refuted precisely by the restriction of the capacities of these defects.

Nor does a lack of confidence arise everywhere simply because knowledge deviates from its object; for when subverting causes and defects are sought with effort and their non-existence is established through their non-perception, trust is justified precisely by the realization of the absence of their contrary, which is pervaded by them. Furthermore, if the existence of error is not admitted, what would be the status of the cognition of two moons? If it is argued that this appearance of duality is due to two cognitions produced in the moon by the rays of the eyes—which, being separated by defects, emerge separately and fall upon the moon—that is not so, because a property of cognition cannot be apprehended by the eye.

If one were to accept that a property of cognition, when apprehended as residing in the object of cognition, is itself apprehended by the very same sense organ that apprehends the object of cognition, then error would be established, because a property belonging to one thing would be apprehended in another. Enough of these excessively provoked Vedic scholars; let us desist.

As for those who, in order to support the absence of error, claim that in the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl, a non-worldly (alaukika) silver is perceived as a real entity—they could never act upon this cognition, because they do not recognize that a non-worldly thing can be a cause for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Praśastapādabhāṣya [162] [pp. 427–428]: Non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) also arises only with respect to the objects of perception and inference. Among these, regarding the object of perception first: non-determination is a mere inquiry as to "what is this? concerning either well-known or unknown things, due to distraction or lack of interest. For example, a person from the Vāhīka region experiences non-determination regarding *panasa* trees and the like. In that case, there is indeed determination (*adhyavasāya*) with respect to existence, substantiality, earthness, treeness, possession of form, branches, and so forth.

The state of being a *panasa* (jackfruit tree) is also directly perceived as persisting among *panasa* trees and as being excluded from mangoes (*āmra*) and so forth; however, due to the absence of instruction, the cognition of its specific name does not occur.

Even regarding an object of inference, for an inhabitant of Nārikela Island, upon seeing only a dewlap, there arises a lack of determination, such as: "What kind of living being could this possibly be?"
*Nyāyakandalī* [162] [pp. 427–429]:

Non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) also arises regarding the objects of perception and inference. The meaning of the word “also” (*api*) is that just as error occurs regarding the objects of perception and inference, so too does non-determination occur. With the intention of stating that non-determination must be explained first for the object of perception and then for the object of inference in sequence, he uses the sequential particle “first” (*tāvat*): non-determination is a mere mental inquiry, such as “What is this?”, arising either due to distraction or lack of interest regarding objects that are familiar or unfamiliar.

Those objects which are well-known are "well-known objects" (*prasiddhārtha*). Regarding those objects previously known, due to distraction—either because the mind is attached elsewhere or because there is no desire for a specific cognition—there is merely a mental consideration (*ālocana-mātra*). Even when a well-known king has passed by, the mere knowledge that "someone has gone by this path," without determining the specific details, is non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*).

Regarding unfamiliar objects, there is indeed no determination due to a lack of full cognition; for example, a person from Vāhīka has no determination regarding *panasa* trees and the like. The meaning is that one born in the region of Takka has no determination regarding *panasa* trees and so forth. Even in that case, however, there is certainly a determination with respect to the existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*), color-form (*rūpatva*), and the branches and so on of the *panasa* tree, because of the ascertainment: "This is a substance," "This is earthen," "This is a tree," "This possesses color-form," and "This possesses branches."

The state of being a *panasa* (jackfruit tree), which persists among *panasa* trees and excludes them from mangoes and other species, is indeed perceived by indeterminate direct perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) itself. However, because there has been no instruction that "the word *panasa* is its name," the apprehension of the specific designation does not occur; that is, the apprehension that "this is denoted by the word *panasa*" does not occur. Rather, there would only be the cognition that "it will have some name or other. This cognition, consisting of the non-determination of a specific name, is what is called "non-ascertainment" (*anadhyavasāya*).

Even regarding the object of inference, there is non-determination on the part of an inhabitant of Nālikera Island; upon seeing merely a dewlap, he thinks, "What kind of living being could there possibly be in this region? Because cows do not exist on Nālikera Island, the people there are unacquainted with the species of cow. When such a person arrives in another land and sees only a dewlap in the forest, having inferred a mere physical mass in a general sense, he entertains a lack of ascertainment regarding the specific genus, thinking, "What kind of living being could there possibly be here? This state of mind consists of non-determination.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is non-determinate cognition (*anadhyavasāya*), according to the etymological derivation that it is "other than determinate cognition," which is the knowledge that ascertains a specific object. But is this not simply doubt (*saṃśaya*), since its nature consists in the absence of ascertainment? No; for there is a difference in their causes and a difference in their essential natures. Furthermore, doubt arises from the recollection of both specific features [of an object], whereas non-determinate cognition can occur even when there is no such specific objective content in the perception. Thus, the distinction is that doubt touches upon two unsettled alternatives, while this [non-determinate cognition] does not.
Moreover, this is not a form of valid knowledge (*vidyā*), because it does not serve as a basis for practical activity (*vyavahāra*).
Praśastapādabhāṣya [163] [pp. 429–430]:
That mental experience which occurs through the very doors of the senses for one whose collection of sense organs has ceased and whose mind is dissolved is dream-cognition (*svapnajñāna*).

How so? When, at night, for the sake of rest or for the digestion of food, a living being who has become exhausted during the day due to bodily activities preceded by conscious intent, the mind—dependent upon the effort induced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from the conjunction of the self and the internal organ—undergoes a continuous series of movements within the heart; and when the mind remains motionless in that region of the self which is devoid of the senses, then it is designated as "one whose mind is dissolved" (*pralīnamanaska*).

When that [mind] has dissolved, the collection of the sense organs comes to rest. In that state, while the continuous flow of the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) proceeds, dream-cognition arises through the door of the sense organs—even though the objects are non-existent—taking the form of direct perception due to a particular conjunction of the self and the mind, and from the latent impression (saṃskāra) known as sleep.
(Nyāyakandalī [163], pp. 429–430)

He speaks for the purpose of defining dream-cognition: "of one whose aggregate of sense-faculties has ceased," and so forth. One whose aggregate of sense-faculties (*indriyagrāma*) has ceased—that is, become desisted from grasping their respective objects—is "one whose aggregate of sense-faculties has ceased. One whose mind (*manas*) is dissolved in its entirety, having been completely withdrawn, is "one whose mind is dissolved" (*pralīnamanaska*).

The mental experience of such a person—whose aggregate of sense-faculties has ceased and whose mind is dissolved—which occurs through the gateway of the senses, which is independent of prior apprehension, which has the nature of discernment, and which originates from the mind alone—that is dream-cognition (*svapnajñāna*).

He demonstrates how and when a person’s mind dissolves and the senses cease by means of the words beginning with "How? When a living being has become exhausted and fatigued during the day due to the bodily activities of the self—such as going and coming—which are preceded by conscious intent, then, for the sake of rest at night—that is, for the cessation of fatigue—and for the sake of the transformation of food and drink already consumed into the state of *rasa* (nutrient fluid) and so forth, [the dissolution occurs] in the mind, depending upon the effort brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and resulting from the conjunction of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

When that continuous flow of activity—that stream of actions—has arisen, and the mind remains motionless within the region of the self in the inner heart, which is devoid of sense organs and free from connection with the external senses, then the person is designated as "one whose mind has dissolved. And when that mind has dissolved, the collection of the sense organs comes to rest, because there is no grasping of objects by the senses when they are not presided over by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

In that state where the mind is dissolved, when there occurs a continuous and frequent activity characterized by the inhalation and exhalation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*), dream-cognition arises—having the form of direct perception and the form of immediate awareness—with respect to objects separated by space and time, even though those objects do not exist [at present]. This arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as sleep, which follows from the name "sleep," and from the object previously experienced.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [164] [pp. 431–432]

That [dreaming] is of three kinds: from the intensity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), from a disorder of the bodily elements (*dhātu-doṣa*), and from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). In that regard, first, due to the intensity of mental impressions: when one who is lustful or angry sleeps while intensely contemplating a certain object, then that very stream of thought arises in the form of a direct perception. Or, due to a disorder of the bodily elements: one of a windy temperament (*vāta-prakṛti*), or one afflicted by wind, sees such things as traveling through the sky; one of a bilious temperament (*pitta-prakṛti*), or one afflicted by bile, sees such things as entering fire or mountains of gold; one of a phlegmatic temperament (*śleṣma-prakṛti*), or one afflicted by phlegm, sees such things as crossing rivers and oceans or snow-capped mountains.

In the case of things already experienced or not yet experienced, whether well-known or unknown, whatever indicates auspiciousness—such as mounting an elephant or obtaining a parasol—all that arises from *saṃskāra* (mental impressions) and *dharma* (merit). Conversely, whatever is the opposite—such as being anointed with oil or riding a donkey or a camel—all that arises from *adharma* (demerit) and *saṃskāra*. In the case of things entirely unknown, it arises solely from the *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen).

Although dream-cognition occurs when the collection of sense-faculties has ceased to function, it is nonetheless nothing but memory because it consists in the reviewing of a past stream of cognitions; thus, this ignorance is of four kinds. Regarding the statement that it is threefold, he asks "Why? and answers: "Because of the intensity of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), due to an imbalance of the bodily elements (*dhātu-doṣa*), and due to unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). *Nyāyakandalī* [164] [pp. 431–432] It is of three types. Why? To this he says: "From the intensity of mental impressions, from a disorder of the bodily humors, and from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)."

Due to the intensity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), when a person filled with desire or anger sleeps while contemplating a certain object—such as a beloved or an enemy—with undivided attention, then that very stream of thought arises through the excellence of those impressions in the form of direct perception, appearing as if the object were present before one's eyes.

The *dhātus* are so called because they sustain the body; they consist of fat, blood, flesh, marrow, bone, semen, and the self (*ātman*). Due to a disorder—meaning their being afflicted by *vāta* and the other humors—a perversion occurs. Thus he says: one of *vāta*-constitution, or one afflicted by *vāta* accumulated due to some cause, perceives such things as traveling through space or running here and there. One of *pitta*-constitution, or one afflicted by *pitta*, perceives such things as entering fire, mountains of gold, or the rising solar disc.
One of *śleṣman*-constitution, or one afflicted by *śleṣman*, perceives such things as crossing rivers and oceans or [climbing] snowy mountains.

Whether things experienced by oneself are unknown to others, or things not experienced by oneself are known to others, or whether things experienced by oneself are indeed unknown to others—whatever auspicious indicators such as mounting an elephant or obtaining a parasol are seen in a dream, all of that arises from both latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*) and merit (*dharma*). Conversely, that which is the opposite of an auspicious indicator, such as anointing with oil, bathing, or mounting a camel, arises from demerit (*adharma*) and latent dispositions.

Regarding objects that are absolutely unknown—such as the moon or the act of eating [the moon], which are not perceived either through their own nature or through another—the cognition arises solely from *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), because there is an absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) for things never before experienced. Although a dream-cognition, occurring due to the intensity of latent impressions, a disorder of the bodily elements, or *adṛṣṭa*, presents a superimposed external form and is thus a misconception (*viparyaya*) because it takes one thing to be what it is not, it is nevertheless mentioned separately because it occurs in a specific state [of consciousness].

Sometimes there occurs a recollection of an object seen in a dream while still in the state of dreaming—thinking, "This was seen by me"—and because that occurs at the end or conclusion of a previously experienced dream, it is called *svapnāntika* (the end of a dream).

To dispel the doubt of someone who might think that dream-cognition is indeed a state occurring when the collection of sense-faculties has ceased, he says: "Even though dream-cognition occurs for one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased, it is nevertheless merely memory (*smṛti*), because it consists of the review (*pratyavekṣaṇa*) and recollection (*anusandhāna*) of a past, previously experienced series of dream-cognitions. He concludes: "Thus, this ignorance (*avidyā*) is fourfold.
[165] Knowledge (*vidyā*) is also fourfold, characterized as perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*laiṅgika*), memory (*smṛti*), and revelation (*ārṣa*).

In this context, that which arises in dependence upon each respective sense-faculty (*akṣa*) is *pratyakṣa* (direct perception). The sense-faculties (*akṣa*) are the organs: the six consisting of the nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear, and mind.
For that [perception] arises with respect to categories of objects such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth.

Nyāyakandalī [165] [pp. 433–436]: Now he divides *vidyā* (valid knowledge): "Valid knowledge is also of four kinds. It is not only ignorance (*avidyā*) that is of four kinds; valid knowledge (*vidyā*) is also of four kinds. It is characterized by perception, inference, recollection, and revelation (*ārṣa*), having the nature of perception, recollection, and revelation.

First, perception is mentioned because it is the cause; immediately after that, inference, because it is preceded by that [perception]; after that, memory, because it exists with respect to objects perceived or inferred; and at the end of the worldly means of knowledge, the mention of the *ārṣa* [intuition], because it belongs to supramundane persons.

He first states the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "In that regard, it is called *pratyakṣa* because it arises depending upon each respective sense-organ (*akṣa*). That which arises depending upon each respective sense-organ is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as direct perception. Furthermore, the fact that an effect is produced from a specific cause also serves as its definition, because it is capable of distinguishing that effect from things of both similar and dissimilar classes. For example, the fact that a barley sprout originates from a barley seed is its defining characteristic; for this very reason, it is designated as a "barley sprout."

If it is argued that pleasure, pain, and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) would also result in being valid direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) because they are produced by the sense faculties, we say no; for [the definition] is qualified by reference to cognition (*buddhi*). Direct perception is that cognition which arises in dependence upon each respective sense faculty (*akṣa*). Since pleasure and the like do not have the nature of cognition, how could there be any such consequence regarding them? If this is so, then the validity of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) is not obtained. True.

This [definition] cannot be obtained from this statement; however, if its validity is intended through an instrumental derivation (*karaṇavyutpatti*)—because it is the cause of determination (*paricchedahetutvāt*), since the investigation of knowledge (*vidyā*) is the subject at hand, which excludes doubt and error—then a certain misconception might arise that "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers only to that which is produced in dependence on the sense organs (*akṣaṃ pratītya yad utpadyate*), namely, that which is born of the external senses, because such a usage is so well-known. To dispel that, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) "each sense organ" (*akṣam akṣam*) is employed. It is made for the purpose of including the comprehension by all the sense organs. It is a *prādi*-compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

The term *pratyakṣa* (perception) is derived from the sense-organ (*akṣa*) with the prefix *prati*; by this, it takes on the gender of its referent, as in "perceptual cognition" (*pratyakṣaṃ jñānam*), "perceptual intellect" (*pratyakṣā buddhiḥ*), or "perceptual conviction" (*pratyakṣaḥ pratyayaḥ*). Since the word *akṣa* is conventionally established in many meanings, he specifies: "the sense-organs (*indriyāṇi*). And since those are said to be of eleven kinds according to the Sāṃkhya school, he provides an exhaustive enumeration to exclude them: "the nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear, and mind. [p.435]

If it were stated that "perception is cognition born of the senses," then memory (*smṛti*) would also be perception; therefore, in order to exclude that [memory] which has non-existent objects, he specifies the object of perception: "for that arises with respect to categories such as substance (*dravya*), etc. The word "for" (*hi*) is used for emphasis. The meaning is that this perception arises only with respect to substances and so forth—namely, only with respect to substances, qualities, actions, and generalities (*sāmānya*)—and not with respect to particularities (*viśeṣa*) or inherence (*samavāya*).

Because substance (*dravya*) is primary, he first states the arising of perception with respect to it: "In the case of substance, for its part... The word "for its part" (*tāvat*) indicates sequence. Perception occurs in a large substance—namely, the three kinds characterized as earth, water, and fire—for what reason? To this he says: "Because of possessing multiple substances" (*anekadravyavattvāt*). Possessing multiple substances means being dependent upon many constituent parts (*avayava*).

The manifestation of form (*rūpa*) is designated as its "emergence" (*udbhava*), which is a property (*dharma*) of form; due to the absence of this [property], there is a lack of perception when light resides in water. From the conjunction of the four [factors], namely the conjunction of the self with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with the object—and from this collection of causes, as well as the presence of the totality of conditions such as heat and so forth—perception occurs; it is stated that [the size of the object] must be "large" (*mahat*) because otherwise perception would not occur.

Because one observes degrees of clarity and lack of clarity in a whole (*avayavin*) corresponding to the excellence or non-excellence of the multiplicity of its parts, possession of multiple constituent substances (*anekadravyavattva*) is the cause [of perceptibility]. Furthermore, since air is not perceived despite possessing magnitude and possession of multiple constituent substances, the manifestation of color (*rūpa-prakāśa*) is the cause [of perceptibility]. Because all cognition serves as a cause for pleasure, pain, and so forth, and because it arises without fixed restriction of place or time, it is produced by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), space (*dik*), and time (*kāla*).

Since perception does not occur without the conjunction of the self and the mind, the conjunction of the mind and the sense organ, and the conjunction of the sense organ and the object, the fourfold contact (*caturvidhasannikarṣa*) is the cause.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [166–170] [pp. 436–437]

First, regarding substance, which is of two kinds: when it is large, possesses multiple constituent substances, and has manifest color, through the fourfold contact [of the object with the sense organ], and when the causal complex such as merit (*dharma*) is present, there arises a mere observation of its own form; then, depending on the qualifiers of generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*), perception arises from the contact between the self and the mind, in the form: "it exists," "it is a substance," "it is earth," "it has horns," "it is white," "it is a cow," or "it is moving.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [166] [pp. 436–437]

If it is argued that, since the contact of the sense organ with its object is the cause [of perception], the perception of the particular must necessarily occur just like the perception of the universal, and therefore doubt and error cannot arise—this is not so, because there is no such necessity. For the universal, having many objects, is perceived by the mere contact of the eye with its own substratum; the particular, however, having fewer objects, requires contact with its own substratum, with its many parts, and with many parts of the eye as well as their parts. Thus, there is no rule for simultaneous perception, due to the difference in the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
For this very reason, there is an indistinct perception from a distance; because the intervening parts of the ocular rays that have disintegrated in the space between do not reach the object.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [167] [pp. 438–439]

Some maintain that perception is exclusively determinate (*savikalpaka*), because it is through its nature as a definitive judgment (*vyavasāyātmakatva*) that it becomes fit for practical activity (*vyavahāra*), since even animals who have not acquired linguistic conventions act upon the conceptualization of objects. To them, he says: "mere observation of the thing-in-itself" (*svarūpālocanamātra*). This means that perception is the mere grasping of the thing-in-itself, free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). It is simply the direct apprehension (*grahaṇamātra*). Perception is [defined as] such.

For if the apprehension of the actual nature of an object by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) were not admitted, then conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) would also be impossible, because there would be no recollection of the word that denotes it. Therefore, one who desires conceptual cognition must also admit non-conceptual cognition; and that [non-conceptual cognition] does not grasp the universal alone, because the particularity (*bheda*) also appears in it. Nor does it grasp the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone, because the form of the universal is experienced and because there is a synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) upon seeing another individual instance.

However, it grasps both the universal and the particular; yet, because it lacks the mental synthesis of other objects, it does not comprehend them by distinguishing them as "this is the universal" and "this is the particular. For it is through the apprehension of the persistence across other individual instances that the universal is distinguished, and through the apprehension of exclusion that the distinction "this is a particular" arises.

And in the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*), because there is no synthesis with other individuals, the two properties of universal and particular—namely, persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—are not apprehended; due to the non-apprehension of those two, there is no distinct apprehension [of them]. However, the apprehension of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) certainly does occur, since that is independent of anything else.

For this very reason, by means of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), there is no apprehension of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) among universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*). This is because such a relationship presupposes the apprehension of difference, whereas non-conceptual perception does not determine the mutual difference between universals and the rest. However, subsequent conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*) does comprehend the nature of universals and particulars; for it is possible for a person who connects one individual with another to perceive through the sense organs the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) as properties, thereby attaining a cognition of that kind. *Nyāyakandalī* [168] [pp. 439–444]

The Buddhists, however, say this: "That which has a manifestation conforming to the presence and absence of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and non-erroneous with respect to the real object; therefore, only that is perception (*pratyakṣa*), not the conceptual (*savikalpaka*). For the latter, being born dependent on latent impressions (*vāsanā*), its manifestation does not conform to the real object and is thus erroneous with respect to the object, like the cognition of [illusory] hair and so forth. Refuting their view, [the author] states that even the conceptual is perception: "From the contact of the self and the mind, depending on the qualifiers of universal (*sāmānya*), particular (*viśeṣa*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*)."

Generality, particularity, substance, quality, and action constitute "generality, particularity, substance, quality, and action. These very things—generality, particularity, substance, quality, and action—are the qualifiers; thus, they are the "qualifiers of generality, particularity, substance, quality, and action. That contact between the self and the mind which depends upon these [qualifiers] results in the cognition "existent substance" as qualified by generality, "earth" as qualified by the particularity of earthness, "horned" as qualified by substance, "white cow" as qualified by quality, and "it moves" as qualified by action.

Perception would be distinguished by its object. Since the conjunction of the four factors is already established by the phrase "from the contact of the four," the repeated mention of this [conjunction of self and mind] is for the purpose of indicating that this is a different sequence from the previous discussion concerning indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*).

How can it be said that determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? For in the cognition "this is a jar," there is indeed perceived an object characterized by a conch-like neck, distinct and differentiated from all else. If it is argued that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a manifestation not produced by the object, and therefore the determination of the object through it is erroneous—then it has been said: [p.441] ... [as stated] ...
"Conceptual construction is a cognitive affliction because it appears as a real object yet fails to correspond to it."

No, because there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) in the activity [of the person]. If it is argued that a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—born from the experience of an object and having its own appearance superimposed as the nature of the object—induces a person toward the location of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) by concealing the difference between the particular and its own appearance, and thereby brings about correspondence; and that this attainment of the object occurs through a mediated connection with the object, like the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel—[we reply: if the conceptual construction does not touch the real entity (*vastu*), how could it superimpose its own appearance as being of the nature of that [entity]? For a superimposition of water upon a locus is never observed when a mass of mirage-rays has not been perceived.

Now, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), by adopting the operation of its cause, directly perceives the object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*); otherwise, it would be impossible for one who seeks causal efficiency to act on the basis of conceptual construction. As it has been said: "Even from that conceptual construction, activity occurs toward the object itself. If this is so, then [conceptual construction] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the object, because it is the cause of a non-contradictory cognition regarding it.

Now, if you think that the moment which is grasped by perception is not determined by conceptual construction, and that which is determined by conceptual construction is not obtained through purposeful action—thus, there is no correspondence with respect to the moment because of their momentariness—[we reply as follows].

However, the kind of moment that is grasped by perception is the very same kind that is determined by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); and the kind that is determined by conceptual construction is the very same kind that is obtained through purposeful action (*pravṛtti*). Thus, with respect to the mere object excluded from what is other (*atadvyāvṛtta-vastumātra*), there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) for one who has not perceived the difference between moments. In this regard, conceptual construction is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, since such an object has already been grasped by perception itself. But conceptual construction arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*) is a means of valid cognition, because it leads to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which had not been attained by any other means of knowledge.

That too is without substance; for neither the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*)—which is of the nature of non-existence—nor a superimposed common form belonging to that [moment], which depends on such exclusion, is grasped by perception as a real entity. This is because the criterion of being an object of cognition (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*) consists in being a cause, and because a non-entity is devoid of all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

The moment (*kṣaṇa*), however, exists as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*); it is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), and it has been stated that it does not persist through the duration of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). How, then, could there be identity of the object? Or, let us grant that there is some single object, whose form is not determined by either conceptual construction or perception, which is fit for purposeful activity and correspondence; even so, conceptual construction does not transcend the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because, like a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhikabuddhi*), it is independent of anything prior in the determination of the object, and because it possesses the capacity to bring about the attainment of what has been determined.

And its status as a valid means of cognition being established, it must be perception itself, because of the absence of inferential signs (*liṅga*) and so forth, and because it follows the presence and absence of the object and the sense faculty.

As for the fact that, although it arises from an object, it does not occur merely upon the impact of the sense faculty like non-conceptual [perception], that is due to the absence of the recollection of the expressive word which acts as a cooperative cause for the sense faculty and the object.

If it is argued that a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which arises immediately after memory is produced by memory alone and not by the sense-organ and its object, because those two are intervened by memory—[we reply: O sir, does an auxiliary cause obscure the inherent power (*svarūpaśakti*) of an entity? What would be the fate of a seed covered by earth and water regarding the production of a sprout? If it is asked what benefit the recollection of a word provides to the sense-organ and its object such that it becomes an auxiliary for them, [the answer is: it is just as [in the case of] conceptual construction. [Page 444]

It follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the object and the sense organ with respect to its own production; the same applies to memory as well. In this regard, the very assistance that memory provides to the sense organ and the object is that these two, which were not producing the effect when alone, do so upon obtaining the cooperation of memory. It has been refuted on the occasion of the rejection of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) that those which do not impart an excellence (*atiśaya*) to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a thing cannot be its auxiliaries (*sahakārin*).

[Objection: It might be argued that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), whereas conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) is not; therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the real object.

Now, what is this "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*)? Is it one cognition consisting of the association with words, and another, distinct cognition apprehending an object consisting of the association with the object itself? That is incorrect, because the alternatives are untenable. Does the cognition consisting of the association with words associate the word with the object, or does it itself become associated with the word? If it associates the word with the object, then in that case too, does it make the object consist of the nature of the word, or does it apprehend it as colored by the form of the word, or does it designate it by means of the word?

Cognition does not, first of all, make the object consist of the nature of the word (*śabdātmaka*), because the object appears even in conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) precisely with its own nature as apprehended by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpakajñāna*), and because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Otherwise, it would be impossible for both those who have mastered language and those who have not to simultaneously determine a single object. Now, if it is argued that [conceptual cognition] grasps the object as colored by the form of the word, that too is incorrect, because such [coloring] is not perceived. Once the object has been apprehended by non-conceptual perception, the word denoting it—which was previously experienced—is remembered due to the perception of its counterpart (*pratiyogin*).

Established through memory, this [word] determines the object while remaining external to it; however, the object is not grasped as being colored by the form of the word, as a crystal might be colored by blue. This is because the word is not visible to the eye, and because the object alone appears in its "this-ness" (*idantā*), just as in non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*). Furthermore, when the designator (the word) is being remembered, there is no impairment whatsoever to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the designated (the object), by which it would fail to attain the status of perception even though there is contact with the sense faculties. As it has been said: "For even when the name is being remembered, it does not obstruct perceptibility."

"For that notion (*saṃjñā*) is indeed indifferent; it is not capable of veiling the form [of the object]. Thus, it is also not well-established that cognition designates an object as conjoined with a word. For the self is conscious; by virtue of its capacity for synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*) and so forth, it recalls the expressive word experienced at the time of the linguistic convention and designates the object by means of that word. It is not the case that "this is a jar" is the cognition, because that [cognition] lacks the capacity for synthesis and so forth. In this way, first of all, cognition does not conjoin the word.

Nor is it conjoined with the word itself, because cognition and its aspect—which is non-different from it—are momentary and unique; thus, being impossible to designate, they are unfit for conjunction with a word. Furthermore, there is no designation of the subjective cognition by means of a word that denotes the object. Now, you might think: conceptual construction has as its object a thing conjoined with a word, and that object, having been conjoined with the word, is itself conjoined with and designated by the word.

And where there is a linguistic convention for a word, that [object] to which the word's convention applies is neither non-momentary nor common; for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the cognition whose object is the particular characteristic, or the mental aspect (*ākāra*) which is the object of that cognition, cannot be both common and non-momentary. Furthermore, even the externality of the cognitive aspect is not distinct from the cognitive aspect itself and is thus strictly unique. Moreover, a universal (*sāmānya*) existing as a real entity does not exist, because it cannot withstand critical analysis.

Therefore, since externalness is superimposed upon each of the mental forms (svākāra) by conceptual constructions (vikalpa), and because their mutual differences are not determined, they are superimposed as a unity through the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*); thus, it follows inevitably by the force of valid cognition that this is where the convention (*saṅketa*) of the word is applied. And in that regard, the conceptual construction, proceeding toward that which is unreal (*alīka*) yet possessed of verbal association, conceptualizes an object that does not exist; hence it is called "conceptual knowledge" (*kalpanājñāna*). As it has been said: "In that [conceptual construction], the form which appears as if it were a single external thing, as if excluded from others, though devoid of reality due to its inability to withstand critical examination. [p.447]

To this it is replied: If the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consists in the apprehension of an object qualified by a universal (*sāmānya*), on the grounds that such a real entity (*vastubhūta*) does not exist, then the nature of conceptual construction would consist simply in having an unreal object (*asadartha*), and not in the apprehension of what is associated with words (*śabda-saṃsṛṣṭa*). In that case, if we were able to establish the existence of the universal through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even though it apprehends what is associated with words, a determinate cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) regarding that object would be nothing but perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is produced from the sense organ and the object.

That which appears as immediate is perception, such as non-conceptual [cognition]; and conceptual cognition appears as immediate. Here, the state of being indirect (parokṣatva) in cognitions is pervaded by not being produced from the sense-objects, as in inference; and the production from sense-objects is contradictory to not being produced from the senses. Since this [production from sense-objects] is perceived in non-conceptual cognition because it exists when that [the presence of the sense-object] exists, there is the "perception of what is contradictory to the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).

If it is argued that there is also a counter-inference (pratipakṣānumāna) stating: "Whatever is preceded by memory is not perception, such as inferential cognition; and conceptual cognition (savikalpakajñāna) is preceded by memory," [we reply: if perceptuality has never been apprehended anywhere, then its negation cannot be established in conceptual cognition, because negation is necessarily preceded by prior apprehension.

Now, [suppose you argue that] it is cognized in non-conceptual [perception]. How is it so cognized? If you say, "by means of the inference based on its occurring when the sense organ and the object are present," then, once the validity of the inference based on its occurring when they are present—which establishes its status as perception—is accepted, the inference that seeks to negate its status as perception is sublated by that very same [inference], which functions in the opposite manner, just as the [inference] "sound is not audible" is sublated by the fact of its being audible. Thus, for now, it is established that cognition consisting of the association with words is not conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Even though it consists of the conjunction with an object, the apprehension of a specific [quality] is not conceptualization (*kalpanā*), because the qualifier, the relation between the two, or the relationship of the excluded and the excluder (*vyavacchedya-vyavacchedaka-bhāva*) are real entities. The apprehension of an object (*arthāvagraha*) is a cognition; through the contact of the sense organ with that object, it arises exactly as the object exists, and it does not proceed by deliberating upon the object. Discernment (*vicāra*), however, is specific cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*). [It takes the form: "This is the qualifier, this is the qualified, this is the relation between these two, and such is the state of affairs in the world."

Having reflected that "the man has a staff" and not "the staff is the man," one subsequently apprehends them as unified, thinking "the man with a staff. If the qualified nature of the object were real, then the cognition of the qualified would arise at the very outset.

If it is argued that [the self] does not exist, and that there is no distinction in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather that the cognition of distinction is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is thus a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); this is difficult for Your Honor to understand. For it is the self (*ātman*)—having grasped each of the qualifiers and so forth and synthesizing them—that perceives the distinction of the object through the sense faculty. Cognition is not insentient, because it lacks the capacity for synthesis and because it does not function by pausing after one operation to engage in another.

The object is indeed qualified by its connection with qualifiers; however, because the perception of the qualifiers and so forth is absent as a cooperative cause, it is not apprehended by the sense organ in that way at first. Once the qualifiers and so forth have been apprehended, it is then apprehended. Thus, the cognition of the qualified object produced by the sense organ is, for its part, a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*). If, due to the fault of being a qualified cognition, it does not qualify as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the matter is difficult to resolve, and we shall desist from further discussion.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [171] [pp. 451–452, 454]

Color, taste, smell, and touch arise through specific sense organs as their cause, due to their inherence in multiple substances, their own inherent particularities, and their contact with their own substrates.
Sound, which inheres in the auditory organ, is perceived by that very organ through the threefold contact.

Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, viscidity, fluidity, velocity, and action are apprehended by both sight and touch, because of their inherence in perceptible substances.
The perception of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort arises from the contact of two [factors]: the self and the mind.

The apprehension of existence, substantiality, quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth—which are inherent in the substrates that are themselves perceived—by means of the sense organs that apprehend those substrates, constitutes the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of persons such as ourselves.

In the *Nyāyakandalī* [171] [pp. 451–455], he states the cause for the arising of perception regarding color and the other qualities: "In color, taste, smell, and touch. A substance that inheres in many constituent parts (*avayava*) is a "multi-substance" (*anekadravya*); [perception arises] because of its inherence (*samavāya*) therein. An intrinsic particularity (*svagato viśeṣaḥ*) exists in color as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*), in taste as "taste-ness" (*rasatva*), in smell as "smell-ness" (*gandhatva*), and in touch as "touch-ness" (*sparśatva*). It is from these [that perception arises].

Due to the contact with their own substrata—that is, from the contact of the sense organs with the substrata of color and the other qualities—knowledge arises regarding color through the eye as its specific cause, regarding taste through the tongue, regarding smell through the nose, and regarding touch through the organ of touch. The restriction of the senses to color and the rest is due to the fact that the specific qualities inherent in each serve as their respective causes; otherwise, there would be confusion due to the absence of such distinctions. As for sound, which inheres in the auditory organ, its perception occurs through the contact of those three [factors] by means of that very organ itself.

By the phrase "from the threefold contact," the contact between the self, the mind, and the sense organs is indicated.
