The contact between the sense organ and its object is stated by the words "inherent in the auditory faculty. "Perception by that alone" means perception by the auditory faculty alone.

Numbers and the other qualities ending with action, when inhering in perceptible substances, are perceived by both sight and touch, just like their substrata. We do not accept that action is perceptible, because when a substance moves, no distinct category of entity other than conjunction and disjunction is perceived. As for this cognition "it moves," it has as its object an action inferred from conjunction and disjunction.

That is without substance: if action, being imperceptible, is inferred from disjunction and conjunction, then since disjunction and conjunction reside in both [the object and its locus], action would have to be inferred in the other locus as well. Furthermore, when a monkey moves from the root to the tip or from the tip to the root, the cognition "the tree is moving" does not arise, even though the tree is the locus of those very same conjunctions and disjunctions.

If it is argued that since the conjunction of this tree-dweller with space and so forth cannot be produced by an action inherent in the tree, one should not infer an action in the tree—then, for the sake of conjunction with another location, there must likewise be a distinct action in the tree-dweller, and the postulation of an action in the tree does not cease at all.

The general rule is that whatever is the locus of the effect is the locus of the cause; if there is a deviation from this in one instance, what confidence can there be in another? If it is argued that since the conjunctions and disjunctions of a monkey with a tree arise even when the monkey moves to another place due to an action inherent in the monkey itself (without being produced by the tree), it is unnecessary to postulate an action in both, we say: not so. For inference functions only to the extent that when a connected mark (*liṅga*) is perceived, it brings to mind its necessary connection (*pratibandhaka*).

As for the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), what is the harm in its being explained otherwise, as in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? Nor is this [complex] conscious like a person, such that it would act out of regard for some purpose. But if one were to postulate that the conjunctions and disjunctions of a single point of space (*vyomapradeśa*) are the causes for the inference of action? It is not possible to postulate this, because the disjunctions and conjunctions residing in supersensible space are themselves imperceptible.

If the motion of a bird flying in the sky were to be inferred from a continuous series of conjunctions and disjunctions with various regions of the earth's sphere, its action would be difficult to apprehend. If it is claimed that a stream of conjunctions and disjunctions with the mass of light pervading the sky constitutes its inferential mark (*liṅga*), then even for one who does not accept this—such as when, due to a wind disorder in the dark, the trembling of a single limb produces the cognition "the tip of my arm trembles" or "my eyebrow moves"—there would arise, based on the tactile sense (*tvag-indriya*) presided over by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), a cognition of action that would be without a [perceptual] basis.
What is the status of the cognition that "lightning flashes" during the darkness of a great storm at night, which lasts for only a moment?

[p.454] Regarding the perception of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, it arises from the conjunction of two—the self and the mind. Cognition and so forth are perceived through inherence in that [self], while those inherent in the self are apprehended through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined with it (*tatsaṃyuktasamavāya*).

Substance, quality, action, and so forth, which are perceived as inherent in their substrates, are apprehended by those sense organs that apprehend their respective supports. As for the universals such as existence (*sattā*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*), they are apprehended by whichever sense organ apprehends their substrate; by that same organ, they too are grasped. In this regard, there is a sixfold contact (*sannikarṣa*): the apprehension of substance through conjunction (*saṃyoga*); the cognition of qualities and so forth through inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*); the knowledge of quality-ness and so forth through inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*); the apprehension of sound through inherence (*samavāya*); the apprehension of sound-ness through inherence in what is inherent (*samaveta-samavāya*); and the apprehension of absence (*abhāva*) through the state of being a qualifier of the related (*sambaddha-viśeṣaṇatā*).

The apprehension of the absence of taste and so forth in color by way of being a qualifier of that which is conjoined and inherent; the cognition of the absence of tasteness and so forth in the universal *rūpatva* (color-ness) by way of being a qualifier of the qualifier of that which is conjoined and inherent; the understanding of the absence of the phoneme *kha* and so forth in the phoneme *ka* by way of being a qualifier of that which is inherent; and the perception of the absence of *khatva* (the universal of *kha*) and so forth in the universal *gatva* (the universal of *ga*) by way of being a qualifier of that which is inherent in that which is inherent—all of these are subsumed under the category of being a qualifier of a related entity (*sambaddhaviśeṣaṇabhāva*).

Others, however, do not accept the postulation of further intermediate relations, because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) alone serve as the causes for perception in all cases according to their respective possibilities. For such is the nature (*svabhāva*) of those entities that they are perceived only through contact with something else. Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because proximity to their own substratum (*svāśraya*) acts as the restrictive factor. He concludes: "This is the perception of people like us. This means: of non-yogins, such as ourselves. *Praśastapādabhāṣyam* [172] [p. 460]

For yogins superior to us who are in a state of meditative union (*yukta*), through a mind assisted by the dharma born of yoga, there arises an unerring perception of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) regarding their own self, other selves, space, direction, time, atoms, air, and the mind, as well as regarding the qualities, actions, universals, and ultimate particulars inherent in them, and regarding inherence itself. Furthermore, for those who are not in a state of union (*viyukta*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises with respect to objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant, due to the power of the assistance provided by the dharma born of yoga, based on the contact of the four factors.

He describes the perception of yogis with the words: "But for those superior to us... Yoga is *samādhi*. It is of two kinds: *samprajñāta* (cognitive) and *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive). *Samprajñāta* is the conjunction of the mind—which has been brought under control in a certain region of the self by means of sustaining effort—with the self, which is distinguished by the desire to know reality. *Asamprajñāta*, on the other hand, is the conjunction of the controlled mind with a certain region of the self, characterized by the absence of intentional objects and the absence of emergence.

In this regard, this higher [yoga] ripens in the final birth for those seeking liberation in order to dissolve the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance; it does not accumulate merit (*dharma*), because it lacks the cooperation of intentional resolve (*abhisaṃdhi*). Nor does it direct one toward external objects, since its transformation occurs within the self alone. The former yoga, however, accompanied by intentional resolve, expands merit.

Because it illuminates that very object for the sake of which there is a desire to know reality, by virtue of that yoga, even those yogins whose yoga has lapsed are called "yogins" due to their inherent fitness. Furthermore, since those whose obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) have not yet been destroyed do not possess the vision of supersensuous objects at that time, he says: "of those who are joined" (*yuktānām*).

For those who have been instructed and established in meditative concentration (samādhi), there arises—by means of a mind aided by the dharma born of yoga—an unerring and non-erroneous perception of the essential nature (svarūpa) within oneself, within other selves, and within the selves of others; likewise with respect to ether, space, time, air, atoms, minds, the qualities and so forth inherent in them, and inherence itself.

By people such as ourselves, the self is always perceived as being permeated by the forms of agency and ownership in the notions of "I" and "mine. Both of these are forms produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body and are not natural; for this very reason, the cognition of "I" and "mine" is proclaimed to be a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), because it grasps a contrary form in all philosophical systems.

However, that which is its essential nature (*svābhāvika-svarūpa*) is perceived by yogis. For when a yogi, with the resolve "May I know the true nature of the Self as it is proclaimed in the Vedānta," withdraws the mind from the external senses and, having fixed it upon a certain locus within the self, practices a continuous flow of contemplation on the Self with one-pointed concentration, then—through the process of instilling those qualities (*dharma*) that bring about the knowledge of reality—the true nature of the Self, freed from the notions of "I" and "mine," becomes manifest to him.

But when one practices a continuous stream of reflection out of a desire to know the Supreme Self, space, time, and so forth, then a dharma of inconceivable power, conducive to the knowledge of the reality of the Supreme Self and other such entities, accumulates within him; and by its force, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) issues forth from the external body and becomes united with the Supreme Self and the rest.

Through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it produces cognition of those [substances]; through inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), of their qualities and so forth; through inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), of [universals] such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*); and through the state of being a related qualifier (*sambaddhaviśeṣaṇabhāva*), it produces cognition of inherence and absence. First, it is observed that for one whose mind is concentrated and who is practicing, there arises knowledge even of the sciences or arts that were previously unknown. In other cases, this is inference: the accumulation of practice regarding the self, space, and so forth, is the cause of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), because it is a specialized form of practice, just like the practice of sciences or arts.
Likewise, there is a gradation of intellect, which in some cases is unsurpassed, because it possesses degrees of excellence, just like the gradation of magnitude.

[Objection: Is it not the case that while there is a gradation of heat in water being heated, no excellence characterized by the attainment of the nature of fire—which would surpass all others—is observed in it? Nor is any limit to the practice of jumping perceived; for there is no such person who, by means of leaping, could traverse the three worlds. [Reply: It is said: A quality (*dharma*) which has a stable substratum and produces a specific excellence within its own substratum reaches the ultimate limit of excellence through the process of repeated practice.

Just as the purification of gold (*kaladhauta*) produced by a continuous process of smelting and heating results in a supreme state of essential refinement, [it is not so with other things]. For instance, water does not possess a stable substratum in which heat could be repeatedly practiced until it reaches its ultimate limit; for when extreme heat is applied, the water itself perishes. Nor does the practice of jumping (*laṅghana*) produce a lasting excellence within its own substratum; for once a previous jump has vanished without leaving a trace (*niranvayavinasta*), a subsequent jump arises—just like something entirely new—due to a different strength and a different effort.

For this very reason, for one who is exhausted by frequent jumping, leaping is reduced compared to what it was before, due to the depletion of physical capacity. Intellect (*buddhi*), however, has a stable substratum and imparts a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) to its own substrate; for we observe that an object not previously grasped is grasped when it is practiced again and again.

Since intellect is cultivated over a long period with devotion and continuity—following a sequence of imparting increasingly superior qualities through repeated prior practice—the attainment of its ultimate excellence, having acquired power through the favor of *yoga*-born merit (*dharma*), is not impossible.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated here—that yogis are not perceivers of objects beyond the senses of those such as ourselves because they possess life-breath (prāṇitva), like ourselves—if this is said by taking "person" in general as the subject (*pakṣa*), then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, a specific kind of person is intended, that is unestablished for the opponent; and if it were established, the inference would contradict the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the very subject (*dharmin*).

Now it is said: this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (a reductio ad absurdum); and a *prasaṅga-sādhana* is not employed for the sake of establishing one's own position, but rather for the purpose of demonstrating an undesirable consequence for the opponent. And that which is undesirable for the opponent can be demonstrated by means of the subject (*dharmin*) and other factors established solely through the opponent's own admission. In that case, one's own realization [of the matter] need not be supported by a formal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the opponent cannot rightly object in this manner: "The subject and other factors are unestablished for you; I do not accept them even when they are established for myself."

To this we reply: Is this *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) an inference (*anumāna*), or something else? If it is something else, its inclusion must be described within the previously stated definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or a new definition must be provided. If, however, it is indeed an inference, then it must proceed preceded by one's own realization, because every inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) functions with the desire to produce a certainty in others just as one has oneself attained certainty.

Otherwise, even the argument "the sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus, like a lotus in a pleasure-pool" would result in the validity of a proof with an unestablished locus (*asiddhāśraya*), since its proponent accepts it as a statement. Furthermore, qualities such as being a living being (*prāṇitva*) have a doubtful pervasion (*sandigdhavyāpti*).

For if even the quality of being a living being were present in this preeminent person who is the subject of dispute, what inconsistency could there be in his being omniscient? Indeed, no contradiction between the two has been observed, since omniscience is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

However, the coexistence of being a living being (*prāṇitva*) and so forth with non-omniscience is doubtful. Is this non-omniscience necessarily concomitant with being a living being as it is for people like us, or is it caused by the absence of the merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), which is known to be the cause of omniscience? This cannot be determined. Therefore, being a living being and the like, whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established, is incapable of serving as a means of inference.

It is not established that the cause of supersensuous knowledge is a quality (*dharma*) born of yoga; how then could our lack of omniscience be suspected on account of its absence? For us, this [yogic *dharma*] is not established, and thus this suspicion arises. Consequently, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established for both parties; how, then, can there be inference?

Having explained the perception of those who are "joined" (*yukta*), he explains that of those who are "disjoined" (*viyukta*) with the words: "Of the disjoined, moreover... Those who, through the excellence of qualities accumulated by the practice of intense yoga, perceive supersensuous objects even while not established in meditative absorption (*asamādhi*), are the "disjoined. For them—whose entire range of objects has become present before them and whose collection of faculties is unimpeded—the favoring influence of yoga-born merit (*yogaja-dharma*) acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakāritā*) through the fourfold contact (*catuṣṭaya-sannikarṣa*), namely the contact of self, mind, sense-organ, and object; and by its power, [they perceive] subtle things.

Direct perception arises with respect to atoms of the mind and so forth, to obstructed objects such as the worlds of the *nāgas*, to remote objects such as the world of Brahmā and so forth, and to [subtle] things.

In that regard, according to the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*: regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), direct perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting merely in the observation of their own nature; the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance (*dravya*) and the rest; the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is the self (*ātman*); and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is the knowledge whose objects are substance and the other categories.

In the arising of the cognition of a universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*) as mere undifferentiated observation; there is no other means of valid cognition in that regard, because it does not possess the nature of a result.

Alternatively, perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that knowledge which arises from the fourfold contact (*catuṣṭaya-sannikarṣa*), being non-erroneous and non-verbal. The objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth; the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is the self (*ātman*); and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is the observation of qualities, defects, or indifference. *Nyāyakandalī* [173] [pp. 461–465]

Thus far, perception has been explained; now the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is distinguished: "In that regard, perception is the mere observation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*). Existence (*sattā*) is the universal; substance-ness, quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth are [lower] universals; and the individuals (*vyakti*) are the particulars. With respect to these, the mere observation of the essential nature—that is, the mere apprehension of the essential nature—free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for the production of valid knowledge (*pramā*).

And "being the most effective means" (*sādhakatamatva*) refers to the excellence (*atiśaya*) that, when it exists, valid cognition (*pramā*) necessarily arises for one who desires to know; whereas when the knower (*pramātṛ*) or the object of knowledge (*prameya*) exist, valid cognition may arise but does not necessarily arise. However, in the case of the indeterminate means of knowledge (*nirvikalpa-pramāṇa*), characterized by the cognition of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa-jñāna*) and so forth, valid cognition characterized by the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya-jñāna*) and so forth necessarily arises—this is the excellence.

The objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) beginning with substance; that is to say, the four categories beginning with substance are the objects of cognition, being the spheres of valid knowledge (*pramiti*), and once such knowledge has arisen, the practical activity of rejection and so forth proceeds with respect to them. The cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is the self (*ātman*), because it is the substratum of consciousness. Valid knowledge (*pramiti*) is the cognition whose objects are substance and the other categories; when indeterminate knowledge of universals and particulars (*nirvikalpa-sāmānya-viśeṣa-jñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then determinate cognition of substance and the other categories is the valid knowledge—this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Is not even the cognition of a universal and a particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-jñāna*), being of the nature of a valid cognition (*pramā*) and consisting in the apprehension of an object, [already] non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)? Therefore, what is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its arising? To this he says: "In the arising of the cognition of a universal and a particular, perception is merely undifferentiated observation (*avibhakta-ālocana-mātra*). It is called "observation" (*ālocana*) because one observes by means of it; it is "merely" that, namely, the contact between the sense organ and the object (*indriya-artha-sannikarṣa*). "Undifferentiated" (*avibhakta*) means simple, that is to say, independent of [any further] cognition.

In the production of the cognition of a universal-cum-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣajñāna*), the sense-object contact (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as it is a cause of valid knowledge; however, it is not so in isolation, but rather by way of being an auxiliary to the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*). But in the production of the cognition of a universal-cum-particular, it is independent of [any prior] cognition and is indeed isolated—this is the intended meaning. To provide the justification for the claim that here "mere sense-object contact" is the means of valid cognition and not the cognition itself, he says: "Not in that... (*na tasmin...*).

Regarding the cognition of a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) and a qualified (viśeṣya), there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in the form of a cognition; for the cognition of the qualifier is not itself a result of cognition, as it lacks the status of being a fruit of knowledge. Indeed, the cognition of the qualified is the fruit of the cognition of the qualifier, whereas the cognition of the qualifier is not the fruit of another cognition, because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (anavasthā). Therefore, the meaning is that regarding the cognition of the qualifier, the mere contact between the sense organ and its object (indriyārthasannikarṣa) alone is the means of valid cognition.

When non-conceptual knowledge of the universal and the particular is the result, then the contact between the sense organ and the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); when the knowledge of the qualified object is the result, then the observation of the universal and the particular is the means of valid cognition—this much has been stated.

Now, since cognitions such as "destruction" and so forth are the results, he states that the cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣyajñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), saying: "Or else... In all objects, due to the contact of four [factors], the mention of "four" is for the sake of illustration. Whether from the contact of two or three factors, that cognition which arises—being non-erroneous (i.e., free from doubt and misconception), non-verbalizable (*avyapadeśya*, meaning not produced by verbal designation, i.e., not generated by words)—is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Doubt, indeed, by presenting an object through its two unstable properties and then leading one to a subject that possesses only one stable property, is false according to its own determination; thus it is excluded by the term "non-false" (*avitatha*). [p.464] For one who is untrained, when the eye is functioning toward a nearby object, the cognition "this is a cow" that arises immediately after hearing a word has the sense organ as its cause as well; otherwise, the perception of specific features such as lines and markings would be impossible.

And that [cognition] is not perception, because it is the sound itself, occurring immediately thereafter, that is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for its production, while the sense organ merely serves as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). Nevertheless, when questioned, one designates it by saying, "This was named by him," but one does not express it thus: "I have perceived this cow through perception. It is for the purpose of excluding such [designation] that the term "non-designatable" (*avyapadeśyam*) is stated.

Valid cognition (*pramiti*) is the perception of qualities, defects, or neutrality. Perception of qualities is the knowledge that something is to be accepted; perception of defects is the knowledge that something is to be rejected; and perception of neutrality is the knowledge that something is neither to be rejected nor accepted—this is valid cognition. This occurs because, once there is an awareness of the essential nature of an object, there arises a recollection of its utility and so forth. When the determination of a thing as a means to pleasure and so on exists, the resulting knowledge of it as something to be accepted becomes the very fruit of the awareness of the object’s essential nature, since the recollections of pleasure and so on function as intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*). As it has been said: "That which occurs in the interval is the operation of the causal factor (*kāraka*)."

Others, however, say this: the cognition that something is a means to pleasure is the perception of its qualities (*guṇadarśana*), and the cognition that it is to be acquired (*upādeyatva*) is that very same thing. The cognition that something is a means to suffering is the perception of its defects (*doṣadarśana*), and the cognition that it is to be abandoned (*heyatva*) is that very same thing. Furthermore, the cognition that "this is neither a means to pleasure nor a means to suffering" is the perception of neutrality (*mādhyasthyadarśana*), and the cognition of indifference (*upekṣājñāna*) is also that very same thing.

All of this is the fruit of perception aided by the proficiency of practice; for one who possesses such proficiency, it arises from the mere apprehension of the nature of the object itself, without depending on the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and because it appears as immediate even to one who has not mentally synthesized the logical mark (*liṅga*).
[From the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*:
Inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika*) is that which is produced from the observation of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

*Nyāyakandalī* [174] [pp. 465–466]: That which arises from the perception of a mark (*liṅga*) is "inferential" (*laiṅgika*). The word "perception" (*darśana*) here denotes apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and not specifically visual cognition, because inference based on what has been inferred (*anumitānumāna*) is also possible. From the perception of a mark, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) having the mark as its object is produced; however, this is not included [in the definition], because it is qualified by the heading of "cognition" (*buddhi*). By the prefix *sam-*, which expresses the sense of "correctly," doubt, error, and memory are excluded.

The meaning of the sentence is that inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika*) arises correctly from the perception and cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, the production of such correct cognition is due to its being a determiner of the object as it truly is (*yathārthaparicchedaka*), because the capacity to determine an object as it truly is is the inherent nature (*kuladharma*) of all cognitions. As for doubt and error, they do not determine the object in the way that it actually exists. We shall explain later that even memory does not determine an object, because it is dependent upon prior experience.

Others, however, eliminate doubt and error by means of the context of knowledge (*vidyā*). And they repeat the phrase, "For that arises with respect to categories such as substance," in order to exclude memory (*smṛti*) which is not born of an object. That is incorrect; for when a meaning is obtainable from the sentence itself, there is no need to rely on the context. Furthermore, because it is not born of an object, if memory were excluded, it would follow that inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*), which has past and future objects, would also be excluded. [175] [p.466] As for the mark (*liṅga*), moreover—
That which is connected with the object of inference, which is well-known to exist where that [object] exists,
and which is absolutely absent when that [object] is absent— that is the mark (liṅga) which brings about inference.

The *Nyāyakandalī* [175] [pp. 466–467] states the definition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) as follows: "The logical mark, moreover... The object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*) one wishes to demonstrate. The meaning is that the logical mark is that which is connected with and resides in that [substratum]. Just as a logical mark residing in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is nonetheless present in the dissimilar class, so too a logical mark residing in only a portion of the subject (*pakṣa*) is indeed connected with the object to be inferred.

If it is argued that, consequently, even the reason "the four kinds of atoms are impermanent because they possess odor" would incur the fallacy of being unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), we say no, because of the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*). That object which is the locus of the exclusion of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Since the exclusion of the probandum and the probans does not occur in their aggregate, but rather occurs in each individually, each one alone constitutes the counter-example.

A "subject" (pakṣa), however, is that wherein the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) is intended by the proponent (vādin) to be established. Now, the proponent does not intend to establish impermanence in a single earthly atom, but rather in all four types of atoms; thus, since the subject is established as being only the collection [of atoms], even the "partially unestablished" (bhāgāsiddha) fallacy is excluded, because there is no connection with the object of inference (anumeya) [in the individual parts]. And it is well known that [the reason] is concomitant with that [subject].

The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), because it is appropriate and because it is that which is to be established. "Established" (*prasiddha*) means well-known in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), which is that in which that [property] is present—that is, in which the property to be proven is present; this excludes the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reasons. "And it does not exist at all in its absence" (*tadabhāve ca nāsty eva*): here too, "that" refers specifically to the property to be proven; since it does not exist at all in the absence of that property to be proven—and not merely in one part of it—it excludes the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason. That mark (*liṅga*) is the inferential indicator, the cognizer of the object of inference (*anumeya*). —Praśastapādabhāṣya [176–177], p. 468.
Kāśyapa stated that a mark which is contrary to this— whether by one or both [of these criteria]— is a non-reason (*aliṅga*), being contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful.

That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred (anumeya) in a particular place or at a particular time, which is well-known to exist in all or some other instance possessing the property to be inferred, and which is known through valid means of cognition to be entirely absent in every instance contrary to the object to be inferred—that alone becomes the mark (liṅga) that leads to the inference of an unestablished object.
*Nyāyakandalī* [176] [pp. 468–472]

Having explained the valid mark (*liṅga*), he explains the fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) with the words: "that which is the opposite of this. That which is the opposite of the aforementioned mark—lacking one or two of the characteristics of a valid mark, being contradictory (*viruddha*), unestablished (*asiddha*), or doubtful (*sandigdha*)—Kaśyapa’s son declared to be a non-mark (*aliṅga*), meaning it does not establish the object to be inferred (*anumeya*). The unestablished lacks [the property] in the object to be inferred, while the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is not excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); thus, these two are the opposites of one characteristic of a valid mark.
It is not present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and is not excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); thus, it is devoid of both characteristics of a valid logical mark (*liṅga*).

He explains the meaning of the verse, "that which is connected with the object of inference," as follows: "yadanumeyena" (that which, by the object of inference). That which is concomitant—that is, connected—with the object of inference, namely the subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis, either in a particular place or at a particular time; and which is established—known through a means of valid cognition—in another instance that possesses the property to be inferred, whether in its entirety or in part, i.e., in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); and which is absolutely non-existent according to valid cognition in every case where the object is the opposite of the object of inference, i.e., in the domain where the property to be proven is excluded—that [is the logical reason] for one whose object is not otherwise established.

The logical mark (*liṅga*) is that which causes the inference of a property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), a property not yet cognized in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). It is stated—"concomitant in a particular place or at a particular time"—in order to demonstrate that the capacity to produce cognition belongs only to that mark which is perceived in the subject of the thesis within the same spatial or temporal limits as those in which its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the property to be proven has been demonstrated in the instance (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

The phrase "established in all [of the subject] or in a part [of it]" is stated for the purpose of showing that even a reason that exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) can function as a valid reason, just like one that pervades all similar instances. Conversely, the phrase "non-existent in all [of the dissimilar instances]" is used to illuminate that even a reason that exists in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) lacks the status of a valid reason, just like one that pervades all dissimilar instances.

Some proponents say this: it is not necessary that a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily be accepted; for even from the statement, "Wherever this [the probandum] is absent, there this [the probans] is also absent," the exclusion of the probans can be understood through the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*). And thus, their own text states: "Therefore, in the case of a dissimilar instance, a locus is not necessarily required here."
"Because even in the absence of that [reason], it is understood from the statement 'it is not there'.

To exclude that [over-extension], he says "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*). The meaning is: that which is known through valid cognition to be non-existent in the case of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparīta*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*), but not by mere word alone. For if mere assertion devoid of valid cognition were possible everywhere, it would follow that the distinction between a valid reason and a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) could not be established. If it is argued: "This definition of a logical mark is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), because it applies to the *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced) and the *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (the mistimed) as well"?

Regarding this, someone says: *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced) and *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (the mistimed) are both included within the *anaikāntika* (inconclusive). This is because *prakaraṇasama* occurs when the subject of the thesis is doubtful with respect to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), whereas *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* operates when the counter-example is certain.

And likewise, the *prakaraṇasama* (the "equivalent to the point at issue") is defined as: "That which is put forward for the sake of a decision, on account of which there is deliberation regarding the point at issue (*prakaraṇa*), is the *prakaraṇasama*. Here, "point at issue" (*prakaraṇa*) refers to the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*), as they are "undertaken" (*prakriyete*) or introduced. The "deliberation" (*cintā*) is the investigation (*vicāra*) concerning them. That [reason] which is adduced for the sake of a decision, because it leaves both sides equal, is the *prakaraṇasama*; it is not capable of determining either one of the two sides.

Just as when there is doubt regarding the permanence or impermanence of sound—due to the non-perception of the properties of permanence [in the case of "sound is permanent because the properties of impermanence are not perceived"] or the non-perception of the properties of impermanence [in the case of "sound is impermanent because the properties of permanence are not perceived"]—an investigation arises; for once one of the two properties is apprehended, the investigation ceases because the determination of the truth has been reached.

In that context, the non-perception of the properties of permanence is taught for the purpose of ascertaining permanence, while the non-perception of the properties of impermanence is taught for the purpose of ascertaining impermanence. However, a reason that does not transcend its counter-position—the non-perception of the properties of permanence—is not capable of leading to a definitive conclusion because it is obstructed by that very counter-position. Furthermore, when this [reason] occurs in a subject (*dharmin*) where a counter-position is possible, it is not restricted to one side; thus, it is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). Likewise, a reason stated when the time has passed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) is also inconclusive, because "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) exists in fire, which is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), even though its heat is ascertained by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This is incorrect. If the probans is a means of cognition merely by virtue of its pervading the subject (*pakṣa*), its presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), then let it be granted that there may be the possibility of a counter-argument regarding the property-bearer to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*); nevertheless, the probandum must still be established by the "neutralized" reason (*prakaraṇasama*) through its own inherent capacity.

If, on the other hand, one is unable to establish [the probandum] because it is beset by a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) and doubt, then the capacity to convey [the conclusion] does not reside in the mere possession of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*). Therefore, the characteristic of "having no counter-argument" (*asatpratipakṣatva*) must also be accepted as another essential feature; for when a counter-argument exists, there is an absence of the status of being a valid reason (*hetu*), whereas when it does not exist, that status is present. The same should be said regarding a reason that is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

If being a logical mark (*liṅga*) were based merely on the three-fold form (*trairūpya*), then since non-heat exists in fire precisely because of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), how could there be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*)? If, however, despite its being produced, non-heat does not exist in fire because heat is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, then, since there is no contradiction with direct perception, the demonstration [of the mark] would not contradict it; thus, another characteristic (*rūpa*), namely "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), must also be adopted.

Therefore, it is stated otherwise: the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is a synonym for the "probandum" (*sādhya*); and that which is capable of being proven becomes the probandum. However, an object for which a counter-argument is possible is not capable of being proven, because a real entity cannot possess two contradictory forms; thus, this [type of reason] is indeed a "property not belonging to the subject" (*apakṣadharma*). Likewise, even that which is contradicted by perception and so forth does not constitute a valid subject, because what is already established in one form cannot be proven in another form.

Therefore, both the *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized by counter-argument) and the *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed) fallacies are already refuted by the very statement "that which is connected with the object of inference," because they rely upon fallacious objects of inference (*anumeyābhāsa*).
— *Nyāyakandalī* [177] [pp. 473–476]

But even so, this [definition] lacks the defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*) because it is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). For there are three kinds of logical reasons (*hetu*): the positive (*anvayin*), the negative (*vyatirekin*), and the positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*). Among these, the positive reason is as follows: "The particular (*viśeṣa*) is denotable (*abhidheya*), because it is cognizable (*prameyatvāt*), like the universal (*sāmānya*). For in this case, everything other than the subject (*pakṣa*)—including both existent and non-existent varieties—is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), because for any cognizer, in relation to any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no such thing as that which is undenotable or uncognizable.

And that which is inexpressible and unmeasurable for a mere person is simply non-existent, like the horn of a horse; nor can it be either a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Furthermore, whatever exists is entirely a similar instance, and in the absence of such [an existent], [the reason] does not exist at all; thus, the definition is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). If it is argued that, due to the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it is simply non-probative (*agamaka*), we say no, because there is no deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

In the case of the principle that "the establishment of one thing follows from the existence of another," positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the cause; however, the perception of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding that concomitance serves as its exception. Indeed, there exists a positive concomitance between the state of being cognizable (*prameyatva*) and the state of being nameable (*abhidheyatva*), because nameability is observed in every instance of the cognizable.

Nor is any deviation observed, nor does even the suspicion of it arise; for whatever object of exclusion one brings to the mind and desires to state to another, all of that necessarily possesses the properties of being knowable (*prameyatva*) and nameable (*abhidheyatva*). Furthermore, there is no distinction such that non-deviation from the contrary (*vipakṣa*) is the cause [of validity] while the absence of a contrary is not. Therefore, knowability implies nameability. And the negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) is as follows: "The living body possesses a self, because it possesses breath and so forth."

Any instance other than this subject (pakṣa) is indeed the counter-example (vipakṣa); nevertheless, the status of [the reason] as a logical mark (hetu) remains because it is not deviant with respect to its connection with the opposite [of the probandum]. The pervasion (vyāpti) of "selflessness" by "being devoid of breath and so forth" has been removed from jars and the like, and the absence of "being devoid of breath and so forth" is perceived in the living body. Through that perception, there is an inference of the removal of selflessness, which is pervaded by that [absence].

Now, you might think: "If an object has not been apprehended, its exclusion cannot be cognized either, because negation has affirmation as its domain. And since the self (*ātman*) is not apprehended anywhere, how can there be a cognition of its exclusion from jars and other things? This is incorrect. For, according to the opponent who maintains that all things are devoid of self (*nairātmya*), the exclusion of the self from jars and so forth is already established.

Once it has been established that for oneself as well, there is a causal relationship between the self and its effects—such as cognition and so forth—within living bodies, then, by the exclusion of cognition and the like from jars and other such objects, it is established that those objects lack a specific connection with the self capable of producing them. This is just as, in the absence of smoke, the absence of fire—which is otherwise incapable of producing it—is established in certain places. If this is so, then the self is indeed already established in living bodies, because the perception of a relation is impossible without the prior perception of the related entities.

Consequently, the negative inference (*vyatirekī-anumāna*) would be redundant, because an instrument cannot function as an instrument when its object has already been accomplished. This is not so, because that which is established for oneself but unestablished for another is precisely what is to be proven (*sādhya*). Nor is there any restrictive reason to maintain that positive concomitance (*anvaya-avyabhicāra*) alone establishes [the probandum] while negative concomitance (*vyatireka-avyabhicāra*) does not. Therefore, since even a negative reason can be a valid *hetu*, the definition "that which is well-known and exists in what is concomitant with it" is underinclusive. On this point, some say that by means of what is established in their own school (*samānatantra*), both the purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) and the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) types are included.

Others, however, describe the definition as both individual and collective: "Connected with the object of inference (*anumeya*), well-known, and present in what is similar to it"—this is the definition of the positive (*anvayin*) reason. "Connected with the object of inference and absolutely absent in its opposite"—this is the definition of the negative (*vyatirekin*) reason. The collective definition belongs to the positive-negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*) reason. The general definition for all three is their status as means of proving the probandum (*sādhyasādhanatva*), just as the general definition of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is their capacity to determine an object as it truly is. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [178] [p.476]

However, that which deviates from one or two of the three characteristics of the mark as previously described does not serve as a mark for the apprehension of the object to be inferred. This very point is stated by the author of the Sūtras: "That which is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), non-existent (*asan*), or doubtful (*sandigdha*) is not a valid indicator (*anapadeśa*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.15).
*Nyāyakandalī* [178] [pp. 476–477]

He explains the meaning of the second verse—that which is contrary to this [is not a valid reason]—as follows: "[But that which is contrary to the aforementioned three-fold mark by one property or by two properties does not constitute a mark for the comprehension of the object to be inferred; this is precisely what the author of the Sūtras states: 'That which is unestablished, non-existent, and doubtful is not a probans' (A 1.2.4). Regarding the term *anapadeśa*: it means that which is not a *apadeśa*, i.e., a reason (*hetu*); thus, *anapadeśa* means "non-reason" (*ahetu*).

"Unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) includes both the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reasons, because they lack establishment in connection with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). "Non-existent" (*asan*) is the inclusion of the unestablished (*asiddha*) reason; for although it may be established in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) along with the property to be proven, it is not a valid reason because it does not occur in the subject (*dharmin*). "Doubtful" (*sandigdha*) is a designation for the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason.

For when that [reason] is observed in the subject (*dharmī*), it remains doubtful whether it is accompanied by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) or devoid of it; it cannot, however, establish one specific property. Because it is seen in both ways, it is not a valid reason (*ahetu*). As for the positive concomitance (*vidhi*), however: where there is smoke, there is fire; and in the absence of fire, smoke does not occur. For one who has established this convention, upon seeing smoke without doubt, there follows the recollection of the constant association (*sāhacarya*), and immediately thereafter, the ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) of fire occurs. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [179–181], p. 477.
*Nyāyakandalī* [179] [pp. 477–478]:

For one who lacks the knowledge that "this is invariably concomitant with that," there exists no status as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for a property (*dharma*), even if it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), within the subject (*dharmin*). To show that, for this reason, the recollection of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-smaraṇa*) is the means for the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), he says: "But the affirmation... (*vidhis tu*).

The "method" (vidhi), however, refers to the manner in which the object of inference is cognized: namely, "where there is smoke, there is fire; in the absence of fire, smoke does not occur. Thus, for a person who has established the convention and recognized the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), upon seeing smoke without doubt—through the cognition that "this is indeed smoke and not vapor or the like"—and through the recollection of its coexistence, he recalls that "where there is smoke, there is fire. From this recollection, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of fire arises, and immediately thereafter, the inference of fire occurs.

[Objection: But in this case, would not a second consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) fail to be obtained? [Reply: It was not obtained; for we have no need for it, since the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is established by the perception of the mark and the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) alone. Nor does it follow that the cognition of the object to be inferred would be indeterminate with respect to direction and location because it occurs immediately after recollection, for the perception of the mark serves as its regulator. Nor is the application (*upanaya*) redundant, because in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), it is introduced in order to establish the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), which has not been established by the other members of the syllogism. (Nyāyakandalī [180], pp. 479–485)
Moreover, sir! What is this so-called "inseparable connection" (avinābhāva)? It is non-deviation (avyabhicāra). From what does it arise?

The Buddhists [hold that concomitance] is due to identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). A fortuitous relationship may or may not exist; thus, there would be no cause for its necessity. In that case, even if there is observation in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and non-observation in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), the absence of deviation (*avyabhicāra*) cannot be known, because the suspicion of the reason's occurrence in the dissimilar class has not been eliminated. However, when the fact of being produced from that (*tadutpatti*) is ascertained, the suspicion is removed, since it is impossible for an effect to acquire its own nature without its cause.

The proof for the arising and destruction of that [effect] as a causal indicator (*kāryahetu*) is established through five types of perception and non-perception: (1) the non-perception of the effect prior to its arising; (2) the perception [of the effect] when the cause is perceived; (3) the subsequent non-perception of the perceived [effect] due to the non-perception of the cause. Thus, there are two non-perceptions and one perception regarding the effect, and perception and non-perception regarding the cause.

Thus, through five types of perception and non-perception, it is ascertained that smoke exists only when fire exists and is absent when it is absent. This very fact—that its existence occurs only when that [cause] exists and its absence occurs when it does not—is what constitutes the effect-nature (*kāryatva*) of an effect; and by means of the cognition of identity (*tādātmya*), the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is also ascertained. For if an entity were to deviate from its own nature (*svabhāva*), it would follow that it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).

The ascertainment of identity (*tādātmya*) is established through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). However, when no such subverting proof operates, even if coexistence is observed hundreds of times, who can prevent the doubt that "this might [nevertheless] exist in the counter-example"?
As it has been said:
"Either from the relation of cause and effect, or from an essential nature (*svabhāva*) that acts as a restrictor..."

"The rule of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is due to the observation of the causal relation or the restrictive nature (svabhāva), not from its observation in the similar class (sapakṣa) or its non-observation in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).

(PV I 33) The restriction of inseparable connection is established by the restrictive factor of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or by the restrictive factor of essential identity (*svabhāva*); it is not [established] by observation in the similar class and non-observation in the dissimilar class.

To this it is replied: Is it the case that wherever there is identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*); or rather, that wherever there is non-deviation, there is identity and causality? The first alternative is not tenable, because even when causality exists, the property of being earthen (*pārthivatva*) and so forth—which is a property of smoke—deviates from fire; and even when identity exists, the property of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) deviates from the *śiṃśapā*. If, on the other hand, it is held that wherever there is non-deviation, there is identity and causality, then it is only once non-deviation is established that those two possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum].

If this is so, let non-deviation alone be the indicator; what is the use of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)? For even an effect does not indicate [its cause] simply by virtue of being an effect, nor does an essential nature indicate [itself] simply by virtue of being an essential nature; rather, it is that which is non-deviant from it. Thus, non-deviation alone is the cause for being an indicator, not identity and causality, because of their deviation. Furthermore, such a position does not stand to reason: smoke is produced by fire, but its qualities such as earthiness (*pārthivatva*) and so forth are not. This is because a real entity (*vastu*) is partless (*nirbhāga*).

Nor is this perceived: that the *śiṃśapā* is of the nature of a tree, yet the tree is not of the nature of the *śiṃśapā*, because it also possesses the quality of being a *dhava*, *khadira*, and so forth; for there is no difference between the two.

If "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatā*), which is common to *dhava* trees and others, is not identical with "śiṃśapā-ness" (*śiṃśapātva*), then these two cannot be one, because difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) is the defining characteristic of difference. If, however, there were non-difference, then just as tree-ness is common to all trees, so too would śiṃśapā-ness be common to all. Furthermore, the establishment of the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is not tenable if there is identity (*tādātmya*), since that relationship depends upon difference. If tree-ness is not apprehended when śiṃśapā-ness is being apprehended, where is the identity? And if it is already apprehended, what is the use of inference?

Now it is said: The subject (*dharmī*) as it exists, its *śiṃśapā*-ness, and its tree-ness—these three are of one and the same nature. Therefore, when that subject is apprehended, tree-ness is necessarily apprehended just like *śiṃśapā*-ness. As it has been stated: "Therefore, when an entity is perceived, all its qualities are indeed perceived.
What other part could there be that is not seen, which would need to be examined by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*)? (PV I.45)

If, on the contrary, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) of "śiṃśapā" has arisen but not a conceptual cognition of "tree," that [absence of the tree-exclusion] is not brought forward by the conceptual cognition of "śiṃśapā"—which arises from the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the word "śiṃśapā" due to the fault of the absence of the recollection of the word "tree," and which terminates in the exclusion of non-śiṃśapās—because that would entail the consequence that all conceptual cognitions are synonyms. Furthermore, there is no relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) between these two exclusions because they are not distinct. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Oh, what supreme skill do the learned possess in connecting the preceding with the following! [p.484] Identity is the seed of inference; yet, there is a mutual difference between the two exclusions (vyāvṛtti) that serve as the probandum and the probans. What kind of sorcery is this? If it is argued: "There is identity between a tree and a *śiṃśapā*, and although there is a difference between the exclusion of non-trees and the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās*—which are determined as having that very nature—there is identity according to how they are determined," then, once that identity is established, by means of the exclusion of non-*śiṃśapās*...

The exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtti*) is to be determined (*adhyavaseyā*) in the subject (*dharmī*); and once that exclusion of non-trees has been determined therein, the establishment of identity (*tādātmyasiddhi*) occurs according to that determination—thus there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayadoṣa*). If it is argued that at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the identity of the two exclusions is established because they are determined as having a single nature, even so, the non-difference between these two is merely conceptual (*kālpnika*). If inference were to proceed even through the superimposition of conceptual construction, then nothing at all would be without a cause.

Even in the case of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), since they are determined as having a single nature, their identity exists according to that determination. If it is argued that because there is no exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), knowability lacks identity with impermanence—this is true; indeed, real identity does not exist. However, identity superimposed by conceptual construction certainly does exist, and it is precisely this that you yourselves have established as the friend of the arising of inference. Therefore, the lack of exclusion from the dissimilar class is equivalent to non-existence.

Furthermore, for that [reason] whose cognition of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpāda*) occurs through the cognition of the absence of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the cognition of its own absence also arises from the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*). And since non-perception is included within inference, it proceeds either through the cognition of identity with its own probandum—the absence of the reason in the counter-example—or through the cognition of origination from that. For that [non-perception] as well, the ascertainment of identity and origination with its own probandum occurs through the cognition of the absence of its occurrence in the counter-example.

Furthermore, the cognition of that non-existence would depend on another non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because of the accepted principle that every negation has non-apprehension as its object. Consequently, due to the resulting infinite regress, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains unestablished; and since identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpāda*) are thus unestablished, neither essential nature (*svabhāva*) nor effect (*kārya*) can serve as a logical reason (*hetu*). Moreover, even in the absence of identity or causality, the relationship between the indicator (*gamaka*) and the indicated (*gamya*) is perceived between the rising of Kṛttikā and the setting of Rohiṇī. Therefore, the claim that "the rule [of concomitance] arises either from the relation of cause and effect or from essential nature" is an unconsidered statement.
*Nyāyakandalī* [181] [pp. 486–490]:

For the relation of some thing with another is necessarily determined by its very nature (*svabhāva*), because it is unconditional (*nirupādhika*). A relation produced by an external condition (*upādhi*) ceases when that condition is removed, but not one that is natural. If the relation of smoke with fire were produced by an external condition, then those conditions would have to be perceived—just as the study [of students] is perceived through the proximity of pupils and teachers. Indeed, there is no reason why the conditions for the relation between fire and smoke, which are repeatedly observed together, should remain unperceived.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) of a perceived object must necessarily be unperceived. For even if those conditions were invariably concomitant with the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the object, the proof of non-deviation would still hold, because the relation established by them would likewise endure as long as the substance exists. If, on the other hand, they are adventitious, then their causes too would have to be perceived; yet to claim that all these adventitious conditions and their causes are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is an excessively cumbersome hypothesis.

And that smoke which lacks limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) might perhaps be perceived independently, just as fire—which is associated with smoke produced by the adjunct of wet fuel—is observed to be smokeless when it has dry fuel as its dominant condition (*adhipatya*). But in no other instance of consciousness does smoke ever appear without fire.

Therefore, when the non-existence of conditions (*upādhi*) that meet the criteria for perception is cognized due to their non-perception, and when it is ascertained that they are not causes because of their deviation (*vyabhicāra*) upon repeated observations of perceived specific locations, times, fuels, and states, there follows the frequent observation of the absence of conditions through the exclusion of all particularities of place, time, and so forth.

By means of the final perception—which, assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from the observation of coexistence and which has eliminated any suspicion of a counter-example—one ascertains the coexistence of the smoke-universal with the fire-universal as being dependent solely upon their own intrinsic nature; thus, one determines the necessary rule (*niyama*) that "this is invariably concomitant with that.

Even though concomitance is apprehended at the first sight, nevertheless, there is no apprehension of the rule (niyama). For mere concomitance is not the rule; rather, it is concomitance that is unconditional (*nirupādhika*). And its unconditionality is to be determined through the practice of repeated observation; thus, by means of a conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) born from the power of apprehending concomitance repeatedly, that [rule] is ascertained.

By this, the objection that—since perception has only existing things as its object—how can there be a grasping of the rule (*niyama*) regarding individual instances that are past or future, is answered. For we do not claim that the grasping of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is restricted to particulars. Rather, when the grasping of pervasion occurs through the universal (*sāmānya*), setting aside the particulars, then the cognition is everywhere free from doubt, because that [universal] is of one and the same form in all cases. Are individuals not included at all in the pervasion? Who indeed says they are not included?

However, this is in a general form, not in a specific one. For this very reason, one who infers fire merely through the cognition of smoke pursues that fire alone and does not attend to its specific qualities.

But if, even when the rule is ascertained everywhere in a general way, a groundless doubt is still entertained, then in your own position as well, what would prevent the operation of inference based on the suspicion of the absence of that relation in instances of fire and smoke separated by space and time—even though the causal relationship has been grasped through perception in those cases where they were observed?

Now it is said: the causal relation is determined through repeated observation, because the suspicion that it might be produced by some adventitious condition (*upādhi*) is not removed by a single observation. Furthermore, repeated observation has universals as its object, since individual momentary entities cannot be observed again and again.

If it is argued that, because the universal is one, the causal relationship—which has as its object the universal that is excluded from both non-fire and non-smoke—is determined once in one instance, it becomes determined everywhere; [we reply: why does this very same rule, which we also determine in all cases, not please you? Furthermore, for you, the causal relationship is not within the range of perception by way of a universal, because according to your experience it is not a real entity (*avastu*), whereas the individuals are of such a nature.

All of these [universals] would have to be apprehended through non-perception. Nor is it logical that there should be a mental synthesis (*saṃkalana*) of past and future individuals, because if the mind possessed independence regarding external objects, it would follow that the blind, the deaf, and others would not exist. Furthermore, if the determination of the causal relationship occurs only with respect to perceived individuals, then inference could not arise regarding unperceived ones, because they are different from those. Moreover, it is not tenable for individuals themselves to stand in the relation of the probandum and the probans, because they lack mutual invariable concomitance (*anvaya*).

Nor can there be a subsumption of these [particulars] under a single universal, because there is no relationship between a real entity (*vastu*) and a non-entity (*avastu*), and because if that which is unrelated were to effect subsumption, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, we do not know what object the determination of the production of that [perception]—which is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—could have, from which the operation of inference (*anumāna*) might proceed.
In this way, in all cases, that which is invariably concomitant with space or time is the mark (*liṅga*) of the other.

In the treatise (*śāstra*), the mention of *kārya* and so forth is made for the purpose of illustration (*vidarśanārtha*) and not for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*). Why? Because we observe exceptions (*vyatireka*). For example: the *adhvaryu* priest’s utterance of "Oṃ, announce! is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *hotṛ* priest who is spatially separated; the rising of the moon is [the mark] of the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lotuses; and the clarity of the water in autumn is [the mark] of the rising of the star Agastya. All such cases are established by the mere statement of a relationship (*sambandhamātra*) in the sūtra: "This belongs to that" (*asyedam*, Vaiśeṣika-sūtra 9.2.1). *Nyāyakandalī* [182] [pp. 491–494]

Thus, in all cases, that which is invariably concomitant with another—whether by way of place (*deśa*) or time (*kāla*)—is the mark (*liṅga*) of the other. For example, smoke is the mark of fire. Likewise, that which is invariably concomitant with a place or invariably concomitant with a time is the mark of the other property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). An example of invariable concomitance by place is the guarding of barley fields by men who are goldsmiths in Kaśmīra, which is the mark of the sprouting of *kemā* shoots among the barley stalks. An example of invariable concomitance by time is the sound of the victory drums in the palace of the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, which is the mark of the king’s awakening. [p. 492]

If inferential capacity were based merely on the inseparable connection of place and time, would this not contradict the Sūtra? For the Sūtra states: "The inferential [cognition] arises from: 'this is the effect of that,' 'this is the cause of that,' 'this is conjoined with that,' 'this is contradictory to that,' and 'this is inherent in that. To this, he replies: "In the treatise, the mention of 'effect' and so forth is made for the purpose of illustration, not for the purpose of restriction. The inclusion of the sun and other examples under the phrase "this is of that" is intended as an illustration of logical marks (*liṅga*), but it is not intended as a restriction that there are only these many types of logical marks. He asks: "How is this so? and provides the answer: "Why? (kasmāt).

He states the answer: "Because of the observation of its absence" (*vyatirekadarśanāt*). Since inference is observed even in the absence of an effect and so forth, the aphorism does not have the purpose of restriction. He demonstrates where there is an absence of effects and so forth: for example, the *oṃ* uttered by the Adhvaryu priest is a mark (*liṅga*) of the Hotṛ priest who is separated [from him].

The *adhvaryu* causes the *hotṛ* to hear the call "Oṃ," and no one else. For one who has previously understood this, upon perceiving the *adhvaryu* uttering "Oṃ" while the *hotṛ* is concealed by a wall or other obstruction, there arises the inference that the *hotṛ* is also present there. Furthermore, the *adhvaryu* is neither the effect, nor the cause, nor the conjoined (*saṃyogin*), nor the contradictory (*virodhin*), nor the inherent (*samavāyin*) of the *hotṛ*; such is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

He states another example: "The rising of the moon [is the sign] of the ocean's swelling," and so forth. When one has understood the rule that when the moon rises, the ocean swells and the night-lotuses (*kumuda*) blossom, for such a person the rising of the moon would be the *liṅga* (logical mark) of both the ocean's swelling and the blossoming of the night-lotuses. Yet, the rising of the moon is not the effect (*kārya*) of either the ocean's swelling or the blossoming of the night-lotuses.

For the rising of the moon is its conjunction with a specific location, and that is the effect of the moon's own motion, not caused by the swelling of the ocean and so forth. Nor is this [rising] the cause of the ocean’s swelling, nor of the blooming of the night-lotuses; for the swelling characterized by surging waves and the blooming characterized by the mutual separation of petals are produced by motions dependent on causes present at that very time—this is what must be said. Likewise, the clarity of the water in autumn is [the effect] of the rising of Agastya.
The clarity (*prasāda*) of water is its purity; this, being perceived in autumn, is the mark (*liṅga*) of the rising of the star Agastya, and not at other times, because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

If there were a mark distinct from effects and so forth, then the definition would be deficient here, because it would fail to encompass all marks. Therefore, he says: "All such [marks] are established by the expression 'this belongs to that' (*asyedam*), which denotes mere relation. Whatever mark is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*)—such as the *adhvaryu* priest making the announcement (*oṃ śrāvayan*)—all that is established and included by the phrase "this belongs to that," which expresses mere relation.

Anticipating the objection that "one thing being the mark of another thing" is not tenable because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*), the author of the Sūtras stated: "This is the mark of this. Although there is no difference in their being distinct entities, by specifying that "this belongs to this probandum," he establishes that "this is the mark of this" and not of everything; thus, he demonstrates that the status of being a mark belongs generally to that which is related [to the specific object].

It has been stated that whatever is inseparably connected with another by way of place, time, and so forth, is the *liṅga* (inferential mark) of that [other]. For only that which is not deviant (*avyabhicārin*) from something is its [mark]; what is deviant from it is not its [mark], because it exists elsewhere as well. Furthermore, O sir! Is there no relationship such as "this is the effect of that"? We say: no. Then for what purpose is the mention of "effect" and so forth? It was said: for the sake of illustration (*nidarśana*).

For it is necessary that, having established the basis in an illustrative example for the sake of a student, some non-deviant mark (*liṅga*) must be shown; thus, "effect" (*kārya*) and so forth are cited in the Sūtra. However, the meaning is not that these alone are the marks.
[Praśastapādabhāṣya 183] [p.495] That [inference], moreover, is of two kinds: the perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and the generally perceived (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Among these, *dṛṣṭa* (perceived) inference occurs when there is no difference in genus (*jāti*) between the known instance and the object to be proven (*sādhya*). For example, having perceived a dewlap on a cow, one recognizes it as a cow upon seeing a dewlap alone in another place. *Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference from general observation) occurs when there is an absolute difference in genus between the known instance and the object to be proven; it proceeds from the persistence of a commonality between the mark (*liṅga*) and the property to be inferred (*anumeya-dharma*). For example, having observed that the activities of farmers, merchants, and princes are fruitful, one infers a fruit for those belonging to the [four] castes and [four] stages of life who act even without aiming at a visible purpose.

The *Nyāyakandalī* [183] [pp. 495–497] explains the division: "That, however, is of two kinds: the perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and the generally perceived (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). The word 'nu' is for the sake of restriction. That inference is of exactly two kinds: one is the perceived, and the other is the generally perceived."

Among those two, *dṛṣṭa* (perceived) inference is that which occurs when there is no absolute difference in genus between the well-known (*prasiddha*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*). When the well-known—the thing previously seen together with the mark (*liṅga*)—and the object to be proven—the thing currently to be inferred—are of an identical genus, the inference that arises is *dṛṣṭa*. For example, having perceived merely the dewlap in a cow, one attains the cognition of a cow in another location.

Previously, because the dewlap was perceived in an individual cow already qualified by the universal "cowness" (*gotvajāti*), there is now likewise an inference of an individual cow qualified by the universal "cowness," provided there is no absolute difference in the universal. This is called "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*). When the universal "cowness" is inferred in another forest from the mere sight of a dewlap—on the grounds that its specific individual (*svalakṣaṇa*) was previously seen in the city—inference based on the persistence of the commonality between the property of the mark (*liṅga*) and the property to be inferred (*anumeya-dharma*) despite an absolute difference in the universals of the well-known instance and the object to be proven is "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

When that which is well-known (*prasiddha*)—that is, perceived together with the mark (*liṅga*)—is the object to be proven (*sādhya*) and the inferable (*anumeya*), and there exists an absolute difference in genus (*atyantajātibheda*) between the two; and when the mark and the property of the inferable (*liṅgānumeyadharma*) have a persistence (*anuvṛtti*) in their respective universals (*sāmānya*), namely the universal of the mark and the universal of the property to be inferred (*liṅgānumeyadharmasāmānya*); then, because of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the universal of the mark with the universal of the object to be proven, the inference that results from this is "inference based on what is observed through generality" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Just as one observes that farmers, merchants, and royal servants possess fruits resulting from their activities, so too is there an inference of fruit for those belonging to the various castes and stages of life who engage in action even without aiming at any visible purpose.

Having observed the fruit of the activity of farmers and others, one infers the fruit of the activity of those belonging to the [four] castes and [four] stages of life (*varṇāśramin*). The fruit of a farmer’s activity is crops and the like; the fruit of the activity of a merchant or a king’s servant is gold, gems, pearls, horses, elephants, and so forth; and the fruit of the activity of those belonging to the castes and stages of life is heaven and the like. Thus, there is an absolute difference in the nature (*jāti*) of these two.
