Nevertheless, the emergence of the inference occurs because the general property of being an activity (*pravṛttitva-sāmānya*) is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) with the general property of having a fruit (*phalavattva-sāmānya*).
For this very reason, this is called *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference from the observation of a general rule), since the rule is perceived through a general property.

Furthermore, regarding the specific result characterized by heaven and so forth which is to be inferred here, the followers of Bṛhaspati (the Cārvākas) maintain that no such rule for this kind of result is observed, since even the engagement of those belonging to the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) has as its sole purpose the mere means of subsistence. To address this, he says: "without aiming at a visible purpose. There certainly exist such persons who, being indeed indifferent to visible results, practice vows such as those of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*);
the inference of this result is based on their engagement, and thus it is not a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). This is the meaning.

*Praśastapādabhāṣya*: In that context, the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the resulting knowledge of fire is the valid cognition (*pramiti*). Alternatively, the knowledge of fire itself is the means of valid cognition, while the perception of its qualities, defects, or neutrality regarding the fire is the valid cognition; this is inference for one's own sake (*svaniścitārtham anumāna*). *Nyāyakandalī*: [184] [pp.497–498] In this regard, the perception of the inferential mark is the instrument of knowledge, and the resulting cognition of fire is the knowledge itself. Or rather, the cognition of fire is indeed the instrument of knowledge, whereas the discernment of the fire’s merits, defects, or indifference is the resulting knowledge. This constitutes inference for one's own sake.

The word *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition), established through its derivation as an instrument (*karaṇa*), does not reach its full meaning without a result (*phala*). Therefore, he demonstrates the distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result: "In that context, the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) is the means of valid cognition. In this context, the knowledge of the mark is the means of valid cognition, according to the etymology "that by which something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate 'nena*). The result of the means of valid cognition is the correct cognition (*pramiti*), namely, the knowledge of fire.

Although there is a difference in objects between the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) and the cognition of that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*) with respect to their arising, nevertheless, because the cognition of the mark also functions toward the production of the cognition of the possessor of the mark, it has the possessor of the mark as its object; consequently, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) do not have different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). He states another alternative: "Or rather" (*athavā*). The cognition of fire is the means of valid cognition; the resulting comprehension (*pramiti*) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition.

The observation of qualities, defects, and neutrality regarding fire consists of: the observation of qualities, which is the knowledge that "this is a means to pleasure"; the observation of defects, which is the knowledge that it is a means to pain; and the observation of neutrality, which is the knowledge that it is neither a means to pleasure nor a means to pain. This is because such a cognition arises when there is knowledge of fire. This is an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). The term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve niṣṭhā*); thus, "ascertained for oneself" (*svaniścitārtha*) means "for the sake of one's own ascertainment"—that is, this is an inference for oneself. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [185], p. 498.

Verbal testimony and the other means of knowledge are also included within inference, because they follow the same procedure. Just as for one who has mastered the conventional relationship between sign and signified, inference regarding an object beyond the senses arises from the perception of a mark and the recollection of its established connection, so too does it arise from words and the like.
*Nyāyakandalī* [185] [pp. 498–505]

Anticipating the objection—"Proponents of other systems also maintain that verbal testimony (*śabda*) and so forth are distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); why then are they not mentioned here?"—the author states "of verbal testimony and the rest" to show that they are not mentioned separately because they are included within these very [means]. [p.499] The inclusion of verbal testimony and the rest within inference (*anumāna*) means their non-distinctness from inference. This is because they share the same method (*samānavidhitva*), that is, because their mode of operation is identical. The meaning is: just as inference proceeds by the force of grasping a pervasion (*vyāpti*), so too do verbal testimony and the others.

"Verbal testimony (śabda) is inference because it brings about the cognition of an object through the force of pervasion (vyāpti), like smoke. He demonstrates this very identity of method with the words "Just as... For a person for whom the convention—that is, the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva)—is well-known, there occurs inference regarding an object beyond the senses through both the perception of the mark (liṅga) and the recollection of that well-known [concomitance]. This consists of the perception of the mark and the recollection of the well-known fact that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. Just as inference occurs regarding an object beyond the senses by means of these two, so too does it occur from verbal testimony and the rest.

For a word does not convey its meaning as long as it is not understood to be non-deviant [from that meaning]; however, when its non-deviance is known, it would function as a logical mark (*liṅga*), like smoke, while conveying that meaning.

On this point, someone objects: in inference, the subject (*dharmin*) is cognized as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). But in the case of inferring an object from a word, what is the subject? It cannot be the object, because at that time it is not being perceived. If you say the word is the subject, then what is its property to be proven? If you say it is "possessing an object," no; for in the case of a mountain and so forth, some relation characterized by conjunction, inherence, or the like, is established between the fire and so on and the mountain, such that the mountain could be proven as qualified by that fire. But no such relation can be determined between a word and its object, by which the word could be proven as qualified by that object.

For the relationship between these two is precisely that of the signified and the signifier; this [relationship] occurs subsequent to the cognition of the object and cannot exist prior to the communication of the object. Furthermore, there is no rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between word and object as there is between fire and smoke, because of their deviation across space and time. This deviation is evident from the use of the word "Yudhiṣṭhira" in the Kali age even though Yudhiṣṭhira himself is non-existent, and from the hearing of the word "Laṅkā" on Jambudvīpa even though Laṅkā itself does not exist.

Therefore, because of its difference from the causal complex of inference, verbal testimony is not inference. For this reason as well, verbal testimony is not inference: because its own object varies according to specific locations. Smoke never deviates from fire in any place; however, verbal testimony deviates from its own object. To illustrate: the word *caura* signifies "cooked food" for Southerners, but it signifies "thief" for those dwelling in Āryāvarta.

Furthermore, if verbal testimony were inference, its validity would have to be ascertained through the cognition of the three marks (trairūpya), not through the cognition of it being spoken by a reliable person (āpta); for if its validity were ascertained through that [latter] cognition, it would indeed be distinct from inference due to its dissimilarity (vaidharmya).

To this it is replied: when the index finger is raised, the inference of the number ten regarding objects separated by space and time does not have that number ten as its subject (*dharmin*), because the number ten is not perceived there. Nor is the positioning of the index finger the subject, because since there is no other relation between the positioning and the number ten being communicated, it is impossible for it to communicate the number as qualified by that [positioning].

Nor do these two share the same location, nor do they exist at the same time; so how can there be the operation of inference? For in the commercial transactions of merchants, such a movement of the index finger is observed to be invariably concomitant with the intention to convey the number ten. If it is argued that its status as a cause for the cognition of the number ten occurs by way of the cognizer’s apprehension of that intention to convey it, then the same applies to the word as well.

First, from the utterance of the word "cow" by a speaker, the intention to express an object possessing a hump and other such features is understood, because it is observed within one's own continuum that the utterance of the word "cow" is preceded by the intention to express a referent. And from that intention to express the referent, the referent itself is inferred. The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the person is the subject (*dharmin*); he possesses the intention to express an object possessing a hump and other such features, because he is the agent of the utterance of the word "cow," just like myself.

If it is argued that since the intention (*vivakṣā*) of non-reliable persons is observed even in the absence of an object, the object is not established by virtue of that intention, then how is it established from a word? [The answer is: because a word devoid of an object is employed through error or with the intent to deceive. If it is argued that the cognition of an object arises from a word spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), then it is the same: the comprehension of the object results precisely from the intention of the reliable person. [p.503]

However, regarding that which possesses the status of an inferential mark (*liṅga*) despite the fact that the word’s referent may deviate in a particular location—whereas smoke does not deviate—the following principle applies: smoke is the mark of fire by virtue of a natural relationship (*svābhāvika-sambandha*). A word, on the other hand, like a gesture, functions through a convention (*saṅketa*) created by human will; wherever it is conventionally established for a certain object by a person, it serves as the mark for that very object by means of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) being understood.

For this very reason, the determination of meaning follows from the fact that it is uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*), just as it does from purposeful action (*ceṣṭā*). This is because, just as smoke characterized by properties such as continuity and upward movement [indicates fire], only a word spoken by a reliable person can possibly not deviate from its meaning. Why, then, is it not assumed that the capacity of a word to convey meaning belongs to it by its primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*)? [It cannot be so assumed] because there is no relationship [between word and meaning]; and if that which is unrelated were to indicate [meaning], it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that there exists an inherent relationship between word and meaning, [we say] no, because a single word is employed for various meanings across different regions.

If it is argued that "wherever this word is employed by people with a specific meaning, it has denotative power (*vācakatva*) there; whereas elsewhere, it has the status of an indicative mark (*liṅgatva*) because it functions in accordance with convention," we say no. For the word *caura* produces the same cognition for both a thief and a cook; in that case, there is no reason for distinction such that it would have denotative power for the thief and the status of an indicative mark for the cook.

Even for the noble ones (*ārya*), the comprehension of meaning from the word "thief" (*caura*) is preceded by a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is a cognition produced by the word "thief," just like the cognition produced by the word "thief" as used by Southerners, which is accepted by both parties. Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of an inherent relationship (*svābhāvikasambandha*). For you, the "relationship" is said to be the inherent expressive power residing in the denotatum of the word, since that very power is what is established in both cases.

As it has been said: "The relation is indeed the capacity (*śakti*) itself. And if the capacity of a word were, by its very nature, fixed upon the denoted object alone, then even one who has not mastered the linguistic convention would perceive the meaning from the word—since the word, the meaning, and their relation would all be present. If it is argued that the relation, when known, is the cause for the cognition of the meaning and not merely by its existence, then it has been said:
because it is a communicator (*jñāpaka*), the relation requires the knowledge of its own self.

"Therefore, even though it exists, that [relation] is not apprehended as the illuminator. What kind of cognition is there of that relation? If you say it is of the form "this word has this meaning as its denotable object" (*vācya*), then from what does that arise? If you say "from the linguistic usage of elders" (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), then let this very cognition—which has the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*) as its objects—be the cause for the comprehension of meaning through the medium of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is precisely what is called "convention" (*saṅketa*) or "acquisition of proficiency" (*vyutpatti*) when it is being produced by elders conversing with one another for the sake of a child standing nearby; why then posit a separate relation?

For the inherent capacity of a word is its nature as speech (*śabdatva*), while its adventitious capacity consists of convention (*saṅketa*) and a specific sequence (*ānupūrvī*). Since the cognition of that object is established through these two capacities alone, the postulation of any further relation is redundant; for when an effect can be accounted for by what is observed, there is no room for the postulation of what is unobserved.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [186–187], p. 506.

"Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) characterized by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* depends upon the authority of its speaker; the authority of the sacred tradition arises from his word" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.3); "And because of indicative marks, [the Veda] is non-eternal" (VS 2.2.32); "The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence" (VS 6.1.1); and "The act of giving is preceded by intelligence" (VS 6.1.3)—because of such statements. *Nyāyakandalī* [186] [pp. 506–510] The sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), which is defined by the *Śruti* (revealed scripture) and the *Smṛti* (traditional law), is dependent upon the reliability of its speaker. This is because the authority of the sacred tradition derives from the fact that it was spoken by him. Furthermore, as stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras: "And because of indicative marks, [the Veda] is non-eternal" (2.2.32); "The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence" (6.1.1); and "The act of giving is preceded by intelligence" (6.1.3). Since these points have been stated, it follows that the Veda is not eternal. Thus, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has established that the Veda is non-eternal. [Objection: If the Veda were non-eternal, then the relationship between words and their meanings would be subject to change. Consequently, one could not attain the knowledge of Dharma through the Veda, just as one cannot know the meaning of a sentence composed by a contemporary person. Moreover, since the Veda is a collection of sentences, it would follow that it is produced by a human being, like the works of Kālidāsa and others. Therefore, the Veda must be eternal. [Response: This is not so. Even if the Veda were eternal, the relationship between words and their meanings would still be subject to change. For instance, the word *agni*, which denotes fire, might come to denote water at some other time. Furthermore, even if the relationship between words and meanings were fixed, the Veda would still fail to convey the knowledge of Dharma, just as the words of a contemporary person do not. And if the Veda were a collection of sentences, it would indeed follow that it is produced by a human being, just like the works of Kālidāsa and others. Therefore, the Veda is not eternal. Even if the Veda were eternal, the relationship between words and meanings could still change. For instance, the word *agni*, which denotes fire, might denote water at some other time. Moreover, even if the relationship between words and meanings were fixed, the Veda would not convey the knowledge of Dharma, just as the words of a contemporary person do not. And if the Veda were a collection of sentences, it would indeed follow that it is produced by a human being, like the works of Kālidāsa and others. Therefore, the Veda is not eternal. [Objection: If the Veda were non-eternal, then the relationship between words and their meanings would be subject to change. Consequently, one could not attain the knowledge of Dharma through the Veda, just as one cannot know the meaning of a sentence composed by a contemporary person. Moreover, since the Veda is a collection of sentences, it would follow that it is produced by a human being, like the works of Kālidāsa and others. Therefore, the Veda must be eternal. [Response: This is not so. Even if the Veda were eternal, the relationship between words and their meanings would still be subject to change. For example, the word *agni*, which denotes fire, might come to denote water at some other time. Furthermore, even if the relationship between words and meanings were fixed, the Veda would still fail to convey the knowledge of Dharma, just as the words of a contemporary person do not. And if the Veda were a collection of sentences, it would indeed follow that it is produced by a human being, like the works of Kālidāsa and others. Therefore, the Veda is not eternal. [Objection: If the Veda were non-eternal

Now, if it is argued that a word conveys meaning only by way of a speaker, then the comprehension of meaning from Vedic sentences would not be possible, because of the absence of a speaker; therefore, he says: "Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) characterized by *Śruti* and *Smṛti* depends upon the authority of a speaker. It is not only secular tradition; even the sacred tradition characterized by *Śruti* and *Smṛti* causes cognition only by depending on the authority of a speaker. A word has defects dependent on the speaker, but it is not inherently defective by its very nature like a foul odor. As it has been said: "In the case of a word, the defects of the cause—the phonemes and so forth—reside in the human speakers."
For a word is not defective by its own nature, just as a fragrance is not foul by its own nature.

If the Veda were eternal, then, due to the absence of an author, there would be no possibility of defects, and its authority would be established beyond doubt. However, if it were of human origin, its authority could not be obtained without hesitation, because we occasionally observe that humans produce statements that are even factually incorrect due to passion, hatred, and other such flaws. To this, he says: "The authority of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) arises from His word."

The word "tat" (that) refers, by way of anticipating what follows, to the speaker distinguished from ourselves who was established in the sūtra, "Nor is there an inferential mark [for the existence] of the Seer other than our cognitions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 6.1.2). Because of his word—that is, because the Veda was composed by that distinguished person—the authority of the Āmnāya, the Veda, is established.

The intended meaning is this: validity is conditioned by the absence of defects, not by eternality; for even though the ear and the mind are eternal, they sometimes lack validity due to adventitious defects. Conversely, even in the absence of eternality, the eyes and other sense organs possess validity when their defects have been removed. Furthermore, it has been established that defects simply do not exist in a particular kind of person. Therefore, the Veda, being conditioned by such a person, possesses validity despite its being of human origin.

For it does not occur to anyone to suspect that one who perceives reality as it is, whose passion and hatred have been extinguished, and who is motivated by compassion to provide instruction, would teach what is contrary to reality.

From what source does this cognition arise that the Veda was composed by a specific person? It arises from the fact that all those belonging to the various castes and stages of life (varṇāśramins) accept its meaning without any disagreement. If the Veda were composed by some arbitrary person, then—just like the words of the Buddha and others—there would not be the performance of its meaning by all investigators without disagreement; for it is possible that someone might perceive its lack of authority and thus experience a contradiction. That which is subject to universal agreement among all people is indeed authoritative, such as perception and other means of valid knowledge.

The Veda is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for all, because it generates non-contradictory cognition, just like perception. As for the fact that the fruit is not observed in some cases despite the performance of rituals whose objects are perceptible, this does not refute its validity, since that non-observation is caused by a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). And that it is caused by such a deficiency is established by the observation of the fruit when the causal complex is present in its proper form.

It is not tenable to claim that the Veda is the word of a reliable person (*āptoktatva*), because at the time of performing its prescribed rites, the diligent practitioners do not remember an author who would be fit for such recollection; thus, the non-existence [of an author] is established. Therefore, he says: "And on account of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is non-eternal. The word "Veda" (*āmnāya*) mentioned in the context of "the authority of the Veda arises from His word" is connected here by virtue of being the subject under discussion; the meaning is that the Veda is understood to be non-eternal due to an indicative mark. He presents this indicative mark: "The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by conscious intelligence (*buddhipūrva*)."
In the Veda, the composition of sentences—the arrangement of sentences—is preceded by intelligence, because it is an arrangement of sentences, like the arrangement of worldly sentences.

He states another mark: "Because it is said that 'the word *dadāti* (he gives) is preceded by intelligence. In the Veda, the word *dadāti* is preceded by intelligence, because it is said that "*dadāti* is [the word for giving]," just like the worldly word *dadāti*.

Furthermore, the argument that [the Vedas] lack an author because no such author is remembered is unproven; for an author is indeed recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) itself: "Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning; there was neither day nor night. He performed austerity. From his performing austerity, the four Vedas were born. Moreover, the reason is inconclusive due to counter-examples such as dilapidated wells and the like.

Thus, since the non-eternality of the Veda is established, and because a doubt regarding its authority arises from the observation of duality in human speech, a person may indeed act upon a perceptible object when there is sometimes a doubt about its purpose; however, regarding an imperceptible object—which is to be accomplished through the expenditure of great wealth and physical exertion—a discerning person will not engage in it until they have ascertained the authority of the statement concerning that object. Furthermore, in the world, the authority of speech is observed to be preceded by the cognition of the speaker's excellence; therefore, in the case of the Veda as well, practice would only be free from doubt if its authority were established in that same manner.

In the *Nyāyakandalī* [187] [pp. 511–517], some say: "The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a statement is not based on its being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess validity intrinsically (*svataḥ*). They should be asked this: what exactly is meant by "validity"? Is it non-deviation from the object (*arthāvyabhicāra*), or is it the determination of the object as it truly is (*yathārthaparicchedakatva*)? It cannot be non-deviation from the object; for even though smoke is invariably concomitant with fire, there are cases where, due to some cause, it does not produce the cognition of fire, and thus lacks validity. Furthermore, regarding blue, yellow, and so forth, each...
Even in the case of an erroneous perception, the eye possesses validity solely by virtue of being the producer of a cognition that corresponds to reality.

Now, if validity consists in being the determiner of an object as it truly is, is that validity known intrinsically (*svataḥ*), or does it arise intrinsically, or does it function intrinsically? If, first of all, the cognition were to know its own validity by itself—namely, "I am the determiner of an object as it truly is"—then a doubt regarding the means of knowledge, such as "Is this [cognition] corresponding to reality or not? would never arise; furthermore, no activity would ever occur based on a mistaken cognition.

Now, if—due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself—the cognition, while not grasping itself, does not grasp its own status as a determiner of reality as it truly is, then another [cognition] must be required for that determination, because there is no apprehension of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) without a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since even the means of knowledge, at the stage of being cognized, is itself an object of knowledge, validity is indeed extrinsic (*parataḥ*). If it is argued that if validity is known by another, the validity of that [second cognition] must be known by yet another, and that by still another, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), we say: there is no infinite regress, because there is no desire to know validity in every instance.

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) determines its object by its very arising, not by having its own validity cognized. Thus, even when the object has been determined, if a doubt arises—due to some cause—as to whether "this is a valid cognition" or "this is not a valid cognition," the person does not act because of uncertainty regarding the object. In that case, for the sake of his engagement, there arises a desire to know the validity [of the cognition] through another means, because as long as validity is not ascertained, the doubt cannot be eliminated.

Furthermore, where a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises such that the stain of doubt has been wiped away—either due to extreme proficiency through repeated practice or because all particular features have been grasped—in that case, since the cognizer has no further desire for certainty regarding the object once that cognition has arisen, there is no desire to ascertain its validity, and thus no pursuit of another means of knowledge. As for one who would still project doubt even there by observing that cognition occurs in two ways, he is unable to project it, because his projection is already refuted by the very certainty regarding that object.
As Maṇḍana stated in the *Brahmasiddhi*:
"For there is no confidence in cognition; it is sublated by knowledge itself.

If it is argued that the inquiry into validity (*prāmāṇya*) is for the sake of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), then in a case where activity occurred due to a doubt about the object while the validity was still undetermined, one who is satisfied with the attainment of the object has no further desire to know the validity. How, then, can the correspondence of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the object be determined through the capacity for activity? It is not so; for even in that case, just as a farmer acts for the sake of testing the seed, one who acts for the sake of testing the validity certainly possesses such a desire regarding the cognition.

However, for one who, due to doubt regarding the validity [of a cognition], has already engaged in activity for the sake of apprehending the object because of that very doubt about the object, the determination of its validity—though not intended by him—occurs through the power of the thing itself once the attainment of the object has fulfilled its purpose; for the capacity for successful activity is never dissociated from validity. Thus, in this way, validity is neither known intrinsically (*svataḥ*), nor does it arise intrinsically.

If cognition, having arisen, subsequently produces within itself the quality of determining its object as it truly is, we might accept its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇyam*). However, seeing that it arises from its own causes with the very nature of a correct apprehension, we consider its validity to depend entirely on something external.

Now, if you think that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) produces its own validity by itself, and thus we do not assert intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇyatva*), but rather that a cognition does not depend on anything other than the collection of causes that produced it for the production of its validity, and this is what is meant by "intrinsic validity"—this too is incorrect.

If indeed the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces a cognition neither deficient nor excessive is the cause of validity, then from where does erroneous cognition arise? If it is argued: "The nature of causes is the production of a cognition corresponding to reality; when this nature is subverted by defects (*doṣa*), then those causes produce a non-corresponding cognition; but when the defects that cause the subversion of the nature are absent, then their nature as the producer of a cognition corresponding to reality remains established," then [we ask]: is that [verbal testimony] based merely on the speaker's cognition?

Does the production of truthfulness in a sentence arise from [the sentence] itself? If that were so, then every sentence would be non-false. Or does the production of truthfulness in a sentence arise from a cognition based on a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? In that case, validity does not stem from the mere nature of the cause, but rather from its quality (*guṇa*). The cause of a word is the cognition of the object; its quality is truthfulness (*yathārthatva*), and its lack of truthfulness is a defect (*doṣa*). Thus, if truthfulness is the cause of a sentence’s validity, then its validity arises solely from the quality of the cause, not from its mere nature.

Furthermore, if the validity of verbal testimony were dependent upon the excellence of its cause, then other types of cognition would likewise be so. Those cognitions under dispute have their validity dependent upon the excellence of their causes, because they are cognitions that are valid, just like a valid cognition dependent on words.

If it is argued that even in the case of verbal testimony, the operation of the excellence of the cause (*guṇa*) lies in the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*), and not in the production of validity (*prāmāṇya*), we say: no. While it may be that due to the excellence’s obstruction of defects, the production of the effect of defects—namely, non-correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatva*)—does not occur, from what [source] does the production of correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*) arise? For when there is an absence of a cause, there is an absence of its effect, but not the occurrence of a contrary effect. If it is argued that this arises from the mere nature of the cognition itself, we say: no, because that [nature] is without distinction [in all cognitions].

For the connection with an object is indeed the distinguishing feature of a cognition; if that [connection] is exhausted merely by counteracting defects and thus fails to be a factor in the production of a cognition that accords with reality (*yathārtha*), then—since the nature [of the cognition] would remain undifferentiated—the sentence would not be restricted to a specific object, because there is no establishment of a distinction from what is undifferentiated. If, on the other hand, it is argued that a sentence produces a cognition only regarding that very object which is its own objective referent, then it follows that the correspondence of the cognition itself is the cause of the sentence’s correspondence with reality, and not its mere nature as awareness. Thus, it arrives at the conclusion that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that [sentence] arises solely from a positive quality (*guṇa*).

Or, even if it be granted that the quality functions toward the absence of defects, nevertheless, the extrinsic nature of validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇyam*) is not lost; for in the production of that [validity], the absence of defects—distinct from the very nature of the causes—is established as possessing causal efficiency through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in all cases.

If it is argued that the absence of error follows from the absence of defects, whereas validity depends solely on the intrinsic nature of the sense organs and other factors, then why not assume instead that the production of validity is obstructed by defects, while error depends solely on the intrinsic nature of the sense organs and so forth? If it is argued that such an assumption is not made because error conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of defects, then the same applies here: since validity is also observed to conform to the positive and negative concomitance of the absence of defects, the [opposite] assumption is equally untenable.
Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that does not depend upon the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the subsequent absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of defects.

Likewise, the operation of a means of valid cognition in producing effects such as purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) is also extrinsic (*parataḥ*), not dependent on its own nature alone; for it generates effects such as activity only when dependent on assistance, hindrance, and so forth. This is the general direction of the argument. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [188], p. 518.
Since comprehension is observed through the gesture of one who is well-known for his expressive performance, that too is nothing but inference.
In the *Nyāyakandalī* [188], p. 518, it is stated:

"The beckoning of the hand is understood from its being bent downwards, and the dismissal is understood from its being thrown upwards away from the face; some desire this to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Against them, he says: 'prasiddhābhinayasya' (of one whose expressive performance is well-known)."

When a person’s well-known gesture—characterized by such things as the contraction of the hand—is performed with a specific intention, it is observed that through that movement, such as the positioning of the hand, there arises the cognition of summoning, dismissing, or other such acts, and not otherwise; therefore, that cognition of knowledge derived from gesture is also nothing but inference (*anumāna*).

[189] [p. 519] Since an authoritative person (*āpta*) conveys the cognition of a *gavaya*, which is otherwise unknown, by means of a cow, this analogy (*upamāna*) is in fact merely the word of an authoritative person (*āptavacana*).
In the *Nyāyakandalī* [189] [pp.

519–523], while demonstrating that comparison (*upamāna*) is included within inference (*anumāna*), he says: "Because an authoritative person (*āpta*) conveys the information about a gavaya, which is not previously known, by means of a cow, comparison is nothing other than the word of an authoritative person (*āptavacana*)."

*Āpti* is the direct perception of an object, its attainment, which is the apprehension of it as it truly is. One who acts by means of that is an *āpta*—one who has directly perceived the nature of things (*sākṣātkṛtadharma*) and is an instructor prompted by the desire to communicate an object exactly as it was seen. By such an *āpta*, namely a forest-dweller who knows the *gavaya* (bos gavaeus), for the sake of a city-dweller who is unacquainted with the *gavaya* and asks "What is a *gavaya* like?", there is the communication of the *gavaya* through its similarity to a cow, in the form of the sentence "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*. This statement of the *āpta* is indeed the means of valid cognition known as *upamāna*.

Since the cognition of the object in that case arises solely from the authority of the speaker, and since the word of a reliable person (*āpta*) is itself inference, the intention is that analogy (*upamāna*) as well is not distinct from inference.
As for those Pūrva-mīmāṃsakas who claim that the word of a forest-dweller is precisely analogy, for them this is nothing but inference.

Even those disciples of Śabarasvāmin who claim that the cognition of similarity—“my cow is similar to this [animal]”—which arises through memory when one sees a *gavaya* in the forest after having previously experienced a cow, constitutes *upamāna* (analogy), that too is nothing but memory. For similarity, like a universal (*sāmānya*), resides completely within each individual instance; it does not exist as a whole distributed across both [the cow and the gavaya] like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). This is because the cognition “this [gavaya] is similar to a cow” arises even when the cow is not being perceived, provided one is perceiving the individual *gavaya* in the forest.
As has been stated by the teachers of Mīmāṃsā:
"And resemblance, like a universal, is completed in each individual;
for it is perceived even when the counter-correlative is not seen.

Even though similarity is complete in each individual instance, although there was previously no cognition regarding the cow that "this is similar to a gavaya" due to the absence of the perception of the gavaya, nevertheless, the cognition of similarity has indeed arisen, occurring solely through the contact with its own substratum. Just as, for example, even in the absence of the cognitions "this is long" or "this is short" because of the non-perception of another counter-correlate, there is a grasping of dimension in its own nature merely through proximity to its own substratum.
Otherwise, how could one who has gone to another place, having apprehended the counter-correlate, determine that "this is long" or "that is short" in relation to it?

If similarity in the cow was not previously grasped by the mere contact of the senses, then it would not be grasped now in the gavaya either; consequently, there would be no restriction that recollection occurs only in the cow upon seeing the gavaya, because there is no distinction between the two cases. If you argue that the restriction of recollection arises because as many general properties as are grasped in the cow—such as having a dewlap, a tail, and so forth—are likewise grasped in the gavaya, we reply: similarity is simply the plurality of common parts existing in both.

If those [individuals] are grasped by means of grasping their respective substrates, then similarity itself has already been grasped. Therefore, when a gavaya is perceived, the cognition of similarity—which takes as its object a cow-individual not present there—is merely a memory produced by a latent impression (saṃskāra) manifested by the sight of a similar thing; it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it is observed that even that which was grasped by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) can become the object of memory; for instance, when a single individual is first grasped by one who has not yet mastered the term, the universal is not yet conceptualized, yet upon the perception of another individual, there occurs a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Even those who maintain that for one who has heard the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) and sees a *gavaya*, the cognition of the relationship between a name and the named—namely, "the word *gavaya* is the name of this [animal]"—arising from the perception of its similarity to a cow, is *upamāna*; for them too, the statement "as is a cow, so is a *gavaya*" and the resulting cognition—"that which is heard of in the world as such is indeed similar to a cow"—are nothing but *āgama* (verbal testimony).

Even that cognition which consists in knowing that what resembles a cow is denotable by the word *gavaya* is indeed inference (*anumāna*), because the word is applied to it. For whatever word is applied without disagreement by experts to a certain object, that word is its denotator. And the word *gavaya* is applied without disagreement by forest-dwellers to that which resembles a cow; therefore, the general cognition that "this too is indeed denotable by the word *gavaya*" is nothing but inference.

When a gavaya is perceived, the cognition of its similarity [to a cow] is a result of perception (*pratyakṣa*), as is the cognition of the individual object (*piṇḍa*) as excluded from the three worlds. Furthermore, the subsequent reflection upon the relationship between the name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*)—which occurs by way of that [similarity]—is likewise produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). This impression arises from the knowledge that the word "gavaya" denotes something similar to a cow, a knowledge which was previously generated by the manifestation of the apprehension of similarity and the operation of the universal (*sāmānya*) [of "cow"]. It is thus like the reflection upon the denotability of other individuals of the same class, which is produced by the latent impression of the conventional knowledge (*saṅketa-jñāna*) regarding a universal established in one instance.

It is simply recollection. For in that case, one reflects: "I previously understood that this very thing has this word as its denotation. Thus, there is no separate means of knowledge called analogy (*upamāna*). *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [190–191] [p. 524]: Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is merely a form of inference based on what is seen; presumption based on what is heard is an inference of an inference.
*Nyāyakandalī* [190] [pp. 524–530]:

"Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of another fact because a perceived or heard object cannot otherwise be accounted for. By demonstrating the utility of separately mentioning the term "heard," the opponent establishes presumption in two ways: presumption from what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) and presumption from what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).

Where a fact, being otherwise inexplicable, leads to the cognition of another fact, that is presumption based on a perceived object (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*). For example, in the case of "Caitra is alive, yet he is not in the house," the absence of Caitra in the house is apprehended through the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (*abhāva-pramāṇa*); and from the hearing of the statement "he is alive," his existence [somewhere] is also apprehended, since one observes that those who are alive reside in a house. Now, it is impossible for a single person such as Caitra to simultaneously exist and be absent in the same place, because there is a contradiction between these two states due to their mutual exclusion (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*).

Thus, this non-existence, while being perceived, is not tenable because of the hearing of the report that "he lives. And since it is untenable, one postulates that in which case it becomes tenable. The absence from the house of one who is alive is not otherwise possible; for if he were not outside, there would be a contradiction with the fact that "he lives," and that very contradiction constitutes its untenability. That contradiction ceases once Caitra's existence outside is cognized.

"Caitra lives and is not at home" [implies] "because he exists outside. When there is a conflict between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one of which has scope (*sāvakāśa*) and the other which lacks scope (*niravakāśa*), *arthāpatti* (presumption) consists in establishing the absence of conflict between them by demonstrating—through the route of the impossibility of the one lacking scope—that the one with scope must have another object. On the other hand, that cognition of another related entity which arises through the recollection of a relation upon seeing a related thing restricted to a particular place and so forth, is inference (*anumāna*). The distinction between these two is due to the difference in the manner in which the knowledge arises, as it has been said:
"In inference, the fact that its birth is dependent upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established."
"But this other [type of] presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) proceeds by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka).

Likewise, there is also presumptive testimony based on what is heard (śrutārthāpatti), where an incoherent statement leads to the postulation of another statement; for example, from the sentence "The fat man does not eat during the day," one postulates the sentence "He eats at night.

In this regard, he first includes *arthāpatti* based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) within inference (*anumāna*), stating: "The *arthāpatti* that contradicts the object of perception is indeed [inference]. "Perceived" (*darśana*) means that which is seen; and "the object of perception" (*darśanārtha*) is an object understood through the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). From that perceived object, the occurrence (*āpatti*)—that is, the understanding—of another object is nothing other than an inference based on contradiction (*virodhi-anumāna*). For whatever has a fixed rule (*niyama*) in a certain way, that very thing serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Here, however, it is precisely an object contradicted by another means of valid cognition that is invariably concomitant with another object; thus, it is the contradictory itself that serves as the logical mark.

This is the intended meaning: if the absence from the house were to imply existence outside merely by virtue of its own inconsistency, then, due to the lack of a restrictive cause (*niyamahetu*), it might imply some other object as well. If you argue that the absence from the house implies another object for the sake of its own consistency, and that no such consistency exists when any other [object] is postulated, we ask: who has stated that its consistency occurs only when existence outside is present? We, however, maintain that even when existence outside is present, the absence from the house remains inconsistent.

It is observed that a substance which is non-pervasive exists in one place and does not exist elsewhere; for example, the sun, being perceived in one location such as the east, is not present in another, such as the west. This is determined by the force of observation alone: the absence of a living person from the house is only possible if they are present inside, and not otherwise. If this is so, is the understanding of "possibility" (tathopapatti) not preceded by the apprehension of a positive concomitance (anvaya)? If that were the case, then presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) would be nothing but inference, because its production is dependent upon positive concomitance.

As for the claim that [the inference] operates when there is a contradiction, that is merely a point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Accordingly, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Devadatta is outside, because, while being connected with life, he is not perceived in the house, just like myself.

He includes presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) within inference: "From hearing, there is an inference based on an inferred [mark]. Upon hearing the statement, "The fat man does not eat during the day," the postulation of his eating at night is an "inference based on an inferred [mark]. This is because one infers the cause—eating at night—from the fattiness, which has been inferred from the statement acting as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Fattiness is the effect of eating; if he were not eating during the day, that fattiness would be inexplicable due to the absence of its cause.

If it is argued that when that [meaning] is untenable, the sentence is also untenable because its meaning is not coherent, then the sentence's untenability consists in the untenability of its meaning, and its tenability consists in the tenability of its meaning; it does not consist in the sentence's own nature being tenable or untenable. For instance, for one who does not eat during the day, the state of being fat—characterized by the fact of eating—is established through the meaning consisting of eating at night, and not through the sentence "eating at night"; thus, due to the untenability of the meaning, that sentence [is deemed untenable].

The object itself, which is the cause of the logical inconsistency, is what must be postulated, not the sentence, because the sentence does not establish the fact. Furthermore, the object being postulated is understood through the object itself; for instance, in the case of corpulence in one who does not eat during the day, there is no deviation from its being the effect of eating at night. Thus, presumption (*arthāpatti*) does not have the word as its domain.

Now, it might be thought: "A meaning is established by a meaning alone; therefore, by that very establishment, the word for it is also established. However, a verbal meaning is established only by a verbal meaning, because there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between it and what is understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For instance, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is said, the lack of establishment of the action due to the absence of an object is not resolved merely by the perception of the bean (*kalāya*) being cooked; even when that [bean] is present, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) "what does he cook? remains unfulfilled.

However, when the object is presented by the word itself, the cognition becomes free from doubt, as in "he cooks vegetables" or "he cooks peas. The statement "the fat man does not eat during the day" is likewise a case of the incoherence of the sentence-meaning; therefore, its resolution must occur through the verbal meaning itself. Thus, one must first seek, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the very sentence that establishes eating at night. Otherwise, there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between eating at night and the word-meanings of the sentence concerning the daytime.

Furthermore, when the conclusion of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) concerns a sentence, the fact of eating at night—the actual object—is not the domain of presumptive testimony, because that is understood from the sentence itself. Nor should it be said that the daytime sentence or its meaning cannot bring about that understanding due to a lack of proximity with the nighttime sentence, for even a sentence is proximate by way of the proximity of its meaning. Moreover, unlike inference, presumptive testimony does not require such proximity, as it functions solely through the mere presence of an inconsistency. As it has been said:
Nor is this second object apprehended again as being the very same object as the first;
for it is concealed by the fact that it is grasped by a conceptualizing consciousness (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*).
"Without having cognized other words, she [the cognition] does not understand the meaning at all;
therefore, this [cognition] is necessarily directed toward the sentence first.
But the sentence itself will cause one to understand the sentence-meaning, because it has already reached that [meaning]. Thus [it is said].

To this it is replied: Words are employed for the purpose of conveying the meaning of a sentence. Since they are individually unable to convey the sentence-meaning—which consists of the mutual connection of word-meanings—because their function would remain incomplete, they require other words that perform the same function. However, where the sentence-meaning has already been conveyed by these [words], there is no further requirement for other words, because their own function has been accomplished.

If it is argued that the meaning established by them is not tenable, let it not be tenable; for the function of a word is not the establishment of the non-contradiction of its meaning, but rather its communication. And that has indeed been accomplished by this [word] even with respect to the sentence concerning the night, though it is not present. For from the sentence "not eating by day," the non-eating of a fat person is understood; and this understanding is both indubitable and non-erroneous, because otherwise there would be no occurrence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) at all.

For it is only when one has ascertained that the fatness established by the absence of eating during the day is otherwise impossible that it is not logical to claim that its justification is untenable; rather, it is for the sake of establishing that justification that [the inference] is sought. But if this [fatness] were doubted or determined to be the opposite, whose justification would there be for the postulation of another fact? Nor is there a mutual contradiction between two facts such that the cognition of one becomes a non-cognition of the other. Therefore, since the word is justified by the very cognition of the fact, it does not depend on another word, as there is no other function to be performed.

But it is well said that "from the hearing of a word there is an inference based on an inference": for it is the very object denoted by that word which, being untenable without another object, seeks out that other object in order to establish itself, following the lead of its own cognition.
Furthermore, probability (*sambhava*) is also nothing but inference, because of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [192] [p.532]:

Some maintain that the knowledge of a hundred within a thousand arises from a distinct means of valid cognition called "possibility" (*sambhava*), on the grounds that a hundred can exist within a thousand. To refute this, he says: "Possibility, too, is nothing but inference because of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*). A thousand is invariably concomitant with a hundred, since it is preceded by it; therefore, the knowledge of a hundred derived from a thousand is indeed inference. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [193–196] [p.533]

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is also nothing but inference; just as an effect that has arisen is a mark for the existence of its cause, so too an effect that has not arisen is a mark for the non-existence of its cause.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [193] [pp. 533–539]

Some maintain that when there is the cognition of the absence of an object of knowledge (*prameya*), there is a sixth means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*), which consists in the cessation of the five means of valid cognition, such as perception, which would otherwise apprehend that object. He refutes this: non-existence is also merely inference (*anumāna*). To explain how: just as a produced effect is a mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of its cause, so too an unproduced effect is a mark for the non-existence of its cause. [Knowledge is the effect of the object of knowledge; its absence is the mark for the absence of the object of knowledge, just as [the presence of an effect] is a mark for the cause.]

Even for one who accepts non-existence (*abhāva*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the knowledge of the non-existence of an object of cognition does not arise merely from the absence of a cognition; for otherwise, it would follow that even an object remote in its own nature (*svarūpa-viprakṛṣṭa*) could be cognized as non-existent. Rather, when the causes of cognition are present, the non-arising of a cognition regarding an object capable of being cognized is the cause for the comprehension of non-existence. Furthermore, there is no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*) between the non-perception of an incapable object and the non-perception of a capable object, because non-existence is devoid of any degrees of excellence (*niratiśaya*).

Therefore, this [non-perception] does not make [an object] known by its own power alone like a sense-faculty; rather, it is the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*) that does not deviate from the absence of the object to be known. However, the non-perception of what is imperceptible (*ayogyānupalambha*) does deviate, because it is possible even when the object is present. By this distinction alone, the non-perception of what is perceptible is the indicator, and nothing else. If this were so, then non-existence would itself be a logical mark (*liṅga*), since it would depend upon the apprehension of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

If, on the other hand, it did not depend upon that, then the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be unavoidable: that all non-existence whatsoever would fail to make anything known, as there would be no distinction between them.

Moreover, when the ground is perceived through the contact of the sense organ, there also arises the cognition of absence, namely, "the ground is without a jar. Why is it not accepted that in that case, the absence is also perceptible, just like the ground? If you argue that the sense organ is connected only with the positive aspect (the ground) because of its suitability [for that], this is not established without further justification.

For fitness is to be understood through its effect; just as an effect is observed to follow the presence and absence of the sense organs when they exist, so too is it observed when they do not exist. Thus, like a positive entity, non-existence (absence) is also indeed fit for apprehension by the senses. And precisely because its effect is observed, some kind of connection with the sense organ will be postulated for it as well.

Now, it might be thought: the absence of anything is not perceived without a locus, because we observe the occurrence and cessation [of activity] governed by rules regarding place and so forth. Furthermore, regarding that which serves as its locus, the operation of the sense organs is required for the perception of that locus itself, but not for the apprehension of the absence; for we observe the perception of absence even when the operation of the sense organs has ceased.

Thus it is said: Suppose someone, having perceived a temple or the like by its own nature, goes to another place; when asked by someone whether Devadatta is in the temple or not, he—desiring to know—realizes at that very moment that he is not there, and having realized this, he declares, "He is not there."

Nor should it be argued that the absence of Devadatta was already apprehended non-conceptually at the time of perceiving the temple, and is now merely being remembered; for while it is reasonable that jars and the like are apprehended non-conceptually through sensory contact—since their own nature is independent of anything else—the nature of an absence, however, which is of the essence of negation, depends upon that very thing whose existence is being negated.

Therefore, since there is no other intrinsic nature for the absence of that [object] apart from its negation, it is impossible to define it there without first defining the nature of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). For this indeed is the distinction between existence and non-existence: that one is apprehended as having a positive form (*vidhirūpatā*), while the other is apprehended by way of the negation of another.

As the author of the *Nyāyavārttika* stated: "The distinction [between existence and non-existence] arises from their being the causes of independent or dependent perception and non-perception; for that which exists is indeed the objective support (*ālambana*) of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) independently, whereas that which does not exist is dependent, appearing by way of the negation of another. If, however, there were a grasping of non-existence (*abhāva*) through its own independence, then it would be indistinguishable from existence. Therefore, there is no grasping of non-existence by means of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*).

As for the further objection: "Was the temple previously perceived as mixed with Devadatta, or as distinct from him? If it was grasped as mixed, then there is no memory of the [temple] alone. If it was grasped as distinct, then it follows that its non-existence was already grasped and is merely remembered later. This too is without substance, because even when the existence or non-existence of Devadatta is not grasped, the temple is grasped by way of its own nature.

Therefore, there is no prior apprehension of non-existence; because of that absence, there is no memory [of it]; nor is any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) perceived at that time. Consequently, when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is remote and has become an object of memory, the very exclusion of the five means of valid cognition—perception and the rest—is itself the means of valid cognition for the apprehension of non-existence. Furthermore, once it is established in one instance that non-existence is determined by a means of valid cognition, it will be established in other cases as well by that same means; thus, it is proven that non-existence is a distinct means of valid cognition.

To this it is replied: When someone who has gone to another place is asked, "Is Devadatta now in the temple? does he understand his current non-existence by means of his current non-apprehension, thinking "He is not here now"? Or does he understand his prior non-existence by means of his prior non-apprehension, thinking "He was not there at the time of entering the temple"? First of all, the current non-apprehension does not constitute a non-apprehension of a perceptible object (*yogyānupalabdhi*), because of the spatial separation.

At present, even the prior absence of Devadatta there remains doubtful, since his arrival is still possible. However, the prior non-apprehension that was capable of determining that prior absence does not persist now, because he has reached another state. And that which is no longer present cannot serve as a cause for cognition.

Nor does it operate while mounted upon memory, because it was not previously cognized. For non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not cognizable by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since its nature is that of an absence (*abhāva*). And if there were a dependence on another non-apprehension, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that this [non-apprehension] determines the object even while itself remaining ungrasped, just like a sense organ; such being the case, how could there be memory of it? Because there is no experience (*anubhava*) of it.

Now, it might be thought: "The non-perception of Devadatta in the temple is sublated by the perception of Devadatta; yet, for one who has gone to another place, that perception has not arisen. Therefore, his non-perception [in the temple] certainly still exists. Even if he has entered another state, there is no difference in the substance itself due to a difference in its state. Let it be so for now in this case.

But where the non-existence of an object was not previously apprehended due to the absence of recollection of its counter-positive, and subsequently, at a later time, through the apprehension of that object, there arises the cognition of the prior absence—namely, "this was not here before"—what is the remedy for that? For the non-perception of that object has indeed ceased by virtue of its perception. Nor can it be argued that the non-perception existed previously and thus serves as a cause for cognition even though it is no longer present now; for if that were so, it would follow that one whose sense organ has perished could still perceive an object.

If it is argued that while the present non-apprehension of that [object] has been sublated by its present apprehension, the prior non-apprehension still remains—and therefore, by means of that which was capable of determining the absence at the previous time, the prior absence is determined—then alas, what learning! Alas, what skill! Non-apprehension is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of apprehension; and since that is singular, having as its limit only the arising of the object, it does not differ according to the distinction between prior and present times. In that case, the present non-apprehension has indeed ceased.

Who other than one whose intellect is as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass can fathom this extremely subtle fragment of discernment—that the prior [state] has not ceased? Therefore, we do not understand how non-existence could be delimited.

How, then, is there the cognition of non-existence regarding a thing that has gone elsewhere after its mere form was perceived, when the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is being remembered? It is through inference: for when a certain counter-positive is being remembered, if a thing which was fit to be remembered is not remembered despite the desire to remember it, then it did not exist at the time of perception. This is just as when a place is being remembered alone, and a jar previously perceived there is not remembered.

Furthermore, when a temple is being remembered, Devadatta—who was capable of being remembered—is not remembered even though there is a desire to remember him. Therefore, it is inferred from the absence of memory that he too was not present at the time the temple was perceived. Even in the case of two things perceived together, it is observed that due to the lack of intensity in the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) or other factors, one is not remembered while the other is; for example, when a verse has been studied, even if one word is not remembered, the other words are remembered.

If it is argued that, in that case, the inference of non-existence based on the non-recollection of one thing when another is recollected is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), [we reply]: even in the case of two objects existing together, due to certain causes, sometimes one is perceived and not the other. Even so, how is the non-existence of a jar established by the perception of the bare ground when the jar is not perceived?
— *Nyāyakandalī* [194] [pp. 539–540].

Now, it might be thought: "The non-apprehension of one thing when there is the apprehension of another that is in contact with cognition is the means of proving its absence, but not every such case. For the very same cognition by which the location is perceived also perceives the jar conjoined with it; and the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the perception of the location is the very same as that for the jar. If the jar were present in the location, it too would have been perceived when the location was being cognized, because they possess an identical causal complex."

And it is not known; therefore, it simply does not exist, because its non-perception cannot be accounted for in any other way. If this is so, then for us as well, the recollection of one thing among two that were co-present in a single cognition is the means of establishing non-existence.

Whatever is the causal complex for the perception of the temple is also the causal complex for the perception of Devadatta when he is conjoined with it; and whatever is the causal complex for the recollection of the temple is also the causal complex for the recollection of Devadatta, because of their association within a single cognition. Therefore, if Devadatta had been present at the time of perceiving the temple, he too would have been recollected when the temple was being recollected, since the causal complex for them is identical.

And it is not remembered; therefore, it did not exist at all, because its non-remembrance cannot be accounted for by any other means—this is the same [argument]. However, the words of a verse are recited in sequence according to the requirements of pronunciation, and they do not coexist within a single cognition. Among them, that for which a particularly vivid latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has been produced is remembered, while the others are not; thus, there is no inconsistency.

Even in the case of an object being thus perceived, that cognition of its prior non-existence—the knowledge that "this was not here before"—is also an inference, provided that the existence of the counter-positive (the object) at a prior time is remembered; for it arises from the absence of the memory of its existence at that time.

As for those who claim that even the absence of memory is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they contradict the *Bhāṣya* which states, "Non-existence too is the absence of a means of valid cognition," as well as the *Vārttika*, which says, "Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with regard to the nature of an object," and so forth. Enough of this prolixity.
*Nyāyakandalī* [195] [pp. 541–543]

However, those who say this—"Since there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) consisting of non-existence, the investigation of its validity is not sound"—should be asked this: what is the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition "it does not exist"? If it is nothing at all, then you have handed over the very hand of victory to the Mahāyānists who desire a consciousness without an objective support (*nirālambana-vijñāna*).

Alternatively, if the ground (*bhūtala*) is the objective support, then even when the ground possesses thorns and the like, the cognition "there is no thorn" would arise, and the resulting activity characterized by walking back and forth without hesitation would be unavoidable.

If it is argued that the cognition "it does not exist" has as its object the bare ground alone, and that when a thorn is present, this "bareness" ceases, resulting in the absence of both cognition and activity [regarding the ground's lack of a thorn], we ask: Is this bareness the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the ground, or is it a distinct attribute (*dharmāntara*)? If it is the nature itself, then since that nature remains unchanged even when a thorn or similar object is perceived, the same fault remains: there would be no cessation of cognition and activity [regarding the ground's lack of a thorn]. On the other hand, if it is a distinct attribute, then a new ontological category (*tattvāntara*) must be established.

Now, if you think that an entity alone undergoes two states—being solitary and being accompanied—in that case, an entity in its solitary state is said to be "mere intrinsic nature" (svarūpamātra) and "isolated" (kevala). When such an entity has a visible counter-correlate (pratiyogin), such as a jar, that is desired to be apprehended, the perception [of the isolated entity] initiates the conventional usage of the non-existence of that jar and so forth.

To this we reply: what meaning for the word "alone" (*ekākī*) have you established here—distinct from both the absence of the jar and the ground—that could serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the negative cognition "it is not"? For a distinct cognition does not arise without a distinct object, nor is a difference in linguistic usage possible [otherwise].

If it is argued that the very oneness which is the intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*) of an entity is what constitutes its "aloneness" (*ekākitva*), then is this oneness the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogirahitatva*), or is it the number one (*ekatvasaṃkhyā*)? The number one persists as long as its substratum exists, even during the state in which the entity has a second. If, on the other hand, "aloneness" is said to be the intrinsic nature consisting in the absence of a counter-correlate, then a distinct object of knowledge (*prameyāntara*) is established.

Surely even for the proponent of non-existence (*abhāvavādin*), the perception of the bare ground is the cause for the cognition of absence, since it is impossible to cognize an absence there if the ground itself is not perceived. In that regard, first of all, the cognition "there is no thorn" does not arise from the apprehension of a ground accompanied by a thorn. Furthermore, if the apprehension of the ground as qualified by an absence were the cause of the cognition of that absence, then the apprehension of the ground as qualified by the absence would follow from the apprehension of the absence, and the apprehension of the absence would follow from the apprehension of the ground as qualified by the absence; thus, one would be admitting that a thing is its own cause.

Therefore, even by you, some state of "aloneness" (*ekākitva*) belonging to the ground—which is distinct from non-existence and distinct from the absence of connection with a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—must be admitted, such that upon the cognition of it there would be the cognition of non-existence, and that alone would trigger our conventional usage of "it does not exist. This too is incorrect, because the very apprehension of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the ground is the cause of the cognition of non-existence.

Nor does it follow that there would be the cognition of this [absence] even when something else co-present is being perceived; for, just like the perception of the bare ground (*bhūtala*), the contact of the sense organ with absence (*abhāva*) is also a causal complex for the apprehension of absence. When thorns or the like are present, their absence does not exist; thus, due to the lack of contact between the sense organ and the object [of absence], there is no cognition of absence even though the ground is being perceived. For it is not the case that because the eye, light, and so forth—which are causes of perception—exist, whatever is not present here must also be cognized there. Thus, in this manner, absence is established. *Nyāyakandalī* [196] [pp. 544–546]

And that [non-existence] is established as fourfold: antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Antecedent non-existence is the non-existence of the effect in its causes prior to its production; [therein, the non-existence of a particular before the production of the effect is antecedent non-existence]. And although it is beginningless, it is non-eternal, because it is destroyed by the production of the effect; for if it were not destroyed, the production of the effect would be impossible.

What is the destruction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)? If it is argued that it is simply the arising of the entity, [we reply: because when an entity has ceased, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving its prior non-existence; for like the entity itself, the parts of the entity that have already initiated their effects also possess the characteristic of being the destruction of prior non-existence.

The falling away from its own nature of that which has arisen is "non-existence through destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). And although it possesses an origin, it is indestructible, because there is no further perception of the entity. Origination is the existence of what previously did not exist; what, then, is the prior non-existence of destruction? For whatever object there is a destruction, the very persistence of that object's own nature is the prior non-existence of that destruction.

Just as the very arising of an entity is the destruction of its prior non-existence, so too the very arising of its subsequent non-existence (pradhvaṃsa) is the destruction of that prior non-existence. It is not to be questioned how that which is non-existent can come into existence, or how that which exists can cease to exist; for the causal capacity of the cause is beyond such inquiry.

The absence of a cow in a horse and the absence of a horse in a cow is mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). This is one and eternal everywhere; for even when a single individual object (*piṇḍa*) is destroyed, it is recognized in another individual object just like a universal (*sāmānya*). And just as a universal is connected with the very individual object that arises by the force of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), and is eternally established by its own nature, so too is mutual non-existence.

However, this much is the distinction: the apprehension of a universal occurs through the mere apprehension of the individual object, whereas the apprehension of mutual non-existence depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), because it must be determined in relation to something else.

"Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is the negation of that which is non-existent. If you argue that absolute non-existence is simply mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), oh, what a confusion on the royal highway! For mutual non-existence is the negation of the identity between two things—such as a cow and a horse—which are established in their own respective natures. Absolute non-existence, however, is the negation of something entirely non-existent, superimposed upon the intellect and unrestricted by space or time; for example, "there is no object of cognition other than the six categories."
Furthermore, if absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) were not admitted, the restriction that there are exactly six categories (*ṣaḍ eva padārthāḥ*) would be difficult to maintain.
Likewise, tradition (*aitihya*), when it is unerring, is simply the instruction of a reliable person (*āptopadeśa*).

*Nyāyakandalī* [197] [p.546]: Tradition (*aitihya*) that is non-false is nothing other than the instruction of a reliable person (*āptopadeśa*). The collection of particles "iti ha" occurs in the sense of a lineage of instruction; here, the suffix *ṣyañ* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*), resulting in the word *aitihyam*. Tradition that is false does not constitute a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all. Tradition that is non-false is simply the word of a reliable person.
