And the word of a reliable person is inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, the intention is that tradition which is non-false does not transcend inference. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [198–200] [p.547]:

Inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a five-membered statement. It should be understood that inference for the sake of others is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself to others—those who are doubtful, mistaken, or ignorant—exclusively by means of a five-membered statement.
(Nyāyakandalī [198], pp. 547–549)

For the purpose of explaining inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), he says: "Inference for others is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a five-membered statement. The collection of words within which the comprehension of the object to be communicated reaches its completion consists of five parts; these are called "members" (*avayava*) with respect to that collection. An "object ascertained by oneself" (*svaniścitārtha*) is an object determined by oneself as being invariably concomitant (*anantarīyaka*) with the probandum (*sādhya*); that is, the logical mark (*liṅga*) that is inseparable from the probandum.

The exposition of that [inference] by means of a five-membered statement—the employment of a five-membered statement capable of generating the cognition of it—is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). For a five-membered statement sets forth the logical mark (*liṅga*) in as many aspects as are required for the mark’s invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) to be fully established; and from the logical mark thus set forth, the establishment of the probandum occurs. It is not the case, however, that the statement itself directly causes the understanding of the probandum, for that would entail the consequence that the probandum is a verbal object (*śābda*).
Therefore, it is precisely the employment of a statement expressing a mark that is invariably concomitant [with the probandum] that is called inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna).

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of a word is that which the word aims at, and that a sentence aims at the probandum (*sādhya*), because it is employed for the purpose of communicating that. They argue that the communication of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is merely an intermediate operation, since a person who is in disagreement cannot understand the probandum through the mere statement of the mark alone; thus they explain it as follows: the probandum is the object ascertained by oneself. Having made the communication of its logical mark the intermediate operation, the communication of that [probandum] by means of a sentence consisting of five members is the employment of a sentence that communicates it;
this is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). [p. 549]

He explains what he has stated himself with the words beginning "by means of five members" (*pañcāvayavenaiva*). Some maintain that a statement consists of only two members; others, of three. To preclude those views, he employs the restrictive particle *eva*: "by means of five members *only*.

One who has doubt regarding the matter to be established is "doubtful" (*saṃśayita*); one who possesses contrary cognition is "mistaken" (*viparīta*); and one who has neither doubt nor misconception, but merely a lack of knowledge, is "uninstructed" (*avyutpanna*). All three are worthy of instruction, because they are devoid of the realization of reality (*tattva*). *Nyāyakandalī* [199], pp. 549–552.

When one employs a collection of words, it is generally recognized within oneself that one intends to convey the connection between the meanings of those words. Subsequently, through the employment of that collection of words, the cognition of the speaker’s intention to convey the connection between those word-meanings serves as the means for inferring the sentence-meaning from the words; however, the cognition of that [sentence-meaning] does not arise directly from the word-meanings. For the Mīmāṃsakas do not admit that what is called a "word-meaning" constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor does the capacity to convey the sentence-meaning emerge in word-meanings that are denoted by words individually for the sake of conveying the sentence-meaning; for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whose function consists solely in the apprehension of its object (*prameya*), cannot bestow a capacity upon that object. Therefore, if word-meanings were to convey the sentence-meaning, they would do so either as logical marks (*liṅga*) or through the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*); in either case, the sentence-meaning would not be verbal (*aśābda*).

Now, do words each convey their respective individual meanings as indicators of the sentence-meaning, or do they convey their own meanings as already mutually related? On this point, some first argue as follows: the communication of meaning by words depends upon linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). And linguistic usage—observed in the worldly interactions of elders such as "Bring the cow" or "Tie up the cow"—occurs with respect to a factor of action (*kāraka*) conjoined with an action, or an action conjoined with a factor of action, but not in isolation from these.
Therefore, it is only word-meanings that are mutually related which are communicated by the words.

On this point it is examined: if, in a sentence such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), the word *gām* alone expresses its own meaning as connected with the meaning of "bring," then the word *ānaya* would be redundant, because its meaning has already been stated. If it is argued that when the meaning of "bringing" is expressed by the word *ānaya*, the word *gām* then expresses its own meaning as connected with the meaning of "bring"—and therefore the word *ānaya* is not redundant—then it follows that the word *ānaya* expresses only its own isolated meaning and thus becomes a denoter of an unconnected meaning (*ananvitābhidhāyin*).

If this [first] word does not denote its own meaning as connected [with others], then the same would apply to every other word; thus, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of meanings as already connected) is abandoned. Now, if it is argued that even by the word *ānaya* ("bring"), its own meaning is denoted as connected with the meaning expressed by the preceding word, then as long as the preceding word has not yet denoted its own meaning, the subsequent word cannot denote its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the preceding word.

As long as the subsequent word does not express its own meaning, so long the preceding word cannot convey its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the subsequent word; thus, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). Now, if you think: "First, the words merely cause the individual word-meanings to be remembered, and subsequently they express their own meanings as connected with those meanings remembered from one another," and therefore there is no mutual dependence—[we reply:]...

That too is without substance; for words have always been perceived as associated with their own meanings in a state of syntactic connection (anvaya), and they are not capable of causing the recollection of a mere word-meaning in isolation from such a connection, since recollection proceeds in accordance with prior experience. In the linguistic usages of elders, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the restriction of the word "cow" (go-śabda) to the object possessing a hump and other such features is grasped, and not to its action, instrumentality, and so forth; for even when those [attributes] vary individually, the word "cow" is observed to be employed.

If it is argued that this word "cow" (*go*), when heard, due to the proficiency gained through repetition, recalls only the object possessing a hump and other such features—never deviating from its association with them—and not the action, instrument, and so forth; then, in that case, the principle that a word denotes only that object with which its association is observed to be restricted applies equally even to the denotation of unrelated meanings. Thus, the word would denote only that specific object where its concomitance has been grasped, and nowhere else.

Furthermore, it is well-established that recollection does not function by depending on a rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*) as inference does; rather, it is based solely on mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus, it occurs even from the sight of a mere counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). As it has been said: "Just as fire is remembered upon seeing smoke, so too a place such as a kitchen is remembered. Therefore, if the word "cow" causes the recollection of the individual cow-thing merely through the perception of its coexistence, it might at times also cause the recollection of those objects that are the counter-correlates of the cow-thing.

However, by necessity, reminding one only of the cow-substance (*gopiṇḍa*), it relies precisely on denotative power (*vācakatva*) directed toward that object, for it is only when this is the case that the restriction is possible. Furthermore, just as you maintain that words in a sentence denote their meanings as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*), so too do you maintain that within a word, the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) denote their meanings as already connected. If the respective meanings are denoted by those two as mutually connected, what other word-meaning remains that could be remembered subsequently? Let us leave aside these words, which have fallen into the camp of the naked wanderers (*nagnāṭaka*). *Nyāyakandalī* [200] [p. 553]

Let us return to the subject at hand. While it may be granted that words convey meaning in this manner, this [definition] does not cohere with the claim that "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*) exists. Either the inferential mark (*liṅga*) or the cognition produced by it is inference; yet neither the mark nor the cognition possesses the quality of being "for the sake of another. If it were argued that inference is called "for the sake of another" because the word expressing the inference is for the sake of another, then one might as well call perception "for the sake of another," since the word expressing perception is likewise for the sake of another?
As it has been said: "Inference belongs neither to the cognition itself nor to its cause; it does not belong to anything else."
And it is not established in either common worldly usage or in the Veda that these two have the purpose of another.

"Since speech is for the sake of another, inference is for the sake of another; why then is it not assumed that perception also serves another's purpose by means of that [speech]? To this we reply: We do not say that because speech is for the sake of another, its object (the thing expressed) must therefore be for the sake of inference. Rather, we say that the five-membered statement, being for the sake of another, is "inference" because it is a cause of inferential knowledge by way of the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*). [Objection: Even so, would there not be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of treating perception—which makes the logical mark known—as metaphorically "inference"? [Reply: There is no such consequence, because the term is not used in common worldly parlance in that context.
Praśastapādabhāṣya [201] [p.554]:

Furthermore, the members [of a syllogism] are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application (*upadeśa*), the illustration (*nidarśana*), the synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*).

Among these, the proposition is the enunciation of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) that is not contradictory [to established knowledge]. The proposition is a mere enunciation for the purpose of bringing the subject (*dharmin*)—as qualified by the property (*dharma*) one wishes to demonstrate—into the scope of the application; for example, "Air is a substance."
In the *Nyāyakandalī* [201] [pp.

554–557], it was stated that a statement consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*). What, then, are those five members? To this he says: "The members, moreover, are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application (*apadeśa*), the illustration (*nidarśana*), the synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*). The word "moreover" (*punaḥ*) is used for the ornamentation of the sentence.

Among those [members of the syllogism], the thesis (*pratijñā*) is the statement of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) that is not contradicted. He explains this himself with the words beginning "that which is intended to be made known," and so forth. That property (*dharma*) which is desired to be established, when it qualifies the subject (*dharmin*), is called the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) or the "position" (*pakṣa*). The mere statement of that—its simple mention without the means of proof—is the thesis. As the wise teach:
"The status of being a thesis belongs to the statement, and the status of being the position belongs to its meaning.

If the reason (*hetu*) is merely the statement of what is to be established (*uddeśamātra*), then it is the thesis (*pratijñā*); since there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through this, it does not deserve to be employed because it is not a constituent part of the proof (*asādhanāṅgatva*). As the Tathāgatas say:
"The statement of the reason indicates that which is capable, even though it is itself incapable;
the statement of the position (*pakṣokti*) from the mere naming of the probandum is not sufficient even indirectly."

Here he says: "In order to establish the scope of the reason (*apadeśa*). A reason (*hetu*) is an *apadeśa*; the thesis (*pratijñā*) is that which establishes—that is, demonstrates—the scope (*viṣaya*) of that [reason]. Indeed, wherever a reason is employed for the sake of proving a probandum (*sādhya*), it is because that [probandum] is already established; however, rather than being so in just any case, it must be restricted to a specific locus (*dharmin*). If that [locus] were not presented, the reason, being without a support, would not function.

If that [proposition] does not occur, there is no establishment of the probandum; therefore, by presenting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*) of the proposition, the subject is brought into proximity as the locus of the reason. Thus, the proposition, by way of demonstrating the locus, sets the reason in motion and is a constituent part of the establishment of the probandum. Accordingly, the *Nyāyabhāṣya* states: "In the absence of the proposition, the reason and other members would not function, being without a locus."

If it is argued that the locus (*āśraya*) of the reason is understood from the application (*upanaya*) alone, we say no; for if the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is absent, even that [application] does not function. Indeed, the application demonstrates the capacity of the means of proof (*sādhana*), characterized by its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Furthermore, the cognizer does not have an initial desire for the means of proof itself, but rather for the probandum (*sādhya*), because the latter is the primary object.

When the probandum (sādhya) is desired, the means of proof (sādhana)—which is a constituent part of its establishment—is required thereafter, and subsequently the capacity of that means of proof; thus, the statement of the probandum itself comes first, and the capacity of the means of proof is not stated beforehand, because it is not required at that time.

If it is argued that "the subject (dharmin) being qualified by the property (dharma) intended to be proven" is a contradiction, because that which is not established cannot serve as a qualifier—this is true; an unestablished thing does not function as a qualifier. However, the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma), once established, is now stated as a qualification of the subject in the proposition (pratijñā) for the purpose of making it known to one who is in disagreement regarding the subject.

For this very reason, the subject (*dharmin*) possesses real "being-a-pakṣa" (*pakṣatā*). This is because, although it is established in its own nature, it is not yet established as being qualified by the property to be proven; thus, it is possible for it to be brought forward in that specific form. The "property-of-being-in-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) of the logical reason (*hetu*) is likewise established in this same way. If one were to prove mere impermanence in general, then the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which is a property of sound, would indeed lack the status of being a property of the subject. However, when impermanence is to be proven specifically with respect to sound itself, this fault does not arise. As the Teachers have said: "This very thing, possessing a dual nature, is both the object to be known and the means of knowing."
"That which is to be understood is by means of an unestablished part, while that which makes it known is by means of an established part.

He states an example of the proposition (*pratijñā*): "Air is a substance. For one who understands air but does not understand its substantiality, the proposition is formulated—"Air is a substance"—to establish it, by specifying air as being qualified by the desired property of substantiality.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [202] [p. 558]

By the inclusion of the term "non-contradictory" (*avirodhi*), those [propositions] that contradict perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), one's own accepted scriptures (*svaśāstra*), or one's own words (*svavacana*) are excluded. For example: "Fire is not hot" contradicts perception; "The sky is a jar" contradicts inference; "[Wine may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa]" contradicts scripture (*āgama*); for a Vaiśeṣika who asserts that "the effect exists prior to its production," it contradicts his own school’s tenets (*svaśāstra*); and "A word does not convey meaning" contradicts one's own statement (*svavacana*). — *Nyāyakandalī* [202] [pp. 558–562]

He states the purpose of including the term "non-contradictory" (*avirodhi*): "By the inclusion of the term 'non-contradictory,' those [propositions] that contradict perception, inference, one's own accepted treatises, or one's own words are excluded. An object intended by the proponent to be established is called the "probandum" (*sādhya*). If only the word "proposition" (*pratijñā*) were used, even a statement contradicted by perception and so forth would be a proposition; however, this is not a proposition because its meaning cannot be established. Therefore, the term "non-contradictory" was included.

The meaning is this: that subject of inference for which there is no contradiction with perception and so forth is "non-contradicted by perception and so forth"; the statement of such a subject is a *pratijñā* (thesis), whereas that for which such a contradiction exists is not a *pratijñā*. What is expressed by this? It is not the case that something is a "probandum" (*sādhya*) merely by virtue of being included within the proponent's intention; rather, that which is fit to be established by proof is the probandum, and only that is the *pakṣa* (position); anything other than that is a fallacious position (*pakṣābhāsa*).

An example of contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth is: "Fire is not hot. This statement, "not hot," is a negation of the sensation of heat. And what is already known is what can be negated, not what is unknown. Furthermore, it is impossible for the heat of fire to be perceived elsewhere; nor is the cognition of that heat in fire inferential, because inference does not function in the absence of perception. When there is a negation of what has been cognized through perception, the inferential negation—which proceeds by accepting the validity of perception—is sublated by that very perception, which functions as its opposite, because its object has been removed.

What is the "removal of the object" (*viṣayāpahāra*)? It is the presentation of a contrary fact. When that occurs, what happens to inference? There is an absence of its arising. For when the heat of fire has been established by a primary perception whose object is uncontradicted, and when that [perception] has already occupied the cognitive space, the cognition of its being non-hot does not arise. This very thing constitutes a contradiction for the reason (*hetu*): namely, that when it is employed to establish non-heat, it fails to produce that cognition because it is contradicted by perception. As it has been said: "When there is a determination of the opposite, there is no room for the other."
"For when its root has not arisen, the object is already taken by the former [reason].

560] If it is argued that because sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) are contradictory, sublation is impossible for that which is invariably concomitant—then if "invariable concomitance" is intended to mean the three-fold character (*trairūpya*), there certainly is sublation of that which is invariably concomitant, as in the case of the very argument: "Fire is not hot, because it is produced. However, if it is said with the intention that invariable concomitance consists in the three-fold character being present while the object is unsublated—that there is no sublation of that which is invariably concomitant—then we say: "So be it" (*om*).
However, in order to specify that its very nature consists in having an object that is not sublated, the term "non-contradictory to perception and so forth" was employed.

Is contradiction with perception a defect of the *pakṣa* (the thesis) or of the *hetu* (the reason)? It is not a defect of the *pakṣa*, because the locus (*dharmin*) remains as it was. Nor is it a defect of the *hetu*, because the [reason] is efficacious within its own domain, whereas everything is equally incapable [of proving anything] outside its own domain. Rather, this is a fault of the proponent who employs a proof regarding what is not its proper domain.

If you maintain that a defect consists in the absence of fitness for the cognition of the intended thesis-meaning and the absence of fitness for its demonstration, then there is likewise a defect in the case of the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). For instance, the proposition "the sky is dense" contradicts inference. By whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) space is apprehended, by that very same means its eternity and partlessness are established; therefore, the proposition "space has dense parts" is contradicted by the inference that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*).

The proposition that "liquor may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa" contradicts scripture (*āgama*). The meaning of the thesis is that liquor, which is fit to be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa, does not become a cause of sin when consumed. Here, milk serves as the example; and the fact that milk is not a cause of sin is to be understood solely through the testimony of the Vedas (*śruti*), the Smṛtis, and the Āgamas.

Since the very same scripture that establishes that drinking milk is not a cause of sin also establishes that drinking liquor is a cause of great sin, the thesis "liquor may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa" contradicts the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the illustrative example.

For the Vaiśeṣika who asserts that the effect exists prior to its production, there is a contradiction with his own school's doctrine. For the Vaiśeṣika engages in debates and the like by accepting the authority of the Vaiśeṣika treatise. Thus, for him to assert that "the effect exists prior to its production" contradicts his own proposition according to his own school, because the Vaiśeṣika treatise establishes that "what is non-existent is produced.

The claim that "a word does not convey its meaning" is self-contradictory. If a word lacks the capacity to convey meaning, then the employment of a word to communicate the sense "a word does not convey its meaning" is untenable. If, on the other hand, this very word is employed for that purpose, then the word's capacity to convey meaning is admitted; thus, there is a contradiction between the proposition and one's own words.

A treatise (*śāstra*) is the exposition of the reality of things as understood through perception and inference. Contradiction with that [treatise] is simply contradiction with perception and inference. Likewise, for one who denies that a word’s capacity to convey meaning is to be apprehended through inference based on the principle of "the existence of the effect following the existence of the cause" (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*), the thesis is indeed contradicted by inference. Why, then, are contradiction with one's own treatise and contradiction with one's own words mentioned separately? To this it is replied: A treatise may also have its root in fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), such as those of the Śākyas and others; in this regard, [there is a distinction] for the Buddhist.

For one who asserts the proposition "everything is non-momentary," there is indeed a contradiction with one's own treatise, not a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). One's own statement might even sometimes be based on what is not a means of valid cognition; therefore, a contradiction with that is not a contradiction with a *pramāṇa*, but rather a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) alone.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [203], p. 563.

The statement of the mark (*liṅga*) is the *apadeśa*. That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred, which is established by its general presence everywhere in things of the same class, and which is entirely absent in everything contrary to it—that is called the mark; the statement of that is the *apadeśa*. For example: "because of possessing action" and "because of possessing qualities" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.13). And thus, possession of qualities exists in that object to be inferred and in all things of the same class, while possession of action exists in all [substances] except for some.
Both of these [properties] do not exist at all in that which lacks a real substance (*adravya*). Therefore, it is established that its verbal expression is the *apadeśa* (the indicative statement).

The *Nyāyakandalī* states: "The *apadeśa* is the statement of the mark (*liṅga*). He explains the meaning of this with the words beginning "that which by the object of inference... and so forth; this is easy to understand. He provides an example: "Because of possessing action and because of possessing qualities" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.13).

In the proposition (*pratijñā*) that "air is a substance" (*dravyam vāyuḥ*), the statement of the mark (*liṅga*) "because it possesses action" (*kriyāvattvāt*) is the *apadeśa* (the formal citation of the reason). In that same proposition, the statement of the mark "because it possesses qualities" (*guṇavattvāt*) is also the *apadeśa*. The presentation of both is for the purpose of demonstrating that both [marks]—that which exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and that which pervades all similar instances—are valid reasons (*hetu*). He says, "And so it is with that," meaning that the definition of a mark applies to both "possessing action" and "possessing qualities."

That possession of qualities exists in the subject (*anumeya*); it exists in all substances that are similar to it, which constitute the entire class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*); and it exists in some, namely in all material substances (*mūrtadravya*), which constitute a portion of the similar instances. Both of these—possession of action and possession of qualities—are entirely absent from non-substances, which constitute the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). The statement of both of these, in the form "because of possessing action" and "because of possessing qualities," is the *apadeśa*, that is, the logical reason (*hetu*). This is established and settled because it is free from defects. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [204] [p.564]
By this, it is stated that the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), the doubtful (sandigdha), and the non-ascertained (anadhyavasita) are not valid reasons (anapadeśa).

Among these, the unestablished (*asiddha*) is of four kinds: unestablished for both, unestablished for either one, unestablished by way of its existence, and unestablished with respect to the object of inference (*anumeya*). Therein, "unestablished for both" is that which is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent, such as: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses parts. "Unestablished for either one" is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product. "Unestablished by way of its existence" is, for example, when vapor is put forward as smoke while fire is to be inferred from the presence of smoke; in this case, the vapor is unestablished as being smoke. "Unestablished with respect to the object of inference" is, for example: "Darkness is earthy because it possesses a black color."

*Nyāyakandalī* [204] [pp. 564–566]: By this statement defining the *apadeśa* (the probans), it is stated by implication that the expressions of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the doubtful (*sandigdha*), and the indeterminate (*anadhyavasita*) are not valid *apadeśas*. By the phrase "coexisting with the object of inference" (*anumeyena sahacaritam*), the non-status of the unestablished expression as an *apadeśa* is stated. By the phrase "well-known in what is of the same class as that" (*tatsamānajātīye ca prasiddham*), the non-status of the contradictory and indeterminate expressions as *apadeśas* is stated. By the phrase "it does not exist at all in its opposite" (*tadviparīte nāsty eva*), the non-status of the doubtful expression as an *apadeśa* is stated; such is the distinction. [p. 565]

Among these—unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), doubtful (*sandigdha*), and unascertained (*anadhyavasita*)—he explains the unestablished: therein, the unestablished is fourfold: unestablished for both, unestablished for either one, unestablished in its existence, and unestablished regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*).

Among these, "unestablished for both" means unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent; for example, [the argument] "sound is impermanent because it possesses parts": since the state of possessing parts is established neither for the proponent nor for the opponent with respect to sound, it is unestablished for both.

The "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*) is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product. Although sound is in fact a product, this reason is unestablished for the Mīmāṃsaka who holds a contrary view. An unestablished reason does not prove the probandum as long as it has not been established itself.

The "unestablished in its very nature" (*tadbhāvāsiddha*) is as follows: when steam is presented as smoke in order to establish fire by means of smoke, that [steam] is unestablished in the nature of smoke—that is, in its actual form as smoke—and is thus called "unestablished in its very nature."

The unestablished in respect of the object of inference (*anumeyāsiddha*) is, for example: "Darkness is earthy because it possesses a black color. There is no such thing as darkness as a distinct substance, since what is perceived is merely the superimposed quality of blackness; therefore, the argument that "the substance darkness is earthy because it possesses a black color" is unestablished in respect of the object of inference, being unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Regarding the term *asiddhānumeya*, the analysis is: "that for which the object of inference is unestablished. Since the rule governing words like *āhitāgni* applies, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is placed first.

Just as a reason (*hetu*) may be unestablished for one party or unestablished for both, so too is the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) twofold. And just as a reason is unestablished for the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*) respectively, or for them both together—due to ignorance, doubt, or misconception—so too is the locus. Furthermore, just as a reason may be unestablished for the proponent due to his ignorance, yet doubtful-unestablished for the opponent; or alternatively, unestablished for the proponent due to his ignorance, yet unestablished through misconception for the opponent.

Alternatively, it may be unestablished through doubt for the proponent (*vādin*) and unestablished through ignorance for the opponent (*prativādin*). Or, it may be unestablished through error for the proponent and unestablished through doubt for the opponent. The same logic should be applied to the locus (*āśraya*) as well. As for those such as the unestablished qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), they are not mentioned separately because they are included within the categories of being unestablished for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*) or unestablished for both (*ubhayāsiddha*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [205], p. 567.

For that which, although present in the subject of inference (*anumeya*), does not exist in all members of its similar class (*tatsamānajātīya*), yet exists in those of the opposite class (*tadviparīta*), is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite; for example: "Because he has horns, therefore he is a horse.
[Nyāyakandalī, p.

567] He explains the contradictory fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*): For that which, although present in the subject of inference, does not exist in all members of its similar class, yet exists in those of the opposite class, is "contradictory" because it establishes the contrary.

When someone, having perceived a horn on a mass of earth hidden within a forest, establishes that "this mass is a horse because it possesses a horn," then that possession of a horn—being non-existent in other masses belonging to the class of horses and yet existing in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) such as cows and buffaloes which are the opposite of horses—is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*), because by the force of its pervasion (*vyāpti*), it establishes non-horseness, which is the opposite of the intended probandum (*sādhya*), namely horseness.

This is an example of a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) that exists in only a portion of the counter-instances (*vipakṣa*), because "having horns" is impossible in all non-horses, such as pillars and the like. An example of a contradictory reason that pervades all counter-instances should be understood as: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. [Prashastapadabhashya 206] That which, while existing in the object of inference (*anumeya*), is common to both similar and dissimilar classes, and being thus common, produces doubt, is called "doubtful" (*sandigdha*). For example: "Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow."

Some maintain that when two contradictory reasons possessing the aforementioned characteristics are encountered together, another type of "doubtful" (sandigdha) reason arises because doubt is observed; for example, regarding whether space is corporeal or incorporeal, the two reasons being its possession of motion and its lack of tangibility. But is this not simply the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason, like the property of not being perceptible to the eye, since neither of these two combined reasons can belong to either of the two possible sides?
And for that reason, we shall state later that it is "non-conclusive" (*anadhyavasita*).
— *Nyāyakandalī* [206] [pp. 568–570]

That which exists in the subject (*dharmin*) to be inferred, and is common to both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), is "doubtful" (*sandigdha*) because it generates uncertainty. For example: "Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow. When this individual body is being proved to be a cow on the grounds of its having horns, then "having horns"—since it is observed in both cows and buffaloes—produces doubt and thus constitutes a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). This is an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason that pervades the similar class but occurs only in a portion of the dissimilar class.

"Pervading both the similar and dissimilar instances" is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable. "Occurring in a portion of both the similar and dissimilar instances" is, for example: "Space is eternal, because it is incorporeal. "Occurring in a portion of the similar instances and pervading the dissimilar instances" is, for example: "Sound is a substance, because it is partless. The term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*)—which is explained by the phrase "existing in both"—refers to that which is common to both similar and dissimilar classes.

Just as a single reason (*hetu*) that produces doubt regarding the subject (*dharmin*) because it is observed in both similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) would be a doubtful fallacious reason (*sandigdha-hetvābhāsa*), so too, when two reasons of equal strength that establish contradictory meanings coincide within a single subject, a doubt is observed; therefore, some have said that this "coincidence of two contradictories" is another type of doubtful fallacious reason. He introduces [this view] in order to refute it, saying: "And in one... (*ekasmiṃśca*).

He provides an example of this: "Just as, with respect to the corporeality or incorporeality of the mind, there are the two reasons of possessing action and being intangible. [The arguments are: "The mind is corporeal because it possesses action, like an arrow," and "The mind is incorporeal because it is intangible, like space. When these two reasons—possessing action and being intangible—which establish contradictory objects are encountered, there arises a doubt regarding the corporeality or incorporeality of the mind. For in this case, neither of the two can be a valid proof, since it is impossible for one thing to possess both natures simultaneously.

Nor does the lack of probative power belong to both [reasons] due to their mutual contradiction, because there is no other possibility apart from being corporeal or incorporeal. Furthermore, no distinction between one or the other reason is perceived by which a determination for one side alone could be made. Therefore, based on the possession of action and the absence of tangibility, a doubt arises regarding the mind as to whether it is corporeal or incorporeal.

And this very point constitutes the difference between the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) and the "neutralized by the context" (*prakaraṇasama*): while the former produces doubt, the *prakaraṇasama*, when employed with respect to a doubtful matter, does not remove that doubt.

But surely this [reason] is indeed uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), because—just like the property of being perceptible by non-visual perception—it cannot belong to either of the two sides of a composite object. Furthermore, the properties of possessing action and lacking touch do not each produce doubt, because they are causes for certain determination (*nirṇaya*).

And this conjunction of those two is indeed uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), because it is impossible for those two combined to exist on either side—whether in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—apart from the mind itself; just as, although *non-visibility* and *perceptibility* each deviate from quality (*guṇa*) individually, their combination is impossible elsewhere apart from quality. Even though the occurrence of two contradictory, non-deviating properties is an uncommon characteristic, nevertheless, its function is solely that of a cause for doubt.

For in the case of a purely negative (vyatirekin) reason, exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) alone is certain; therefore, it serves as a cause for a definitive conclusion regarding the subject (pakṣa). However, in the case of an unshared (asādhāraṇa) reason, the exclusion is inconclusive (anaikāntika), because such exclusion is possible not only from the dissimilar instances but also from the similar instances (sapakṣa). In that regard, if the possession of odor were to establish permanence by virtue of being excluded from impermanent things, would it not also establish impermanence, since it is likewise excluded from permanent space? Yet the establishment of both cannot occur, because a single entity cannot possess two contradictory natures.

Nor is there a lack of establishment for both [the presence and absence of the property], because no other alternative exists. Therefore, due to the possession of odor, doubt arises regarding earth as to whether it is eternal or non-eternal. As Bhaṭṭa Miśra has said: "Where a unique property exists, that [property], by way of its own absence and because of the contradiction of its being neither [of the two alternatives], is the cause of our doubt."

And as for what the author of the *Nyāyavārttika* said—that "the state of being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajatva*) consists in having disjunction-produced disjunction (*vibhāgajavibhāga*) as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and this is not possible except in the case of sound"; thus, because it is excluded from all [other] things, it is a cause of doubt. To this he replies: "We shall say that, therefore, it is not determinative (*anadhyavasita*). The meeting of two contradictory [properties] is the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason]; and because it is uncommon, we shall say that this is "not determinative" (*anadhyavasita*). What would be stated? We shall say that an uncommon property does not effect determination (*adhyavasāya*), but rather, it does not effect doubt; such is the meaning.

Praśastapādabhāṣya [207] [p. 571]: Now, it may be argued that in the treatise, the observation of two possibilities in various instances is pointed out as a cause of doubt. This is not so; doubt does not arise from the mere observation of two objects. Rather, the observation of two objects is the sole instrumental cause for the production of doubt. Furthermore, if those two were of equal strength, they would mutually contradict one another and thus fail to produce a definitive conclusion, rather than serving as causes for doubt. Moreover, those two are not of equal strength, because one of them—the subject of inference—is sublated by scripture (āgama). This, however, is merely a specific type of contradiction (viruddha-bheda).

*Nyāyakandalī* [207] [pp. 571–576]. Having established that the "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is not a cause of doubt, he raises an objection regarding its contradiction with the *Śāstra*. "Now, in the *Śāstra*, it is taught in various places that 'perceiving in two ways' (*ubhayathā-darśana*) is a cause of doubt. This refers to "perceiving in two ways," which is stated in various places in the *Śāstra* as follows: "Perceiving a single substratum (*dharmin*) together with two contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharma*) is a cause of doubt. As it is said: "Having seen what was seen before, doubt arises" (*vai. a. 2.2.20*).

18) Just as intangibility is observed in the self (ātman) along with formlessness, and is likewise seen in the mind (manas), so too is activity observed in the atom (paramāṇu) along with materiality. Therefore, having observed that activity is seen in the atom along with materiality—just as intangibility was seen in the self along with formlessness—a doubt arises: "Is the mind material, or is it formless?"

"Because it is seen in both ways—as seen according to its nature and as seen contrary to its nature—there is doubt" (Nyāya Sūtra 2.2.19). For instance, the mind is "seen" in one way together with "action-possessingness," which is invariably concomitant with corporeality; therefore, it is "not seen" in that same way together with "tangible-possessingness," which is invariably concomitant with incorporeality. Thus, "because it is seen in both ways," there is doubt: is the mind corporeal because it possesses action? Or is it incorporeal because it lacks tangibility? Such is the meaning of the sūtra.

Thus, for one who rejects that the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is a cause of doubt, there is a contradiction with the treatise (*śāstra*). He resolves this: "There is no doubt, because of the perception of two distinct objects. As for what you said—that there is a contradiction with the treatise—that is not so, because doubt arises from the perception of two distinct objects. He explains this very point: "In the production of doubt, the perception of two distinct objects is the cause."

When a doubt arises regarding a subject (*dharmin*) that possesses an upward nature—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—the cause of that doubt is the prior perception of the object in both ways, that is, its perception together with both the states of being a post and being a person; it is not, however, caused by the conjunction of two contradictory properties in a single subject. Therefore, the intended meaning of the Sūtra is not that doubt arises from the occurrence of two contradictory and non-erroneous properties.

And thus, "seen as seen" (dṛṣṭavaddṛṣṭa) means this: having seen an object already perceived—whether it be a post or a person—as being "seen as seen," that is, existing in a manner identical to other previously seen posts or persons (meaning, similar to other posts or persons), and then seeing it again in another place or at another time, when no distinguishing feature is perceived due to some cause, doubt arises.

The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "it is seen" (dṛṣṭam ca) implies that even though an object was not previously seen, doubt arises upon seeing it as similar to both a post and a man—objects already seen. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, another sūtra—namely, "seen as it was," "seen as it was not," and "seen as both"—demonstrates doubt produced by the recollection of the specific qualities of a single object. A person previously seen is "seen as it was" in whichever particular state he was observed, whether shaven-headed or with matted hair; from that, he is "seen as it was not" when seen in another distinct state at a later time. Thus, for one who does not perceive the specific state but remembers it, there arises a doubt regarding that very same person's prior, unstable, and dual states.
The meaning of the sūtra is that there might arise a doubt as to whether this person is now shaven-headed or whether he has matted hair;

however, the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is not a cause for doubt, because it is never actually employed in practice. For if the first reason is understood to possess the aforementioned definition, then the object determined from it remains exactly as such, and thus there is no employment of a second reason, since its application would be sublated by the cognition already established.

Now, if this [reason] does not possess the characteristics as previously described, then this very same fault must be stated; what is the use of a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*)? A counter-inference that is contradictory does not deviate from its object; thus, the first reason is "contradictory and non-deviating" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*), and its fault is precisely this: the possibility of a contrary inference. If it is argued that when a counter-position is established by the second [reason], the first lacks the capacity to prove its own probandum (*sādhya*), we reply: if the first, like the second, is endowed with the characteristics of a valid inference, then the first is not incapable of proving its point.

If that [reason] is not a prover, then what confidence can there be in any other inference? If you say it is because it is not a prover due to the absence of two forms in the real entity (*vastu*), who has said that the real entity does not possess two forms? For in whatever way a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) makes an object known, that alone is its true nature (*tattva*).

Now, if this matter—that a single entity cannot possess both natures—is established by very firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and cannot be otherwise, then there is no such thing as an equality of strength between those two, because one of them is in accordance with reality; so how can there be doubt? If it is argued: "Even though in the actual state of things neither of the two possesses conformity to reality, nevertheless, due to the non-perception of any distinction between them, there may arise the conceit of an equality of strength," let it be so; even then, because of that equality of strength, the first [cognition] would be [sublated] by the subsequent one.

Just as [the latter] is obstructed, so too is the latter obstructed by the former; thus, due to mutual obstruction, neither would be capable of establishing its own probandum, yet they do not produce doubt. This is because, through the mere non-perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣānupalambha*), there is no presentation of both contradictory particulars. Thus he says: "And when those two are of equal strength, because of their mutual contradiction, they would fail to produce a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), but they do not serve as a cause for doubt."

[Objection: "Is it not the case that whatever entity exists must be either corporeal (*mūrta*) or incorporeal (*amūrta*), and no other category besides the corporeal and the incorporeal is perceived? Therefore, even though neither corporeality nor incorporeality is perceived in the mind, for one who considers the non-existence of both or the existence of both to be impossible, doubt regarding one of the two alternatives certainly arises. [Reply: True, it does indeed arise; however, it is not due to the conjunction of two contradictory and non-deviating properties (*viruddhāvyabhicāri-dharma*), but rather because of its being an entity (*vastutva*).

For the fact of being an entity, which has been observed to be concomitant with both corporeality and incorporeality, brings those two to mind through the medium of memory when it is perceived in the mind.

Having granted for the sake of argument that the two reasons possess equal force, the status of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) as a cause of doubt was refuted; however, these two do not actually possess equal force. This is because, regarding one of them—the thesis that "the mind is formless" (*amūrtaṃ manaḥ*)—its absence is established by scripture (*āgama*), since the mind is atomic (*aṇu manaḥ*) according to the sūtra (A. 7, Bhā. 1, Sū. 23). If, on the other hand, this sūtra is not authoritative and the mind is indeed all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), then there would be no proof whatsoever for the existence of the mind, and thus the reason "because it is intangible" (*asparśatvāt*) in the argument "the mind is formless" would be unestablished in its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Now, the non-simultaneity of cognitions establishes [the existence of] the mind; however, this is sublated by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (dharmin). For if the mind possesses atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*), the non-simultaneity of cognitions is possible; whereas if the mind were all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), it would be in contact with all the sense organs simultaneously, which would entail the occurrence of cognitions all at once.

What is the fault in the subject of inference (*anumeya-uddeśa*) being in contradiction with scripture (*āgama*)? To this he says: "But this is merely a variety of the contradictory (*viruddha*). The meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is as follows: this subject of inference contradicted by scripture is merely a sub-variety of those fallacious propositions (*pratijñābhāsa*) already excluded by the term "non-contradictory" (*avirodhin*), namely those contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth; it is not a separate fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) called "doubtful" (*saṃdigdha*). Rather, it is simply a variety of the contradictory. This is the sense of the particle "but. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, pp. 577–578.

That which exists in the object of inference (*anumeya*) and is present only among things of its own class and not among those of a different class is "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*); it is called "inconclusive" (*anadhyavasita*) because it does not serve as a cause for certain determination. For example: "The effect pre-exists [in the cause], because it arises. This is subsumed under the statement: "That which is unestablished is not a valid reason" (*Vaiśeṣikasūtra* 3.1.15).

[Page 578] But has this not been stated in the *Śāstra* as a cause for doubt: "Because a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣa*) is observed in two ways among things of equal class that are distinct entities" (NS 2.2.22)? No, because it serves a different purpose. It was said that doubt does not arise regarding sound because a distinguishing feature is perceived in it; however, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) cannot be a distinguishing feature of any one among the categories such as substance (*dravya*), but rather it becomes a universal (*sāmānya*). Why? Because among things of equal class that are distinct entities—namely, the various divisions of substance and so forth—one by one...

When it is stated that "doubt arises because a particular property is observed in two ways," this is not a cause for doubt; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of doubt arising regarding all six categories. Therefore, doubt arises solely from the perception of a commonality (*sāmānya*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [208] [pp. 577–581]

The "undetermined" (*anadhyavasita*) is said to be the uncommon fallacious reason (*asādhāraṇa-hetvābhāsa*). He explains it as follows: that which exists in the subject (*anumeya*), but does not exist in either its similar or dissimilar classes, is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to one or the other; because it is a cause for non-determination, it is called "undetermined. For example: "The effect exists [prior to its production], because it is produced. When it is to be proven that every effect exists even prior to its production, the reason "because it is produced" belongs to the Sāṃkhyas.

Since it is absent in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as space and absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) such as a sky-flower, it does not lead to a definitive determination regarding either side. The Sāṃkhyas maintain that "origination" (*utpatti*) is simply the manifestation later of that which was previously unmanifest in the form of a capacity to produce a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, for them, the reason "because of origination" is not unestablished (*asiddha*) in itself. He asks: by which statement of the author of the Sūtras is this "unascertained" (*anadhyavasita*) fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) subsumed? He replies: it is included under the statement, "This is an unestablished non-indicator" (*aprasiddho 'napadeśaḥ*, NS 3.1.15).

An uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), like an inconclusive one (*anaikāntika*), produces doubt; therefore, its inclusion under the rule "that which is doubtful and not stated" (*saṃdigdhaścānapadeśaḥ*) is appropriate, rather than under the term "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*). With this intention, he says: "But surely this cause of doubt has been stated in the treatise: 'Because a specific feature is observed in two ways—among those of the same class and among those belonging to a different category. In the phrase "among those of the same class and among those belonging to a different category," the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*).

The specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) of things arises from their being distinct from other entities belonging to the same class; for example, the possession of odor in earth is a specific characteristic that distinguishes it from other substances as well as from qualities and actions.

Regarding sound (*śabda*), the specific property of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is observed. Is this its distinction from things of the same class (*sajātīya*), such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, or from things of a different class (*vijātīya*)? If sound is a quality (*guṇa*), then this distinction is from things of the same class, namely color and so forth; but if it is a substance (*dravya*) or an action (*karman*), then it is from things of a different class. Thus, because of the audibility of sound, there arises a doubt as to whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action. When the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) has thus demonstrated the contradiction with the Sūtra, [the author] says: "No, because it has another purpose" (*nānyārthatvāt*).

This is not the meaning of the Sūtra—that a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is a cause of doubt—but rather its meaning is something else entirely. He demonstrates that very meaning with the words "because of the perception of a specific quality in sound" (*śabde viśeṣadarśanāt*), etc. Having established that "sound is that object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing," the author of the Sūtra stated: "In regard to that, there is doubt as to whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action" (VaiSū 2.2.25).
This is the meaning of that statement: regarding that object apprehended by the sense of hearing, there is a doubt as to whether it is a substance, or a quality, or perhaps an action.

Regarding this, another has said: "By you, who state that there is doubt concerning sound when it is apprehended by the auditory organ, you have stated that the very fact of being apprehended by the auditory organ is the cause of the doubt. And since being apprehended by the auditory organ is a specific property (*viśeṣa*), doubt is untenable upon the perception of that [specific property]."

For doubt is preceded by the recollection of two contradictory [features], and such recollection does not arise from the perception of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), because that [unique property] is never perceived along with any particularity—this being the objection raised by the opponent, the author of the Sūtras has provided this rebuttal: "Audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is not a particularity of any one among substances and so forth; audibility is not a particularity of any one among substances, qualities, or actions, but rather it is simply a universal (*sāmānya*) common to them."

It is established; why? Because it has been stated that the specific difference (*viśeṣa*) of each individual among the various categories—substance and so forth—is observed in two ways: among those of the same class and among those that are different entities. "Differences" (*bhedāḥ*) means those which are differentiated; the "differences consisting of substance and so forth" (*dravyādibhedāḥ*) are simply substance, quality, and action. Among these, the specific difference of each individual substance, quality, or action from those of the same class and from those that are different entities is "observed in two ways."

Is the specific property of earth (*pṛthivītva*), which distinguishes it from other classes, observed together with substantiality (*dravyatva*)? Is the specific property of color (*rūpatva*), which distinguishes it [from other qualities], observed together with quality-ness (*guṇatva*)? Is the specific property of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇatva*), which distinguishes it [from other actions], observed together with action-ness (*karmatva*)? Even for sound, its specific property of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is observed together with quality-ness. Therefore, this too, in its form as a specific property, is indeed a generality (*sāmānya*) of substances and the rest. Consequently, it is logical that it serves as a cause of doubt in that form.

Furthermore, that which is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) is not a cause of doubt, because it does not cause the recollection of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*); thus he says, "it is not a cause of doubt. Although it should have been stated in the Sūtra as "from things of the same class and from things belonging to other classes," the use of the locative case implies this meaning as well. For instance, upon perceiving the specific property of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) in sound, there arises the doubt: "Is it a substance, a quality, or an action?"

Because the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*) of each of the divisions—substance (*dravya*) and so forth—are observed among their own homogeneous classes (*sapakṣa*) and among heterogeneous classes (*vipakṣa*). What is meant by this? A specific characteristic is observed in substance, quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*); and in sound (*śabda*), audibility (*śravaṇatva*) is observed as its specific characteristic. Therefore, due to the presence of this specific characteristic, there arises doubt regarding whether it belongs to the category of substance and the others.

If even an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) were a cause of doubt, then there would be the undesirable consequence of doubt regarding all six categories, because they all possess uncommon properties; and from that, there would follow the consequence of doubt never ceasing. Thus he says: "Otherwise, there would be the consequence of doubt regarding all six categories. He concludes with: "Therefore..."

A common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is one observed to have a concomitance with two contradictory particulars; it is capable of causing the recollection of those two. The point of the summary is that doubt arises precisely from the perception of such a common property, and not from the perception of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [209] [p. 582]

The illustration (*nidarśana*) is of two kinds: by similarity (*sādharmya*) and by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Among these, the demonstration of the concomitance of the general nature of the mark (*liṅga-sāmānya*) with the general nature of the object to be inferred (*anumeya-sāmānya*) is the illustration by similarity. For example: "Whatever possesses action is observed to be a substance, as for instance an arrow. And the demonstration of the absence of the mark in the absence of the object to be inferred is the illustration by dissimilarity; for example: "Whatever is not a substance does not possess action, as for instance existence (*sattā*). — *Nyāyakandalī*, p. 582.

In order to define the nature of the example (*nidarśana*), he says: "The example is of two kinds: by similarity (*sādharmya*) and by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). The distinction is as follows: that statement by which the concomitance (*anugama*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is demonstrated is the example by similarity; that statement by which the exclusion of the probans through the exclusion of the probandum is demonstrated is the example by dissimilarity. Among those two, he states the example by similarity with the words beginning "tatrānumeya... (there, the object of inference...).

That is indeed clear. He states the illustration by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nidarśana*) with the words "in the case of the opposite of the object of inference" (*anumeya-viparyaye*), and so forth. That too is indeed clear.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [210], p. 583.

By this, fallacious examples (*nidarśanābhāsa*) are excluded. They are as follows: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is seen to be incorporeal is eternal, such as an atom, such as action, such as a pot, such as darkness, and such as space. And: "Whatever is a substance is seen to possess activity. These are the fallacious examples based on similarity (*sādharmya-nidarśanābhāsa*), which are respectively: unestablished in the mark (*liṅga-asiddha*), unestablished in the object to be inferred (*anumeya-asiddha*), unestablished in both (*ubhaya-asiddha*), non-concomitant (*ananugata*), and concomitant with the opposite (*viparītānugata*). *Nyāyakandalī* [210] [pp. 583–585]

By this, fallacious illustrations (*nidarśanābhāsa*) are excluded. Although they are not actual illustrations, they appear as if they were illustrations due to some commonality; thus, they are "fallacious illustrations" because they resemble illustrations. By this statement of the definition of an illustration, they are effectively excluded, since they lack that defining characteristic.

As long as the nature of fallacious illustrations (*nidarśanābhāsa*) is not understood, it is impossible to either avoid them in one's own statement or to criticize them in the statement of another; therefore, he explains their nature: for example, "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is incorporeal is seen to be eternal, such as an atom, such as an action, such as a pot, such as darkness, or like space; and whatever is a substance is seen to possess motion. And so forth.

The fallacious examples based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are those where the mark (*liṅga*), the probandum (*anumeya*), or both are unestablished (*asiddha*), as well as those that are non-concomitant (*ananugata*) or conversely concomitant (*viparītānugata*). For example: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom (*paramāṇu*). This is a fallacious example where the mark is unestablished (*liṅgāsiddha*), because an atom lacks incorporeality. "Like action (*karman*). This is one where the probandum is unestablished (*anumeyāsiddha*), because action lacks eternity. "Like a pot (*sthālī*). This is one where both are unestablished (*ubhayāsiddha*); for in a pot, neither the property to be proven—eternity—nor the means of proof—incorporeality—is present.

The example "like darkness" (*tamaḥ*) is one where the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*). Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), there is no such thing as "darkness," where could the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans be stated? The example "like space" (*ambaravat*) is a fallacious illustration (*darśanābhāsa*) because it lacks positive concomitance (*ananugata*). For although both eternality and incorporeality exist in space, it does not state that "whatever is incorporeal is necessarily eternal"; rather, it merely says "like space."

Nor does this statement lead to the cognition of the existence of the probandum and the probans in space for one who has not accepted [the premise]; therefore, this is a non-concomitant fallacy of the example (*nidarśanābhāsa*). The claim that "whatever is a substance is seen to possess action" is a case of inverse concomitance (*viparītānugata*). Furthermore, in the argument "Air is a substance because it possesses action," action-possessingness is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and substantiality is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). And since the pervasion is restricted to the pervaded alone, it does not reside conjointly in both like conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for the pervader would otherwise deviate from the pervaded.

Even in cases where there is co-extensive pervasion, such as between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), where the pervaded (*vyāpya*) also possesses the nature of being a pervader (*vyāpaka*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is nevertheless based solely on its character as being pervaded, and not on its character as being a pervader; for that latter form [of pervasion] can also exist in cases of deviation (*vyabhicārin*).
As the Teachers have taught:
"Although the pervaded is grasped as a pervader in reality..."
"Even when there is an excess [of the pervader], it would not establish the pervaded because it is not contradictory [to its absence].

Therefore, pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be shown as residing in the pervaded (*vyāpyagatatvena*), as in: "Whatever has action is a substance. It is not shown as residing in the pervader (*vyāpakagatatvena*), because that [pervasion] is absent therein; thus, this is a case of following the reverse order (*viparītānugata*). Regarding the compound *liṅgānumeyobhayāśrayāsiddha*: "the mark (*liṅga*), the object of inference (*anumeya*), both (*ubhaya*), and the substratum (*āśraya*)"—those for whom these are unestablished (*asiddha*) are "those for whom the mark, the object of inference, both, and the substratum are unestablished" (*liṅgānumeyobhayāśrayāsiddha*). The construction is: those for whom the mark, the object of inference, both, and the substratum are unestablished, and those who are non-concomitant (*ananugata*), and those who follow the reverse order (*viparītānugata*).
Praśastapādabhāṣya [211] [p.585]:

That which is impermanent is observed to be corporeal, as for example action, as for example an atom, as for example space, as for example darkness, like a jar; and that which is motionless is a non-substance—these are the fallacious illustrations of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), namely: those where the mark is absent from both the prover and the probandum, those where the substratum is unestablished, and those where the exclusion is either non-existent or contrary.

The *Nyāyakandalī* [211] [pp. 585–586] explains the fallacious examples of negative concomitance (*vaidharmyanidarśanābhāsa*) with the words beginning "that which is impermanent," etc. "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; that which is impermanent is corporeal, like action"—this is a fallacious example of negative concomitance where the mark (*liṅga*) is not excluded [from the counter-example], because action lacks corporeality. "Like an atom"—this is one where the mark is not excluded from the object of inference (*anumeya*), for eternality (the property to be inferred) is not excluded from the atom. "Like space"—this is one where the mark is excluded from both [the subject and the object of inference], for neither incorporeality nor eternality is excluded from space.

The example "like darkness" (*tama*) is one where the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*). For in ultimate reality, darkness itself does not exist; what, then, would be the basis for the exclusion of the probandum and the probans? The example "like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*) is one where there is no exclusion (*avyāvṛtta*). Although there is indeed an exclusion of the probandum and the probans in the case of a jar, one does not state it in the form "whatever is impermanent is corporeal. Since the opponent does not achieve an understanding of the exclusion of the probandum and the probans when it is not stated in that way, this is therefore an instance of non-exclusion (*avyāvṛtta*).

"That which is inactive is not a substance" is the exclusion by way of contrariety (*viparītavyāvṛtta*). Just as the probandum (*sādhya*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), so too is the absence of the probandum the pervaded and the absence of the probans the pervader.
As it has been said:
"The nature of being governed and being the governor in two entities is considered to be such [as described]."
"Those two very same [properties] are perceived in reverse in the case of their absences.

In that context, regarding the argument "Air is a substance because it possesses motion," one ought to state "it is devoid of motion" in order to demonstrate the pervasion in the counter-example (viparyaya-vyāpti). However, this [proponent] does not say that; rather, he says: "Whatever is devoid of motion is not a substance. But in this way, there is no pervasion, because space, although devoid of motion, is still a substance. Therefore, this is a fallacious example based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya-nidarśanābhāsa), as it fails to exclude the two contrary cases.

The mark (*liṅga*), the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), and both together constitute "the mark, the object to be inferred, and both. Those for whom these are not excluded are so described. That whose locus (*āśraya*) is unestablished is "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*). The explanation is that there are four types: that which is not excluded from the mark, the object to be inferred, and both; that which is unestablished in its locus; that which is non-excluded (*avyāvṛtta*); and that which is excluded in the opposite way (*viparītavyāvṛtta*). — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [212], p. 587.

In the context of an illustration (*nidarśana*), "corroboration" (*anusandhāna*) refers to the application (*anvānayana*) or connection to the object of inference (*anumeya*) of the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) which was previously observed together with the generality of the property to be inferred. Corroboration is that statement by which the general mark—which has been stated merely as a property of the object of inference, whose capacity to prove is not yet perceived, and which was seen in the illustration together with the generality of the property to be proven—is connected to the object of inference. For example: "And thus, air possesses motion.
Furthermore, having perceived its non-existence in the absence of the object of inference, one concludes: "But air is not thus devoid of motion.
*Nyāyakandalī* [212] [pp. 587–589]

In the context of an illustration (*nidarśana*), *anusandhāna* (corroboration) is the application (*anvānayana*)—that is, the demonstration of the presence—in the object of inference (*anumeya*) of the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) which was observed together with the general property to be inferred (*anumeyasāmānya*). An illustration (*nidarśana*) is an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) because in it the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is shown (*nidarśyate*) as being certain. That statement by which the application—that is, the demonstration of the existence—in the object of inference, the subject of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*), of the general mark which was observed and cognized together with the general property to be proven in that illustration, is performed, is *anusandhāna*.

The logical mark (*liṅga*), which has been shown in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as being inseparable from the property to be proven (*sādhyāvinābhūta*), is subsequently applied to or established in the subject (*pakṣa*); this is according to the etymological derivation [of *anvaya*] as "that by means of which [the mark] is connected. He explains his own statement precisely with this: "the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) is stated merely as the property to be inferred (*anumeyadharma*). The intention is that immediately after the proposition (*pratijñā*), the logical mark is stated as a reason (*hetu*) merely in the sense that "it exists in the object to be inferred through its exclusion from other things" (*vastuvyāvṛttyā*), but its actual presence in the locus (*dharmī*) has not yet been asserted.

The capacity of the logical mark (*liṅga*) to establish the probandum consists of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Since this capacity is not previously understood through the statements of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), that statement by which the mark—whose capacity was thus unperceived—is connected with the object of knowledge in which it is observed together with the generality of the property to be proven, is called "connection" (*anusandhāna*).

This is the intended meaning here: a word is employed for the sake of another in whatever way the other’s desire to know arises; and when the probandum (*sādhya*) has been stated, the cognizer develops an expectation regarding the probans (*sādhana*), namely, "How is this established? However, there is no such expectation regarding the capacity of the probans, because the desire to know its capacity is preceded by the comprehension of its own nature.

And when the probans is expected, the statement of the reason (*hetu*) being uttered expresses only the essential nature of the reason, not its property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), since a single word cannot have two distinct meanings.

When the reason has been cognized, if there arises a desire to know its capacity—namely, "How does this possess the nature of a reason?"—then, because the cognition of the probandum is inseparable from the cognition of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), once the concomitance has been stated by means of the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the subsequent possibility of the reason, whose capacity has now been ascertained, within the subject (*pakṣa*) is what is to be investigated. Therefore, the application (*upanaya*) must be accepted immediately after the example for the purpose of understanding the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). [Objection: The status of being a feature of the subject is understood through the very power of the statement of the reasonhood.

If it is argued that [the reason] is unproven because it possesses a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*), then by the very power of its expression, pervasion (*vyāpti*) will also be obtained; since that which is unrelated cannot function as a reason (*hetu*), even an example (*udāharaṇa*) need not be stated.

If it is argued that because even a non-common [reason] can be designated as a cause through error, there is no absolute cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) from that [reason], and thus pervasion (*vyāpti*) is demonstrated by means of the example (*udāharaṇa*); [we reply: since we observe the designation of something not existing in the subject (*dharmin*) as a cause due to delusion, the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not thereby established; therefore, the application (*upanaya*) must be stated for the purpose of ascertaining the existence of the mark (*liṅga*) residing in the example within the subject.

If it is asked: "How can there be an establishment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) even from that [statement of application], since the application is seen even when [the reason] is unestablished due to error? [The reply is: "How can there be an establishment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) from that [statement of example], since the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is seen even for one whose invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is unestablished due to delusion? If it is argued: "In the example, the ascertainment of the positive concomitance follows the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion, and not by mere words, because the latter would be no different in all cases," [then we reply: "In the application (*upanaya*) as well, the ascertainment of its being a property of the subject follows precisely from the means of valid cognition that grasps the property of the subject; it does not arise from mere words."

If it is argued that the conformity to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) occurs solely through the statement of the reason (*hetu*), because it would otherwise be impossible; then, by that same impossibility of being otherwise, there will be conformity to the means of valid cognition which apprehends pervasion (*vyāpti*).
