If it is argued that since the statement of the reason has another purpose, it lacks the capacity for application (*upanaya*), and therefore its presentation is performed by means of the example (*udāharaṇa*); then let this same method be followed here as well—enough with such far-fetched possibilities!

"Let it be that the application (*upanaya*) exists; however, is the statement of the reason (*hetu*) then redundant? No, for if the reason were not stated, there would be no comprehension of the nature of the proof (*sādhana*). Consequently, since the desire to know its capacity would be impossible, there would be no engagement with the statements of the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the other members. Thus says the *Nyāyabhāṣya*: "In the absence of a reason, of what would the status as a means of proof be demonstrated?
(Praśastapādabhāṣya, pp. 590–591).

*Pratyāmnāya* (the conclusion) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the purpose of producing certainty in others regarding that which was indicated as the object of inference and remains unsettled. *Pratyāmnāya* is the restatement of the proposition for the purpose of producing certainty in others—whose capacities have been stimulated by the other members of the argument, such as the reason (*hetu*), and who are presented with a completed sentence—regarding that which was indicated as the object to be established and remains unsettled; therefore, [sound] is indeed a substance (*dravya*).

For if this [conclusion] were absent, the preceding members—whether taken collectively or individually—would lack the capacity to express that meaning. If it is argued that this is not so because the meaning is already understood [by implication], we say no, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To explain: immediately after the proposition (*pratijñā*), one need only state the reason (*hetu*); since learned persons will recall the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the understanding of the meaning will follow. Therefore, the completion of the purpose occurs right here. *Nyāyakandalī* [213] [pp. 590–591]

He demonstrates the form of positive concomitance (*anusandhāna*) as follows: "And likewise, air possesses action. He states the negative concomitance (*vaidharmyānusandhāna*): "Having perceived the absence of one [property] in the absence of the inferable [subject], he declares: 'But air is not thus inactive.'"

He explains the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*): "The conclusion is the restatement of the proposition for the purpose of producing certainty again in others regarding that which was indicated as the object of inference and which remains uncertain. When the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has been indicated by the statement of the proposition as the object of inference—that is, as that which is to be established—and it remains uncertain within that very subject of the proof (*sādhyadharmin*), the conclusion is that verbal expression by which its restatement is made through repetition. Thus, it is called the conclusion.

For what purpose is there a restatement of that which has already been stated? To this he says: "In order to bring about certainty in others. First, the probandum (*sādhya*) was stated, but it was not yet certain, because the probandum is not established by the mere statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*). Once the reason (*hetu*) has been shown and the efficacy of that reason has been explained, certainty is produced through the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*); thus, its utility is established. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning, "designated as the object to be understood," and so forth.

Initially, the ascertainment of the probandum for others does not occur through the mere statement [of the proposition]. Once the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the reason has been demonstrated by means of the members [of the syllogism]—the reason, the example, and the application—and the capacity for the comprehension of the inferable has arisen in them, the ascertainment is produced by a "complete" statement rather than an "incomplete" one when the restatement (*pratyāmnāya*) is made. For this purpose, the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) proceeds; its example is: "Therefore, it is indeed a substance."

Is the probandum (sādhya) determined by the members [of the syllogism] themselves, such as the reason (*hetu*) and so forth; what, then, is the purpose of the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*)? To this he replies: "For if this were absent... The members, beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*), each terminate in their own individual meaning; in the absence of the conclusion, they are unable to convey a single unified meaning because they are independent. But when this [conclusion] exists, they are embraced by the expectancy for that meaning and enter into a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva*), whereby they become capable [of conveying the whole]; thus, the conclusion is appropriate. He raises the objection once more: "Because its meaning is already understood..."

The intention here is as follows: whatever collection of conditions constitutes the means of comprehension in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), that very same collection also constitutes it in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). This, however, is the distinction: in one's own realization, this [collection] is synthesized by oneself; in the realization of another, it is made known to the other. Furthermore, while the object is understood by oneself through the power of the logical mark (*liṅga*), that same [mark] is the communicator for the other as well. The verbal statement, however, fulfills its purpose merely by introducing the logical mark.

And it has been established that the logical mark (*liṅga*)—endowed with the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—is set forth by the members [of the syllogism] beginning with the reason (*hetu*). Since the comprehension of the object is possible through that much alone, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is redundant. To this, he replies: "No, because of the risk of over-extension. A sentence conveys only the capacity of the logical mark, not the object itself.

However, its capacity consists not merely in external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) and the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); for even when these are present, there are cases of the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) and the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) reasons which lack probative force. Rather, its capacity also includes having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*). As long as both of these are not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the suspicion that a counter-argument might exist cannot be dispelled.

Even when the property-bearer (*dharmin*) has been withdrawn from the proof, the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) is untenable; therefore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of contrary evidence (*viparītapramāṇa*). By this [conclusion], the means of knowledge that apprehends the absence of contrary evidence is shown. Once that absence has been established and the non-existence of the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) and "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) fallacies has been ascertained, the proof, whose capacity has been made manifest, establishes the probandum; such is the utility of the restatement (*pratyāmnāya*).

In this regard, if a rejection is made of the view that even what is not explicitly stated can be understood through implication (*sāmarthya*), then the example (*udāharaṇa*) and other members must also be rejected; for when the reason (*hetu*) is stated immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*), the understanding of the meaning occurs naturally for the learned, since they themselves will recall the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

This is what is meant: inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not directed toward one who has already understood, because it would be useless. Nor is it possible to determine how much of the subject matter the person to be instructed has understood and how much they have not, since the mental states of others are difficult to discern. Furthermore, it is not logical to compose a statement merely in accordance with that [person's] capacity, because the capacities of those who understand vary.

Therefore, when instructing another, one should communicate through speech only that much of the meaning as is established by the actual nature of things (vastuvṛtti) for the sake of proving the reason; one should not proceed in accordance with the particularities of the listener.
As it has been said:
"The thing itself must be stated; the purpose is accomplished [by the thing], not by reference to persons."
For who indeed would follow the cognitions of one whose objects are misconceived?

He concludes: "Therefore, the completion of the meaning occurs right here. Because the full capacity of the reason (*hetu*) is perceived only when there is a conclusion (*nigamana*), therefore it is in this very conclusion that the completion of the meaning—that which is to be proven (*sādhya*)—is reached, meaning the finality of its cognition. Alternatively, the construction is as follows: because the absence of contrary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not understood without the conclusion, therefore the completion and finality of the meaning—the efficacy of the correct reason—occurs in this very [conclusion].

Having already described the nature of each individual component, he now explains them collectively by means of a question, beginning with "How? and so forth. When there is a desire to know one of two properties—whether sound is eternal or non-eternal—the word "sound" is stated as qualified by the property of non-eternality alone, which is not yet established, through the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*): "Sound is non-eternal. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [215–216] [pp. 594–595]

How so? By the statement "sound is impermanent," sound is expressed as being qualified merely by impermanence which has not yet been established. By the statement "because it follows immediately upon effort," only the property that serves as the means of proving impermanence is denoted. By the statement "in this world, whatever follows immediately upon effort is seen to be impermanent, as for example a jar," only the concomitance of the general property of the probans with the general property of the probandum is stated.

"Always not produced immediately after an effort, as for example space"—by this, the absence of the probans where the probandum is absent is demonstrated. And thus, while sound is seen to be produced immediately after an effort, it is not, like space, not produced immediately after an effort; through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the application of the general property of the probans, whose capacity has been observed, to sound is understood.
Therefore, by the statement "sound is impermanent," the completion of the intended meaning—that sound is indeed impermanent—is understood.

Therefore, the communication of one's own intended meaning to others is accomplished solely by means of a five-membered statement; thus, this *parārthānumāna* (inference for the sake of others) is established.

In this regard, when the expectation arises as to "what is the reason (*hetu*)?", the mere property that serves as the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*) for impermanence is expressed by the statement of the reason: "because of being produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*), which means "because of being perceived immediately after effort, having previously been non-existent. By the use of the word "mere" (*mātra*), he demonstrates that the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are not explicitly stated [by the reason alone].

When one has understood the means of proof (*sādhana*), the question arises: "How does this [means] lead to the understanding of the probandum (*sādhya*)? In response to this inquiry regarding the capacity of the means of proof, the example—"Whatever in this world is produced immediately after an effort is seen to be impermanent"—merely establishes the concomitance (*anugama*) of the general form of the means of proof with the general form of the probandum; it does not establish any other essential nature. This is the meaning of the word "mere" (*mātra*).

By means of the negative example (*vaidharmya-nidarśana*), "that which is eternal is not produced immediately after an effort," the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is demonstrated: "whatever is produced immediately after an effort is impermanent. This has been observed; however, when there is a desire to know whether that [property] exists in sound or not, it is stated: "and thus sound is produced immediately after an effort," just as a jar is produced immediately after an effort, so too is sound produced immediately after an effort.

Nor is it the case that, by means of the consideration [of the reason] as being non-consequent upon effort like space, one perceives the application—that is, the presence—of "being consequent upon effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva) in the subject *śabda*, which has its capacity observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is observed; for example, although external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is possible in the case of "whatever is produced is seen to be non-hot, as in a jar," it may sometimes happen that a produced composite of light (*tejo 'vayavī*) is not non-hot, because that would contradict valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, when external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is possible—namely, that "whatever is produced by effort is impermanent"—and there arises a doubt regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as "perhaps sound, though produced by effort, might not be impermanent," which would render the reason (*hetu*) non-probative, there follows the restatement (*pratyāmnāya*): "therefore, sound is impermanent. The meaning is: because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing its permanence, therefore sound is impermanent; it does not exist as permanent.

By this term, which expresses the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is brought forward that apprehends the absence of any contrary evidence; once that absence has been established and doubt regarding the opposite has ceased, one understands the probandum (*sādhya*) without hesitation through the force of the means of valid cognition that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*), as the reason—whose invariable concomitance has been demonstrated—is applied to the subject (*dharmin*). One requires nothing further. By this method of restatement (*pratyāmnāya*), the completion of the intended meaning—that "sound is indeed impermanent"—is understood through certainty.

However, those who maintain that the meaning of the conclusion (*nigamana*) consists in the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) justify its purposefulness as follows: "The fact of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is one thing in the case of a jar, and another in the case of sound. Even if the jar's state of being produced is pervaded by impermanence, does it follow on that account that the same must hold for what pertains to sound? To one who is thus confused, even when the reason’s presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) have been shown, there might still be no cognition of the probandum; therefore, by means of the conclusion, through the pronoun "therefore" (*tasmāt*), [the probandum is established] in a general sense.

Having recalled the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the positive instance (*pravṛtta*), the impermanence of sound is established: because it is understood in a general sense that "whatever is produced is impermanent," but not in a specific sense, therefore sound is impermanent by virtue of being produced. And in this position, the absence of the fallacies of *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced) and *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (the mistimed) is demonstrated by the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) itself, since having no counter-thesis and having a non-sublated object are among the defining characteristics of a thesis.

Others, however, by the word "therefore" (tasmāt), refer specifically to the three-fold nature [of the reason], as follows: "Since it is observed that whatever is produced is impermanent; since sound is produced; and since there is no possibility of a counter-argument or a sublation—therefore, because of its being produced, sound is impermanent."

He concludes: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Since the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhyapratīti*) culminates in the perception of the complete capacity of the proof (*sādhanasāmarthya*) within the five members alone, and nothing further is required, it follows that the demonstration of an object ascertained by oneself is performed by a sentence consisting of exactly five members—neither fewer nor more. On this basis, it is established and settled that this five-membered sentence is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). *Nyāyakandalī* [216] [pp. 597–598]

However, those who maintain that perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and assert that inference is not a means of valid cognition, should be asked this: Is it only that single perception of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—the very nature of which is being cognized—that is the means of valid cognition, or is it all [perceptions] alike? It cannot be that only one is the means of valid cognition, because there is no reason for another [perception] to lack validity when its causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is identical to it.

Now, is it the case that everything—whether past, future, or residing in another person—is a directly perceived particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and thus a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? How is this determined? If you say it is because [the object] belongs to the same class as the individual instance of the cognition currently being experienced, then the validity of inference based on essential nature (*svabhāvānumāna*) has been admitted.

In this same manner, the status of inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must also be stated after critical examination. Furthermore, who is it that is being established [as an object] by the claim that perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition? It cannot be one's own self, because it is the establisher [of the argument]. If it is another person, is that person one who already accepts [the truth], or one who rejects it? It cannot be one who already accepts it, because there would be the futility of establishing what is already accepted. If it is one who rejects it, the rejection residing in another person cannot be known through perception.
If it is argued that [the absence of a means of knowledge] is inferred by the mark (liṅga) of speech, then the validity of inference based on an effect (*kāryānumāna*) is established.

By what means of knowledge is it proven that "inference is not a valid means of knowledge"? Perception has positive entities as its object; it is not capable of negating anything. If it is understood through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), then this would be an inference having non-apprehension as its mark. And thus it has been said by the Buddhists:
"Because of the establishment of the general nature of both the means of knowledge and its opposite, and because of the cognition of another cognition..."
"And there is the existence of other means of valid cognition, because of the negation of something.
— *Pramāṇaviniścaya* 1.2 [p. 598]

The meaning of the *Vārttika* is that because of the establishment of the general categories of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its absence, because of the comprehension of another's cognition, and because of the negation of some object, there exists inference (*anumāna*)—as a distinct means of valid cognition from perception—characterized by the logical marks (*liṅga*) of essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [217] [pp.
598–599]: Determination (*nirṇaya*) is the certain knowledge arising from the observation of specific characteristics; it is the opposite of doubt (*saṃśaya*).

This very [process] is either perception or inference. That which arises from the observation of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) as an opponent to doubt is "ascertainment through perception" (*pratyakṣanirṇaya*). For example, when a doubt arises—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—due to the observation of the mere similarity of height between a post and a person, while their specific features remain unperceived and one recalls both sets of specific features; then, upon seeing the head, hands, and so forth, the definitive cognition that "this is indeed a person" is ascertainment through perception.

When doubt arises as to whether this is a cow or a gavaya upon seeing only its horns, the definitive cognition that "this is indeed a cow" upon subsequently seeing its dewlap is *anumānanirṇaya* (ascertainment through inference).
— *Nyāyakandalī* [217] [pp. 598–599]

Some maintain that *nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and inference; in response to them, he says: "arising from the observation of a specific feature," and so forth. Where doubt has arisen due to the non-perception of specific features, the definitive knowledge produced therefrom by the observation of a specific feature is *nirṇaya*. It is the opposite of doubt, for when it arises, doubt is destroyed. As Maṇḍana states in the *Vibhramaviveka* [p. 599]:

Indeed, when a post has been ascertained by its verticality, people do not waver; "they waver" means they doubt. Although every cognition that is of the nature of ascertainment (*niścaya*) is a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), nevertheless, because of the strength of common usage regarding what occurs at a subsequent time, it is described as being the opposite of doubt. While explaining his own summary statement, he demonstrates the inclusion of definitive conclusion within perception and inference: "This very thing is perception and this is inference, which [arises] from the observation of a specific feature."

"That which arises as the opposite of doubt is determination (*nirṇaya*). He explains through the subsequent textual passage that "that determinative knowledge which pertains to the object of perception is perceptual determination (*pratyakṣa-nirṇaya*); and that determinative knowledge which pertains to the object of inference is inferential determination (*anumāna-nirṇaya*).
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p. 599 [218].

Memory is that which has as its object what was previously perceived, heard, or experienced; it arises from a specific contact between the self and the mind dependent upon the observation of a sign, desire, recollection, and so forth, and from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by vivid perception, repetition, or interest; it is the cause of subsequent determination, desire, recollection, and aversion regarding objects not currently grasped.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [218] [pp. 599–601]

He explains the definition of memory (*smṛti*) with the words "the desire to see a mark" (*liṅgadarśanecchā*), and so forth. "The seeing of a mark," "desire," and "recollection"—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the "attention" (*praṇidhāna*) and other factors mentioned in the *Nyāya-sūtra* are included. "From a particular conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon those [factors]" is the statement of the causes of memory. The "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) of the conjunction of the self and the mind consists precisely in its being assisted by the seeing of a mark and the other factors; for memory does not arise from this [conjunction] alone.

Just like the observation of a mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is also a causal condition for memory; thus he says: "And from an impression produced by a cognition characterized by intensity, repetition, or interest. A "sharp cognition" (*paṭupratyaya*) is a more vivid cognition; from that, an impression is born. Therefore, although a sharp cognition may arise in some cases from the knowledge of the touch of grass while walking, it does not become an impression capable of being grasped—as is the case with a verse (*anuvāka*) recited only once.

For one who has grasped [the material], practice—characterized by repeated grasping through recitation—is the cause of *saṃskāra*, because it is observed that an *anuvāka* (section of a text) is mastered when such practice exists. Furthermore, even when an object of extreme wonder is perceived only once, the observation of memory at a later time shows that grasping with reverence (*ādara*) is also a cause of *saṃskāra*. The phrase "in those things seen, heard, or experienced" is a mention of the objects.

"In those seen" means in those perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); "in those heard" means in those understood through verbal testimony (*śabda*); "in those experienced" means in those inferred (*anumita*)—this is the meaning. "The cause of subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), desire, memory, and aversion" is the definition by way of its effects. That which remains or is left over is called "the remainder" (*śeṣa*). "Subsequent" (*anu*) refers to that which occurs after; "reflective awareness" (*vyavasāya*) is the act of ascertainment; thus, *anuvyavasāya* is "subsequent reflective awareness."

The term *śeṣānuvyavasāya* refers to the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that follows; specifically, it is the cognition of the object to be inferred which arises immediately after the initial cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*). The cause of this [subsequent awareness] is the recollection of the invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*). The recollection of something being a means to pleasure is the cause of desire. The recollection of the first word is the cause of the recollection of the second word. The recollection of something being a source of pain is the cause of aversion.

The form (*ākāra*) of memory is precisely "that" (*tat*); therein, the pastness of the object—that is, its having been previously experienced—is cognized, and thus memory has a past object. For this very reason, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because in determining an object by demonstrating that its object was the domain of a previous experience, it is dependent upon that prior experience regarding the delimitation of the object. Inferential knowledge, however, while dependent on another for its arising, is entirely independent in the delimitation of its own object, unlike memory.
Therefore, because there is no cognition of an object through a connection with a prior experience— as the teachers, whose intellects are supreme among all, have stated in the *Tantraṭīkā*:
"Memory is held to be a cognition whose object is the object of a prior cognition."
"Without a prior cognition, its validity is not apprehended. And as they say in this verse:
"In that case, the validity of that prior cognition is accepted;
by the mere presentation of it, the remembrance fulfills its purpose."

As for those who claim that memory lacks authority because it arises from what is not an object [of direct perception], the refutation is that inference concerning past and future objects would likewise lack authority.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [219] [pp. 601–602]

The knowledge that arises for the seers who are the authors of the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*)—concerning objects beyond the senses, such as *dharma* and so forth, whether recorded in texts or not recorded—in the past, future, or present, through the contact of the self and the mind and by virtue of a particular merit (*dharma*), and which reveals things as they truly are, is called *ārṣa* (the seer’s intuition). This occurs extensively among the divine seers, and occasionally among worldly people as well; for example, when a young girl says, "My brother will come tomorrow; my heart tells me so."

Why is the vision of the perfected ones (*siddhadarśana*) not a distinct form of knowledge? Because the vision of those who have attained perfection through eye-salve, foot-ointment, the sword, or pills—beings who perceive visible objects regarding things that are subtle, concealed, or distant—is nothing other than perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, if it is claimed that the vision of the ripening of merit and demerit by celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial beings, based on the movements of planets, constellations, and so forth, is intended [as a distinct knowledge], that too is merely inference (*anumāna*).

Now, if it is claimed that there is a perception of dharma and so forth that does not depend on a logical mark (*liṅga*), even that is included within one of the two—either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or the cognition of a seer (*ārṣa*); such is the understanding.
*Nyāyakandalī* [219] [pp. 601–603]

He explains the *ārṣa* [type of knowledge]: "Of the authors of the *āmnāya*. The *āmnāya* is the Veda; its authors are the seers (*ṛṣis*). Of them, there arises—due to the contact of the self and the mind—that intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*) which is a direct report of the self and a direct awareness of the nature of others, regarding things past, future, or present, beyond the senses, transcending the path of the senses, such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), space, time, and so forth, whether they are recorded in texts or not, and whether they are established by scripture or not.

The wise declare that knowledge which arises free from doubt and error is *ārṣa* (sage-like). That manifestation of an object which occurs in the absence of the senses, inferential marks, and so forth, is *pratibhā* (intuition); the wise call this very *pratibhā* "prātibha. When the objection is raised that its arising is impossible due to the absence of a cause, this was stated: "from a particularity of merit (*dharma-viśeṣāt*)."

That which is distinguished is a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*); a distinction that is itself a property is a "property-distinction" (*dharmaviśeṣa*). From such a property—namely, an excellence born of austerity and meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—there arises intuitive insight (*pratibhā*). This intuitive insight occurs, for the most part and in great abundance, among the divine sages (*devarṣis*), while it happens only occasionally among ordinary people. For example, a young girl says: "My brother will come tomorrow; my heart tells me so. And this is not doubt, because there is no contact with two opposing alternatives (*ubhayakoṭi*).
Nor is it error, because it is subsequently confirmed; therefore, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Some maintain that the vision of perfected beings (*siddhadarśana*) is also a separate branch of knowledge (*vidyā*); in order to refute this, he says: "The vision of perfected beings is not a separate knowledge. He establishes this very point with the words beginning "Why? and so forth. Those who are the perceivers of objects possessing their own nature—which are visible, capable of being seen, and which include the perfections such as the ointment for the feet (*añjanapādalepa*)—are called "perfected beings" (*siddhas*).

The perception of those seers of the visible—who have attained perfection through ointments and other means—regarding objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant, which consists of an experience dependent upon the senses, is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, if the vision of perfected beings regarding the movement of planets and constellations among celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial creatures, as well as their observation of the ripening of merit and demerit, is intended to be "perception of the perfected" (*siddhadarśana*), that too is merely inference (*anumāna*), because the movement of the planets and so forth serve as inferential marks (*liṅga*).

Now, if the perception of dharma and so forth by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) is held to be independent of inferential marks (*liṅga*), it is included within one of the two: perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inspired knowledge (*ārṣa*). If the perception of dharma and so forth arises from the sense organs, then it is perception; if it is independent of the sense organs, then it is inspired knowledge—this is the meaning. He concludes: "Thus, cognition (*buddhi*). This means that cognition has been explained according to the sequence of the text just mentioned. The word "iti" indicates the end of the section. *NK_5_G2ṭXT Guṇa 2; Praśastapādabhāṣyam [220] [p.603]*

Pleasure has the characteristic of favor (*anugraha*). When desired objects such as garlands are present, pleasure arises from the contact of the self and the mind—dependent upon merit (*dharma*) and other factors—and from the perception of the desired object through the sense organs; it is that which produces favor, attachment, and clarity of the eyes and other faculties. In regard to past objects, it is born of memory; in regard to future objects, it is born of volition (*saṅkalpa*). However, that which manifests for the wise even in the absence of recollection, desire, or volition toward objects, has its cause in knowledge, tranquility, contentment, and a particular state of merit.

*Nyāyakandalī* [220] [p.604]: Since it is an effect of the intellect (*buddhi*), he explains pleasure immediately after the intellect: "Pleasure is characterized by favor. That by which one is favored is "favor" (*anugraha*); the meaning is that it has the characteristic of favor, that is, its nature is favor. For pleasure, by virtue of its agreeable nature, favors the person while producing an experience of its own object. He explains this very point with the words: "A garland and so forth."

Pleasure (*sukha*) is that which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects when desired objects—such as garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth—are present; it depends upon merit (*dharma*) and other factors. Even when a desired object is present before the senses, pleasure does not arise for one who is distracted by another object; therefore, the perception of the desired object is understood to be its cause. Furthermore, since pleasure is absent in one who is separated from the object, it is understood that the contact with the object is also a cause.

By the phrase "from dharma, etc.," the word "etc. includes such states as composure (*svasthatā*). The description of the effect is that it produces favor (*anugraha*), attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*), clarity of the eyes (*nayanādiprasāda*), and so forth. Favor is a cognition whose object is pleasure. Attachment is passion. Clarity of the eyes and so forth is purity; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the clarity of the face is included. Pleasure is the producer of these.

Through the arising of a wholesome state (*śaikṣa*), self-experience is produced; that itself is a benefit to oneself. When pleasure arises, there is clarity of the face and other features. Attachment to the means of pleasure arises from pleasure itself. Regarding past [objects], pleasure born of memory occurs through the recollection of previously experienced means of pleasure. Regarding future [objects], it arises from the mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) that "this will be mine."

As for that [bliss] which manifests for the wise—those possessed of self-knowledge—even when there are no recollections of sense objects, no mental constructions (*saṃkalpa*) regarding objects, no object present, and no recollection or construction present, it has as its cause the specific qualities of knowledge, tranquility, contentment, and dharma. Knowledge is self-knowledge; tranquility is the mastery of the senses; contentment is the state of not desiring anything beyond what is necessary for the maintenance of the body; and the specific dharma is preeminent dharma characterized by cessation (*nivartaka*). Thus, it has these four as its causes.

However, for those who assert that pleasure is merely the absence of suffering, there is a contradiction with the experience of its nature as bliss (*ānanda*), as well as the impossibility of accounting for the two types of activity—namely, "I shall attain what is beneficial" and "I shall avoid what is harmful.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [221] [p. 604]

Suffering has the characteristic of being harmful (*upaghāta*). When there is the presence of undesirable objects such as poison, suffering arises from the contact between the self and the mind, depending on the perception of what is undesired, the contact of the sense organs with their objects, and factors such as demerit (*adharma*); it is that which has intolerance, injury, and dejection as its causes. Regarding past objects such as snakes, tigers, or thieves, it is born of memory; regarding future objects, it is born of conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*). — *Nyāyakandalī*, p. 605 [221]

Because it is the opposite of pleasure (*sukha*), he explains suffering (*duḥkha*) immediately thereafter: "Suffering has the characteristic of affliction. Affliction (*upaghāta*) is that by which one is afflicted; thus, it has the characteristic of affliction, meaning its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is affliction. When suffering arises, because its nature is contrary [to the self], it afflicts the self while producing an experience directed toward itself as its object. He elucidates this with the passage beginning "the perception of the undesirable" (*aniṣṭopalabdhi*). This "intolerance" (*amarṣa*) is what is meant by "aversion" (*dveṣa*).

Injury (*upaghāta*) is the experience of suffering; wretchedness (*dainya*) is a lack of luster; these are its causes. When suffering exists, there is injury to the self characterized by that experience. Regarding past objects such as snakes and so forth, it arises from memory; regarding future objects, it arises from conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*). This is to be explained in the same manner as pleasure. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [222] [pp. 605–606]

Desire (*icchā*) is the longing for what has not yet been attained, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon pleasure and so forth, or depending upon memory. It is the cause of effort, memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*). Desire, longing, passion, resolve, compassion, detachment, hypocrisy, disposition—these and others are varieties of desire.

Desire (*kāma*) is the wish for sexual intercourse. Longing (*abhilāṣa*) is the wish for food and drink. Attachment (*rāga*) is the wish to repeatedly delight in sense objects. Resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is the wish for an action that is not yet imminent. Compassion (*kāruṇya*) is the wish to remove the suffering of others without regard for one’s own interest. Detachment (*vairāgya*) is the wish to abandon sense objects due to perceiving their defects. Guile (*upadhā*) is the wish to deceive others. Intent (*bhāva*) is a wish hidden within. Varieties of wish arise from the differences in actions, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) or the desire to take away (*jihīrṣā*). *Nyāyakandalī* [222] [pp. 605–606]

Desire (*icchā*) is the longing for what has not yet been attained, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another. That longing which, regarding an unattained object, seeks it for one's own sake—thinking "may this be mine"—or that longing which seeks it for the sake of another—thinking "may this belong to him"—is desire. And it arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon pleasure and so forth, or upon memory.

A desire arises for an object that is a means to happiness in the future; and upon the arising of that desire, the happiness to be accomplished by that object—even though it is future—is a causal factor (*nimittakāraṇa*) because it is established by the intellect. As the author of the *Nyāyavārttika* states: "Because the fruit is the motivator. When the cause of happiness has passed, memory is the cause for the arising of desire. Effort, memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*) are its causes.

From the desire for appropriation (*upādāna*), there arises an effort conformable to it; from the desire to remember, there arises remembrance (*smaraṇa*); for one who engages in prescribed rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* out of a desire for their fruit, merit (*dharma*) is produced; for one who engages in prohibited acts out of passion (*rāga*), demerit (*adharma*) is produced. Since desire and so forth also exist, why are they not mentioned? To this he says: "Desire," etc. [p. 606]

He demonstrates that which was stated—that desire and the like are specific varieties of longing (*icchā*) and not distinct ontological entities: "Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for sexual union. The word *kāma*, when used without a qualifying prefix, applies specifically to the longing for sexual union; its application elsewhere occurs only through its association with another word, as in "one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) should sacrifice. Longing (*abhilāṣa*) is the desire for food. Food (*abhyavahāra*) means eating; the desire for that is longing. Attachment (*rāga*) is the desire for repeated enjoyment of sense objects.

Furthermore, the meaning is that *rāga* (attachment) is the desire for the enjoyment of sense objects. *Saṅkalpa* (volition) is the desire for an action that is not yet imminent; it is the desire to perform an object that has not yet come into being. *Kāruṇya* (compassion) is the desire to eliminate the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest. That desire to remove or dispel the suffering of others, without aiming at any personal goal or purpose whatsoever, is compassion. *Vairāgya* (dispassion) is the desire to renounce sense objects due to perceiving their defects—that is, through the realization that they are causes of suffering.

The desire to deceive others, the desire to mislead others, is *upadhā* (hypocrisy). That desire which is hidden within but manifested through outward signs is *bhāva* (disposition). Varieties of desire arise from the differences in actions, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the desire to take (*jihīrṣā*). The desire to act is *cikīrṣā*, the desire to take is *jihīrṣā*, and the desire to go is *jigamiṣā*; thus, these varieties of desire arise from the differences in actions. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [223] [p. 606]

Hatred (*dveṣa*) has the nature of burning. That state, in which one exists, whereby one considers oneself as if set ablaze, is hatred. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon pain or upon memory. It is the cause of effort, memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*). Anger (*krodha*), malice (*droha*), resentment (*manyu*), intolerance (*akṣamā*), and indignation (*amarṣa*) are the varieties of hatred.

Aversion (*dveṣa*) consists of the nature of burning. He explains this with the words "when that exists," and so forth. This is clear. And it arises from the contact of the self and the mind, depending either on pain or on memory. [When a cause of pain is present and being experienced, aversion toward the pain produced by it arises from that pain. When the cause of pain is past, aversion arises from the memory of the pain born from it. It is the cause of effort, merit, and memory.

The effort "I shall think of this" arises from hatred; toward those who cause the subversion of the meaning of the Vedas, there is *dharma* (merit) through hatred, and toward those intent on protecting that [Vedic] meaning, there is *adharma* (demerit) through hatred. Memory also arises from hatred; whoever hates someone remembers that person constantly. Anger (*krodha*), malice (*droha*), resentment (*manyu*), intolerance (*akṣamā*), and impatience (*amarṣa*) are varieties of hatred. Hatred that causes a momentary disturbance of the body, senses, and so forth is anger. Malice is hatred that is characterized by unobserved transformation and results in long-term injury.

*Manyu* is inwardly concealed hatred toward one who has done harm, when one is unable to retaliate. *Akṣamā* is hatred for the virtues of others. *Amarṣa* is hatred arising from the humiliation of one's own virtues.

In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, effort (*prayatna*) is synonymous with *saṃrambha* (agitation) and *utsāha* (zeal). It is of two kinds: that preceded by the vital breath (*jīvana-pūrvaka*), and that preceded by desire and aversion (*icchā-dveṣa-pūrvaka*).

Among these, that which is preceded by life-force (*jīvana-pūrvaka*) is the impeller of the continuous flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna* in one who is asleep, and at the time of awakening, it is the cause for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) reaching other sense organs. The production of this [action] preceded by life-force arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

The other [type of action], however, is the cause of activity capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and it is that which sustains the body. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon desire or upon aversion.
*Nyāyakandalī* [224] [pp. 607–608]:

Effort (*prayatna*), exertion (*saṃrambha*), and enthusiasm (*utsāha*) are synonyms. It is of two kinds: that preceded by life-force (*jīvana-pūrvaka*) and that preceded by desire and aversion (*icchā-dveṣa-pūrvaka*). Life-force is the conjunction or connection of the embodied self, accompanied by the ripening of the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*), with the mind; effort preceded by that performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, he says:

Regarding the phrase "preceded by life" (*jīvanapūrvaka*): the activity of inhalation and exhalation in one who is asleep must have effort as its cause, because it is an activity of inhalation and exhalation, just like the activity of inhalation and exhalation in one who is awake; and since at that time desire and aversion—which are causes of effort—are not possible, it follows that the effort inferred from the movement of inhalation and exhalation is indeed preceded by life. Not only is this effort preceded by life and the impeller of inhalation and exhalation, but it is also the cause of the internal organ's contact with other sense organs at the time of awakening from sleep.

The conjunction of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the sense-organ, which is inferred from the apprehension of objects, is produced by an activity of the internal organ preceded by effort; for it is a conjunction of the internal organ and a sense-organ, like the conjunction of the internal organ and a sense-organ during the waking state. Thus, its being preceded by effort is established. Its production—referring to that [conjunction] which is preceded by life—is due to the conjunction of the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*), depending upon merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); "life" is defined as the conjunction of the self and the mind depending upon merit and demerit; therefore, the meaning is that its production arises from that [conjunction]. [p.608]

The other [type of effort], however, is preceded by desire and aversion; it is the cause of an activity capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and it is that which sustains the body. When gravity is present, the effort preceded by desire acts as the sustainer of the body that would otherwise fall. And that [effort] arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon desire and aversion. Effort directed toward the acquisition of the means to what is beneficial is preceded by desire; effort directed toward the abandonment of the means to suffering is preceded by aversion. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [225] [p. 608]

Gravity belongs to water and earth; it is the cause of the action of falling. It is imperceptible and is to be inferred from the action of falling. It is opposed to conjunction, effort, and momentum (*saṃskāra*). Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are like those of the color and other qualities of atoms of water and so forth.

*Nyāyakandalī* [225] [pp. 608–609]: "Gravity belongs to water and earth" is the statement of its substratum. "The cause of the action of falling" is the definition of its effect. "It is imperceptible" is a description of its nature; the meaning is that gravity is not grasped by any sense organ.

As for those who claim that heaviness (*gurutva*) is perceptible by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*), there follows the undesirable consequence that one would perceive the heaviness of a substance situated below just as one perceives its touch, because the sense of touch cannot depend on anything other than its own direct contact (*svasannikarṣa*) when perceiving an object. As for the fact that the heaviness of something situated above is perceived, that is due to the inference of the downward movement of the hands and so forth. If it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), how can it be perceived? To this he says: "It is to be inferred from the action of falling" (*patanakarmānumeyam*).

That which is the falling of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*), by which an inherent non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) inhering in the same object is inferred—that alone is, for us, heaviness (*gurutva*). By this, the following argument put forward by others is refuted: "Because the specific effect of the heaviness of the composite, namely its distinct downward bending (*avanativiśeṣa*), is not perceived, there is an absence of heaviness in the composite. For [otherwise] it would follow that the composite itself could not fall. If it is argued that its falling occurs precisely because of the heaviness of its parts, then those parts too are composites in relation to their own parts.

"Falling" means, in every case of an effect, the cessation of that [gravity]. Now, if gravity is postulated in parts because falling would otherwise be impossible for them due to the weight belonging to their own constituent parts—which are in a different substratum—then it must likewise be postulated in the whole (*avayavin*), since the logic is the same. As for the fact that no excess in the effect of the whole's gravity is perceived, that is because the difference between the gravity of the parts and the gravity of the whole is extremely slight;
just as when a large substance is being weighed, the distinct effect of the gravity of other subtle substances surrounding it is not perceived.

It is opposed by conjunction, effort, and momentum (*saṃskāra*). Gravity possesses opposition toward conjunction, effort, and momentum—which is known as *vega*—because when obstructed by them, it does not perform its own effect. Thus, for one mounted on a swing, there is no falling due to obstruction by conjunction; there is no leaning of the body due to obstruction by effort; and there is no falling of an arrow, a splinter, or similar object thrown outward due to obstruction by momentum.

Furthermore, its establishment regarding eternality and non-eternality is like that of the color and other qualities of water-atom constituents (*ab-paramāṇu*). Just as the color and other qualities of non-atomic (i.e., composite) matter are eternal, so too is gravity (*gurutva*) in both earth-atoms and water-atoms. And just as in the case of a substance that is an effect of water and so forth, color and other qualities arise through the prior process of the qualities of the causes and perish upon the destruction of their substratum, so too does gravity.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [226] [pp. 609–611]

Fluidity (*dravatva*) is the cause of the action of flowing (*syandana*). It resides in three substances. It is of two kinds: natural (*sāṃsiddhika*) and incidental (*naimittika*). Natural fluidity is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water. Incidental fluidity is a common quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) of earth and fire. [p.610]

The production of the eternal and non-eternal states of natural fluidity is like that of gravity. If it is argued that this is inconsistent with the nature of natural fluidity because we observe [snow and hail] as conglomerates, we say no; for when water-atoms (āpya-paramāṇu) are conjoined with divine heat (divya-tejas), their mutual conjunction—which is termed a "conglomerate" (saṅghāta)—is what initiates the substance. By means of this, the fluidity of the atoms is obstructed, and thus fluidity does not arise in the resulting effects, such as snow and hailstones.

And the occasional [color] of earth and fire is produced by conjunction with fire. How so? When action arises in the atoms—the causes of substances such as clarified butter, lac, beeswax, and the like—due to conjunction with fire and depending on momentum (*vega*), then from the disjunctions produced thereby, there follows the destruction of the conjunctions that originate the substance; upon the cessation of the effect-substance, substantiality (*dravyatva*) arises in the independent atoms due to conjunction with fire and depending on heat (*auṣṇya*). Then, when action arises in those [atoms] due to conjunction of the self and the atom, depending on the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the experiencers...

From those conjunctions, an effect-substance is produced through the sequence beginning with dyads; and in that substance, simultaneously with the production of color and other qualities, fluidity is produced through the sequence of the qualities of the causes.
(Nyāyakandalī [226], pp. 609–611)

Fluidity (*dravatva*) is the cause of the action of flowing (*syandana*). The meaning is that whatever is the cause of the action of flowing is fluidity. It subsists in three substances; that is, it subsists in earth, water, and fire. "But that is of two kinds"—the sense of the word "but" (*tu*) is that while gravity (*gurutva*) is of one kind, fluidity is of two kinds. These are the occasional (*naimittika*) and the natural (*sāṃsiddhika*). Fire-contact is the "occasion" (*nimitta*); that which is the effect of this is the occasional.

*Saṃsiddhika* (inherent) means established by its own nature; that is to say, it is independent of conjunction with fire. *Saṃsiddhika* fluidity is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water, because it does not exist elsewhere. *Naimittika* (accidental) fluidity is a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) of earth and fire, because it is a common quality. Regarding the inherent fluidity, its eternity, non-eternity, and production are like those of gravity (*gurutva*). Just as gravity inherent in an eternal substance is eternal, and that inherent in a non-eternal substance is preceded by the qualities of the cause and effect and perishes upon the destruction of its substratum, so too is inherent fluidity.

Here, an objection is raised: "If it is argued that [water] cannot possess the nature of a substance established by its own inherent nature (*sāṃsiddhika*) because it is observed as an aggregate, then since substances such as snow and hail—which are composed of water—are observed to be aggregates and are observed to be solid, it is incorrect to say that the status of water as a substance is established by its own inherent nature. The author replies: "By the divine... Since fluidity is perceived in all water as something established by its own inherent nature, it is first of all certain that fluidity is indeed established by the inherent nature of water.

However, in cases such as snow and hail where fluidity does not arise in the effect, there occurs a mutual conjunction of aqueous atoms conjoined with celestial fire, termed a "conglomeration" (*saṅghāta*), which initiates the substance. This is because the fluidity of the atoms initiating the snow and hail is obstructed by that [conjunction]. It is inferred from the observation elsewhere that even in the case of a solid substance like salt, its fluidity is obstructed by conjunction with fire. Thus, by the conjunction with fire, the fluidity of the atoms is obstructed.

The fact that salt possesses fluidity is understood from the observation that, like snow or hailstones, it becomes liquid after a lapse of time. As for the melting of snow, hailstones, and the like, that which is the melting of a solid substance is understood to result from contact with terrestrial fire, as in the case of gold and other metals. Since the melting of snow, hailstones, and so forth is indeed a form of melting, we therefore rely here upon contact with fire alone as the cause, as its causal efficiency has been observed in this context.

Having explained inherent fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*), he explains occasional fluidity (*naimittika-dravatva*): "Occasional fluidity belongs to earth and fire, and is produced by conjunction with fire. Being questioned by one who does not know how this is so, he provides the proof, beginning with the words "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*) and so forth.

In the case of substances such as clarified butter, lac, and beeswax, when action arises in their constituent atoms due to contact with fire, there occurs a disjunction resulting from that action; this leads to the destruction of the conjunctions that originate the substance of clarified butter and the like. Once the substance of clarified butter and so forth has ceased to exist, fluidity is produced in those independent atoms through contact with fire.

Immediately thereafter, when fluidity has arisen in the atoms, an action is produced due to the conjunction of the soul and the atoms, which depends upon the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of the experiencers. When, through the mutual conjunctions of the atoms resulting from that action, a composite substance arises by way of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, then at the very moment that color and other qualities arise, fluidity is produced from the fluidities of the constituent causes. This same sequence applies even to the melting of snow, hailstones, and the like.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [227] [p. 611]

Viscosity (*sneha*) is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water; it is the cause of cohesion, smoothness, and so forth. Like gravity (*gurutva*), its eternity, non-eternity, and production are also [to be understood] in the same way.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [227] [p. 611]

Viscosity (*sneha*) is a non-specific quality (*aviśeṣaguṇa*) that is the cause of cohesion (*saṃgraha*), smoothness (*mṛjā*), and so forth. Cohesion is the cause of the attainment of a state of massing (*piṇḍībhāva*) among substances such as flour-meal (*saktu*) when they are joined together; it is a specific type of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*). Smoothness is the purification of the body produced by rubbing with unguents and the like. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), softness is also included; viscosity is the cause of these. Like gravity (*gurutva*), its production as eternal or non-eternal is also determined. Gravity is eternal in atoms (*paramāṇu*), and in an effect (*kārya*), it is preceded by the qualities of its causes and perishes upon the destruction of its substratum; viscosity is likewise. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [228] [p. 611]

Formative force (*saṃskāra*) is threefold: velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*). Among these, velocity arises from action dependent upon a specific cause in the five corporeal substances; it is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a fixed direction, is opposed by a specific conjunction with a substance possessing touch, and in some cases, it is produced through the sequence beginning with the qualities of its cause.
*Nyāyakandalī* [228] [p.612]

Latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*) are of three kinds: velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthāpaka*). Among these, velocity arises from action (*karman*) depending on specific causes within the five corporeal substances. Action produces velocity in the five substances—earth, water, fire, air, and mind—and nowhere else, because [velocity] does not exist there by itself. It depends not only on specific causes such as pushing or striking, for there is an absence of velocity in slow motion. It is the cause of the continuous succession of actions in a restricted direction.

The meaning is that it is the cause of the continuity of action precisely in the direction toward which the velocity was produced by that action. It is opposed by a specific conjunction with a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat*). Velocity is destroyed by a specific conjunction with a substance possessing touch—one characterized by the extremely tight binding of its constituent parts—which itself is of a specific nature. However, a weak velocity is destroyed by mere conjunction with a substance possessing touch, as in the case of an arrow that has traveled a great distance and is obstructed by still air.

In some cases, it arises following the sequence of the qualities of its causes. For the most part, velocity is born of action; however, in certain instances—such as in a composite water-substance composed of parts possessing velocity—it is also produced from the velocities of its constituent causes.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya [229–230], p. 613)

The quality of the self known as *bhāvanā* (mental impression) is the cause of memory and recognition regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced; it is opposed to knowledge, intoxication, pain, and so forth. It is produced by intense, repeated, or respectful cognitions. A sharp mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind when there is a marvelous object, depending upon a sharp cognition—for example, as in the case of a person from the South seeing a camel.

When knowledge, arts, physical exercises, and so forth are being practiced, from each successive cognition—which depends upon the preceding latent impression (saṃskāra) regarding that very object—there arises, due to the conjunction of the self and the mind, a latent impression of superior intensity.
*Nyāyakandalī* [229] [pp. 613–614]

The *bhāvanā* (mental impression) is a quality (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*). Specifically, that which is designated as *bhāvanā* is a latent disposition (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the self. Regarding the phrase "in respect of things seen, heard, or experienced": this is a statement of its function, meaning it is the cause of memory and recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) with regard to objects previously seen, heard, or experienced. The term "seen, heard, or experienced" should be understood as referring to objects cognized even through error, since memory is observed to occur in those cases as well. It is opposed by knowledge, intoxication, pain, and so forth; that is, a mental impression is destroyed by a counteracting cognition.

For one afflicted by vices such as gambling, there is the destruction of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) due to the forgetting of what was previously studied. Even through intoxication, there is the destruction of latent impressions, because the memory of the past is lost in one intoxicated by liquor. Latent impressions are also destroyed by the suffering of death and so forth, because there is an absence of recollection of experiences from other lives. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), pleasure and the like are included, since one who is attached to enjoyment or who is angry lacks memory of previous occurrences. [Latent impressions are also produced] by intense practice, respect, and vivid cognition.

A latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises from a vivid cognition, from the cognition of repetition, and from the cognition of intense interest. From a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, contingent upon a vivid cognition, a vivid latent impression arises with respect to a marvelous object. For example, as in the case of a Southerner seeing a camel. Because the camel’s form has never been experienced by a Southerner before, it is a marvelous object; from seeing it, a vivid latent impression arises in him, because it generates a memory of the experience of the camel even at a later time.

He demonstrates the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of repeated practice with the words "in sciences, arts, athletics, and so forth. "Science" refers to treatises, scriptures, and the like; "art" refers to activities such as leaf-carving; "athletics" refers to physical exertion in weaponry and the like. When these are being practiced, with respect to that very object previously grasped, an excellence of latent impression arises from the contact of the self and the mind, depending upon each preceding latent impression. This excellence persists for a long time and brings about a much clearer recollection.

For it is not the very first experience that deposits a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*), because there is no recollection of the object at that initial stage. Nor is the subsequent experience alone the cause of it, as that would render prior practice useless. Therefore, its production occurs from the final experience, which depends upon the penultimate latent impression; this follows a sequence in which each successive experience, depending on the preceding latent impressions, produces increasingly superior latent impressions. *Nyāyakandalī* [230] [pp. 614–617]

This, however, is investigated here: when knowledge is being practiced, is the meaning conveyed by the sentence (*vākya*), or is it conveyed by the *sphoṭa*? Why is there doubt? Because of conflicting views. Some say that the *sphoṭa* conveys the meaning; others, however, say it is the word (*yakam*). Therefore, what is the conclusion? That the *sphoṭa* is the conveyor of the meaning.

For if the word were not distinct from the phonemes, and the sentence were not distinct from the words, then there would be no comprehension of meaning at all. To explain: the phonemes do not individually manifest a cognition whose object is the meaning, because the remaining phonemes would otherwise be redundant. Furthermore, their collective aggregate is impossible, since the preceding phonemes no longer exist at the time of the perception of the final phoneme.

If it is argued that because phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, they possess a collective aggregate (*samudāya*), even so, their cognition does not persist; and if those which are not being cognized were to convey meaning, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the meaning being understood at all times. For there is no distinction whatsoever between those [phonemes] that have been cognized and then are no longer being cognized, and those that are never cognized at all.

If it is argued that the phonemes previously perceived, having ascended to memory (*smṛti*), are the causes of comprehension? If indeed memory also occurs sequentially, then—as with the phonemes themselves—there is no simultaneity (*sāhitya*); for at the time of perceiving the third phoneme, the memory of the first phoneme has already vanished. Furthermore, the simultaneous arising of memories is not even to be suspected, because of the prohibition against the simultaneity of cognitions (*jñāna*).

Now, if it is maintained that first there is the cognition of the initial phoneme, which produces a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); thereafter follows the cognition of the second phoneme, which, together with the previous impression, generates a distinct, cumulative impression; and by this sequence, a final impression arises that has all the phonemes as its object, and simultaneously produces a single recollection (*smṛti*) having all the phonemes as its object—then the [postulated] sequence is abandoned.

Sequence (*krama*) is indeed priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*); and that must be based either on space or on time. Neither of these two finds any scope among the phonemes (*varṇa*), because they are all-pervading (*sarvagata*) and eternal (*nitya*). However, the sequence of phonemes could be based on the sequence of cognitions; yet, since that [sequence] has vanished when [the phonemes] are revolving within a single recollective cognition (*smṛtibuddhi*), it is only those [phonemes] which are themselves devoid of sequence that possess the capacity to convey meaning.

Furthermore, in cases such as *tatsaraḥ* (that lake), *rasaḥ* (taste), *vanam* (forest), *navam* (new), *nadī* (river), and *dinam* (day), there would be no cognition of a difference in meaning because the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves are non-different, and because the order [of phonemes] is not a factor in the cognition [of meaning]. Yet, this difference in cognition does exist; since it is inexplicable on the basis of the phonemes alone, it necessitates a further, distinct cause. Thus is the proof of the *sphoṭa*.

Now, it may be argued that even the *sphoṭa* does not convey meaning unless it is manifested, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the meaning at all times. Furthermore, its manifestation cannot arise from the phonemes (*varṇa*), because according to the reasoning already stated, they lack the capacity either individually or when combined in succession; therefore, the comprehension of meaning would be impossible even from the *sphoṭa*.

On this point, they say: the sounds belonging to the element of air, which follow upon various efforts, each individually manifest the *sphoṭa* indistinctly as being of the nature of this or that phoneme; yet, by obtaining the assistance of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) left by each preceding object, they cause the *sphoṭa* to appear clearly at the end. Thus, at the conclusion, there is experienced a single, clear reality of meaning—one in which all distinctions and recollections of individual phonemes have subsided, which is devoid of sequence and partless.

For if the word were merely the phonemes themselves, it could not be apprehended by a single cognition; thus, the cognition would result in being without an objective support (*anālambana*). Furthermore, the conventional expression, "We understand the meaning from the word," would not be tenable. Therefore, there must exist some single entity distinct from the phonemes, from which the meaning becomes manifest.

This being the case, it is replied: When words such as "Guṇaratnābharaṇa," "Kāyasthakulatilaka," or "Pāṇḍudāsa" are being uttered, only the phonemes occurring in succession are perceived; there is no cognition of any object distinct from the phonemes at the end. For if, after that [object] was previously cognized as consisting of phonemes, its own true nature were subsequently cognized, then the falsity of the prior cognition would be determined, just as the cognition of silver is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl.

Nor is there such a cognition as "this is not a phoneme, but rather the *sphoṭa*. Furthermore, this cognition which reflects upon a single object does not manifest a distinct entity; rather, like the cognition of a "forest," it takes as its objective support merely the collection of phonemes. People employ the expression "we understand the meaning from the word" while accepting nothing other than the collection of phonemes.

Furthermore, that which is not perceived through direct perception cannot be established by means of another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), due to the absence of any such means. If it is argued that the impossibility of accounting for the cognition of meaning otherwise (*arthapratītyanyathānupapatti*) is that means, then do you maintain that the *sphoṭa* is the cause of the comprehension of meaning while it remains unperceived, or while it is being perceived? If it were the cause while unperceived, it would follow that there would be a constant cognition of meaning at all times.

It has been stated that there is no cognition of such a [sphoṭa]; furthermore, the cognition of meaning follows the very presence of the phonemes themselves. Therefore, it is better that some means for the communication of meaning be adopted in accordance with the established linguistic usage of these [phonemes] alone; it is not reasonable to postulate something unperceived, like a flower in the sky. Nor does this imply that there would be a cognition [of meaning] when there is a difference in the sequence of the phonemes, a difference in the speaker, or an intervention.

For cognitions of those objects are not caused by [sounds] that have a reversed order, that follow different speakers, or that are separated by space and time; for the capacities of entities are to be inferred from their effects. Their capacities are postulated exactly as their effects are observed from them. As the wise teach:
"However many letters there are, of whatever kind they may be, and whatever their capacity for conveying a particular meaning may be known to be, they convey that meaning in precisely that way."

For this very reason, there is a difference in meaning in words such as *nadī* and *dīna*, due to the difference in their sequence. If it is objected that "there is no sequence among phonemes; how then could it be a constituent part (*aṅga*) of them?", we say no, because for those [phonemes] which possess origination and which do not pervade [their locus], a priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) based on space and time is possible. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that neither individually nor collectively [the phonemes] possess the capacity—that too shows that the opponent has not considered the [true] position.

Although the phonemes (*varṇa*) are non-durable, nevertheless, the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) directed toward them, arising in succession, combine to produce the cognition of the word-meaning. Alternatively, the final phoneme, depending on either the impression of the preceding phonemes or their recollection, is the conveyor of meaning. Just as multiple impressions combine to produce a single recollection, this has been established in the discussion on duality (*dvitva*).

Now, you might think that it is illogical for the perception of the *āśraya* (locus) to arise from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is the phoneme (*varṇa*). For latent impressions, having their birth brought about by the apprehension of a particular object, are capable of producing memory only regarding that same object, not some other effect. As Maṇḍana stated in the *Sphoṭasiddhi*: "Latent impressions, indeed, being manifested by the appearance of the form of a certain thing, produce their fruit only with respect to that; therefore, cognition [of the word] is not postulated as being directed toward the external object."

That too is incorrect; for, because they are deposited by individual experiences in accordance with the comprehension of word-meanings, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) whose objects are the phonemes are deposited as possessing powers that are distinct from the latent impressions that cause memory. This is because they are understood through their very effect to be of such a nature. Or, even if these impressions were of the nature of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), their capacity to convey meaning would still be established, since they arise only when those [phonemes] exist.

For he who postulates the *sphoṭa* must also postulate that the *sphoṭa* possesses the power to convey meaning; thus, there is a redundancy of postulation (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Since it is simpler to postulate merely the capacity of the *saṃskāra*, which is established for both parties, this alone is what ought to be postulated. As it has been said by the proponents of Nyāya:
"Even though the status of the *saṃskāra* as the cause of memory is established, its capacity for other effects is not obstructed."
Thus, since the cognition of an object is possible from the phonemes themselves by means of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the postulation of *sphoṭa* is incorrect.
[From the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, p.

616]: When one, having fixed the mind upon the eye with effort, desires to see an object not previously seen, there arises an intense cognition (*ādarapratyaya*)—like the sight of a flash of lightning. Depending upon that, from the conjunction of the self and the mind, an excellence of mental impression (*saṃskārātiśaya*) is produced, just as it occurs from seeing silver or golden lotuses in Devahrada lake.

The *Nyāyakandalī* [231] [p. 618] demonstrates the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by an impression of intensity (*ādara-pratyaya*) with the words "by effort," and so forth. Intensity (*ādara*) is an excellence of effort; for one who desires to see an object from afar, that perception of the object which occurs like the sight of a flash of lightning is the impression of intensity. From the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon that very [intense impression], an excellence of latent impression is born, because it is not destroyed even after a long period of time has elapsed. An example of this is: as when, in the Devahrada lake, there is the sight of silver and golden lotuses.

Having learned the report that silver and golden lotuses are seen at midnight on the full moon day of the month of Caitra when it is conjoined with the Citrā constellation at Devahrada, those who have gathered there out of a desire to see them remain with their minds fixed upon their eyes through great effort as midnight approaches. When the lotuses rise, because they are seen for even a moment and because of the resulting conviction born of their regard, an excellence of mental impression (*saṃskārātiśaya*) arises which becomes the cause of a clearer recollection even at a later time.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [232] [p. 618]

Elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*), however, residing in tangible substances that possess a dense arrangement of parts and persist over time, restores its own substratum—which has been altered—to its original state. The effect of elasticity is observed in the modifications of both stationary and moving things, such as bows, branches, horns, tusks, bones, threads, and cloths, when they have been bent or compressed. Its properties regarding eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of gravity (*gurutva*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [232] [pp. 618–619]

He explains *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity) with the words: "But *sthitasthāpaka*... The word "but" (*tu*) is used to distinguish *sthitasthāpaka* from the impression (*saṃskāra*) called *bhāvanā*, because while the latter resides in substances that lack touch (*asparśavat*), the former resides in substances that possess touch (*sparśavat*). Residing in tangible substances characterized by dense and compact arrangements of parts, *sthitasthāpaka* restores its own substrate—which has been altered, bent, or otherwise displaced—to its original state, making it straight again just as it was before.
