To those who, on account of its non-perception by direct observation (*pratyakṣa-anupalambha*), maintain that *sthitisthāpaka* does not exist, he says—showing its existence through its effect—"in the modifications of the stationary and the moving. "Bent" (*bhugna*) means made crooked or contracted; "made to return to their former state" (*saṃvartita*). Thus, "bent and made to return to their former state" refers to those [modifications]; in them, the effect of *sthitisthāpaka* is observed.

What would be said? In the case of bows, branches, and so forth, when they are bent and then released, that which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the first action—conjoined with the same object (*ekārthasamaveta*)—that exists for the sake of restoring them to their prior state is the *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) formation (*saṃskāra*), because no other [cause] is possible. Others, however, considering "in those that are bent and restored" (*bhugnasaṃvartiteṣu*) to be a qualification of "in threads and so forth" (*sūkṣmatrādiṣu*), explain it as: "in those threads and so forth which have been bent and then restored."

Its eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of gravity (*gurutva*). The meaning is that just as gravity is eternal in atoms, non-eternal in effects, and preceded by the qualities of its causes, so too is the elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).

Dharma is a quality of the person (*puruṣa*). It is the cause of what is dear, beneficial, and liberation for the agent; it is supersensible (*atīndriya*); it is incompatible with the cognition of final bliss; it arises from the contact between the person and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) when there is a pure intention (*abhisaṃdhi*); and it has specific means as its cause for those belonging to the various castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).

Its means of accomplishment, however, are substances, qualities, and actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti for those belonging to the various classes and stages of life (varṇāśramins), existing in the relationship of general and particular.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [233] [pp. 619–622]

Dharma is a quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*). The meaning is that whatever is Dharma is a quality of the person and not a capacity of action (*karmasāmarthya*). It is the cause of the agent’s pleasure, welfare, and liberation. "Pleasure" is happiness; "welfare" is the means to happiness; and "liberation" is the absolute cessation of the nine specific qualities of the self (*ātmaviśeṣaguṇa*). One should explain it thus: Dharma is that which is the cause of the agent’s pleasure and so forth alone.

However, it is not the case that dharma is defined as that which is a cause of pleasure and so forth for the agent alone; for we hear in scripture that the fruit of satisfaction resulting from a *śrāddha* performed by a son accrues to the father. Furthermore, when a *kārīrī* sacrifice is performed by one desiring rain, we observe that the fruit of rain also relates to another person situated nearby.

In such scriptural injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is heard that heaven is to be produced by means of sacrifice; thus, the action is revealed to be a means for attaining the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). And that which connects a person with the highest good is *dharma*. Therefore, sacrifice and the like alone are *dharma*, not a quality of the person. For instance, they call one who performs a sacrifice "righteous" (*dhārmika*). This is incorrect, because an action that is momentary cannot have the relationship of being a means to a result that arises at a later time. Now, it might be argued:

Action is momentary, yet the fruit of heaven arises at a later time; moreover, an effect cannot arise from a cause that has already perished, and yet it is revealed in scripture that sacrifices and the like are causes. Since this would otherwise be impossible, one must postulate some power of action (*karmasāmarthya*) that persists until the time of the fruit’s production and is conducive to its arising, by means of which the scripturally stated efficacy of actions as instruments for attaining results is fulfilled. And because it is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition, it is designated as *apūrva* (the "unprecedented").
As it has been said:
"Action enjoined for the sake of a fruit is momentary, yet it leads to a result that occurs after a long interval."
Since its accomplishment cannot be otherwise, even this unprecedented [factor] is postulated.

To this it is replied: the capacity of an action does not reside in an action that is momentary, because when the possessor of power has perished, it is impossible for that capacity to persist without a substratum. Furthermore, at that time, the fruit such as heaven is yet to come; it cannot serve as the substratum for the capacity. If, however, heaven were to arise immediately after the performance [of the rite], then the postulation of the *apūrva* (the unseen force) would be useless, and its enjoyment would be unavoidable.

And is it not the case that there is no experience [of the fruit] because of the absence of a distinguished body, sense organs, and so forth? If that is so, then I did not come into existence at that time, because heaven has as its very nature that which is to be enjoyed. To claim that the nature of happiness exists even when it is not being enjoyed is merely a postulation based on unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the *apūrva* does not reside in the fruit. Nor is it possible for a fruit directed toward the self to arise from an *apūrva* inherent in space and other such elements.

Furthermore, an effect that is a real entity cannot logically exist without a substratum; therefore, its arising must be admitted as occurring only within that which is inherent in the self (the substrate). This being the case, it would not possess the capacity for that action, because the capacity of one thing does not inhere in another. If it is argued that even for one thing, a capacity inherent in another is desired, since that capacity is to be inferred from the effect—then it has been said:
"For capacity is indeed inferred from the effect, and it is perceived only as residing in that [substratum] wherein it is found."

"It must be understood as residing in that [action], whether its locus be itself or something else. This is incorrect; for when the possessor of power has perished, we do not observe the mere power—being independent of that possessor—producing an effect. By this, the following argument of Maṇḍana in the *Vidhiviveka* is also refuted: "Because it is produced by that [action], it is the power [of the action]. Since it is produced by the sacrifice, the effect would belong to the sacrifice and not to the power; for a fruit does not arise from an action assisted by the *apūrva*. Therefore, once the action has ceased, it is from the *apūrva* alone—assisted by factors such as place, time, and state—that [the fruit arises].

The production of the fruit is itself the unprecedented (*apūrva*) means of attaining the highest good (*śreyas*). As for the scriptural statement regarding the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the sacrifice and so forth, it must be accepted in accordance with the authoritative evidence that this occurs through the generation of the *apūrva*, and not directly. This being the case, it is logical that *dharma* is a quality of the person. Even the designation of *dharma* applied to the sacrifice and so forth is due to its being a means to the *apūrva*, just as the term "heaven" (*svarga*) is used for that which is a means to [the attainment of] pleasure.

For the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which is enjoined as a means to heaven, is praised by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) as being continuously a means to pleasure; furthermore, since [the word "heaven"] is used when there is a connection with pleasure—as in the case of sandalwood and the like—and is not used in its absence, the word "heaven" (*svarga*) is based upon pleasure. Although it denotes pleasure alone, its application to that which is a means to pleasure occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, since the cognition of a means to pleasure is established, it is redundant to assume a dual denotative power [of the word].

In this way, the word *dharma* is also employed by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote its accomplishment (*tatsādhana*), because the cognition of both is established through a single denotation; thus, there is no occasion for postulating a dual denotative power. This is the method of the logicians (*tārkika*).

That which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is not perceived by any sense organ by those who are not yogis; such is *dharma*. It is opposed to the consciousness of final bliss. Since *dharma* is an effect, it must necessarily be perishable; moreover, the destruction of anything is never found to be causeless. If its destruction were due to something else, it would not necessarily persist until the time of the production of its fruit.

Furthermore, the fruit of some dharma is to be enjoyed for many thousands of years; if that [dharma] were destroyed by its very first enjoyment, there would be no production of fruit at a later time. Moreover, it is not possible for a partless entity (*nirbhāga*) such as *adṛṣṭa* (dharma) to undergo destruction part by part. Therefore, it is only the final pleasure that is destroyed by perfect knowledge (*samyagvijñāna*), which destroys the dharma. As for those who maintain that dharma is eternal, for them the departure from the body (*prāyaṇa*) is impossible, because there would be no exhaustion of dharma and adharma. [The cause of rebirth is] the conjunction of the person (*puruṣa*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self (*ātman*), like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. It arises from a pure intention (*abhisandhi*). A pure intention is a specific volition (*saṃkalpa*) free from hypocrisy (*dambha*) and other such defects; from that, Dharma is born. It is caused by the specific means prescribed for those belonging to the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. The *āśramins* are the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). The meaning is that their Dharma is produced by the means enjoined with reference to each respective class and stage of life. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [234] [pp. 622–623]

In that regard, the general duties (*dharma*) are: faith in the sacred law, non-violence, benevolence toward living beings, truthfulness in speech, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from guile, avoidance of anger, ritual ablution, the use of pure substances, devotion to the specific deities, fasting, and vigilance.
For the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the common means of accomplishing dharma are sacrifice, study, and giving.
The specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa are receiving gifts, teaching, officiating at sacrifices for others, and the sacraments prescribed for his own caste.

For the Kṣatriya, it consists of the proper protection of subjects, the restraint of the wicked, not retreating in battles, and his own purificatory rites. For the Vaiśya, it consists of buying and selling, agriculture, cattle-rearing, and his own purificatory rites.
For a Śūdra, there is dependence on the preceding castes, and his rites are performed without mantras.

As for those belonging to the stages of life (āśramins), the student (brahmacārin) residing in the teacher’s household must perform the duties prescribed by his own scripture—namely, service to the teacher, tending the sacred fire, gathering fuel, and the practice of begging for alms—as well as the avoidance of honey, meat, sleeping during the day, applying collyrium to the eyes, anointing the body with oil, and so forth.
*Nyāyakandalī* [234] [pp. 622–624]

From where should the means for accomplishing dharma, which transcends the senses, be sought? To this he says: "But of that... Śruti is the Veda, heard precisely from the mouth of the teacher through a specific performance and not grasped by being written down; Smṛti is the word of Manu and others. By these two, [the means] are enjoined—that is, propounded. Substances, qualities, and actions, existing in the relationship of general and particular, are the general means of accomplishing dharma.

In this regard, the means for accomplishing dharma are described in their general form for all social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas): faith in dharma, clarity of mind toward dharma; non-violence, which is the resolve not to harm living beings. Since the performance of prohibited injury does not result in adharma, nor does its mere absence give rise to dharma, the resolve not to injure—being prescribed by rule—is indeed a means for accomplishing dharma. Benevolence toward beings is the act of favoring living creatures.

Truthfulness is speech that accords with reality. Non-stealing is the resolve, "I shall not take the property of others without authorization according to the scriptures," rather than merely the absence of taking another's property, which is a negative state. Celibacy is the avoidance of consorting with women; this too is of the nature of a resolve. Integrity is purity of intention, because actions performed with a pure motive serve as means for attaining *dharma*.

The avoidance of anger is the renunciation of anger, and that too consists essentially of mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Ablution is bathing. The practice of pure substances is the regular use of pure items such as sesame seeds and the like on certain festival days (*parvan*) as a means for accomplishing dharma. Devotion to a specific deity means devotion to a deity recognized by the three Vedas (*trayī*). Fasting is the resolve to abstain from food on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and other such occasions.

Heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the necessary performance of obligatory and occasional rites. These—sacrifice (*ijyā*), study (*adhyayana*), and charity (*dāna*)—are the common means of achieving *dharma* for all three classes, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; they are the general means of achieving *dharma*. Sacrifice is the performance of rituals such as the *yāga* and *homa*. Study is the recitation of the Vedas. Charity is a specific intention (*saṃkalpa*) resulting in the transfer of one's own property to another.

Although charity certainly exists for the Śūdra as well, this [set of duties] is stated as a specific means of achieving *dharma* for the three higher castes with reference to the kind of charity performed within sacrifices and similar rites.

He sets forth the specific and unique means for the accomplishment of dharma for the Brāhmaṇa: receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*). Receiving gifts is the acceptance of wealth from a distinguished person; teaching is well known; and officiating at sacrifices is the performance of priestly duties (*ārtvijya*). These are the means for the accomplishment of dharma for the Brāhmaṇa, because he has the right to perform dharma with wealth acquired solely through these very methods. Furthermore, the forty-eight sacraments (*saṃskāras*) prescribed for his own caste are the means for the accomplishment of dharma for the Brāhmaṇa by way of producing fitness for the completion of Vedic rites.

The specific duties of a Kṣatriya are as follows: the proper protection of subjects, the preservation of subjects who follow righteous conduct, the restraint of the wicked, and the punishment of the corrupt according to the scriptures; non-retreat in battles, the engagement of weapons until victory is achieved or until the end of one's life; and the performance of his own purificatory rites.

For the Vaiśya, the means of accomplishing dharma are buying and selling, agriculture, and cattle-rearing. Buying is the acquisition of goods from another after giving a price; selling is the giving of one's own goods to another after receiving a price. Agriculture is the sowing and planting of seeds in cultivated land. Cattle-rearing is the tending of cows, goats, sheep, and so forth. These are the instruments for the fulfillment of dharma for the Vaiśya, because wealth acquired through these very means serves as an auxiliary to dharma. For the Śūdra, dependence upon the preceding castes and ritual acts performed without mantras are the instruments for fulfilling dharma.
*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [235] [p.624]:

For a householder who has completed his studies and vows (*vidyāvratasnātaka*) and has performed his duties, there is the performance of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*)—known as those for beings, humans, gods, ancestors, and Brahman—at morning and evening, using wealth acquired through the *śālīna* or *yāyāvara* modes of livelihood. Furthermore, when capacity exists, there is the performance of the permanent cooked sacrifices (*pākayajña-saṃsthā*) according to the rules of the single fire (*ekāgni*), as well as the oblation sacrifices (*haviryajña-saṃsthā*) such as the *ādhāna* and others, and the soma sacrifices (*somayajña-saṃsthā*) such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others, during the intervals between these; and likewise, the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the procreation of offspring.

For the student (*brahmacārin*) or the householder, there is dwelling in the forest (*vanavāsa*), as well as the wearing of bark garments, skins, and the maintenance of hair, beard, nails, and body hair. For one established in the forest, there is the eating of forest-grown food, sacrificial remnants, and the remains of offerings made to guests. In the *Nyāyakandalī* [pp. 624–626], the means for accomplishing the duty (*dharma*) of those belonging to the stages of life (*āśramin*) is stated. Regarding the student who dwells in the teacher’s family: he who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with its auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*) and its secret doctrines (*sarahita*), is the "teacher" (*guru*). For the student who is habituated to dwelling in that teacher's family or household, there are the observances prescribed by his own scripture; these are the duties ordained by the scripture specifically concerning the student.

[Service to the teacher, tending the fire, gathering fuel, and the practice of begging for alms; as well as the avoidance of honey, meat, sleeping during the day, and the use of ointments and collyrium—these constitute the means for accomplishing dharma in the form of vows. Service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) means attending upon the teacher. Regarding "service to the teacher, the fire, fuel, and begging": *ācaraṇa* refers to the performance of these acts. The performance of service and begging consists in their actual execution. The performance regarding the fire is the daily oblation (*homa*) into the fire. The performance regarding fuel is the fetching of fuel from the forest for the sake of the fire; such is the distinction.

He describes the foundation of dharma for the householder: "for one who has bathed after completing his studies and vows. One who has studied the vow undertaken for the sake of Vedic study and has then relinquished it is a *vidyāvratasnātaka*; for such a householder who has taken a wife—that is, who has formally accepted a spouse—the performance of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), known as those for beings, humans, gods, ancestors, and Brahman, must be carried out morning and evening with wealth acquired through the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* modes of livelihood.

To the extent that a granary or a jar is filled with grain, or for as long as there is sustenance for three days or one day—that much, when brought by another and given with faith, the acceptance of which constitutes the *śālīna* mode of life. Moving from house to house without accepting anything from another, taking up the alms-bowl (*cakra*) and wandering for alms, is the *yāyāvara* mode of life.

The performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—in the evening, in the morning, and in the afternoon—by means of wealth acquired through those two [duties], is the means for fulfilling the dharma of a householder. The offering of oblations (*bali*) to all beings is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*). The honoring of guests is the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*). The burnt offering (*homa*) is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). The ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). In the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), there is the recitation of the Vedas. Furthermore, when one has the capacity, there is the performance of the obligatory cooked-sacrifices (*pākayajñasaṃsthā*) according to the rules of the single fire (*ekāgni*). This is the performance.

"One fire" refers to the *aupāsana* fire. Its ritual procedure consists of its formal adoption at the time of marriage. By means of this fire, there is the performance—provided one has the capacity—of the *pākayajña* sacrifices, which are specific types of cooked-sacrifices such as the *aṣṭakā*, *pārvaṇa*, *caitrī*, *āśvayujī*, and others, which are obligatory and must necessarily be performed. [This also applies to] the *haviḥ-yajña* sacrifices beginning with the *agnyādheya*, and the *soma-yajña* sacrifices beginning with the *agniṣṭoma*.

Performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is the means for accomplishing *dharma*. By the term "establishment of the fires" (*agnyādheya*), the laying of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is designated—that which is performed by a Brāhmaṇa in the spring. The "sacrificial sessions consisting of oblations" (*haviryajñasaṃsthā*) refers to the specific types of oblation sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the Four-Monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the Agrahāyaṇī, and so forth. The phrase "Agniṣṭoma and so forth" refers to the seven specific types of Soma sacrifices—the Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśin, Vājapeya, Atirātra, Aptoryāma, and [the others]—which are called the "sacrificial sessions consisting of Soma" (*somayajñasaṃsthā*). As for the expression "in the interval" (*yadantareti*).

The avoidance of sexual intercourse in the form of a vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) at times other than the prescribed period is a means for achieving *dharma*. Furthermore, the procreation of offspring is also a means for achieving *dharma*, according to the Vedic revelation: "Through a son, one conquers the worlds. He describes the means for achieving *dharma* for one dwelling in the forest: "Whether he be a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) or a householder," because of the scriptural statement: "On whatever day faith arises in him, on that very day he should go forth. Thus, when faith has been attained, the forest-dwelling of a celibate student occurs.

For that householder practicing the vow of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), the means for accomplishing *dharma* consist of wearing bark garments, skins, and keeping the hair, beard, nails, and body hair; eating wild fruits and roots, eating the remnants of the fire-oblation (*huta-śeṣa*), and eating the remnants of what has been offered to guests. However, for one who has performed the *prājāpatyā* sacrifice, given away his entire property as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), established the sacred fires within himself, entrusted his wife to his son, and has gone forth into the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), there is neither fire-oblation nor the reception of guests.

As for one who has set out for the forest together with his wife and his sacred fires, his food consists of the remnants of oblations and the remnants of what was offered to guests. Praśastapādabhāṣya [236] [p.626]:

For one who has renounced the world—whether he belongs to any of the three [orders], is endowed with faith, has granted perpetual fearlessness to all beings, has relinquished his own ritual duties, and is vigilant in the observances (yama)—the accomplishment of yoga consists in the thorough discernment of the six categories.
"Virtue arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon these means and the clarity of one's disposition, without aiming at any visible purpose.
(*Nyāyakandalī* [236], pp. 626–628).

He explains the duty of the ascetic with the words "of the three": even when adopting the stage of life of an ascetic, there is no fixed rule; for if faith is present, one becomes a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) who is still a student (*brahmacārin*), or one may be a householder (*gṛhastha*), or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). It is with this intention that he says "of any one of the three."

For one who possesses faith and mental clarity, having granted perpetual fearlessness to all beings and having adopted the resolve of non-malice—thinking, "Beings must never be harmed by me"—and having renounced and abandoned his own optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), he remains vigilant regarding the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). Non-violence, truthfulness, and so forth are the *yamas*, as the venerable Patañjali said: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*. Austerity, purity, and so forth, however, are the *niyamas*.

As that very Blessed One said: "Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas). However, the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya* states that for each stage of life (āśrama), there is a specific observance that serves as a means to dharma. For one who is diligent in these and does not transgress them, the accomplishment—that is, the production—of a particular meditative absorption (samādhi) capable of generating self-knowledge through the discernment of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha-prasaṃkhyāna*), which is the knowledge of the reality of the six categories, is the means to dharma for the renunciant.

He explains how these accomplish *dharma* with the words "and it is seen. When these practices are performed without aiming at purposes such as gain or honor—that is, without attachment—then, depending upon the purity of disposition (*bhāva-prasāda*) and the purity of intention (*abhiprāya-viśuddhi*), *dharma* arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind.

For one who is daily struck by sufferings, who has come to know in reality that sense-objects are the sole cause of suffering and is thus dispassionate, who desires the absolute cessation of suffering, and who—having heard it said that "the unerring manifestation of the Self is the means of its removal" and that "its basis is a particular state of meditative concentration"—has renounced all desire-driven actions and intends to practice *samādhi*.

For one who has abandoned a village abounding in things antagonistic to yoga and has resorted to the forest, having purified the self through *yama* and *niyama*, a dharma that turns back [the mind] arises from the practice of *samādhi*. From that, a superior *samādhi* arises; from that, another even more superior dharma; and from that, yet another most superior *samādhi*. By this sequence, in the final birth, such a specific *samādhi* matures which cannot be overcome even by the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*).

For it is observed that when one attentively contemplates some desired object, the mind becoming one-pointed upon it, there occurs a lack of awareness even toward powerful objects present nearby; just as an archer who has hit his mark does not perceive even a king passing by while in practice. And so the venerable Patañjali says: "Its cessation [of mental fluctuations] is achieved through practice and dispassion. When concentration has thus matured, the knowledge that directly realizes the nature of the Self arises. As the followers of Kapila have said: "Thus, from the practice of the principles, [the realization arises]: 'I am not,' 'nothing is mine,' 'I do not exist'—without remainder."

"From the absence of error, pure and absolute knowledge arises. Therefore, for the sake of self-knowledge, the ascetic practices the means of yoga. Knowledge has as its sole fruit the manifestation of the object of knowledge; since the nature of the Self is attained even through scriptural knowledge of the Self, one might ask: "What is the use of making it perceptible through the practice of meditation? No, for that which is beyond the senses lacks the capacity to sublate perceptual knowledge. In its essential nature, the Self is neither an agent nor an enjoyer, but is indeed indifferent.

In this regard, the notion of agency and enjoyership expressed as "I" and "mine," which is produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the connection between the body and the senses, is false, because it consists in perceiving that which is not [the Self] as being that. And from this arise attachment toward agreeable things and aversion toward disagreeable things; from these two come engagement and withdrawal; from those, merit and demerit; and from those, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). As it has been said by the followers of the Sugata:
"When there is a self, there is the conception of another; from the division of self and other, there arise grasping and aversion. All states of existence are bound up with these two."

This entire conventional cognition, permeated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is exceedingly powerful and established by nature; it is a perception (*pratyakṣa*) through which this conviction arises. In contrast, the knowledge of the reality of the self derived from scripture (*śruti*) is momentary, lacks corroboration through experience, and is indirect (*parokṣa*). Furthermore, a more firmly established appearance of perception cannot be negated by an appearance that is indirect.

For even if one has understood through other means of knowledge that sugar is sweet, the appearance of bitterness produced by a defective sense organ, along with the resulting onset of suffering, does not cease even after a hundred repetitions. Therefore, for the sake of direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*) must be cultivated. When concentration is perfected, through its power, the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*)—which is the opposite of being an agent and an enjoyer—becomes manifest. Due to the contradiction between knowledge and ignorance regarding the same object, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" are eradicated; thus, although the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) still exists, it no longer touches the Self. And so it has been said by the followers of Kapila:
Therefore, when the sevenfold form has ceased through the power of its purpose,
the Puruṣa, established in himself like a spectator, beholds Prakṛti as she has desisted from further procreation.

By means of that true knowledge being present, the Puruṣa—like a spectator, indifferent, established in his own nature, and unmixed with the intellect (buddhi) due to its being defiled by the fluctuations of *rajas* and *tamas*—beholds Prakṛti, whose productivity has ceased; that is to say, she has turned away from the seven forms [of effects], because her capacity to generate experience has ceased, owing to [the presence of] knowledge, virtue, dispassion, and power, as well as non-virtue, ignorance, passion, and lack of power.

Although this latent impression of delusion (*mohavāsanā*) is beginningless and the direct realization of truth (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) has a beginning, nevertheless it is suppressed by this [realization]; for the apprehension of reality is the supreme strength of the intellects.

Non-dharma (*adharma*) is also a quality of the self (*ātman*). It is the cause of misfortune and transgression for the agent, is beyond the reach of the senses, and brings about the cessation of the consciousness of final suffering. Its means of accomplishment are those prohibited in the scripture, which are the opposites of the means of accomplishing dharma, such as violence, falsehood, theft, and so forth; the non-performance of what is enjoined, and negligence. These, depending upon a corrupt intention and the conjunction of the self and the mind, result in the production of non-dharma.

From a predominant *dharma* characterized by activity—which belongs to one who is ignorant and possessed of passion and hatred, and which is accompanied by a small amount of *adharma*—there arises a conjunction with desirable bodies, senses, objects, pleasures, and so forth, in accordance with one's latent dispositions (*āśaya*), within the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Prajāpati, the ancestors, and humans. Likewise, from a predominant *adharma* accompanied by a small amount of *dharma*, there arises a conjunction with undesirable bodies, senses, objects, sufferings, and so forth, in the states of existence as hungry ghosts and animals.

Thus, from *dharma* characterized by activity that is accompanied by *adharma*, there occurs the continuous cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) again and again among gods, humans, animals, and denizens of hell.

*Nyāyakandalī* [237] [pp. 629–630]: Adharma is also a quality of the self (*ātmaguṇa*). Not only dharma, but adharma as well, is a quality of the self. It is the cause of misfortune and transgression for the agent. "Misfortune" refers to the means of suffering, and "transgression" refers to suffering; adharma is the cause of both. [The meaning is that it is supersensible (*atīndriya*), i.e., not perceived by any sense organ. It is opposed to the cognition of the final suffering. It is destroyed by the correct cognition of the final suffering.

The means for that [unrighteousness] are prohibited in the treatise; they are the opposites of the means for righteousness, such as violence, falsehood, theft, and so forth. Violence is the harming of others. Falsehood is speaking untruth. Theft is the taking of another's property not in accordance with the scriptures. Such things, which are the opposites of the means for righteousness and are prohibited in the treatise, are the means for unrighteousness. Also included are the non-performance of what is enjoined and negligence. Non-performance of what is enjoined is the failure to perform that which must necessarily be done.

Negligence (*pramāda*) is a transgression not preceded by conscious intent; these two are also means for the production of demerit (*adharma*). He demonstrates how demerit arises from these: "And depending upon these and a corrupt intention (*abhisandhi*), demerit arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind. Where there is the performance of a means for demerit preceded by desire, there a corrupt intention is the cause; however, in the case of what is done unintentionally, negligence is its cause.

Having thus stated the proof for what is not the Dharma (*adharma*), he now states the thesis (*sādhya*) with the words beginning "among the ignorant" (*aviduṣu*). He who conceives of himself as "I am the agent and the enjoyer," and who, from the perspective of ultimate reality, conceives of external and internal objects—which are actually means to suffering—as means to happiness, is the ignorant person (*avidvān*). Overwhelmed by thirst for his own enjoyment, he becomes attached to objects superimposed as means to happiness, and he becomes hostile toward that which obstructs them.

From that dharma which is the cause of its manifestation—specifically from the dharma performed with the aspiration for rebirth, thinking "May I become a god or a gandharva"—there arises, as a result of that preeminent cause, a connection with desirable bodies and so forth that correspond to one's intentions and actions. Even in the abodes of Brahmā, Indra, and others, there is a certain degree of the intermingling of suffering; and there is no experience of suffering other than from unrighteousness (adharma).

And since there is no cause for suffering other than unrighteousness (*adharma*), it has been stated [in the verse] that [the results arise] from that which is accompanied by even a small amount of unrighteousness. To demonstrate that for one whose *dharma* is superior, the body and so forth become superior; for one whose *dharma* is more superior, they become more superior; and for one whose *dharma* is most superior, they become most superior—it was said [in the verse], "conformable to their disposition" (*āśayānurūpaiḥ*). The word *iṣṭa* (desired) is connected with each member beginning with "body," because it is employed immediately after the copulative compound (*dvandva*).

Likewise, from excessive unrighteousness (*adharma*), there occurs a conjunction with undesirable bodies and so forth in the states of the *preta* and animal births. Even in the state of a *preta* and the like, there is some slight pleasure, and that is the effect of righteousness (*dharma*); therefore, it was said [in the verse] "accompanied by a small amount of dharma. He concludes: "Thus" (*evam*). *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [238–239–240] [pp. 631–632]

However, from an action performed preceded by knowledge and without a desire for its fruit, there arises for one born into a pure family—who seeks the means to eliminate suffering, has approached a teacher, and has produced knowledge of the reality of the six categories—the cessation of ignorance. Consequently, being dispassionate, there is an absence of passion and hatred; due to this absence, there is no production of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Through the exhaustion of previously accumulated merit and demerit by means of experience, and having produced the happiness of contentment and the dissolution of the body, when passion and the like cease, there remains only the *dharma* characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Having attained the happiness born from the vision of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), one desists. Then, due to cessation, for the self which is now seedless, there is the cessation of the body and so forth; since the body and so forth do not arise again, liberation is the state of tranquility, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [238] [pp. 631–632]

Having thus established that *saṃsāra* proceeds from [ignorance regarding] the *dharma*, he now establishes *apavarga*: "But through knowledge preceded by [this realization]," etc. He who has attained the knowledge—"By my very nature I am indifferent (*udāsīna*), and all these external and internal objects are merely means to suffering"—becomes free from thirst for the pleasures of seen and heard-of objects. Without desire for fruits such as "May I be thus" or "May these [pleasures] be mine," he performs the other prescribed actions which are necessary to be done as means to cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Therefore, from action performed preceded by knowledge, one’s birth occurs in a pure family. For one of low birth, faith does not arise; for one lacking faith, the desire to know is not accomplished; for one who lacks the desire to know, there is no self-knowledge; and for one devoid of that, there is no attainment of liberation.

Therefore, action performed without intending its fruit, which is conducive to liberation, brings about birth in a pure family. For one born into a pure family and daily afflicted by sufferings, there arises an inquiry into the means for the cessation of suffering, [in the form of the thought]: "How indeed might this cessation of my suffering come about? Having thus developed this inquiry, he approaches a teacher; and from the instruction of that teacher, he acquires a scriptural knowledge of the reality of the six categories.

Thereafter, through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), [the truth] becomes directly perceived. For one in whom the knowledge of reality has arisen, ignorance together with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) ceases. Upon that cessation, erroneous cognition vanishes; and for one who is dispassionate and whose impressions of attachment and aversion have been severed, there is no production of merit and demerit due to the absence of attachment and aversion. For activities bound by the impressions of afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*) sprout like rice grains covered by husks.

When the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, they no longer link to a new effect, like husked grains of rice. As the Blessed Lord Patañjali said: "When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. And as the Blessed Lord Akṣapāda said: "There is no further activity for one whose afflictions have been destroyed, in order to link to a new existence. Furthermore, there is the cessation of previously accumulated merit and demerit through their being experienced, and through other karma that has the result of cessation (*nivṛtti*) as its cause.

Having produced the happiness of contentment and physical exhaustion, the *dharma* characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), being solitary, brings about the happiness born from the vision of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-darśana*) and then ceases. "Cessation" (*nivṛtti*) is that by which *saṃsāra* is brought to an end; that whose characteristic is cessation is "characterized by cessation," a *dharma* whose nature is cessation. Once the cessation of passion and other afflictions has occurred, this solitary *dharma* remains established, and having produced the happiness of contentment and physical exhaustion, it effects the happiness born from the vision of the ultimate truth—that is, the happiness born from the realization of the Self (*ātman*). Having performed that, it ceases.

Because it is the rule for the cessation of actions that lead to humiliation, at that time, for the seedless self (*ātman*), when the body and so forth have ceased, there is no further production of a body and so forth; liberation (*mokṣa*) is thus a subsiding like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.

When, having attained the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-darśana*), merit (*dharma*) has ceased, then for the seedless self—devoid of the merit and demerit (*adharma*) which are the seeds of the body and so forth—once the produced bodies and so forth have ceased due to the exhaustion of karma, and future ones do not arise due to the absence of a cause, liberation is the non-production of a body again, just as there is a subsiding and non-reappearance of a fire once its fuel is burnt. Thus, the non-production of a body again is liberation.

*Nyāyakandalī* [239] [pp. 632–636]: This is now being examined: Is liberation attained through knowledge alone, or through the combination of knowledge and action? We maintain that it is through the combination of knowledge and action. For one whose desire for other things has ceased and who has desisted from optional (*kāmya*) rites, the obligation to perform obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites does not cease; for these are prescribed for any initiated Brāhmaṇa. And the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) is indeed a Brāhmaṇa, since his caste has not been extinguished.

If, while being qualified for it, he were to neglect those duties that must necessarily be performed, his demerit would accumulate day by day; and due to that accumulation, he would remain bound and not be liberated. As it has been said:
"Those actions which are performed for the sake of desire, and those which are prohibited..."
"They bind even one who does not perform the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites.

If it is argued that the non-performance of what is enjoined is a mere absence (abhāva), and that an absence cannot be a cause for a positive state (bhāva), and therefore sin (pratyavāya) does not arise from this—[we reply: no, because sin is possible due to the performance of something else when that which was enjoined is left undone. For it is not accepted that absence has causal efficacy in its own right, but rather as subordinate to a positive entity. Furthermore, a person possessing a body does not do nothing at all with body, speech, or mind during the time of the Sandhyā and other such rites, since they still perform actions such as maintaining the body. As it has been said:

The prior non-existence of actions that exists in cases such as the non-performance of prescribed duties is not removed by its being a real entity (vastu), even though it brings about undesirable results.

"Doing something else at the time [prescribed for a rite] instead of what ought to be done, the insentient person incurs sin (*pratyavāya*) by that very act; he is not produced by non-existence alone. The meaning is that he is not produced by mere non-existence. Sin arises from the performance of prohibited acts, whereas the mere maintenance of the body and so forth is not prohibited. If one asks, "What fault is there if he practices yoga during the *saṃdhyā* even while performing those [prohibited acts]?"—that is not so. Because of the rule of absolute necessity (*avaśyakartavyatā*) regarding what is enjoined for that specific time, the performance of mere bodily maintenance and the like is effectively prohibited.

For one who practices that [prohibited act], there certainly arises demerit (pratyavāya) caused by the performance of what is forbidden. Now, if it is argued that the knowledge of the Self alone—having attained a state of clarity through cultivation practiced over a long period, with devotion and without interruption—eradicates passion, hatred, and delusion along with their very roots, and thereby also eradicates the demerit caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties, that is incorrect.

For when practice becomes clear in a particular domain, the apprehension of reality arises therein and dispels doubt and error; however, its capacity to bring about another entity has never been observed before. If, moreover, the knowledge of the Self were to obstruct karmas, it would obstruct even those karmas whose fruits have already begun to manifest; in that case, liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) would be utterly remote, since the body would fall away immediately after the realization of reality, as all karmas would have dissolved.

And there exists this person who, although all ignorance has been ceased by the vision of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), perceives the entire world as a mere appearance like a painted image; he is free from attachment even toward a single thing, and while experiencing the specific karma whose fruit has already begun (*prārabdha-phala*), he awaits the fall of the body—just as the rotation of a potter’s wheel continues by the force of its momentum even after the potter’s activity has ceased. Thus says the Śruti: "For the wise man, even while living, is liberated from both joy and sorrow. And so say the followers of Kapila:

"Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, when dharma and the other [causes] no longer function as causes, he remains with his body sustained by the force of the *saṃskāras*, like the whirling of a potter's wheel. Regarding the phrase "when dharma and the others no longer function as causes," the meaning is: when the afflictions (*kleśas*) along with their latent impressions (*vāsanās*) have been eradicated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there is an absence of the acquisition of auxiliary causes for dharma and the rest. If it is argued that "karmas whose results have not yet begun do not manifest and are dissolved through the knowledge of reality," we say no; because they too are karma, they cannot be destroyed by knowledge, just like karma that has already begun to yield its fruit (*ārabdhaphala*).

As for the teaching, "And his actions are exhausted when He, who is both the high and the low, is seen," its meaning is this: when knowledge exists, future actions are not performed. It does not mean, however, that actions already produced are destroyed by knowledge. Accordingly, another scripture states: "Action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, once performed must necessarily be experienced; it is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons. And so forth.

If knowledge does not destroy actions, how can there be the exhaustion of actions accumulated over many thousands of births? [The answer is: Through experience and through actions impelled for that purpose. If it is asked, "How can there be exhaustion in a single birth of those [actions] which are infinite?"—no, because there is no fixed rule regarding time. Just as actions are accumulated with each birth, so too are they exhausted through experience. Those actions, however, which have not been exhausted, are destroyed by one who knows the Self and who does not accumulate new [karma], gradually, through experience and through [the exhaustion of] actions. As it has been said:

"One who knows the nature of the self, while performing [actions], effects the exhaustion of karma through experience; after thousands of millions of ages, perhaps one such person is liberated. Thus it is said.

Thus, because non-performance of what is enjoined results in transgression (*pratyavāya*), and because that transgression is a cause of bondage, there can be no cessation from it through other means; therefore, one who desires liberation and wishes to prevent transgression must perform the enjoined duties at the proper times—consistent with the practice of yoga and like the eating of alms—as long as the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) has not become manifest. Even for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) whose self-reality has become manifest, these duties continue as long as the maintenance of the body persists.

However, for one who is established solely in the Self, whose liberation is imminent, and whose prior karma has been exhausted, those [objects] simply vanish due to the absence of external consciousness. At that time, there arises only the knowledge of the Self—which is clarified by the power of matured *samādhi*, brought to its ultimate fruition through the cultivation of detachment, which has induced non-duality regarding objects and uprooted all latent impressions of error, having made the internal organ one-pointed—and not external perception, because of the cessation of the activity of the external senses.

In that state, what possibility is there for the performance of ritual acts? Thus says the Śruti: "They say he does not hear; he has become one. They say he does not see; he has become one," and so forth. At that time, there is also no sin arising from non-performance, because for one who is unaware that "this is the twilight prayer" and the like, and who lacks the realization "I am a Brāhmaṇa," there is a total loss of eligibility for ritual acts. As it has been said: "How could one who no longer conceives the ego-identification with being a Brāhmaṇa engage in ritual acts?"

Furthermore, for one whose all activities have ceased and who remains like a piece of wood, even the injury of living beings is no longer possible. As for the fact that his body persists for some time—even though he has seen what was to be seen, exhausted what was to be exhausted, mastered his mind, and is free from the perception of objects, memory, volition, pleasure, pain, and so forth, being absorbed in samādhi fixed upon Brahman—that is due to the non-termination of the knot of karma whose fruition is longevity, which is the sole cause for the maintenance of the body.

When, however, the attainment of that duration of time occurs for which the body must be maintained as the fruition (*vipāka*) of karma, then, through the performance of its own function, karma is completely severed; with the cessation of karma, the body—which is its effect—ceases. Upon that cessation, since its effect, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), also perishes, the self attains isolation (*kaivalya*). In this regard, there is a cooperative functioning (*sambhūyakāritā*) because the knowledge of the reality of the self and the prescribed karmas both operate toward the obstruction of those karmas that are the cause of bondage.

For one who knows the self as distinct from the body and so forth, and who does not attribute benefit or harm to the self, there occurs the cessation of the notions of "I" and "mine. Consequently, because passion and aversion toward benefactors and malefactors respectively cease to exist, the indifferent person does not engage in action. Thus, there is no accumulation of future wholesome or unwholesome karma; and as for previously accumulated karma, it is exhausted through experience and by further actions. Furthermore, any transgression caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties is prevented precisely by the performance of those prescribed duties.

When the karma of this present life is exhausted and the body ceases to exist, and because of the absence of any other cause there is no further arising of a body for the next life, the self remains in its own essential nature. As it has been said:
"By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil;
and by purifying knowledge through repeated practice, one brings it to fruition."
"Through practice, a person whose consciousness has reached maturity attains liberation.
Thus, this path has also been adopted by others.

"Purification of the being occurs through action; the determination of the self occurs through knowledge. Liberation arises from the practice of both, through their combined union. — *Nyāyakandalī*, pp. 636–637.

Furthermore, what is the nature of the self (*ātman*) by which its abiding is called liberation? Some say it is the nature of bliss (*ānanda*). That is incorrect, because it cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpa*). Is that bliss experienced in liberation, or not? If it is not experienced, then even though it exists, it does not distinguish itself from non-existence, because it is not being enjoyed. If it is experienced, then the cause of that experience must be stated. And we do not perceive any cause for its arising when the body, sense organs, and so forth have ceased to exist.

If it is argued that the conjunction with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the cause [of cognition], we say no; for the mind, when seized by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), acts as a mere auxiliary, and thus—being overridden by the destruction of all seeds of good and evil—it does not function in accordance with the Self's inclination.

If it is argued that [the mind] favors the self through the assistance of *dharma* born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), then since even *dharma* born of yoga is necessarily perishable due to its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), what would favor the mind once that [dharma] has perished? Alternatively, if it is thought that the insentient self, even when liberated, is no different from a stone—for that too neither experiences pleasure nor pain—and if the liberated self were likewise [insentient], what difference would there be between the two? Therefore, the self possesses an innate consciousness (*citi*); when that is drawn outward by the senses, then...

It becomes extroverted. But when the senses have ceased their activity, it then immerses itself in its own self, which is of the nature of bliss. For this Self of consciousness, if it illumines anything whatsoever, yet if it remains indifferent in the state of liberation, then even though it exists, it is as if it does not exist at all. If it is argued that it would be better to conceive of the Self as being merely insentient (*jaḍa*), it is said in reply: Is this nature of bliss belonging to consciousness innate, or is it produced by some other cause? In the first place, there is no cause for illumination in the state of liberation, because it has been stated that the body, the organs, and so forth—the causes thereof—have dissolved.

If it is intrinsic (*svābhāvikī*), then bliss (*ānanda*) should be experienced even during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārāvasthā*), since both consciousness (*citi*) and its objects (*caittrya*) are present. If it is argued that there is no experience due to the obstruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no; for since eternal consciousness has as its very nature the favoring of bliss, its essential form (*svarūpa*) does not fall away—what, then, would be the purpose of an obstruction? Or, if its essential form were to fall away, what permanence could there be in that nature? Therefore, eternal bliss, being perceived by eternal consciousness, is perceived without distinction in both states.

But this is not the case, because during the state of *saṃsāra*, pleasure is experienced as something that arises and ceases, its cognition being dependent upon the objects and the sense organs. Therefore, there is no eternal pleasure belonging to the self; and due to the absence of such pleasure, the state of liberation (*mokṣa*) does not consist in the experience of it. Rather, it is simply the abiding in one's own essential nature (*svarūpasthiti*), characterized by the total cessation of all the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self. That this is the true human goal (*puruṣārtha*) has been established accordingly. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [241] [pp. 637–639]

Sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), perceptible by the auditory organ, momentary, opposed to both its cause and its effect, produced from conjunction, disjunction, and sound, subsisting in a specific location, and having causes that are both similar and dissimilar. It is of two kinds: characterized as phonemes (*varṇa*) and characterized as noise (*dhvani*). Among these, the phoneme-characterized begins with the letter *a* and so forth; the noise-characterized is caused by conch shells and the like.

In that regard, the production of what is characterized as *varṇa* (articulate sound) proceeds as follows: from the conjunction of the self and the mind, there arises a desire to utter a *varṇa*, contingent upon memory; immediately after that, an effort (*prayatna*) occurs; and depending upon that effort, an action is produced in the air (*vāyu*) due to the conjunction of the self and the air. That air, moving upward, strikes the throat and other locations; then, depending upon the conjunction of the air with those locations and the conjunction of those locations with space (*ākāśa*), the production of *varṇa* occurs. Even that which is not characterized as *varṇa* (non-articulate sound) is produced from the conjunction of the drum and the stick, contingent upon that, and from the conjunction of the drum and space. It is also produced from the division of the bamboo joints, contingent upon that, and from the division of the bamboo and space.

Furthermore, from sound—which is produced by conjunction and disjunction—there arises a series of sounds, just like a series of waves. Thus, through this series, the sound that has reached the region of the ear is apprehended. Since there is no going or coming on the part of either the ear or the sound, and since what has not been reached is not perceived, the existence of the series is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
Thus ends the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
*Nyāyakandalī* [241] [pp. 637–639]

Sound is a quality of the ether (*āmbara*), that is, a quality of space (*ākāśa*). But surely number and other qualities could also be qualities of space; how then can this be the definition of sound? To this he says: "perceptible by the ear. The meaning is that sound is that which is a quality of the ether while being perceptible by the ear. In order to refute the opponent's misconception, he says: "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*). Sound perishes very quickly and is not eternal, because it is no longer perceived after its utterance.

Since there is no evidence for their existence, there is no room for the hypothesis that the manifesters [of sound] are momentary; for recognition is explained as having the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object—just as in the case of a flame—and because the distinctions of intensity, dullness, and so forth, establish a distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*). The first sound, which is cognized by both cause and effect, is contradicted by its own effect; the last sound is contradicted by its own cause, the penultimate sound, since there is no other cause for its destruction; whereas those in the middle are contradicted in both ways.

It is produced from conjunction, disjunction, and sound. The distinction is that the first sound is born from conjunction and disjunction, whereas that which follows it is born from sound alone. It exists in a specific location; the meaning is that it does not pervade its substratum. This has already been established. It has causes that are both similar and dissimilar in kind. A sound born from sound has a cause that is similar in kind. That which is born from conjunction or disjunction has a cause that is dissimilar in kind. It is of two types: characterized as phonemes (*varṇa*) and characterized as resonance (*dhvani*). The phoneme-type begins with the letter *a* and so forth; the resonance-type originates from conch shells and the like.

In that regard, among those two, the production of the phoneme-characteristic (*varṇalakṣaṇa*) is now described. From the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon the recollection of a previously experienced phoneme, a desire arises when it is necessary to produce the utterance of a similar phoneme. Thence comes effort; depending upon that effort as the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), an action arises in the internal air (*kauṣṭhyavāyu*) from the conjunction of the self and the air, which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

And that air, moving upward, strikes the throat and other locations; it strikes regions such as the heart, the throat, and the palate. Immediately after that impact, from the conjunction of the location—such as the throat—with the internal air, which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and depending upon that conjunction as the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), the production of the phoneme occurs from the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), which is the conjunction with space at that location.

Sound characterized by the absence of color (avarṇalakṣaṇa) also arises from the conjunction of a drum and a stick, depending upon the velocity residing in the stick, [and] from the conjunction of the drum and space. In this case, the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), while the conjunction of the drum and the stick, as well as the velocity residing in the stick, are the efficient causes (nimittakāraṇa). Furthermore, sound is produced from the disjunction of a section of a bamboo joint and from the disjunction of the bamboo and space.

And from the word itself, he explains the production of sound: from a sound produced by conjunction and disjunction, there arises a series of sounds like a series of waves. Just as from one water-wave another wave arises in the space immediately adjacent to it, and from that yet another, and from that yet another—in this sequence a series of waves occurs—so too, from a sound that has arisen, another sound arises in the space immediately adjacent to it; and since there is no coming or going for these two, there is perception only of what has reached [the sense organ]. From that, yet another [sound arises], and from that...

In this manner, a series of sounds (*śabdasantāna*) comes into being. Thus, there is the perception of the final sound once it has reached the location of the auditory organ (*śrotradeśa*) by means of that series.

[Objection: From what source is this conceptual construction established? To this he says: "Of the auditory organ and the sound. The auditory organ does not travel to the location of the sound, nor does the sound travel to the location of the auditory organ, because both are devoid of motion. There is no perception of that which is not reached, because the sense organs function only through contact (*prāptakāritva*). Furthermore, perception cannot be accounted for by any other means.

And it is observed that in a series of waves, even though they perish at their own place of origin, there is an attainment of another location through a succession of similar effects initiated in a location immediately adjacent to them, depending upon their own proximity; by this, a sound-series (*śabda-santāna*) is postulated. Nor is there an infinite regress, because the sound-series persists for as far as the internal air (*kauṣṭhya-vāyu*), which serves as its efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), continues to follow. For this very reason, sound is not perceived against the wind, due to the obstruction of the internal air.
This path has been thoroughly traversed by logicians; therefore, we have here explained only the essential purport of the commentary, and no further reasoning has been stated.
May this pure system, strung together with its qualities and polished by the luster of reasoning, be placed upon the heart like a necklace of pearls.
Thus ends the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) in the *Nyāyakandalī*, a commentary on the *Padārthapraveśa* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Śrīdhara.
Now follows the determination of the category of action (*karmapadārthanirūpaṇam*).

Praśastapādabhāṣya [242] [pp. 640–641]: All five actions, beginning with upward throwing (utkṣepaṇa), possess the relation of being "action" (karmatva). They share the following characteristics: inherence in a single substance; momentariness; subsistence in corporeal substances; possession of no qualities; possession of gravity, fluidity, effort, or conjunction as their cause; opposition to their own effect, which is conjunction; being the cause of conjunction and disjunction independently of other causes; being a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa); initiating effects that inhere in themselves and in other substrates; not initiating effects of the same class; and not initiating substances. Furthermore, they possess a specific, restricted genus.
And the distinction [of time] consists in its being the initiator of effects characterized by spatial direction.
*Nyāyakandalī* [242] [pp. 640–642]:
To the seed of the sprout of the world, the bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra...
Homage to the one whose crown is the crescent moon, who is like a moon dripping with the nectar of primordial wisdom.

Explaining the mutual similarity among throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the others, as well as their dissimilarity to other categories of entities, he says: "Of throwing upwards and the others. *Karmatva* (the state of being action) is a generality (*sāmānya*); the connection with that belongs only to throwing upwards and the others. Regarding "residing in a single substance" (*ekadravyavattva*): at one time, only one action exists in a single substance; since one action exists in one and the same substance, this is called "residing in a single substance."

If there were a simultaneous inherence of two contradictory actions in a single substance, then, due to their mutual obstruction, there would be no production of conjunctions and disjunctions with specific points of space; consequently, the definition of action as "the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction" would be lost. Alternatively, if there were the occurrence of two non-contradictory actions, then since the conjunctions and disjunctions with that place and substance would be accounted for by one alone, the postulation of a second would be redundant.

In this way, a single action does not exist in more than one place, because when one [substratum] moves, no movement is perceived in another due to that action. Momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) means the state of being destroyed very quickly. Existing in corporeal substances (*mūrtadravyavṛttitva*) means existing in substances that possess delimited dimensions. Being devoid of qualities (*aguṇavattva*) means being free from [inherent] qualities. Being produced by gravity, fluidity, effort, or conjunction. Being opposed to conjunction with its own effect.
Being destructible by conjunction, which is its own effect—not by disjunction—because that would entail the impossibility of a subsequent conjunction.

It is a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction. The meaning is that while, for instance, the initiation of velocity depends upon specific instances of pushing or striking, the initiation of conjunction and disjunction does not depend upon pushing and so forth. It is an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); the meaning is that while qualities may also be instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), actions are not so, but rather are exclusively inherent causes. It is the initiator of effects that are inherent in both itself and another substratum.

The state of being an originator [of action] consists in initiating an effect characterized by conjunction and disjunction that inheres both in its own substratum and in another substratum. [Furthermore, there is] the non-origination of like-kind [action]. If action were to originate another action, there would be no cessation of motion for one who is moving. If it is argued that the cessation of motion at the end occurs due to the cessation of desire, effort, and so forth, then desire, effort, and the like alone must be the cause of each subsequent action, and not action itself.

The action under dispute does not have another action as its cause, because it is an action, like the final action. Alternatively, the action under dispute is not something to be accomplished by another action, because it is an action, like the initial action. [It possesses] the property of not being the originator of a substance, because a substance is produced when the action has ceased due to the subsequent conjunction. [It possesses] the property of being associated with specific universals; this means that each among the [five types of actions], such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), is associated with the universal "upward-throwing-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth. All of these are the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) of all five. He explains precisely how they produce effects distinguished by direction: "In that regard... (*tatra*).

In that context, *utkṣepaṇa* (upward motion) is the action produced from gravity, effort, and conjunction, which occurs in the limbs of the body and in things connected to them, and which causes conjunction with upward regions and disjunction from downward regions. The action that causes conjunctions and disjunctions contrary to that is *avakṣepaṇa* (downward motion).

The disjunction and conjunction of the foremost parts of a straight substance with their respective locations, by which action the whole becomes curved, is contraction (*ākuñcana*). By the reverse of that, when disjunction and conjunction arise, the action by which the whole becomes straight is expansion (*prasāraṇa*).

That which is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with indefinite directions and locations is *gamana* (going). These five kinds of action are, among the limbs of the body and their related objects, both perceptible (*sat-pratyaya*) and imperceptible (*asat-pratyaya*). That which is other than these occurs among them and others as imperceptible; that is indeed *gamana*. It is incorrect to maintain that there are five classes of actions, because there is no distinction from *gamana*. *Nyāyakandalī* [243] [pp. 642–643]

That action which, in the case of the limbs of the body such as the hands and so forth, or in objects connected to them such as pestles and the like, arises from gravity, conjunction, and effort, having as its cause conjunction with the upper parts and disjunction from the lower parts, is *utkṣepaṇa* (throwing upward). The action that has as its cause conjunctions and disjunctions contrary to that is *avakṣepaṇa* (throwing downward). The meaning is that *avakṣepaṇa* is the action which has conjunction with a lower region as its cause and disjunction from an upper region as its cause.
"Moving forward" (rju-gati) means that it is produced by the regions of space and so forth connected to the parts of that stone; this is the connection with the word "by which action.
The meaning is: when, due to the disjunction of the parts of the stone from the lower region, there occurs the production of conjunction with the upper region.

"Accompanied by cognition" (*satpratyayam*) means that it occurs either preceded by volitional effort (*prayatnapūrvakam*) or not preceded by volitional effort (*aprayatnapūrvakam*). "That which is other" (*yadanyat*): among these limbs of the body, or in other substances such as a pestle and so forth, whatever action arises that is not produced by cognition—that is, distinct from the aforementioned [five types]—is merely "going" (*gamana*). The opponent objects: "Regarding actions"—namely, throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest—it is incorrect to claim that there are five classes of action, because all of them are indistinguishable and non-different from "going. This is the meaning of the objection. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [244] [p. 644]

For every momentary action, as soon as it arises, produces conjunctions and disjunctions with the upper, lower, or lateral parts of its own substratum—parts consisting of nothing more than the interstices between atoms—and since the cognition of "going" is indistinguishable in all these cases, therefore all action is indeed merely going.

No, because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to their respective classes. Here, for instance, there is the cognition "upward throwing" and elsewhere "downward throwing," and so on; in every such case, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions are observed according to their classes, from which the distinction between universals and particulars is understood as their cause. Furthermore, due to the specific prefixes such as *ut* and others, and because they initiate effects characterized by specific directions, the distinction of their defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*) is also established.
*Nyāyakandalī* [244] [p.644]

He states that there is indeed no distinction among all [these actions] because they involve motion, beginning with the words "for everything" (*sarvaṃ hi*). Since we observe the cognitions "it moves upward" and "it moves downward" in relation to throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, this entire category—throwing upwards and the rest—is nothing but motion (*gamana*).

He refutes this, saying "No. That which you have stated is not correct, because among actions such as throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*), one observes the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions within each respective class. Just as *gotva* (cowness) is postulated because one observes the recurrence of a cognition within the class of cows through its exclusion from the class of horses and so forth, so too, since one observes the recurrence of a cognition within each class of throwing upwards and the rest through its exclusion from others, there must be the postulation of universals such as *utkṣepaṇatva* (the nature of throwing upwards). This explanation is easy to understand.

Regarding the word "teṣām" (of these): the particle *api* (also) in the phrase "upalakṣaṇabheda api" (there is also a difference in the indicator) is to be understood as following the phrase "kāryārambhāt" (from the commencement of an effect). An "indicator" (*upalakṣaṇa*) is a genus (*jāti*), because by means of it an individual (*vyakti*) is indicated—that is, it is made known as being distinct from others. Thus, the meaning here is this: not only is the distinction between the genera of upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*), downward motion (*apakṣepaṇa*), and so forth established through the observation of inclusive and exclusive cognitions, but it is also established from the commencement of specific effects characterized by particular directions due to the difference in prefixes such as *ud-* and others.

Others, however, maintain that because those actions such as throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth initiate specific effects in particular directions due to the distinctions among prefixes like *ud* and others, both a difference in their defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇabheda*) and a difference in their cognition (*pratipattibheda*) are established. For if there were no difference, then just as throwing upwards would be the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with the upper direction, so too would throwing downwards and the other types of action be.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [245] [pp. 645–647]

[Even so, the restriction that there are exactly five is untenable, because even in the case of going out, entering, and so forth, we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to their respective classes. If it is maintained that a distinction of universals (*jāti*) is accepted in the case of throwing upwards and so forth because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to their respective classes everywhere, [and if it is argued that similarly in the case of going out, entering, and so forth, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions occur due to a difference in effects], then [the answer is]: no, for in the case of throwing upwards and so forth as well, [the distinction arises] precisely from a difference in effects.

There would follow the consequence of the persistence and exclusion of cognitions. Now, if it is argued that there is a specific reason why, despite the existence of the persistence and exclusion of cognitions within similar groups, a distinction of genus (*jāti*) belongs only to throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, and not to going out (*niṣkramaṇa*) and so forth—[we reply: no, because of the consequence of the confusion of genera (*jātisaṅkara*). If the persistence and exclusion of cognitions were due to a distinction of genus in the case of going out and so forth, the confusion of genera would result. How so?

It is observed that when two observers move from one room to another room, they simultaneously have the cognitions of "going out" and "entering," as well as the cognitions "he enters" and "he goes out" at the doorway. However, when the curtain or other such barriers are removed, there is neither the cognition of entering nor the cognition of going out; rather, there is only the cognition of "moving."

Likewise, when a reed or bamboo leaf falls into a tube, many observers simultaneously perceive the notions of whirling, falling, and entering; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (*jāti-saṅkara*). However, no such confusion of cognitions is observed in the case of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the other [motions]. Therefore, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions regarding upward throwing and so forth are due to differences in their respective universals, whereas in the case of exiting and so forth, they are due to differences in their effects.

If it is asked, "How can there be a difference in cognitions simultaneously?"—that is to say, if it is thought that just as there is no confusion of universals (*jāti*), so too there is no confusion of multiple actions, then how can there be simultaneous cognitions of whirling, falling, and entering within a single object by various observers?

To this we reply: No, because of the difference between the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts with spatial directions on the one hand, and those of the whole on the other.
