For an observer who perceives the successive conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts with various spatial points on their sides experiences the cognition of rotation; whereas one who observes the disjunction of the whole from an upper spatial point and its conjunction with a lower point experiences the cognition of falling.

Furthermore, for one who perceives conjunction within the interior of a tube and disjunction at its exterior, the cognition of "entering" arises; thus it is established that the difference in cognitions regarding exiting and so forth is due to the difference in their effects. Let it be granted that the difference in cognitions regarding upward throwing and so forth is due to the difference in their generic classes (*jāti*), but the difference in cognitions regarding exiting and so forth is due to the difference in their effects.
*Nyāyakandalī* [245] [pp. 645–647]

The opponent objects: "Even so. If a universal is admitted in the case of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth because one observes the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions within each respective class, then one must also admit "going out-ness" (*niṣkramaṇatva*) and so forth in the case of going out and so forth, since one likewise observes the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions within each respective class. Consequently, the restriction that there are "only five" [universals] would be untenable.

Now, if it is argued that the difference in cognitions regarding actions such as "going out" (niṣkramaṇa) and so forth arises from a difference in their effects (*kāryabheda*) and not from a difference in their universal (*jātibheda*), then the same would apply to actions such as "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*). To this he says: "Because of the difference in their effects, [the universals] in those [actions]. He answers: "No. If universals such as "going-out-ness" (*niṣkramaṇatva*) were admitted, then there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (*jātisaṅkara*). The meaning is that the inherence (*samavāya*) of multiple contradictory universals in a single individual instance (*vyakti*) would result.

Being asked "How so?", he replies: "Of two observers. When a person goes from one room to another room, there are two observers of that person; regarding a single instance of action, two cognitions are observed: the cognition of "going out" and the cognition of "entering. For the person standing in the room from which the person departs has the cognition "he is going out," while the person standing in the room where he enters has the cognition "he is entering."

If these two cognitions were seen to be produced by [distinct] universals (*jāti*), then the fault would be the coexistence of two mutually contradictory universals—namely, "exit-ness" (*niṣkramaṇatva*) and "entrance-ness" (*praveśanatva*)—within a single individual entity. For instance, when a person enters or exits through a doorway in a house consisting of many rooms, those observers situated in the preceding and succeeding rooms perceive the person as "exiting" or "entering" at the doorway, even though he is merely moving from one room to another within that very same single house.

But when the curtain and so forth have been removed—that is, when the screen situated in the middle has been taken away—then there is neither a cognition of entering nor a cognition of exiting; rather, there is only a cognition of going. Therefore, the intention is that there is only going, and the difference in cognitions in that case is produced by adventitious conditions (upādhi).

He states another example: "In the same way, in the case of a tube (*nālikā*)," where *nālikā* is a designation for a hollow pit. He states a distinction regarding his own position: "And it is not thus. He concludes: "Therefore... [On page 647] he asks: "How can there be a single action in a single substance, and how then is there the cognition of multiple simultaneous actions? He explains this with the words beginning "Now, if it is thought... Here, the phrase "To this we say" marks the commencement of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

What you have stated is not correct, because there is a distinction between the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts and the whole as characterized by direction. The explanation of this is easy to understand: the cognition of "whirling" arises from the actions of the parts which cause conjunctions and disjunctions on the sides; whereas the cognitions of "falling" and "entering" arise from the action of the whole due to the difference in their effects. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [246] [pp. 647–649]

Now, is "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) a synonym for "action-ness" (*karmatva*), or is it another universal (*sāmānya*)? From what source does this doubt arise? Because, just as there is the cognition of "action" in the case of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth when they are combined, there is likewise no difference in the cognition of "going" (*gamana*); therefore, it is understood that it is a synonym for "action-ness. However, since it is designated by a specific name just like throwing upwards and the rest, it might therefore be another universal.

No, because "action-ness" (*karmatva*) is a synonym. Just as there are the terms "self-ness" (*ātmatva*) and "person-ness" (*puruṣatva*), so too is "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) merely a synonym for action-ness. If it is asked, "For what purpose was 'going' mentioned by means of a specific designation?"—no, it is for the purpose of including whirling and so forth. The mention of "going" was made in order to include whirling, falling, vibrating, and the like, which are not already included by the terms "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so on. Otherwise, it would follow that only those four which were stated with specific designations would also be the objects of the general and specific designations.

Alternatively, let there be another universal, *gamanatva* (the nature of going), which resides only in actions such as whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and the like, which cause conjunctions and disjunctions with spatial directions and locations that are not fixed; and the word "going" (*gamana*) should be understood as being applied figuratively (*bhākta*) to upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, on the basis of the commonality of being the agent of conjunctions and disjunctions with its own substratum.
*Nyāyakandalī* [246] [pp. 647–649]

Let it be granted that there is a distinction in the cognition of upward-thrusting (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the other [motions] due to a difference in their generic classes (*jāti*). Now, is "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) a synonym for "action-ness" (*karmatva*), or is it a different, further universal (*sāmānya*)? The proponent asks: "On what basis do you have this doubt? The intention is that such a doubt is here untenable. The opponent establishes the doubt by saying: "In all [of them]," etc.

Just as in all actions such as throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) there is the cognition of action based on the characteristic of motion, so too in those [actions] there arises the cognition of "going" (*gamana*), such as "it goes upward," "it goes downward," "it goes to the base region," or "it goes to the tip region. Therefore, it is understood that "the nature of going" (*gamanatva*) is a synonym for "the nature of action" (*karmatva*), because it pervades all particular instances of action.

As for the fact that "going" (gamana) is mentioned separately by a specific name, like throwing upwards and so forth, it follows that "going-ness" (gamanatva) would be a distinct lower generality (apara-sāmānya), because it is enumerated at the occasion of defining its internal subdivisions.

When doubt has been raised in this manner by the opponent, the Teacher says: "No. Doubt should not be entertained. Why? Because "the state of going" (*gamanatva*) is a synonym for "the state of action" (*karmatva*). He explains this: "The state of going is indeed a synonym for the state of action, just like the state of selfhood (*ātmatva*) and the state of personhood (*puruṣatva*). Just as the state of personhood is a synonym for the state of selfhood because it pervades all distinctions, so too the state of going is a synonym for the state of action. Now, he raises an objection: "For what purpose was 'going' mentioned separately by means of a specific designation?"—this is the point of the challenge introduced by "atha."

The author gives the reply: "No. Movements such as whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth are not included—that is, they are not subsumed—by the terms "throwing upward" (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest. If the mention of "going" (*gamana*) were not made, then those [movements] would not be included within the category of action (*karman*). However, only those specifically designated by their particular names, such as throwing upward and so forth, would be the objects of the general designation "action. Since movements like whirling are also well-known in common worldly usage as being actions, the mention of "going" is made separately for the purpose of including them; such is the meaning of the text. [p. 649]

Alternatively, let there be another universal, "going-ness" (*gamanatva*). To which things does that belong? To this he says: [it belongs] to that which has no fixed direction or location. Why, then, is there the cognition of "going" (*gamana*) with respect to upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest? To this he says: "But the word 'going'... Since the mention of the word "going" is intended as an illustration, the cognition of "going" with respect to upward throwing and so forth must also be explained as being figurative (*bhākta*). He states the basis for this metaphorical usage: "Because of the commonality of being the agent of conjunctions and disjunctions with its own substratum."

Motion produces conjunctions and disjunctions of its own substratum, and upward motion (utkṣepaṇa) and the others do so as well; by this much similarity, the conventional usage of "motion" (*gamana*) is applied to upward motion and the rest.

Why, by this same similarity, is the conventional usage of "upward motion" and the rest not applied to [ordinary] motion? Why is the conventional usage of "young boy" (*māṇavaka*) not applied even to fire, given the similarity of tawny color, reddishness, and so forth? If it is argued that metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) does not occur when the cause is present, but rather the cause is postulated once the conventional usage is established—then this is precisely the solution here as well.
The *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [247] [pp. 649–656]:

The rule for action based on the cognition of existence (*sat-pratyaya*). How so? When one desires to raise up or lower the hand in relation to acts such as sacrifice, study, giving, or agriculture, then an effort (*prayatna*) arises in the self with respect to the region of the hand. From the conjunction of the self and the hand, depending upon that effort and gravity (*gurutva*), motion occurs in the hand; and as it does in the hand, so it occurs in all the limbs of the body, such as the feet, and in the body itself.

How does it occur even in relation to things connected to that [body]? When, having grasped a club with the hand, one forms the desire, "I shall lift up the club with my hand," immediately thereafter, a volitional effort (*prayatna*) arises; from the conjunction of the self and the hand, depending upon that effort, at the very same time that the action of upward-lifting (*utkṣepaṇa-karman*) arises in the hand, at that same time, from the conjunction of the hand and the club, depending upon that very same effort, an action also arises in the club. Then, once the club has been lifted high, the desire for that purpose ceases.

Again, a desire to throw [the pestle] arises. Immediately thereafter, depending upon that [desire], an effort is produced; and depending upon that effort, from the two aforementioned conjunctions, simultaneous actions of throwing occur in both the hand and the pestle. Then, by means of the final action of the pestle, a conjunction called "impact" (abhighāta) is produced between the mortar and the pestle. That conjunction, depending upon the velocity residing in the pestle, produces an action of upward-leaping in the pestle that has no further cause (apratyaya).

Depending on the impact of that action, the pestle initiates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Depending upon that [impression], the conjunction between the pestle and the hand produces an uncaused action in the hand.

Even though the previous impression has perished, the conjunction between the pestle and the mortar—because it is a specific kind of conjunction capable of producing a potent action—is able to assist in the initiation of that new impression.

Alternatively, the very same potent prior latent impression (*saṃskāra*), not being destroyed by the impact, remains present; therefore, there is no further initiation of a latent impression in that which already possesses one. Consequently, at the very moment when the action of upward throwing occurs in the pestle due to the impact independent of a conscious effort, at that same moment, the action of upward throwing also occurs in the hand—though independent of a conscious effort—due to the conjunction of the hand and the pestle depending upon that very same latent impression.

The procedure for movement in the case of objects released from the hand: how so? When the desire to throw a javelin (*tomara*) arises by grasping it with the hand—namely, "I shall throw the javelin with my hand"—thereafter follows an effort (*prayatna*). Depending upon that effort, from the two aforementioned conjunctions, there simultaneously arise the actions of drawing toward oneself in both the javelin and the hand. And when the hand has been extended, the effort intended for that drawing toward oneself ceases.

Immediately thereafter, the desire arises, "I shall throw it far or near, horizontally or upwards. Following that, there occurs an effort corresponding to that desire; depending upon this effort, the conjunction of the hand with the javelin, known as *nodana* (impulsion), takes place. From that, an action produced in the javelin—depending upon the impulsion—initiates a latent momentum (*saṃskāra*) within it. Then, by means of both that momentum and the impulsion, actions continue to occur as long as there is no separation between the hand and the javelin.

Then, once the impulsion has ceased following the separation, subsequent to that formative force (*saṃskāra*), there arise actions—either upward, obliquely, far, or near—in accordance with the effort, until the fall.

The same principle of motion applies to objects released from a machine as well. How so? Suppose a strong man, having practiced his exercises, steadies the bow with his left hand, fits an arrow with his right, and grasping the string together with the arrow by means of his fist, forms the desire to draw it back, thinking, "I shall draw this strung bow."

Immediately thereafter, as soon as an action of attraction arises in the hand from the contact between the self and the hand depending upon that effort, at that very moment, an action arises in the bowstring and the arrow from the contact between the hand and the bowstring depending upon that same effort; and actions arise in the two ends of the bow from the two contacts between the bowstring and the ends of the bow, depending upon the contact between the hand, the bowstring, and the arrow characterized by effort—all of this occurring simultaneously.

When the bow has been drawn thus to the ear, the cognition that "it must not be drawn further than this" arises; from that [cognition], there occurs the destruction of the effort intended for that drawing. Thereafter, a desire to release [the arrow] arises, and following that, an effort [is produced]. Depending upon that [effort], from the contact between the self and the fingers, there is motion in the fingers. From that [motion], there is the disjunction between the string and the fingers. From that disjunction, there is the destruction of the contact. When that [contact] has perished, due to the absence of the obstructing factor, the elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) residing in the bow—

When it places the bow, which had been drawn into a circle, back into its natural state, then, depending upon that very impression (*saṃskāra*), an action arises in the bowstring and in the arrow due to the contact between the bow and the string. Depending upon its own cause, that [action] produces an impression in the bowstring. Depending upon that [impression], the contact between the arrow and the string is the "impulsion" (*nodana*); from that, the initial action in the arrow initiates an impression in the arrow, depending upon that impulsion.

Therefore, from that *saṃskāra* acting as an auxiliary to the impulsion (*nodana*), actions continue to occur as long as there is the separation of the arrow from the bowstring; once the impulsion has ceased due to that separation, the subsequent successive actions arise solely from the *saṃskāra* of the arrow itself, without further effort. Why do many actions occur sequentially? Because of the multiplicity of conjunctions. But the *saṃskāra* is singular, because there is no cause for dependence upon an intervening action. Thus, action governed by the self has been described as having both a real basis (*sat-pratyaya*) and an unreal basis (*asat-pratyaya*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [247] [pp. 649–656]:

"The rule for action based on true cognition"—the meaning is that a type of action preceded by volitional effort (*prayatna*) is now being described. To the question "How so?", he replies: "In the case of things intended to be done. When a person desires to raise or lower his hand while sacrifices and other such acts are intended to be performed, then an effort arises in a region of the self where the hand is located.

Depending upon that effort as its instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), motion arises in the hand from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) consisting of the conjunction with the self residing in the self. Even though effort exists, because it is impossible to perform upward or downward throwing for that which is devoid of gravity, gravity also functions as a cause. As in the case of the hand, so it is for all the limbs of the body, such as the feet, and for the body itself.

In the case of the production of action in the foot, effort (*prayatna*) residing in that portion of the self (*ātmapradeśa*) associated with the foot is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), while the conjunction of the foot and the self (*pādātmasaṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). This should be understood to apply everywhere regarding the production of action in the limbs of the body. Furthermore, in the production of action in the body as a whole, the conjunction of the body and the self is the non-inherent cause, and effort residing in that portion of the self associated with the body is the efficient cause.

The meaning of the question is: how does action arise even in those things connected to it, that is, even in the parts of the body? When one, having grasped a pestle with the hand, forms the desire, "I shall lift up the pestle with my hand," immediately after that desire, an effort arises from the simultaneous desire to lift both the hand and the pestle—namely, "I shall lift the pestle upward with my hand"—and this effort, being produced, is specifically capable of lifting them both simultaneously.

At the very same time that the action of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) arises in the hand from the conjunction of the self and the hand—which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—depending upon that specific effort as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), there also arises an action in the club from the conjunction of the hand and the club, depending upon that same effort produced for both purposes; this occurs due to the simultaneity of the causes.

Then, when the club has been raised far upward, the desire for that purpose ceases; the desire to lift it ceases. Again, the desire to cast it down arises—the meaning is that the desire to cast the club down with the hand arises. Immediately after that, effort (*prayatna*) occurs; and that too, as it arises, arises as something distinct, just like the effort to lift it.

Depending upon that effort, from the two aforementioned conjunctions—namely, the conjunction of the self and the hand, and the conjunction of the hand and the pestle—there arise simultaneously the actions of throwing in both the hand and the pestle. Then, by means of the final action of the pestle, a conjunction called "impact" (*abhighāta*) is produced between the mortar and the pestle. The meaning is that, through another action of the pestle which has been thrown, a conjunction inherent in both the mortar and the pestle is produced, which serves as the cause for the pestle's upward rebound.

That conjunction, depending on the velocity residing in the pestle, produces the action of upward motion in the pestle without an external cause and without being preceded by effort. In the production of that action of upward motion, the impact is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), the velocity residing in the pestle is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and the pestle is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). That action, depending on the impact, initiates a latent disposition (*saṃskāra*) in the pestle; and the action of upward motion, depending on the conjunction called impact which is its own cause, initiates velocity in the pestle.

Depending upon that impression (*saṃskāra*), the conjunction of the hand and the club, acting as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), produces an upward motion in the hand as well, even without being preceded by volitional effort (*aprayatnapūrvakam*).

That previous downward-projecting momentum residing in the pestle has also been destroyed by the impact. In its absence, how could the upward-moving action in the pestle—characterized by the momentum of rising—begin without a cause? Since there would be no efficient cause (*apekṣākāraṇa*), he says: even though the previous momentum has perished, nevertheless, the conjunction of the pestle and the mortar produces a potent action that generates a momentum which, in turn, produces an action. Why? Because it is a specific kind of conjunction; that is, because it is a particular conjunction.

What follows from this if it is so? To that he replies: it becomes capable of assisting—that is, capable of aiding—in the undertaking of the formative impression (*saṃskāra*) of that action. On this view, the actions of flying up belonging to the hand and the mace occur sequentially; however, due to their rapid occurrence, they are perceived as simultaneous.

He states another alternative: "Or rather, the very same previous potent *saṃskāra* remains without being destroyed due to the impact; because it is produced by a specific cause, this extremely powerful *saṃskāra* is not destroyed even by conjunction with a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat*). Therefore, there is no initiation of a further *saṃskāra* in that which already possesses a *saṃskāra*; hence, the previous *apakṣepaṇa-saṃskāra* has not been destroyed. Thus, it is understood that there is no initiation of a further *saṃskāra* in the mace (*musala*) while it already possesses the previous *saṃskāra*."

At the very time when the upward motion of the pestle occurs without an external cause due to an impact dependent on its own latent momentum (*saṃskāra*), at that same time, the upward motion of the hand also occurs without an external cause due to the contact with the lower part of the pestle, which depends on that very same latent momentum. In this view, the simultaneity of the upward motions of both the hand and the pestle is indeed real.

Regarding the question of how the process of motion occurs in objects released from the hand: when the question is asked how the process of motion—that is, the manner of going—arises in substances released from the hand, he says: when, having grasped a javelin (*tomara*), the desire to throw it arises, namely, "I shall throw the javelin with my hand"; immediately thereafter, depending upon that effort and the aforementioned conjunctions—both the conjunction of the [upper] arm and the hand, and the conjunction of the hand and the javelin—there arise simultaneously two actions of drawing toward oneself in both the hand and the javelin.

"Simultaneous attraction" means that it is impossible to lift [an object] without first attracting it. When the hand is extended, the effort for the purpose of attracting it ceases; thus, the effort whose purpose was the attraction of those two—the club and the mallet—ceases because of the production of an opposing effort of extension. [p. 654] "Immediately after that" means immediately after the extension. Then, the desire arises: "I shall throw it sideways, upwards, far away, or near."

Immediately following that, there arises an effort corresponding to it: when there is a desire to throw sideways, an effort to throw sideways is produced; when there is a desire to throw upwards, an effort to throw upwards is produced; and when there is a desire to throw far, a great effort is produced, whereas when there is a desire to throw nearby, a relaxed effort is produced—this is the meaning of the term "corresponding" (*tadanurūpa*).

With reference to that [hand], the contact of the hand with the *tomara* (javelin), termed "impulsion" (*nodana*), is the cause of their simultaneous movement—both for the *tomara*, which is the object of impulsion, and for the hand, which is the agent of impulsion. Therefore, from that contact termed "impulsion," which depends on the aforementioned effort conforming to desire, motion arises in the *tomara*. That motion does not depend on the impulsion; rather, it initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*) within that *tomara*. Subsequently, through both that momentum and the impulsion, further motions continue to occur as long as there is no separation between the hand and the *tomara*.

Then, once the impelling force has ceased due to separation, subsequent to that momentum, there arise actions—either oblique, far-reaching, or near-reaching—that correspond to it until the falling; this means that for the javelin, actions corresponding to the momentum continue to occur until its descent.

The method of movement even for those released from a machine is as follows: How so? One who is strong, having practiced physical exercise and trained with weapons, steadies the bow with his left hand, grasping it firmly; with his right hand, he fits an arrow to it, joins the arrow to the string, and taking hold of the string together with the arrow by means of his fist, he forms the intention: "I shall draw this strung bow. *Jyā* is a name for the bowstring, and *iṣu* is a designation for the arrow.

The string and the arrow together constitute "jyeṣū"; that which exists together with the string and the arrow is "sajyeṣū. This indicates the form of the desire: "I shall draw this bow. Immediately thereafter, when an action of drawing arises in the hand from the conjunction of the self and the hand—dependent upon that effort—at that very same moment, an action arises in the string and an action in the arrow, due to the conjunction of the hand and the string and the conjunction of the hand and the arrow, respectively, both depending upon that same effort.

Two actions occur simultaneously at the two ends of the bow, depending upon the conjunctions of the string with the two ends, which themselves depend upon a specific effort characterized by the conjunction of the hand and the string; all this happens at once due to the simultaneity of the causes. Likewise, when the bow has been drawn back to the ear, there arises the cognition: "By this hand, nothing further need be moved. Consequently, there is the destruction of the effort whose purpose was that drawing of the bow.

Then there is the desire to release the arrow and the bowstring. Immediately after that, there is an effort for the sake of release; from the conjunction of the self and the fingers, which depends upon that effort, arises the action of the fingers. From that [action] arises the disjunction of the fingers from both the arrow and the bowstring.

Then, from that disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction between the arrow and the string-finger; when that conjunction has perished, because of the absence of an obstructing factor, the stabilizing impression (*sthitisthāpaka-saṃskāra*) residing in the bow restores the bow—which had been drawn into a circle—to its original state. At that time, depending upon that impression, an action arises in both the bowstring and the arrow due to the conjunction between the bow and the string.

That action, depending on its own cause and depending on the conjunction of the bowstring, produces in the string a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as velocity (*vega*). That conjunction of the arrow and the string, depending upon that latent impression, is called "impulsion" (*nodana*), because it is the cause of the simultaneous movement of both the impelled arrow and the impelling quality [the string]. Therefore, the first action produced in the arrow from that impulsion, depending on the impulsion, initiates a latent impression in the arrow. From that latent impression, aided by the impulsion, as many actions continue to occur as there is separation between the arrow and the string.

When the impulsion ceases due to separation, subsequent actions continue to arise solely from the latent impression (saṃskāra) known as velocity (vega), until the fall; the fall of the arrow and of this [body] occurs due to the exhaustion of the momentum that counteracts gravity.

Here, an objection is raised: "Why are there many actions occurring sequentially? The intention of the objection is: why is it postulated that there are many sequential actions within the interval of an arrow released from a bowstring? Why is not a single action alone postulated? The response is: "Because of the multiplicity of conjunctions. It is established that an action terminates with a final conjunction. Since many conjunctions are observed in the interval of the discharged arrow, it is therefore accepted that there are many actions.

The impulse (*saṃskāra*), however, is single; for in the interval [between the initial action and the fall], there is no cause for its dependence on further action. Action, depending on either *nodana* (pushing) or *abhighāta* (striking), initiates an impulse, but not action alone, because of the absence of velocity (*vega*). Furthermore, in the interval, there is neither *nodana* nor *abhighāta*. Therefore, a specific impulse produced by the action of the arrow—depending upon the contact with the bowstring—persists until the fall.

And to the extent that its power for performing an action is diminished, to that same extent the action produced becomes progressively weaker, distinguished by degrees such as "slower" or "very slow. For example, the fruit of a young tree is drawn out [grows], whereas that of an old tree is drawn away [falls].

In the case of the four external gross elements when they are not presided over [by a conscious agent], motion occurs solely as movement, being independent of causes such as conjunction with air and so forth. (Praśastapādabhāṣya [248]) [pp. 657–659]

In this context, *nodana* (impulsion) is that specific kind of conjunction which, depending on gravity, fluidity, momentum, and effort—either collectively or individually—is the cause of action that results in non-separation; from it, action occurs in all four great elements (*mahābhūta*), as for example in the earth known as mud. *Abhighāta* (impact) is that specific kind of conjunction which, depending on momentum, is the cause of a single action that results in separation; from it also, action occurs in the four great elements, as for example when hard objects such as stones fall upon one another.

Likewise, when that which is called mud is being pushed or struck by feet and the like, there occurs a conjunction—dependent on either the pushing or the striking, or dependent on both—which is a "conjunction with what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*). From that as well, action arises even in those parts that are neither pushed nor struck.
*Nyāyakandalī* [248] [pp.657–659]

He summarizes: "In this way. In external great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are not presided over [by a conscious agent], motion alone occurs from impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth, without a causal basis [for other types of action]. The meaning is that in external things not presided over by the self—which is the unique correlate—there occurs only the action called "motion" (*gamana*), which is not preceded by effort, and not actions in the form of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the like. It has been stated that in the great elements, action arises from impulsion and so forth.

Now, what is this "impulsion" (*nodana*)? To this he says: "In that context, impulsion is a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) which depends upon gravity, fluidity, effort, and velocity, either collectively or individually. How is this particular conjunction designated as "impulsion"? To this he says: "Impulsion is the cause of an action that does not result in mutual disjunction. That is, impulsion is the cause of an action which does not produce a separation between the object being impelled and the impeller.

What is meant by this? By means of this conjunction, the impeller (*nodaka*) impels the object to be impelled (*nodya*), and not otherwise; therefore, this is called "impelling" (*noga*). As for where impulsion (*nodana*) is the cause of action, he says here: "as in the case of earth known as mud. When a stone pellet placed gently on top of mud gradually sinks down together with the mud, then the conjunction of the stone and the mud, dependent upon gravity, is impulsion.

When mud is lifted a great distance with effort and struck by a stone, then the conjunction dependent on gravity, effort, and momentum is "impulsion" (*nodana*); when it is struck by water, then the conjunction dependent on all [three] is "impulsion"—this should be inferred according to the circumstances as they occur.

That conjunction which depends on momentum (*vega*) and is the cause of a single action that produces disjunction is *abhighāta* (impact). That particular kind of conjunction which is the sole cause of that very action from which the mutual disjunction of the object struck and the striker arises is *abhighāta*. From this as well, action occurs in the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as when hard objects like stones and the like fall upon one another.

Impulsion (*nodana*) is the cause of only one action that results in mutual non-separation, not of one that results in mutual separation; likewise, impact (*abhighāta*) is also the cause of only one action that results in mutual separation, not of one that results in mutual non-separation—this is what is meant by "the cause of one action."

He explains "conjunction with the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*): when the earth known as mud is being pushed or struck by feet and the like, the conjunction that depends on either the push or the strike, or on both, is "conjunction with the conjoined. From that [conjunction] as well, motion arises even in those parts which are neither pushed nor struck.

In one case, when the earth is being pushed or struck by a foot, motion is observed even in those parts that are neither pushed nor struck. In that instance, the cause of the motion in the moving parts is their conjunction with a part of the earth that is being pushed or struck. Where a striking substance, having struck a portion of the earth, moves downward slightly and then rebounds upward, the cause of the action in those other parts is the conjunction of the conjoined (saṃyuktasaṃyoga), which depends on both factors. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [249] [p.659]

Falling is that downward motion which occurs due to gravity when there is an absence of conjunction, effort, or velocity that counteracts gravity, as in the case of a pestle, a body, or similar objects. Among these, the first [motion] is due to gravity alone, while the second and subsequent ones are due to both gravity and momentum (*saṃskāra*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [249], p. 659.

He states that gravity is the cause of action: "In the case of earth and water, when there is an absence of conjunction, effort, or velocity that counteracts gravity, the downward motion resulting from gravity is called falling. As it has been stated regarding the pestle, the body, and so forth: in the absence of the conjunction with the hand which obstructs gravity, the downward motion of the pestle occurs due to gravity; this is falling."

Thus, in the absence of an effort that counteracts gravity, there is the falling of the body; and in the case of a discharged arrow, there is falling in mid-course due to the absence of velocity and because of gravity. Among these, the first motion arises from gravity, while the second and subsequent motions arise from both gravity and the residual momentum (*saṃskāra*). In the case of objects such as a pestle, the initial motion occurs due to gravity, and by that motion a residual momentum is produced. Thereafter, the successive motions are generated by both gravity and the residual momentum, since the causal efficacy of each of the two has been determined individually in other instances. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [250] [pp. 660–661]

The downward gliding of waters from a high place to a low place, which occurs when they have become a stream, is due to their fluidity (*dravatva*). How so? The fluidity of the whole is obstructed by its conjunction with the surrounding banks; the fluidity of the parts is also obstructed by that very same [conjunction] as it inheres in the same object; and the fluidities of the successive parts are obstructed by the conjunctions of those conjoined [parts].

But when the breach of the dam is made by means of a certain measure, then, because the fluidity of the composite whole is obstructed on all sides, there is no commencement of activity. However, for the fluidity of the parts situated near the dam, there is the attainment of functional activity due to the absence of any obstruction to the successive fluidities of the subsequent parts.

Then, there is the successive movement of those very [atoms] in conjunction. Thereafter, when the previous substance has perished, a long substance is initiated by the parts remaining in a continuous series. And in that case, fluidity (*dravatva*) arises through the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes. [In that process, the action that arises in the composite whole when the conjoined causes move in a continuous series] is called "flowing" (*syandana*).
*Nyāyakandalī* [250] [pp. 660–661]

He explains the causality of fluidity (*dravatva*): "The downward gliding of waters that have become a stream from high ground to low ground is flow (*syandana*) due to fluidity. The meaning is that the downward gliding of waters, which is flow, arises from fluidity. [The question is: "How so? [The answer is: "On all sides. When there is contact with obstructions on all sides—that is, contact with banks—the fluidity of the whole (*avayavin*) is obstructed and does not produce flow.

The fluidity of the parts (*avayava-dravatva*) is also obstructed by that very same [obstructive contact] through its inherence in the same substrate. In whichever part there is a direct conjunction with the obstruction, the fluidity residing in that part is obstructed by that very conjunction with the obstruction. However, the subsequent fluidities of the parts are obstructed by conjunct-conjunctions (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*); for the fluidity of another part is obstructed because of its conjunction with the part that is conjoined with the obstruction.

By this very principle—that the fluidity of another is obstructed due to conjunction with that [obstructing factor]—the successive instances of fluidity are each obstructed. However, if a breach in the dam is made even slightly, then there is no commencement of the effect by the fluidity of the whole (avayavin) which is obstructed on all sides; for there is no exit through a small opening created in one part for a large-sized whole that is obstructed on all sides by a very long dam.

However, for the fluidity of the parts situated near the dam, there occurs the attainment of functional activity (*vṛttilābha*), because it is possible for a small portion of the parts to exit by that path. And when that [fluidity] attains functional activity, due to the absence of any obstruction, the other fluidities of the parts will also attain functional activity and thereby perform their own effects.

Therefore, there is a movement only of those parts that are already in contact. The part situated nearest the dam moves first; after that, the one situated next to it, and then the one situated next to that—by this sequence, all the parts move forward. And as they move, they do not move while occupying mutually distinct locations; rather, they move in such a way that they remain in mutual contact. It is for the purpose of illuminating this fact that it is said: "there is a movement only of those that are conjoined."

Furthermore, this does not mean that there is merely a gliding forward of those very same original conjunctions, because a different configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is perceived. Therefore, upon the destruction of the previous conjunctions and the destruction of the prior substance, a long substance is produced by the parts—parts which remain in a continuous series and exist in a state of mutual conjunction. And in that case, fluidity (*dravatva*) arises through the process beginning with the qualities of the causes; fluidity is produced in the longer composite whole from the fluidities of its constituent parts.

And in that case, when the constituent causes move in a continuous series, the action that arises in the composite whole due to fluidity is called "flowing" (*syandana*). When that fluidity has arisen, as the constituent parts—the causes—move in a continuous series, that is, in a state of succession without occupying distinct locations, the action that arises in the composite whole due to fluidity is termed flowing.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [251] [p. 661]

Action arising from *saṃskāra* (elasticity/disposition) is illustrated by the case of arrows and the like. Similarly, when parts of a wheel or similar object undergo conjunctions and disjunctions with specific directions and locations on their sides, that action of the whole which—caused by its own *saṃskāra*—is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with non-specific directions and locations, is called "revolving" (*bhramaṇa*). [Such are the various types of motion.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [251] [pp. 661–662]

It was stated that action arises from *saṃskāra* (elasticity/disposition) in the case of arrows and the like, as well as in the case of wheels and the like. The word "tathā" (so/likewise) requires the word "yathā" (just as), because of the constant syntactic connection between the relative pronoun (*yat*) and the demonstrative pronoun (*tat*). The meaning is: just as action is said to arise from *saṃskāra* in the case of arrows and so forth, so too does it occur in the case of wheels and so forth.

He demonstrates this very point: when conjunctions and disjunctions with specific directions and locations arise for the parts [of a wheel], that action which belongs to the whole (*avayavin*)—caused by its *saṃskāra* and characterized by conjunctions and disjunctions with non-specific directions and locations—is called "revolving" (*bhramaṇa*).

When there is the production of disjunctions and conjunctions of the parts with those specific directions and locations that are adjacent [to them], then, due to the momentum (*saṃskāra*) of the whole, there arises an action which is the cause of disjunctions and conjunctions in all directions with non-specific directions and locations; that is rotation (*bhramaṇa*). First, an action is produced in the wheel as a whole due to conjunction with a stick. Subsequent actions arise from impulsion (*nodana*), impact (*abhighāta*), and from momentum born of prior action.

Thus, when the wheel is joined with the staff, the initial action in that part of the wheel joined with the staff arises from the conjunction with the staff; in other parts, it arises from conjunction with what is already conjoined. The subsequent actions in the part of the wheel joined with the staff arise from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and from impulsion (*nodana*). For other parts, they arise from the latent impression and from conjunction with what is conjoined. But upon the removal of the staff, they arise solely from the latent impression itself in the wheel and its parts. He concludes: "Such are the various types of motion. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [252] [p. 662]

Regarding the action in the wind known as *prāṇa*, it arises from the conjunction of the self and the wind, depending upon desire, aversion, and effort; for in the waking state, its conformity to desire is observed, whereas in the case of one who is asleep, it depends upon the effort that precedes the act of living.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [252] [p. 662]

Regarding the action in the wind called *prāṇa*: for a waking person, the action in the wind called *prāṇa* arises from an effort preceded by desire and aversion, due to the contact between the self and the wind. How is this known? He says: because its conformity to desire is observed. In the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and so forth, the activity of the vital breath is perceived as following the dictates of desire.

When dust enters the nostrils, the activity of breath occurs even out of aversion for the sake of its removal; therefore, it is understood to be preceded by effort. In the case of one who is asleep, the activity of breath arises from the conjunction of the self and the vital air (vāyu) dependent upon the effort that precedes life. The argument is as follows: The activity of breath in one who is asleep is produced by effort, because it is an activity of breath, like the activity of breath in one who is awake. And that [activity] does not have desire or aversion as its antecedent, because desire and aversion are absent in one who is asleep.
Therefore, it is determined to be preceded solely by the maintenance of life, since the sustenance of the vital breath is preceded by that [life].

*Praśastapādabhāṣya*: Although ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), space (*dik*), and the self (*ātman*) possess the nature of substance (*dravya*), they are devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*) because, like universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, they are formless (*amūrtatva*). Form (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading (*asarvagata-dravya-parimāṇa*), and action follows from it; that [form] does not exist in ether and the others. Therefore, there is no connection with action for them. *Nyāyakandalī*: [253] [p.663] Action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction. It is of two kinds: produced by effort (*prayatnajanya*) and produced by impulse (*vegajanya*). Effort is a quality of the self. Impulse is a quality of earth, water, fire, air, and mind. Action exists in the nine substances—earth, water, fire, air, mind, self, ether, time, and space. Among these, the action of the self is of two kinds: that which is produced by effort and that which is produced by impulse. The action of the mind is produced by effort alone. The action of earth, water, fire, and air is of three kinds: produced by effort, produced by impulse, and produced by conjunction. The action of ether, time, and space is non-existent. Why? Because they are devoid of form. Form is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading. Action conforms to that [form]. Since that [form] does not exist in ether and the others, there is no connection with action for them. Thus, the absence of action in ether, time, space, and the self has been established. This concludes the section on action. Now, the section on qualities begins. Quality is dependent upon substance, does not possess qualities, and is the cause of conjunction and disjunction. It is of twenty-four kinds: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, weight, fluidity, viscidity, sound, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and impression. Among these, color resides in earth, water, and fire. Taste resides in earth and water. Smell resides in earth. Touch resides in earth, water, fire, and air. Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, and fluidity reside in the nine substances beginning with earth. Weight, fluidity, and viscidity reside in earth, water, and fire. Sound resides in ether. Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and impression reside in the self. Among these, color is of seven kinds: white, blue, yellow, red, green, brown, and variegated. Taste is of six kinds: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. Smell is of two kinds: fragrant and foul. Touch is of three kinds: cold, hot, and temperate. Number is of three kinds: unity, duality, and plurality. Dimension is of four kinds: small, large, long, and short. Separateness is of two kinds: absolute and relative. Conjunction and disjunction are each of two kinds: produced by action and produced by conjunction. Remoteness and proximity are each of two kinds: based on direction and based on time. Weight is heaviness. Fluidity is of two kinds: natural and artificial. Viscidity is the cause of the cohesiveness of liquids. Sound is the quality of ether. Intellect is knowledge. Pleasure is satisfaction. Pain is suffering. Desire is longing. Aversion is hatred. Effort is exertion. Merit is the cause of desirable results. Demerit is the cause of undesirable results. Impression is the cause of memory. These are the twenty-four qualities. Among these, color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, weight, fluidity, viscidity, sound, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and impression are qualities. They are dependent upon substance, do not possess qualities, and are the causes of conjunction and disjunction. This concludes the section on qualities. Now, the section on action begins. Action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction. It is of two kinds: produced by effort and produced by impulse. Effort is a quality of the self. Impulse is a quality of earth, water, fire, air, and mind. Action exists in the nine substances—earth, water, fire, air, mind, self, ether, time, and space. Among these, the action of the self is of two kinds: that which is produced by effort and that which is produced by impulse. The action of the mind is produced by effort alone. The action of earth, water, fire, and air is of three kinds: produced by effort, produced by impulse, and produced by conjunction. The action of ether, time, and space is non-existent. Why? Because they are devoid of form. Form is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading. Action conforms to that [form]. Since that [form] does not exist in ether and the others, there is no connection with action for them. Thus, the absence of action in ether, time, space, and the self has been established. This concludes the section on action. Now, the section on inherence begins. Inherence is the relation between things that cannot exist separately. It is one, eternal, and all-pervading. It is the cause of the cognition "this is in this. This concludes the section on inherence. Now, the section on non-existence begins. Non-existence is the negation of existence. It is of four kinds: prior non-existence, posterior non-existence, mutual non-existence, and absolute non-existence. Prior non-existence is the state before production. Posterior non-existence is the state after destruction. Mutual non-existence is the negation of identity. Absolute non-existence is the negation of a thing where it is never found. This concludes the section on non-existence. This concludes the *Nyāyakandalī*. This concludes the commentary on the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*. This concludes the *Nyāyakandalī*. Why is the production of action not considered in the case of space and the other [factors], just as it is in the case of the four great elements? To this he says: although space, time, direction, and the self possess the status of substances (*dravya*), they are devoid of action because they are formless (*amūrta*), like universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth. Being possessed of action is pervaded by having form (*mūrtatva*); and since form does not exist in space and the others, therefore possession of action also does not exist. He explains this very point with the words beginning "form" (*mūrti*), which is clear. —Praśastapādabhāṣya [254] [pp. 663–667]

In the case of one who possesses a body and is awake, the action of the mind for the purpose of connecting with another sense organ arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on an effort preceded by desire or aversion; for we observe the perception of other objects through other sense organs according to one's intention. In the case of one who is asleep, at the time of awakening, it arises from an effort preceded by the vitalizing impulse (*jīvana-pūrvaka-prayatna*).

The action of departing (*apasarpaṇa-karma*) and the action of entering (*upasarpaṇa-karma*) arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). How so? When there is the exhaustion of the two types of merit (*dharma*) that accompany life, or their mutual suppression, then, due to the deficiency of those two which were aids to life, the effort preceded by them also ceases. Upon the cessation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the action of departing—which is the cause of separation from the dead body—is produced by the other two, merit and demerit (*adharma*), which have acquired their functional state and are aided by the conjunction of the self and the mind.

Then, having departed from the body, it becomes connected with a subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) produced by those very same factors of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). Transferred by that [subtle body], it goes to heaven or hell and becomes connected with a body corresponding to its latent disposition (*āśaya*); thus, the movement toward [the new body] is caused by karma for the purpose of that conjunction.

Furthermore, there is the going to and returning from a desired location of the mind projected outward by yogis; likewise, at the time of creation, karma driven by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) effects the connection with a newly arisen body.

In this same way, whatever else among the great elements has its cause unperceived by means of either direct perception or inference, yet is capable of producing benefit or harm, that too is brought about by the unseen (adṛṣṭa). Examples include: the motion of atoms at the beginning of creation; the upward and horizontal movement of fire and air; the agitation of the great elements; the movement of consecrated gems toward a thief; and the attraction of iron toward a magnet. Thus ends the section on the category of action (*karmapadārtha*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.

In the *Nyāyakandalī* [254] [pp. 663–667], he states the cause of action in the mind: "possessing a body" (*savigraha*). For a waking person, when the mind possesses a body—that is, when the mind is embodied—action occurs for the sake of connecting with another sense organ, arising from effort preceded by desire and aversion, such as the conjunction of the self and the mind. Effort preceded by desire and aversion is the cause of the movement of the mind in a waking person. How is this known? To this he says: because the perception of objects through another sense organ is observed to follow one's intention.

In the waking state, it is observed that the apprehension of objects by other sense organs, such as the eye and so forth, occurs without deviating from one's intention. When a person desires to grasp form (*rūpa*), he then perceives form; when he desires to grasp taste (*rasa*), he then tastes the taste. Furthermore, there is no capacity for external sense organs to grasp their objects without a connection to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Therefore, it is understood that an action arises in the mind (*manas*) preceded by effort (*prayatna*) which is itself preceded by desire (*icchā*) and aversion (*dveṣa*).

At the time of awakening from sleep, [the action] depends upon an effort preceded by the vital force (*jīvana*). For the sake of connecting with another sense organ at the time of awakening, an activity arises in the mind due to the contact between the self and the mind, which depends upon an effort preceded by the vital force. Furthermore, the actions of moving away and moving toward [the body] arise from the contact between the self and the mind, depending upon the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). He explains this very point by means of a question beginning with "How so? and so forth. "Life" (*jīvana*) is a specific contact between the self and the mind; in the performance of its own function, dharma and adharma serve as its auxiliary causes.

When there is the exhaustion, destruction, or mutual suppression of those two [merit and demerit] through experience, or when they fail to produce their own effects due to mutual obstruction, then—given the deficiency or absence of merit and demerit which are the companions of life, and consequently the deficiency or absence of the effort preceded by life due to that deficiency—the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) is obstructed. When that has ceased in the body, those two merits and demerits, whose results are to be experienced in another body, have attained their functional state (*labdhavṛttika*).

Because [the self] is bound by merit and demerit whose fruits are to be experienced with the present body, no effect is produced by the merit and demerit whose fruits are to be experienced in another body. However, when the merit and demerit to be experienced with the present body have been exhausted, then the acquisition of activity—that is, the absence of obstruction—occurs for the merit and demerit to be experienced in another body.

From those two—dharma and adharma—which have attained their functional operation, and which are distinct from the karma to be experienced in the present body, there arises, through the auxiliary cause of the conjunction of the self and the mind, an *apasarpaṇa* (departure) action that causes the separation of the mind from the dead body. In the production of this *apasarpaṇa* action, the conjunction of the self and the mind is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), the mind is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and dharma and adharma, having attained their functional operation, are the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Thereafter, immediately following that, the mind—which has emerged from the dead body—becomes connected with a subtle translocating body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) produced from those very same *dharma* and *adharma* which have acquired their functional activity. Transferred into that—that is, transferred into that subtle translocating body—the mind goes to heaven or to hell. Having gone there, it becomes connected with a body corresponding to its desires and corresponding to its karma.

Whether in heaven or in hell, whatever body has arisen, the mind must necessarily have a connection with it; otherwise, experience would be impossible in that location. Furthermore, the mind cannot connect with another body without traveling, as it is not all-pervasive like the self. And such travel over such a great distance is not possible for the mind alone, because—except for the state following the great dissolution—the mind, being devoid of a body, lacks the karma necessary for movement.

Therefore, it is postulated that a body—extremely subtle and beyond the reach of perception—is produced by atoms which, through the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), initiate activity and proceed via the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, closely following the deceased physical body. And because it possesses the property of carrying the mind across to regions such as heaven or hell, transcending the dead body, it is called the "conveying" (*ātivāhika*) body.

Between death and birth, the activity of the mind arises only when it is supported by a body; for, while being distinct from the mental activity occurring during the state immediately following the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), it is nonetheless mental activity, like the mental activity observed in the functioning of a visible body. Furthermore, scripture here serves as corroborative evidence, for such scripture is seen to corroborate this, just as in the case of the mental activity observed in a visible body. And the movement [of the mind] is for the sake of its conjunction with that [body];
thus, for the sake of the mind’s conjunction with a newly born body—whether in heaven or in hell—there is the movement of the mind toward that body.

Furthermore, for yogis, there is the going to and returning from a desired location by means of the mind that has been projected outward—that is, drawn out externally. Likewise, at the time of creation, the connection with a newly formed body is brought about by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen moral force) acting upon the mind.

Not only this much; all other things as well, which have causes unperceived by either direct perception or inference, yet are capable of producing benefit or harm within the great elements (*mahābhūta*), are also brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). For example: the action of atoms at the beginning of creation; the upward and horizontal movements of fire and wind respectively; the agitation and motion of the great elements and the terrestrial globe; the movement of consecrated gems toward a thief at the time of examination; and the attraction of iron toward a magnet—all these are brought about by the unseen force.
"Action is the supreme reality, the basis for attaining beneficial results and abandoning those that are harmful; let it be placed in your heart with diligent effort."

Thus ends the category of action (*karmapadārtha*) in the *Nyāyakandalī*, a commentary on the *Padārthapraveśa* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrīdhara. Now follows the determination of the category of generality (*sāmānyapadārtha*).

Praśastapādabhāṣya [255] [pp.668–669]: Generality (sāmānya) is of two kinds: the higher (para) and the lower (apara). It pervades all its own objects, is non-different in nature, and subsists in many. It is the cause of the cognition of recurrence in one, two, or many things, and it exists continuously in its substrates through its identity with their own forms as the cause of the cognition of recurrence.

How so? Because, when knowledge arises through a continuous series based on a universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to each individual object (*piṇḍa*), and because of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the causal conditions of repeated practice, there is that which persists as a recurring factor through the reflection upon the series of past cognitions; that is the universal.
Victorious are those who are the causes of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the world!
From the Supreme Self of the universe [arise] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.

He explains *sāmānya* (generality): "Generality is twofold, namely the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). This has already been explained on the occasion of the enumeration (*uddeśa*). Some maintain that every generality is omnipresent (*sarvagata*); in order to refute that, he says: "It is omnipresent within its own domain. That generality which is perceived in a particular individual (*piṇḍa*) is its own domain; it is omnipresent—that is, inherent (*samaveta*)—in all such [individuals], because it is cognized everywhere therein. As for the absence of omnipresence in everything, non-perception itself is the proof.

It is of a non-different nature, that is, it has an undivided intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*). The meaning is this: by whatever intrinsic essence a universal (*sāmānya*) exists in one individual (*piṇḍa*), by that very same intrinsic essence it exists in another individual as well, because there is no difference in the cognition thereof. That which exists in many individuals is "multilocated" (*anekavṛtti*). And the fact that it exists in many places while having an undivided intrinsic essence must be established on the strength of actual experience (*pratītisāmarthya*). For indeed, when a matter is understood through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no such thing as an "inconsistency."

Even duality and so forth, being of an undifferentiated nature, exist in many [individuals]; therefore, no distinction from the universal (*sāmānya*) is found there. To this he says: "The cause of the cognition of the persistence of its own essential nature in one, two, or many [individuals]. The universal produces a cognition that follows its own essential nature in a single individual, in two individuals, or in many individuals.

Since the cognition "this is a cow" occurs even when a single individual, two, or many individuals are perceived, whereas duality and so forth do not occur in this way—this is the distinction. The meaning of the definition is that *sāmānya* (the universal) is that which, while residing in many, is the cause of a cognition that follows the nature of the self [of the object] across one, two, or many instances. He explains this very point with the words: "without difference from its own nature."

That which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) in one individual (*piṇḍa*) is also present in another individual; therefore, that which exists in substrates through non-difference, by way of continuity, without cessation, and without abandoning each preceding individual, being the cause of the cognition of recurrence and the cause of the perception of the conformity of its own essential nature, is the universal (*sāmānya*).

"How so? is the question of the opponent. The meaning is: how is the existence of a universal (*sāmānya*) understood among multiple individual objects (*piṇḍa*)? He provides the answer: "In each individual object. When a cognition arises in such a way that it depends upon the universal in relation to each individual object, a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced by the resulting repeated cognition (*abhyāsapratyaya*). Because of the recollection (*smaraṇa*), which consists in the retrospective observation (*pratyavekṣaṇa*) of the past continuum (*prabandha*) or flow (*pravāha*) of cognitions, that which persists as a recurring element is the universal.

What is being said? Having perceived a universal in one individual (piṇḍa), its recognition in another individual leads to the understanding that it subsists in many. For this very reason, the subverting arguments (*bādhakahetu*) in this case are set aside due to their contradiction with perception.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [256], p. 670.

In this regard, the highest universal, existence (*sattāsāmānya*), is solely the cause of the recurring cognition [of "existent"]. Just as there is a recurrence of the cognition "blue, blue" with respect to mutually distinct objects such as leather, cloth, and woolen blankets due to their connection with a single substance that is blue, so too there is a recurrence of the undifferentiated cognition "existent, existent" with respect to substances, qualities, and actions which are mutually distinct. And since that [cognition] must arise from a connection with something else [than the individual entities], that which is that "something else" is established as existence (*sattā*). Because the recurrence of the cognition "existent, existent" occurs through connection with existence, it is therefore a universal alone.
*Nyāyakandalī* [256] [p.670]:

Having previously stated that generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds, the higher and the lower, he now explains this in detail. Among these, the higher is the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), which is solely the cause of the cognition of inclusion (*anuvṛttipratyaya*). Although existence is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he nevertheless states an inference for one who is in disagreement: "Just as in things mutually distinct," and so forth. This is clear.

The persistence of the cognition "existent, existent" with respect to substances and the other categories is based on a distinct [underlying] cognition, because it is a persistence of cognition among diverse things, like the persistence of the cognition "blue" in leather, cloth, and so forth. Since existence (*sattā*) produces the persistence of cognition in the three categories—substance and the rest—and does not produce their exclusion, the meaning of the conclusion is that it is a universal (*sāmānya*) alone, not a particular (*viśeṣa*).
*Praśastapādabhāṣya* [257] [pp. 671–672]

Furthermore, substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, are both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), because they serve as the causes for the notions of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Among these, substance-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the notion of inclusion among earth and the other substances, which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of the notion of exclusion from qualities and actions. Likewise, quality-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the notion of inclusion among color and the other qualities, which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of the notion of exclusion from substances and actions.

Likewise, *karmatva* (the nature of action) is a universal (*sāmānya*) because it is the cause of the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) among mutually distinct actions such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), and it is a particular (*viśeṣa*) because it is the cause of the exclusive cognition (*vyāvṛttihetu*) from substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*).

In this same way, the status of being both universal and particular is established for *pṛthivītva* (earthness), *rūpatva* (color-ness), *utkṣepaṇatva* (upward-throwing-ness), *gotva* (cowness), *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness), *paṭatva* (cloth-ness), and so forth, which reside in living and non-living things, because they are the causes of both inclusive and exclusive cognitions. These categories, beginning with *dravyatva* (substanceness), are primarily universals because their scope is extensive; however, they are figuratively termed "particulars" because they distinguish their own substrates.

Furthermore, substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, are both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), because they serve as the causes for inclusive and exclusive cognitions respectively. Substance-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the inclusive cognition regarding substances; it is a particular because it is the cause of the exclusion [of substances] from qualities and actions. Quality-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the inclusive cognition regarding qualities; it is a particular because it is the cause of the exclusion [of qualities] from substances and actions.

Likewise, "action-ness" (karmatva) is a generality because it is the cause of a recurring cognition among throwing upwards and other actions which are mutually distinct; it is a particularity because it is the cause of differentiation from substances and qualities.

Since earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like, like substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, are the causes of both inclusive (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtti*) cognitions, they possess the nature of being both generalities (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*); thus he says, "In this way. Generalities residing in living beings are such as cowness (*gotva*), horseness (*aśvatva*), and so on; generalities residing in non-living things are such as potness (*ghaṭatva*), clothness (*paṭatva*), and so on. Is the status of being a generality for substantiality and the like real? Or is it the status of being a particular? Or is it both? To this he replies: "These... [p.672]

The nature of being common (*samāna*) is "generality" (*sāmānya*); this definition of generality exists in [categories such as] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like. However, the definition that "it distinguishes its own substratum from everything else" as "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) does not apply to them. Therefore, these [categories] are primarily only generalities and not particulars; they receive the designation "particular" only figuratively. For a particular indeed distinguishes its own substratum from everything else, and since substantiality and the like also distinguish their own substratum from those of a different class, the figurative usage proceeds on the basis of this much similarity.
—Praśastapādabhāṣya [258–259] [p. 672]
Because of the difference in their characteristics, it is established that these are distinct categories from substance, quality, and action; for this very reason, they are eternal.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [258] [p. 672]

Substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the other [universals] are not distinct from substance and the rest; therefore, it would be improper to define their functions separately. To this, he says: "Because of the difference in definition" (*lakṣaṇabhedāt*). Substance-ness and the others are cognizable by a cognition of a recurring form (*anugatākāra*), whereas individual substances and the like are cognizable by a cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttibuddhi*). Therefore, because of the difference in definition—that is, the difference in cognition—these [universals] such as substance-ness are categories distinct from substance, quality, and action. For this very reason, they are also eternal.

Precisely because the universal is distinct from substance and the other categories, it is therefore eternal. If there were no distinction between the universal and substance and so forth, then upon the destruction of the substance and the rest, the universal would be destroyed, and upon their production, it would be produced; however, since they are distinct, this rule does not apply.
(Nyāyakandalī [259], pp. 673–675)

On this point, some say: the inclusive cognition (*anugatabuddhi*) establishes the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, that cognition does not manifest two independent entities—one characterized as the universal and the other as the particular—with respect to each individual object (*piṇḍa*). Nor is there a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between them, because [the cognition] does not arise in the form "this possesses cowness" (*gotvavān*). Rather, this is a cognition grasping identity (*tādātmya*), because of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of a single nature in the form "this is a cow," and because neither of the two exists as a distinct intrinsic nature apart from the other.

For positive concomitance (*anuvṛttatā*) is the very nature of "cowness" as it is of any other universal, and negative exclusion (*vyāvṛttatā*) is the inherent character of an individual cow as it is of other individuals. However, the nature of "cowness" as excluded from other universals and the inherent character of the individual cow as excluded from other individuals cannot be specified for one another without their being mutually identical.

Furthermore, it is not tenable that the very same thing is both its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and its correlate (*sambandhin*), because that which lacks an intrinsic nature cannot have a relationship. Therefore, the reality of the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) consists precisely in their mutual identity. This being so, the doctrine of non-difference-in-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*) is also established. For just as one perceives "the brindled cow is a cow," so too does one perceive "the black-spotted cow is a cow. Nor is there any sublation for anyone such that "only the brindled cow is a cow, not the black-spotted one."

However, there is one commonality for all: "This is a cow; that too is a cow. In this regard, by the force of such cognition, once it is established that the cowness inherent in a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow) exists within the nature of a *bāhuleya* (a black cow), its difference from the *śābaleya* is also established. For this alone constitutes the difference of a universal from a prior individual: namely, its consisting in other individuals. And this alone is its nature as a universal: namely, its consisting in both. To claim that difference and non-difference are contradictory in a single thing is a fallacy.

If you ask why, it is because it is not appropriate for you, who understand reasoning, to say this now. Where the intellect is subverted by what is contrary to that [reality], yet that which is always cognized as being exactly so by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) exists, then to assert a contradiction in such a case is itself contradictory.

If it is argued that this is not seen elsewhere, does even perception follow what has been seen, as inference does? Then this [perception] is destroyed by the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Or, if it functions by its own inherent capacity (*svasāmarthya*), then a thing is exactly as it appears; it cannot be rejected on the grounds of not being seen elsewhere, for that would entail the rejection of all existent things.

Therefore, because it possesses arising and destruction when the individual instances arise and perish, and because it persists while other instances persist, the universal is both eternal and non-eternal; it is not, however, exclusively eternal.

This being the case, it is replied: Does the cognition that apprehends a non-distinct form for both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) apprehend their non-difference? Or does it apprehend two forms that are mutually distinct? In the first alternative, there would be only a single entity; for the two cannot possess a single nature, since the definition of non-difference is the state of being cognizable by a cognition that apprehends a non-distinct form. In the second alternative, however, there is a direct contradiction; for the very cognition of distinct forms is indeed the cognition of difference.

When that [inherence] exists, there is simply no apprehension of non-difference between those two; how then can non-difference be established between two distinct things? How, then, is there the cognition of identity (*tādātmya*)? We say: not in any way whatsoever. If, first of all, a single form is experienced, this is the cognition of a single object alone, not of both. If, on the other hand, two forms are experienced, then the occurrence of such a cognition is impossible.
