As for the undivided awareness "this is a cow," that is due to the power of inherence (*samavāya*).

For in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there is the appearance of a mixture of two things; but the greatness of inherence (*samavāya*) is this: that here the two related entities are perceived as if they were fused into one, like a ball of clay and fire, and the universal (*jāti*) itself is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, even though there is a difference, the nature of the individual is not extracted separately from the universal, as is the case with a jujube fruit from its bowl. Nevertheless, their perception does indeed occur through mutual exclusion, since the individual is perceived at a distance even when the "cowness" (*gotva*) is not grasped.

Even when one individual lump is not perceived, the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is apprehended through another lump; therefore, the position of the logicians (*tārkika*) is that the universal is absolutely distinct from the individual.
[From the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, §§260–263, pp. 676–677:

Because of the restriction of their occurrence to [specific] substances and so forth, and because of the difference in their cognitions, they are mutually distinct. On the other hand, each universal is a single entity because there is no difference in its definition across its own substrates, and because it possesses the defining characteristic of a universal.

Even though universals have unlimited spatial extension, they nevertheless pervade their own entire range of objects due to the restriction of their defining characteristics and the restriction of the causal complex. Furthermore, because the relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) do not exist in the intervals between them, they are not designated there.
Thus ends the category of the universal in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
*Nyāyakandalī* [260] [p.676]:

Due to the restriction of their occurrence to substances and so forth, and due to the difference in their cognitions, there is mutual distinctness among them. The universals such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) are each restricted to substances and so forth alone. Furthermore, differences in cognition are observed regarding these; therefore, because of the restriction of their occurrence to substances and so forth, and because of the difference in their cognitions, there is a mutual distinction among substanceness and the other universals.

It was previously stated merely as a proposition that the universal (*sāmānya*) is non-different in nature; now, he establishes this through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "Because its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is non-distinct with respect to each of its own substrata (*svāśraya*), and because there is an absence of a defining characteristic of difference, it is one. A "defining characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is that by which something is characterized—namely, a cognition (*jñāna*) having a recurrent form (*anugatākāra*). Because it is non-distinct—that is, lacking differentiation—with respect to each individual instance (*piṇḍa*), and because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a defining characteristic of difference—that is, of distinction—the universal is one among its own substrata; the meaning is that it possesses a non-different essential nature (*abhinnasvabhāvatva*).

Regarding what was stated previously—that a universal inheres everywhere within its own domain and nowhere else—the author states the reason for this with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). Even though universals have unlimited locations and no fixed location because they are connected with whatever individual (*piṇḍa*) arises here or there, nevertheless, due to the restriction—meaning the necessity—of the specific configuration of parts which serves as the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) or manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*), and due to the restriction of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces the individual, they inhere everywhere within their own domain and nowhere else.
*Nyāyakandalī* [261] [pp. 677–678]

This is what is meant: the specific configuration of the dewlap and so forth is the manifester of "cowness" (gotva); the specific configuration of the mane and so forth is that of "horseness" (aśvatva); and the specific configuration of the particular neck and so forth is that of "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva), because of the necessity of their respective cognitions. Furthermore, these specific configurations are not common to all individual objects (piṇḍa), but rather occur only in their respective restricted instances.

In this regard, although every universal is capable of being connected with another individual object—just as it is with its own [manifesting] object—nevertheless, the inherence (*samavāya*) of a particular universal occurs only in that individual where its manifestor is possible, and not elsewhere. Thus, the restriction regarding the connection of a universal is also due to the restriction of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For this is the nature of causes such as threads, that when a substance is produced by them, only "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) inheres therein, and nothing else.

For this is the greatness of the lump of clay and other such materials: that when a substance is being produced by them, it is *ghaṭatva* (the state of being a jar) alone that inheres in it, and nothing else.

A universal (*sāmānya*) does not travel from one place to another and then become connected elsewhere, because it is devoid of action (*niṣkriyatvāt*). Furthermore, if it did not previously exist there, then its connection with the lump being produced at that moment would be impossible. Yet, a connection with the newly produced lump is observed everywhere; therefore, the view of some—that everything exists everywhere—is refuted by the statement: "In the interval, they are unnameable because of the absence of the modes of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)."

"Intermediate space" (*antarāla*) may refer to ether (*ākāśa*), the substance of direction (*dig-dravya*), still air, or the absence of corporeal substances. In these, there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*). Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their existence while remaining entirely unconnected. Therefore, universals are not designated as being in the intermediate space; the meaning is that they do not exist there. How, then, are they connected with the individual object (*piṇḍa*) arising therein? Through the causal capacity (*kāraṇa-sāmarthya*) [of the universal].

For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) occurs either between that which has come from elsewhere or between that which is already situated right there. In contrast, inherence (*samavāya*) is of a different nature: wherever the causes operate toward the production of a composite whole, it occurs right there within that whole—due to the causal capacity of the factors—even for a universal (*sāmānya*) that has not come from elsewhere nor is already situated there, because the power of things cannot be questioned.
*Nyāyakandalī* [262] [pp. 678–681]

Regarding this, the Buddhists say: "Since no single form is perceived among the various particularities that are being cognized—just as there is no single thread-form in a string of jewels—the universal (sāmānya) does not exist at all. This is incorrect, because when multiple individual cows are being experienced, a cognition of a common form is possible by virtue of their being distinct from individual horses and other such animals.

If there were nothing at all that persists as one among the mutually distinct individuals such as the brindled cow and others, then just as the individual cows and horses are perceived as mutually distinct, so too would the individual cows be perceived [as distinct from one another]. Or, just as the individual cows are perceived as having a common form, so too would the individual cows and horses be perceived [as having a common form], since there would be no distinction [between these two cases].

However, when cow-individuals are perceived as necessarily possessing a similar form, they project a certain single form that is common to their own class and excluded from horses and the like, either because they perform a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*) or because they have a single cause (*ekahetutva*). If it is argued that there is a unity among the cow-individuals themselves, [we reply: no, for in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), even the causes of individuals and the effects of individuals—which are mutually distinct just like the individuals themselves—cannot possess unity.

Furthermore, if oneness were due to having a single cause, there would be no oneness among individual entities produced from diverse causes. Yet, a difference in causes is observed even for those things that possess an identical nature; for example, fire arises from the friction of wood, from lightning, and also from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta) agitated by the rays of the sun.

If unity were to result from performing a single function, then even heterogeneous things would have to be considered one, for we observe that functions such as carrying loads or yielding milk are performed by individuals such as buffaloes just as they are by individuals such as cows; consequently, a cow that neither yields milk nor carries loads would not be a cow.

Furthermore, in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), what could be the object associated with a word? It cannot be the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because being momentary and excluded from everything else, it cannot be the referent of a linguistic convention. Nor can conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) be the meaning of a word, because it too is momentary and unique.

If it is argued that the object of a word is the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*), is this form of conceptual construction distinct from the conceptual construction itself, or non-distinct? If it is distinct, is it common to all conceptual constructions, or does it differ with each individual conceptual construction? If it were common, then there would be no difference between this and a universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, for you [the Yogācāra], this is a property of cognition, whereas for us [the Naiyāyikas], it is a property of the object, because it is perceived as being directed outward; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.

If this mental aspect (*ākāra*) is distinct from cognition, it differs with each individual cognition; or if it is indeed non-distinct from cognition, in either case it lacks the capacity for association with words, because—just like cognition itself—it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) for it.

If it is argued that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), by means of a causal succession, imposes its own form as being external because it obstructs the arising of that [external object], and thus conceptualizes it—therein lies the association with words (*śabda-saṃsarga*)—[we reply: the form of conceptual construction, which is superimposed as being external, exists as something distinct for every individual conceptualization. This is because its nature is dependent solely upon conceptual construction; thus, when a conceptualization arises, it appears as if arising, and when it perishes, it appears as if perishing. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the application of linguistic convention does not follow after such [illusory] distinctions.

Now it is said: Just as one conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) superimposes its own appearance as being an external object upon a cow, another conceptual cognition likewise superimposes such [an appearance]. Furthermore, each conceptual cognition grasps only its own form and is not capable of discerning the difference between forms superimposed by one another, because that [discernment of difference] depends upon the apprehension of both. And because that [difference] is not apprehended, the unity of the forms superimposed by the conceptual cognitions is established, and it is said that there is a single object for the conceptual cognitions.

And that very universal (sāmānya), being of the nature of non-existence due to its absolute lack of difference from the forms of conceptual construction superimposed upon external objects, is said to consist of four [mental] aspects together with the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) and the cognition of that [particular], making five aspects in total. This, being designated by the term "superimposed externality," is the object associated with verbal expression. The very determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [universal] is the determination of the particular characteristic, because the former is superimposed as having the nature of the latter.

This [exclusion of others] has the nature of the exclusion of other things and is common to both existence and non-existence, because of the linguistic usage "the cow exists" and "the cow does not exist. For if it were of the nature of existence (*bhāva*), the usage "the cow exists" would be impossible, because it would be a tautology. Furthermore, the usage "it does not exist" would not be employed, because of contradiction. Likewise, if it were of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), the usage "it does not exist" would be a tautology, while "it exists" would be contradictory. As it has been said: "One should not say 'the jar exists,' since the jar is already existent.
Nor should one say 'it does not exist,' because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence."

And for this very reason, there is the appearance of unity even among distinct individuals. For this [object] is the domain of all conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*); and because it is one, the conceptual cognitions are also one. Because they too are one, their causes—the non-conceptual cognitions (*nirvikalpaka*) that occur with respect to each individual object—are also one. And because those are one, there is the comprehension of the unity of the individuals which are their causes. As it has been said:
"Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), cognition is non-differentiating."

"Because they share the status of being the cause of a single cognition, even individuals possess non-difference. This too is incorrect, because the conceptual construction [required to support it] is untenable. The Buddhist monks (bhikṣus) assert that the universal is a superimposed unity resulting from the non-apprehension of the difference between the forms of conceptual cognitions. To this we reply: Is the superimposition of non-difference merely the non-apprehension of the difference between the forms of these cognitions, or is it the apprehension of non-difference that constitutes the superimposition? It cannot be the first alternative, for that would entail the superimposition of difference as well; just as the difference between the forms of conceptual cognitions is not apprehended, so too their non-difference is not apprehended.

In that case, just as there is the superimposition of non-difference due to the non-apprehension of difference, there would also follow the superimposition of difference due to the non-apprehension of non-difference; consequently, the engagement in linguistic usage appropriate to non-difference would be impossible. Furthermore, it is not tenable to say that the apprehension of non-difference is itself the superimposition of non-difference, because according to the theory of self (ātmavāda), a single perceiver of many things perceives both their difference and non-difference. According to the theory of selflessness (nairātmyavāda), however, there is no single perceiver of multiple objects at all, because each conceptual construction (vikalpa) is restricted solely to its own internal form.

Or, let it be granted that there is some single entity that perceives multiple objects; even so, without a single underlying cause (*nimitta*), there can be no apprehension of non-difference among distinct forms. Or, if such an apprehension were to occur, it would also apply to the forms of cows, horses, snakes, and so forth, since there would be no distinction between them.

If it is argued that even in the case of things having the form of a cow, there exists a single cause, namely the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*), then who are these "non-cows" by whose exclusion unity is superimposed upon those things having the form of a cow? If it is said that "those which are not cows are non-cows," then who are the cows? If it is said that "those which are not non-cows are cows," then the nature of non-cows is defined by their being excluded from the nature of cows once the nature of cows has been defined; and the nature of cows is defined by the exclusion of non-cows once the nature of non-cows has been defined. Thus [it results in a circularity].
Because when one is not apprehended, the other is not apprehended, there is a non-apprehension of both. As the venerable [author] has said:
"And the non-cow would be established as that which is excluded; moreover, it consists in the negation of the cow."

In that case, it must be stated that the cow itself is what is negated by the negative particle; for if the cow is not established, there is no "non-cow," and in the absence of that, how could there be a cow? Thus [it is said].

Now, [you may argue that] the meaning of a word is "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha), which consists in the non-superimposition of externality? To this also it is said: what is this so-called "exclusion"? Is the exclusion of the non-cow a positive entity (bhāva) or a non-entity (abhāva)? If it is a positive entity, is it of the nature of a cow-individual (gopiṇḍa) or of the nature of a non-cow individual? If it were of the nature of a cow-individual, it would first of all be unique (asādhāraṇa); and it has already been stated that a word does not function with respect to a unique object. Even if it were of the nature of a non-cow individual, this same fault would apply, and furthermore, there is this additional defect.

In that case, it would follow that the meaning of the word "cow" is "non-cow. But if you maintain that the reality of *apoha* is a real entity (*vastubhūta*) distinct from the individual object (*piṇḍa*) and common to many [individuals], then the disagreement concerns merely the nature of the word. Furthermore, if *apoha* is held to be of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*) because its form consists in the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), then it could not be apprehended by perception, since the definition of the apprehended (*grāhya*) is precisely that which generates cognition; moreover, a non-entity is characterized by the total absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, since there can be no grasping of a convention regarding an object not apprehended through perception, a word simply does not apply to non-existence. Moreover, when that [non-existence] is being cognized, the listener’s activity would not be directed toward an object, because existence and non-existence are distinct and lack a relationship.

If it is argued that activity toward a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) occurs through non-discrimination when there is a cognition of absence as having the nature of that particular characteristic—just as it has been said: "The engagement of cognizers occurs through an error that unifies the perceptible object and the conceptualized object, even though [the mind] does not possess the actual configuration of those objects" (PVSV 39,7f)—that is incorrect. For, as long as [the particular characteristic] is not being perceived, it is impossible to superimpose the nature of absence upon it.

Furthermore, at that time, there is no comprehension of the object by the hearer, because the word has the non-existent as its object and there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Yet, there is indeed comprehension of the object from the word; therefore, even non-existence is not the meaning of a word. Nor is there any other single basis for it. This entire range of objects, being mutually excluded, experienced as new at every moment, is not cognized through words.

Nor can even that which is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be the object of rejection or acquisition, because its capacity [to produce an effect] has not yet been fully ascertained. Yet, there exists verbal usage (*vyavahāra*), and there exists the worldly course of life (*lokayātrā*)—which is preceded by direct perception and is inherent to all living beings—aimed at the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. It is this very [course of life] that establishes a single universal (*sāmānya*) amidst distinct individuals.

When one observes the application of words directed toward such an object, it is because one has determined, by way of belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*), the fitness for that purposeful action (*arthakriyā-yogyatā*); thus, people proceed to act even regarding an object not previously experienced.
"The cognition that follows through diverse [individuals] is based upon a universal (*jāti*);
in its absence, this worldly course of life would not proceed at all.
Thus ends the category of the Universal in the *Nyāyakandalī*, a commentary on the *Padārthapraveśaka*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrīdhara.
Now follows the definition of the category of particularity (*viśeṣa*).
Praśastapādabhāṣya [264] [pp. 684–687]:

Those which exist in the ultimate [entities] are "ultimate" (*antyāḥ*); they are "particularities" (*viśeṣāḥ*) because they serve to differentiate their own substrates. They reside one by one in each of the eternal substances—which are devoid of destruction or origination—namely, atoms, ether, time, space, self, and mind; they are the causes of the cognition of absolute distinction.

Just as in the case of people like us, a distinction in cognition regarding cows and the like—differentiated from horses and the like—is observed to be caused by the similarity of form, quality, action, parts, and conjunction, as in the expressions: "a cow," "white," "swift-moving," "fat," "humped," or "possessing a large bell."

Likewise, for these distinguished yogins, regarding eternal atoms that are identical in form, quality, and activity, as well as liberated selves and minds—for which no other cause is possible—there arise from certain causes a differentiation of cognitions such that "this is distinct" and "that is distinct" with respect to each substrate, and there also arises the recognition "this is that very same atom" even when the atom is perceived at a distance in space and time; those are the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*).

If, however, without the final particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), there were for yogins—due to the quality born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*)—both the cessation of conceptual cognition (*pratyayavyāvṛtti*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), what would follow? It is not so. Just as from the quality born of yoga a cognition of "white" does not arise regarding what is not white, nor is there recognition of that which has never been seen before; if such were to occur, it would be false. Likewise, in this case as well, without the final particularity, neither the cessation of conceptual cognition nor recognition can occur for yogins due to the quality born of yoga.

If it is argued that, as in the case of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), the exclusion of cognition is postulated as inherent in atoms themselves, we say no, because of identity (*tādātmya*). In this world, with respect to things that do not possess a certain nature, a cognition arises due to another cause, as for example, the cognition of jars and the like arises from a lamp; but the cognition of a lamp does not arise from another lamp. Or, just as the impurity of horse-flesh and such is inherent in them alone, while others become impure through contact with them, so too here, due to identity, the exclusion of cognition occurs inherently in other particularities, and through contact with them, it occurs in atoms and the like.
Thus ends the category of Particularity (*viśeṣa*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Salutation always to the one who bears four faces, who ordains the four ages, the four Vedas, and the four castes, and who is eternally devoid of the state of death.

For the sake of a detailed explanation, he says: "Those which exist in the ends (*anteṣu*) are the *antyāḥ*. Because they abide at the end of production and destruction, eternal substances are denoted by the word "end" (*anta*); the meaning is that they exist—that is, they are situated—within those [substances]. They are called "particularities" (*viśeṣa*) because they particularize and differentiate their own substrates from all [others]. He explains this with the words beginning "in those devoid of destruction and commencement," where "devoid of destruction and commencement" is the gloss for the term "end" (*antya*).

The phrase "causes of the cognition of absolute exclusion" is an elaboration of the statement "because they distinguish their own substratum. The expression "existing one by one in each substance" means that a single *viśeṣa* exists in relation to each and every substance. Since the exclusion of a substratum from others is accomplished by a single *viśeṣa* alone, the postulation of multiple *viśeṣas* would be redundant. How this constitutes the definition of *viśeṣas* has been explained previously.

Anticipating the objection that "the statement of their definitions is appropriate only when the existence of particularities (*viśeṣa*) is established, not when it is unestablished," he introduces the text with the words "Just as... (*yathā*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate the existence of these particularities:

"Just as among cows and the like, there is observed a differentiation of cognition for people such as ourselves—based on a common form, [such as] 'cow'; based on a quality, [such as] 'white'; based on an action, [such as] 'swift-moving'; based on parts, [such as] 'fat' or 'humped'; and based on conjunction, [such as] 'possessing a large bell'—with respect to horses and the like."

Likewise, for yogins who perceive what is otherwise imperceptible to us, there exist ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣas*). These are those causes—found among atoms that are identical in form, quality, and activity, as well as among liberated selves and minds—which, because no other cause is possible, result in the exclusion of cognitions such that, with respect to each substrate, the cognition arises: "This one is distinct from that one."

Just as there is a difference in cognition regarding individual cows and other entities for people like us, so too must there be a difference in cognition among those who perceive atoms and the like, due to their mutual distinction, since a difference in individuals is possible. Nor is this difference in individuals alone the cause [of the difference in cognition], because doubt is observed even when such an entity is perceived, as in the case of a *sthāṇu* (a post or stump) and similar objects. Furthermore, there is no other cause, because the generic form (*ākṛti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) are identical [in all atoms].

Furthermore, no variation in cognition is observed to be without a cause; therefore, that which is its cause is a particularity (*viśeṣa*). Atoms, though separated by space and time, become objects of recognition for someone because they possess both universals and particulars, like jars and other such things. Moreover, recognition regarding an object previously perceived does not occur without the apprehension of a particularity; therefore, it has as its cause a particularity.

Here he raises an objection with the words "If, however... The meaning of the objection is this: just as yogins possess the perception of supersensuous objects through the power of dharma born of yoga, so too will the exclusion of cognitions and recognition occur even without a specific [particularity].

He refutes this, saying: "It is not so. Just as for yogins there is no cognition of whiteness in what is not white, and recognition would not occur regarding that which has never been seen before; if it were to occur, it would be a false cognition. Likewise, without the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), neither the exclusion of cognitions nor recognition can possibly exist. The intention is that while the perception of supersensuous objects arises from the merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), a cognition devoid of any objective cause does not arise from this [particularity].

He raises an objection again: "Now, regarding the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*). First of all, even in the case of ultimate particulars, there can be no possibility of further particulars because it would lead to an infinite regress. [The opponent asks: "Just as for yogins, the differentiation of cognition occurs through the particulars themselves without requiring further particulars, so too will it be in the case of atoms; what is the use of postulating [further] particulars? To this, he gives the answer: "No."

What you have said is not so, because of identity (*tādātmya*). He explains this very point with the word "here" (*iha*): in things that do not possess that nature, there arises a cognition caused by something else, but not in things that do possess that nature. For example, in non-luminous objects such as jars and the like—which are of the nature of absence—there occurs illumination due to a lamp and the like, which are luminous by nature; however, the illumination in a lamp does not come from another lamp, but rather from itself alone. Or, for instance, horse-flesh and the like are impure by their very nature, and they cause sin for the toucher through contact with them.

Through connection with that [impurity], others become impure. Likewise here as well, because they possess the nature of absolute exclusion due to identity (*tādātmya*), the exclusion of cognition regarding ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) occurs by themselves—that is, from their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone—and not through connection with other particulars. However, in the case of atoms and so forth, which do not possess that identity and which have common characteristics, the exclusion of cognition is logically possible only through the connection with a particular (*viśeṣa*), and not from the essential nature alone. "In all eternal substances, which are mutually similar, the particulars (*viśeṣas*)—the causes of differentiation—reside individually."
Thus ends the category of "Particularity" (viśeṣa) in the Nyāyakandalī commentary on the Padārthapraveśa, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrīdhara.
Now follows the definition of the category of inherence (*samavāya*).
Praśastapādabhāṣya [265] [pp. 688–689]:

Inherence is that relation between things that are inseparably connected (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support (*ādhāryādhārabhūta*), which is the cause of the cognition "it is here. It is that relation by virtue of which there arises the cognition "this is here" with respect to substances, qualities, motions, universals, and particulars—whether they stand in the relation of cause and effect or not—which are inseparably connected and exist as the supported and the support; and it is that by virtue of which there is the non-separation (*aviṣvagbhāva*) of those things that are not all-pervading and whose distinctness has been apprehended. This is the relation called inherence.

How so? Just as the cognition "there is curd in this bowl" is observed to occur when a relation exists, so too are there observed such cognitions as: "the cloth is here in these threads," "the mat is here in these *vīraṇa* grasses," "quality and action are here in this substance," "existence (*sattā*) is here in substance, quality, and action," "substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is here in this substance," "quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is here in this quality," "action-ness (*karmatva*) is here in this action," and "ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣāḥ*) are here in this eternal substance. From the observation of these cognitions, it is known that a relation exists among these. *Nyāyakandalī* [265] [pp.688–690]
Salutations to you, the destroyer of worldly existence, the cause of the dissolution and creation of the universe, whose body is stainless knowledge, the moon-like Śambhu.

For the purpose of defining inherence (*samavāya*), he says: "Inherence is that relation between things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition 'here'. This has already been explained at the occasion of the enumeration (*uddeśa*). What are those inseparable things whose relation is inherence? To this he says: "Of substance, quality, action, universal, and particular. Whether they exist as cause and effect or not as cause and effect is left unstated, as it is not eternal.

The rule is that inherence (*samavāya*) occurs between parts and wholes; between impermanent substances and their qualities; between eternal substances and the qualities inherent in them; between eternal qualities and their possessors; and between causes and effects. Furthermore, the rule is that inherence occurs between things that are not related as cause and effect—namely, eternal substances and their qualities, universals and their possessors, and ultimate particulars and their possessors—provided they are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*). Likewise, the rule is that this applies to those existing in the relationship of the supported and the support.

Inherence (*samavāya*) is that cause from which the cognition "this is here" arises, and by virtue of which there occurs the non-separation, non-distinctness, and lack of independence among things that are not all-pervasive, which abide in fixed locations, and whose distinctness has been apprehended—that is, whose difference in essential nature has been apprehended; for it is observed that the mutual conjunction of two distinct things is produced by a relation.

He establishes this very point by means of a question beginning with "How so?"—just as the cognition "curd is in this bowl" is observed when there is a relation between the bowl and the curd, so too, because cognitions such as "the cloth is in these threads" are observed, it is known that there exists a relation between these [entities], such as the threads and the cloth. Cognitions such as "the cloth is in these threads" have a relation as their cause, because they are uncontradicted cognitions of "being here," just like the cognition "curd is in this bowl.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [266] [p. 690]

And this [conjunction] is not a *saṃyoga* (conjunction), because the related things are not established as separate (*ayutasiddha*), because the causes such as the action of one of the two are impossible, because it is never seen to end in disjunction (*vibhāga*), and because there exists only the relationship between the locus and that which is to be located.
— *Nyāyakandalī* [266] [p. 690]

Now, one might argue that this must be a conjunction (*saṃyoga*). To this he says: "And this is not a conjunction. This relationship between threads, cloth, and so forth, is not a conjunction. Why? He says in response: "Because the related entities are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*). For conjunction occurs only between things that are separably established (*yutasiddha*), whereas this [relationship] is between things that are inseparably established. Furthermore, a conjunction would have to be produced by the action of one of the two, produced by the action of both, or produced by another conjunction. [But this is not the case here.]

In this case, however, the absence of causes such as the action of either one of the two [relata] is due to the fact that the capacity to produce an entity resides in the cause itself. It is observed that conjunction (saṃyoga) ends in disjunction (vibhāga) and is destroyed by disjunction, whereas this is not the case for inherence (samavāya). Conjunction occurs even between two independent things, as in the case of two fingers held upright; this [inherence], however, occurs only between a substratum and that which is supported. Therefore, this is not conjunction, but rather something entirely distinct from it. — *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [267] [p. 691]

And that [inherence] is a distinct category from substance and the others, because its definition differs from existence (*bhāva*). Just as existence, as well as substanceness (*dravyatva*) and the rest, are distinct entities from their own substrates and from one another—because they produce cognitions corresponding to themselves within their own loci—so too inherence is a distinct category from those five categories, because the cognition "it is here" is observed in relation to them.
(Nyāyakandalī [267], p. 691)

This being the case regarding *samavāya* (inherence), he establishes its difference from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories, stating: "And that [inherence] is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) from substance and the rest. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the difference in its definition (*lakṣaṇabheda*), like existence (*bhāva*). He explains this with the words "Just as... *Bhava* refers to the great universal (*mahāsāmānya*) of existence (*sattā*). By the word "and the rest" (*ādi*) in the phrase "substance-ness and the rest," qualities-ness (*guṇatva*) and so forth are included.

Just as there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature regarding existence (*bhāva*) in its own substrata—namely, substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*)—such that there is the cognition "existent, existent" (*sat-sat*); and as there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature regarding substantiality (*dravyatva*) in its own substrata—the substances—such that there is the cognition "substance, substance" (*dravya-dravya*); and as there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature regarding quality-ness (*guṇatva*) in its own substrata—the qualities—such that there is the cognition "quality" (*guṇa*); and as there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature regarding action-ness (*karmatva*) in its own substrata—the actions—such that there is the cognition "action" (*karman*): because it is the agent of these, [existence] is the cause of the notions of substantiality and so forth.

Inherence possesses the nature of being a distinct entity from its own substrata and so forth, as well as from one another; likewise, because the cognition "herein" (iheti) is observed with respect to the five categories, inherence is a category distinct from those five.

[Praśastapādabhāṣya 268] Nor is it manifold like conjunction, because its indicative mark is non-distinct—just like existence—and because there is no indicative mark of particularity. Therefore, like existence, inherence is one and the same everywhere.

[Objection: But if inherence (*samavāya*) is one, then since there is a single relation between substances, qualities, and motions on the one hand, and their qualifiers—such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*)—on the other, would it not follow that there is a confusion of categories (*padārthasaṅkara*)?

[Reply: No, because of the restriction of the container and the contained (*ādhārādheyaniyama*). Even though inherence is one and independent everywhere, there is nevertheless a restriction of the container and the contained. How so? Because substantiality exists only in substances, quality-ness only in qualities, and action-ness only in actions.

Why is this so? Because of the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Here, because the positive concomitance of the cognition whose cause is inherence (*samavāya*) is observed, it is understood that inherence is one and the same everywhere. Because the negative concomitance of the causes of cognitions such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is observed, their specific restriction is known.

Just as, even though the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between a bowl and curd is one, there exists a restriction regarding the relationship of substratum and superstratum; likewise, although inherence is one and the same for substance-ness and the rest, there is a restriction of container and contained due to the difference in the powers of the manifested and the manifestor.
*Nyāyakandalī* [268] [pp. 692–694]:

Regarding whether this [inherence] is one or many, he says: "And it is not manifold like conjunction. Just as conjunction is manifold, inherence is not so. Why? He says: "Because its indicative mark is non-different from that of existence, and because there is an absence of any indicative mark of difference."

Just as, because the definition of the cognition "existent, existent" is without distinction—that is, non-differentiated—everywhere, and because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a particularity or difference, there is a single entity everywhere; in the same way, because the definition of the notion "here [is]" is without distinction everywhere, and because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition for difference, inherence (*samavāya*) is one everywhere. He concludes with the words "therefore."

He points out [the flaw]: "If inherence is one"—that is, if inherence is a single entity, then whatever is the connection of substantiality (*dravyatva*) with earth and the other substances would be the very same as the connection of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) with qualities and of action-ness (*karmatva*) with actions.

In this regard, just as the conjunction with "substance-ness" (dravyatva) exists in earth and the other [elements], such that they possess substance-ness, so too, because that same conjunction is possible in qualities (guṇa) and so forth, those too would possess substance-ness. And just as the conjunction with "quality-ness" (guṇatva) exists in color-form (rūpa) and the like, such that color-form and the rest [possess quality-ness], so too, because that same conjunction exists in substances and actions (karman), those two would also possess quality-ness. In this way, one must demonstrate the confusion of categories even among actions.

He provides the resolution: "No. Nor is there a confusion of categories (padārtha). Why? Because of the restriction of the locus and the located (ādhārādheya-niyama). Substantiality (dravyatva) does not exist merely through the presence of inherence (samavāya); rather, substantiality exists because of the inherence of substantiality. And that inherence occurs only in substances, not in qualities (guṇa) or actions (karman); therefore, they do not possess substantiality. This should be explained in the same way for qualities and actions as well. He explains this summary statement with the words beginning, "Even though inherence is one," and so forth.

"Independent" (*svatantra*) means that it does not exist through any other relation, such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*). "Manifested" (*vyakta*) is the subordinate term. He objects again: "Why is this so?"—the meaning is: why do you know that "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) exists only in substances, "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) only in qualities, and "action-ness" (*karmatva*) only in actions? He replies: "Because of the observation of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekadarśanāt*).

The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the cognition caused by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is observed among substances, and its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is observed among qualities and actions; likewise, the positive concomitance of the cognition caused by "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is observed among qualities, and its negative concomitance is observed among substances and actions; similarly, the positive concomitance of the cognition caused by "action-ness" (*karmatva*) is observed among actions, and its negative concomitance is observed among substances and qualities. Therefore, from this observation of positive and negative concomitance, the restriction (*niyama*) of substance-ness and the other categories is known. The explanation of this is easy to understand.

If inherence (*samavāya*) is without distinction, how can this restriction exist—that inherence of "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) occurs only in earth and the other substances, inherence of "qualityness" (*guṇatva*) only in color and the other qualities, and inherence of "actionness" (*karmatva*) only in upward throwing and the other actions, and not elsewhere? To this he says: "Just as... Even though conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is one, a restriction regarding the relationship of container and contained between a bowl and curd is observed, due to the restriction of capacity (*śakti*). Only the bowl is the container and only the curd is the contained; the curd is not the container, nor is the bowl the contained.

Likewise, even though inherence (samavāya) is one, there is a restriction regarding the locus and the located for universals such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) due to the difference in their manifesting and manifested powers (*vyaṅgyavyañjaka-śakti*). What is meant by this? The power that manifests substance-ness belongs only to substances; therefore, substance-ness inheres only in substances and not elsewhere. This should be explained in the same way for qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) as well.
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [269], p. 695.

Even though the relation is non-eternal, it does not possess the non-eternality of conjunction, because, like existence (*bhāva*), it is without a cause. Just as it has been stated that existence is eternal because no cause for it is apprehended through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is inherence (*samavāya*). For no cause whatsoever of this [inherence] is apprehended through any means of valid cognition.
*Nyāyakandalī* [269] [p. 695]

When the doubt arises as to whether this [inherence] is impermanent or indeed permanent, he says: "even when the related terms are impermanent. Just as conjunction is not impermanent even when its two related terms are impermanent, so too inherence is not impermanent even when its two inherent terms are impermanent, because—like existence—it is causeless. He explains this with the words beginning "just as," and so forth.

For when the related entities (*sambandhin*) are destroyed, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is destroyed, because those two related entities are its inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*). However, the related entities are not the cause of inherence (*samavāya*), because they are merely the relata. How these two are not the cause has already been demonstrated. Therefore, even upon the destruction of the related entities, this [inherence] does not perish, because it is recognized as persisting in other substrates, just like existence (*sattā*).
— *Praśastapādabhāṣya* [270], pp. 695–698.

By what mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*), moreover, does inherence (*samavāya*) reside in substances and the other categories? It cannot be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because that is a quality (*guṇa*) and thus must depend upon a substance. Nor can it be inherence itself, because inherence is a single entity. And there is no other mode of subsistence. [p.696] It is not through identity (*tādātmya*). Just as for substances, qualities, and actions—which are of the nature of "being" (*sat*)—there is no further connection with existence (*sattā*); likewise, for inherence, which is indivisible and consists of the very nature of subsistence, there is no other subsistence. Therefore, its subsistence is within its own self.

For this very reason, inherence (*samavāya*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because it does not occur in perceptible objects—unlike existence (*sattā*) and other such properties—and because there is no self-referential cognition (*svātmagatasaṃvedana*) of it. Therefore, in this system, inherence is inferable by means of the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus ends the section on the category of inherence in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
It is completed.
Having satisfied Maheśvara by means of the power of his yogic practice,
he composed the Vaiśeṣika treatise; homage to that Kaṇabhuj.
Thus ends the commentary on the six categories, beginning with substance, composed by Praśastapāda.

*Nyāyakandalī* [270] [pp. 695–701]: Is inherence (*samavāya*) related to its relata or unrelated? It cannot be unrelated, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor can its relation be of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because conjunction subsists only in substances. Nor can it be inherence itself, because inherence is unitary. Furthermore, there exists no other mode of subsistence apart from conjunction and inherence.

How, then, does this [inherence] function? To this he says: "By what mode of functioning (*vṛtti*) does inherence reside in substances and so forth? The intention is that it does not reside [there] because of the absence of a mode of functioning. He resolves this by saying "no. It is not the case that it does not reside because of the absence of a mode of functioning; rather, because its nature is identity (*tādātmya*), this very [inherence] is the mode of functioning itself. For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is produced, and even though it consists of a mode of functioning, it possesses another mode of functioning, since the inherence in the cause is the defining characteristic of the effect.

Inherence has no other mode of existence (*vṛtti*). Therefore, its existence is by its own self, that is, by its very nature, and not through another mode of existence; this is the meaning. For this very reason, it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because, like "existence" (*sattā*) and other universals, it lacks a mode of existence within perceptible objects. Just as "existence" and the like possess a mode of existence in perceptible things—and are thus perceived by the senses through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)—such a possibility of existence does not exist for inherence itself.

Therefore, this [inherence] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because the capacity of a sense organ to apprehend an entity is observed only when it depends upon conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). If there exists a sensory cognition whose object is inherence, then the statement that there is no relation is mere idle chatter (*pralāpa*). If, on the other hand, such a cognition does not exist, then that very point must be stated; to this he says: "And because of the absence of a cognition residing in its own nature. Just as there is a manifestation of conjunction by means of the sense organ, there is no such manifestation of inherence, because one perceives the two related entities as being in a state of massed unity (*piṇḍībhāva*); therefore, this [inherence] is not perceptible. He concludes: "Therefore... [p.697]
That which brings about the mutual conjunction of distinct things should be understood as inherence (samavāya), for it is that which obstructs their independence.
Thus ends the category of inherence (*samavāya*) in the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on the *Padārthapraveśa*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrī Śrīdhara.
This *Nyāyakandalī* is like a terrace on the peak-path of Mount Sumeru— delightful with its golden form and standing as the highest of all. 1.
Proclaiming the virtues of her own unassailable school,
this Nyāyakandalī shatters the tenets established by others.
In Dakṣiṇarāḍhā, there was a village named Bhūrisṛṣṭi belonging to twice-born men of meritorious deeds, which was a refuge for many learned people.
From this ocean-like [lineage], there arose the moon of the earth, the venerable Brahmin Bṛhaspati, who brings joy to the world. (4)
Therefore, he became a great ocean of the jewels of pure virtues, a tree providing support for the creepers of knowledge,
and a clear intention that was a flowing stream of various glories.
The one named Baladeva possesses the power of the perfection of movement. || 5 ||
To him,
who possessed abundant fame, there was a wife named Abbokā, born of a pure lineage, whose virtues were honored, and who was herself virtuous.
Possessing beautiful shade, yielding large fruit, having many branches, and providing refuge for birds,
he became known as Śrīdhara, a lofty wish-fulfilling tree for those who seek his aid.
He has produced this beautiful *Nyāyakandalī*, which is suitable for hearing by those refined by learning, beneficial to the six categories [of Vaiśeṣika], and pleasing.
In the Śaka year nine hundred and thirteen, this Nyāyakandalī was composed by the venerable Śrīdhara, at the request of the illustrious Pāṇḍudāsa Bhaṭṭa. (9)
